How this curriculum works:
What this is, how it is arranged, and what it asks of you.

**Every lesson teaches its point in full.** Nothing here says *"read Thompson chapter 4"* and stops. The material is the lesson; the sources are where you go to go further, to check it, or to see the thing itself.

**And every lesson ends by directing practice.** For a subject like this, practice is not a drill. It is one of six things:

| Kind of practice | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Read the document** | the section of the Constitution the lesson just explained |
| **Compare two accounts** | Thompson and Giliomee on the Great Trek |
| **Check the number** | take a figure from an argument and find it in StatsSA or the Budget Review |
| **Place a source** | read a page and say what it is doing before judging whether it is right |
| **Trace a thing to its origin** | a property dispute today back through the 1913 Act |
| **Follow it live** | a bill through PMG, a judgment through the Court's own collections |

**None of it is required to understand the lesson.** It is how the lesson becomes yours rather than something you once read.

**The order.** Twelve stages, arranged so no lesson depends on a later one:

| Stages | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **how to read the subject** — method, before any content |
| **2–6** | **the history**, from before 1652 to the Constitution in 1996 |
| **7–10** | **the machinery** — the Constitution, the institutions, the economy, the parties and the press |
| **11** | **1994 to now** |
| **12** | **the live arguments** |

**Stage 1 is first and it is not optional.** It is the one stage whose absence would make every other stage misleading, because a reader who cannot place a source reads a committed account as a neutral one. Everything after it assumes you can.

**There are no dates, no pacing and no gates.** Work through it in order, repeat what has not landed, and stop when you want to.

**There is a card deck**, and it covers the skeleton: the legislation, the institutions, the constitutional sections people cite, and the numbers that recur. **It deliberately does not cover the contested parts**, for a reason the next lesson gives: a card asserts, and the contested parts are not to be asserted.

**On the sources.** Each lesson names its own. Two kinds:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Books you own** | eighteen of them, in `~/Media/Books` |
| **Free material online** | and this subject's free material is extraordinary — the state publishes, and the archives are open |

**The free side is not a consolation prize here.** The TRC report, the Zondo reports, the Constitution, every Constitutional Court judgment, every parliamentary committee's proceedings, every Budget Review, every census, every election result since 1999, the whole 1996–98 *TRC Special Report* television series, and three hundred scholarly books from HSRC Press — **all free, all primary or near-primary.** For the period after 1994 the free material is *better* than any book, because it is the thing itself rather than an account of it.

**A convention you will meet throughout.** Anything that can change with an election, a reshuffle or a court date is written as a **dated snapshot**:

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the ANC governs nationally in a coalition formed after the May 2024 election.

**The teaching around a snapshot never depends on the snapshot being current.** So when a snapshot goes out of date, the lesson is still right and the stale part is the one in bold with a date on it. **The municipal elections are on 4 November 2026**, so several snapshots in stage 11 will be out of date within weeks of this being written. That is by design.

**Practice.** Read the goal in the next lesson, then come back and decide whether this arrangement serves it. If you think a stage is in the wrong place, say so — the order is a judgement, not a fact.
What it is for, and what it is not:
The goal, stated precisely, because it is unusual and it governs everything after it.

**The goal: understand the country you live in well enough to follow an argument about it, and know which parts are contested.**

**Not to arrive at a position.**

**That second sentence is the whole design.** It is not neutrality for its own sake, and it is not an inability to decide. It is a judgement about the subject: **almost every account of South African politics is written from inside a commitment**, and a reader who does not notice that will adopt the commitment of whatever they happened to read first and mistake it for having thought about it.

**So the aim is a different skill from agreeing or disagreeing.** It is being able to say: *this book is doing something. Here is what. Here is what it is good for and here is where it will mislead me.*

**What that means in practice, lesson by lesson:**

| Where a question is | The material |
| --- | --- |
| **Settled** | **teaches the answer.** The 1913 Act's provisions are not contested. |
| **Live** | **gives the strongest form of each side**, and says what evidence would settle it |
| **Unsettleable on present evidence** | **says so**, and says why |

**The middle row is the hard one and the one that makes this curriculum different.** It is easy to give a weak version of the side you disagree with. The rule here is the opposite: **each side gets its best argument, made by someone who holds it.**

**And "what evidence would settle it" is the test that keeps that honest.** If a disagreement cannot be connected to anything that would resolve it, it is not a disagreement about facts — it is a disagreement about values, and that is worth knowing too, because it means more research will not help.

**What this curriculum is not:**

| Not | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A political education** | it will not tell you how to vote |
| **A defence of the settlement, or an attack on it** | **that is one of the four big disagreements** — stage 1 covers it as a disagreement |
| **A history of Southern Africa** | other states appear only where they bear on this one |
| **Neutral in the sense of having no content** | it takes positions on facts constantly; it declines to take them on contested interpretations |
| **Complete** | see the thin spots in `sa-politics.md` |

**One honest tension worth naming.** "Not arriving at a position" is itself a position, and some people — including serious historians — regard it as evasion. The argument against this curriculum's posture goes: *in a country built on a specific injustice, treating the question of what to do about it as an open argument with two good sides is itself a side.*

**That argument deserves to be taken seriously and this curriculum does not accept it**, for one reason: the alternative is a curriculum that tells you what to think, and you can get that anywhere. **What is scarce is the equipment to read the ones that do.**

**But the force of the objection is real in one specific way, and the material respects it:** declining to adjudicate an interpretation is not the same as declining to state a fact. **Where the historical record is clear, the material says so plainly** — the dispossession happened, the numbers are known, the laws said what they said. **It is the *meaning* of those facts, and what follows from them, that is left open.**

**The practical payoff.** When you finish, you should be able to pick up any book, article or speech on this subject and, within a page or two, say what tradition it comes from, what it is trying to establish, what it will be good on, and what it will quietly skip. **That is a durable skill. A position is not.**

**Practice.** Find a recent opinion piece about South African politics. Before deciding whether you agree, write down what it is trying to establish and what it needs you to accept in order to get there. Then decide.
Establish what a source is before readin:
The one rule the rest of the curriculum rests on, and the five questions that apply it.

**The rule: establish what a source is before reading it for facts.**

**Why this subject particularly.** Every country's history is written by interested parties, but South Africa has a specific feature: **the major accounts were written as interventions in a live political conflict, often by participants, and several of them were written to establish a claim to land or to legitimacy.** Reading them for facts without knowing that is like reading a prospectus for an assessment of a company.

**The five questions, in order:**

**1. Who wrote it, and when?** The *when* matters more than usual here, because the subject's scholarship broke into distinct periods and a 1960 book and a 1990 book on the same events are often not disagreeing — they are answering different questions with different evidence.

**2. What tradition does it come from?** The next lesson covers the schools. A book from the liberal tradition and one from the revisionist tradition will agree on nearly every date and disagree on nearly every cause.

**3. What is it trying to establish?** Not its subject — its **claim**. *The Afrikaners* is about the Afrikaners; what it is trying to establish is that they were a people with a coherent history and genuine predicament rather than simply the architects of apartheid. **Knowing the claim tells you where to be careful.**

**4. What would it have to leave out?** Every account leaves things out, and the pattern of omission is more informative than the errors. An account of the transition that barely mentions the violence of 1990–94 is telling you something about what it thinks the transition was.

**5. Is it a source *about* its subject, or a source *of* its subject?** The distinction that does the most work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A source *about*** | an account, to be assessed for accuracy |
| **A source *of*** | **evidence of its own author's thinking**, which cannot be wrong in the same way |

**An Afrikaner nationalist history of the Great Trek is a poor source *about* the Trek and an excellent source *of* Afrikaner nationalism.** Same book, two uses, and conflating them is the commonest mistake in this field.

**What the rule is not.** It is not an excuse to dismiss a source by labelling it.

| Not this | But this |
| --- | --- |
| *"Giliomee is an Afrikaner, so discount him"* | *"Giliomee is writing his own people's history, so expect the predicament to be rendered with unusual sympathy and the victims with less"* |
| *"The revisionists were Marxists, so ignore them"* | *"They were looking for economic function, so they will find it where it is and sometimes where it is not"* |
| *"Thompson is a liberal, so he is biased"* | *"Thompson assumes a trajectory toward liberal democracy, so apartheid will appear as a deviation rather than as a development"* |

**The left column is a way of not reading. The right column is reading.**

**And the inverse error, which is worse: treating a source as neutral because it does not announce itself.** The most committed accounts are frequently the ones written in the most measured prose. **A textbook tone is a style, not an absence of position.**

**The test for whether you have actually placed a source: can you predict it?** If you know what a book is doing, you can guess how it will handle an episode before you read that chapter — what it will emphasise, what it will call the thing, how much space it will give. **When your predictions start coming true, you have placed it.**

**A worked example.** Three accounts of the 1913 Natives Land Act:

| Account | What it emphasises |
| --- | --- |
| **Liberal** | the Act as a betrayal of the Cape's non-racial franchise tradition; the moment the trajectory went wrong |
| **Revisionist** | the Act as **labour policy** — destroying the African peasantry to force men onto the mines |
| **Afrikaner nationalist** | the Act as a settlement of a land question, and largely as a *British* measure |
| **Africanist** | the Act as it was experienced — Plaatje's *Native Life in South Africa*, written in response |

**All four are about the same statute and none of them is lying.** They are selecting, and the selection is the argument.

**Practice.** Take any one source from the list in this curriculum and answer the five questions on it before reading a word of its content. Then read twenty pages and check your answers. Then do the same for the next source, and compare the two accounts of a single episode they both cover.
The schools, and what each one is for:
The five traditions in South African historiography, in the order they arrived, and what each is good for.

**Why this matters more here than elsewhere.** The schools did not merely disagree about interpretation. **They disagreed about what the subject was** — whether the history of South Africa is the history of white settlement, of class formation, of African societies, or of a nation's making. That choice determines everything downstream.

**1. The settler tradition.** Nineteenth century into the early twentieth — **George McCall Theal** above all.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject is** | white settlement and its advance |
| **Africans appear as** | an obstacle, or a backdrop |
| **Good for** | its own evidence; Theal transcribed archives that were later lost |
| **Why it is dead** | its premises are no longer arguable |

**It is included because its claims survived it.** "Empty land", the idea that Bantu-speakers and Europeans arrived simultaneously, and the framing of frontier wars as unprovoked attacks all entered school curricula and public argument from here and are still met today.

**2. The liberal tradition.** From the 1920s — **W. M. Macmillan**, **C. W. de Kiewiet**, later **Leonard Thompson**, **Rodney Davenport**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject is** | the making of a society, and the failure of its liberal possibilities |
| **The driver** | **ideas and politics** — racial attitudes, policy choices |
| **Apartheid appears as** | **irrational**: a deviation from a trajectory, economically self-harming |
| **Good for** | narrative, chronology, political detail, fairness |
| **Weakness** | **if apartheid was irrational, who was it for?** The question the next school asked |

**Thompson is this tradition's best single-volume statement**, and the thing to watch for is the assumed trajectory: progress toward a liberal order, from which everything else is a departure.

**3. The Afrikaner nationalist tradition.** From the early twentieth century — **Gustav Preller**, **F. A. van Jaarsveld**, in a quite different register **Hermann Giliomee**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject is** | the formation and survival of a people |
| **The Trek appears as** | a founding, often providentially framed |
| **The republics appear as** | legitimate states destroyed by imperial aggression |
| **Good for** | **it is the primary source of the thing itself** — what apartheid's architects believed |
| **Weakness** | the obvious one |

**Giliomee requires care because he does not belong here simply.** He is an Afrikaner liberal, highly critical of apartheid, writing the most serious history of Afrikaner nationalism there is. **Place him by what he is trying to establish — that these were people with a predicament — not by his ethnicity.**

**4. The revisionist, or radical, tradition.** The 1970s, mostly from British universities — **Harold Wolpe**, **Martin Legassick**, **Frederick Johnstone**, **Colin Bundy**, **Shula Marks**, **Stanley Trapido**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject is** | **class formation and the structure of capitalism** |
| **The driver** | the demand for cheap labour |
| **Apartheid appears as** | **functional, not irrational** — it produced the labour the mines needed |
| **Its central claim** | Wolpe's: the reserves subsidised wages by bearing the cost of reproducing labour |
| **Good for** | causation, the economy, and demolishing "apartheid was merely prejudice" |
| **Weakness** | **functionalism** — if everything served capital, nothing is explained by anything else |

**This is the school that changed the field.** Feinstein's economic history is downstream of it, and no serious account since treats apartheid as economically inexplicable.

**5. Social history, and the Africanist turn.** From the late 1970s — the **Wits History Workshop**, **Belinda Bozzoli**, **Charles van Onselen**, and in the pre-colonial period **Carolyn Hamilton**, **Bernard Mbenga**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject is** | **experience**, and African societies on their own terms |
| **The method** | oral history, local studies, "history from below" |
| **Good for** | everything the other four schools render as structure or statistic |
| **Weakness** | hard to aggregate; a hundred excellent local studies is not a national account |

**The Cambridge volumes are substantially this tradition's settlement with the others**, which is why they read as consensus with a visible line rather than as a single argument.

**And a sixth, still forming: post-1994.** No settled name. Its features: **the struggle's own history becoming official history**, and a critical reaction to that; **the economy of the present** displacing apartheid as the central problem; and **Simpson's** kind of narrative, written close enough to events that its reputation is not yet made.

**The practical use of all this:**

| If you want | Read |
| --- | --- |
| **What happened, in order** | the liberal tradition |
| **Why it happened** | the revisionists |
| **What it was like** | social history |
| **What the architects thought** | the nationalist tradition, as a primary source |
| **The pre-colonial period** | the Africanist turn; nothing earlier is usable |
| **The present** | documents, not books |

**Practice.** Take one episode both Thompson and Feinstein cover — the mineral revolution will do — and read each on it. Write down what each one thinks the episode *was*. Then predict how Giliomee will handle it, and check.
The four big disagreements:
The four live questions in this subject, each stated as both sides at their strongest, with what would settle them.

**Know these before reading anything, because every substantial account takes a side on at least one and most do not announce it.**

---

**1. Was apartheid a continuation of segregation, or a break with it?**

| Continuity | Break |
| --- | --- |
| The architecture was built 1910–48: the 1913 Land Act, the 1923 Urban Areas Act, the colour bar, the 1936 removal of the Cape African franchise | 1948 brought **system** where there had been accumulation: a coherent ideology, total legal coverage, and the deliberate destruction of what segregation had tolerated |
| The National Party inherited a segregated state and tightened it | Population registration, Group Areas, Bantu Education and the homeland project have no real precedent |
| Smuts's governments did most of the groundwork | **Grand apartheid** — separate nationhood — was a genuinely new idea |

**What it decides:** how much 1948 matters, and whether apartheid was an Afrikaner project or a South African one. **Also who is responsible** — which is why it is not a dry question.

**What would settle it:** nothing cleanly, because it is partly definitional. **But it is testable in one respect:** if continuity is right, the *rate* of change in the laws and in measurable outcomes should not jump at 1948. Feinstein's series let you look. **Stage 4 does.**

---

**2. Did apartheid fall to internal resistance, to economic failure, or to the end of the Cold War?**

| Resistance | Economy | The Cold War |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The 1980s made the country ungovernable; the unions, the UDF, the townships | Growth stalled from the 1970s; the shortage was **skilled** labour, which apartheid forbade producing | The USSR's collapse removed the ANC's patron **and** the NP's best argument |
| Sanctions and disinvestment bit | The Rubicon speech crashed the currency; debt had to be rescheduled | 1989–90 is too tight a coincidence to ignore |
| The regime negotiated because it was losing | The state could no longer afford itself | De Klerk could act once communism was no longer the threat |

**What it decides:** an enormous amount about the present. **If resistance won, the settlement was a victory and its beneficiaries earned it. If the economy failed, the transition was a managed handover. If the Cold War ended it, South Africans were less the authors of their own liberation than any account likes.**

**What would settle it:** the timing. **Each explanation predicts a different sequence**, and the archives of the period — the NP's own deliberations, in particular — bear on it. The O'Malley interviews are evidence because they were taken *as it happened*.

---

**3. Was the negotiated settlement a victory, or a compromise that left economic power untouched?**

| A victory | A compromise |
| --- | --- |
| Universal franchise, a justiciable Bill of Rights, no civil war — in 1990 none of that looked likely | **Political power changed hands and economic power did not.** Land, mines, banks and boardrooms stayed where they were |
| The Constitution is among the most ambitious in the world | The sunset clauses protected the old civil service; property rights were entrenched in s25 |
| The alternative on the table was partition or war | The debt was honoured, the Reserve Bank kept its independence, and GEAR followed |

**This is the live argument in South African politics.** Almost every current dispute — land, BEE, NHI, the fiscus — is a continuation of it.

**What would settle it:** not a fact, but **a counterfactual**, which is why it will not be settled. **What *can* be established is what was actually on the table**, and the O'Malley archive and the CODESA records make that unusually checkable. **Stage 6 works through it.**

---

**4. Is the post-1994 state's failure a matter of corruption, or of design?**

| Corruption | Design |
| --- | --- |
| The institutions were sound and were captured; Zondo documents how | The state was built for a different job — **a developmental state staffed by a liberation movement**, with cadre deployment as policy |
| Where capture was resisted — the courts, the Reserve Bank, StatsSA — the institutions held | Municipal failure is near-universal, not concentrated where theft was worst |
| Remove the thieves and the machine works | **Capacity, not honesty, is the binding constraint** |

**What it decides:** whether the answer is prosecution or reconstruction.

**What would settle it:** **this one is genuinely tractable.** The Auditor-General's outcomes, municipal performance data and StatsSA's service-delivery series let you ask whether failure tracks theft. **Zondo answers the first question and explicitly not the second** — a point the commission makes about itself.

---

**How to use these four.** When you read anything on this subject, ask which of the four it is answering. **Most books are answering one and assuming the others**, and the assumptions are where the argument actually lives.

**Practice.** Pick the disagreement you find most interesting and write the side you do *not* instinctively hold, as strongly as you can, in a paragraph. Then find a source that holds it and check whether you got it right.
Placing the eighteen books on this shelf:
The library you have, placed — what each book is for, what it is doing, and where it will mislead you.

**Eighteen books on this subject in `~/Media/Books`.** Placed against the schools from two lessons ago.

**The spine:**

| Book | Tradition | For | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Thompson & Berat, *A History of South Africa* (4th ed.)** | **liberal** | **the narrative, start to finish.** The one to read first | an assumed trajectory toward liberal democracy; apartheid as deviation |
| **Cambridge vol. 1 (to 1885)** | **Africanist / consensus** | **the pre-colonial period and the colonial era, properly** | multi-author, so the line shifts between chapters |
| **Cambridge vol. 2 (1885–1994)** | consensus | **the standard reference** for the century that matters most | same |
| **Feinstein, *An Economic History of South Africa*** | **downstream of the revisionists** | **causation.** The material spine of the whole subject | economic explanation can crowd out everything else |
| **Simpson, *History of South Africa: From 1902 to the Present*** (OUP, 2022) | **post-1994, narrative** | **the only book here that reaches the present** | written close to events; its reputation is not made |

**Those five will carry most of the curriculum.** Thompson for shape, Cambridge for depth, Feinstein for why, Simpson for the modern half.

**The committed ones, which are not lesser:**

| Book | What it is doing | Use it as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Giliomee, *The Afrikaners*** | establishing that the Afrikaners were a people with a predicament, not only the authors of apartheid | **the serious history of Afrikaner nationalism** — and a source *of* that nationalism's self-understanding |
| **Blackman, *Rogues' Gallery*** | establishing that corruption is continuous in South African history, not a post-1994 arrival | **excellent on detail, polemical by design.** Journalism as history |

**Giliomee is the most important book on this shelf after the spine**, and the reason is in the four disagreements: you cannot assess disagreement 1 without a serious account of what the Afrikaner nationalists thought they were doing, and nobody else has written one this good.

**The military and the wars:**

| Book | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Stapleton, *A Military History of South Africa*** | **the long arc** — Dutch–Khoi wars to the end of apartheid, in one frame |
| **Knight, *The Boer Wars* I (1836–1898)** | **the wars before the war**, which most accounts compress into a sentence |
| **Knight, *The Boer Wars* II (1898–1902)** | the campaign |
| **Evans, *The Boer War: South Africa 1899–1902*** | the war in detail |

**Four books on warfare is more than this curriculum needs**, and the reason to have them is specific: **the frontier wars and the South African War are where land changed hands**, and the detail of how is what later political claims rest on.

**The two about religion, which are not a digression:**

| Book | Why it is here |
| --- | --- |
| **Hofmeyr, *History of the Church in Southern Africa*** | **apartheid needed a theology and the Dutch Reformed Church supplied one.** Also the mission churches, which produced much of the African elite |
| **Chidester, *Wild Religion*** | religion and the state **after** 1994 — the Constitution's religion clauses, and what filled the space |

**And one that is not a source at all.** *The Unauthorised History of South Africa*, by "Stienie Dikderm" (Penguin Random House SA), is **comedy** — its chapter on the Khoisan is a joke about the word *Bush*. **It is named here so that nobody, including you in two years, wires it in by mistake.**

**What the shelf is missing**, said plainly:

| Gap | What fills it |
| --- | --- |
| **Anything from the liberation movement's own side at book length** | **free archives** — SAHO, the Mandela Foundation, Wits Historical Papers |
| **A constitutional law text** | **the Constitution itself**, plus the Court's own judgments |
| **The economy after 1994** | **the Budget Review, StatsSA, and HSRC's *State of the Nation* series** |
| **State capture at length** | **the Zondo reports** — five parts, free, and far more detailed than any book |
| **Local government** | the Auditor-General's outcomes |
| **What South Africans think** | **Afrobarometer** |

**Which is the point the first version of this curriculum got half right.** It said the library was thin after 1994 and filled the gap with primary documents. **The library is not thin after 1994 — Simpson covers it — but the documents are still better**, because for the present the thing itself beats an account of it.

**Practice.** Open Thompson and Giliomee at their treatment of the same episode — 1948 is a good choice — and read both. Write one sentence on what each thinks happened, and one on what each thinks it meant. The first sentences should be close. The second two should not be.
Primary and secondary, and why the line:
The distinction every history course teaches, and the two ways it behaves oddly in this subject.

**The standard distinction:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary** | produced at the time, by a participant or an observer — a statute, a letter, a speech, a census, a photograph, a trial transcript |
| **Secondary** | written afterwards, about the primary material — a history book |

**And the standard advice: prefer primary where you can get it.** Which for this subject is unusually often, because the archives are open and free.

**The first oddity: a committed secondary source is a primary source of its own commitment.**

From the source-placing lesson, in its sharpest form:

| Book | As a source *about* its subject | As a source *of* something |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A 1950s Afrikaner nationalist history of the Trek** | poor | **excellent evidence of what apartheid's architects believed about themselves** |
| **A 1980s ANC publication on the armed struggle** | partial | **the movement's own self-understanding at the time** |
| **Theal's history** | superseded | **the origin of claims still made today** |
| **Giliomee** | **good** | and also a document of post-apartheid Afrikaner self-reckoning |

**So "is this primary or secondary" is the wrong question.** The right one is **"primary to what?"** — and the answer can be *"secondary about the Trek, primary about 1938."*

**The second oddity: a great deal of this subject's primary material was produced by bodies whose job was to establish a version of events.** Commissions, trials, parliamentary debates and official statistics are all primary — and all produced inside a dispute.

| Primary source | Produced in order to |
| --- | --- |
| **The 1913 Act** | effect a policy. **It says what it says, and that is not in doubt** |
| **The Tomlinson Commission (1955)** | assess whether the homelands could be made viable. It found they could not, with investment the state declined to make |
| **The Fagan and Sauer reports (1948)** | **argue for opposite policies**, on the same evidence |
| **The TRC report** | establish a record and enable amnesty |
| **Zondo** | establish what happened and refer it onward |
| **A census** | count — and, before 1994, **count people into racial categories that the counting helped to create** |

**That last row is the point.** An apartheid-era census is primary evidence of the population *and* of the state's categories, and the categories were not natural. **Using the numbers without the categories imports the state's framework silently.**

**The hierarchy that actually works for this subject:**

| Most reliable | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. The text of a law** | not contested. **Read the Act, not a summary of it** |
| **2. A court's order** | what was actually decided |
| **3. Official statistics, with their definitions** | reliable *as defined* — see the next two lessons |
| **4. A commission's record of evidence** | testimony given under oath |
| **5. A commission's findings** | **a finding, not a verdict** — the next lesson |
| **6. Contemporaneous accounts by participants** | honest and partial |
| **7. Retrospective accounts by participants** | memory, plus reputation management |
| **8. Secondary accounts** | **where the interpretation lives** |

**Note that 8 is last and is still indispensable.** The hierarchy ranks *reliability about facts*, not *usefulness*. A statute tells you nothing about why it was passed; that is what the books are for.

**The one trap in preferring primary sources**, which is worth stating because this curriculum pushes you toward them: **a primary source can be perfectly reliable and completely misleading.** The 1913 Act's text is exactly what it says and tells you nothing about the 1,500 families evicted in its first year. **Plaatje's *Native Life in South Africa* tells you that, and it is a polemic.**

**So: primary for what happened, secondary for what it meant, and both for anything that matters.**

**Where to find the primary material, free:**

| Want | Go to |
| --- | --- |
| **A statute** | Open Gazettes, or the department's site |
| **A judgment** | the Constitutional Court's own collections |
| **The TRC** | the full report, and the televised hearings |
| **Zondo** | all five parts |
| **The transition** | **the O'Malley interviews, taken as it happened** |
| **Trial records** | Wits Historical Papers; the Mandela Foundation archive |
| **Documents, speeches, pamphlets** | South African History Online |
| **Numbers** | StatsSA, Treasury, the Reserve Bank, the Auditor-General |

**Practice.** Take one claim from any secondary account in your library and trace it to a primary source. Then write down what the primary source does and does not support. Most of the time it will support less than the claim, and the gap is the historian's inference — which is their job, not a failing.
A commission is not a court:
The distinction most often collapsed in public argument about both the TRC and Zondo, and why it matters.

**The claim people make:** *"Zondo found him guilty."* **He did not. He could not.**

**What a commission of inquiry is.** Appointed by the President under **section 84(2)(f)** of the Constitution, operating under the **Commissions Act 8 of 1947** and its own terms of reference. It can subpoena, take evidence under oath, and publish findings.

**What it cannot do:**

| Cannot | Who can |
| --- | --- |
| **Convict** | a criminal court |
| **Impose a sentence** | a criminal court |
| **Order compensation** | a civil court |
| **Make binding law** | Parliament, or a court's precedent |
| **Guarantee its findings stand** | **its findings are reviewable** |

**What it can do:**

| Can | |
| --- | --- |
| **Establish a record** | sworn testimony, documents, a published account |
| **Make findings** | on the balance of what it heard |
| **Recommend** | prosecution, legislation, dismissal |
| **Refer** | to the NPA, which then decides independently |

**So a finding is a conclusion by a body that heard evidence, not a determination of guilt.** The standard of proof is lower, the rules of evidence are looser, and — the crucial part — **the person found against may not have had a criminal trial's protections.**

**The two commissions this curriculum leans on:**

| | **TRC** | **Zondo** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Established by** | **the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995** | presidential proclamation, 2018, after the Public Protector's *State of Capture* report recommended it |
| **Chaired by** | Archbishop Desmond Tutu | **Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo** |
| **Unusual power** | **it could grant amnesty** — a real legal consequence | none; it referred |
| **Report** | **vols 1–5 in 1998, vols 6–7 in 2003** | **five parts, January to June 2022** |
| **Status of findings** | findings, not convictions | findings, not convictions |

**The TRC's amnesty power is why it is not simply a commission.** Its Amnesty Committee could extinguish criminal and civil liability for a disclosed act — which is a court-like power, granted by statute, and the price of the disclosure. **That trade is the single most argued-about feature of the South African transition**, and it belongs to disagreement 3.

**Zondo's referrals are why it is not a prosecution.** The commission found, and handed to the **National Prosecuting Authority**, which exercises its own discretion under section 179 of the Constitution. **A referral is not a charge.** The gap between the volume of Zondo's findings and the volume of prosecutions is one of the live arguments in stage 12 — and reading it as *"nothing happened"* or as *"he was found guilty and walks free"* both mistake what a commission is.

**Why collapsing the distinction is not pedantry.** Three consequences:

| If you treat a finding as a verdict | |
| --- | --- |
| **You overstate what is established** | and your argument collapses when the finding is reviewed |
| **You understate the state's failure** | **the absence of prosecutions is the story**, and it disappears if you think the finding already settled it |
| **You lose the ability to criticise a commission** | a commission can be wrong, and saying so is not denialism |

**And commissions are reviewed.** The courts have set aside findings of inquiries and of the Public Protector on review — most visibly where a body acted beyond its powers or without a fair hearing. **That is the system working, not a scandal.**

**A related distinction worth keeping separate: the Public Protector is not a commission.** It is a **Chapter 9 institution**, permanent, created by the Constitution. And its remedial action is **binding unless set aside on review** — which the Constitutional Court held in *Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly* (2016), the Nkandla judgment. **So the Public Protector has more legal force than a commission of inquiry, and less than a court.** Stage 8 does the institutions properly.

**The three-way test, to carry through the rest of this curriculum:**

| A says | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **court** | **decided**, with precedent and consequence |
| **commission** | **found**, on evidence it heard, reviewable, with no consequence of its own |
| **Public Protector** | **directed**, binding unless reviewed |

**Practice.** Open any part of the Zondo report at a finding about a named person and read how it is worded. Note the verbs. Then find how many of that part's referrals had resulted in charges — and note the date you checked, because the answer moves.
How to read a judgment:
Court judgments are free, they are the most reliable account of what was decided, and there is a right order to read them in.

**Why bother.** Two reasons. **The Constitutional Court decides the arguments this subject is about** — property, housing, healthcare, the powers of the President, the binding force of the Public Protector. And a judgment is the one kind of source where **the reasoning is published in full by the people who did the deciding.**

**The citation, which you need in order to find anything:**

```
Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign (No 2)
    2002 (5) SA 721 (CC)
```

| Part | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **`Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign`** | the parties. **The first name is the one who brought this appeal, not necessarily the original plaintiff** |
| **`2002`** | year of the report volume |
| **`(5)`** | volume number that year |
| **`SA`** | the series — *South African Law Reports* |
| **`721`** | first page |
| **`(CC)`** | **the court** |

**And the neutral citation, which is how you search for it:**

```
[2002] ZACC 15
```

**`ZACC` is the Constitutional Court; `ZASCA` the Supreme Court of Appeal; `ZAGPPHC` the Gauteng Division, Pretoria**, and so on. **Neutral citations are stable and free to look up**, which is why they are the better handle.

**The courts, in order of authority:**

| Court | |
| --- | --- |
| **Constitutional Court (CC)** | **the highest court on all matters** since 2013 |
| **Supreme Court of Appeal (SCA)** | appeals |
| **High Court divisions** | first instance for most constitutional matters |
| **Specialist courts** | Labour, Land Claims, Competition, Electoral, Equality |
| **Magistrates' courts** | no constitutional jurisdiction to speak of |

**Reading order — and this is the part that saves time:**

**1. The order, at the end.** Skip to it first. **The order is what was actually decided**; everything before it is why. A judgment that reads like a sweeping victory often ends in an order that grants very little, and the reverse happens too.

**2. The headnote, if the report has one.** A summary written by the reporter, not the court. **Useful and not authoritative** — do not quote it.

**3. The first few paragraphs.** Courts state the question. *"The issue in this appeal is whether…"* **If you cannot say what the question was, you cannot use the judgment.**

**4. The reasoning**, which is where the law is made.

**5. The separate judgments.** Concurrences and dissents, and both matter: **a dissent is frequently where the next decade's argument comes from.**

**The two words that decide what a judgment is worth as authority:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`Ratio decidendi`** | **the reasoning the decision needed.** Binding on lower courts |
| **`Obiter dictum`** | said in passing, not needed for the outcome. **Persuasive, not binding** |

**Quoting an obiter remark as though it settled the law is the commonest error in public argument about judgments**, and it happens constantly with the socio-economic rights cases, because the judgments contain a great deal of eloquent framing that is not the holding.

**The judgments this curriculum returns to**, so you meet them in context rather than cold:

| Case | What it settled |
| --- | --- |
| ***Certification of the Constitution*** (1996) | **the Court refused to certify the first draft** — the Constitutional Assembly had to go back |
| ***S v Makwanyane*** (1995) | the death penalty |
| ***Grootboom*** (2000) | **what a socio-economic right requires** — reasonableness, not a minimum core |
| ***Treatment Action Campaign*** (2002) | ordering the state to provide nevirapine |
| ***EFF v Speaker*** (2016) | **the Public Protector's remedial action binds unless reviewed** |
| ***Glenister*** (2011) | an anti-corruption body must be adequately independent |
| ***My Vote Counts*** (2018) | party funding must be disclosed |

**None of those is a detail.** Each one is an answer to a question this subject keeps asking, given by the body entitled to answer it, in public, for free.

**Where to read them.** The **Constitutional Court's own collections** publish every judgment of that court. **The Court also publishes a media summary with each judgment** — a plain-language account of what was decided, written by the Court itself, which is the single most useful free resource for a non-lawyer.

**The limit to keep in mind.** A judgment tells you what the law is, **not whether the order was carried out.** *Grootboom* was decided in 2000; Irene Grootboom died in 2008 still without a house. **The judgment and its implementation are two different subjects**, and conflating them produces both naive constitutionalism and lazy cynicism.

**Practice.** Open the Court's collections and read the media summary of *Grootboom*, then its order, then its first five paragraphs. Write down the question and the answer in one sentence each. Then do the same for *Treatment Action Campaign* and note how the orders differ in how specific they are.
How to read a statistic:
Numbers in this subject are reliable and routinely misused, and the misuse is almost always the definition rather than the arithmetic.

**Start from the right assumption: South Africa's official statistics are good.** StatsSA is competent, independent, publishes its methods, and survived the capture period with its reputation intact. **When a number is wrong in an argument, the number is usually right and the claim about it is not.**

**The five questions to ask of any figure:**

**1. Who produced it?**

| Producer | Treat as |
| --- | --- |
| **StatsSA** | **authoritative, with the definition attached** |
| **The Reserve Bank** | authoritative on monetary and financial series |
| **National Treasury** | authoritative on what the state plans to spend |
| **The Auditor-General** | authoritative on whether it was spent lawfully |
| **A department** | **check it against the AG** |
| **A party, a union, a lobby** | a real number, selected |
| **A news article with no source** | **find the source or drop the claim** |

**2. What exactly is being counted?** The question that does nearly all the work. Three examples that recur:

| Figure | The definition that decides it |
| --- | --- |
| **Unemployment** | **two official rates, 10 points apart** — the next lesson |
| **The population** | Census 2022 counted about **62 million**. A census undercounts, and StatsSA publishes its estimate of by how much |
| **"The budget for X"** | **allocated, adjusted, or actually spent?** Three different numbers, all published |

**3. Over what period, and against what baseline?** A change is meaningless without both. *"Crime is up 8%"* — on last quarter, last year, or 1994? **Quarter-on-quarter figures in a seasonal series are the commonest honest mistake.**

**4. Is it a level or a rate?** *"Unemployment fell"* can mean the rate fell while the number of unemployed rose, **if the labour force grew faster.** Both statements are true and they imply opposite things.

**5. What is the denominator?** The one to check when a figure seems extraordinary.

| Claim | The denominator question |
| --- | --- |
| *"X% of the budget goes to public servants"* | of the consolidated budget, or of non-interest spending? |
| *"Y% of land is still white-owned"* | **of all land, of farmland, of registered title?** All three circulate, and they differ |
| *"Z% pay no tax"* | of adults, of workers, of registered taxpayers? |

**The land figure is worth dwelling on** because it is the most-cited contested number in South African politics, and the disagreement is almost entirely about the denominator and the category. **Stage 9 does it properly.** For now: when you meet it, ask what is in the bottom of the fraction.

**Inequality, and what the Gini coefficient is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **a single number from 0 to 1** summarising how unequally something is distributed. 0 is everyone equal; 1 is one person with everything |
| **South Africa's** | **about 0.63**, which is among the highest measured anywhere |
| **The catch** | **it depends on what you measure** — income before tax, income after tax and transfers, or consumption — and the three give meaningfully different answers |

**So "the most unequal country in the world" is a defensible claim that needs its measure named.** After taxes and social grants the figure falls appreciably, which is a real fact about South African redistribution and is routinely omitted by both sides — by one because it weakens the indictment, by the other because it shows how much lifting the grants are doing.

**Two habits worth building.**

**Go to the release, not the headline.** StatsSA publishes a media release and the full publication with every survey. **The release states the definitions in the first two pages**, and reading them takes four minutes.

**Write the definition down with the number.** *"33.6% (official definition, QLFS Q2 2026)"* is a usable figure. *"33.6%"* is a number that will be wrong in six months and you will not know when.

**And one piece of advice specific to this subject: dated figures, always.** Every number in this curriculum's material carries its date and its definition, because a curriculum that says *"unemployment is 33.6%"* is wrong by the next quarter, while one that says *"33.6% on the official definition in Q2 2026"* stays right forever and tells you to go and look.

**Africa Check as a teaching source.** It fact-checks South African public claims **and shows its working** — which source it went to, what the definition was, and why the claim failed or held. **Read a few of its checks for the method rather than the verdicts.**

**Practice.** Take any claim with a number in it from a recent South African news story. Find the original release it came from. Write down the definition, the period and the denominator. Then decide whether the claim survives.
The two unemployment rates:
The most important number in South African politics, the two official versions of it, and why the argument uses both.

**StatsSA publishes two unemployment rates and both are official.** They differ by about ten percentage points. **Which one a speaker uses tells you something about what they are arguing.**

**The definitions, which come from the Quarterly Labour Force Survey:**

| | **Official (strict)** | **Expanded** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Not employed** | required | required |
| **Available to work** | required | required |
| **Actively looked for work in the last four weeks** | **required** | **not required** |
| **Includes discouraged work-seekers** | **no** | **yes** |

**The whole difference is the search requirement.** A person who wants work, is available for work, and has stopped looking because there is no work to look for is **employed in neither rate's numerator** — but is counted as unemployed in the expanded rate and as *outside the labour force* in the official one.

**And the official definition is the international standard**, used by the ILO and by most countries, which is why it is the one in international comparisons.

**The numbers, dated:**

> **As of Q2 2026** (StatsSA, QLFS, released August 2026):
> **official rate 33.6%**, up from 32.7% in Q1;
> **expanded rate 43.8%**;
> **labour underutilisation 46.3%**;
> **8.5 million unemployed**, **16.7 million employed**;
> **youth (15–34) 47.4%**; **women 37.5%** against **men 30.3%**.

**Go and get the current figure before using any of that.** The structure of the gap is the durable fact; the levels move every quarter.

**Why the gap is so large here, and why that is itself the finding.** In most economies the two rates are a few points apart. **Ten points apart means an enormous number of people have stopped looking** — which is not a measurement artefact but a description of the labour market. **The discouraged work-seeker is the characteristic South African economic figure**, and the official rate is the one that does not see them.

**Which is the whole argument about which rate to use:**

| Using the official rate says | Using the expanded rate says |
| --- | --- |
| **compare us with other countries** | **comparability matters less than the size of the problem** |
| searching is evidence of participation | **in an economy with no jobs, not searching is rational** |
| the standard is the standard | the standard was built for labour markets unlike this one |

**Both are honest positions.** What is not honest is switching between them to suit the direction of the point — quoting the expanded rate to show catastrophe and the official rate to show improvement. **Watch for that; it is extremely common.**

**The other figures that travel with these, each with its own definition problem:**

| Figure | The catch |
| --- | --- |
| **Youth unemployment** | **which ages?** StatsSA uses 15–34 for "youth"; the international convention is 15–24. **The two differ by a lot** |
| **The absorption rate** | the share of working-age people who are employed. **Often more informative than the unemployment rate**, because it is immune to the search definition |
| **The labour force participation rate** | and this is where the discouraged go |
| **The NEET rate** | not in employment, education or training. **The number that best captures the youth problem** |

**The absorption rate deserves promoting.** Because it is *employed ÷ working-age population*, it sidesteps the entire strict-versus-expanded dispute. **If you want one number for how much of the country is working, it is that one** — and it is published in every QLFS.

**What the number does not tell you**, which matters for stages 9 and 12:

| |
| --- |
| **The informal sector is counted but probably undercounted** — StatsSA says so |
| **It is a household survey**, so it measures what people report |
| **It says nothing about wages**, and a job is not the same as a living |
| **It is national**, and the provincial and municipal spread is enormous |

**And the political use of all this.** Unemployment is the number every South African party campaigns on, so it is the number most often cited without its definition. **When you hear it, ask: which rate, which quarter, and which age band.** Three questions, and they separate an argument from a slogan.

**Practice.** Download the most recent QLFS from StatsSA and find all four figures — official, expanded, absorption and the youth rate — along with the quarter. Write them down with their definitions. Then find a recent political statement using an unemployment figure and work out which one it used, and whether it said so.
How to read a party document:
Parties publish far more than manifestos, and the manifesto is the least informative of it.

**The mistake: reading election manifestos to find out what a party intends.** A manifesto is written to win votes, cleared by a communications team, and binds nobody. **The documents that tell you what a party thinks are the ones written for its own members.**

**The hierarchy, for the ANC — which matters most because it has governed since 1994 and its internal process is unusually public:**

| Document | What it is | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **National Conference resolutions** | **adopted policy**, every five years | **the highest. This is where ANC policy is made** |
| **Discussion documents** | circulated before a conference, arguing positions | **the argument in the open**, before it is resolved |
| **National General Council** | mid-term review, between conferences | real |
| **NEC statements** | the National Executive Committee between conferences | binding on the organisation |
| **The January 8th statement** | the annual address on the anniversary of its founding | **priorities for the year, in the movement's own voice** |
| **The election manifesto** | a campaign document | **lowest** |

**So the sequence to read is: discussion document → conference resolution → what government actually did.** The gap between the second and third is the most informative thing about the ANC in power, and it is checkable because all three are published.

**Why the ANC's documents read strangely to an outsider.** It is a **liberation movement** that became a party, and the vocabulary comes from that: the National Democratic Revolution, the national democratic society, the motive forces, the balance of forces, the two-stage theory, cadre deployment, democratic centralism. **That is not jargon for its own sake** — it is a coherent analytical framework, derived partly from Marxism-Leninism, and reading the documents without it makes them opaque.

**And it means ANC documents are doing something unusual: they are internal analysis made public.** A discussion document frequently contains a franker assessment of the party's own failures than anything its opponents produce. **That is a resource, and it is free.**

**The other parties, in brief:**

| Party | What to read |
| --- | --- |
| **DA** | federal congress resolutions and policy documents; it publishes a formal policy suite |
| **EFF** | **the Founding Manifesto (2013)** and its "seven cardinal pillars", which have barely changed |
| **IFP** | a long and specific position on traditional authority and federalism |
| **The newer parties** | manifestos, mostly, because they have not yet had the internal process that produces anything else |

**The founding documents, which are a different kind of source entirely:**

| Document | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Freedom Charter (1955)** | adopted at the Congress of the People at Kliptown. **Short, and still quoted on every side of the land and economy arguments** |
| **The Harare Declaration (1989)** | the ANC's terms for negotiation |
| **The RDP (1994)** | the first programme of the new government |
| **The National Development Plan (2012)** | the current official long-term plan, and the one everyone cites and nobody implements |

**Read the Freedom Charter.** It is two pages, it is free, and both the claim that the settlement honoured it and the claim that it betrayed it are made by people who have not. **"The people shall govern" and "the national wealth… shall be restored to the people" are in it; so is "all shall have equal rights to… own property."**

**The four questions for any party document:**

**1. Who adopted it, and could they bind anybody?** A resolution of a national conference is policy. A discussion document is an argument. A minister's speech is neither.

**2. What is its audience?** Members, voters, investors, or a faction. **A document aimed at investors and one aimed at a branch will describe the same policy in incompatible language, honestly.**

**3. What is it responding to?** Party documents are usually arguments against someone, frequently inside the same party. **Identifying the opponent tells you the real subject.**

**4. Did anything follow?** The only test that matters. **Resolutions on land, on the Reserve Bank's mandate and on state banks have been adopted repeatedly and not implemented, and the reasons are a central subject of stages 11 and 12.**

**Where to find them, free.** Parties publish their own; **South African History Online** holds the historical ones including the Freedom Charter and the movement's documents across the exile decades; **PMG** records what happened when policy met a parliamentary committee.

**One warning.** A party's own account of its history is a source *of* that party and not *about* the events — the distinction from earlier in this stage. **This applies to the ANC's history of the struggle exactly as it applies to Afrikaner nationalist history of the Trek**, and treating one as testimony and the other as evidence is the most common asymmetry in writing about South Africa.

**Practice.** Read the Freedom Charter — all of it, it takes ten minutes. Then find one current argument that cites it and check whether the citation is fair. Then find the most recent ANC national conference resolutions on one subject you care about, and ask what followed.
How to read the press, and who owns it:
The press is where you will meet this subject daily, and its structure in South Africa is unusually concentrated and unusually contested.

**Why ownership matters more than usual.** South Africa has a free press, a constitutional guarantee of it, and a small number of owners. **A handful of groups produce most of what is read**, so the question *"who owns this title"* is answerable and informative in a way it would not be in a larger market.

> **As of 14 October 2026**, the main groupings. **Ownership in this sector changes often — verify before relying on it:**

| Group | Titles |
| --- | --- |
| **Media24** (Naspers) | News24, City Press, Rapport, Netwerk24 |
| **Arena Holdings** | Sunday Times, Business Day, Financial Mail, Sowetan |
| **Independent Media** (Sekunjalo) | The Star, Cape Times, Mercury, IOL |
| **Caxton** | The Citizen and a large stable of local papers |
| **Mail & Guardian** | independent |
| **Daily Maverick** | **independent, reader-funded** |
| **SABC** | **state-owned public broadcaster**, with a statutory mandate |
| **eMedia** | eNCA, e.tv |
| **Newzroom Afrika** | independent broadcaster |
| **amaBhungane**, **GroundUp**, **Viewfinder** | **non-profit, specialist, free to republish in part** |

**Three structural facts to hold.**

**1. The SABC is not a state broadcaster in law and has repeatedly been one in practice.** It is a public broadcaster with an independent board and a charter, **and its editorial independence has been a live political fight for its whole existence** — before 1994 as an instrument of the government, and after it through a series of board and management crises. **Its news is worth reading and its history is a subject in itself.**

**2. The non-profit investigative outfits do work the commercial press cannot fund.** **amaBhungane broke a great deal of what became state capture**; GroundUp covers social-grant administration, housing and local government with a consistency no daily matches. **Both are free.** This is not a marginal part of the landscape — it is where several of the biggest stories of the last decade came from.

**3. There was a captured newspaper, and it is the best available case study.** *The New Age* and the television channel *ANN7* were Gupta-owned, launched in 2010 and 2013, funded substantially by advertising and subscriptions from state-owned enterprises and government departments, and closed in 2018. **Zondo examined the arrangement.** Read some of it: **it is the clearest demonstration available of what a newspaper looks like when its purpose is not journalism**, and it trains the eye.

**How to read a South African news story — five habits:**

**1. Separate the reporting from the framing.** The facts in a story are usually right; the selection and the adjectives are the argument. **South African political reporting is generally factually careful and rarely neutral in emphasis.**

**2. Find the document.** Most political stories are about a document — a report, a judgment, a committee meeting, a tender. **The document is usually free**, via PMG, the Court's collections, the Gazette or the Auditor-General. **The story is a summary; read what it summarises when it matters.**

**3. Watch for the single anonymous source.** South African political journalism relies heavily on factional leaking, which means **a story can be accurate about what someone said and be entirely a move in an internal fight.** *"Sources close to"* a faction is evidence about that faction.

**4. Distinguish an allegation, a finding and a conviction** — the three-way test from the commission lesson. **Headlines collapse all three constantly.**

**5. Check who benefits from the story existing.** Not as cynicism, as information. A leaked report lands at a moment, and the moment is often the point.

**The Press Council**, which is worth knowing exists: a self-regulatory body with a Press Code and an ombud; its rulings are public and are a usable record of where a title has been found wanting. **Independent Media withdrew from it in 2016**, which is itself a fact about the landscape.

**And the things the press does badly here, named:**

| Weakness | |
| --- | --- |
| **Local government** | **almost unreported** outside the metros, which is where most failure is |
| **Parliament's committees** | **PMG exists because the press does not cover them** |
| **Economic data** | reported by headline, rarely by definition |
| **Follow-through** | a scandal is covered at the allegation and rarely at the outcome |

**That fourth one is the most useful thing to know about reading South African news: the story usually stops before the end.** A prosecution announced, a commission established, a report promised — and then silence, not because nothing happened but because the follow-up is not a story. **Which is why the primary sources matter: the NPA's own reporting, the AG's outcomes and the court rolls are where you find out what became of it.**

**Practice.** Take any political story from this week and find the document behind it. Then read the document's relevant part and compare it with the story. Note what the story selected and what it left. Then try to find out what happened to a scandal from two years ago, and notice how much harder that is.
The Gazette, where the law actually appe:
Where South African law is published, and the step between a signed Act and a law in force that almost everyone misses.

**The *Government Gazette* is the official journal of record.** Nothing is law until it appears there.

**What is published in it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Acts of Parliament**, once assented to | |
| **Proclamations** | including **commencement dates** |
| **Regulations** made under an Act | **where most of the operative detail lives** |
| **Notices** | appointments, expropriations, company and liquidation notices, tenders |
| **Provincial gazettes** | nine of them, for provincial legislation |
| **Local notices** | municipal by-laws and tariffs |

**The sequence by which a bill becomes an enforceable law:**

| Step | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. A bill is introduced** and published for comment | |
| **2. Parliament passes it** | the committee stage is where it changes — see PMG |
| **3. The President assents and signs** | |
| **4. It is published in the Gazette** | **now it is an Act** |
| **5. It commences** | **either on publication, or on a date fixed by proclamation** |

**Step 5 is the one people miss, and it is where a great deal of South African politics happens.**

**An Act can be signed and not in force.** If the Act says *"this Act comes into operation on a date determined by the President by proclamation"*, then **the President decides when — or whether — it ever starts.** Sections can be brought into force separately. An Act can sit signed and dormant for years.

**Which makes "the law was passed" and "the law applies" two different claims**, and the gap between them is a political instrument. **Before asserting that something is law, check whether it has commenced**, and the proclamation is in the Gazette.

**Regulations, which are the other place the detail hides.** An Act typically sets a framework and empowers a minister to make regulations. **The regulations decide what the Act actually does** — thresholds, procedures, forms, exemptions — and they are made by a minister, gazetted, and changeable without going back to Parliament.

**So: for what the state may do, read the Act. For what it actually does, read the regulations.** And a great many arguments about "the law" are arguments about regulations, which is a much lower bar to change.

**The three documents to be able to tell apart:**

| | Made by | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **An Act** | **Parliament** | Parliament |
| **A regulation** | **a minister**, under an Act | **that minister** |
| **A policy, framework or plan** | a department | the department. **Not law at all** |

**That third row is worth its own warning.** A White Paper, a framework, a strategy and a plan are **not law**. The National Development Plan is not law. A departmental policy is not law. **They matter politically and they bind nobody**, and treating one as law is a common error in both directions — claiming an obligation that does not exist, and dismissing a real one.

**Where to read it, free.** **Open Gazettes South Africa** holds the largest freely available collection of the *Government Gazette*, with the original PDFs made searchable — which solves the real problem, because the official publication is a scanned image and historically very hard to search.

**Why this matters for the history, not just the present.** **Apartheid was legislated**, which means **its entire architecture is in the Gazette** — every Act, every proclamation declaring a group area, every removal notice. **The documents that destroyed communities are public and searchable.**

| To find | Look for |
| --- | --- |
| **A group area declaration** | a proclamation under the Group Areas Act for that place |
| **A homeland's "self-government"** | the proclamation, and the Act behind it |
| **A banning order** | a notice under the Suppression of Communism Act or its successors |
| **A removal** | the notice naming the land |

**That is a different kind of knowledge from reading a history of forced removals.** It is the paperwork, in the state's own voice, and it is free.

**A caution about reading old law.** An Act as originally passed is not the Act as amended, and apartheid-era statutes were amended constantly. **The version that matters is the one in force at the date you care about**, and consolidated versions of repealed legislation are harder to find than current ones. **For a historical question, the original Act plus its amending Acts; for a current one, a consolidated version.**

**Practice.** Find one Act passed in the last two years and check whether it has commenced — and if so, on what date and by what instrument. Then find the regulations made under an Act you have an opinion about, and read them. Then search Open Gazettes for a group area proclamation covering a place you know.
The words that carry an argument:
Vocabulary in this subject is not neutral, and the choice of word is frequently the whole claim.

**The point. In most subjects you can describe a thing and then argue about it. Here a great many things have two or three names, and each name contains a position** — so the describing has already done the arguing.

**This lesson is not about avoiding loaded words.** It is about noticing them, including your own.

**The pairs, with what each choice asserts:**

| The thing | The words | What the choice asserts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The 1835–40s migration inland** | **Great Trek** / Boer migration / *die Groot Trek* | "Great" makes it a founding; "migration" makes it a movement of people |
| **The upheaval of the 1820s–30s** | **Mfecane** / *Difaqane* / the wars of Shaka / **"the time of troubles"** | the name carries the *cause* — see stage 2 |
| **The territories** | **homeland** / **bantustan** / self-governing territory / **Bantu area** | "homeland" accepts the premise; "bantustan" rejects it; the official terms are the state's own |
| **Where the state put people** | **location** / **township** / **informal settlement** / squatter camp | "location" is the older official word; "informal settlement" is current official language |
| **1966–89 in northern Namibia and Angola** | **the Border War** / the Angolan War / **the Namibian liberation struggle** / the Bush War | whose war it was, and whether it was a defence or an occupation |
| **Armed members of the liberation movements** | **terrorist** / **freedom fighter** / **cadre** / insurgent | the standard example, and the ANC was on the US terrorism list until 2008 |
| **July 2021** | **unrest** / **riots** / **looting** / **attempted insurrection** | **a live dispute with legal consequences** — stage 11 |
| **Changing who owns land** | **land reform** / **restitution** / **redistribution** / **expropriation** / **land grab** | the first four are distinct legal mechanisms; the fifth is a judgement |
| **The 2010s** | **state capture** / corruption / **radical economic transformation** | "capture" claims a system; "corruption" claims individuals |
| **Racial preference in law since 1994** | **transformation** / **employment equity** / **affirmative action** / reverse discrimination | |
| **The country** | **South Africa** / RSA / **Azania** | "Azania" is a claim about legitimacy, used by the PAC and others |
| **The policy** | **apartheid** / **separate development** / *eie volk, eie reg* | **"separate development" is the state's own later euphemism** and tells you who is speaking |

**Two words that are legally defined, which puts them in a different category.**

**"Black" has two meanings and one of them is in a statute.** In ordinary South African usage it may mean African specifically, or it may mean African, Coloured and Indian together. **The Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment Act 53 of 2003 defines "black people" as a generic term meaning Africans, Coloureds and Indians** — so in any discussion of BEE, employment equity or procurement, the broad meaning is the legal one. **A great deal of confused argument about BEE statistics comes from mixing the two.**

**"Coloured" is a category the apartheid state created and the democratic state still uses.** It was a legal classification under the Population Registration Act, it is an identity many people hold, and it remains an official statistical and employment-equity category. **It is not a slur in South African usage and it is not a natural kind either**, and the tension between those two facts is a real political subject — particularly in the Western Cape, and particularly in arguments about whether the category's members were beneficiaries or victims of the old order, which is one of stage 12's arguments.

**One doctrinal distinction that looks like a synonym and is not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Non-racial** | **race is not a legitimate political category at all.** The Congress tradition's position, and the Constitution's |
| **Multiracial** | **races exist and should be represented.** The position non-racialism was formulated against |

**The ANC's tradition is non-racial, not multiracial, and the distinction was fought over for decades** — it is why the Congress Alliance was organised in separate congresses that nevertheless denied the legitimacy of the separation. **Using the words interchangeably erases an argument that mattered enormously.**

**How to handle all this, in three rules:**

**1. Use the word the context requires and know what it carries.** This curriculum uses "Great Trek" because that is what the event is called; it does not thereby endorse "great".

**2. When a dispute is about the word, say so.** *"What is called the Mfecane"* is sometimes the only honest construction.

**3. Notice your own.** The words that feel neutral to you are the ones you absorbed from whatever you read first. **That is the thing this whole stage exists to make visible.**

**Practice.** Take a news story and a history chapter on the same episode and list every word each uses for the central thing. Then write the episode's name as each side would. Then check which version came naturally to you, and ask where you got it.
What would change your mind:
The closing lesson of the method stage, and the one habit that makes everything after it useful.

**The question: for each thing you believe about this subject, what would have to be true for you to be wrong?**

**If there is no answer, the belief is not about the world** — it is an allegiance, a value, or a mood. **All three are legitimate and none of them is improved by more reading**, which is useful to know, because you can stop looking for evidence that was never going to arrive.

**Why this closes stage 1.** The four previous lessons taught you to place a source, read a report, check a number and notice a word. **This one is what you do with those abilities**: apply them to your own positions, which is harder and is the only thing that stops the equipment being used solely on other people.

**The three kinds of claim, and what settles each:**

| Kind | Settled by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Factual** | **evidence, straightforwardly** | *the 1913 Act reserved about 7% of the country for African occupation* |
| **Causal** | **evidence, with difficulty** | *the reserves subsidised mine wages* |
| **Evaluative** | **not by evidence** | *the settlement was worth its cost* |

**Most arguments about South Africa mix all three in one sentence**, and separating them is most of the work. **"The settlement left economic power untouched and that was a betrayal"** is a causal claim and an evaluative one joined by "and" — and the first is checkable while the second is not.

**Writing a falsifier, worked.** Take the four big disagreements and ask what would move you:

| Disagreement | A falsifier |
| --- | --- |
| **Continuity or break at 1948** | **a measurable discontinuity, or its absence.** If the rate of change in land dispossession, urban removals and wage gaps does not jump after 1948, continuity gains |
| **What ended apartheid** | **sequence.** If the NP's own records show the decision taken before the economic crisis bit, the economic account weakens |
| **Victory or compromise** | **what was actually on the table.** If the CODESA and O'Malley records show the ANC could have had more and chose not to take it, "compromise" gains; if they show it could not, "victory" does |
| **Corruption or design** | **whether failure tracks theft.** If the worst-governed municipalities are not the most looted ones, design gains |

**Each of those is a real research programme and each is at least partly answerable from free sources.** That is the payoff of stage 1: not neutrality, but **knowing which of your positions could be checked and where to check them.**

**The four honest failure modes, including the one this curriculum risks:**

| Failure | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Motivated reading** | reading only the tradition you already hold, and finding it convincing |
| **Both-sidesing** | **treating every question as evenly balanced**, including the ones that are not |
| **Sophisticated paralysis** | knowing enough about every account's limitations to never conclude anything |
| **Collecting disqualifications** | learning to place sources only in order to dismiss them |

**The second and third are this curriculum's own risks** and it is worth naming them. **"Not arriving at a position" is a rule about contested interpretations, not about facts** — and a reader who comes out of it unable to say that the dispossession happened, that the laws said what they said, or that the numbers are what they are has learnt the posture and missed the point.

**The distinction that keeps it straight:**

| |
| --- |
| **Facts are to be stated.** The record is clear on a great deal, and saying so is not taking a side |
| **Interpretations are to be held with their reasons**, and changed when the reasons change |
| **Values are to be held knowingly**, and not mistaken for conclusions |

**A practical habit: write the number of your confidence.** Not precisely — just *"fairly sure"*, *"it seems likely"*, *"I have no idea"*. **Three levels are enough.** The value is that it forces the question, and it makes it possible to notice later that you were confident about something you had no business being confident about.

**And the test of whether stage 1 worked**, which is also the test of this whole curriculum:

> **Can you state the position you disagree with, in its strongest form, well enough that someone who holds it would recognise it as their own?**

**If yes, you can follow the argument.** If no, you know what you have been reading.

**What comes next.** Stage 2 goes to before 1652, and the first thing it does is apply this stage to a specific case: **the Mfecane debate, which is the clearest fight in South African historiography and the best worked example of everything stage 1 has taught.**

**Practice.** Pick the three things you are most confident about regarding South African politics. For each, write what would change your mind and whether that evidence exists or could exist. Then mark each one "fairly sure", "likely" or "no idea". Keep the list; come back to it at the end of stage 12.
Why this stage exists, and the claim it:
Fourteen lessons for several thousand years, and the honest reason the proportion is what it is.

**The claim this stage exists to dismantle.** Taught in South African schools for decades, and still met in argument:

> *When Van Riebeeck landed in 1652, the interior was empty. Bantu-speaking peoples were migrating south at the same time as Europeans were moving north. They met in the middle. Neither has a prior claim.*

**Every substantive part of that is false**, and the dating has been known for sixty years. **Why it persisted is the interesting question, and the answer is that it did work**: if nobody was there first, then conquest was settlement, and land taken was land found.

**So the stage's job is not to narrate several thousand years.** It is to establish four things firmly enough that the political claim cannot be rebuilt on them:

| What | Against |
| --- | --- |
| **The subcontinent was occupied continuously for tens of thousands of years** | "empty land" |
| **Bantu-speaking farmers were settled in what is now South Africa from the early centuries CE** | "simultaneous arrival" — they were there **more than a thousand years** before 1652 |
| **The Cape was Khoe and San territory, densely used, with an economy and a politics** | "unoccupied" |
| **There were states, towns and long-distance trade** | "no civilisation to displace" |
