| --- | --- |
| **It made the Transvaal the centre of gravity** | the poorest state became the richest |
| **It created Johannesburg** | an immigrant industrial city in a pastoral republic |
| **It made the republic's institutions inadequate** | from the republics lesson |
| **It gave Britain an interest it did not have in 1880** | **the empire's monetary system ran on gold** |
| **It created the two classes that fought over the state** | mine owners, and white workers |

**And it set the terms of the war.** The next lessons are about how a dispute over a goldfield became the largest war Britain fought between 1815 and 1914.

**Practice.** Work out how a business responds to rising costs when it cannot raise its price, and list every option. Then read Feinstein on mine wages and find the 1911-to-1970 comparison. Then state Wolpe's claim in your own words, and ask what it predicts about state policy toward the reserves — then check that prediction against stage 4.
The mining labour system:
How several hundred thousand men a year were recruited, moved, housed and returned — and the regional system it built.

**The problem the industry faced in the 1890s.** It needed unskilled labour on a scale the region had never supplied, at wages low enough for a fixed gold price, **and it was in competition with itself.**

**The last point is the one to understand.** Mines bidding against each other for scarce labour push wages up. **So the industry's first move was to stop bidding.**

**Monopsony, institutionalised:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Chamber of Mines**, 1889 | the collective body |
| **WNLA** — the Witwatersrand Native Labour Association, **1900** | **a single recruiting agency for the whole industry**, with a maximum permissible wage |
| **The NRC** — Native Recruiting Corporation, **1912** | for South African and High Commission Territory recruitment |
| **Agreed maximum wages** | **the mines set a ceiling and did not break it** |

**A single buyer facing many sellers sets the price.** That is monopsony, it is a textbook mechanism, and the South African gold mining industry is one of the clearest historical examples of it operating at scale for decades.

**The geographical reach, which is what made it work.** The industry recruited from an area far larger than South Africa:

| Source | |
| --- | --- |
| **Mozambique** | **the single largest external source for much of the period**, under the 1909 Mozambique Convention — Portugal supplied labour, South Africa guaranteed rail traffic through Delagoa Bay and remitted part of the wages in gold |
| **Lesotho** | a very large share of adult men, from the Lesotho lesson |
| **Malawi (Nyasaland), Botswana, Eswatini, Zambia, Zimbabwe** | substantial |
| **South Africa** | the reserves of the Transkei, Ciskei, Zululand, the northern Transvaal |

**The Mozambique Convention is worth naming** because it shows the system as diplomacy: **a treaty by which one colonial state supplied labour to another's mines in exchange for railway revenue.** Wages were partly paid at home in gold at a favourable rate, which gave the Portuguese administration a revenue stream from its own population's labour.

**So the "South African" mining economy was a regional system from the beginning**, and that has a modern consequence: **the labour-sending areas are now independent countries whose economies were built around remittances, and the retrenchments of the 1990s and after fell on them.** Stage 9 picks it up.

**Chinese labour, 1904–10, which is an episode worth knowing.** After the South African War, African labour did not return to the mines at pre-war wages — **workers declined the terms, which is itself evidence the wage was below a market rate.** The industry's answer was to import about **63,000 indentured Chinese workers** on three-year contracts, confined to compounds, barred from skilled work and from trading.

| And it backfired politically | |
| --- | --- |
| **In Britain** | **"Chinese slavery" became a major issue in the 1906 general election** and contributed to the Liberal landslide |
| **In South Africa** | white labour objected to any cheap labour, Chinese included |
| **Outcome** | **repatriation completed by 1910** |

**The episode demonstrates two things.** That the industry would reach anywhere for labour at its price; **and that white workers' objection to cheap labour was about competition, not about the workers' welfare** — which is the Black Flag pattern from the diamonds lesson.

**The migrant system's mechanics**, which were stable for most of a century:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A recruiter in a rural district** | often working through chiefs and traders |
| **An advance** | which created a debt, and so an obligation |
| **Rail transport** to the Rand | in the company's hands |
| **Medical examination and classification** | and rejection of the unfit |
| **A contract of nine to twelve months** | signed with a thumbprint |
| **The compound** | for the duration |
| **Deferred pay** | a portion held and paid on return home — **which guaranteed the return** |
| **Repatriation** | at the end |

**Deferred pay is the clever part.** Holding back wages until the worker reached home ensured he went home, kept the system circular, and transferred part of the wage into the rural economy where it supported the family the wage did not have to cover. **It is Wolpe's mechanism, administered.**

**The human cost, which the mechanics conceal:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Silicosis and tuberculosis** | from rock dust. **Hundreds of thousands of men were disabled over the century**, returned home sick, and compensated minimally or not at all |
| **Accidents** | gold mining at depth is among the most dangerous industrial work there is; **tens of thousands died** |
| **Family separation** | eleven months a year, for decades, as a structural feature |
| **The urban consequence** | single-sex compounds in a city, with the social effects that follow |
| **The rural consequence** | **a rural economy of women, children and the old**, with agriculture declining because the labour was gone |

**The silicosis point has a modern legal tail worth knowing.** A class action on behalf of mineworkers with silicosis and tuberculosis was certified by the South Gauteng High Court in 2016 and **settled in 2018 for a reported figure of around R5 billion**, with a trust established to pay claimants. **The injuries of the system described in this lesson are being compensated, partially, in this decade** — which is as direct a line from 1890 to the present as this curriculum contains.

**And the rural consequence is the thing to carry into stage 4.** The reserves did not fail by accident. **An economy whose adult men are absent for eleven months a year cannot develop**, and the migrant system guaranteed that absence for sixty years before the homelands were declared unviable and then declared independent anyway.

**Practice.** Find out what proportion of gold mine labour came from outside South Africa at its peak. Then read the terms of the Mozambique Convention and note what each party got. Then look up the silicosis class action settlement and note the number of claimants. Then work out what eleven months' absence a year does to a family's ability to farm.
The compound, the pass and the colour ba:
Three institutions that between them created the South African labour market, and the moment two of them were written into statute.

**All three were working practice before they were law**, which is the pattern: **the state codified what the industry had already built.**

---

**1. The compound.** From Kimberley, as the diamonds lesson described: **fenced, guarded single-sex barracks, housing the workforce for the duration of a contract.**

**What it accomplished:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Immobilised the workforce** | a worker in a compound cannot take a better offer |
| **Excluded families** | so no housing, schools, or settled community had to be provided |
| **Prevented organisation** | by controlling who entered and who spoke to whom |
| **Made the worker's whole life the employer's** | food, sleep, medical examination, recreation |
| **Made the wage a single man's wage** | which is the arithmetic of the whole system |

**That last row is the economic function.** A wage that need only feed one man for eleven months is a fraction of a wage that must support a household permanently. **The compound is how the migrant system was physically possible**, and it survived until hostels replaced it and then survived as hostels.

**And the hostels are a live political fact.** Single-sex hostels on the Rand were the site of much of the violence of 1990–94, and their conversion to family housing has been policy for thirty years and is incomplete. **Stage 11 returns to them.**

---

**2. The pass.** A document a black person was required to carry authorising presence, movement or employment.

**The lineage, which is long:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cape, eighteenth century** | passes for Khoekhoe |
| **1809 Caledon Code** | formalised |
| **1828, Ordinance 50** | **abolished** — from the Ordinance 50 lesson |
| **Kimberley, 1870s** | reinvented for the diggings |
| **ZAR Law 23 of 1895** | the Rand's system |
| **Post-1902 Transvaal** | consolidated |
| **1923 Natives (Urban Areas) Act** | **nationalised** — stage 4 |
| **1952 Natives (Abolition of Passes and Co-ordination of Documents) Act** | **the reference book — and note the title** |

**That 1952 title is the single best illustration in South African law of stage 1's lesson on words.** An Act that extended the pass system to women and made a single document compulsory nationally was named for the **abolition** of passes, because it replaced several documents with one. **It is not a mistranslation or an irony; it is deliberate drafting.**

**What a pass did, economically:** it made the labour market administratively controlled rather than free. **A worker could not move to where wages were higher**, because presence required authorisation tied to employment. **The pass is what prevented wage competition from doing its ordinary work**, and it is why monopsony held for decades.

---

**3. The colour bar**, which is the one with the most instructive legislative history.

**Customary first.** From the 1890s, skilled and supervisory work on the mines was held by white workers — initially because the skills were imported with the men from Californian and Australian mining, then because white workers organised to keep it so.

**Then statutory:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1911, Mines and Works Act** | **regulations reserved certificates of competency** — blasting above all — **for whites and Coloureds in practice**, excluding Africans from skilled underground work |
| **1923** | **a court struck the regulations down** as beyond the Act's powers |
| **1926, Mines and Works Amendment Act** | **the colour bar re-enacted, this time explicitly** |

**The 1923–26 sequence is worth dwelling on.** A court found the racial reservation unlawful; **Parliament passed a new Act to make it lawful.** It is the clearest demonstration available that the discrimination was legislative choice rather than administrative drift — and it happened under the **Pact government** of the National Party and the Labour Party, elected in 1924 on exactly this platform. **Stage 4 takes it up.**

**Who the colour bar was for, and this is the lesson's central point.** Not the mine owners. **The industry wanted the cheapest competent labour and repeatedly tried to replace white miners with cheaper black ones.** The colour bar was won by **white labour**, against capital, by political means.

| Interest | Wanted |
| --- | --- |
| **The mine owners** | **to dilute skilled work** and pay less for it — "the dilution of labour" |
| **White miners** | **statutory protection** of their jobs, since they could not compete on wage |
| **Black workers** | access to skilled work, and had no vote |

**So the structure of South African racial labour policy is a bargain between white labour and the state, against capital, at black workers' expense.** The 1922 Rand Revolt — the next-but-one stage's subject — is that bargain's violent moment, and the 1924 election is its political settlement.

**Which complicates the functional account from the gold lesson, and this curriculum's posture requires saying so.** Wolpe's argument explains the migrant system and the reserves very well. **It explains the colour bar badly**, because the colour bar raised the industry's costs and the industry fought it. **The liberal tradition's objection — that some apartheid measures were economically irrational — lands precisely here.**

**The resolution most historians now accept: there were two systems with different logics.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The migrant-labour and reserve system** | **functional for capital.** Cheap labour, subsidised reproduction |
| **The colour bar and job reservation** | **functional for white workers**, costly for capital, delivered by politics |

**Apartheid was both, and the tension between them is a real force in the period after 1948** — which is why stage 5 can show the mining industry lobbying against influx control while the state tightened it.

**Practice.** Read the title of the 1952 Act aloud and then read what it did. Then find the 1923 judgment that struck down the colour bar regulations and the 1926 Act that restored it, and note the gap in months. Then work out, from this lesson, which of the two logics each of the following serves: the compound, the pass, the blasting certificate, the reserve.
The Cape franchise, and the non-racial e:
For sixty years one South African colony had a franchise with no racial bar in it — and the slow destruction of it is the most instructive sequence in the subject.

**The institution. The Cape's 1853 constitution gave the vote to adult men meeting a property or wage qualification, with no mention of race.**

| The qualification, 1853 | |
| --- | --- |
| **Occupation of property worth £25**, or | |
| **wages of £50 a year**, or £25 with board and lodging | |
| **Male, adult** | |
| **Race** | **not mentioned** |

**This was deliberate.** The imperial government, influenced by the missionary lobby from the Ordinance 50 lesson, insisted on a colour-blind qualification; the Cape's own merchants and officials largely accepted it, partly from principle and partly because a qualified franchise would in practice return few non-white voters.

**And it was real, not decorative.** By 1909 **African and Coloured voters were roughly 15% of the Cape electorate**, and in a number of eastern districts they held the balance between parties — which meant candidates campaigned for their votes, and African newspapers and political organisations formed around the fact.

**What it produced, which is the part that matters most for the next century:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African voters with real leverage** in specific constituencies | |
| **An African press** — **John Tengo Jabavu's *Imvo Zabantsundu*** from 1884 | |
| **African political organisations** working through electoral and constitutional means | |
| **A political language** of British liberty, constitutional rights and petition | |
| **An African elected representative** — **Walter Rubusana**, to the Cape Provincial Council in 1910 | |
| **A belief that the system could be worked** | which shaped African politics until the 1940s |

**Rubusana is worth knowing: the only African ever elected to the Cape Provincial Council**, in 1910, and he lost the seat in 1914 when Jabavu stood against him and split the vote. **That is the whole history of African electoral representation in white South Africa, and it is one man for four years.**

**Now the destruction, and it is a masterclass in how to remove a right without repealing it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1887, Parliamentary Voters Registration Act** | **excluded land held under communal tenure from counting toward the property qualification.** Removed roughly 20,000 African voters at a stroke |
| **1892, Franchise and Ballot Act** | **raised the property qualification to £75 and added a literacy test** — write your name, address and occupation |
| **1894, Glen Grey Act** | individual tenure granted in a form **specifically excluded** from the franchise qualification |

**Note what none of those did: mention race.** Each is a facially neutral adjustment to a qualification — tenure form, monetary threshold, literacy — **and each was designed and understood to reduce the African vote.** The Glen Grey Act is the most elegant: it gave individual land title, which would ordinarily qualify a man to vote, **in a statutory form drafted so that it did not.**

**This is the Ordinance 50 pattern from earlier in this stage, in its purest form:**

> **The right is preserved and the qualification is adjusted until the right is empty.**

**And it is the pattern to recognise in the present.** Any argument about a facially neutral requirement — a documentation rule, a threshold, a qualification — is an argument whose effects are the question, not whose wording is.

**What happened at Union, which is stage 3's last lessons.** The 1909 South Africa Act preserved the Cape franchise **in the Cape only**, and protected it with an entrenchment: it could be altered only by a **two-thirds majority of both Houses sitting together.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1910** | entrenched, Cape-only, and no equivalent in the other three provinces |
| **1936, Representation of Natives Act** | **African voters removed from the common roll** — passed with the required two-thirds, because the United Party and the National Party combined |
| **1951–56** | **Coloured voters removed**, after a constitutional crisis in which the government enlarged the Senate and reconstituted the Appellate Division to get the majority |

**The 1936 and 1956 removals are stage 4 and stage 5's material.** What belongs here is the structural observation: **the entrenchment held for twenty-six years and then did not, because an entrenchment is only as strong as the legislature's unwillingness to assemble the majority.** The 1950s crisis is the clearest demonstration in South African history that a procedural safeguard will not stop a determined parliament — **which is one reason the 1996 Constitution has a justiciable Bill of Rights and a court with the power to strike legislation down**, rather than relying on special majorities alone. **Stage 7 makes that connection explicitly.**

**The historiographical argument about the Cape franchise, since there is one.** Two readings:

| The liberal reading | The critical reading |
| --- | --- |
| **A genuine non-racial tradition**, destroyed by the north's racism at Union — the road not taken | **a qualified franchise that admitted a tiny elite** and legitimated the exclusion of everyone else |
| It produced real African political participation | **on terms set by property**, and it was whittled down by the Cape's own parliament, not by the Transvaal's |
| Its removal was a defeat worth mourning | **the Cape's liberals voted for the 1892 Act** |

**Both have strong evidence and the second is the one less often heard.** The 1887 and 1892 restrictions were passed by the Cape parliament, under Cape governments — **including Rhodes's, with Afrikaner Bond support.** The non-racial franchise was narrowed by the colony that is credited with it, two decades before Union.

**Practice.** Read the 1853 qualification and work out who it would and would not have enfranchised in a rural district. Then read what the 1887 Act excluded and estimate its effect. Then find how the Glen Grey Act's land tenure was worded so as not to qualify a man to vote. Then ask which of the two readings above you find stronger, and what would change your mind.
Rhodes, the Chartered Company and the Ra:
A diamond fortune turned into a colony, a premiership and a failed coup — and the raid that made the war almost certain.

**Cecil Rhodes, in four capacities at once by 1895:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Chairman of De Beers** | roughly 90% of world diamond production |
| **A major gold magnate** | through Consolidated Gold Fields |
| **Prime Minister of the Cape Colony** | from 1890, **governing with Afrikaner Bond support** |
| **Managing director of the British South Africa Company** | which held a royal charter to administer territory |

**The combination is the point.** No comparable concentration of corporate, political and quasi-sovereign power existed elsewhere in the empire, and it was held by one man who regarded the three as a single project.

**The Cape premiership, and the Bond alliance.** Rhodes governed in coalition with **Jan Hofmeyr's Afrikaner Bond** — the organised Cape Dutch interest. **That alliance is frequently forgotten and it explains his domestic legislation:** the Bond's farmers wanted labour and land, and Rhodes delivered.

**The Glen Grey Act, 1894**, which Rhodes called "a Bill for Africa":

| Provision | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Individual land title** in the Glen Grey district, **one allotment per man** | breaking communal tenure, and creating a landless majority of sons |
| **The allotments excluded from the franchise qualification** | from the last lesson |
| **A labour tax** — ten shillings on men who had not worked outside the district for three months in the year | **forcing wage labour** |
| **District councils** with limited powers | a model of separate local administration |

**Read those four together and the Act is a blueprint.** Individual tenure insufficient to support a family, a tax payable only in cash, and no vote — **which produces migrant labourers.** Rhodes said in parliament that the Act was intended to teach the African "the dignity of labour", and the labour tax says what that meant.

**And Glen Grey's district council model is the ancestor of the Bunga and then of the homeland administrations** in stages 4 and 5. **Rhodes's "Bill for Africa" was a prototype, and it was treated as one.**

**The British South Africa Company, 1889.** A royal charter authorising a private company to acquire and administer territory north of the Transvaal — **to make treaties, maintain a police force, and govern.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1888, the Rudd Concession** | obtained from **Lobengula** of the Ndebele — mineral rights, on terms Lobengula understood differently from the way they were presented in London |
| **1889** | the charter granted on the strength of it |
| **1890** | the occupation of Mashonaland |
| **1893** | **the Matabele War** — Lobengula's kingdom destroyed by Company forces with Maxim guns |
| **1895** | the territory named **Rhodesia** |

**A private company conquering a kingdom under a royal charter is worth pausing on.** It is the nineteenth century's characteristic institution — the VOC at the start of this stage, the BSAC at the end — and the Rudd Concession's disputed interpretation is the standard mechanism: **a document signed by a ruler who was told it meant one thing and which was used in London to mean another.**

**The Jameson Raid, December 1895 – January 1896.** The plan: **an armed incursion into the Transvaal, timed to coincide with an uprising of uitlanders in Johannesburg, which would produce a new government and British supremacy over the goldfield.**

| What happened | |
| --- | --- |
| **29 December 1895** | **Dr Leander Starr Jameson rides in from Pitsani with about 600 men**, without waiting for the rising |
| **The Johannesburg rising** | **did not happen.** The Reform Committee could not agree and had not armed |
| **2 January 1896** | **Jameson surrenders at Doornkop** |
| **January 1896** | **Rhodes resigns as Prime Minister of the Cape** |
| **The Reform Committee** | tried; four leaders sentenced to death, commuted, then fined |

**A fiasco, and the consequences were enormous — all of them in the opposite direction from the intention:**

| Consequence | |
| --- | --- |
| **Kruger's position strengthened** | he had been embattled; he was now the victim of an attempted coup |
| **The republics allied** | the Transvaal and the Orange Free State concluded a **military alliance in 1897** |
| **The Transvaal re-armed** | large purchases of Mauser rifles and Creusot artillery, which is why the Boers fought as well as they did in 1899 |
| **Afrikaner opinion in the Cape turned** | **the Bond's alliance with Rhodes ended**, and Cape Afrikaners' sympathies moved to the republics |
| **British official complicity** | **the Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, was implicated** — the parliamentary inquiry's failure to pursue it was widely understood as a cover-up |
| **Internationally** | the Kaiser's congratulatory telegram to Kruger, which inflamed British opinion |

**So the Raid armed the enemy, cemented the alliance, destroyed the one cross-national political coalition in the subcontinent, and left the British government's good faith in ruins** — four years before the war it was meant to make unnecessary.

**The deeper structural point, which is why this is not merely a colourful episode.** The Raid demonstrated that **the mining interest would use force to obtain a government it could work with**, and that the imperial government would let it try. **After 1896 Kruger's government could not credibly be asked to trust British intentions about anything** — which is the context for the failure of the negotiations in the next lesson.

**And it is why the "uitlander franchise" grievance was never going to be settled by concession.** Kruger had reason to believe that enfranchising the Rand's immigrant majority would hand the republic to the mining companies by vote, having just seen them attempt it by force.

**Rhodes afterward.** He remained a member of the Cape parliament and a BSAC director, campaigned in the 1898 Cape election, and died in 1902 during the war. **His will founded the Rhodes Scholarships, and the statue at the University of Cape Town was removed in 2015 after the Rhodes Must Fall protests** — which stage 11 covers, and which is the clearest instance in recent South African politics of a nineteenth-century figure becoming a live political question.

**Practice.** Read the Rudd Concession's text and then read what the BSAC charter was granted on the basis of. Then read Rhodes's own stated purpose for the Glen Grey Act and list the Act's four mechanisms against it. Then list the Raid's consequences and mark which, if any, served its intention.
The road to war:
How a dispute over the voting rights of immigrant miners became the largest war Britain fought between Waterloo and 1914.

**The dispute, as stated at the time.** The Transvaal had a large immigrant population on the Rand — **the uitlanders** — who paid most of the taxes and could not vote. The republic had progressively lengthened the residence requirement for naturalisation, to **fourteen years** by 1890. Britain demanded five.

**Why that could not be conceded, from Kruger's side.** The arithmetic:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Boer electorate** | perhaps 30,000 men |
| **The uitlander male adult population on the Rand** | **comparable, and growing** |
| **So a five-year franchise** | **would hand control of the republic to a population with no attachment to it**, much of it in the mining companies' employ |
| **And the companies had just tried a coup** | from the Raid lesson |

**So the franchise demand was, in effect, a demand that the republic vote itself out of existence**, and Kruger understood it that way. **His counter-offers — seven years, then five with conditions — were real, and were rejected as insufficient.**

**Why it could not be dropped, from the British side, and here the stated and the real reasons diverge.**

**The stated reason: the rights of British subjects.** Genuine as a political argument in Britain, and the uitlander petitions were real.

**The structural reasons:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gold** | **the empire's monetary system ran on the gold standard**, and the largest supply in the world was in a foreign state |
| **Supremacy** | **Milner's objective**, stated in his own correspondence: British paramountcy in South Africa, which an independent, rich, re-arming Transvaal denied |
| **The mining industry's costs** | the republic's concession monopolies — dynamite above all — and its labour administration were expensive for the mines |
| **The deadlock of the route** | an independent Transvaal with its own railway to Delagoa Bay could bypass British ports |
| **Confederation** | the long-standing imperial aim of a single South African dominion, impossible with two independent republics |

**Milner, who matters more than any other individual in causing the war.** **Alfred Milner became High Commissioner in May 1897** with the settled view that the republics must be brought under British supremacy and that a crisis was the way to do it.

**His method is documented in his own letters**, which is unusual and makes the historiography unusually tractable: **he deliberately pressed a grievance he considered insoluble, in order to force the issue.** He wrote of wanting to "work up to a crisis" and considered the franchise question useful because it was both popular in Britain and unacceptable in Pretoria.

**So on the question of who caused the war, the evidence is better than for most such questions:**

| Account | Standing |
| --- | --- |
| **Milner and Chamberlain deliberately engineered it** | **strongly supported by their own correspondence.** The dominant view |
| **Kruger's intransigence made it inevitable** | real, and it was intransigence about a demand that would have ended the republic |
| **The mining capitalists drove it** | **argued, and more complicated** — the industry was divided, and some houses feared a war's disruption more than they wanted the republic changed |
| **Gold alone explains it** | too simple; gold explains the British interest and not the timing |

**The third row deserves care, because "the war was fought for the mining houses" is a popular claim with mixed evidence.** Some magnates — Beit, Wernher — supported intervention; others did not; and the industry's collective behaviour before 1899 is not that of a unified lobby for war. **The interest was real and the agency was Milner's.**

**The sequence to the war:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1897** | Milner arrives; the republics conclude a military alliance |
| **1898** | Kruger re-elected as State President |
| **March 1899** | the uitlander petition, with tens of thousands of signatures |
| **31 May – 5 June 1899** | **the Bloemfontein Conference.** Milner and Kruger meet. Kruger offers a seven-year franchise with conditions; Milner insists on five and the conference **collapses in five days** |
| **August–September 1899** | further offers and counter-offers; Britain begins moving troops to Natal |
| **9 October 1899** | **Kruger issues an ultimatum**: withdraw the troops within 48 hours |
| **11 October 1899** | **war** |

**The ultimatum is Kruger's great tactical error and his only real option.** Issuing it made the Transvaal the aggressor in the eyes of British and world opinion, which Milner wanted. **Not issuing it meant waiting while British reinforcements arrived** — the republics' only military advantage was that they could mobilise faster than the empire could deploy. **He chose to strike first, which was militarily correct and politically fatal.**

**The forces, which explain the war's shape:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The republics** | **roughly 60,000 men at most**, including foreign volunteers and later Cape and Natal rebels. **Mounted, with Mauser magazine rifles and modern Creusot and Krupp artillery** |
| **Britain** | **eventually about 450,000 imperial troops** — from Britain, Australia, Canada, New Zealand, India |
| **Boer advantages** | mobility, marksmanship, knowledge of ground, no uniforms to aim at |
| **British advantages** | numbers, artillery, the sea, and an empire's resources |

**The Boer system is worth understanding as an institution rather than a militia.** From the commando lesson: **burghers were legally obliged to turn out mounted and armed, electing their own field officers.** That produced excellent light cavalry and a command structure that could not compel obedience — **generals persuaded rather than ordered, and sieges were abandoned when burghers went home to their farms.**

**Practice.** Read Milner's correspondence on wanting to work up to a crisis, and then read Kruger's franchise offers in sequence. Then work out the arithmetic of a five-year franchise against the Boer electorate. Then decide, on the evidence, who you think caused the war — and write down what would change your mind.
The war: the conventional phase:
Eight months in which an empire was humiliated and then brought its weight to bear — and the events every South African has heard of.

**Phase one: the Boer offensive, October to December 1899.** The republics struck into Natal and the northern Cape before British reinforcements arrived, and laid siege to three towns.

| Siege | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ladysmith** | Natal; the main British force bottled up |
| **Kimberley** | **with Rhodes inside it**, and a diamond company's resources |
| **Mafeking** | **Baden-Powell commanding**, for 217 days |

**The sieges were the republics' strategic mistake.** Their advantage was mobility; investing it in three static positions surrendered it. **A thrust to Durban or the Cape ports was available in October 1899 and was not attempted** — partly because the commando system could not sustain an offensive far from home, and partly because the Boer leadership's aim was defensive: hold what they had until Britain tired or Europe intervened.

**Black Week, 10–15 December 1899** — three British defeats in six days:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Stormberg** | 10 December |
| **Magersfontein** | 11 December. **The Highland Brigade caught in the open before entrenchments** |
| **Colenso** | 15 December. Buller's attempt to relieve Ladysmith fails |

**The British losses were not large by later standards.** The shock was that a European army with modern artillery had been defeated three times in a week by farmers. **It produced a crisis of confidence in Britain, the replacement of the commander-in-chief, and the Army reforms of the following decade** — the 1899–1902 war is one of the reasons the British Army of 1914 was what it was.

**The tactical reason for Black Week is worth knowing because it is the first modern war.** The combination of **magazine rifles with smokeless powder, entrenchments, and barbed wire** against **close-order infantry assault** produced slaughter. The Boers could not be seen, fired fifteen aimed rounds a minute, and held prepared positions.

**Every lesson of 1914–18 was available in 1900**, and was observed by foreign military attachés from Germany, Russia, France, Japan and the United States. **It was largely not learned.**

**Phase two: the British counter-offensive, February to September 1900.** **Roberts and Kitchener** arrive with overwhelming force and change the method — flanking marches rather than frontal assault, and mounted infantry in quantity.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **15 February 1900** | **Kimberley relieved** |
| **27 February 1900** | **Paardeberg.** Cronjé's force surrounded and surrendered — about 4,000 men. **And the date was the anniversary of Majuba**, which the British noted publicly |
| **28 February 1900** | **Ladysmith relieved** |
| **13 March 1900** | **Bloemfontein taken** |
| **17 May 1900** | **Mafeking relieved** — and the news produced extraordinary celebrations in Britain |
| **5 June 1900** | **Pretoria taken** |
| **24 May 1900** | the Orange Free State annexed as the **Orange River Colony** |
| **1 September 1900** | **the Transvaal annexed** |

**By September 1900 the British government considered the war over.** Both capitals taken, both republics annexed, Kruger gone into exile in Europe. **Roberts went home. Elections were held in Britain on the strength of it.**

**It was not over.** The next lesson is the twenty months that followed, which cost more lives than the first eight months and which decided the peace.

**Two things in this phase that the standard accounts underweight.**

**1. Black participation, on both sides, on a large scale.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **With the British** | **perhaps 10,000 or more armed** as scouts, guards and auxiliaries; **and on the order of 100,000 employed** as drivers, labourers, and transport workers |
| **With the Boers** | ***agterryers*** — mounted servants who looked after horses, carried equipment and in practice often fought. **Numbering in the thousands to tens of thousands** |
| **Mafeking** | **the Barolong defended a section of the perimeter**, and bore a disproportionate share of the siege's starvation |

**Both nationalist traditions wrote this out.** The Afrikaner account could not admit black combatants on either side; the British account preferred a white man's war; **and the 1902 peace then excluded Africans from its settlement on the basis that it had been.** The recovery of this record is relatively recent, and Stapleton's military history and the war's centenary scholarship are where to find it.

**2. The Cape and Natal rebels.** Dutch-speaking colonists in the Cape who joined the republics — several thousand. **They were tried after the war and disenfranchised**, which is one reason the Cape's Afrikaner political mobilisation after 1902 was so intense.

**And one episode worth knowing for its later political life.** **Jan Smuts**, then the Transvaal's young State Attorney, led a commando deep into the Cape Colony in 1901. **Thirty-eight years later he took South Africa into the Second World War on Britain's side**, and his opponents never let the country forget which side he had fought on in this one.

**Practice.** Find the casualty figures for Magersfontein and note how the attack was made. Then read what foreign military observers reported about entrenchments and magazine rifles. Then look up the Barolong role at Mafeking and compare it with how the siege is usually described. Then read the terms of the annexation proclamations of May and September 1900 and note what Britain thought it had achieved.
The guerrilla phase, the farms and the c:
Twenty months after the war was declared over — and the methods that ended it, which are the ones South Africans remember.

**Why it continued.** The capitals were taken and the field armies broken, **and a commando does not need a capital.** Under **Christiaan de Wet**, **Koos de la Rey**, **Louis Botha**, **Jan Smuts** and others, perhaps 20,000 men dispersed and fought a mounted guerrilla war across a territory the size of western Europe.

**Their method:** attack railways, convoys and isolated posts; live off the country and off captured supplies; never accept a general engagement; and outlast British political will.

**Kitchener's answer, in four parts**, and it is the part of the war that shaped South African memory:

**1. The blockhouse and wire system.** Roughly **8,000 blockhouses** connected by barbed wire along the railways and across the veld, dividing the country into compartments — **about 6,000 kilometres of wire**.

**2. Drives.** Columns of mounted troops sweeping a compartment toward the wire, to trap commandos against it.

**3. Scorched earth.** **Farms burned, crops destroyed, livestock killed or removed, wells fouled.** Systematic, on written orders, across both republics. **The aim was to remove the commandos' supply base, which was the farms of their own families.**

**4. Concentration camps**, which followed directly from the third: **the families removed from the burned farms had to be put somewhere.**

**The camps, and the numbers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **White internees** | **on the order of 110,000–160,000** passed through the camps |
| **White deaths** | **about 28,000**, of whom **roughly 22,000 were children** |
| **Black internees** | **on the order of 115,000**, in separate camps |
| **Black deaths** | **at least 14,000–20,000 recorded**, and the records are poorer, so the true figure is likely higher |

**The causes of death were disease — measles, typhoid, dysentery — in camps that were overcrowded, badly sited, short of water, with inadequate rations and insufficient medical staff.** The mortality was not a policy of killing; **it was the consequence of interning a civilian population without the means to keep it alive**, which is a different charge and a serious one.

**Emily Hobhouse**, who matters. A British woman who visited the camps in 1901, documented the conditions, and published. **Her report caused a political storm in Britain**, led to the government-appointed **Fawcett Commission**, and to reforms that reduced mortality substantially in the war's last months.

**She is a national figure in South Africa** — buried at the Women's Monument in Bloemfontein — and a largely forgotten one in Britain. **That asymmetry is itself a fact about how the war is remembered.**

**The black camps, and why they were forgotten.** Separate, worse supplied, less visited, poorly recorded. **Their inmates were the families of farm workers and tenants displaced by the same farm burning**, and many of the men were employed by the British army. **Hobhouse did not visit them; the Fawcett Commission's remit did not cover them; and neither the Afrikaner nor the British account of the war had a place for them.**

**The recovery of this record is recent** — substantially since the 1990s — and it is one of the clearest cases in this subject of a historiographical gap that was not a mystery but an absence of interest. **The camp registers exist.**

**How the war ended.** The commandos were ground down: by attrition, by the loss of their supply base, by exhaustion, and by the knowledge that the camps were killing their families. **De la Rey and De Wet were still in the field and still winning engagements in 1902** — which is why the surrender was a political decision rather than a military collapse.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **April–May 1902** | negotiations at Pretoria and Vereeniging |
| **The Boer delegates divided** | **the *bittereinders* — "bitter-enders" — wanted to continue** |
| **The argument that carried it** | the camps, the exhaustion of the civilian population, and the fear that the Afrikaner people would not survive another year |
| **31 May 1902** | **the Peace of Vereeniging signed** |

**The vote among the Boer delegates was 54 to 6 for peace**, and the division between those who accepted the surrender and the *bittereinders* who did not **is a fault line in Afrikaner politics for the next fifty years** — Botha and Smuts on one side, Hertzog's and later Malan's tradition drawing on the other. **Stage 4's politics is partly a continuation of this argument.**

**The totals, for scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **British and imperial military deaths** | **about 22,000**, the majority from disease |
| **Boer combatant deaths** | **roughly 6,000–7,000** |
| **Civilian deaths in the camps** | **about 28,000 white, and at least 14,000–20,000 black** |
| **Cost to Britain** | over £200 million, far beyond any estimate |

**So the war's largest category of death was civilian, in camps, mostly children.** That is the fact Afrikaner nationalism was built on, and it was not a myth — **which is why dismissing Afrikaner grievance as merely self-serving does not work.** The grievance was real; what was done with it is the subject of stage 4.

**And the comparison that is always made, and the care it needs.** The term "concentration camp" is correct and contemporary — it was the British term. **The camps were not extermination camps and the comparison with the 1940s is not apt**; the deaths were from disease and neglect rather than from a programme of killing. **Making that distinction is not minimising, and refusing to make it is not honouring the dead.**

**Practice.** Find the camp mortality figures by month and look at what happened after the Fawcett Commission's reforms. Then read a passage of Hobhouse's report. Then look up the black concentration camps and note how much less is written about them, and why. Then read the Vereeniging vote of 54 to 6 and consider what the six were arguing for.
Vereeniging, and the peace that excluded:
The treaty that ended the war, and the one clause in it that decided the next ninety years.

**Signed 31 May 1902**, at Pretoria, by the republican leadership and by Kitchener and Milner.

**The terms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Independence** | **surrendered.** British sovereignty accepted |
| **Amnesty** | for burghers — **except Cape and Natal colonial rebels**, who were tried and **disenfranchised** |
| **No death penalty** | for acts of war |
| **Language** | **Dutch permitted in schools where parents wished it, and in the courts** |
| **Rifles** | could be kept, under licence |
| **Money** | **£3 million** for restocking and repairing farms, plus loans |
| **Self-government** | military rule to be replaced by civil administration, **leading to representative institutions** |

**For a defeated side that had lost its states, those are generous terms**, and they were meant to be: Milner's aim was a reconciled white South Africa under the Crown, and a punitive peace would not produce one. **The £3 million proved far too little against the destruction, which became a grievance of its own.**

**And then Article 8.**

> **The question of granting the franchise to Africans was deferred until after the introduction of self-government in the new colonies.**

**Read what that does.** The Transvaal and the Orange River Colony would get self-government — which meant **a white electorate**, since no African franchise existed there. **That electorate would then decide whether Africans should vote.** The answer was never in doubt.

**So the clause does not deny the franchise. It assigns the decision to the people certain to refuse it.** The mechanism is the same one as the Cape's 1887 and 1892 Acts from the franchise lesson: **not a prohibition, a procedure with a predictable outcome.**

**Why it was in the treaty.** The Boer negotiators insisted on it; the British conceded it. **Milner and Chamberlain had, before and during the war, used the condition of Africans in the republics as part of the justification for intervening** — the uitlander grievance was the stated cause, but the republics' racial order featured in British public argument.

**And the peace abandoned it in a sentence.** That is the charge African political leaders made at the time and have made ever since, and **it is well founded.** Britain went to war partly in the name of the rights of people under Boer rule, and settled the war by guaranteeing that the most numerous of them would have no rights at all.

**What African leaders said at the time**, which is worth knowing because it establishes that the betrayal was identified immediately rather than in retrospect. The Cape's African press and the emerging political organisations protested; the **South African Native Congress** petitioned; and the expectation that British victory would extend the Cape franchise northward was publicly and bitterly disappointed.

**The hope had been reasonable.** The Cape had a non-racial qualified franchise under British rule; the republics did not; **the natural inference from a British victory was that the Cape model would spread.** Instead the opposite happened: in 1910 the Cape's franchise was quarantined in one province, and in 1936 it was abolished.

**And black participation in the war made the exclusion sharper**, from the war lessons: **tens of thousands had served the British effort as scouts, labourers, transport drivers and armed auxiliaries.** The Barolong had defended part of Mafeking's perimeter and starved for it. **None of that purchased anything in the settlement.**

**The *bittereinder* division, continued.** The Boer delegates voted 54 to 6 for peace. **The division between those who signed and those who would not accept it runs through Afrikaner politics for fifty years:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The signatories' tradition** | **Botha and Smuts** — accept the British connection, work within the empire, build white South African unity |
| **The irreconcilable tradition** | **Hertzog**, and later Malan and the National Party — the republic deferred, not abandoned |
| **1914** | the **Maritz rebellion**, when Smuts took South Africa into the war against Germany and some *bittereinders* rose against him |
| **1948** | the tradition that would not sign Vereeniging takes power |

**So Vereeniging did not end the republican project; it postponed it by fifty-nine years.** The Republic of South Africa was declared in 1961, and the 1960 referendum that produced it was fought in explicitly these terms.

**The structural reading, and this is how to hold the whole episode.** The war was fought between two white polities over the control of a goldfield. **The peace settled that question and, in settling it, converted the racial arrangements of the defeated republics into the basis of the new order** — because the price of white reconciliation was that the victors would not impose their colony's franchise on the vanquished.

**White unity was bought with African exclusion.** That is the transaction, it is stated in Article 8, and the next three lessons are its working out.

**Practice.** Find the text of the Peace of Vereeniging and read Article 8 in the original wording. Then read one African organisation's protest from 1902 or 1903 and note what it expected. Then list the terms the Boers obtained and ask what Britain got in exchange for each.
Reconstruction, Milner, and anglicisatio:
Four years of Crown colony government that rebuilt the state, failed at its cultural project, and drafted the blueprint for segregation.

**The period. From 1902 to 1906–07 the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony were governed directly, with Milner as High Commissioner and effectively as proconsul.**

**What Milner wanted:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A reconstructed economy** | the mines working, the farms restocked |
| **An integrated administration** | railways, customs, native affairs across the four colonies |
| **A British majority** | through immigration, so that self-government would be safe |
| **Anglicisation** | **English as the language of the state and the schools** |
| **Then a self-governing British South Africa** | within the empire |

**His instrument was the "Kindergarten"** — a group of very able young Oxford men appointed to the administration: **Lionel Curtis, Patrick Duncan, Philip Kerr, Richard Feetham, John Buchan**. **They mattered beyond South Africa**: several became significant imperial figures, and the ideas about imperial federation worked out here circulated for decades.

**What he achieved:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Administrative integration** | the **Inter-Colonial Council** (1903), the **Central South African Railways**, and the **Customs Union** of 1903 — **the institutional groundwork of Union** |
| **The mines restarted** | with Chinese indentured labour from 1904, from the mining lesson |
| **A modern bureaucracy** | in colonies that had not had one |
| **Agricultural and veterinary services, land settlement schemes** | |

**And the integration point is the one that matters.** By 1906 the four colonies shared railways, customs and a native affairs apparatus. **Union in 1910 was in large part the political ratification of an administrative merger Milner had already carried out** — which is why it happened so quickly once self-government was granted.

**What he failed at, and failed spectacularly: anglicisation.**

**The policy.** English as the medium of instruction in state schools, with Dutch restricted to a few hours a week — which Vereeniging permitted, since it guaranteed Dutch "where parents wished it" and the state schools were the state's.

**The response:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The CNO schools** | ***Christelike Nasionale Onderwys*** — Christian National Education. **Private Dutch-language schools, funded largely by donations from the Netherlands**, set up in opposition |
| **Enrolment** | substantial, at real cost to families who had lost everything |
| **The political effect** | **language became the central symbol of Afrikaner identity** |
| **The cultural effect** | **a push toward Afrikaans rather than Dutch** as the written language of the people — the *Tweede Taalbeweging* |

**So the attempt to make South Africa English produced Afrikaans as a literary and political language**, and the generation that fought the schools fight built the cultural institutions of Afrikaner nationalism: **the language movement, the newspapers, the teachers' associations, and eventually the organisations of stage 4.**

**It is one of the clearest cases in this subject of a policy producing its own opposite.** Milner wanted to dissolve Afrikaner identity; **the schools fight gave it a cause, a grievance and an institution.** And the grievance was strengthened immeasurably by the camps: a people who had lost 22,000 children were being told their children would be taught in English.

**And the political failure.** Milner's hoped-for British majority never arrived — British immigration was far below what he needed. **When the Liberal government in Britain granted the Transvaal self-government in 1906, the 1907 election returned *Het Volk*, Botha's party, to power.** The Orange River Colony returned the **Orangia Unie** in 1907. **Within five years of military defeat the Boer leadership governed both colonies by election.**

**Milner left in 1905.** His project's one durable success was the administrative integration that made Union possible, and its chief by-product was the nationalism that captured the Union in 1948.

**Now the thing in this period with the longest consequences, and it is not usually given this weight.**

**The South African Native Affairs Commission — SANAC — 1903–05**, chaired by **Sir Godfrey Lagden**, appointed by Milner to recommend a common native policy for the four colonies and the territories.

**What it recommended:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Territorial separation** | **African land purchase restricted to defined areas** |
| **Separate political representation** | **Africans on a separate roll**, voting for a limited number of representatives, rather than on the common roll |
| **A common policy** across the colonies | |
| **Recognition of chiefly authority** in the reserves | |
| **No extension of the Cape franchise** northward | |

**That is the blueprint for the next eighty years.** Read the list against what followed:

| SANAC recommended | Enacted |
| --- | --- |
| **Territorial separation of land purchase** | **the Natives Land Act, 1913** |
| **A separate roll** | **the Representation of Natives Act, 1936** |
| **Chiefly administration of reserves** | the Native Administration Act 1927, then the Bantu Authorities Act 1951 |
| **A common national policy** | Union, 1910 |

**So the segregation architecture of stage 4 was drafted by a commission in 1905, under British Crown colony government, before the Union existed and forty-three years before the National Party took power.**

**Which bears directly on the first of the four big disagreements — continuity or break at 1948.** SANAC is the strongest single piece of evidence for continuity: **the design was British, imperial, pre-Union and pre-National Party**, and 1948's government inherited a nearly complete legal structure. **Stage 4 is substantially the story of that structure being built by governments nobody calls apartheid governments.**

**Practice.** Find SANAC's recommendations and set them beside the 1913 and 1936 Acts. Then read about the CNO schools and work out what they cost the families who used them. Then list Milner's five objectives and mark which succeeded — and note that the one that succeeded was the one he cared least about politically.
African and Coloured politics before Uni:
The organisations, newspapers and delegations that opposed the Union settlement — and why knowing them changes how 1912 reads.

**The common account: African political organisation began with the South African Native National Congress in 1912.** It did not. **There were thirty years of organised African and Coloured politics before it**, and the ANC was a federation of existing bodies rather than a founding.

**The organisations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Imbumba Yama Nyama**, 1882, Port Elizabeth | **the first African political organisation in South Africa.** Its name means roughly "hard, solid sinew" — unity |
| ***Imvo Zabantsundu***, 1884 | **John Tengo Jabavu's newspaper**, at King William's Town — the first African-edited newspaper, and a political institution in its own right |
| **The South African Native Congress**, 1898, Cape | with its paper *Izwi Labantu* — **a rival to Jabavu's position** |
| **The African Political Organisation (APO)**, 1902 | **Coloured**, Cape-based, led from 1905 by **Dr Abdullah Abdurahman** |
| **The Natal Native Congress**, 1900 | |
| **The Transvaal Native Congress** | and others in each colony |
| **The Natal Indian Congress**, 1894 | from the indenture lesson |

**What they had and what it rested on, from the franchise lesson: the Cape vote.** These were organisations of a mission-educated, property-holding, enfranchised elite, working through petition, the press, deputations and electoral leverage. **Their political language was British constitutionalism** — the rights of subjects, the Queen's promises, the rule of law — **and that was not naivety; it was the only language the system recognised, and it had occasionally worked.**

**The division between Jabavu and his rivals is worth knowing** because it is the first instance of a recurring split. Jabavu's *Imvo* was aligned with Cape liberal politicians and counselled working with them; *Izwi Labantu* and the SANC were more confrontational and aligned differently. **Accommodation against confrontation, with each side accusing the other of selling out or of futility** — it is the argument that recurs in 1912, in 1949, in 1960, in the 1980s and in 1993.

**Then the Union crisis, 1908–09**, which produced the first national African political action.

**The South African Native Convention, Bloemfontein, March 1909.** Delegates from across the four colonies and the territories met to oppose the draft South Africa Act. **It is the first national African political gathering in South African history**, and it is the direct institutional ancestor of 1912.

**Its objections to the draft Act:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No African franchise** outside the Cape, and no extension | |
| **A colour bar on membership of Parliament** — **"British subjects of European descent"** | so even a Cape African voter could not be represented by an African |
| **The Cape franchise left vulnerable** | entrenched only by a special majority |
| **No protection for African land or rights** in the new state | |

**And the delegation to London, 1909.** A mixed deputation went to lobby the imperial parliament:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Led by W. P. Schreiner** | **a former Prime Minister of the Cape Colony** — a white liberal who took the African case to London against his own country's settlement |
| **Including** | **Jabavu**, **Walter Rubusana**, **Abdullah Abdurahman**, Thomas Mapikela, Daniel Dwanya, Matt Fredericks |
| **They were received** | by the Colonial Secretary, and by members of both Houses |
| **The outcome** | **the South Africa Act passed unamended** |

**Schreiner's role deserves naming.** He had been Cape premier, he lost his career over his opposition to the war and then to the Act's racial clauses, and **he argued in London that the Act would make the African's position worse than it had been under the republics it had defeated.** He was right.

**Why it failed, and the answer is structural rather than a matter of persuasion.** The British government's priority was a self-governing dominion of reconciled whites. **The settlement's whole premise was that Britain would not impose the Cape's franchise on the north** — Article 8 of Vereeniging, from the last lesson. **Amending the Act's racial clauses would have meant reopening the peace.**

**So the imperial parliament heard the case, acknowledged its force, and passed the Act.** Some members spoke against it; the Act went through; and **the dominion was created with a formal racial bar on parliamentary membership.**

**What that failure taught, which is the lesson's point.** Thirty years of petition, press and deputation — conducted with skill, within the system's own terms, by men the system had educated — **produced nothing when the imperial interest ran the other way.**

| Conclusion drawn | By whom |
| --- | --- |
| **Organise nationally rather than by colony** | **the 1912 founders** |
| **Appeal to Britain is still the route** | the dominant view until the 1940s |
| **Petition will not work and something else is needed** | **the Youth League of 1944**, thirty-two years later |

**And so the SANNC, 8 January 1912, Bloemfontein.** Convened by **Pixley ka Isaka Seme**, a Columbia- and Oxford-educated lawyer; **John Langalibalele Dube** the first president; **Sol Plaatje** the first secretary-general.

**It was a federation of the existing bodies**, it included chiefs as well as the educated elite, and **its founding purpose was to do nationally what the colonial organisations had done separately.** Its first great campaign was against the 1913 Natives Land Act, which stage 4 opens with — and Plaatje's ***Native Life in South Africa*** (1916) is that campaign's document and one of the essential primary sources of South African history.

**Practice.** Read the South African Native Convention's 1909 objections and check each against the final text of the South Africa Act. Then find Schreiner's argument in London and note what he predicted. Then read the first chapter of Plaatje's *Native Life in South Africa* — it is free on South African History Online — and note what he says the 1913 Act did to specific families.
The National Convention and Union, 1910:
Thirty-three white men in a room for four months, and the constitution they produced — which governed South Africa for fifty-one years.

**The Convention.** Met in **Durban from October 1908** and then in **Cape Town**, reporting in **February 1909**.

| Delegates | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cape Colony** | 12 |
| **Transvaal** | 8 |
| **Natal** | 5 |
| **Orange River Colony** | 5 |
| **Southern Rhodesia** | observers |
| **African, Coloured or Indian delegates** | **none** |
| **Women** | none |

**The principal figures:** **Jan Smuts**, the draft's chief architect; **Louis Botha**; **J. B. M. Hertzog**; **John X. Merriman**, the Cape premier; **M. T. Steyn**, the former Free State president; **Sir Percy Fitzpatrick** and **Sir Thomas Smartt** from the Cape's progressive side; **F. R. Moor** of Natal.

**Note who is in that list: the men who had led the republics in the war, drafting the constitution of a British dominion six years after losing it.** Smuts, who had raided the Cape with a commando in 1901, wrote the constitution. **That is the white reconciliation Milner wanted, achieved by his failure.**

**The decisions, and each is a choice with consequences:**

**1. Unitary, not federal.** Natal wanted a federation and was outvoted. **Smuts and Steyn pressed for a unitary state and got it.**

**The consequence is the most important structural fact in twentieth-century South Africa.** A unitary parliament with sovereign power and no justiciable bill of rights meant **a bare majority could do anything** — which is how the segregation statutes of stage 4 and the apartheid statutes of stage 5 were passed, and why no court could stop them. **Compare it with 1996 in stage 7, where the answer was the opposite on every point.**

**2. The franchise left to each province as it stood.**

| Province | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cape** | **the non-racial qualified franchise retained** — entrenched, requiring a two-thirds majority of both Houses sitting together |
| **Natal** | a franchise framed to exclude in practice |
| **Transvaal, Orange River Colony** | **whites only** |

**No extension, no uniformity, and the Cape's exception quarantined in one province** where it could be outvoted in the national parliament by the three that had none.

**3. A colour bar on Parliament itself.** Members of the House of Assembly had to be **"British subjects of European descent"**. **So a Cape African voter could vote — and could not be represented by an African.** Walter Rubusana sat on the Cape Provincial Council and could not have sat in Parliament.

**That provision is the one the 1909 London delegation objected to most sharply**, and it is the clearest statement of what the Union was.

**4. Two official languages, entrenched.** **English and Dutch** — Afrikaans was added in 1925 — protected by the same two-thirds requirement as the Cape franchise. **The language clause held for the whole life of the Union; the franchise clause did not.**

**5. Three capitals**, which is the compromise everyone knows and nobody can defend:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pretoria** | administrative — the executive |
| **Cape Town** | legislative — Parliament |
| **Bloemfontein** | judicial — the Appellate Division |

**A horse-trade between the Transvaal, the Cape and the Free State**, and it survives in the present: **the Constitution still has Cape Town as the seat of Parliament, and the cost and absurdity of moving the government twice a year is a live argument** — stage 12 touches it.

**6. A Senate with nominated members**, including four appointed for their "thorough acquaintance with the reasonable wants and wishes of the coloured races" — **representation for Africans by white appointees, without their participation.** The Senate's composition becomes the instrument of the 1950s constitutional crisis in stage 5.

**7. Provision for later incorporation** of the High Commission Territories and Rhodesia. **Never exercised** — from the Lesotho lesson, and Rhodesia voted against joining in 1922.

**The ratification:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The four colonial parliaments** | approved |
| **Natal** | held a **referendum**, which approved by roughly three to one |
| **The imperial parliament** | passed it as the **South Africa Act 1909** |
| **31 May 1910** | **Union** — **eight years to the day after Vereeniging** |

**The date was chosen.** Union came into being on the anniversary of the peace, which is as explicit a statement of what the settlement was as a calendar can make.

**The first government: Louis Botha as Prime Minister**, with Smuts in several portfolios and **Hertzog as Minister of Justice.** The party was the **South African Party**, a fusion of the colonial parties.

**And the opposition that formed immediately.** Hertzog left the cabinet in 1912 over his insistence on Dutch-language rights and "South Africa first", and founded the **National Party in 1914.** **So the party that would govern from 1948 to 1994 was founded four years after Union, by a member of its first cabinet, over language and the British connection.**

**Practice.** Find the South Africa Act 1909 and read sections 35 and 137 — the entrenched clauses — and the qualification for membership of the Assembly. Then list the Convention's seven decisions and mark which survive in the 1996 Constitution. Then note the date of Union and the date of Vereeniging, and ask who chose it.
What 1910 settled, and what it deferred:
The stage's conclusion: a settlement among whites that created a state and left every other question open — and a list of when each one came due.

**What Union settled.**

| Settled | |
| --- | --- |
| **White reconciliation** | Boer and Briton in one state, with the republican leadership governing it |
| **The territorial shape** | the four colonies into one country, which is the South Africa of today minus the territories |
| **A sovereign parliament** | unitary, supreme, with no court able to review its legislation |
| **The language question** | **two official languages, entrenched** — and it held |
| **Economic integration** | railways, customs and a single market, largely accomplished by Milner before 1910 |
| **The mining economy's political security** | a stable state governing the goldfield |
| **Dominion status** | within the empire, self-governing |

**That is a real achievement and it should be said so.** Eight years after a war that killed tens of thousands of civilians, the combatants had a functioning joint state with an elected government and a durable language compromise. **Very few post-war settlements manage that.**

**It was achieved by excluding four-fifths of the population from it.**

**What Union deferred, and when each came due:**

| Deferred | Came due |
| --- | --- |
| **The African franchise** | **1936** — removed from the common roll |
| **The Coloured franchise** | **1951–56** — removed after a constitutional crisis |
| **Land** | **1913** — three years. **The Natives Land Act** |
| **Urban residence** | **1923** — the Natives (Urban Areas) Act |
| **The industrial colour bar** | **1911, struck down 1923, re-enacted 1926** |
| **The position of Indians** | contested continuously; the Ghetto Act of 1946, then stage 5 |
| **The republic** | **1961** |
| **The High Commission Territories** | **never** — Lesotho, Botswana and Eswatini became independent instead |
| **Whether Africans would be citizens at all** | **answered "no" in 1970**, by the Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act |
| **The whole settlement** | **1990–96** |

**Reading that table is the point of this stage.** Every item in the right-hand column is a stage in this curriculum, and **each one is a cheque written in 1910.**

**The structural statement, which is how to carry 1910 forward.** The Union converted the arrangements of four colonies into the law of one state:

| From | To |
| --- | --- |
| **The Cape's qualified non-racial franchise** | **a provincial anomaly, outvoted and then abolished** |
| **Shepstone's Natal system of indirect rule** | **the national model for administering Africans** |
| **The republics' whites-only constitutions** | **the national norm** |
| **The mining industry's labour system** | **national labour law** |
| **SANAC's 1905 blueprint** | **the legislative programme of the next thirty years** |

**So the Union chose, from among the arrangements available, the most restrictive of each** — and that was not an oversight. **It was the price of the reconciliation in the left-hand column of the first table.**

**Which brings the stage back to the four big disagreements from stage 1, and the first of them in particular.**

**Was apartheid a continuation of segregation or a break with it?** This stage has assembled the evidence for continuity:

| Evidence for continuity, from stage 3 |
| --- |
| **The pass, the compound and the colour bar** were working institutions by 1900, built by an industry |
| **SANAC drafted the territorial and political segregation blueprint in 1905**, under British rule |
| **The 1910 constitution** made a sovereign parliament with no judicial check — the instrument apartheid later used |
| **Article 8 of Vereeniging** assigned the franchise question to a white electorate |
| **The Cape franchise was narrowed by the Cape's own parliament** in 1887 and 1892 |
| **Indirect rule through chiefs** was invented in Natal in the 1840s |

**Stage 4 will assemble the rest, and stage 5 will put the case for the break.** What this stage establishes is that **the case for continuity is strong and rests on the period before the National Party existed** — which means the first disagreement cannot be settled by pointing at 1948.

**And the honest counterweight, so the stage does not close by deciding what stage 1 said not to decide.** Nothing in this stage produced population registration, the Group Areas Act, the destruction of the Cape Coloured franchise, Bantu Education, the homelands project or the security state. **Those are after 1948, they are different in kind as well as in degree, and the argument for a break rests on them.** Stage 5 makes it.

**One last thing, which is the counterfactual worth holding.** The Cape's franchise existed. **It could have been extended.** The 1909 delegation asked for exactly that, a former Cape premier argued for it in London, and some British parliamentarians agreed.

**It was not extended because white unity was the priority and African exclusion was its price.** That is a choice made by identifiable people at an identifiable meeting, recorded in a published Act — **not a historical inevitability**, and the fact that it was a choice is why the four big disagreements are arguments about responsibility and not only about causation.

**Practice.** Write out the deferred-questions table from memory and check it. Then take the continuity evidence and write the strongest reply to it you can — you will need stage 5's material, so come back to this after it. Then find the 1909 delegation's request and the Convention's reasoning for refusing it, and decide what you think of each.
The Natives Land Act, 1913:
The Union's third year, and the single most consequential statute in South African history.

**The Act. Natives Land Act 27 of 1913.** What it did, in three provisions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Africans could not buy or lease land outside the "scheduled areas"** | and whites could not buy inside them |
| **2. The scheduled areas were defined by schedule** — **about 7.3% of the country** | a map of where conquest had stopped, from stage 3 |
| **3. Sharecropping and labour tenancy on white farms were prohibited** | the "Free State clause", and it bit immediately |

**The 7% figure is the one everyone knows, and it is worth being precise about what it measures.** It is the share of the country's land area in which the African majority — roughly two-thirds of the population — could lawfully acquire land. **It was raised on paper to a target of about 13.6% in 1936**, which the next lessons cover, and the target was never fully met.

**But the third provision is the one that did the immediate damage**, and it is the one usually underweighted.

**What sharecropping was.** Across the Free State and the Transvaal, African families farmed white-owned land on shares — **they supplied the labour, draught oxen, implements and seed, and gave the owner a portion of the crop.** Many were prosperous. They had livestock, ploughs, and in some cases more capital than their landlords.

**Why white farmers wanted it ended.** Not because it was unprofitable — because they wanted **labourers rather than partners.** A sharecropper with his own oxen and plough could bargain; a wage labourer with nothing could not. **And African tenants were outcompeting some white farmers on the same land.**

**So the Act's effect in 1913 was mass eviction.** Families who had farmed the same land for a generation were given a choice: **stay as servants on terms the owner set, or leave with their stock and find somewhere to go.** There was nowhere to go, because the scheduled areas were full and they could not buy.

**Plaatje's record of it, which is the next lesson, follows families on the roads in the winter of 1913 with their cattle dying as they moved.**

**And one detail that is both legally important and generally missed: the Act's land provisions did not initially apply in the Cape.** The reason is stage 3's: **land ownership was a franchise qualification in the Cape**, and the Cape franchise was entrenched by the South Africa Act. **A statute barring African land purchase there would have altered an entrenched franchise, requiring a two-thirds majority.** So the Cape was excluded — and the exclusion lasted until the 1936 legislation handled both questions together.

**Which tells you something about how the entrenchment worked: it did protect something, for a while, and when it was finally overcome both the franchise and the land went in the same session.**

**Why the Act was passed in 1913 specifically.** Three pressures converging:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The farmers** | wanted labour, and wanted African competitors off the land |
| **The mines** | wanted the reserves maintained — **Wolpe's mechanism from stage 3**: the reserve subsidised the wage |
| **SANAC's 1905 blueprint** | **territorial separation of land purchase, recommended under British rule** — stage 3's reconstruction lesson |

**The Act is where the farm lobby and the mining lobby agreed**, and that is why it passed easily. **Farmers got labour; mines kept the reserves; and the two interests that fought over everything else were aligned on this.**

**What the Act did not do, because the distinction matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It did not expropriate land already owned** | existing African freehold title outside the scheduled areas — the "black spots" — survived until the removals of stage 5 |
| **It did not create the reserves** | they existed; the Act **froze and nationalised** them |
| **It did not apply to the Cape** at first | as above |
| **It did not fix the figure at 7% forever** | 1936 raised the target, and delivery lagged |

**The long consequences, which is why this is the most consequential statute:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The 1913 date is the cut-off for restitution** | **the Restitution of Land Rights Act 1994 allows claims for dispossession after 19 June 1913.** So this Act's date governs the entire post-apartheid land restitution programme — and everything before it, including stage 3's conquest and all Khoe and San dispossession, falls outside |
| **The reserves became the homelands** | stage 5 |
| **Rural African agriculture was destroyed as an independent sector** | and has never recovered |
| **The migrant labour system was secured** | with a legal floor under it |
| **The 7%/13% figures** | are the arithmetic of every land argument since |

**The restitution cut-off is the one to hold.** It is a deliberate choice made in 1994: **1913 as the date the modern dispossession begins, for reasons of administrability** — records exist after it and largely do not before. **The consequence is that the longest dispossessions are the least claimable**, and stage 9 and stage 12 both argue about it.

**Practice.** Find the text of the 1913 Act and read the schedule, then find a map of the scheduled areas. Then read the Free State clause and work out what it required of a sharecropping family. Then look up the Restitution of Land Rights Act's cut-off date and ask who it includes and who it does not.
Plaatje, and the campaign against the Ac:
The first national African political campaign, the book it produced, and what its failure established.

**Sol Plaatje**: interpreter, newspaper editor, linguist, novelist, translator of Shakespeare into Setswana, **first secretary-general of the South African Native National Congress**. And the author of the single most important primary source on the 1913 Act.

**The campaign, in sequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1913** | the Act passes. The SANNC resolves to oppose it |
| **1913–14** | **Plaatje travels through the Free State and Transvaal recording what the Act was doing** |
| **1914** | **a deputation to London** — Dube, Plaatje, Rubusana, Saul Msane, Thomas Mapikela |
| **August 1914** | **the First World War begins.** The deputation's case is overtaken |
