| **The response** | the Colonial Secretary declines to intervene: the Union is self-governing, and the Act is its internal affair |
| **1916** | **Plaatje publishes *Native Life in South Africa*** in London, to fund and sustain the campaign |
| **1919** | **a second deputation**, to the Versailles peace conference and to Britain. Also unsuccessful |

**Why appeal to London at all?** Because from stage 3's franchise lesson it was the strategy available: the Cape's constitutional tradition, petition, and the claim of British subjecthood. **And in 1909 the London route had at least been heard.**

**What 1914 established, and it is the campaign's real result: self-government meant Britain would not intervene.** The 1909 delegation had failed to amend the Act; the 1914 delegation failed to get Britain to disallow a Union statute at all. **After 1914 there was no external authority to appeal to, and African politics had to find something else.**

**It took thirty years to find it.** The Youth League of 1944, which stage 4 ends near, is the answer — and the intervening decades of petition and deputation are the evidence that the earlier strategy was exhausted.

***Native Life in South Africa*, and why to read it.** It is free on South African History Online.

**What it is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reportage** | **Plaatje on a bicycle, through the winter of 1913, recording evictions family by family** |
| **Political argument** | against the Act, addressed to a British readership |
| **A record of a world ending** | African commercial farming in the Free State, as it was destroyed |
| **A source of itself** | **the voice and the political reasoning of the African elite of 1913**, in its own words |

**The passage everyone quotes is the Kgobadi family**, evicted with their stock, moving along the roads in winter, their cattle dying, **and burying their child by the roadside at night because they had no right to be on any land on which to dig a grave.** It is the most-cited paragraph in South African political writing and it is reportage, not rhetoric.

**Why it matters as evidence, in stage 1's terms.** It is **primary** for the Act's effects — an eyewitness, naming places and families, within months. **It is also a polemic with a purpose**, and Plaatje says so: he wrote it to move British opinion. **Both facts hold, and the first is not weakened by the second.** The evictions are corroborated by other sources; what Plaatje adds is detail no official record kept.

**The book's other function, which is easy to miss.** It documents **that African farmers were prosperous**, with stock and implements and surpluses to sell. **That is the claim the Act's defenders needed to be false** — and it is the claim that makes the Act legible as the destruction of a competitor rather than the protection of a dependent.

**Plaatje's own place, in stage 1's terms.** He was:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A mission-educated member of the Cape's enfranchised elite** | and wrote in its political idiom |
| **A believer in the imperial connection** | which the 1914 failure did not immediately shake |
| **A cultural nationalist of a different kind** | *Mhudi*, his novel, is the first by a black South African in English; his Setswana work preserved a language |
| **Politically unsuccessful in his lifetime** | the Act stood for eighty-one years |

**And the SANNC's position after 1914.** Divided, as it had been in stage 3's Jabavu split: some arguing for continued constitutional appeal, others for industrial action, and the organisation itself small, under-funded and without a mass base. **The mass base arrives in 1919 with the ICU**, four lessons from here, and the ANC does not acquire one until the 1950s.

**The honest assessment of the campaign.** It failed completely. **The Act was not amended, Britain did not intervene, the evictions proceeded, and the SANNC had no means of resistance beyond publicity.**

**What it produced was a record and a lesson.** The record is still the best source on 1913. **The lesson — that the imperial appeal was dead and that an organisation without mass support cannot resist a statute — was learned slowly and at great cost**, and the arguments inside African politics for the next forty years are arguments about it.

**Practice.** Read the Kgobadi passage in *Native Life in South Africa*, and then read another chapter for its detail on African farmers' prosperity. Then find the Colonial Secretary's response to the 1914 deputation. Then write down what options African political organisation had after 1914, and which were tried.
The Natives (Urban Areas) Act, 1923:
The statute that decided African urban life for sixty years, and the single sentence of doctrine behind it.

**The doctrine first, because the Act is its implementation.** The **Stallard Commission** of 1922, reporting on the Transvaal's local government, stated the principle:

> **The native should only be allowed to enter urban areas, which are essentially the white man's creation, when he is willing to enter and to minister to the needs of the white man, and should depart therefrom when he ceases so to minister.**

**Read it carefully, because every element of urban apartheid is in it:**

| The sentence says | Which produces |
| --- | --- |
| **the city is "essentially the white man's creation"** | **no African claim to urban space** |
| **"allowed to enter"** | **permission, and therefore permits** |
| **"to minister to the needs"** | **presence justified only by employment** |
| **"should depart when he ceases"** | **no unemployed Africans in cities; removal when work ends** |

**That is the temporary sojourner doctrine**, and it governed South African urban policy from 1923 to the 1980s. **The Group Areas Act, influx control, the Section 10 rights of stage 5, and the pass raids all execute it.**

**The Act. Natives (Urban Areas) Act 21 of 1923.** Its provisions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Segregated locations** | municipalities empowered — and later obliged — to establish separate African townships |
| **Removal powers** | Africans could be required to move to them from other parts of a town |
| **Influx control** | municipalities could restrict African entry to a proclaimed area |
| **Registration of service contracts** | and so pass control tied to employment |
| **"Surplus" removal** | **Africans not employed could be removed from an urban area** |
| **The Native Revenue Account** | **locations had to be financed from African rents and beer-hall profits** — not from general rates |

**That last provision is the one with the longest consequences and it is almost never discussed.** African townships were required to be **self-financing**: the services were paid for out of the rents and from the municipal monopoly on beer sales to Africans.

| Consequence | |
| --- | --- |
| **Townships were under-serviced by design** | the revenue base was the poorest population in the city |
| **The municipal beer hall became a political target** | — attacked in protests from the 1920s through to 1976 and after |
| **Local government's financial geography was set** | **a pattern that survives: the 1996 settlement inherited municipalities whose tax base and whose population were in different places** |

**Stage 8's local government lesson and stage 9's fiscal lesson both begin here.** The structural problem of South African municipal finance — service obligations in the townships, rateable value in the suburbs — was created by the requirement that the locations pay for themselves.

**What the Act did not do.** It did not stop urbanisation. **Africans came to the cities in increasing numbers for the next sixty years**, because the work was there and the reserves could not support the population. **Influx control slowed, criminalised and brutalised the movement without reversing it** — which is the central finding of the Fagan Commission in 1948, at the end of this stage.

**The statistics make the point.** The urban African population grew continuously through every period of influx control, and by the 1946 census it had roughly doubled since 1921. **A policy that was enforced with millions of arrests over decades did not achieve its stated objective at any point.**

**Which raises the question stage 1's method requires: if it did not work, what was it for?**

| Answer | Standing |
| --- | --- |
| **It did work, at its real purpose** — **controlling the terms on which labour was available**, not the number | **the strongest reading.** A worker who may be removed is a worker who cannot bargain |
| **It worked as a mechanism for distributing labour** | directing workers to farms and mines rather than cities |
| **It was ideologically necessary** | the temporary sojourner doctrine required an apparatus whether or not it succeeded |
| **It failed and was persisted with** | which happens, and is the liberal tradition's reading |

**The first is the functional account from stage 3 applied to urban policy**, and the evidence for it is that the pass system's effect on wages and on organisation was large while its effect on urban growth was small.

**The 1937 amendment, worth naming** because it tightened the Act considerably: it required municipalities to remove "surplus" Africans, restricted entry further, and barred Africans from acquiring property in urban areas outside the locations. **By 1937 the doctrine was fully legislated** — eleven years before 1948.

**And the pattern from stage 3 again:** this is **national legislation codifying what Kimberley, the Rand and Shepstone's Natal had already built.** The compound, the pass and the location were working institutions; **the Union's parliament made them the law of the country.**

**Practice.** Read the Stallard formulation and map each clause onto a later apartheid law. Then find the Native Revenue Account provision and work out what it meant for township services. Then find urban African population figures for 1921, 1936 and 1946, and judge whether influx control achieved its stated aim.
The 1922 Rand Revolt:
An armed insurrection by white workers under a red flag, with a slogan nobody can forget, and the election it decided.

**The cause: the Chamber of Mines tried to cut costs.** From stage 3's gold lesson — the gold price was fixed, the ore was getting poorer, and after the war the industry was squeezed. **The largest saving available was to replace expensive white semi-skilled miners with cheaper black workers**, by altering the ratio of white to black underground.

**That is "the dilution of labour", and it is precisely what stage 3 said the colour bar existed to prevent.** The industry had been trying since the 1890s; in December 1921 it announced it would do it.

**The strike, and then the rising:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **January 1922** | white mineworkers strike; coal and engineering follow |
| **February** | negotiations fail; **commandos form** — organised on the Boer model, with elected officers |
| **early March** | **a general strike is declared, and the Rand rises** |
| **10–14 March** | **armed insurrection.** Police stations attacked, suburbs held, black workers attacked and killed in the townships |
| **Smuts's response** | **martial law, 20,000 troops, artillery, tanks and aircraft** — bombing was used on the Rand |
| **by mid-March** | suppressed |
| **Casualties** | **about 200 dead** |
| **After** | **four strikers hanged**, many imprisoned; the strike lost; the colour bar diluted |

**The slogan, which is the thing everybody knows and which is worth understanding rather than merely quoting:**

> **Workers of the world, unite and fight for a white South Africa.**

**It is not a confusion.** It is the exact statement of the position: a militant labour movement, with real socialist elements and Communist Party involvement, whose material interest was **the statutory protection of white jobs against cheaper black competition.** From stage 3's Black Flag pattern: white workers threatened from above secure protection by excluding black competitors, not by being protected from capital.

**The Communist Party's part is genuinely awkward and is argued about.** The CPSA, founded in 1921, supported the strike. **Some members fought in the commandos; the party's position was that this was a workers' rising against capital, and the racial element was an error to be corrected later.** The party's subsequent reckoning with 1922 — and the 1928 Native Republic thesis two lessons from here — is partly a response to it.

**And black workers were attacked during the rising**, which is not incidental. **The insurrection included racial violence in the townships**, and no account of 1922 as a straightforward class struggle survives that fact.

**Why Smuts suppressing it cost him the country.** He won in March 1922 and lost the election in June 1924.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The method** | **aircraft and artillery against white workers** was unforgivable to a large part of the white electorate |
| **The Afrikaner dimension** | **many of the strikers were Afrikaners recently off the land** — the poor whites of two lessons from here — and the commandos used the republican military form |
| **The memory of 1899–1902** | Smuts using imperial methods against Afrikaners was read in that light |
| **The alliance it produced** | **Hertzog's National Party and Creswell's Labour Party formed a pact** |
| **1924** | **the Pact wins. Smuts loses office** |

**So 1922 is the moment the two strands that became apartheid's political base fused:** Afrikaner nationalism and organised white labour, **against the mining industry and the party that governed for it.** The Pact government's programme in the next lesson is the direct result.

**The structural lesson, and it is the clearest instance of stage 3's two logics in collision:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Capital wanted** | **to employ black workers in skilled jobs** at lower wages — i.e. to erode the colour bar |
| **White labour wanted** | **statutory protection**, which raised the industry's costs |
| **The state in 1922** | **sided with capital, by force** |
| **The state from 1924** | **sided with white labour, by statute** |
| **Black workers** | had no vote, were attacked during the rising, and bore the cost of both outcomes |

**That table is the political economy of twentieth-century South Africa in five rows.** And it refutes any account in which capital and apartheid are simply identical: **in 1922 the mining industry was trying to do what the colour bar forbade, and white workers rose against it.**

**Which is the strongest single piece of evidence for the liberal tradition's objection from stage 1** — that significant parts of the racial order were economically irrational and were imposed on capital by politics. **The migrant and reserve system was functional for capital; the colour bar was not.** Stage 4's next lesson shows white labour collecting its winnings.

**Practice.** Read the slogan and write out what material interest it expresses. Then find out what the Chamber of Mines proposed in December 1921 and what the ratio change would have meant. Then list Smuts's actions in March 1922 and the 1924 election result, and work out the connection. Then decide which of stage 3's two logics 1922 supports.
The Pact government, and civilised labou:
White labour collects its winnings: a programme of state employment, statutory protection and industrial policy that built the white working class.

**The government. The 1924 election brought in the Pact** — **Hertzog's National Party** with **Creswell's Labour Party** — on a platform of protecting white workers and asserting South African interests against imperial and mining ones.

**What it did, and the list is a coherent programme rather than a set of measures:**

**1. The civilised labour policy, 1924.** A circular instruction: **the state and its agencies were to employ "civilised" labour at "civilised" rates.**

| The euphemism | The meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **"Civilised labour"** | **white labour** — defined as workers whose standard of living conformed to European standards |
| **"Civilised rates"** | wages sufficient to maintain that standard |

**And the instrument was state employment.** The South African Railways and Harbours, the Post Office and public works were directed to replace African workers with whites:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Railways** | **the largest single employer of poor whites.** Thousands of African workers were displaced by whites at several times the wage |
| **Public works and municipalities** | the same |
| **The effect** | **a state-funded solution to the poor white problem** |

**2. The 1925 Wage Act.** A Wage Board to set minimum wages in unregulated industries.

**And here is the mechanism worth understanding, because it is subtle and effective.** The Act was racially neutral on its face — it set minimum wages by occupation. **Its purpose and effect was to price black workers out of jobs white workers wanted**: if the minimum wage for a job is set at a "civilised" level, an employer will prefer a white worker at that wage to a black one at the same wage. **A minimum wage, used as a colour bar.**

**That is the substitution pattern from stage 3's Ordinance 50 lesson, in its most sophisticated form** — a measure that is race-blind in text, protective in intent, and exclusionary in effect. **And it is why arguments about minimum wages in South Africa still carry this history.**

**3. The Mines and Works Amendment Act, 1926.** From stage 3: the colour bar struck down by a court in 1923 and **re-enacted explicitly by this government.** The reason the Pact existed, delivered in its second year.

**4. The Industrial Conciliation Act, 1924.** Registered trade unions, recognised collective bargaining — **and defined "employee" so as to exclude pass-bearing Africans.** So African workers were outside the entire industrial relations system: **they could not register a union, could not bargain legally, and their strikes were criminal.**

**That exclusion lasted until 1979**, which is stage 5's Wiehahn Commission. **Fifty-five years in which the majority of the industrial workforce had no legal collective voice** — and it is the single most important fact about South African labour history.

**5. Industrial policy: protection and state enterprise.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Tariff protection, 1925** | for domestic manufacturing — jobs for white workers |
| **ISCOR, 1928** | **the state steel corporation**, created because private capital would not. The Iron and Steel Industry Act |
| **Later: ESCOM (1923), SASOL (1950), IDC (1940)** | **a tradition of state-owned industry** |

**The parastatal tradition begins here, and it matters for stage 9 and stage 11.** Eskom, Transnet, Denel, SAA and the rest descend from a deliberate policy of state enterprise, created to industrialise and to employ whites, **which means the state-owned enterprises at the centre of state capture were built as instruments of racial employment policy.** That is not a reason for anything in particular; it is the lineage.

**6. Afrikaans made an official language, 1925.** From Dutch, by statute — the schools fight of stage 3 reaching its conclusion.

**What the programme accomplished, which is the part to take seriously.** It worked.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Poor white unemployment** | substantially reduced by state employment |
| **A white working class** | **created and secured**, with wages far above African wages and rising |
| **Industrialisation** | real, behind tariffs, with state capital |
| **Afrikaner upward mobility** | begun — and the institutions of the next lesson accelerated it |

**It is one of the most successful programmes of state-directed social uplift of its era**, and it was for one racial group, funded by the exclusion of another. **Both halves of that sentence are the point.**

**The cost, measured:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African workers displaced from state employment** | in the tens of thousands |
| **African wages** | held down by the Wage Act's mechanism and by exclusion from bargaining |
| **The wage gap** | **widened substantially** through the period |
| **African workers' legal position** | outside the industrial system entirely, until 1979 |

**And the political lesson, which is this stage's throughline.** The Pact government was **elected**, by a white electorate, on an explicit platform of racial protection in employment, **and it delivered what it promised.** It was not a government of extremists; it was a coalition of nationalists and labour that did what its voters had asked.

**Which bears on the first big disagreement from stage 1.** The civilised labour policy, the 1926 colour bar, the 1924 exclusion of Africans from industrial law and the 1923 Urban Areas Act were all in place by 1937. **Apartheid's labour and urban architecture was built by the Pact and by Hertzog's governments, twenty-four years before 1948.**

**Practice.** Read the civilised labour circular and note the definition of "civilised". Then work out how a racially neutral minimum wage operates as a colour bar. Then find the 1924 Industrial Conciliation Act's definition of "employee" and note what it excluded and until when. Then list the state corporations founded between 1923 and 1950.
The Native Administration Act, 1927:
The statute that put the African majority outside the ordinary law of the country, and the clause used against political speech for sixty years.

**Native Administration Act 38 of 1927.** Its central provisions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Governor-General is declared "Supreme Chief" of all Africans** | **in Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State**, and the doctrine was later extended |
| **Rule by proclamation** | the Governor-General could legislate for the reserves **by proclamation, without Parliament** |
| **Power to depose chiefs** and appoint them | so chiefly authority became a delegation from the state |
| **Power to move communities** | **a whole "tribe" could be ordered to relocate by proclamation** |
| **"Native law" recognised and codified** | as the state's officials understood it |
| **A separate court system** | chiefs' courts and Native Commissioners' courts, with their own appeal structure |
| **Section 29** | **an offence to utter words with intent to promote hostility between Africans and Europeans** |

**The Supreme Chief doctrine is from Shepstone's Natal, in stage 3** — the colonial governor as paramount chief, with the powers of a chief and none of the obligations. **The 1927 Act made it national.**

**What it accomplished, and it is more radical than it first reads.**

**1. Two legal systems, by race.** An African's civil status, marriage, succession and local disputes were governed by codified "native law" in a separate court hierarchy. **An African and a white person in the same town were under different law for a range of matters.**

**And the codified version was not the living custom.** Officials wrote down what they understood customary law to be, in the 1920s, and that written version then governed — **frozen, simplified, and systematically more patriarchal than the practice it recorded**, because the officials recording it asked chiefs and headmen rather than women.

**That matters now.** Customary law is recognised in the 1996 Constitution, and the question of which customary law — the living practice or the colonial codification — has been litigated repeatedly. **The Constitutional Court's answer has been *living* customary law**, which is stage 7's material, and the 1927 codification is what it was distinguishing itself from.

**2. Legislation without Parliament.** Rule by proclamation meant the reserves were governed by executive decree. **No debate, no vote, no publication beyond the Gazette.** From stage 1's Gazette lesson: this is where you find it.

**3. The power to move people.** **A proclamation could order a community off its land.** This is the legal instrument behind the forced removals of stage 5 — the machinery existed from 1927, and what changed after 1948 was the scale of its use.

**4. Section 29, and this is the provision to remember.** An offence to say anything "with intent to promote any feeling of hostility between natives and Europeans".

| Why it is so broad | |
| --- | --- |
| **Almost any political statement about racial injustice** | can be charged as promoting hostility |
| **Truth is not a defence** | the offence is the intent to promote hostility, not falsehood |
| **It was used extensively** | against ICU organisers, against the Communist Party, against ANC speakers, for decades |

**Section 29 is the ancestor of the security legislation of stage 5** — the Suppression of Communism Act, the Riotous Assemblies amendments, the banning orders. **The technique of criminalising political speech by defining its effect rather than its content starts here**, in a government that is not usually called repressive.

**And the chiefs, which is the Act's most consequential long-term effect.**

**By making chiefly office a state appointment, the Act transformed what a chief was:**

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| Authority from lineage, and from followers who could leave | **authority from the state, which could depose you** |
| Accountable downward, in part | **accountable upward** |
| Could resist colonial demands | **could be replaced for resisting** |
| Paid by tribute | **paid a stipend** |

**So the Act created a class of officials wearing the clothes of traditional authority**, and it is the origin of the deepest division in twentieth-century African politics: **between chiefs who worked within the system and the political organisations that regarded them as instruments of it.**

**That division runs through everything after.** The Bantu Authorities Act of 1951 and the homelands of stage 5 are built on it; **the 1950s rural revolts — Witzieshoek, Sekhukhuneland, Pondoland — were substantially revolts against state-appointed chiefs**; and the position of traditional leaders in the 1996 settlement, and the Traditional Leadership legislation since, are still arguing about it. **Stage 8's lesson on traditional authority picks it up directly.**

**And a complication, because the picture is not simply collaboration.** Some chiefs used the position to protect their people and obstruct the state; some were deposed for it; **and Albert Luthuli, ANC president from 1952, was a chief deposed for his politics.** The institution was compromised and the individuals varied, and treating "the chiefs" as a single political category is the error the ANC itself made at times and corrected.

**Practice.** Find the Act's Supreme Chief provision and compare it with Shepstone's Natal system from stage 3. Then find section 29 and work out what political statement could not be charged under it. Then look up one 1950s rural revolt and establish what the grievance was.
The poor white problem:
Three hundred thousand destitute white South Africans, a study funded from New York, and the most successful anti-poverty programme in the country's history.

**The problem. By the 1920s a large part of the white population was very poor.**

**How it happened:**

| Cause | |
| --- | --- |
| **Land subdivision** | from stage 3's loan-farm inheritance system: the frontier ran out, and farms were divided until they could not support a family |
| **The South African War** | **farms destroyed, stock killed, and the £3 million from Vereeniging far short of the damage** |
| **Drought and stock disease** | rinderpest in the 1890s, East Coast fever, drought cycles |
| **Commercialisation of agriculture** | mechanising farms needed capital, and capital went to the already-solvent |
| **Bywoners displaced** | white tenant farmers on others' land, pushed off as agriculture commercialised |
| **No skills for industry** | a population raised on farms, with limited schooling, arriving in cities |

**The *bywoner* is the key figure.** A white tenant or sharecropper on another white man's farm — **and when commercial farming arrived, the bywoner was displaced exactly as the African sharecropper was by the 1913 Act.** The difference was that the bywoner could vote.

**The Carnegie Commission, 1932** — and its origin is worth noting. **The study was funded by the Carnegie Corporation of New York**, which had conducted similar work on poor whites in the American South. Five volumes, published in 1932.

**Its findings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Roughly 300,000 "very poor" whites** | out of a white population of about 1.8 million — **about one in six** |
| **Concentrated among Afrikaners** | rural, and newly urban |
| **Causes** | the Commission emphasised economic and environmental factors, education and health, rather than character |
| **Recommendations** | education, health services, agricultural support, and state intervention in employment |

**The Commission's framing mattered as much as its findings.** It treated white poverty as a **structural** problem requiring state action, not as individual failure — **and that framing legitimised the interventions of the previous lesson** and of the twenty years after.

**What was done, which is the part to weigh:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The civilised labour policy** | from the last lesson: state employment, at protected wages |
| **The Railways** | the single largest absorber of poor whites |
| **ISCOR and the parastatals** | industrial employment, created by the state |
| **Compulsory free education** for whites | and schools built |
| **Agricultural support** | subsidies, marketing boards, credit, debt relief |
| **Housing** | state housing schemes |
| **Health services** | and the Commission's recommendations acted on |
| **The Afrikaner economic movement** | the next lesson |

**And it worked.** Within a generation white poverty in South Africa was largely eliminated. **By the 1960s the Afrikaner population had moved from being disproportionately poor and rural to being substantially urban, employed, educated and middle-class** — one of the fastest social transformations of a population in the twentieth century.

**The two things to hold about that, simultaneously.**

**First: it demonstrates that the state could do it.** Mass poverty in a population of two million was ended within thirty years by deliberate policy — education, employment, housing, health, and protected wages. **The programme is evidence against any claim that poverty of that scale is intractable.**

**Second: it was for one group, and it was substantially funded by the exclusion of another.** The jobs came from displacing African workers; the protected wages were possible because African wages were suppressed; the agricultural subsidies went to farms worked by labour with no rights. **The programme's success and its racial basis are the same fact.**

**This is the sharpest instance of this stage's pattern**, and it is why the period matters so much for the present. **Stage 9's arguments about redistribution, about a developmental state, about BEE and about what the state can accomplish all have this as their precedent** — and both sides cite it. One says: *look what a determined state did for a poor population in thirty years.* The other says: *look who paid for it.*

**And a detail that closes the loop.** In **1984 the Second Carnegie Inquiry into Poverty and Development in Southern Africa** reported, directed by **Francis Wilson** at the University of Cape Town — **the same funder, fifty-two years later, studying black poverty.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The First Carnegie Commission, 1932** | white poverty. **Acted on, comprehensively** |
| **The Second Carnegie Inquiry, 1984** | **black poverty**, on a vastly larger scale. Published under apartheid, and its recommendations not acted on by that state |

**The symmetry is exact and it was intended by the organisers.** Reading the two reports beside each other is the single most efficient way to understand what this stage is about — **the same methodology, the same funder, the same country, two populations, and two entirely different political responses.**

**Practice.** Find the Carnegie Commission's 1932 estimate of poor whites as a share of the white population. Then list the interventions that followed and the decades over which white poverty fell. Then find the Second Carnegie Inquiry of 1984 and compare its framing with the first's. Then decide what you think the 1932–60 experience proves about what a state can do, and what it proves about who pays.
Afrikaner nationalism: the institutions:
How a poor, defeated, rural population captured a state in forty-six years — by building institutions, deliberately, and recording that they were doing it.

**The starting point, 1902.** Afrikaners were a defeated people: two republics destroyed, 28,000 dead in camps, farms burned, a third of the population destitute, and governed in English.

**The end point, 1948.** An Afrikaner nationalist party in government, which it held for forty-six years.

**That did not happen by sentiment.** It happened through institutions, and the institutions are nameable.

**1. Culture and language.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The CNO schools**, from 1903 | stage 3: the schools fight that made language the identity's core |
| **Afrikaans made official, 1925** | from Dutch |
| **The Afrikaans Bible, 1933** | **the single most important cultural event** — a language with a scripture is a language with standing |
| **The FAK, 1929** | ***Federasie van Afrikaanse Kultuurvereniginge*** — the umbrella for cultural organisations, festivals, music, language |
| **The 1938 centenary** | stage 3: the ox-wagon trek, the crowds, and the national mobilisation |
| **The Voortrekker Monument, 1949** | |

**The Bible in 1933 deserves its weight.** Until then, Afrikaans was the spoken language and Dutch the language of religion. **Translating the Bible made Afrikaans a language of ultimate seriousness** — and it was carried out by the churches, which is the next item.

**2. The churches.** The three Afrikaans Reformed churches — the NGK and its sisters — provided:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A national organisation** | in every town and district |
| **A moral framework** | and from the 1930s a theological justification for segregation |
| **Welfare** | which reached the poor whites directly |
| **Legitimacy** | **the policy could be presented as a calling, not an interest** |

**Hofmeyr's church history in your library is the source for this**, and the theological argument — the diversity of nations as divinely ordained, the Tower of Babel read as authority for separation — is worth reading in the original, because it was taken seriously by serious people and it was formally repudiated by the NGK only in the 1980s and after.

**3. The Broederbond.** Founded **1918**, secret from **1921**: an invitation-only network of Afrikaner men — teachers, ministers, civil servants, academics, farmers, businessmen.

| What it did | |
| --- | --- |
| **Coordinated** | across the cultural, economic, religious and political organisations |
| **Placed people** | in education, the civil service, the parastatals |
| **Initiated** | the FAK, the economic congress, the Reddingsdaadbond |
| **Deliberated policy** | **apartheid's specifics were worked out substantially in its circles** |
| **Membership** | **included National Party leaders from Strijdom onward**, and a large part of the senior civil service |

**Its secrecy is the reason it is a conspiracy theory and a documented fact at once.** Its existence and membership were exposed repeatedly — by the *Sunday Times* in 1963–64 and comprehensively by Wilkins and Strydom's *The Super-Afrikaners* in 1978, which published a membership list. **So the organisation was real, its influence was real, and the accounts of its omnipotence were overdrawn.** Stage 1's method applies: a secret network's power is systematically hard to measure and therefore systematically over- and under-estimated.

**4. Capital — ***volkskapitalisme***.** The explicit project of building Afrikaner-owned business.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sanlam and Santam, 1918** | insurance — **the first large Afrikaner financial institutions** |
| **Volkskas, 1934** | a bank |
| **The 1939 *Ekonomiese Volkskongres*** | Bloemfontein. **A national congress on the economic position of the Afrikaner** |
| **Federale Volksbeleggings, 1940** | an investment company, out of the congress |
| **The Reddingsdaadbond, 1939** | **a mass savings and mutual-aid movement** — small contributions from many, channelled into Afrikaner enterprise |
| **Rembrandt, 1948** | Anton Rupert's tobacco company, from the same movement |

**The Reddingsdaadbond — "rescue action league" — is the mechanism to understand.** A poor population cannot accumulate capital individually. **Pooling small savings through an organisation with cultural authority could.** It is a mutual-aid and development-finance movement, built on ethnic solidarity, and it worked.

**5. Labour.** Afrikaner trade unions and the capture of existing ones — the Mineworkers' Union above all, and the *Blankewerkersbeskermingsbond*. **The 1922 rising's constituency, organised nationally.**

**6. The party.** The National Party from 1914, the Purified National Party from 1934, the Reunited National Party from 1940 — and the 1948 victory.

**Now the thing to take from all of this, which is why it is a lesson rather than a list.**

**Afrikaner nationalism is the best-documented case available of a national identity being deliberately constructed.** Not discovered — **constructed**, by identifiable organisations, with budgets, over four decades, with the intention stated in their own minutes.

| What was built | |
| --- | --- |
| **A language** | standardised, given a Bible, made official |
| **A history** | stage 3's Trek, made into a founding by Preller and the centenary |
| **A theology** | which the churches later repudiated |
| **A capital base** | by pooled savings |
| **A political vehicle** | and a civil service to staff |
| **A sense of a *volk*** | with a destiny and a grievance |

**And the grievance was real**, which is the part that makes it work and the part that critics of nationalism most often miss. **The camps happened. The anglicisation happened. The poverty happened.** A constructed identity built on real injuries is far more powerful than one built on invention, and Giliomee is the historian to read on how it felt from inside.

**The analytical payoff for the rest of this curriculum.** Every claim you will meet about any South African identity — African, Afrikaner, Zulu, Coloured, "the nation" — **can be examined the same way: who built this, when, with what institutions, and against what.** The question is not whether an identity is "real"; it is how it was made and what it was made for. **Stage 10's lesson on the ANC as a movement applies exactly this method to the other side.**

**Practice.** List the six institutional categories and name one organisation in each. Then find the Reddingsdaadbond's method and work out how pooled small savings become industrial capital. Then read one Afrikaans theological argument for separation from the 1930s or 1940s, and then find the NGK's later repudiation of it. Then apply the six categories to another South African identity and see what you can fill in.
The ICU, and the first mass movement:
A union that reached a hundred thousand members in the 1920s, mostly in the countryside, and collapsed in a decade — and what both facts teach.

**The ICU — the Industrial and Commercial Workers' Union**, founded in **Cape Town in January 1919** by **Clements Kadalie**, a teacher from Nyasaland.

**What made it unprecedented.** Everything before it — the organisations of stage 3, the SANNC — was an elite body of the mission-educated, working by petition. **The ICU was a mass organisation with dues-paying members in the tens of thousands, and its reach was rural.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Founded** | among Cape Town dock workers; the 1919 dock strike was its launch |
| **Peak** | **mid-1920s. Membership claims ran to 100,000 and higher** — the records are unreliable and the real figure was probably around 100,000 |
| **Reach** | **Natal, the Orange Free State, the Transvaal countryside** — farm workers, labour tenants, sharecroppers |
| **Press** | ***The Workers' Herald*** |
| **Politics** | a mixture of trade unionism, Garveyism, Christian millenarianism and land grievance |

**The rural reach is the extraordinary part and it is what distinguishes the ICU from everything before and most things after.** Farm workers and labour tenants on white farms — **the people the 1913 Act had evicted and reduced** — joined in large numbers. **In the Free State and Natal countryside the ICU was, for a few years, a genuine mass movement of the rural dispossessed.**

**And that is why it was so dangerous to the state and so attractive to its members.** From the 1913 Act lesson: the Free State clause had destroyed sharecropping and made labour tenants of people who had been partners. **The ICU arrived in that countryside with a promise.**

**The promise, and this is central to understanding it: the ICU was not only a union.** Its meetings were revivalist; its message included the expectation that the land would be returned; **and in places members understood joining as participation in a coming deliverance.** Historians have documented farm workers believing that an ICU card would restore their land, and organisers who encouraged it.

**Which is a strength and the seed of the collapse.** A movement that promises deliverance can mobilise enormously and cannot deliver.

**Why it collapsed, in five causes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No shop-floor base** | **it organised where there was no bargaining structure.** A farm worker's union has no plant, no negotiating counterpart, and no strike that does not end in eviction |
| **No financial discipline** | dues were collected and not accounted for; the organisation had no structure to spend them through |
| **State and farmer repression** | section 29 of the 1927 Act from two lessons ago, evictions, prosecutions, violence |
| **Factionalism** | **the 1927–28 split**, with **A. W. G. Champion** taking the Natal membership as the **ICU yase Natal** |
| **The legal exclusion** | from the Pact lesson: **Africans were excluded from the definition of "employee" in the 1924 Industrial Conciliation Act**, so the ICU could not register, could not bargain lawfully, and its strikes were criminal |

**That last cause is the structural one and it deserves the weight.** The ICU was trying to be a trade union in a country where the law said the people it organised were not employees. **It was not out-competed; it was legislated out of existence as a union** — and no African union had a legal existence until 1979.

**And a complication worth noting: Kadalie brought in a British adviser, William Ballinger, in 1928, to impose administrative order.** The attempt to turn a movement into an orderly union accelerated the splits rather than saving it. **Whether the ICU could have been saved by better administration is argued, and the structural answer above suggests it could not.**

**What the ICU established, and this is why it is a lesson:**

| Lesson | Taken by |
| --- | --- |
| **African workers would join a mass organisation in enormous numbers** | **everyone afterwards.** The question was never whether support existed |
| **Rural organisation is possible and extremely hard to sustain** | the ANC's rural weakness for decades is the counter-evidence |
| **A movement needs a structure that can survive its founder** | the ANC's eventual answer: branches, constitutions, elected leadership |
| **Without legal standing, industrial action means eviction and prosecution** | **which is why the 1979 Wiehahn reforms changed everything** — stage 5 |
| **Promising deliverance mobilises and then discredits** | and the charge recurs |

**Its place in the lineage.** The ICU's collapse left a vacuum that the ANC did not fill for twenty years — **the ANC of the 1930s was smaller and weaker than the ICU had been at its peak.** The organisational tradition the ICU began was taken up by:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Communist Party's union work** | the next lesson, and the 1940s unions |
| **The Council of Non-European Trade Unions**, 1941 | which organised the wartime manufacturing workforce |
| **The African Mineworkers' Union**, 1941 | and the 1946 strike, four lessons from here |
| **SACTU, 1955** | and then the unions of the 1970s and 1980s |

**Kadalie himself** ended his career in East London, running a much smaller organisation, and died in 1951. **The movement he built is the first mass political organisation in South African history, and it lasted about ten years.**

**Practice.** Find the ICU's membership claims and what historians think the real figure was. Then work out why a farm workers' union in 1925 had no available industrial action. Then find the 1924 definition of "employee" again and note that the ICU's whole membership was outside it. Then list the five causes of collapse and mark which were internal and which were imposed.
The Communist Party and the Native Repub:
A small party with disproportionate influence, the 1928 directive that split it, and the reason it mattered for the next sixty years.

**The party. The Communist Party of South Africa, founded 30 July 1921** in Cape Town, from the International Socialist League and other groups.

**Its first years, and the problem in them.** The CPSA was initially **white-dominated and economistic**: it understood South Africa as a capitalist society with a working class, and it took the organised working class to be the white one, because that was the one with unions.

**Hence 1922.** From the Rand Revolt lesson: the party supported the white miners' strike, some members fought in the commandos, and the slogan about a white South Africa flew over a strike the party backed. **The party's own later assessment of 1922 is critical, and it had to be.**

**Then 1928, and the directive.** The Comintern instructed the CPSA to adopt the **"Native Republic" thesis**:

> **An independent native South African republic as a stage towards a workers' and peasants' republic, with full protection and equal rights for all national minorities.**

**What it claimed, in three moves:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. South Africa's primary contradiction is national, not simply class** | **the African majority is a colonised nation**, and its liberation is the first task |
| **2. So the struggle has two stages** | **national liberation first**, then socialism |
| **3. Whites are a "national minority"** | with rights protected in the republic to come |

**The consequences inside the party were severe.** The thesis was resisted by much of the existing leadership — **Sidney Bunting** among them, who argued it was imposed from Moscow and misread the country — and the resulting conflict produced expulsions, including Bunting's in 1931, and the party nearly collapsed through the 1930s.

**And then the thesis won, and it won for the next sixty years.** Because:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It was analytically right about the country** | a theory that treated the African majority as incidental could not explain South Africa |
| **It made alliance with African nationalism possible** | **a communist party that puts national liberation first can work with the ANC** |
| **Africanisation of the party followed** | **Moses Kotane**, general secretary from 1939, had argued in his 1934 "Cradock letter" for exactly that — an Africanised party rooted in local conditions |

**The two-stage theory is the single most important idea in the South African left**, and its consequences run to the present:

| Where it leads | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Congress Alliance** | ANC, SAIC, SACTU, the Coloured People's Congress and the Congress of Democrats — stage 5 |
| **The SACP–ANC relationship** | the party dissolved itself in 1950 ahead of the Suppression of Communism Act and **re-formed underground as the SACP in 1953**, working inside the ANC |
| **The National Democratic Revolution** | **the ANC's own analytical framework**, from stage 1's lesson on reading party documents — it is this thesis, in the ANC's vocabulary |
| **The post-1994 argument** | **"the NDR's first stage is complete; when does the second begin?"** — which is a live argument inside the ANC alliance, in stage 12 |

**So reading a current ANC discussion document and finding "the national democratic revolution", "the motive forces" and "the balance of forces" is reading the 1928 thesis's descendants.** That is why stage 1 said the vocabulary is a coherent framework rather than jargon.

**The party's practical importance, which exceeded its size.** It never had many members. It had:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Organisers** | in the unions the ICU had failed to sustain — **CNETU from 1941, the African Mineworkers' Union** |
| **A non-racial membership** | **the only political organisation in the country with white, African, Coloured and Indian members on equal terms**, which mattered enormously for who could do what |
| **Training and theory** | and later, access to the Soviet bloc |
| **Individuals** | Kotane, J. B. Marks, Bram Fischer, Ruth First, Joe Slovo, Yusuf Dadoo, Albert Nzula |
| **Discipline** | which is the quality the ICU lacked and the ANC of the 1930s lacked |

**And its non-racial character is the historically decisive thing.** In a country where every other organisation was racially defined by law or by choice, **the CPSA was the place where people of different races did politics together** — which is why so much of the Congress Alliance's cross-racial machinery was built by communists, and why the National Party could present the whole opposition as a communist front with a grain of plausibility.

**Which is the complication, and this curriculum's posture requires it.** Three honest difficulties:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Comintern connection was real** | the 1928 thesis was directed from Moscow, and the party followed Soviet lines through the purges, the Nazi–Soviet pact and after |
| **Soviet support for the liberation struggle was real** | training, arms and funding, which the ANC needed and the West did not provide |
| **The party's internal history includes expulsions and silences** | which its own later accounts address unevenly |

**And the 1990s question that follows: how much did the alliance's socialist commitments survive the settlement?** That is the third big disagreement from stage 1 — victory or compromise — and the SACP's own answer has shifted. **Stage 6 and stage 12 take it up.**

**Practice.** Read the 1928 Native Republic thesis in its original wording and identify the two stages. Then read Kotane's 1934 Cradock letter. Then find a recent ANC discussion document and count how many of the thesis's terms appear in it. Then write down what the two-stage theory implies about when economic transformation should happen, and ask whether that is what happened.
Women's politics, and the anti-pass camp:
Thirty years before the campaigns everybody knows, women ran the first successful civil disobedience in South African history — and then were refused membership of the organisation they supported.

**1913, the Orange Free State.** The provincial authorities required African women in towns to carry residential passes — a requirement not imposed on women elsewhere.

**The campaign:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Who** | African and Coloured women in Bloemfontein, Winburg, Jagersfontein and other Free State towns |
| **Leaders included** | **Charlotte Maxeke**, and local women's organisations |
| **The method** | **refusal to carry passes, deputations, and mass marches to municipal offices** |
| **The scale** | hundreds marched; **many went to prison rather than pay fines** |
| **The result** | **the pass requirement for women in the Free State was suspended** |

**It worked.** That is the thing to notice. **The first sustained civil disobedience campaign in South African history was run by women in 1913 and it achieved its objective** — and it is far less well known than the campaigns of 1952 and 1956.

**Charlotte Maxeke**, who deserves to be known: **the first black South African woman to earn a university degree** — Wilberforce University, Ohio, 1901 — a founder of the **Bantu Women's League in 1918**, and a presence in African politics for forty years. **She is the figure the 1913 campaign is built around**, and the ANC Women's League traces itself to her league.

**And then the thing that is hard to read.** The SANNC, founded in 1912, **did not admit women as full members.** Women could be "auxiliary" members, supporting the organisation, without voting rights within it.

**Full membership came in 1943.** Thirty-one years.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1912** | SANNC founded. **Women not full members** |
| **1918** | **the Bantu Women's League**, founded because the Congress had no place for them |
| **1931** | Maxeke continues organising; the League's work goes on outside the Congress's structures |
| **1943** | **women admitted as full members of the ANC** |
| **1948** | **the ANC Women's League** formally established |
| **1954** | **FEDSAW** — the Federation of South African Women — founded, non-racial |
| **1955** | **the Women's Charter** |
| **9 August 1956** | **20,000 women march on the Union Buildings** against the extension of passes to women. **Now a public holiday** |
| **1950s–60s** | **rural women's revolts**, notably against cattle dipping and Bantu Authorities |

**The 1956 march is the one everybody knows, and the 1913 campaign is its direct ancestor** — the same grievance, in the same country, forty-three years apart, because the 1952 Act had extended passes to women nationally. **The 1913 suspension had been a local victory on a national trend.**

**Now the other 1930 fact, and it is a cold one.**

**The Women's Enfranchisement Act of 1930 gave the vote to white women only.**

**Work out what that does.** From stage 3's franchise lesson, African and Coloured voters were about 15% of the Cape electorate.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1930** | **white women enfranchised — the white electorate roughly doubles** |
| **1931** | **the property and literacy qualification removed for white men in the Cape** — so poor whites who had not qualified now voted |
| **The arithmetic** | **the Cape's black voters' share of the electorate was cut roughly in half** |
| **1936** | **and then they were removed from the common roll entirely** |

**So the extension of the franchise to white women was simultaneously a genuine advance for them and an instrument of dilution.** It was understood as such at the time: **the measure's effect on the Cape's non-racial franchise was discussed in the debates.**

**That is worth sitting with, because it is the kind of fact that fits no simple narrative.** A real expansion of democratic rights, for one group, used to reduce another's — and the white women's suffrage movement in South Africa had, for decades before, generally pressed for the vote on the existing qualified basis, which would have enfranchised black women too. **The measure that passed did not.**

**The rural women's revolts, which are the most under-taught resistance in South African history.** Through the 1940s and 1950s, in the reserves:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Against cattle dipping and culling** | which killed stock and was enforced by state-appointed chiefs |
| **Against Bantu Authorities** | the chiefs of the 1927 Act |
| **Against passes for women** | |
| **Natal, 1959** | the **beer-hall protests** — women destroying municipal beer halls, from the 1923 Act's Native Revenue Account |
| **Pondoland, 1960** | the **Mpondo revolt**, suppressed with killings and a state of emergency |

**The beer-hall protests connect directly to stage 4's third lesson.** The 1923 Act required locations to be financed from African rents and **municipal beer sales**. **So women whose husbands' wages were going into a state monopoly on liquor attacked the monopoly** — and it was the most widespread rural and township women's action of the period.

**Why women's politics was separate, and then was not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The grievances were partly different** | passes for women, beer halls, cattle, children's schooling, food prices |
| **The organisations excluded them** | until 1943 |
| **The methods were often more confrontational** | because the constitutional routes were male and elite |
| **FEDSAW in 1954 brought it together** | non-racial, with the Women's Charter |
| **And the Charter's demands** | went beyond the Freedom Charter's on the position of women |

**The Women's Charter of 1954 is worth reading beside the Freedom Charter of 1955.** It is more explicit about the household, about women's legal status, and about the double burden — **and the extent to which the Freedom Charter absorbed it is a real question**, as is the extent to which the 1996 Constitution did. **Stage 7's equality lesson and stage 12 both return to it.**

**Practice.** Read about the 1913 Free State anti-pass campaign and note what it achieved. Then look up the Women's Enfranchisement Act of 1930 and work out its effect on the Cape electorate's composition. Then read the Women's Charter of 1954 and the Freedom Charter of 1955 side by side, and list what the first demands that the second does not.
Fusion, 1934:
The two men who fought each other for twenty years merging their parties — and why that merger was the precondition for removing the African franchise.

**The sequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1929** | **the "black manifesto" election.** Hertzog's National Party campaigns on the danger of African political rights and wins a majority |
| **1929–33** | **the Depression.** Commodity prices collapse; farm debt becomes unpayable |
| **1931–32** | **South Africa stays on the gold standard** after Britain leaves it, which makes its exports dearer and deepens the slump |
| **December 1932** | **the gold standard abandoned**, after a former judge, Tielman Roos, resigned from the bench to campaign against it and threatened to split the government |
| **1933** | Hertzog and Smuts form a coalition |
| **1934** | **Fusion** — the National Party and the South African Party merge into the **United South African National Party**, the **United Party** |
| **1934** | **D. F. Malan leads nineteen MPs out**, forming the ***Gesuiwerde* — Purified — National Party** |

**Why they fused.** The economic crisis, and the exhaustion of the quarrel. **Hertzog had got what he most wanted** — Afrikaans official, South African nationality defined, the Statute of Westminster confirming dominion sovereignty in 1931, and the republican question deferred. **Smuts wanted the British connection preserved, which Fusion did.** The two leaders' remaining differences had become manageable.

**And Malan's breakaway is the event that matters most.** The Purified National Party took the irreconcilable tradition — stage 3's *bittereinders*, the republicans, the Broederbond's political wing — out of the governing coalition and into opposition.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fusion created** | **a broad centre party of English and Afrikaans whites**, governing with a large majority |
| **And left outside it** | **a purely Afrikaner nationalist party**, with the cultural and economic institutions of the last lesson behind it |
| **Which in 1948** | **won** |

**So Fusion is the moment the National Party became what it would be in 1948** — not a coalition of Afrikaner interests with others, but the vehicle of a nationalism with its own institutions, free of the compromises of office.

**Now the thing this lesson exists to establish, and it is a point about constitutional mechanics.**

**From stage 3: the Cape's non-racial franchise was entrenched in the South Africa Act.** It could be altered only by **a two-thirds majority of both Houses sitting together.**

**No single party could assemble that.** Hertzog had tried to remove the African franchise repeatedly through the 1920s — the "Hertzog bills" were introduced and reintroduced from 1926 — **and he could never get two-thirds.**

**Fusion gave him two-thirds.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1926–33** | Hertzog's bills fail for want of a two-thirds majority |
| **1934** | **Fusion** |
| **1936** | **the Representation of Natives Act passes at a joint sitting, 169 votes to 11** |

**Read that vote.** One hundred and sixty-nine to eleven. **The removal of the African franchise from the Cape common roll was carried by the merged centre party of English and Afrikaans South Africa, not by the National Party** — which was in opposition, and voted for it too.

**That is the single most important fact in this stage for the first big disagreement from stage 1.** The measure which, more than any other, defined African political exclusion for the next fifty-eight years **was passed in 1936, by a government of Hertzog and Smuts, twelve years before the National Party took power** — and with only eleven dissenting votes in a joint sitting of both Houses.

**The eleven are worth knowing**, because they are the entire parliamentary opposition to it: **a small group of liberals, including Jan Hofmeyr**, Smuts's own deputy, who broke with his government on this and whose reputation rests substantially on it.

**Eleven out of one hundred and eighty.** The entrenchment from stage 3 had held for twenty-six years, and it fell the moment a government existed that could assemble the numbers. **Which is the lesson stage 3 drew: a procedural safeguard is only as strong as the legislature's unwillingness to meet it.**

**And it tells you what the 1948 election was and was not about.** It was not about whether Africans should vote — **that had been settled in 1936 by both of the parties contesting 1948.** The next lessons establish what it actually was about.

**Practice.** Find the Hertzog bills of the 1920s and the reason they failed. Then find the 1936 joint sitting vote and the names of the eleven. Then work out what Fusion made possible that neither party alone could do. Then write down what this does to the claim that apartheid began in 1948.
The 1936 Acts: the franchise:
The removal of the African vote, what replaced it, and the ten years in which the replacement was shown to be worthless.

**The Representation of Natives Act 12 of 1936.** What it did:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African voters in the Cape removed from the common roll** | the franchise of stage 3's lesson, ended |
| **Placed on a separate communal roll** | electing **three white members** of the House of Assembly for the Cape |
| **Four white senators** | elected indirectly by Africans across the country |
| **The Natives Representative Council** | created — **and it is the part to understand** |

**So Africans did not lose the vote entirely in 1936.** They lost the **common roll** — the vote that counted in the same constituencies as everyone else's, where a candidate had to seek it. **What replaced it was separate representation by white people, in numbers fixed by statute, that could never affect an outcome.**

**Three MPs out of 150, and they could not be African.** The colour bar on parliamentary membership from stage 3's Union lesson still stood.

**The Natives Representative Council**, which deserves its own treatment because its fate is the lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Composition** | **22 members** — 12 elected by Africans, 4 nominated, 6 white officials |
| **Chaired by** | the Secretary for Native Affairs |
| **Powers** | **none. Purely advisory** |
| **Could** | debate, pass resolutions, make recommendations |
| **Could not** | legislate, veto, compel, or require an answer |

**Why African leaders participated anyway.** It was the only national forum available, it had elected members, and the argument for using it was the argument that had governed African politics since stage 3: **work the institutions you are given, and build a record.**

**The men who served on it were the senior African political figures of the period** — including ANC leaders — and their participation was contested within African politics from the start. **The Youth League of 1944 regarded it as collaboration; the All African Convention's tradition rejected it on principle.**

**And then 1946 settled it.** From the mineworkers' strike lesson, three lessons from here: when the 1946 African Mineworkers' Strike was broken by police, **the Council adjourned in protest.**

**The remark that killed it** was made by a Council member, Paul Mosaka:

> **We have been talking to a toy telephone.**

**The Council never functioned effectively again, and it was abolished in 1951.** Ten years of advisory participation, ending with its members concluding in public that the body had never been connected to anything.

**That conclusion is the hinge of twentieth-century African politics.** It is why:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The 1949 Programme of Action** | adopted boycott, strike and civil disobedience |
| **The 1952 Defiance Campaign** | happened |
| **The ANC's method changed** | from deputation to mass action, after forty years |

**So the Natives Representative Council is the most consequential failed institution in South African history**, and it failed in a specific way worth naming: **it was not ignored, it was consulted.** Its members were received, their resolutions were read, and nothing followed. **A participation mechanism with no power is more corrosive of faith in a system than exclusion is**, because it produces evidence.

**Which is a general point worth carrying to stage 8 and stage 12.** When you meet a consultative body, a council, a forum or an advisory panel, the question is not whether it exists or who is on it. **It is whether anything it says can oblige anybody to do anything.** The Council could not, and its members eventually said so in those words.

**The fate of the separate representation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1936–1960** | three white MPs for African voters in the Cape |
| **The MPs themselves** | included **Margaret Ballinger** and **Helen Joseph's contemporaries**; they were a real if tiny liberal presence, and they used the platform |
| **1959, Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act** | **the three seats abolished**, on the argument that Africans would be represented in their homelands instead |
| **1960** | **the last African representation in the South African Parliament ends** |

**And Margaret Ballinger is worth naming**: elected on the African roll in 1937, she served until 1960, and she and the other native representatives were among the very few voices in Parliament consistently opposing segregation legislation. **Their position was itself contested — whether to occupy a token seat at all — and they argued it both ways over twenty-four years.**

**The Coloured franchise, for completeness and because the sequence differs.** Coloured voters in the Cape remained on the common roll in 1936. **They were removed in the 1950s** — the Separate Representation of Voters Act of 1951, upheld only after the constitutional crisis of stage 5, in which the government enlarged the Senate and reconstituted the Appellate Division to get the two-thirds majority.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African common roll vote** | **removed 1936**, by Fusion, with the NP voting for it |
| **Coloured common roll vote** | **removed 1956**, by the National Party, after four years of constitutional conflict |

**Twenty years apart, by two different governments, by two different methods** — and both ending in the same place.

**Practice.** Read the 1936 Act's provisions on the separate roll and count the seats against the size of the Assembly. Then find Mosaka's "toy telephone" remark in its context. Then work out what distinguishes a consultative body with power from one without, and keep the test for stage 8. Then compare how the African and Coloured franchises were removed, and what each required.
The 1936 Acts: the land:
Where the 13% comes from, the Act that promised it, and the promise that was never kept.

**The Native Trust and Land Act 18 of 1936**, passed in the same session as the franchise Act and traded against it.

**The trade is the thing to understand.** Hertzog's position, held since the 1920s, was that **Africans should lose political rights in the common system and receive more land in exchange.** The two 1936 Acts are the two halves of that bargain:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Representation of Natives Act** | **takes the vote** |
| **The Native Trust and Land Act** | **promises the land** |

**What the land Act provided:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The South African Native Trust** | a state body **to buy land for African occupation** |
| **"Released areas"** | additional land, defined by schedule, **in which African purchase was permitted** |
| **The target** | the 1913 scheduled areas of about 7.3% **plus released areas, to reach roughly 13.6%** |
| **Chapter IV** | **tightened labour tenancy and squatting on white farms** — limits on how many African families a farm could carry |

**So the famous figure is from 1936, not 1913.** The 1913 Act gave about 7%; **the 1936 Act set a target of about 13%** — for a population that was then roughly two-thirds of the country's people.

**And the target was not met.** Land acquisition by the Trust proceeded slowly and incompletely, obstructed by price, by white farmers' resistance to sales, by the state's unwillingness to pay, and then by the arrival of a government with a different plan. **By the end of apartheid the actual area was roughly 13% including the homelands — approaching the target on paper and never delivering the quality or the usability it implied.**

**The second half of the Act, which is the half that hurt immediately: Chapter IV.**

**From the 1913 lesson: the Free State clause had destroyed sharecropping there.** Chapter IV extended and tightened the attack on **labour tenancy** nationally:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Limits on the number of African families per white farm** | |
| **Registration and licensing** of labour tenants | |
| **Power to remove "surplus" families** | |
| **Enforcement that increased over the following decades** | |

**The effect was another wave of evictions**, and it continued into the 1960s. **The destruction of African farming as an independent activity, begun in 1913, was completed by the 1936 Act and the removals that followed it.**

**The numbers, as far as they are established.** Over the whole period of removals — 1913 to the 1980s — **the figure usually given for forced removals is around 3.5 million people.** The bulk of that is after 1960 and belongs to stage 5, and the legal machinery is 1913, 1927 and 1936.

**Why the land promise was always going to fail, and this is the analytical point.**

**The arithmetic does not work, and it was known not to work.** From stage 3's Tomlinson reference and the agricultural evidence of the period:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **13% of the land** | for about two-thirds of the population |
| **And the land itself** | **the worst of it** — the scheduled areas were where conquest had stopped, which is to say the least desirable |
| **Without capital, extension services, irrigation or markets** | all of which went to white agriculture |
| **With the adult men absent** | eleven months a year, from stage 3's migrant system |

**So even full delivery of the 1936 target could not have supported the population**, and the state's own commissions said so repeatedly — Tomlinson in 1955 most explicitly, which stage 5 covers.

**Which raises the question that stage 3's Wolpe lesson answers: if the reserves could not support the population, what were they for?**

| Answer | |
| --- | --- |
| **To subsidise wages** | the family subsists partly on the land, so the wage need not cover a household |
| **To hold the population** that the cities would not accept | the temporary sojourner doctrine of the 1923 Act |
| **To provide a political destination** | **so that Africans could be said to have rights somewhere else** — which is 1959 and 1970 |
| **Not to be viable** | **and the policy required that they not be**, because a self-sufficient reserve would not supply labour |

**The last row is the uncomfortable conclusion and the evidence supports it.** Reserve agriculture was not supported in any way that could have made it self-sufficient; **the labour supply depended on its inadequacy.** That is the functional account at its strongest, and it is why the reserves were maintained and underfunded simultaneously for sixty years.

**The modern tail, which makes this the stage's most live lesson.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1913 is the restitution cut-off** | from the first lesson of this stage |
| **The 13% figure** | is the baseline of every land redistribution target since 1994 |
| **The former homelands** | hold a large share of the rural population on communally administered land with **insecure individual tenure** — a direct inheritance |
| **Labour tenants' rights** | legislated for in 1996 and still substantially unresolved |
| **Section 25 of the Constitution** | stage 7, and the amendment argument of stage 12, is about this |

**And the figure arguments from stage 1's statistics lesson come back here.** *"Whites own 72% of farmland"* or *"black South Africans own 4% of land"* — **both have circulated, both have a denominator, and stage 9 does the arithmetic properly.** What this lesson gives you is where the baseline came from: **a schedule in a 1936 Act, implementing a bargain in which the vote was traded for land that was never fully transferred.**

**Practice.** Find the 1936 Act's released areas schedule and the target percentage. Then find out how much the Native Trust actually acquired. Then read Chapter IV's provisions on labour tenants and work out what they required of a family. Then write down the trade Hertzog proposed, and whether either half of it was delivered.
African politics between the wars:
Two decades in which the ANC nearly disappeared, the alternatives that arose, and the generation that changed the method.

**The ANC's condition, 1920s–30s: weak.** From the ICU lesson: the ANC of the 1930s was smaller and less influential than the ICU had been at its peak. Its presidents in the period:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **John Dube**, 1912–17 | |
| **Sefako Makgatho**, 1917–24 | |
| **Josiah Gumede**, 1927–30 | **visited the Soviet Union, returned advocating radical alliance, and was deposed for it** |
| **Pixley ka Isaka Seme**, 1930–37 | a founder, and the organisation declined further under him |
| **Zaccheus Mahabane** | |
| **Alfred Xuma**, 1940–49 | **the rebuilder** |

**Gumede's deposition in 1930 is the period's defining internal event.** He had attended the Comintern-linked congress in Brussels and the Soviet Union, and returned arguing for alliance with the Communist Party and for a more confrontational politics. **He was voted out by a conservative membership of chiefs and professionals.** The ANC chose moderation and nearly expired.

**What the organisation lacked:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Members** | a few thousand at best, in a population of millions |
| **Money** | it was repeatedly insolvent |
| **A structure** | branches existed intermittently |
| **A method** | deputation and resolution, which the 1914 and 1919 failures had discredited |
| **Youth** | the leadership was elderly and professional |

**The alternatives that arose, and this is the part usually left out.**

**1. The All African Convention, 1935.** Convened in Bloemfontein in December 1935 **to oppose the Hertzog bills** — the 1936 Acts of the last two lessons. Chaired by **D. D. T. Jabavu** — the son of stage 3's newspaper editor.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It was larger than the ANC** | and drew every organisation together |
| **It failed to stop the bills** | which passed in 1936 |
| **It then became a standing federal body** | and declined |

**2. The Non-European Unity Movement, 1943**, and the tradition it carried, which this curriculum's posture requires including because it is the road not taken.

| The NEUM's position | |
| --- | --- |
| **Non-collaboration** | **refuse to participate in any segregated institution** — no Natives Representative Council, no advisory boards, no separate rolls |
| **The boycott as principal weapon** | |
| **Unity of all the oppressed** | African, Coloured and Indian, against racial division of the struggle itself |
| **Suspicion of the Congress tradition** | as elite, as prone to collaboration, and later as nationalist rather than socialist |
| **Figures** | **I. B. Tabata**, **Ben Kies**, the Cape's teachers' organisations |

**It was strongest in the Cape, especially among Coloured teachers and intellectuals**, and its intellectual output was substantial. **It never built a mass base and is largely written out of the ANC-centred account** — which is the stage 1 problem of a victor's history, and it is worth knowing that a principled anti-collaborationist position existed, was argued at length, and lost.

**The argument between them is still live.** Participate in a flawed institution and build a record, or refuse and keep your hands clean? **The Natives Representative Council's collapse in 1946 was the NEUM's best vindication** — and the ANC's eventual mass mobilisation was the answer to the charge that it had achieved nothing.

**3. Xuma's reconstruction, 1940–49.** **Alfred Bitini Xuma**, a medical doctor educated in the United States and Scotland, became ANC president in 1940 and rebuilt the organisation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Paid off its debts** | and put its finances in order |
| **Revised the constitution**, 1943 | **and admitted women as full members** — the women's politics lesson |
| **Built branches** | |
| **The Doctors' Pact, 1947** | with Dadoo and Naicker — from stage 3's indenture lesson, the alliance with the Indian Congresses |
| ***Africans' Claims in South Africa*, 1943** | |

***Africans' Claims* is the document to read.** Drafted in response to the **Atlantic Charter** — Roosevelt and Churchill's 1941 declaration of war aims including self-determination — **it asks for the Charter's principles to be applied in South Africa**, and sets out a bill of rights: universal franchise, equality before the law, land, education, freedom of movement.

**It is the direct ancestor of the Freedom Charter of 1955 and, at a distance, of the 1996 Bill of Rights** — and its method is the old one: a reasoned claim, addressed to the authorities, invoking their own stated principles.

**It was ignored.** Smuts's government did not respond to it substantively.

**4. The Youth League, 1944**, and this is where the method changes.

**Founded by a generation in their twenties and thirties:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Anton Lembede** | first president, and the League's intellectual force. **Died in 1947, aged 33** |
| **A. P. Mda** | who succeeded him |
| **Walter Sisulu**, **Oliver Tambo**, **Nelson Mandela** | |
| **Jordan Ngubane** | |

**Their diagnosis:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Deputations have failed for thirty years** | and the evidence is the whole record of this stage |
| **The ANC is a club** | of professionals and chiefs, without members |
| **The people must be the force** | not the organisation's respectability |
