| **Africanism** | **Lembede's position: African self-reliance, African leadership, African nationalism** — initially suspicious of alliance with Indians, whites and communists |

**The Africanist element matters and it did not prevail.** Lembede's early position was that the struggle must be led by Africans alone; **Sisulu, Tambo and Mandela moved toward the alliance politics of the Congress Alliance**, and the Africanists who did not eventually broke away in 1959 to form the **Pan Africanist Congress**. **Stage 5 covers the split.**

**What the Youth League produced: the 1949 Programme of Action** — boycott, strike, civil disobedience, non-cooperation. **Adopted by the ANC's national conference in December 1949**, eighteen months after the National Party took power, **and it is the beginning of the mass politics of the 1950s.**

**So the sequence, which is the stage's conclusion on African politics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1912–1944** | **petition, deputation and resolution. Comprehensively unsuccessful** |
| **1946** | **the Natives Representative Council's collapse** closes the consultative route |
| **1949** | **the Programme of Action** opens the mass route |
| **1952 onward** | and the Defiance Campaign follows |

**Practice.** Read *Africans' Claims in South Africa* (1943) and note which of its demands appear in the 1996 Bill of Rights. Then read the Youth League's 1944 manifesto and note its criticism of the ANC. Then find the NEUM's argument for non-collaboration and state it as strongly as you can. Then decide which position the 1946 Council collapse vindicates.
The war, and the Afrikaner split:
The parliamentary vote that divided Afrikaner politics, the paramilitary movement that followed, and a future prime minister interned as a security threat.

**4 September 1939. The House of Assembly votes on whether to enter the war against Germany.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hertzog, the Prime Minister** | **argued for neutrality** |
| **Smuts, his deputy** | argued for war |
| **The vote** | **80 to 67 for war** |
| **Hertzog** | **resigned.** Smuts became Prime Minister |

**The Fusion government of 1934 broke on the question five years after it was formed.** And the vote cut across the merged party rather than between the old ones — which is why it was a crisis rather than a defeat.

**Why neutrality had support, and the case is not simply pro-German.**

| Argument | |
| --- | --- |
| **The dominion's sovereignty** | **the Statute of Westminster of 1931 had made South Africa's belligerency its own decision.** Neutrality was the exercise of a right only recently won |
| **The 1899–1902 memory** | **fighting for Britain, thirty-seven years after Britain's camps** |
| **The Smuts question** | from stage 3: he had led a commando into the Cape in 1901, and his opponents never stopped mentioning it |
| **Genuine republican principle** | the British connection was the thing the tradition existed to end |
| **And, for some, sympathy with Germany** | which existed and which the above does not reduce to |

**Both things are true and the proportions are argued about.** Giliomee is the serious guide to how the neutrality position was held by people who were not pro-Nazi; **and the Ossewabrandwag's trajectory shows how much of it was.**

**What followed, politically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **January 1940** | **Hertzog and Malan reunite** — the *Herenigde Nasionale Party*, the Reunited National Party |
| **Later 1940** | **Hertzog leaves it**, over Malan's republicanism and his refusal to guarantee English-speakers' rights. He retires |
| **So** | **Malan inherits the whole nationalist tradition**, and the Purified Party's line prevails |
| **1943 election** | **Smuts wins decisively** — the war was going well and the UP's majority increased |
| **1948** | and then he lost |

**Hertzog's exit is the end of an era and it is a small tragedy.** The man who had fought for Afrikaans, for the republican principle and for the 1936 Acts was pushed out of the party he had founded for insisting that English-speaking whites be guaranteed equal treatment. **The tradition had moved past him.**

**The Ossewabrandwag**, founded 1939 — "ox-wagon sentinel", named from the 1938 centenary:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | a mass Afrikaner cultural and **paramilitary** movement |
| **Membership claims** | up to several hundred thousand, which is unverifiable and probably inflated |
| **Leader from 1941** | **Hans van Rensburg**, an admirer of German National Socialism |
| **Its *Stormjaers*** | carried out **sabotage** — power lines, railways, post offices — and were involved in robberies and bombings |
| **The state's response** | **internment without trial** |

**And the detail that matters most: among those interned was B. J. Vorster**, held from 1942 to 1944 — **and Prime Minister of South Africa from 1966 to 1978.**

**That is worth stating plainly.** A future South African prime minister was interned by a South African government during the Second World War as a security threat on account of his membership of a pro-German paramilitary organisation. **It was used against him for the rest of his career, including by his own side's opponents.**

**Oswald Pirow's "New Order"** was the other wing: a former Hertzog cabinet minister advocating an explicitly national-socialist state for South Africa. **Malan's National Party kept its distance from both**, which is a politically important fact: **the party that took power in 1948 had positioned itself as the constitutional nationalist option against the paramilitary and the fascist wings.**

**Whether that distance was principle or calculation is argued.** Malan needed respectability and the Broederbond's political judgement was that power would come by election. **The paramilitary route was tried, failed, and discredited itself** — which left the party.

**What the war did to the country, which is the next lesson's subject but belongs noted here:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Industrial expansion** | **manufacturing overtook mining and agriculture** in share of output |
| **African urbanisation** | accelerated enormously, as the next lesson shows |
| **Influx control relaxed in practice** | because industry needed workers |
| **African political expectations raised** | **by the Atlantic Charter, by African service in the war, and by the rhetoric of fighting fascism** |
| **A hundred thousand and more black South Africans served** | in non-combatant roles, unarmed by policy, and came home to the pass laws |

**That last row is the 1902 pattern from stage 3 repeating.** Africans served in a war fought in the name of freedom and self-determination, were not armed, and returned to no change in their position. ***Africans' Claims in South Africa*, from the last lesson, is the document that said so at the time** — and it was written in 1943, while the war was still being fought.

**Practice.** Find the 4 September 1939 division list and note how the vote cut across the United Party. Then read the neutrality case as Hertzog made it, and separate the sovereignty argument from the sympathy argument. Then look up Vorster's internment and the dates, and note when he became Prime Minister. Then read *Africans' Claims* again with the war's rhetoric in mind.
Wartime urbanisation and the squatters:
The decade in which the temporary sojourner doctrine was disproved by events, and the movement that built Soweto.

**The economic change, which drove everything.** The war cut South Africa off from imported manufactures and gave it a captive market and a military demand.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Manufacturing** | **overtook both mining and agriculture** in share of output during the 1940s |
| **The workforce it needed** | **urban, semi-skilled, and permanent** — not migrant |
| **Where it got it** | **African workers from the reserves and the farms** |
| **Influx control** | **relaxed in practice from about 1942 to 1944**, because the war effort needed the labour |

**That relaxation is the crucial administrative fact.** The pass system was not repealed; **enforcement was reduced because the state needed workers in factories** — which demonstrates what the system was for. **When labour was needed in cities, the controls eased; when it was not, they tightened.**

**The scale of the movement.** The urban African population grew very rapidly through the 1940s — **by roughly half over the decade** — and by the 1946 census the number of Africans in the cities was approaching the number of whites.

**And there was nowhere to put them.** From the 1923 Act lesson: **townships were required to be self-financing out of African rents and beer-hall profits.** No municipality had built housing at anything like the rate required, and none had the revenue base to.

**So people built their own, and this is the squatter movement.**

**James Mpanza, Orlando, 1944.** Mpanza — a man with a criminal past, a religious conversion and extraordinary organising ability — **led thousands of sub-tenants out of overcrowded Orlando onto vacant municipal land and established a settlement.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The organisation** | ***Sofasonke*** — "we shall all die together" |
| **The method** | **occupy, organise, collect dues, run a committee, resist removal** |
| **Scale** | thousands of families, then tens of thousands across the Rand |
| **Other leaders** | **Oriel Monongoaha**, **Schreiner Baduza** and others led further occupations |
| **The state's response** | **it could not remove them.** It had to provide site-and-service land instead |

**And that is why Mpanza is called the father of Soweto.** The emergency camps and serviced sites the authorities laid out in response to the occupations — Moroka, Jabavu and the rest — **became the townships that were consolidated as Soweto.** The city's largest African settlement exists in the shape it does because of an organised land occupation the state could not reverse.

**Monongoaha's recorded remark catches the logic exactly:**

> **The Government is like a man who has a cornfield which is invaded by birds. He chases the birds from one part of the field and they alight in another part… We squatters are the birds.**

**Why the state could not simply remove them, which is the lesson's analytical content:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Numbers** | tens of thousands of families, organised |
| **The labour was needed** | **by the industries the war had built** |
| **There was nowhere to remove them to** | the reserves could not absorb them, from the 1936 land lesson |
| **Housing would have had to be built** | and the 1923 Act's financing rule made that impossible at scale |
| **Removal meant force on a scale** | the wartime state was not prepared to use |

**So the squatter movement established, by demonstration, that the urban African population was permanent.** That is the finding the Fagan Commission made two lessons from here — **and the squatters had made it first, on the ground, by living there.**

**What else the decade produced:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African trade unions, growing** | **CNETU** — the Council of Non-European Trade Unions, 1941 — organising the new manufacturing workforce, with Communist Party organisers |
| **The African Mineworkers' Union**, 1941 | and the 1946 strike, next lesson |
| **Bus boycotts** | **Alexandra, 1940 and 1943–44** — tens of thousands walking nine miles each way to work rather than pay a raised fare. **And they won** |
| **Food and rent protests** | across the Rand |
| **Rising African wages** | **in real terms, for the first time in decades**, because manufacturing competed for labour |

**The Alexandra bus boycotts deserve the mention.** Ordinary people, walking eighteen miles a day for weeks, defeated a fare increase twice. **It is the clearest demonstration in the period that mass action worked where deputation did not** — and the Youth League, from the last lesson, was watching.

**And the rising wages point matters for the functional account.** Where African workers were not held by the pass system and monopsony — **in wartime manufacturing, where employers competed** — wages rose. **That is the control case for stage 3's claim about mine wages**, and it supports it: the flat mine wages were not a market outcome.

**Which sets up 1948 precisely.** By 1946 South Africa had:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A permanent, growing urban African population** | which no one could remove |
| **A manufacturing economy** | that needed it |
| **Rising African wages and growing unions** | |
| **Mass action that was winning** | boycotts, strikes, occupations |
| **And a white electorate** | that found all of it alarming |

**The 1948 election was fought on what to do about this**, and the two answers were on the table as formal reports. **The next lessons are those two reports and the election between them.**

**Practice.** Find urban African population figures for 1936 and 1946 and calculate the growth. Then read Monongoaha's remark about the birds and the cornfield. Then look up what site-and-service areas were laid out in response to the Orlando occupation and what they became. Then find the Alexandra bus boycott's outcome, and note how long people walked.
The 1946 mineworkers' strike:
Sixty thousand men out on the gold mines, broken by police in four days, and the political consequence that outlasted it.

**The union. The African Mineworkers' Union, founded 1941**, president **J. B. Marks** — a Communist Party member, which is how the union came to exist: from stage 4's Communist Party lesson, the party supplied the organisers the ICU's collapse had left absent.

**The demand: ten shillings a day.** Against a prevailing wage that was a fraction of it, and against the structure of stage 3's gold lesson — **monopsony recruitment, agreed maximum wages, real wages flat since 1911.**

**The strike:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **12 August 1946** | **it begins.** Between 60,000 and 70,000 men out on a dozen or more mines |
| **The compound system** | from stage 3 — which meant the strike had to be organised **inside** guarded barracks, and that the state's response could be concentrated at the gates |
| **The state's response** | **police baton charges, and shooting.** Men driven back underground at gunpoint, stope by stope on at least one mine |
| **16 August** | broken |
| **Official deaths** | **nine**, and the real figure is probably higher |
| **Injuries** | over a thousand |
| **After** | the union's leadership prosecuted; **the AMWU effectively destroyed**; **Marks and others charged with sedition** |

**And a detail that places it: the Communist Party's entire national executive was prosecuted** over the strike, in a trial that ran into 1948. **The state treated the strike as an insurrection.**

**Why it failed, in the terms this stage has established:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No legal standing** | from the Pact lesson: **Africans were excluded from the definition of "employee" in the 1924 Act**, so the strike was criminal by definition |
| **The compound** | organising and supplying a strike inside a guarded compound is close to impossible |
| **Migrant composition** | a workforce on nine-month contracts, from across the region, with no urban base |
| **No strike fund** | and men with no savings |
| **Monopsony** | the employers were a single bargaining unit; the workers were not |
| **Force** | applied immediately and without restraint |

**Every structural feature the industry had built since Kimberley worked exactly as designed.** The strike is the test that proved the system.

**Now the political consequence, which is why this lesson is here.**

**The Natives Representative Council was in session.** From the franchise lesson: the advisory body created in 1936, twelve of whose members were elected by African voters.

**When the strike was broken, the Council adjourned in protest** — and refused to continue. **Its members, the senior African political figures of the period, publicly concluded that the body was useless.**

**Paul Mosaka's remark, which is the sentence to remember:**

> **We have been talking to a toy telephone.**

**And another member, Dr Moroka, moved the adjournment.** The Council met once more in 1947 and never functioned again. **It was abolished in 1951.**

**So 1946 did two things:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It demonstrated that industrial action without legal standing could be crushed** | **by force, in four days** |
| **It ended African participation in the consultative institutions** | **by the participants' own decision** |

**Both routes closed in the same week.** And the conclusion the Youth League had been arguing since 1944 — from the politics lesson — was now the conclusion of the ANC's elders as well.

**The line from 1946 to 1949 is direct:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **August 1946** | the strike broken; the Council adjourns |
| **1947** | the Council's last meeting; the Doctors' Pact |
| **1948** | **the National Party takes power** |
| **December 1949** | **the ANC adopts the Programme of Action** — boycott, strike, civil disobedience |
| **1952** | **the Defiance Campaign** |

**The Programme of Action is usually read as a response to the National Party's victory, and it is only partly that.** The method changed because the alternatives had been exhausted **before** 1948 — by the 1914 and 1919 deputations, by the 1936 Acts, by the Council's record, and by 1946. **The new government made it urgent; it did not make it necessary.**

**One more consequence worth naming.** The 1946 strike and the Communist Party's role in it gave the National Party its central campaign theme for the next forty years: **that African political and industrial organisation was communist-directed.**

| The claim | The reality |
| --- | --- |
| **"The strike was communist-organised"** | **the union's leadership was substantially Communist Party** — so the claim had a factual basis |
| **"Therefore African grievances are not real"** | **which does not follow**, and the wage evidence from stage 3 shows why |
| **"Therefore the response is security legislation"** | **which is what happened** — the Suppression of Communism Act of 1950 |

**That is the structure of the argument the apartheid state made for forty years**, and it is worth seeing it assembled here, from a real fact and an invalid inference. **Stage 5's security state is built on it.**

**And the mineworkers' demand of ten shillings a day was not met.** Mine wages rose substantially only after **1973**, when the Durban strikes and then the oil shock and the gold price change the industry's position — **twenty-seven years later.**

**Practice.** Find the 1946 strike's demand and the prevailing wage, and express one as a multiple of the other. Then find Mosaka's remark in the Council's record. Then trace the line from August 1946 to December 1949 and decide how much of the Programme of Action is a response to 1948. Then find when African mine wages began to rise substantially, and count the years.
Fagan and Sauer: the two reports:
Two commissions, two answers to the same question, published a year apart — and an election fought between them.

**The question both reports addressed: African urbanisation is permanent and growing. What should the state do?**

**From the last two lessons, the facts both commissions had:** a permanent urban African population, a manufacturing economy dependent on it, squatter settlements that could not be removed, growing unions, and mass action that was winning.

---

**The Fagan Commission** — formally the **Native Laws Commission**, appointed by Smuts's government in 1946, chaired by **Judge Henry Fagan**, reporting in **1948**.

**Its findings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African urbanisation is a permanent, irreversible economic fact** | driven by industry's demand for labour and the reserves' inability to support the population |
| **Total territorial segregation is impossible** | **the economy depends on African labour in the cities** |
| **The migrant labour system is harmful** | to families, to productivity, and to social stability |
| **Influx control cannot stop urbanisation** | **it has not, over twenty-five years, and it will not** |

**Its recommendations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Accept a settled, permanent urban African population** | |
| **Relax influx control** | and administer movement rather than prohibit it |
| **Stabilise labour** | encourage families in the cities instead of migrant men |
| **Build housing** | and accept the cost |
| **Keep the reserves** | but stop pretending they could absorb the population |

**What Fagan was not.** **It was not a proposal for political rights.** It recommended no franchise, no end to residential segregation, no equality. **It was a pragmatic economic argument for accepting urbanisation and administering it humanely** — which is why it is sometimes described as the liberal option and is better described as the pragmatic one.

**And its diagnosis has worn extremely well.** Everything Fagan said about influx control's futility was confirmed over the following thirty-eight years, **and the apartheid state itself conceded it in 1986 when influx control was abolished** — stage 5's lesson. **Fagan was right, in 1948, and the country spent four decades establishing it.**

---

**The Sauer Report**, 1947 — the National Party's own commission, chaired by **Paul Sauer**, written for the party's 1948 platform.

**Its findings and recommendations, which are the same thing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Total separation is the goal** | ***apartheid*** — the word enters national politics here |
| **Africans belong in the reserves** | which are their national homes |
| **Urban Africans are temporary** | **the Stallard doctrine of 1923, restated and intensified** |
| **Migrant labour only** | families to remain in the reserves |
| **No permanent urban African population** | and existing settlement to be reversed |
| **Separate development** | the reserves to be developed as separate polities |
| **Segregation to be total** | residence, work, transport, education, marriage, politics |

**And the two reports are not a difference of degree.** They are opposite answers:

| | **Fagan** | **Sauer** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Urbanisation is** | **permanent** | **reversible** |
| **Influx control** | **relax it** | **tighten it** |
| **The family** | **in the city** | **in the reserve** |
| **The goal** | administer the inevitable | **reverse it** |
| **The reserves** | cannot absorb the population | **must be made to** |
| **The economy** | needs settled urban labour | can run on migrants |

**So the 1948 election was a choice between accepting the facts and attempting to reverse them**, and that is an unusually clean description of an election.

**The National Party won, and the thirty years that followed are the attempt to reverse them** — the Group Areas Act, the removals, the homelands, the pass system at its most intense, influx control enforced with millions of arrests. **Stage 5 is that attempt.**

**And the outcome is known.** By 1986 influx control was abolished, by 1990 the policy was being dismantled, and the urban African population was larger than Fagan had projected. **Sauer's programme was pursued for thirty-eight years with the full force of a state and it did not work** — which is the single most important empirical fact about apartheid and it was predicted, in a published government report, before the policy began.

**Two things that follow, and they pull in different directions.**

**First, for the "was apartheid irrational" question from stage 1's disagreements.** Fagan is the liberal tradition's best evidence: **the state was told, in advance, by its own commission, that the policy could not work, and it proceeded.** That is not functional behaviour.

**Second, and against that: it worked at something else for forty years.** It did not reverse urbanisation. **It did control the terms of labour, suppress wages, prevent organisation, and transfer enormous resources to the white population** — and it did that successfully until the 1970s. **So "it failed" needs the question "at what?"**

**Which is stage 5's subject, and the reason this curriculum puts the two reports at the end of stage 4: everything after 1948 is a test of a hypothesis that had already been refuted on paper.**

**Practice.** Read Fagan's central finding on the permanence of urbanisation. Then read Sauer's recommendation on the same question. Then set the two side by side and note that both commissions had the same evidence. Then list what Sauer's programme achieved by 1986 and what it did not, and decide what that proves.
1948: how it was won:
The election that is treated as the beginning, the numbers that decided it, and what they tell you about what 1948 was.

**26 May 1948.**

| | Seats |
| --- | --- |
| **National Party** | **70** |
| **Afrikaner Party** | **9** |
| **National Party + Afrikaner Party** | **79** |
| **United Party** | 65 |
| **Labour Party** | 6 |
| **United Party + Labour** | **71** |
| **Native representatives** | 3 |

**And the votes:**

| | Share |
| --- | --- |
| **NP + Afrikaner Party** | **about 41%** |
| **UP + Labour** | **about 53%** |

**The National Party took power with a minority of the votes cast**, and it governed for forty-six years.

**How a minority of votes produced a majority of seats:**

| Mechanism | |
| --- | --- |
| **Rural weighting** | **constituencies could be "loaded" or "unloaded" by up to 15%** from the national average, and rural seats were systematically under-populated |
| **Where the NP's support was** | **rural and small-town Afrikaner districts** — exactly the over-represented ones |
| **Where the UP's was** | **cities**, especially English-speaking urban seats — the under-represented ones |
| **First past the post** | so efficient distribution matters more than total votes |
| **The electoral pact** | **the NP and the Afrikaner Party did not oppose each other**, so the anti-UP vote was not split |

**And Smuts lost his own seat**, at Standerton, which he had held for decades.

**So 1948 was not a landslide of opinion.** It was a narrow seat victory, on a minority of the vote, delivered substantially by the rural weighting of constituencies — **and no one expected it, including the National Party.**

**Which bears directly on how 1948 is read.** Three claims to separate:

| Claim | Standing |
| --- | --- |
| **"White South Africa voted for apartheid in 1948"** | **false as stated.** A majority voted against the parties that formed the government |
| **"Apartheid was imposed by a minority"** | **true of 1948, and not of what followed** — the NP's support grew at every election to 1977 |
| **"1948 was the beginning of segregation"** | **false.** This whole stage is the refutation |

**The second row matters.** The National Party won 41% in 1948 and progressively more thereafter — a majority of votes by the 1950s, and large majorities by the 1960s and 1970s. **So the policy was ratified by the white electorate repeatedly after it was introduced.** An account resting on the 1948 minority has to deal with that.

**Why the NP won, in the terms this stage has built.** Five causes, and the relative weights are argued:

**1. The urbanisation panic.** From the last three lessons: a permanent, growing urban African population, squatter settlements, growing unions, wage pressure, mass action that was winning. **The NP offered to reverse it; the UP offered Fagan.** For a white electorate alarmed by what it saw on the Rand, Fagan's pragmatism read as surrender.

**2. The Afrikaner institutional machine.** From the institutions lesson: the Broederbond, the FAK, the churches, the economic movement, the unions, the schools. **Forty years of institution-building, mobilised.**

**3. Afrikaner grievance, still live.** The camps, anglicisation, the 1922 suppression, the war and the internments, and Smuts as the man who had taken South Africa into Britain's wars twice.

**4. The poor-white and white-labour constituency**, from the civilised labour lesson, which the UP's industrialists did not speak for.

**5. The electoral system**, as above — which converted a minority into a government.

**And one cause that is often cited and is weaker than it looks: that the UP had no answer.** It had Fagan. **The problem was that Fagan's answer required accepting something the electorate did not want to accept**, and Smuts did not campaign on it. **He had received the report and had not acted on it** — which left the UP defending a status quo that everyone agreed was failing, against a party with a programme.

**What changed after 1948, and what did not — which is this stage's closing judgement.**

**What was already in place before May 1948:**

| |
| --- |
| **The 1913 and 1936 land Acts** — 7%, then a 13% target |
| **The 1923 Urban Areas Act and the Stallard doctrine** |
| **The 1927 Native Administration Act** — Supreme Chief, rule by proclamation, section 29 |
| **The pass system**, nationally |
| **The industrial colour bar**, statutory since 1926 |
| **Africans excluded from the definition of "employee"** since 1924 |
| **The civilised labour policy** and the parastatals |
| **The African franchise removed from the common roll** — **1936, by Fusion, 169 to 11** |
| **The Natives Representative Council** — created 1936, defunct by 1946 |
| **SANAC's 1905 blueprint**, largely executed |

**That is the architecture, and the National Party inherited it.**

**What 1948 brought that was new is stage 5's subject**, and it is substantial: population registration, prohibition of mixed marriage, Group Areas, Bantu Education, the homelands as separate nations, the security state, and the attempt — unprecedented in scale — **to reverse urbanisation rather than merely to control it.**

**So the answer to the first big disagreement from stage 1 is not "continuity" or "break". It is: continuity in the architecture, break in the ambition.**

| |
| --- |
| **Every major mechanism of racial control existed before 1948** |
| **What was new was the attempt to make it total, systematic and permanent** — and to reverse the urbanisation that the previous order had merely regulated |
| **Which required a scale of coercion the segregation state had not used** |
| **And it failed, as Fagan had said it would** |

**That formulation is defensible and it is not a dodge** — the evidence for each clause is in stages 3, 4 and 5. **And it means that the question "when did apartheid begin" has no single answer**, which is itself the finding.

**Practice.** Write out the 1948 seat and vote figures from memory. Then work out how the rural loading produced the result. Then take the list of what was in place before 1948 and mark which items you had previously thought were apartheid measures. Then write your own answer to the continuity-or-break question, in one paragraph, and keep it to compare after stage 5.
What apartheid was: the four pillars:
The stage's map: what was actually built between 1948 and 1960, organised so the thirty lessons after it have somewhere to sit.

**The word.** *Apartheid* is Afrikaans for "apartness" or "separateness". It entered national politics with the **Sauer Report of 1947**, from stage 4, and it was the National Party's 1948 election platform.

**And the state's own later preference was "separate development"** — stage 1's lesson on words: the euphemism tells you who is speaking, and the shift from *apartheid* to *separate development* in official language happened in the 1960s as the first word acquired its international meaning.

**The four pillars. Everything in this stage is one of these:**

---

**Pillar 1 — Classification.** Every person assigned to a race, by law, with a register.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Population Registration Act, 1950** | the national register and the classification |
| **Why it is first** | **every other apartheid law depends on knowing who is what.** Group Areas, Bantu Education, job reservation and the franchise all require a classified population |

**This is the pillar that makes the rest administrable**, and it is the next lesson.

---

**Pillar 2 — Separation of space.** Where people may live, work, travel and be.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Group Areas Act, 1950** | urban residential segregation, by proclamation |
| **The 1913 and 1936 land Acts** | inherited from stage 4 |
| **The pass system and influx control** | inherited, and intensified |
| **Forced removals** | **about 3.5 million people** |
| **The homelands** | and eventually their "independence" |
| **Reservation of Separate Amenities Act, 1953** | **petty apartheid** — benches, beaches, entrances, counters |

---

**Pillar 3 — Separate and unequal institutions.** Education, health, labour, local government.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bantu Education Act, 1953** | and the Coloured and Indian equivalents |
| **Extension of University Education Act, 1959** | separate universities, and exclusion from the existing ones |
| **Job reservation** | under the Industrial Conciliation Act of 1956 |
| **Bantu Authorities Act, 1951** | separate administration through chiefs, from stage 4's 1927 Act |
| **Separate everything else** | hospitals, transport, sport, pensions, courts |

---

**Pillar 4 — Suppression of opposition.** The security apparatus.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Suppression of Communism Act, 1950** | banning of organisations and persons |
| **Public Safety Act, 1953** | **states of emergency** |
| **Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1953** | penalties for civil disobedience |
| **The 90-day, 180-day and then indefinite detention laws** | from 1963 |
| **Terrorism Act, 1967** | **section 6: indefinite detention without trial, incommunicado** |
| **The Bureau of State Security, the Security Branch, the Special Branch** | |

---

**And one distinction that organises the whole period: petty against grand apartheid.**

| | **Petty apartheid** | **Grand apartheid** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What** | **segregated amenities, signage, social separation** | **territorial and political separation** |
| **Instruments** | Separate Amenities Act, local by-laws | **Group Areas, removals, the homelands, citizenship** |
| **Visible to visitors** | **yes, and internationally notorious** | less so |
| **Dismantled** | **from the late 1970s and through the 1980s** | **the core, maintained to the end** |
| **The point** | humiliation and the reinforcement of hierarchy | **the denial of political claim on South Africa** |

**That distinction matters for reading the 1980s.** When the state removed "whites only" signs, opened hotels and desegregated sport, **it was conceding petty apartheid while intensifying the grand variety** — and foreign observers consistently misread the first as reform of the second. **The lesson on PW Botha's reforms is about exactly this.**

**The periodisation this stage uses:**

| Period | Character |
| --- | --- |
| **1948–58, Malan and Strijdom** | **building the legal architecture.** Classification, Group Areas, Bantu Education, the security laws |
| **1958–66, Verwoerd** | **grand apartheid.** The homelands as nations, separate development, the Republic, and Sharpeville |
| **1966–78, Vorster** | **enforcement and the security state.** Detention, Soweto, Biko, and the first economic trouble |
| **1978–89, PW Botha** | **Total Strategy** — reform of petty apartheid, the 1983 constitution, the townships' revolt, the states of emergency, and the stalemate |
| **1989–90, de Klerk** | which is stage 6 |

**What this stage is careful about, under stage 1's rules.** Two things:

**The facts are not in dispute and are stated.** The laws said what they said; the removals happened; the deaths in detention are counted; the TRC and the courts established a great deal. **This curriculum does not treat any of that as contested.**

**The interpretations are.** Why it was built, whom it served, why it lasted so long, why it ended, and whether it was a continuation or a break — **all four of stage 1's big disagreements run through this stage**, and it gives both sides of each.

**One thing to hold from the start.** Apartheid was **legislated** — openly, in a parliament, by elected governments, with debate recorded in Hansard and every statute printed in the Gazette. **It was not a secret and it was not a coup.** From stage 1's Gazette lesson: the entire architecture is public, searchable and free to read.

**Which means a question worth carrying through the whole stage: at each point, who knew, and what did they say?** The answer is almost always that everyone knew, because it was in the statute book.

**Practice.** Write out the four pillars and put each of these in one of them: the pencil test, Meadowlands, the Terrorism Act, job reservation, the Transkei's independence, a bench marked "Europeans Only". Then look up one apartheid statute in the Gazette and note its date and number. Then write down what you expect the strongest argument for the "break" reading to be, and check it at the end of this stage.
Population Registration, and classificat:
The Act that made the rest possible — a national register of race, the tests used to decide it, and what a reclassification meant for a family.

**Population Registration Act 30 of 1950**, with the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act the first statutes of apartheid.

**What it did:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A national population register** | with every person's race recorded |
| **An identity number** | encoding the classification |
| **Three primary categories** | **White, Coloured, and Native** — later *Bantu*, later *Black* |
| **Subcategories of Coloured**, by proclamation from 1959 | **Cape Coloured, Malay, Griqua, Chinese, Indian, Other Asiatic, Other Coloured** |
| **A Race Classification Board** | to decide disputed cases and hear appeals |

**Why it is the foundational statute.** Every other apartheid law operates on a classified population:

| Law | Needs to know |
| --- | --- |
| **Group Areas** | which group you belong to, to say where you may live |
| **Bantu Education** | which school system you enter |
| **Job reservation** | which jobs are closed to you |
| **The pass laws** | whether you need a pass at all |
| **Mixed Marriages** | whether a marriage is lawful |
| **The franchise** | whether you may vote |

**So the register is the machine's index.** Without it, nothing else can be administered — which is why it came first and why it was the last thing repealed, in 1991.

**The tests, which is where it becomes grotesque.** The Act's definition of "white person" was someone who **"in appearance obviously is, or who is generally accepted as, a white person"** — and excluding anyone who, though appearing white, was generally accepted as Coloured.

**So the statutory tests were:**

| Test | |
| --- | --- |
| **Appearance** | as judged by an official |
| **General acceptance** | **what the community treated you as** — habits, speech, education, employment, where you lived, whom you associated with |
| **Descent** | in practice, through records and inquiry |

**Note what "general acceptance" means as a legal test.** It makes race a social fact to be determined by evidence about how neighbours and employers behaved — **which is an accurate description of how race works and a monstrous thing to put in a statute**, because it means the classification could turn on which school a child had attended or which church a family went to.

**And the methods officials used, which were not in the Act:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Examination of hair, skin, facial features** | |
| **The "pencil test"** | **a pencil pushed into the hair; if it stayed, that counted against a white classification.** Never statutory, widely used |
| **Inspection of family members** | |
| **Inquiries to employers, neighbours, schools, ministers** | |
| **Examination of the ears, the gums, the nail beds** | |

**The pencil test is the detail everyone knows, and it is worth being precise: it was not law.** It was administrative practice, which is in some ways worse — **a legal classification with life-defining consequences, decided in part by an unwritten test officials had devised.**

**What a classification decided, for one person:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where you could live** | and therefore whether you would be removed |
| **Where your children could go to school** | and what they would be taught |
| **What work you could do** | and what you would be paid for it |
| **Whom you could marry** | and whether you had committed a crime by doing so |
| **Whether you needed a pass** | and could be arrested for not having it |
| **Which hospital, which bus, which beach, which bench** | |
| **Whether you could vote** | |
| **From 1970, which country you were a citizen of** | |

**And the reclassifications, which are the part that makes the system's arbitrariness undeniable.** The government published annual figures of people reclassified from one race to another.

| |
| --- |
| **People moved from Coloured to White, and from White to Coloured** |
| **From Native to Coloured, and back** |
| **From Indian to Coloured, from Chinese to White** |
| **Hundreds of cases a year, for decades** |

**So the state's own statistics recorded that its classifications were wrong, in hundreds of cases a year, and were corrected** — which is a statistical admission that the categories did not correspond to anything findable.

**What that did to families.** The classification was individual. **So a family could be split: siblings classified differently, a child classified differently from a parent.**

| Consequence | |
| --- | --- |
| **A reclassified child** | **had to change schools**, and could no longer live in the family's area |
| **A reclassified spouse** | **made the marriage unlawful** under the Mixed Marriages Act |
| **A family split** | **lived in different group areas, legally** |
| **Appeals** | took years, cost money, and were heard in public |

**And "passing"** — a person classified Coloured living as white, or the reverse — **was a criminal matter and a constant anxiety**, with the attendant phenomena: families cutting off relatives, people never visiting home, siblings pretending not to know each other.

**The two cases that stand for the rest.** **Sandra Laing**, born in 1955 to white Afrikaner parents and classified white, reclassified Coloured at the age of eleven on the basis of her appearance, expelled from her school, and reclassified white again after her father's legal action. **She is the best-documented case and she is one of many.**

**And the Chinese and Japanese anomaly**, which exposes the system's logic completely:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **South African Chinese** | **classified Coloured** |
| **Japanese visitors and businessmen** | **treated in practice as "honorary whites"** |
| **Why** | **trade.** Japan was an important buyer of South African minerals |

**The categories bent for commerce and did not bend for anything else.** Which tells you what they were.

**The repeal. The Population Registration Act was repealed in 1991** — among the last of the pillars to go, because dismantling it meant dismantling the administrative basis of everything.

**And one modern consequence to carry forward.** The post-1994 state **still uses racial classification** — for employment equity, for B-BBEE, for redress monitoring — **on the basis of self-identification rather than official determination.** Stage 9 and stage 12 both argue about it, and the argument's terms are set by this lesson: **the categories were invented by this statute, they corresponded to nothing findable, and they now describe real distributions of wealth and opportunity that nothing else measures.**

**Practice.** Find the Act's statutory definition of "white person" and read the "generally accepted" test. Then find the government's published reclassification figures for any year and note the categories of movement. Then read Sandra Laing's case. Then consider: if the categories were invented and arbitrary, why does the present state still use them — and what would be lost by stopping?
Mixed Marriages and the Immorality Act:
The first apartheid statute, the one that reached furthest into private life, and the prosecutions it produced for thirty-six years.

**Two Acts, passed in the government's first two years:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act 55 of 1949** | **the very first apartheid statute.** Marriage between a white person and a person of another race prohibited and void |
| **Immorality Amendment Act 21 of 1950** | extended the existing prohibition on sexual relations across the colour line — the 1927 Immorality Act had barred it between whites and Africans — **to relations between whites and all other races** |

**Note the order.** Before the population register, before Group Areas, before Bantu Education — **the first thing the government legislated was whom people could marry and sleep with.**

**That ordering is informative and it is argued about.** Two readings:

| Reading | |
| --- | --- |
| **It reveals the ideology's core** | apartheid was fundamentally about biological separation and racial purity, and everything else followed |
| **It reveals the politics** | **it was the cheapest and most popular measure available**, satisfying the electorate immediately at no economic cost, while the harder architecture was drafted |

**Both have support, and the second is often underweighted.** The marriage and sex laws cost the economy nothing, required no expenditure, displaced nobody, and spoke directly to the anxieties the 1948 campaign had mobilised. **They were, in political terms, free.**

**How the Immorality Act was enforced, which is the part that is hard to read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Police surveillance** of suspected couples | |
| **Raids on homes**, at night | |
| **Evidence collected** | bedding, underclothing, medical examination |
| **Neighbours' reports** | and the encouragement of them |
| **Public trials** | with the details reported in newspapers |
| **Sentences** | imprisonment, and for whites often a suspended sentence with the non-white partner imprisoned |

**The asymmetry of sentencing is documented and consistent.** And the social consequences frequently exceeded the legal ones: **loss of employment, expulsion from a community, and a number of suicides**, which were reported at the time.

**The scale. Thousands of prosecutions over the Acts' lifetime** — the figure usually given is in the region of 11,000 convictions under the Immorality Act's race provisions between 1950 and 1985, and the number of investigations was far higher.

**The arithmetic of the Act's futility is worth stating.** South Africa's Coloured population — several million people by the 1980s — **is substantially the descendant population of exactly the relationships the Act prohibited**, over three centuries, from stage 3's slavery lesson. **The state was criminalising in 1950 the process that had produced one of the groups it was classifying.**

**The churches, and a point stage 4 set up.** The Dutch Reformed Church supported the legislation and provided theological argument for it. **The English-speaking churches opposed it with varying firmness; the Catholic and Anglican churches more consistently.** And in the 1980s the Reformed churches' own reversal on apartheid began substantially with this area, because the biblical case for prohibiting marriage was the weakest part of the whole theological edifice.

**The repeal, 1985**, and it is a telling date:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1985** | **both Acts repealed**, under PW Botha |
| **Why then** | **petty apartheid was being dismantled while grand apartheid was intensified** — from the pillars lesson. Repealing the sex laws cost the state nothing structurally and bought international credit |
| **What was not repealed in 1985** | **Group Areas** — so a legally married mixed couple **still could not live together lawfully** in most of the country |

**That last row is the clearest single illustration of the petty/grand distinction.** From 1985 a mixed marriage was lawful and **the couple had no lawful place to live**, because the Group Areas Act stood until 1991. **The reform was real and it was also, in the most literal sense, unlivable.**

**Why this lesson matters beyond itself.** Three reasons:

**1. It is the limit case of state reach.** Any argument about what a state can and should regulate meets this at one end. **The apartheid state legislated the bedroom, enforced it with police, and tried it in public.**

**2. It shows the ideology was not only economic.** From stage 1's disagreements: the revisionist tradition explains the migrant labour system and the reserves extremely well, **and the Mixed Marriages Act is not explained by labour economics at all.** It cost money to enforce and produced no labour. **This is the liberal tradition's second-best piece of evidence, after Fagan.**

**3. It is the reason the TRC heard about private life.** The harms of apartheid were not confined to detention and killing; **a great many people's lives were deformed by whom they were forbidden to love**, and the record of that is thinner because it was private and shameful and the law made it criminal.

**Practice. Find the 1949 Act's date and confirm it was the first apartheid statute.** Then find the Immorality Act's conviction figures and the sentencing pattern between partners. Then establish what year the Acts were repealed and what year Group Areas was, and work out what a mixed married couple's legal position was between those dates.
The Group Areas Act:
The statute that redrew every South African city, how its machinery worked, and why its map is still the country's.

**Group Areas Act 41 of 1950**, re-enacted and consolidated in 1957 and 1966.

**What it did: it empowered the state to declare any area for the exclusive occupation and ownership of one racial group**, and to remove everyone else.

**The machinery, which is the part to understand, because it was designed to be slow and irreversible:**

| Step | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Investigation** | the **Group Areas Board** investigates an area, holds hearings, takes representations |
| **2. Proclamation** | the area is **declared** for a group, by notice in the Gazette |
| **3. Disqualification** | everyone of another group becomes a **"disqualified person"** — unlawfully occupying their own home |
| **4. Permits** | temporary permits issued, to allow a wind-down |
| **5. Expropriation** | property acquired by the state, at **a valuation the state set** |
| **6. Removal** | occupants moved, usually to a new township on the city's edge |
| **7. Redevelopment** | the land sold or developed for the designated group |

**Four features of that machinery decided its effects.**

**The hearings were real and did not matter.** Communities made representations, hired lawyers, submitted evidence. **The Board heard them and the proclamations followed.** From stage 4's Natives Representative Council: a consultative process with no power to oblige anybody produces a record and no outcome.

**The valuations were set by the state and were low.** Owners were compensated at prices well below what the land was worth once rezoned — **so the removal transferred wealth as well as people**, and the recipients were the developers and buyers of the cleared land.

**"Disqualified person" is the legal fiction that did the work.** A family in a house they owned, in which they had lived for generations, became an unlawful occupier by a notice in a newspaper. **No individual wrongdoing, no court, no finding — a gazetted proclamation.**

**And permits made it gradual.** A community was not removed at once; **it was hollowed out over years as permits expired, businesses lost their licences, schools closed and services were withdrawn.** By the time the bulldozers came, many had already gone. **That was the design.**

**Who it moved.** The Act applied to all groups in principle. **In practice it moved Coloured and Indian communities overwhelmingly**, out of inner cities and established suburbs, and it moved African communities under the overlapping provisions of the 1923 Urban Areas Act and the homeland legislation.

| Group | Share of removals under Group Areas |
| --- | --- |
| **Coloured** | **the largest number by far** |
| **Indian** | very large relative to population |
| **African** | removed mainly under other statutes |
| **White** | **a very small number**, and generally with better compensation |

**That distribution is the Act's signature.** It was, in its day-to-day operation, principally a machine for removing Coloured and Indian people from valuable urban land — **and that is why the Coloured and Indian experience of apartheid is distinct**, and why Group Areas rather than the pass laws is the central grievance in those communities' memory.

**The commercial dimension, which gets less attention than the residential.** The Act also governed **where businesses could trade**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Indian trading communities** | **destroyed in town after town** — businesses built over generations, in locations chosen for passing trade, moved to a township with no customers |
| **Permits to trade** | required, and refused |
| **The effect** | **the elimination of a commercial class**, which is a distinct kind of loss from a residential removal |

**Why its map is still the country's**, which is the lesson's conclusion and the reason it matters now.

**A city's shape is extremely durable.** Group Areas determined, for every South African city:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where the townships are** | **far from the centre, on the wrong side of a buffer** |
| **Where the industrial land is** | often between the township and the suburbs, as a buffer |
| **Where the transport runs** | long commutes, built in |
| **Where the rates base is** | from stage 4's Native Revenue Account — in the suburbs |
| **Where land is cheap and where it is dear** | |

**None of that changed in 1991, or in 1994, or since.** The Act was repealed; **the city it built is still there**, because moving a city requires building another one.

| The consequence | |
| --- | --- |
| **Commuting** | **among the longest and most expensive in the world as a share of income** |
| **Spatial inequality** | measurable, and it has barely moved since 1994 |
| **The cost of housing delivery** | **cheap land is far out, so state housing reproduces the pattern** |
| **Municipal finance** | service obligations and rateable value in different places |

**That last point is the one stage 8's local government lesson and stage 9's fiscal lesson both turn on**, and stage 12 argues about: **post-apartheid housing policy has delivered millions of houses, overwhelmingly on cheap peripheral land, which has deepened the spatial pattern Group Areas created.** Whether that was avoidable is a live argument.

**Practice.** Find the Group Areas proclamation for an area you know, in Open Gazettes, and read what it declared. Then find a map of your nearest city's group areas and compare it with a current map of where people live. Then work out the distance from a township you know to the city centre, and what the taxi fare is as a share of a minimum wage.
Forced removals: the method and the numb:
About three and a half million people moved by the state, in five distinct programmes, over about twenty-five years.

**The figure. The number usually given is around 3.5 million people forcibly removed between 1960 and 1983**, and the source matters: it comes from the **Surplus People Project**, a five-volume independent survey published in 1983–85, which remains the standard reference. **It is an estimate with a method, not an official count** — the state did not publish a total — and it is the figure the TRC and subsequent scholarship use.

**The five programmes, because "forced removals" is not one thing:**

**1. Group Areas removals.** From the last lesson: urban Coloured and Indian communities, and some African, out of proclaimed areas.

**2. "Black spot" removals.** African-owned freehold land outside the scheduled areas — **land bought and titled before the 1913 Act, which that Act had not expropriated.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What they were** | **communities with title deeds**, some since the nineteenth century |
| **Why they were removed** | **they were inside areas designated white** |
| **The legal basis** | the 1927 Act's power to move communities by proclamation, from stage 4 |
| **The best-known** | **Mogopa**, removed in 1983–84 — a community with title that resisted for years and was removed at night |

**The black spots are the removals that most clearly defeat any "the land was never theirs" argument**, because the communities held registered title in the state's own deeds office.

**3. Homeland consolidation.** The homelands were patchworks of non-contiguous pieces. **Making them look like territories meant moving people to join the pieces up** — hundreds of thousands moved to make a map tidier.

**4. Farm removals.** From stage 4's 1936 Chapter IV: limits on labour tenants per farm. **As agriculture mechanised through the 1960s and 1970s, farmers needed fewer workers and the law let them remove the rest** — the largest and least documented category.

**Why least documented: nobody counted.** A family removed from a farm where they had lived for three generations, with no title and no record, **leaves no paper.** The Surplus People Project's estimate for this category is the softest number in the total and probably the largest.

**5. Urban relocation and influx control.** People endorsed out of cities for lacking section 10 rights — the next lessons — and transported to a homeland.

---

**The method, which was consistent:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Notice** | sometimes months, sometimes days |
| **Trucks** | **the government lorry is the universal image of a removal** |
| **Demolition** | **houses knocked down behind the departing families**, so return was impossible |
| **The destination** | a numbered site on bare ground, frequently with **a tin latrine and a water point and nothing else** |
| **Compensation** | a small sum, or a site, or nothing |
| **Resistance** | met with police, prosecution and delay until it exhausted itself |

**The destinations deserve their own note, because the word "resettlement" conceals them.** The relocation sites were:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On marginal land** | in homelands with no work |
| **Without services** | water trucked in, no electricity, no clinic, no transport |
| **Without an economy** | **nothing to do** — the characteristic feature |
| **With high mortality** | **infant mortality in some resettlement areas was among the highest recorded anywhere**, documented by Francis Wilson's work and the Second Carnegie Inquiry from stage 4 |

**Dimbaza, Limehill, Sada, Ilinge, Thornhill, Botshabelo** — the names of the resettlement camps. **Dimbaza became internationally known through the 1973 documentary *Last Grave at Dimbaza*, filmed clandestinely and banned in South Africa**, which showed the children's graves.

**And the demographic consequence, which is the thing to grasp about what removal meant.** A resettlement area's population was disproportionately **women, children and the old** — because the working-age men were migrants elsewhere. **The removals created settlements of dependants without economies, far from work, which is why they had famine-level child mortality.**

---

**Resistance, and it was real:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sophiatown, 1955** | the ANC's "Ons dak nie, ons phola hier" campaign — and the removal proceeded |
| **Mogopa, 1983–84** | years of legal and physical resistance; removed |
| **Driefontein** | **its leader, Saul Mkhize, shot dead by a policeman in 1983** |
| **Magopa, KwaNgema, Mathopestad** and others | the 1980s anti-removal movement, with church and legal support |
| **The outcome** | **a few removals were stopped or reversed in the 1980s**, as the state's capacity and will weakened |

**And the 1980s is when it stopped being possible.** The anti-removal campaigns, the Black Sash's monitoring, the Surplus People Project's documentation and international attention made removals politically expensive. **The programme wound down before apartheid did.**

---

**The restitution tail.** The **Restitution of Land Rights Act 1994** allows claims for dispossession after 19 June 1913, from stage 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Claims lodged by the 1998 deadline** | **about 80,000** |
| **Mostly urban** | Group Areas removals, where title and records existed |
| **Settled mostly in cash** | rather than land — because the land was built on |
| **Rural claims** | slower, more complex, more often restored in land |
| **A reopening of the claims window in 2014** | **struck down by the Constitutional Court in 2016** on procedural grounds |

**So the restitution programme has substantially completed the urban claims and has had far more difficulty with the rural ones** — which is stage 9's material, and one of stage 12's arguments.

**Practice.** Find the Surplus People Project's estimate and its method. Then find one black spot removal — Mogopa is the best documented — and establish that the community held title. Then watch or read about *Last Grave at Dimbaza*. Then look up how many restitution claims were lodged and what share were settled in cash rather than land.
Sophiatown, District Six, and the black:
Three removals in detail, because the aggregate number conceals what the thing actually was.

**Why these three.** Sophiatown and District Six are the most documented urban removals, with enormous cultural records. **The black spots are the least documented and the most legally indefensible.** Between them they cover the method.

---

**Sophiatown.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where** | four miles from central Johannesburg |
| **What it was** | **a freehold township** — one of the few places in Johannesburg where Africans could own land, because it had been laid out before the 1923 Act's restrictions |
| **Population** | **around 65,000**, African, Coloured, Indian and Chinese |
| **Character** | **the centre of African urban culture** — jazz, journalism, writing, football, gangs, shebeens, churches. *Drum* magazine's world |
| **Why it had to go** | it was freehold, it was mixed, it was close to white suburbs, and **its existence contradicted the temporary sojourner doctrine** |

**The removal began on 9 February 1955** and ran over several years. **Residents were moved to Meadowlands**, in what became Soweto, and the land was cleared and rebuilt as a white suburb **named Triomf** — "triumph".

**The naming is the single most quoted fact about Sophiatown** and it is accurate: the suburb built on the cleared township was officially called Triumph. **It was renamed Sophiatown in 2006.**

**The resistance.** The ANC campaigned against the removal under the slogan **"Ons dak nie, ons phola hier"** — a mix of Afrikaans and township argot, roughly *"we're not moving, we're staying here"*. **It failed.** And its failure was a significant moment in the internal argument about method: **a well-organised, well-publicised campaign by the ANC at the height of its 1950s mobilisation could not stop a removal.**

**What was lost that the number does not capture.** Sophiatown produced a generation: **Can Themba, Bloke Modisane, Es'kia Mphahlele, Todd Matshikiza, Miriam Makeba, Hugh Masekela, Trevor Huddleston's parish.** The freehold meant permanence, and permanence had produced an urban culture that was not a township's culture. **The removal was understood at the time as the destruction of a specific possibility** — that Africans might have a city of their own in the city.

---

**District Six.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where** | **central Cape Town**, on the slopes below Devil's Peak, minutes from the city |
| **What it was** | mixed, poor, dense, old — **Coloured predominantly, with Muslim, Jewish, African and white residents**, going back to the nineteenth century |
| **Population removed** | **about 60,000** |
| **Declared white** | **11 February 1966** |
| **Removals** | **through to the early 1980s** |
| **What happened to the land** | **mostly cleared and left empty** — and that is the extraordinary part |

**The land stayed vacant for decades.** The Cape Technikon was built on part of it; **most of District Six was bulldozed and never redeveloped**, and much of it is still open ground in the centre of Cape Town.

**Which answers the question of whether these removals were economically motivated.** District Six was valuable central land and it was cleared and then not used. **The removal was not profitable; it was ideological** — and it is therefore the other side of the Group Areas lesson's point about wealth transfer. **Sometimes the land was taken for value, and sometimes it was taken because the community's existence was intolerable.**

**And it is the most visible monument apartheid left.** Empty ground in the middle of a city, for sixty years, visible from every road into Cape Town. **The District Six Museum** is one of the country's most important, built by former residents around the recovery of the street names and the family records.

**Restitution.** District Six was one of the earliest and most prominent claims. **Land was returned and a small number of families have been resettled**, slowly and with much frustration; **most claimants had not been housed decades later**, and the delay is one of the standard illustrations of restitution's practical difficulty.

---

**The black spots.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What** | **African freehold land, with registered title, outside the scheduled areas** |
| **Origin** | bought before the 1913 Act, sometimes in the nineteenth century, often by church-assisted community purchase |
| **Why removed** | the title was inconvenient and the land was in a white area |
| **The mechanism** | the 1927 Act's power to move a community by proclamation |

**Mogopa**, the best-documented:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A Bakwena community** in the western Transvaal, **with title since the 1910s** | |
| **Resisted for years** | legal action, publicity, church support, international attention |
| **Services destroyed first** | **the school demolished, the water pumps removed, the clinic closed** — the hollowing-out method from the Group Areas lesson |
| **Removed in February 1984** | **at night, with police, after the community had refused to leave** |
| **Returned after 1994** | and the community's reconstruction has been difficult |

**Driefontein**, in the same campaign: **its leader Saul Mkhize was shot dead by a policeman at a community meeting in 1983.** The policeman was acquitted. **Driefontein was not removed** — the resistance, and the death, made it too costly.

**So the black spots establish two things.** That **registered title gave no protection** — which disposes of any argument that the dispossessed simply had no legal claim. **And that resistance sometimes worked, in the 1980s, when the state's will was failing.**

**Why these three together.** Sophiatown shows what was destroyed culturally and that organised campaigning failed in 1955. **District Six shows that the motive was not always economic.** The black spots show that law and title were no defence. **And the three together are why the aggregate figure of 3.5 million is a number that needs opening.**

**Practice.** Find the date Sophiatown's removal began and the name the suburb was given. Then look at a satellite image of District Six today and find the empty ground. Then read about Mogopa's removal and note the sequence of what was destroyed before the people were moved. Then find out how many District Six claimants have been resettled, and when.
Suppression of Communism, and the securi:
The statute that criminalised opposition by redefining a word, and the thirty-year escalation of detention law that followed it.

**Suppression of Communism Act 44 of 1950.** Its importance is not that it banned the Communist Party. **It is the definition.**

**The Act defined "communism" to include** — and this is close to the statutory language — **any doctrine or scheme which aims at bringing about any political, industrial, social or economic change within the Union by the promotion of disturbance or disorder.**

**Read what that catches:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Any campaign for political change** | that might cause disorder |
| **A strike** | |
| **A boycott** | |
| **A protest march** | |
| **Advocating a universal franchise** | if pursued by any means the state called disorderly |

**No Marxism required.** From stage 1's lesson on words: **the statute uses a word everybody thinks they understand and defines it to mean something else entirely** — and then the state could truthfully say that those it banned had been named under the Communism Act.

**The powers it gave the minister, without a court:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Declare an organisation unlawful** | |
| **"Name" a person as a communist** | placing them on a list |
| **Ban a named person** | from gatherings, from organisations, from areas, from employment |
| **Banning orders** | **a form of house arrest, imposed administratively** |
| **Ban a publication** | |
| **Prohibit a person from being quoted** | **so a banned person's words could not be published, at all** |

**The banning order deserves explanation because it is the characteristic instrument of the period.** A banned person typically could not:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Attend any gathering** | — and "gathering" was defined to include **being with more than one other person at a time** |
| **Enter a school, a court, a factory, a township** | depending on the order |
| **Leave a magisterial district** | |
| **Be quoted** | so journalists could not report them |
| **Hold office** in any listed organisation | |

**So a banned person was socially erased without trial, by ministerial signature, renewably**, and breach was a criminal offence. **Hundreds of people were banned**, some for decades.

**And the CPSA's response, which is worth noting: it dissolved itself in June 1950, before the Act came into force**, and re-formed underground as the **South African Communist Party in 1953** — from stage 4's lesson.

**Then the escalation, and the dates are the thing to hold:**

| Year | Instrument |
| --- | --- |
| **1950** | **Suppression of Communism Act** — banning, naming, listing |
| **1953** | **Public Safety Act** — **states of emergency**, with rule by regulation |
| **1953** | **Criminal Law Amendment Act** — heavy penalties for protest offences, explicitly to break the Defiance Campaign |
| **1956** | **Riotous Assemblies amendments** — **banishment**: a person could be ordered to a remote place and kept there |
| **1960** | **Unlawful Organizations Act** — **the ANC and PAC banned** |
| **1962** | **"Sabotage" Act** — sabotage defined very broadly, with a **minimum sentence of five years and a maximum of death**, and **the onus of proof reversed** |
| **1963** | **90-day detention** — detention without charge, renewable |
| **1965** | **180-day detention** |
| **1967** | **Terrorism Act, section 6** — **indefinite detention, incommunicado, with no access to a court, a lawyer or a family** |
| **1969** | **Bureau for State Security (BOSS)** established |
| **1982** | **Internal Security Act** — consolidation; **section 29** detention |

**Three features of that escalation are the pattern to recognise.**

**1. Each step removed a protection rather than adding a crime.** 90 days became 180 became indefinite. **The direction is always toward the executive and away from the courts.**

**2. The onus of proof was reversed.** Under the sabotage provisions, **once certain acts were proved the accused had to prove they had not intended the prohibited purpose.** That is the reversal of the presumption of innocence, by statute, for political offences.

**3. The courts were progressively excluded.** Section 6 of the Terrorism Act provided that **no court could pronounce on the validity of a detention or order a detainee's release.** The judiciary's acquiescence in this is one of the genuine controversies about the South African legal profession, and the TRC's legal-sector hearings addressed it.

**What section 6 detention meant in practice.** Indefinite, solitary, incommunicado — **and this is the provision under which people died.** From the security-state lesson later in this stage: **at least 73 deaths in security detention are documented, Steve Biko's in 1977 the best known.** The absence of access and of judicial oversight is what made the deaths possible.

**Now a point this curriculum's posture requires, about how the laws were used.**

**They were used overwhelmingly against non-violent opposition.** The Suppression of Communism Act banned organisations, newspapers and individuals whose activity was speech and organisation. **The sabotage and terrorism laws were used against armed activity and also against anyone the state chose to charge** — from stage 1's commission lesson: these were trials, with convictions, and the convictions covered a very wide range of conduct.

**And they were used against whites too**, which is politically significant: **Bram Fischer, Ruth First, Helen Joseph, the Liberal Party's members, the Christian Institute's Beyers Naudé** — banned, detained, imprisoned. **Beyers Naudé is the notable case**: a Broederbond member and NGK minister who broke with apartheid, was expelled from both, and was banned.

**The legal profession's record is mixed and is worth knowing.** Advocates and attorneys defended political trials at real cost — **and the courts upheld the statutes, because the statutes were valid under stage 3's sovereign-parliament doctrine.** There was no constitution to appeal to.

**Which is the structural point this stage keeps making and stage 7 answers: with a sovereign parliament and no justiciable bill of rights, a lawfully passed statute is simply the law**, and the judge's only question is what it means. **The 1996 Constitution's entire design is a response to that.**

**Practice.** Find the 1950 Act's definition of communism and list five lawful political activities it covers. Then find section 6 of the Terrorism Act 1967 and read what it says about the courts. Then find a banning order's standard terms and work out what a banned person's daily life would be. Then look up Beyers Naudé.
The pass system at its height:
The most-enforced law in South African history, the section that decided whether you could be in a city, and the arrest numbers.

**The statute with the misleading name.** From stage 1's words lesson: the **Natives (Abolition of Passes and Co-ordination of Documents) Act 67 of 1952.**

| What the title says | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| **Abolition of passes** | **replaced several documents with one — the reference book — and made it compulsory** |
| **Co-ordination of documents** | and **extended the system to women**, phased from 1956 |

**The reference book — the *dompas***. A booklet containing identity, classification, employment record, tax receipts, influx-control endorsements and permissions. **Required to be carried at all times and produced on demand.** Failure was a criminal offence.

**And then the provision that actually governed urban life: section 10.** The Natives (Urban Areas) Amendment Act of 1952 provided that no African could remain in an urban area more than 72 hours unless they qualified under one of four categories:

| | **Section 10 rights** |
| --- | --- |
| **10(1)(a)** | **born in the area and permanently resident there** |
| **10(1)(b)** | **worked continuously for one employer for ten years, or been lawfully resident for fifteen** |
| **10(1)(c)** | **the wife, unmarried daughter, or son under eighteen of a qualifying person** — and dependent on them |
| **10(1)(d)** | **holding a permit** issued by a labour bureau |

**Those four categories decided the shape of millions of lives, and the detail is where the cruelty is.**

**Read 10(1)(b) carefully.** Ten years **with one employer** — so a worker who changed jobs started again. **A dismissal in year nine destroyed a decade of qualification**, and the employer knew it.

**Read 10(1)(c) carefully.** A wife's right to be in the city **derived from her husband's**. So:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If he died** | **she could lose the right to remain** |
| **If he lost his qualification** | so did she |
| **If they separated** | she could be endorsed out |
| **A son at eighteen** | **lost the right derived from his father** and needed his own |

**The eighteenth birthday provision is the one that broke families.** A young man born and raised in a township, on his father's qualification, **had to qualify in his own right at eighteen or be endorsed out to a homeland he had never seen.** Thousands were.

**"Endorsed out"** is the term for it: a stamp in the reference book cancelling the right to be in the area, and removal to a homeland.

**The labour bureaux**, which allocated the rest. A person without section 10 rights could work in a city only on a permit, obtained through a bureau that **directed labour where the state wanted it** — to farms and mines rather than to cities, because those were the employers that could not compete for workers.

**So the pass system was a labour-allocation mechanism as much as a control on movement**, which is the functional reading from stage 3 and is well supported here: **the bureaux existed to supply agriculture and mining with workers who would otherwise have gone to cities for better wages.**

**The arrest figures, which are the thing to know.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pass-law arrests ran at hundreds of thousands a year** | peaking well above 300,000 and in some years far higher |
| **Over the system's life** | the figure usually given is **on the order of 17 million arrests for pass offences** |
| **The courts** | dealt with them in bulk, in minutes per case |
| **The consequence for an individual** | a fine, imprisonment, or a farm-labour sentence |

**That last point deserves its own note.** Pass offenders were, for a period, **sent to work on white farms as an alternative to prison** — a system exposed in the 1950s press, notably by *Drum* and by Ruth First's reporting. **A criminal justice system supplying agricultural labour.**

**The scale is the thing to hold.** Seventeen million arrests is not a policy with excesses. **It is the most intensively enforced body of law in the country's history**, applied to a population for being in the wrong place, and it ran for decades.

**What it did to daily life:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Carrying the book, always** | and the fear of having left it |
| **Raids** | in trains, streets, workplaces and homes, at any hour |
| **Separation** | men in cities on contract, families in homelands |
| **Dependence on employers** | who held your qualification in their hands |
| **The 72-hour rule** | which made visiting family a criminal risk |

**And the women's dimension, from stage 4's lesson.** Passes for women were the single most resisted element: **the 1913 Free State campaign, the 1956 march of 20,000 on the Union Buildings, and sustained local resistance through the late 1950s.** The extension to women was slowed and was completed.

**The abolition, and the date matters: 1986.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1986** | **influx control and the pass laws abolished** |
