| **Why** | **they had failed**, exactly as Fagan said in 1948 — from stage 4. Urbanisation had not been reversed; enforcement was consuming the police; and the 1980s townships were ungovernable |
| **What replaced it** | **"orderly urbanisation"** — and in practice the economics of where anyone could afford to live |
| **What did not change** | **the geography.** Group Areas stood until 1991, and the cities' shape stands now |

**So the pass system is the clearest case of an apartheid policy formally abandoned by the apartheid state itself**, four years before de Klerk's speech, **on the grounds that it did not work.** And that concession is one of the most important facts for stage 5's final lesson on why apartheid ended.

**Practice.** Find section 10 and write out the four categories. Then work out what happened to a township-born man on his eighteenth birthday, and to a widow. Then find annual pass-arrest figures for any 1970s year. Then find the 1986 abolition and the government's stated reason for it.
Bantu Education:
The policy stated in public by the man who made it, what it did to a generation, and the paradox in its results.

**Bantu Education Act 47 of 1953.** What it did administratively:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African education transferred** | from the four provinces to the **central Native Affairs Department** |
| **Mission schools** | **required to register and accept state control, or lose their subsidy** |
| **Syllabus** | set centrally, with a new curriculum |
| **Funding** | tied substantially to African taxation, in the pattern of stage 4's Native Revenue Account |
| **Medium of instruction** | mother-tongue in the lower primary years, which the next lessons show becoming explosive |

**The mission schools' destruction is the immediate effect.** From stage 3 and stage 4: **mission schools had educated the entire African political and professional class** — Plaatje, Jabavu, Seme, Luthuli, Mandela, Tambo, Sobukwe.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Most churches transferred their schools** | having no means to run them unsubsidised |
| **The Catholic Church largely kept its schools** | **funding them from its own and overseas resources**, at great cost |
| **The Anglican Church under Trevor Huddleston** | closed St Peter's in Johannesburg rather than hand it over — *"the school that would not be a Bantu school"* |
| **The effect** | the independent educational route out of the system was closed |

**Now the statement, which is why this lesson quotes at length.** **Hendrik Verwoerd**, as Minister of Native Affairs, in the Senate in 1954:

> **There is no place for him in the European community above the level of certain forms of labour… What is the use of teaching the Bantu child mathematics when it cannot use it in practice?**

**That is the policy, in the responsible minister's own words, in Hansard.** It is not an opponent's characterisation. **It is why arguments about whether apartheid's educational effects were intended have an unusually short route to an answer.**

**And the companion statement, on the purpose:** education should train Africans **for their place in a separate society** — so mathematics, science and the professional curriculum were not merely under-provided; **they were considered inappropriate.**

**The spending, which measures the policy:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Per-capita spending ratios** | **by the 1970s roughly ten to one, white to African**, and at some points wider |
| **Teacher qualifications** | African teachers trained to a lower standard, in larger numbers, and paid far less |
| **Class sizes** | **double sessions and "platoon" systems** — two shifts a day through one building |
| **Facilities** | frequently no electricity, no library, no laboratory |
| **Books** | charged for |

**And now the paradox, which is the most interesting thing about Bantu Education and is usually omitted.**

**Enrolment rose enormously.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African school enrolment in 1953** | under a million |
| **By the mid-1970s** | **several million** |
| **Literacy** | rose substantially |
| **Secondary enrolment** | rose, more slowly and then sharply in the 1970s |

**The state expanded African schooling massively while deliberately limiting its quality and content.** Both halves are true and they are not in tension once you see the purpose: **a semi-skilled industrial economy needed workers who could read an instruction and not workers who could qualify as engineers.**

**So the policy produced, by the 1970s, exactly what it had not intended: a large, literate, schooled, urban generation** — educated enough to read, to organise and to understand their position precisely, and denied the education that would have given them anywhere to go.

**That generation is the one that made 1976**, and the next lessons are about it. **The policy's quantitative success produced its political defeat**, which is a pattern worth recognising: **an authoritarian state that needs literate workers cannot keep them politically quiet.**

**The language flashpoint.** From 1974–75 the department enforced a requirement that **certain secondary subjects be taught in Afrikaans** — arithmetic and social studies in Afrikaans, general science and others in English, with mother-tongue instruction below that.

| Why it was intolerable | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pupils and teachers mostly could not teach or learn in it** | and were being examined in it |
| **It was the language of the state** | and of the police |
| **It guaranteed failure** | in a system where failure meant no future |
| **It was imposed** | without consultation, against the advice of school boards |

**That is the immediate cause of the Soweto uprising of 16 June 1976**, and the lesson on it is nine lessons from here.

**The long consequences, and this is why Bantu Education is arguably apartheid's most enduring damage.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A generation under-educated** | and then a second, through the disruption of the 1980s |
| **"Liberation before education"** | the 1980s school boycotts' slogan — and the lost schooling was real |
| **The teaching corps** | trained in a deliberately limited system, and still substantially in service decades later |
| **Mathematics and science** | **the deficit that has proved hardest to close** |
| **The 1996 settlement inherited it** | **and school outcomes remain the most-cited evidence of apartheid's persistence** |

**That last row is where stage 9 and stage 12 pick it up.** South African educational outcomes are poor by international comparison and extremely unequal internally, **thirty years after the policy ended** — and the argument about how much of that is apartheid's inheritance and how much is post-1994 failure is one of the sharpest in the country. **Both sides have real evidence, and the honest position is that it is both.**

**Practice.** Find Verwoerd's 1954 Senate statement in full and read the paragraph around it. Then find per-capita education spending by race for a year in the 1970s. Then find African enrolment figures for 1953 and 1975 and note the increase. Then find the 1974–75 Afrikaans instruction directive and work out what it required of a Soweto schoolteacher.
The universities, and higher education:
How the open universities were closed, the ethnic colleges that replaced them, and why those colleges produced the state's most effective opponents.

**The position before 1959.** Three routes existed for black students:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fort Hare**, founded 1916 | **the premier black university in southern Africa** — and its alumni list is extraordinary: **Mandela, Tambo, Sobukwe, Biko's generation, Robert Mugabe, Julius Nyerere, Kenneth Kaunda, Seretse Khama** |
| **The "open" universities** | **Wits and the University of Cape Town** admitted black students — in small numbers, with social segregation, but admitted |
| **UNISA** | correspondence study, which remained open throughout |

**The alumni list matters politically.** Fort Hare educated the founding presidents of several African states and most of South Africa's liberation leadership. **A single institution, open for forty years, produced the leadership of a continent's independence movements** — which the South African government noticed.

**Extension of University Education Act 45 of 1959.** The title is another of stage 1's examples: **it restricted university education.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Black students barred** from the existing universities | except by **ministerial permit**, rarely granted |
| **Fort Hare taken over** | by the state, and designated **for Xhosa-speaking students** |
| **New ethnic university colleges created** | each for a designated group |

**The institutions, and their designations:**

| College | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Fort Hare** | **Xhosa** |
| **University College of the North (Turfloop)** | Sotho, Tswana, Venda, Tsonga |
| **University College of Zululand (Ngoye)** | **Zulu** |
| **University College of the Western Cape** | **Coloured** |
| **University College, Durban (Westville)** | **Indian** |
| **Later: Medunsa, Vista, the homeland universities** | |

**And the design was explicit.** Ethnically defined institutions, located remotely, with white staff and state-appointed rectors, **teaching a curriculum aimed at producing the professional and administrative class the homelands would need.** The colleges were to be the universities of separate nations.

**The open universities' response**, which is a real and limited piece of resistance:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Wits and UCT opposed the Act** | on grounds of **academic freedom** — a formal institutional position |
| **The protest** | annual, ceremonial, and sustained for decades — the plaques and the academic freedom lectures |
| **Its effect** | **none on the legislation** |
| **The honest assessment** | **they objected and then complied for thirty years**, admitting black students only by permit |

**And their position has been reconsidered since.** The academic freedom tradition was genuine and it was also the defence of institutional autonomy by universities that were, in their composition and culture, part of the order they objected to. **The 2015 Rhodes Must Fall and Fees Must Fall movements in stage 11 made exactly that argument about their inheritors.**

**Now the thing this lesson exists for: the colleges produced the opposition.**

**The South African Students' Organisation — SASO — was founded in 1968–69, at and around these institutions**, by students including **Steve Biko** at the University of Natal's black medical school, with Turfloop and the other colleges as its base.

**Why the ethnic colleges became Black Consciousness's home**, and the mechanism is worth understanding:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They concentrated politically conscious black students** | in residential institutions, away from white society |
| **They had no white students** | **so the question of multiracial student politics did not arise**, and an autonomous black politics could form |
| **They were run paternalistically** | by white staff, with petty authoritarianism that politicised everybody |
| **Their graduates faced a ceiling** | educated for a role in a system they rejected |
| **The ANC and PAC were banned** | from 1960 — **so there was a vacuum, and students were the only organised constituency left** |

**That is the central irony of the 1959 Act, and it is not a small one.** The state built segregated institutions to produce a compliant black professional class, **and the institutions produced the movement that broke the political silence of the 1960s.** Turfloop's 1972 graduation address by Onkgopotse Tiro — attacking Bantu Education from the platform, which got him expelled and later killed by a parcel bomb — is the emblematic moment.

**Fort Hare's own trajectory is the saddest part.** From the premier institution in southern Africa to an ethnic college under state control, **and its alumni list ends in the 1950s.** The place that educated Mandela, Tambo and Sobukwe spent thirty years as a Xhosa college in the Ciskei.

**The repeal and after.** The Act's restrictions were eased from the 1980s as the "white" universities began admitting black students in growing numbers under permits and then freely, and **the formal system ended with the 1990s.**

**What was inherited in 1994:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A deeply stratified system** | historically white institutions with endowments, libraries and research capacity; historically black institutions without |
| **The merger programme** of the early 2000s | which consolidated and renamed many institutions |
| **A funding and access problem** | **which produced Fees Must Fall in 2015** — stage 11 |
| **The "historically disadvantaged institution" category** | still in use in funding policy |

**So the 1959 Act's institutional geography is still the sector's geography**, in the same way that Group Areas is still the cities'. **Stage 9's education lesson and stage 12 both come back to it.**

**Practice.** Find Fort Hare's alumni list for the 1940s and 1950s and count the heads of state. Then read the 1959 Act's title and its provisions, and note the mismatch. Then find where SASO was founded and by whom. Then read Tiro's 1972 Turfloop graduation address and what happened to him.
Bantu Authorities, and the homelands beg:
The policy that distinguishes apartheid from segregation — governing the African majority as separate nations, and the statutes that built it.

**This is grand apartheid, and it is the part with no real precedent.** Stage 4 established that the pass laws, the land Acts, the colour bar and the urban doctrine were all in place before 1948. **The homeland project was not.**

**Bantu Authorities Act 68 of 1951**, the first step:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Abolished the Natives Representative Council** | from stage 4 — the advisory body that had declared itself a toy telephone in 1946 |
| **Created a hierarchy** | **tribal authorities** under chiefs → **regional authorities** → **territorial authorities** |
| **Built on the 1927 Act** | from stage 4: the Supreme Chief doctrine, rule by proclamation, and chiefs as state appointees |
| **The theory** | Africans would exercise political rights **through traditional structures in their own areas**, not in the common system |

**So the Act's logic: if Africans have political institutions somewhere, their exclusion from Parliament is not a denial of political rights but an allocation of them.** That is the argument grand apartheid rests on, and everything after builds it out.

**Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act 46 of 1959**, Verwoerd's measure and the one that states the doctrine:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Eight — later ten — "national units"** | defined ethnically: **Transkei, Ciskei, KwaZulu, Bophuthatswana, Venda, Gazankulu, Lebowa, QwaQwa, KaNgwane, KwaNdebele** |
| **Each to progress** | through self-government toward independence |
| **Commissioners-General** | appointed to each |
| **And the price** | **the three white representatives of African voters in Parliament were abolished** |

**That last row is the trade and it is explicit.** From stage 4's franchise lesson: the 1936 Act had left Africans three white MPs. **The 1959 Act removed them, on the argument that Africans would now be represented in their own national units instead.**

**So the sequence of African parliamentary representation, complete:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1853–1936** | **Cape common roll, qualified, non-racial** |
| **1936–1960** | **three white MPs on a separate roll** |
| **1960–1994** | **none** |

**Why "nations" rather than one African population**, and this is the ideological core:

| The claim | |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa contains many nations** | a white nation and several African nations, each with its own language, custom and territory |
| **Each nation has the right to self-determination** | in its own homeland |
| **So there is no racial discrimination** | **only the separate development of distinct peoples** |
| **And the white nation's exclusive claim to 87% of the land** | follows from its being one nation among several |

**That argument is the state's own, it was made in international forums for thirty years, and it is the reason "separate development" replaced "apartheid" in official language.** Stage 1's words lesson: the euphemism is doing argumentative work, and the work is this.

**What is wrong with it, stated in the terms the argument invites.** Four objections, and they are the ones made at the time:

| Objection | |
| --- | --- |
| **The nations were partly constructed by the state** | **ethnic classification was administered**, and people were assigned to nations they had not chosen. From stage 4's institutions lesson: the method is the one Afrikaner nationalism used on itself, applied by a state to others |
| **The territory was absurd** | **13% of the land for two-thirds of the people** — from stage 4's 1936 lesson — in non-contiguous fragments |
| **The economies could not work** | which the state's own commission said: the next lesson |
| **Nobody asked** | **no homeland's population was consulted on whether it wished to be a nation** |

**And the fifth objection is the decisive one: the policy's purpose was revealed by the citizenship provision of 1970**, three lessons from here, which used the homelands to strip South African citizenship from Africans. **A self-determination argument that results in the removal of citizenship is not a self-determination argument.**

**The ethnic assignment is worth one more note** because it has modern consequences. The homelands' boundaries and the ethnic categories they institutionalised — **Zulu, Xhosa, Tswana, Venda, Pedi, Tsonga, Swazi, South Sotho** — were given administrative reality by the policy: **school language, chiefly authority, identity documents, and eventually a passport.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Were the ethnic identities invented?** | **no** — they existed, with real histories |
| **Were they politicised and hardened by the policy?** | **substantially yes** |
| **Does that matter now?** | **yes.** The IFP's Zulu nationalism in stage 6, and the ethnic dimension of the 1990–94 violence, are partly this inheritance |

**Which is the careful position: pre-existing identities, selected, bounded, given institutions and made politically salient.** The same analysis stage 4 applied to Afrikaner nationalism, and the same conclusion: **the question is not whether an identity is real but who gave it these particular institutions and for what.**

**Practice.** List the ten homelands and the ethnic group each was designated for. Then read the 1959 Act's provision abolishing the African representatives in Parliament, and note what it was traded against. Then state the self-determination argument as strongly as you can, and then state the four objections. Then decide which objection is strongest and why.
Tomlinson, and the viability question:
The state's own commission on whether the homelands could work, what it recommended, and the decision not to do it.

**The commission.** Appointed in 1950 under **Professor F. R. Tomlinson** to report on the socio-economic development of the "Bantu areas". **It worked for four years, produced a report of enormous length, and was published in summary in 1955.**

**It is the single most important document in the history of apartheid policy**, because it is the state asking, in detail, whether its central project was feasible — and getting an answer.

**What it found:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reserves could support, on the existing basis, only a fraction of their population** | the commission's assessment was that the areas could carry roughly **half to two-thirds** of the people then in them, by agriculture |
| **Land was overstocked and eroding** | from generations of overcrowding |
| **Agriculture was not viable** | on holdings of the existing size, with the existing methods and no capital |
| **Industry did not exist** | and would not arise without investment |
| **The population was growing** | and the policy proposed to add to it |

**And what it recommended, which is the part to know, because the scale is the point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Massive capital investment** | **about £104 million over ten years**, as a first instalment |
| **Consolidation of the land** | into contiguous blocks, by purchase |
| **Industrialisation inside the areas** | which meant **admitting white capital**, because no other capital existed |
| **A full-time farming class** | on **viable, larger holdings** — which necessarily meant **a landless majority** |
| **Towns, services, infrastructure** | |

**The commission was not an opponent of apartheid.** It accepted the policy's objectives and asked what they would cost. **Its answer was: this much, and it will work only if you do all of it.**

**What Verwoerd did with it:**

| Recommendation | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| **£104 million over ten years** | **refused.** A small fraction was allocated |
| **White capital in the reserves** | **refused** — it would compromise the areas' African character. **Border industries outside them instead**, from the 1960s |
| **A full-time farming class on viable holdings** | **refused** — it would create a landless class and the state needed the reserves to hold people |
| **Land consolidation** | **accepted in principle**, pursued slowly and incompletely |

**So the state's own commission said the homelands required a given scale of investment and a given reorganisation of land, and the government declined both while proceeding with the policy.**

**That is the fact that makes the viability argument unanswerable in one direction** — and it is why this lesson exists. **The homelands' failure was not a surprise, an accident or an unforeseen outcome. It was reported in advance by the state's own commission and the remedy was refused.**

**Why Verwoerd refused, and the reasons are coherent on their own terms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cost** | £104 million was a very large sum and the white electorate would have paid it |
| **White capital in the reserves** | would have created white interests inside the homelands, which contradicted the separation |
| **A landless class in the reserves** | **would have had to go somewhere — the cities** — which is exactly what the policy existed to prevent |
| **And the fourth reason, which the functional account supplies** | **viable reserves would not supply migrant labour.** From stage 3's Wolpe lesson: the labour system depended on the reserves being insufficient |

**That fourth reason is where the interpretations diverge, and this is one of the cleanest cases for stage 1's method.**

| Reading | |
| --- | --- |
| **The functional reading** | **the refusal was rational.** Viable homelands would have ended the migrant labour supply, so the policy required their non-viability. **Verwoerd's decision served the labour system** |
| **The ideological reading** | **the refusal was doctrinal.** White capital and a landless class were incompatible with separation as a principle, and Verwoerd sacrificed viability to consistency |
| **The fiscal reading** | the money was not there, and the electorate would not vote it |

**All three have support and they are not exclusive.** The strongest form of the composite: **the policy's ideological requirements and the economy's labour requirements pointed the same way, and the cost pointed the same way again** — so the refusal was overdetermined.

**What followed, which confirms the analysis.** The border industries policy of the 1960s: **factories sited just outside the homeland boundaries**, with incentives, so that workers could live in the homeland and work in South Africa.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The logic** | development "for" the homeland without capital inside it |
| **The effect** | **daily and weekly migrancy**, with the worker's home in a homeland and the job in South Africa |
| **The reading** | **the homelands as labour dormitories**, which is what the functional account predicts |

**And the resettlement camps from the removals lesson are the other half of it:** populations placed in the homelands with no economy, surviving on remittances and pensions. **Tomlinson had said the areas could support a fraction of their existing population; the state proceeded to increase it by about 3.5 million people.**

**The comparison that settles the viability question empirically.** From stage 3's Lesotho lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Lesotho** | **a real state, with real sovereignty, international recognition, aid, and its own government** — in the same geography, with the same mountains and the same lost arable land |
| **And it could not support itself either** | depending on mine remittances, water sales and imports |

**So even genuine independence in that geography did not produce self-sufficiency** — which means the homelands' economic failure was partly structural and not only a consequence of the refusal to invest. **Both things are true: the geography was unforgiving, and the state declined the remedy its own commission specified.**

**Practice.** Find Tomlinson's assessment of what proportion of the population the reserves could carry. Then find the recommended investment figure and what was actually allocated. Then read Verwoerd's reasons for rejecting white capital in the reserves. Then set Lesotho beside the Transkei and work out what each tells you about viability.
The Coloured vote and the constitutional:
Five years in which a government was defeated in court, enlarged the Senate, enlarged the court, and won — and the reason the 1996 Constitution looks as it does.

**The target.** From stage 3: the **Cape's Coloured voters remained on the common roll** after 1936. Removing them required the **entrenched-clause procedure — a two-thirds majority of both Houses sitting together.**

**The government did not have two-thirds. It tried anyway.**

**The sequence, and it is worth following closely because it is the only time a South African court seriously obstructed the apartheid state:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1951** | **the Separate Representation of Voters Act** passed as **ordinary legislation**, by simple majority |
| **1952, *Harris v Minister of the Interior*** | **the Appellate Division strikes it down.** The entrenched clauses are binding; a simple majority cannot do this |
| **1952** | the government creates a **"High Court of Parliament"** — Parliament itself, sitting as a court, to review the judges |
| **1952, *Minister of the Interior v Harris*** | **the Appellate Division strikes that down too** |
| **1953** | **the government wins a general election**, increasing its majority — but still short of two-thirds |
| **1955, the Senate Act** | **the Senate enlarged from 48 members to 89**, with the additional members nominated so as to deliver the government's majority |
| **1955, the Appellate Division Quorum Act** | **the Appeal Court enlarged from five judges to eleven for constitutional cases**, with the new appointments the government's |
| **1956** | **the South Africa Act Amendment Act passes at a joint sitting with the required two-thirds.** Coloured voters removed to a separate roll electing four white MPs |
| **1957, *Collins v Minister of the Interior*** | **the enlarged court upholds it** |

**Read what happened there.** A court held legislation invalid. The government **changed the composition of the legislature and of the court** until the result changed. **And every step was lawful** — the Senate Act and the Quorum Act were valid statutes of a sovereign parliament.

**That is the lesson, and it is the most important constitutional lesson in South African history:**

> **A procedural entrenchment cannot restrain a government willing to change the procedure. Only a supreme constitution with a court empowered to strike down amendments can.**

**And it is exactly why the 1996 Constitution is built the way it is.** From stage 7:

| 1910–1983 | 1996 |
| --- | --- |
| **Parliament sovereign** | **the Constitution supreme** |
| **Entrenched clauses by special majority** | **a Bill of Rights, justiciable** |
| **Courts could interpret, not invalidate** | **the Constitutional Court can strike down legislation, including constitutional amendments on some grounds** |
| **The Senate could be enlarged at will** | **amendment requires 75% for the founding provisions, 66⅔% generally, plus provincial concurrence** |
| **The court's composition at the government's discretion** | **the Judicial Service Commission**, with a prescribed composition |

**Every one of those right-hand entries is a response to the left.** The 1950s crisis is the negative template of the South African constitutional order, and the people who drafted 1996 — many of whom were lawyers who had lived through this — said so.

**The resistance, which is worth recording because it was white and large and it failed.**

**The Torch Commando**, 1951–53: a protest movement of Second World War veterans, led by the fighter ace **"Sailor" Malan**, opposing the government's constitutional method.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Scale** | **membership claimed up to a quarter of a million** — one of the largest protest movements in white South African history |
| **The grievance** | **the rule of law and the constitution**, not racial equality as such |
| **Its limit** | it could not decide whether to admit black members or to oppose apartheid itself, and it did neither |
| **Outcome** | **collapsed by 1953** |

**The Torch Commando's failure is instructive about white opposition generally.** It mobilised enormous numbers against the government's *methods* and could not survive the question of whether it opposed the government's *purpose*. **The same fracture runs through white liberal politics for the next forty years** — and the United Party's decline, the Progressive Party's founding in 1959 with one MP, and the Liberal Party's dissolution in 1968 are its history.

**What happened to Coloured representation after 1956:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1956–68** | **four white MPs**, elected on a separate Coloured roll |
| **1968** | **separate representation abolished entirely**, and the **Coloured Persons Representative Council** created — advisory, from stage 4's toy-telephone pattern |
| **1980** | the Council abolished |
| **1983** | **the tricameral parliament** — a separate Coloured chamber, which stage 5's later lesson covers, and which was boycotted |
| **1994** | the common roll, universal |

**So Coloured South Africans lost the common roll vote in 1956, were offered three successively less meaningful substitutes, and regained it in 1994** — thirty-eight years.

**And one consequence that matters for the present.** The Western Cape's distinctive politics — **the only province the ANC has not won since 1994** — has several causes, and this history is one of them. **A population removed from the common roll by the National Party, then removed from its homes by the Group Areas Act, and then offered a chamber in 1983 that its own organisations boycotted**, has a political memory that does not map onto the national one. **Stage 10 and stage 12 both return to it.**

**Practice.** Follow the sequence from 1951 to 1957 and write down what the government changed at each step. Then list the four 1996 constitutional features that answer it. Then read about the Torch Commando and identify the question that destroyed it. Then count the years between 1956 and 1994.
The Defiance Campaign, 1952:
The first mass civil disobedience campaign of the apartheid era, the date it was launched on, and the reason it ended.

**The decision.** From stage 4: the ANC adopted the **Programme of Action** in December 1949 — boycott, strike, civil disobedience. **The Defiance Campaign is its first full application.**

**The planning.** A **Joint Planning Council** of the ANC and the **South African Indian Congress**, from 1951 — the Doctors' Pact of 1947 in operation. **Jointly organised from the start**, which matters: it is the Congress Alliance's first joint action.

**The date, which was chosen.** The campaign was launched on **26 June 1952** — and the timing was deliberate against the **1952 tercentenary celebrations of Van Riebeeck's landing**, from stage 3's first lesson. **The state was celebrating three hundred years of white settlement; the campaign was the answer.**

**The method: deliberate, public, non-violent breach of specific laws, by volunteers who courted arrest.**

**The six laws selected:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The pass laws** | entering a city without a permit; not carrying a reference book |
| **The Group Areas Act** | entering a location without a permit |
| **The Separate Amenities Act** | **using facilities reserved for whites** — benches, entrances, waiting rooms, post office counters |
| **The curfew regulations** | being out after hours |
| **The Bantu Authorities Act** | |
| **The Suppression of Communism Act's banning orders** | attending gatherings |

**The method's logic, and it is the classic one: fill the jails.** Volunteers broke a law openly, gave their names, refused bail and refused to pay fines, and went to prison. **The aim was to make the laws unenforceable by making their enforcement unaffordable.**

**The scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Volunteers arrested** | **about 8,500** over roughly six months |
| **Mandela's role** | **volunteer-in-chief**, organising the batches |
| **Geographic spread** | strongest in the eastern Cape — **Port Elizabeth and East London** — and in the Transvaal |
| **Participation** | African, Indian, Coloured and a small number of white volunteers |

**And the effect on the ANC, which is the campaign's most durable result:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ANC membership before** | **roughly 7,000** |
| **ANC membership after** | **around 100,000** |

**That is the transformation.** The ANC had been, from stage 4, a small organisation of professionals and chiefs. **The Defiance Campaign made it a mass organisation** — and every subsequent phase of its history depends on that.

**It also produced the leadership of the next forty years.** Mandela, Sisulu, Tambo, Dadoo, Kathrada, and **Albert Luthuli**, who became ANC president in 1952 after being deposed as a chief for refusing to abandon his politics — from stage 4's lesson on chiefs.

**Why it ended, and this is the part to understand.**

**Two things happened in late 1952.**

**First, riots.** In October and November there were outbreaks of violence in **East London, Port Elizabeth, Kimberley and Johannesburg**, in which people were killed, including a white nun in East London. **The ANC's leadership denied responsibility and the evidence is that the campaign's own volunteers were disciplined and non-violent**; the riots arose separately, in townships under pressure, and the state attributed them to the campaign.

**Which is the structural vulnerability of mass non-violent action: it cannot control everyone it mobilises**, and a single violent incident is available to the state as the campaign's meaning.

**Second, and decisively, the state legislated.** From the security lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1953** | **penalties for protesting against a law**: fines, imprisonment up to three years, and **whipping**. And heavier penalties for inciting others |
| **Public Safety Act, 1953** | **states of emergency**, with government by regulation |

**The Criminal Law Amendment Act was written to destroy the Defiance Campaign and it worked.** Filling the jails depends on the penalty being bearable. **When the penalty became three years and a whipping, the supply of volunteers stopped.**

**That is the campaign's lesson, and it is a hard one: non-violent civil disobedience works against a state with limits, and the apartheid state removed its limits by statute within a year.**

**What the campaign established:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Mass support existed** | 8,500 volunteers and 100,000 members proved it |
| **Joint action across racial organisations worked** | and the Congress Alliance followed |
| **The ANC became a mass organisation** | permanently |
| **Non-violent mass defiance could be legislated against** | and was |
| **The state would not be shamed into concession** | which is the finding that leads, eight years later, to the armed struggle |

**And the international dimension began here.** The campaign put South Africa on the **United Nations agenda** in 1952, and the UN's involvement in apartheid — resolutions, the Special Committee, and eventually sanctions — dates from it.

**The comparison everyone makes, and its limit.** The campaign's method is Gandhi's, from stage 3's indenture lesson — **developed in South Africa, exported to India, and brought back.** The ANC's leadership was explicit about the lineage.

**The limit is that Gandhi's satyagraha had worked against a colonial power with a metropolitan public opinion it had to answer to.** The National Party answered to a white electorate that approved of what it was doing. **There was no equivalent pressure point, and the campaign's failure established that.**

**Practice.** Find the six laws the campaign targeted and the date it was launched, and work out why that date. Then find the ANC's membership figures before and after. Then read the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1953 and note the penalties. Then write down why filling the jails stopped working.
The Freedom Charter, 1955:
The document the Congress tradition has argued about for seventy years, how it was written, and the three clauses that are still live.

**The event. The Congress of the People, at Kliptown, Johannesburg, 25–26 June 1955.** About **3,000 delegates**, from across the country, meeting on open ground.

**How it was drafted, which is the part that gives it its authority.** Not by a committee. **The Congress Alliance sent out "freedom volunteers" to collect demands** — on scraps of paper, at meetings, in townships and villages and farms — asking people what they wanted in a free South Africa.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Submissions collected** | **thousands** — the figure usually given is around ten thousand |
| **Drafting** | a committee worked the submissions into a document |
| **Adoption** | clause by clause, at Kliptown |
| **The police** | **surrounded the gathering on the second day and took names and documents**, which is how the Treason Trial's evidence was gathered |

**The Alliance that convened it** — and the composition is the thing the next lesson's split is about:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The African National Congress** | |
| **The South African Indian Congress** | |
| **The South African Coloured People's Organisation** | |
| **The Congress of Democrats** | **white** |
| **The South African Congress of Trade Unions (SACTU)** | from 1955 |

**The Charter's clauses, as headings:**

| |
| --- |
| **The People Shall Govern!** |
| **All National Groups Shall Have Equal Rights!** |
| **The People Shall Share in the Country's Wealth!** |
| **The Land Shall Be Shared Among Those Who Work It!** |
| **All Shall Be Equal Before the Law!** |
| **All Shall Enjoy Equal Human Rights!** |
| **There Shall Be Work and Security!** |
| **The Doors of Learning and Culture Shall Be Opened!** |
| **There Shall Be Houses, Security and Comfort!** |
| **There Shall Be Peace and Friendship!** |

**Read it.** It is two pages, it is free, and **both the claim that the 1994 settlement honoured it and the claim that it betrayed it are made constantly by people who have not.**

**The three clauses that are still live, in the exact words that matter.**

**1. On the economy:**

> **The mineral wealth beneath the soil, the banks and monopoly industry shall be transferred to the ownership of the people as a whole.**

**That is a nationalisation clause and it says what it says.** Which is why:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is cited by the left** | as the Charter's economic commitment, abandoned after 1994 |
| **It is cited by the right** | as evidence the ANC's economic intentions were always socialist |
| **Mandela's 1990 statements** | affirmed nationalisation as policy; **by 1992–94 it was no longer policy** — stage 6 |
| **The EFF's founding position** | **is this clause** |

**2. On the land:**

> **The land shall be shared among those who work it.**

**Note what it does and does not say.** "Among those who work it" is not "returned to those dispossessed", and it is not "redistributed by race". **It is a formulation about labour on the land**, which is a different principle from restitution — and the difference matters for stage 9's land lesson, where the three mechanisms (restitution, redistribution, tenure reform) rest on different principles and only one of them is the Charter's.

**3. On national groups:**

> **All national groups shall have equal rights.**

**This is the clause the Africanists rejected**, and the next lesson is the split it produced. **The objection: "national groups" concedes that South Africa contains distinct national groups** — which is the premise of apartheid's own separate-development argument from the homelands lesson. **The Africanist position was that there is one nation, Africa's, and that recognising groups imports the enemy's framework.**

**And the drafting history fuels the objection.** The Charter was drafted by a committee in which white and Indian Congress members were prominent, with **Lionel "Rusty" Bernstein** generally credited with the drafting. **The claim that it was therefore not the authentic voice of the African majority was made at the time** and is one of the PAC's founding arguments.

**How to assess that claim, in stage 1's terms.** The evidence for the Charter's authenticity is the collection process — **thousands of submissions from ordinary people.** The evidence for the objection is the drafting — **a committee shaped the result, and committees have views.** Both are true; **the dispute is about how much the drafting changed, and the submissions' originals are substantially lost**, so it cannot be settled.

**The Charter's later career, which is the real measure of it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1956** | **used as evidence of treason** — the next lesson |
| **1960s–80s** | the ANC's foundational document in exile; **"Charterist" becomes the name for the ANC-aligned tradition**, against Black Consciousness and against the PAC |
| **1983** | **the UDF adopts it** — a national front of 600 organisations, built on it |
| **1990s** | the basis of the ANC's negotiating position on rights |
| **1996** | **much of it is in the Bill of Rights** — equality, dignity, assembly, movement, housing, health care, education, labour rights |
| **And one part is not** | **the nationalisation clause**, and section 25 protects property instead |

**That last comparison is the sharpest way to read the third big disagreement from stage 1** — victory or compromise. **Set the Charter beside the 1996 Bill of Rights:**

| Charter | 1996 Constitution |
| --- | --- |
| The people shall govern | **universal franchise, achieved** |
| All shall be equal before the law | **section 9, achieved** |
| Houses, security and comfort | **section 26, as a progressively realisable right** |
| Doors of learning opened | **section 29** |
| Work and security | **section 23 labour rights** |
| **Mineral wealth, banks and monopoly industry to the people** | **not in it.** Section 25 protects property |
| **Land shared among those who work it** | **section 25(5)–(9): restitution, redistribution and tenure reform, subject to compensation** |

**Eight of ten, substantially delivered; two, not.** And the two are the economic ones. **That table is the argument, and both sides are reading the same document.**

**Practice.** Read the whole Freedom Charter — ten minutes. Then set its economic clause beside section 25 of the Constitution. Then find the Africanist objection to "all national groups" and state it as strongly as you can. Then decide what the table above shows, and what would change your mind.
The Treason Trial:
One hundred and fifty-six people charged with treason over a political document, a trial that ran for four years, and a complete acquittal that changed the state's methods.

**The arrests. In the early hours of 5 December 1956, police arrested 156 people across the country** and flew them to Johannesburg.

**Who they were:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The entire senior leadership of the Congress Alliance** | **Albert Luthuli** (ANC president), **Mandela**, **Sisulu**, **Tambo**, **Yusuf Dadoo**, **Monty Naicker**, **Helen Joseph**, **Lilian Ngoyi**, **Ruth First**, **Joe Slovo**, **Ahmed Kathrada**, **Z. K. Matthews** |
| **Composition** | **105 Africans, 21 Indians, 23 whites, 7 Coloureds** — which is itself a statement about the Alliance |

**The charge: high treason**, carrying the death penalty. **The alleged conspiracy: to overthrow the state by violence and replace it with a communist one.**

**And the principal evidence was the Freedom Charter.**

**That is the trial's centre.** The state's case was that the Charter from the last lesson was **a blueprint for a communist state**, and that the campaign to achieve it necessarily involved violence, so that the whole Congress movement was treasonable.

**The trial's course:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **December 1956** | arrests |
| **1957** | **the preparatory examination** — a committal proceeding that took a year |
| **1957** | charges against **61 accused withdrawn** |
| **1958** | the indictment quashed; **a new indictment against 30** |
| **1958–1961** | **the trial itself**, before a special court of three judges at Pretoria |
| **1960** | **the Sharpeville emergency intervenes**; the accused are detained under the emergency while on trial, and the defence team withdraws for a period in protest |
| **29 March 1961** | **all remaining accused acquitted** |

**The judgment's reasoning, which is the thing to know.** The court found:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC did seek to replace the state** | **with a radically different one** |
| **The Freedom Charter was its programme** | and the Charter did envisage fundamental change |
| **But the state had failed to prove** | **that the ANC had a policy of violence** |
| **Nor that it was a communist organisation** | |
| **Therefore** | **no treason.** Acquitted |

**So a South African court, in 1961, having heard four years of the state's evidence, found that the ANC's programme was not violent and that it was not communist** — which is a finding of some weight against the characterisation on which the next thirty years of security policy rested.

**And it was a fair trial, which is worth saying plainly.** The special court conducted itself properly, the defence — led by **Israel Maisels** and **Bram Fischer** — was given room, and the judges decided against the government on the evidence. **The apartheid judiciary's record is mixed and this is the best of it.**

**What the trial cost, which was the point even without a conviction:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Four and a half years** | of the leadership's time and attention |
| **Attendance in court** | daily, for the accused, from across the country |
| **Livelihoods** | lost |
| **Defence costs** | enormous, funded substantially from abroad — the **Treason Trial Defence Fund** |
| **Organisational paralysis** | during the most important years of the 1950s |

**So the state achieved by process what it failed to achieve by verdict**, which is a pattern: **the trial as an instrument of attrition.** The same technique recurs — in the 1980s treason trials, in the Delmas trial, and in the lawfare of later decades.

**The consequence that matters most, and it is the reason this lesson sits here.**

**The acquittal taught the state that the courts were unreliable.**

| And its response was to stop using them | |
| --- | --- |
| **1962–63** | **the sabotage law, with reversed onus and minimum sentences** |
| **1963** | **90-day detention without charge** |
| **1967** | **indefinite detention under section 6, with no court access** |
| **Banning orders** | **ministerial, no trial** |
| **Banishment** | ministerial |

**From the security lesson: each step moved power from the courts to the executive.** The Treason Trial is why. **A state that cannot convict its opponents of treason in four years will find a procedure that does not require conviction** — and section 6 detention is a procedure in which the court has no role at all.

**And one more consequence, in the other direction.** The trial created the political generation. **Four years in a courtroom together, across racial organisations, built the relationships of the Congress Alliance's leadership** — and the accused repeatedly said so afterwards. **The state assembled the movement's leaders in one room for four and a half years.**

**Luthuli during the trial**, and the detail that places it: **Albert Luthuli, one of the accused, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1960** and granted a ten-day passport to collect it in Oslo in 1961 — **while under a banning order, from a country prosecuting him for treason.** He returned to his banning order and died in 1967.

**Practice.** Find the number and racial composition of the 156 accused. Then find the court's finding on whether the ANC had a policy of violence. Then list the security statutes passed between 1962 and 1967 and note which require a trial. Then look up Luthuli's Nobel Prize and the terms on which he was allowed to collect it.
The PAC split, and 1959:
The division inside African nationalism over whether the struggle should be African or multiracial — the organisation it produced, and the campaign that changed everything.

**The disagreement, from stage 4's Youth League lesson.** **Anton Lembede's original Africanism** held that the struggle must be led by Africans, for Africans, without alliance with whites, Indians or communists. **Sisulu, Tambo and Mandela moved away from it toward the Congress Alliance.** The Africanists did not.

**What they objected to, specifically:**

| Objection | |
| --- | --- |
| **"All national groups shall have equal rights"** | from the Charter lesson: **it concedes that South Africa contains distinct national groups**, which is apartheid's own premise |
| **The Congress of Democrats** | **a white organisation inside the Alliance** — and in the Africanist reading, a communist one steering African politics |
| **Multiracialism against non-racialism** | **the Alliance was organised as separate racial congresses**, which the Africanists said institutionalised race even while denying it |
| **The leadership's caution** | the Charter's committee drafting, the deputations, the legalism |
| **Who the land belongs to** | **"Africa for the Africans"** — the land is African, and whites are settlers with no inherent claim |

**That fourth and fifth are the live ones and they are still live.** The question of whether whites in South Africa are **fellow citizens** or **settlers** is the single deepest division in the country's political thought, and 1959 is where it was formalised.

**The split.** The Africanists were defeated at the ANC's 1958 Transvaal conference, walked out, and on **6 April 1959 founded the Pan Africanist Congress.**

**The date was chosen.** **6 April is Van Riebeeck's day** — from stage 3's first lesson, and the holiday the Defiance Campaign had been launched against in 1952. **Founding an African nationalist party on the anniversary of the Dutch landing is a statement.**

**Robert Sobukwe**, its first president: a lecturer in African languages at Wits, a former Youth League Africanist, and by every account the most formidable intellect in the generation.

**The PAC's positions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Africanism** | **one nation, African, with no "national groups"** |
| **Membership** | **African only**, in practice |
| **"Africa for the Africans"** | and Sobukwe's definition of an African: **anyone who owes loyalty only to Africa and accepts majority rule** — which is more open than the slogan sounds |
| **Pan-Africanism** | alignment with Nkrumah's Ghana and the continental movement |
| **Method** | **"positive action"** — immediate, dramatic, mass defiance, without the Charterists' phased planning |

**Sobukwe's definition of an African deserves the emphasis**, because the PAC is routinely described as racially exclusive and his formulation was not: **loyalty and acceptance of majority rule, not descent.** The practice was more exclusive than the formulation; both are the record.

**Then the anti-pass campaign, and the detail that matters.**

**The ANC had announced an anti-pass campaign for 31 March 1960.** The PAC, nine months old and needing to establish itself, **announced its own for 21 March** — ten days earlier.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The PAC's method** | **men would leave their passes at home, present themselves at police stations, and demand to be arrested** |
| **Sobukwe's instruction** | explicit: **absolute non-violence** |
| **The aim** | fill the jails, break the pass system, and do it immediately |
| **Sobukwe himself** | **walked to Orlando police station on the morning of 21 March and was arrested** |

**And at Sharpeville, which the next lesson is about, the police opened fire.**

**So the PAC's first campaign produced the massacre that defined the era**, and the organisation was banned within three weeks of it.

**The two organisations' fates after 1960, which is the part to know:**

| | **ANC** | **PAC** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Banned** | **April 1960** | **April 1960** |
| **Armed wing** | **Umkhonto we Sizwe**, Dec 1961 | **Poqo**, 1961–62 |
| **Exile** | **built a substantial organisation** — diplomacy, training, the Soviet bloc, the OAU, the UN | **fractured into factions**, repeatedly |
| **Leadership** | Tambo in exile for thirty years; Mandela imprisoned and became the symbol | **Sobukwe imprisoned, then detained on Robben Island under a clause renewed annually for him specifically, then banished to Kimberley; died 1978** |
| **Internally** | the UDF's Charterist tradition from 1983 | **influence substantially passed to Black Consciousness** |
| **1994** | **62.6% of the vote** | **1.2%** |

**The "Sobukwe clause" is worth naming.** The General Law Amendment Act of 1963 contained a provision allowing the annual renewal of his detention by ministerial order — **a statute with one man in mind, renewed every year for six years.** He was then banished to Kimberley under house arrest until his death.

**Why the ANC prevailed and the PAC did not — four reasons, and the first is the largest:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Organisational capacity in exile** | **the ANC built an apparatus; the PAC split** |
| **The alliance** | which gave the ANC Indian, Coloured and white members, international networks, legal and medical professionals, and the SACP's discipline — **exactly what the Africanists objected to** |
| **Soviet support** | which followed from the alliance |
| **Sobukwe's removal** | the PAC lost its one unifying figure immediately and permanently |

**So the Africanist critique's substance — that alliance with whites and communists would compromise African leadership — was answered in practice by the fact that the alliance worked and the alternative did not.** Which is not the same as the critique being wrong, and stage 12's arguments about economic transformation are its descendants.

**The PAC's intellectual afterlife is larger than its electoral one.** Black Consciousness in the 1970s, from a later lesson, is substantially Africanist in inheritance; **the EFF's land position echoes "Africa for the Africans"**; and the question Sobukwe put — **whose country is this** — is asked constantly.

**Practice.** Read Sobukwe's definition of an African and compare it with the slogan. Then find the Charter's "national groups" clause and the Africanist objection to it. Then establish the two anti-pass campaign dates and which came first. Then look up the Sobukwe clause and how many times it was renewed.
Sharpeville, and the turn to armed strug:
The day everything changed, the three weeks that followed, and the decision that the next thirty years rested on.

**21 March 1960, Sharpeville**, a township near Vereeniging.

**What happened.** Following the PAC's campaign call from the last lesson, a crowd gathered at the police station — the estimates range widely, from around 5,000 to 20,000 — **to present themselves for arrest without passes.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The police** | about 300, reinforced, with Saracen armoured vehicles |
| **Around 1.15pm** | **the police opened fire** without an order to disperse being effectively given, and continued firing as the crowd fled |
| **Killed** | **69**, including **8 women and 10 children** |
| **Wounded** | **more than 180** |
| **And the forensic finding** | **most of the dead were shot in the back** |

**Langa, Cape Town, the same day:** a march and police action in which **three were killed.**

**The "shot in the back" finding is the fact that made Sharpeville what it became.** It establishes that the crowd was fleeing, which disposes of the self-defence account the police gave, and it was established at the time.

**What followed, in three weeks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Immediately** | strikes, marches and protest across the country |
| **30 March** | **Philip Kgosana leads about 30,000 people from Langa and Nyanga into central Cape Town** — one of the largest marches in South African history. He is persuaded to disperse the crowd on a promise of a meeting, and is then arrested |
| **30 March** | **a state of emergency declared.** About **18,000 detained** |
| **8 April** | **the Unlawful Organizations Act. The ANC and the PAC banned** |
| **9 April** | **Verwoerd shot and wounded** at the Rand Easter Show by a white farmer; he recovers |
| **1 April** | **UN Security Council Resolution 134** — the Council's first substantive action on apartheid |
| **Economically** | **capital flight, a collapse in share prices, and reserves falling sharply** |

**Kgosana's march is the forgotten part and it is extraordinary.** Thirty thousand people walked into the centre of Cape Town, the city was effectively theirs, **and a 23-year-old student dispersed them on an undertaking that was not honoured.** The counterfactual — what would have happened had they stayed — is one of the great unanswered questions of South African history.

**Why Sharpeville is the turning point, in five respects:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Internationally** | **it made apartheid a world issue.** The UN Security Council acted; South Africa's isolation begins here; **21 March is now the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination** |
| **2. Economically** | **the first capital flight** — and it established that political crisis had a price |
| **3. Legally** | **the banning of the ANC and PAC** closed legal political organisation for the African majority. **For thirty years there was no lawful African political party** |
| **4. The Commonwealth** | South Africa left in 1961, rather than face expulsion over apartheid |
| **5. Strategically** | **it ended the argument about non-violence** |

**The fifth is this lesson's substance.**

**The decision. With the organisations banned, their leaders detained or in exile, the Defiance Campaign's method legislated against in 1953, and Sharpeville demonstrating the state's willingness to shoot, the ANC's leadership concluded that non-violent methods had been exhausted.**

**Umkhonto we Sizwe — "Spear of the Nation", MK — was formed in 1961, and its first operations were on 16 December 1961.**

**The date is chosen again: 16 December is the Day of the Vow**, from stage 3's Great Trek lesson. **Blood River's anniversary.**

**MK's founding manifesto stated the reasoning:**

> **The time comes in the life of any nation when there remain only two choices: submit or fight. That time has now come to South Africa.**

**The strategy, initially, and the distinction is important:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sabotage, not terrorism** | **targets were installations — pylons, government offices, railway signals — chosen to avoid loss of life** |
| **Why** | to demonstrate seriousness and force negotiation, **without a race war** |
| **Luthuli's position** | **the ANC president remained committed to non-violence**, and MK was constituted as a separate organisation precisely so that the ANC's own position was formally preserved |
| **The SACP's role** | substantial — the party had reached the same conclusion, and much of MK's early leadership was jointly ANC and SACP |

**The Luthuli point is the one most often got wrong.** The ANC did not become an armed organisation in 1961. **MK was established as a separate body, and the ANC's formal position remained Luthuli's** — which allowed him to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo in December 1961, days before MK's first attacks. **The arrangement was a fiction and it was a deliberate one.**

**The PAC's parallel: *Poqo*** — "pure" or "alone" — **from 1961, which was more diffuse, more locally organised, and which carried out attacks involving deaths**, including of civilians. **It was broken by the state in 1963** with mass arrests.

**And the white armed grouping, which is usually omitted: the African Resistance Movement**, 1964, a small group of mostly young white radicals, whose **station bombing in Johannesburg killed a woman and injured others.** Its member John Harris was hanged in 1965 — **the only white person executed for a political offence under apartheid.**

**What the turn to armed struggle achieved militarily, honestly assessed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Militarily** | **very little.** MK never threatened the state's security |
| **Politically** | **a great deal.** It established that the movement would not acquiesce, and it gave the struggle a form international supporters could support |
| **Symbolically** | **enormous.** Rivonia, Mandela's statement, and the movement's survival in exile |
| **Strategically** | **it made the ANC the recipient of Soviet and OAU support**, which built the exile organisation |
| **In the 1980s** | the armed struggle's real function was **to make the townships' resistance part of something national** |

**The honest historiographical point for stage 1's second disagreement — what ended apartheid.** If the armed struggle never threatened the state militarily, then it cannot be the cause by itself. **The resistance account rests on the 1970s and 1980s mass movements, not on MK's operations** — and the next lessons build that case.

**Practice.** Find the Sharpeville casualty figures and the finding on where the dead were shot. Then look up Kgosana's march of 30 March and what he agreed to. Then find MK's founding manifesto and the date of its first operations, and work out why that date. Then find Luthuli's Nobel acceptance date and compare it with MK's first attacks.
Rivonia, and the silent decade:
The trial that removed the movement's leadership for a generation, the statement that made Mandela, and the decade of quiet that followed.

**The raid. On 11 July 1963 police raided Liliesleaf Farm at Rivonia**, north of Johannesburg — MK's underground headquarters — and arrested most of its high command, with the documents.

**Mandela was already in prison.** Arrested in August 1962 and sentenced in November to five years for incitement and leaving the country without a passport. **He was brought from prison to be the first accused at Rivonia.**

**The accused:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Nelson Mandela** | |
| **Walter Sisulu**, **Govan Mbeki**, **Raymond Mhlaba**, **Elias Motsoaledi**, **Andrew Mlangeni** | |
| **Ahmed Kathrada** | |
| **Denis Goldberg** | **white** |
| **Lionel Bernstein** | **acquitted** |
| **James Kantor** | charges withdrawn |

**The charge: sabotage, not treason.** And that choice is the Treason Trial's legacy, from two lessons ago: **the 1962 sabotage law carried the death penalty, reversed the onus of proof, and was far easier to prove than treason.** The state had learned.

**The evidence: Operation Mayibuye**, a document found at the farm setting out a plan for guerrilla warfare — insurgent units, external bases, a general uprising. **Whether it had been adopted as policy or was a draft under discussion was disputed by the accused and is still argued**; the state treated it as the plan, and the court substantially accepted that.

**The defence's strategy, and it is unusual.** The accused did not deny MK's existence or their part in sabotage. **They admitted it and justified it** — which converted the trial into a political platform at the risk of their lives, since the charge carried death.

**Bram Fischer led the defence.** A Free State Afrikaner of distinguished family, a QC, and a member of the underground Communist Party — **which the state did not know while he was conducting the defence.** He was arrested the following year, convicted, and **died in custody in 1975**. He is among the most remarkable figures in this history.

**Mandela's statement from the dock, 20 April 1964.** Four hours. It is free to read and it is the single most important political text in modern South African history. **Its closing passage:**

> **I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination. I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities. It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.**

**Three things about that statement, as a document.**

**The "black domination" clause is doing deliberate work.** It is addressed to white South Africa and to the world, and it commits the movement to non-racialism at the moment it is being prosecuted as a racial threat. **From stage 1's method: that is what the statement is for.**

**It is an argument, not a plea.** The bulk of it explains why sabotage was chosen, why non-violence had been abandoned, what MK's strategy was and was not, and what the ANC wanted. **It was written to be read as a historical document, and it has been.**

**And he said it expecting to be hanged.** The sentence was not known; the charge carried death; the words "prepared to die" were a calculation about what the sentence would mean politically.

**The verdict, 11 June 1964; the sentence, 12 June: life imprisonment** for eight of the accused. **Bernstein acquitted.** The judge, Quartus de Wet, declined the death penalty — for reasons that have been argued about ever since, with international pressure and the probable consequences generally credited.

**Where they went. Goldberg, as a white prisoner, to Pretoria Central. The rest to Robben Island.**

**And then the silent decade, which is the period's real subject.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC and PAC** | banned since 1960 |
| **Their leadership** | **imprisoned, exiled, or dead** |
| **MK's internal structures** | **broken** by Rivonia and the arrests that followed |
| ***Poqo*** | broken by 1963 |
| **The ARM** | broken by 1964 |
| **Trade unions** | African unions had no legal standing, from stage 4 |
| **The press** | constrained, and banned persons could not be quoted |

**For roughly ten years — 1964 to 1973 — there was no significant organised internal opposition.** The state had won, comprehensively, and said so.

**What filled the decade instead:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Exile politics** | the ANC's external mission under **Tambo**, building an organisation, diplomacy and training. **Thirty years of it** |
| **Robben Island** | **which became the movement's university.** Political education, discipline, the formation of a leadership cadre — and the relationships that governed South Africa after 1994 |
| **Economic boom** | the next-but-one lesson: the highest growth in South African history |
| **And then, from 1968–69** | **Black Consciousness** — a new generation, with no organisational memory of the ANC, in the universities apartheid had built |

**Robben Island's role deserves its emphasis.** Thirty years of political prisoners in one place, with time, produced: **a systematic political education programme, a disciplined organisational culture, the "University of Robben Island", and — crucially — the negotiating leadership of 1990.** Mandela's own account is that his understanding of Afrikaners and of what a settlement would require was formed there.

**And the prison's conditions were severe** — hard labour in the lime quarry, which permanently damaged eyesight; censorship; one visit and one letter every six months initially. **The conditions improved over the decades, substantially through the prisoners' own organised resistance.**

**Practice.** Read Mandela's statement from the dock in full — it takes an hour and it is free. Note what proportion of it is explanation rather than appeal. Then look up why sabotage rather than treason was charged, and what the 1962 Act changed. Then read about Bram Fischer. Then list what organised internal opposition existed in 1968, and compare it with 1958.
Verwoerd, the Republic, and separate dev:
The prime minister who turned segregation into a theory of nations, the referendum that made a republic, and his assassination.

**Hendrik Verwoerd.** Minister of Native Affairs 1950–58, Prime Minister 1958–66. **Trained in psychology, an academic, editor of *Die Transvaler*** — and the figure conventionally called the architect of apartheid.

**Why the title is roughly right.** The architecture was substantially built before him, from stage 4. **What Verwoerd supplied was the theory that made it a system rather than a collection of measures** — and the administrative will to carry it through.

| His contribution | |
| --- | --- |
| **Bantu Education** | his Act, and his statement of its purpose |
| **The homelands as nations** | the 1959 Promotion of Bantu Self-Government Act |
| **"Separate development"** | the doctrine, and the vocabulary |
| **The rejection of Tomlinson** | from that lesson: the decision not to fund viability |
| **The Republic** | |
| **Administrative thoroughness** | **the most systematically implemented social engineering of its era** |

**The doctrine, stated as he stated it.** Not that whites were superior — that was the older segregationist register. **That South Africa contained several distinct nations, each entitled to self-determination in its own territory**, and that apartheid was therefore not discrimination but decolonisation.

**That reframing is Verwoerd's work and it should be understood as an intellectual achievement of a repellent kind.** It gave the policy:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An answer to the UN** | **self-determination is the UN's own principle** |
| **An answer to the churches** | diversity of nations as divinely ordained |
| **An answer to decolonisation** | **apartheid as Africa's own decolonisation**, running in parallel with Ghana's and Nigeria's |
| **A trajectory** | so the policy was going somewhere, which segregation was not |
| **And a defence against the franchise argument** | Africans were not disenfranchised; **they were enfranchised elsewhere** |

**The timing matters. Verwoerd took office in 1958, the year before Ghana's independence had been followed by the rest of the continent's.** Macmillan's "wind of change" speech was delivered to the South African Parliament in **February 1960** — a British Prime Minister telling that House that African nationalism was the future. **Verwoerd replied immediately and in person**, and his separate-development doctrine is the answer he had already prepared: **South Africa would decolonise too, into its own nations.**

**The Republic.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The referendum** | **5 October 1960** — **whites only** |
| **Result** | **52.3% in favour** |
| **The Republic declared** | **31 May 1961** |
| **The date, again** | **Vereeniging 1902, Union 1910, Republic 1961** — all on 31 May |
| **The Commonwealth** | **South Africa left**, having withdrawn its application to remain after other members' objections to apartheid |

**Fifty-nine years after Vereeniging, the republican project of stage 3's *bittereinders* was complete** — and it was completed by a 52% majority of white voters, in a referendum from which the majority of South Africans were excluded. **The date was chosen to say exactly what it said.**

**Leaving the Commonwealth is the first real cost of apartheid internationally**, and it was paid willingly: **Verwoerd returned from London to a hero's welcome.** English-speaking white South Africans had voted against the republic in substantial numbers, and the 1961 settlement is the moment Afrikaner nationalism stopped needing them.

**What the 1960s looked like under him:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Opposition** | **crushed** — Rivonia, the bannings, the silent decade |
| **The economy** | **booming**, the next lesson |
| **Removals** | accelerating |
| **The homelands** | self-government legislated, Transkei first in 1963 |
| **International isolation** | beginning, and not yet costly |
| **White confidence** | **at its height** |

**The assassination. On 6 September 1966 Verwoerd was stabbed to death in the House of Assembly by Dimitri Tsafendas**, a parliamentary messenger of Greek-Mozambican background.

**Tsafendas's case is strange and worth a line.** He was found unfit to stand trial on grounds of mental illness — he spoke of a tapeworm directing him — **and was detained for the rest of his life, dying in 1999.** Later research has argued that his political motives were real and that the insanity finding was convenient for a state that did not want a political assassination; **the question is genuinely unresolved.**

**Verwoerd's legacy, assessed in the terms this stage uses.**

**What he achieved:** the policy's most complete implementation, its most coherent justification, the Republic, and a decade of white security.

**What he did not:** make it work.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The homelands** | **not viable, and he had been told so and declined the remedy** |
| **Urbanisation** | **not reversed** — the African urban population grew throughout |
| **International acceptance of separate development** | **never achieved by any state** |
| **The economic ceiling** | the next lesson: his education policy produced the skills shortage that ended the boom |

**And the deepest contradiction is in the education lesson.** Verwoerd's Bantu Education expanded African schooling enormously while deliberately limiting its content — **and the economy he was building needed skilled workers his policy forbade producing.** That contradiction is the subject of the next lesson and of the Wiehahn reforms fifteen years later.

**Practice.** Find Macmillan's "wind of change" speech and Verwoerd's reply, and read them together. Then state the separate-development argument in Verwoerd's own terms, as persuasively as you can. Then list the three events on 31 May and work out what the choice of date asserts. Then look up the 1960 referendum's franchise and its result.
The homelands as independent states:
Four states recognised by one country, their governments, and the function they performed.

**The programme. From self-government to "independence", on the 1959 Act's trajectory.**

**The four that took it — the TBVC states:**

| | Independent |
| --- | --- |
| **Transkei** | **1976** |
| **Bophuthatswana** | **1977** |
| **Venda** | **1979** |
| **Ciskei** | **1981** |

**And the six that did not:** KwaZulu, Lebowa, Gazankulu, QwaQwa, KaNgwane, KwaNdebele — **all took self-government and refused independence.**

**The refusals are politically the more important fact.** And the most important refusal was **Mangosuthu Buthelezi's KwaZulu.**

| Buthelezi's position | |
| --- | --- |
| **Accepted self-government** | and the Chief Minister's office |
| **Refused independence** | **repeatedly and publicly**, on the ground that it would denationalise Zulu South Africans |
| **Founded Inkatha in 1975** | as a cultural and then political movement |
| **Opposed sanctions and the armed struggle** | which made him acceptable to Western governments and to Pretoria |
| **And opposed apartheid** | in his own terms |

**That combination made him the most consequential and most contested black political figure of the period** — a homeland leader who used the homeland platform against the policy's central aim, and whose organisation became, in the 1980s and 1990s, the ANC's principal violent antagonist. **Stage 6 and stage 10 both take him up properly.**

**Why independence mattered so much to the state.** Because of the next lesson: **independence was the mechanism for removing South African citizenship from Africans.** A self-governing homeland's people were still South African; **an independent one's were not.**

**So the four independences removed the citizenship of about eight million people**, and the six refusals preserved it for the rest. **That is what Buthelezi's refusal was about and why it was the single most effective act of obstruction in the policy's history.**

**What the TBVC states actually were:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Recognised by** | **South Africa, and each other. No other state, ever** |
| **Territory** | **non-contiguous fragments** — Bophuthatswana was in **seven pieces** |
| **Economies** | **dependent on South African transfers**, migrant remittances, and later casinos and border industries |
| **Governments** | **one-party, with security legislation copied from South Africa's and used freely** |
| **Leaders** | **Kaiser Matanzima** (Transkei), **Lucas Mangope** (Bophuthatswana), **Patrick Mphephu** (Venda), **Lennox Sebe** (Ciskei) |

**And their internal repression is a part of this history that the ANC-centred account underplays.** The homeland governments detained, tortured and killed their own opponents:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ciskei under Sebe** | **a notorious security police**, detentions, deaths |
| **Transkei under Matanzima** | emergency rule, detentions, opposition suppressed |
| **Bophuthatswana under Mangope** | detention and suppression of unions |
| **The TRC** | **heard extensively about homeland security forces**, and its findings cover them |

**So the homelands produced black-governed states that practised the repression of the state that created them** — which is a fact both the apartheid government and the liberation movement found awkward, for opposite reasons.

**The casinos and the odd economics**, worth knowing because they explain the landscape:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gambling was illegal in South Africa** | and legal in the homelands |
| **So** | **Sun City in Bophuthatswana**, and casinos in the Transkei and Ciskei |
| **Also** | **"adult" entertainment and boxing** prohibited in South Africa |
| **The result** | **resorts serving white South Africans, in nominally foreign countries forty minutes from Johannesburg** |
| **And the cultural boycott's sharpest edge** | **"I ain't gonna play Sun City"** — the 1985 Artists United Against Apartheid record, which made the arrangement internationally notorious |

**The 1980s instability, which is how the project ended:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Transkei, 1987** | **a coup — Bantu Holomisa takes power**, and aligns with the ANC |
| **Bophuthatswana, 1988** | **a coup against Mangope, put down by the South African Defence Force** — which reveals the sovereignty exactly |
