| **Ciskei, 1990** | **a coup — Oupa Gqozo**, whose forces killed 29 ANC marchers at **Bisho in September 1992**, a central event of stage 6 |
| **KwaNdebele, 1986–89** | a sustained popular revolt against independence, which **defeated the independence proposal** |

**The 1988 Bophuthatswana coup is the decisive illustration.** South African troops restored a foreign head of government to power in his own country. **No one could pretend after that.**

**The end. The 1993 interim constitution reincorporated all ten homelands into South Africa**, and the 1994 election was held across the whole territory. **The TBVC states' independence lasted between thirteen and eighteen years and was recognised by nobody.**

**What was inherited:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Administrations** | **absorbed into the new provinces**, with their staff — a major source of post-1994 capacity problems |
| **Debt and pension liabilities** | |
| **Land under communal tenure** | administered by traditional authorities — stage 9's tenure problem |
| **The poorest regions of the country** | and they remain so, measurably |
| **Traditional leadership structures** | whose place in the new order had to be negotiated — stage 8 |

**The former homelands are still visible in every South African development statistic**, which is the most durable thing the policy produced.

**Practice.** List the four TBVC states and the four that refused. Then find Buthelezi's stated reason for refusing independence and connect it to the next lesson. Then look up the 1988 Bophuthatswana coup and who restored Mangope. Then find a current map of South African poverty and compare it with a map of the former homelands.
Citizenship, 1970:
The statute that made every African South African a foreigner in waiting — apartheid's logical endpoint, and the eight million people it denationalised.

**The Act. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act 26 of 1970**, later the National States Citizenship Act.

**What it did:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every African South African was assigned citizenship of a homeland** | **whether or not they had ever been there** |
| **Assignment was by** | language, ethnic classification, descent, or administrative decision |
| **It applied to everyone** | **including people born in Johannesburg to parents born in Johannesburg** |
| **And then** | **when a homeland became "independent", its citizens ceased to be South African** |

**That is the mechanism, and it is the point of the whole homeland project.**

**Work through what it means for one person.** A man born in Soweto in 1940, whose family had lived in Johannesburg for three generations, speaking Setswana:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1970** | **declared a citizen of Bophuthatswana**, a territory he has never visited |
| **1977** | **Bophuthatswana becomes "independent"** |
| **Therefore** | **he is no longer a South African citizen.** He is a foreign national in the city of his birth |
| **His status in South Africa** | a migrant worker, present on permit, under influx control |
| **His children** | citizens of Bophuthatswana |

**That is not an interpretation. It is what the law provided, and it was applied to about eight million people.**

**The numbers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Denationalised by the four independences** | **roughly 8 million people** |
| **Assigned homeland citizenship in total** | **the entire African population** — around 15 million by 1970 |
| **The intended endpoint** | **if all ten homelands had taken independence, no African would have been a South African citizen** |

**Read that last row again, because it is the policy's destination.** The logical completion of separate development was **a South Africa with no African citizens at all** — a country in which the majority of the people living and working in it were foreigners.

**Connie Mulder, Minister of Plural Relations, said so in Parliament in 1978:**

> **If our policy is taken to its full logical conclusion… there will be not one black man with South African citizenship.**

**That is the state's own formulation, from the responsible minister, in Hansard.** From stage 1: the strongest evidence about what a policy was for is frequently the government's own statement of it.

**Why it was done, in two registers.**

**The stated reason: self-determination.** From the Verwoerd lesson — Africans would have full political rights in their own nations, and therefore needed none in South Africa.

**The functional reason: it answered the demographic argument.** The white electorate's central anxiety was that whites were a minority. **Denationalisation solved it arithmetically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa's population, counted as it was** | **about 70% African** |
| **South Africa's population, excluding homeland citizens** | **a white plurality or majority, depending on which homelands were counted** |
| **So** | **apartheid's demographic problem was solved by redefining the denominator** |

**That is stage 1's statistics lesson, applied by a state to its own census.** And it was applied: official population figures in the late 1970s and 1980s excluded TBVC citizens, so **published South African statistics of the period undercount the population and overstate every per-capita figure.** Anyone using 1980s South African data needs to know which population it covers.

**What it did to people practically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Passports** | TBVC passports, which almost nowhere accepted |
| **Travel** | and therefore effectively none |
| **Pensions and benefits** | transferred to homeland administrations, and reduced |
| **Employment in South Africa** | as a foreign migrant, on permit |
| **Section 10 rights** | from the pass lesson — and these interacted brutally |
| **The right to be anywhere** | contingent on a permit from a state one was not a citizen of |

**The resistance, and it was substantial.** Denationalisation was the single most resented element of the policy, and it is why six homelands refused independence:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **KwaZulu under Buthelezi** | **refused on exactly this ground** — and KwaZulu's population was the largest, so the refusal preserved millions of citizenships |
| **KwaNdebele, 1986–89** | **a popular revolt that defeated an independence proposal** — one of the few outright defeats the policy suffered |
| **KaNgwane** | refused, and resisted a proposed transfer to Swaziland |
| **Urban communities** | resisted assignment and reassignment constantly |

**The reversal:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1986, Restoration of South African Citizenship Act** | **partial** — restored citizenship to some TBVC citizens **permanently resident in South Africa**, which left millions out |
| **1993–94** | **full restoration**, with the reincorporation of the homelands and the interim constitution |
| **1994** | everyone voted |

**The 1986 partial restoration is itself informative.** It came in the same year as the abolition of influx control, from the pass lesson — **the year the state conceded that its urban policy had failed.** Having conceded that Africans were permanently in the cities, it had to concede that they could not all be foreigners. **The two concessions are the same concession.**

**Why this lesson is the hinge of stage 5.** Because it answers the question the whole stage poses.

**Separate development claimed to be self-determination. Its statutory endpoint was the removal of citizenship from the majority of the population without their consent.** A self-determination argument whose implementation strips nationality from the people it claims to liberate is not a self-determination argument — **and the minister said in Parliament that this was the intended conclusion.**

**That is the clearest single reason the "break" reading of 1948 has force**, from stage 4's closing lesson. **No segregation government before 1948 proposed to denationalise the African population.** It required the homeland theory, and the homeland theory was Verwoerd's.

**Practice.** Find the 1970 Act and read how homeland citizenship was assigned. Then find Mulder's 1978 statement in Hansard. Then take a 1980 South African population figure and establish whether it includes TBVC citizens. Then list the six homelands that refused independence and the reason each gave.
The 1960s boom, and the ceiling:
The fastest economic growth in South African history, why it happened, and the constraint that apartheid itself had built into it.

**The numbers.** Through the 1960s the South African economy grew at roughly **5.5 to 6 per cent a year** — **among the fastest growth rates in the world for that decade**, comparable with Japan's and well above Western Europe's.

**And it happened in the decade of Sharpeville, Rivonia, the removals and the Republic.** The relationship between repression and growth is the lesson's subject.

**Why it grew — six causes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Political stability, achieved by repression** | **the silent decade.** Investors who fled after Sharpeville returned from 1963, when the state had demonstrably won |
| **2. Cheap and controlled labour** | from stage 3's whole apparatus — monopsony, pass law, no legal unions |
| **3. Import substitution behind tariffs** | from stage 4's Pact policy, matured |
| **4. Foreign capital** | direct investment and loans, substantial through the decade |
| **5. State investment** | the parastatals — Eskom, ISCOR, SASOL, the railways — building infrastructure |
| **6. Gold** | a reliable export earner, with costs controlled |

**The first cause is the uncomfortable one and it should be stated plainly.** Foreign investment returned **after** the state had crushed its opposition. **The capital flight of 1960 reversed once the ANC was banned, its leadership imprisoned and the townships quiet.** That is the historical record and it is the strongest evidence for the claim that international capital was, in the 1960s, a beneficiary and an enabler.

**Which bears on stage 1's second disagreement — what ended apartheid.** If capital flowed **in** when repression succeeded, then capital's later withdrawal in the 1980s was a response to repression's **failure**, not to its existence. **That is the economic account's own logic, and it is a less flattering version than the one usually told.**

**Now the ceiling, which is this lesson's point and is Feinstein's central argument about the period.**

**The economy ran out of skilled workers.**

| The mechanism | |
| --- | --- |
| **Industrial growth needs skilled labour** | technicians, artisans, supervisors, clerks |
| **The white population was small** | and fully employed by the mid-1960s |
| **Immigration could not fill it** | though the state tried hard, with assisted white immigration |
| **The African population was large and available** | |
| **And apartheid forbade training or employing them in skilled work** | **the colour bar from stage 3, job reservation from the 1956 Act, and Bantu Education from this stage** |

**So the economy hit a constraint that the political system had created and could not relieve without dismantling itself.**

**That is the strongest form of the claim that apartheid became economically irrational** — and note the word *became*. From stage 3's gold lesson: **cheap unskilled labour was functional for a mining economy.** For a manufacturing economy needing skills, **the same policy was a binding constraint.**

| Era | Apartheid's labour policy was |
| --- | --- |
| **Mining, to the 1940s** | **functional** — cheap unskilled migrant labour was exactly what was needed |
| **Manufacturing, from the 1960s** | **dysfunctional** — the skills the economy needed were the ones the policy forbade |

**That table resolves a good deal of the argument between the liberal and revisionist traditions from stage 1.** They are describing different economies. **The functional account is right about the first period and the irrationality account is right about the second**, and the transition is in the 1960s.

**What the state did about it, and the sequence is revealing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1960s** | **denial, and white immigration** |
| **Late 1960s onward** | **"floating" the colour bar** — jobs quietly reclassified so Africans could do them at African wages, with union agreement |
| **1970s** | **training schemes for Africans in semi-skilled work**, cautiously |
| **1979** | **Wiehahn** — African unions recognised, job reservation abolished. Four lessons from here |
| **1980s** | the whole labour order unravelling |

**The "floating colour bar" is the thing to notice.** Rather than repeal the bar, the state and the unions allowed specific jobs to be reclassified downward — **so an African could do the work at a lower wage and a white worker moved up.** It relieved the constraint and preserved the principle, which is the classic form of apartheid's economic management.

**The 1970s reprieve, which complicates the story.** Just as the constraint bit, **the gold price was freed in 1971 with the end of Bretton Woods, and it rose enormously** — from $35 an ounce to several hundred dollars by 1980.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The windfall** | **vast.** Export earnings, state revenue and the balance of payments all transformed |
| **The effect** | **it postponed the reckoning by most of a decade** and funded the military build-up of Total Strategy |
| **And then** | **the gold price fell through the 1980s**, at the same time as sanctions, debt and rebellion |

**So the 1970s gold boom is why apartheid survived the 1970s**, and its reversal is part of why the 1980s were terminal. **Stage 5's final lesson weighs it.**

**One number that belongs here.** From stage 3: **real black mine wages were roughly no higher in 1970 than in 1911.** Over the same decade that the economy grew at 6% a year.

**And then they rose sharply after 1973** — the Durban strikes, two lessons from here, and the gold windfall. **Which establishes the causal direction: the wages were not held down by the market, and when the political constraint on organisation weakened, they moved.**

**Practice.** Find South African GDP growth rates by year for the 1960s and compare with Japan's and West Germany's. Then find when foreign investment returned after Sharpeville and what had happened politically by then. Then read Feinstein on the skilled labour constraint. Then find the gold price in 1970 and in 1980.
Black Consciousness, and Biko:
The movement that broke the silence of the 1960s, its central argument about the mind, and the death that made it international.

**The context, from the Rivonia lesson: by 1968 there was no significant legal internal opposition.** The ANC and PAC banned, their leaders imprisoned or exiled, the unions without standing, the decade quiet.

**And from the universities lesson: the state had built segregated ethnic colleges**, which concentrated politically conscious black students in residential institutions with no white students and nothing else to do.

**The founding. The South African Students' Organisation — SASO — formed in 1968 and constituted in 1969**, with **Steve Biko** as its first president.

**The break it made was from NUSAS** — the National Union of South African Students, liberal, multiracial and white-led. **Biko's argument for leaving was the movement's founding idea:**

| The argument | |
| --- | --- |
| **White liberals in a multiracial organisation set its terms** | by education, confidence, resources and habit — **however good their intentions** |
| **So black students in NUSAS were junior partners** | in their own liberation |
| **And the posture of gratitude** | was itself part of the damage |
| **Therefore** | **black people must organise separately, and lead** |
| **"Black man, you are on your own"** | |

**And the crucial move, which is why Black Consciousness is not a racial nationalism: the redefinition of "black".**

> **Black** means, in Biko's usage, **all those who are by law or tradition politically, economically and socially discriminated against and who identify themselves as a unit in the struggle towards the realisation of their aspirations.**

**So "black" includes African, Coloured and Indian** — and **excludes** those so classified who collaborate. **It is a political category, defined by position and commitment, not by descent.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Apartheid's categories** | **African, Coloured, Indian** — separate, ranked, and designed to divide |
| **Black Consciousness's category** | **black** — one, chosen, and designed to unite |
| **The word "non-white"** | **rejected** — it defines people by what they are not |

**That redefinition is the movement's most durable achievement.** "Black" in the broad, political South African sense comes from here, and from stage 1's words lesson: it is still the sense used in the B-BBEE Act, though by a very different route.

**The central argument, which is psychological and is the thing to understand.** Biko's claim was that **the deepest injury of apartheid was to the mind**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Oppression had been internalised** | as inferiority, deference, self-doubt, and the acceptance of white standards as standards |
| **So liberation had to begin there** | **"the most potent weapon in the hands of the oppressor is the mind of the oppressed"** |
| **Which means** | psychological liberation is **prior** to political liberation, not a consequence of it |
| **And it can begin now** | **without permission, without an organisation the state can ban, and without waiting** |

**That is why the movement could grow in a decade when organised politics was impossible.** Consciousness cannot be banned. **It was a political strategy chosen for conditions in which nothing else was available**, and it worked.

**What it built:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **SASO**, 1968–69 | students |
| **The Black People's Convention**, 1972 | a political movement |
| **Black Community Programmes** | clinics, literacy, self-help — **practical work, deliberately, as consciousness in action** |
| **The Zanempilo clinic** | at King William's Town, which Biko ran while banned |
| **Black Theology** | with the churches |
| **Writing** | ***I Write What I Like***, Biko's collected columns, which is the text to read |

**Its relation to the ANC tradition, which was tense.** Black Consciousness was Africanist in inheritance, from stage 5's PAC lesson, and it rejected:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Charterist multiracialism** | **"all national groups"** — the same objection the PAC had made |
| **White participation in the leadership** | on the NUSAS argument |
| **The exile organisations' remoteness** | and their claim to direct internal politics |

**And yet most of its surviving leadership eventually went into the ANC or the UDF**, and the movement's generation — radicalised by it, organised in the 1980s — became the Charterist mass movement's cadre. **The relationship is one of the most argued-about questions in the movement's history.**

**Biko. Born 1946, expelled from medical school for his politics, banned in 1973 to King William's Town, and detained on 18 August 1977 under section 6 of the Terrorism Act.**

**What happened:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In detention at Port Elizabeth** | interrogated, and sustained **severe head injuries** |
| **Examined by district surgeons** | who recorded findings and did not act on them |
| **11 September 1977** | **driven roughly 1,100 kilometres to Pretoria, naked, in the back of a Land Rover**, unconscious |
| **12 September 1977** | **died on a cell floor in Pretoria**, aged 30 |
| **The Minister of Police, Jimmy Kruger** | said publicly that Biko's death **"leaves me cold"** |
| **The inquest, 1977–78** | **found no one responsible** |

**The exposure.** The **Rand Daily Mail** and the editor **Donald Woods** — a friend of Biko's — reported the death and the inquest. **Woods was banned and fled the country.** The international reaction was immediate and large.

**The consequences:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **October 1977** | **18 Black Consciousness organisations banned**, with **two newspapers including *The World***, and dozens detained |
| **November 1977** | **UN Security Council Resolution 418 — a mandatory arms embargo**, the first mandatory sanction against South Africa |
| **The doctors** | **the medical profession's failure became a major scandal**, and the two district surgeons were eventually disciplined, years later, after a long campaign |
| **1997** | **five former security policemen applied to the TRC for amnesty**, admitting involvement. **Amnesty was refused**, because they did not make full disclosure and the killing was not found to have a political objective in the required sense |
| **Prosecution** | **never.** The NPA declined to prosecute; the family's objections are on record |

**The TRC amnesty refusal is the detail to hold.** Biko's killers admitted involvement, were refused amnesty, **and were never prosecuted** — which is stage 11's argument about Zondo's referrals, prefigured twenty years earlier.

**And the medical profession's failure is the part that is least comfortable and most instructive.** Doctors examined a man with brain injuries in police custody and recorded findings consistent with the police account. **The South African Medical Association's handling of it took years to correct and remains a standard case in medical ethics teaching worldwide.**

**Practice.** Read Biko's definition of "black" and compare it with the B-BBEE Act's from stage 1. Then read one essay from *I Write What I Like*. Then find the chronology of his detention and death and the inquest's finding. Then look up the TRC's amnesty decision on his killers and the reason amnesty was refused.
The Durban strikes, 1973:
A hundred thousand workers out with no union and no leaders, and the movement it started — which became the most effective opposition apartheid faced.

**January 1973, Durban.** About 2,000 workers at **Coronation Brick and Tile** stopped work and demanded a wage increase.

**Within three months:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Workers out** | **around 100,000** |
| **Factories affected** | **more than 150**, across the Durban–Pinetown industrial area |
| **Demands** | **wages**, almost entirely |
| **Organisation** | **none — no union, no committee, and deliberately no identifiable leaders** |

**The leaderlessness was a tactic, and a good one.** From stage 4: African workers were excluded from the definition of "employee", so unions had no standing and strikes were criminal. **A strike with named leaders produced prosecutions.** A strike with none produced a mass of workers at a factory gate with nobody to arrest.

**It worked.** Employers, faced with a stopped factory and no one to negotiate with, **conceded wage increases.**

**Why 1973, and the conditions are the lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Wages had stagnated** | from stage 3 and the boom lesson: **real black wages had barely moved in sixty years** |
| **Inflation was rising** | so real wages were falling |
| **The economy was tight** | labour was scarce in a growing manufacturing sector |
| **And employers could pay** | which the concessions proved |
| **The political vacuum** | from the Rivonia lesson — no ANC, no PAC, nothing to be prosecuted as |

**And there was a small, important intellectual input.** In Durban a circle around the academic **Rick Turner** and the **Institute for Industrial Education** had been working on exactly this — **worker organisation as the available route when political organisation was banned.** Their argument was that the factory was the one place the state's controls did not reach, because production had to continue.

**Turner was banned in 1973 and assassinated at his home in January 1978**, shot through a window. **No one was ever charged.**

**What the strikes started:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1973–79** | **the independent union movement** — small, unregistered unions built on shop-floor organisation, with elected shop stewards |
| **1979** | **FOSATU** — the Federation of South African Trade Unions, with a deliberately **non-political, shop-floor "workerist"** orientation |
| **1979** | **Wiehahn** — the next lesson, which legalised them |
| **1985** | **COSATU** — the Congress of South African Trade Unions, with around half a million members at its launch, **and an explicitly political alignment** |
| **1980s** | **the most powerful organised opposition in the country** |

**The "workerist" against "populist" argument inside the movement matters and is still live.** FOSATU's position was that **unions should build worker power on the factory floor and not subordinate themselves to a nationalist movement**; the Charterist position was that the struggle was national and the unions were part of it. **COSATU's 1985 formation and its 1987 adoption of the Freedom Charter settled it in the Charterists' favour** — and the question of whether that was right is one of stage 12's arguments, because it is the lineage of COSATU's current position inside the governing alliance.

**Why the strikes were the beginning of the end, and this is the claim to weigh.**

**From stage 5's whole architecture: apartheid's labour order rested on African workers having no legal standing, no bargaining power and no organisation.** The Durban strikes demonstrated, in three months, that:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Workers would act without organisation** | |
| **Employers would concede** | because stopping production cost more than the wages |
| **The state could not prevent it** | without shutting the factories |
| **And the law against unions was useless** | **it prevented recognition, not action** |

**That last point is the structural discovery.** Outlawing unions did not prevent strikes; **it prevented the orderly settlement of strikes.** Employers were facing illegal stoppages with no procedure, no recognised counterpart and no agreement that would hold.

**And it was employers who pressed the state to change the law** — which is the Wiehahn lesson, and one of the clearest instances of capital's interests diverging from apartheid's.

**What the 1973 strikes did to wages**, which answers stage 3's question empirically:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Real black wages 1911–1970** | **roughly flat** |
| **Real black wages from 1973** | **rose substantially**, and continued rising through the decade |
| **What changed** | **not the market, which had been tight before. The workers' capacity to act** |
| **Which establishes** | the sixty flat years were produced by the suppression of organisation, not by productivity or supply |

**That is the control experiment for the whole functional account**, and it comes out in the functional account's favour.

**Practice.** Find the Durban strikes' scale and the fact that they had no formal leadership, and work out why. Then find real black manufacturing wage series across 1970 to 1980 and note the break. Then read about Rick Turner and the Institute for Industrial Education. Then state the workerist and the Charterist positions on unions and politics, each as strongly as you can.
Soweto, 1976:
The day schoolchildren marched against a language rule and were shot, and the year that followed, which no one controlled.

**The grievance, from the Bantu Education lesson.** From 1974–75 the Department of Bantu Education enforced a requirement that **certain secondary school subjects be taught in Afrikaans** — arithmetic and social studies in Afrikaans, other subjects in English.

**Why it was intolerable:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Teachers could not teach in it** | and pupils could not learn in it |
| **Examinations were in it** | so it guaranteed failure |
| **It was the language of the police and the state** | |
| **School boards had objected** | and were ignored |
| **And failure meant no future** | in a system where education was the only route |

**The organising.** Protests at individual Soweto schools from early 1976; the formation of an action committee that became the **Soweto Students' Representative Council**; **Tsietsi Mashinini** among its leaders; and the influence of Black Consciousness from the last lesson, which had been building among school students through SASO's work.

**16 June 1976.** Between 10,000 and 20,000 school students — the estimates vary — marched through Soweto toward Orlando Stadium.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The march** | peaceful, with placards |
| **The police** | blocked it; dogs, then teargas, then **live fire** |
| **The first deaths** | **Hastings Ndlovu**, and **Hector Pieterson**, aged about twelve |
| **The photograph** | **Sam Nzima's image of Mbuyisa Makhubo carrying Hector Pieterson**, with Hector's sister Antoinette beside them — **which became the defining image of apartheid worldwide** |
| **By nightfall** | Soweto was in revolt; buildings burning, including administration offices and beer halls |

**Nzima's photograph deserves a note.** It was published within a day, went worldwide, and **Nzima was harassed into leaving journalism and placed under police surveillance.** A single photograph did more to internationalise apartheid than a decade of diplomacy, which is why the state treated the photographer as a threat.

**And the beer halls burning is not incidental** — from stage 4's 1923 Act lesson: **the municipal beer monopoly financed the townships' own administration.** Students burning beer halls were attacking the fiscal basis of the system that governed them, and they knew it.

**What followed, and this is the part the date obscures.**

**16 June was not an event; it was the start of about eighteen months of revolt.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Spread** | **to more than a hundred townships** across the country within weeks |
| **Duration** | **through 1976 and into 1977** |
| **Forms** | school boycotts, marches, attacks on government property, **and attacks on councillors and police** |
| **Deaths** | **the Cillié Commission's official figure was 575**, of whom **134 were under eighteen**. Other estimates run higher, toward 700 |
| **Detentions** | thousands |

**The casualty figure is worth stating carefully.** The commission's 575 is the official count and it is generally regarded as an undercount; **the figure usually cited in the literature is between 575 and 700.** From stage 1's statistics lesson: it is the state's own commission's number and should be quoted as such.

**The consequence that changed everything: exile.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Thousands of young people left the country** | across the Botswana, Lesotho, Swaziland and Mozambique borders |
| **Where they went** | **to the ANC and, in smaller numbers, the PAC** |
| **What they did** | **joined MK** |
| **The effect on the exile movement** | **transformative** — the ANC had been an organisation of exiles in their forties and fifties with no internal base. **It now had thousands of recruits in their teens and twenties, radicalised, from the townships** |

**That is why 1976 matters more than its casualty figure.** The movement in exile had been decapitated in 1964 and had no internal constituency. **1976 supplied it with a generation** — and the MK of the 1980s, the underground of the 1980s, and much of the ANC's leadership after 1994 is the class of '76.

**The second consequence: the townships were never governed again.**

**From 1976 the state's administrative control of African townships was progressively lost.** The pattern that becomes the 1980s:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **School boycotts** | recurring |
| **Attacks on councillors** | who had no legitimacy and could not be protected |
| **Administration buildings burnt** | |
| **Rent and service boycotts** | |
| **The police as an occupying force** | rather than a civil authority |

**Which is the beginning of what the 1980s called "ungovernability"**, and stage 5's later lessons follow it.

**The third consequence: international.** 1976 and then Biko's death in 1977 produced:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **UN Security Council Resolution 418, 1977** | **the mandatory arms embargo** |
| **Sporting and cultural isolation** | deepening |
| **Divestment campaigns** | beginning in earnest in the United States and Europe |
| **The Sullivan Principles, 1977** | American companies' code of conduct — a corporate response to pressure |

**And the state's own response, in two directions at once**, which is the pattern of the following decade: **the October 1977 bannings** of eighteen Black Consciousness organisations and two newspapers, **and the appointment of the Wiehahn and Riekert commissions in the same year** — repression and reform, simultaneously, which is the next two lessons.

**16 June is now Youth Day**, a public holiday, and the Hector Pieterson Museum stands near where he was shot.

**Practice.** Find the Afrikaans medium directive of 1974–75 and what subjects it covered. Then find the Cillié Commission's death toll and the proportion under eighteen. Then look up Sam Nzima's photograph and what happened to him. Then find estimates of how many young people left the country after 1976 and where they went.
The security state: detention, torture,:
What the security apparatus actually did, how much of it is established, and by what process it became known.

**A note on sources first, because this is the subject where it matters most.** Most of what follows is established by:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The TRC** | **amnesty applications in which perpetrators described their own acts**, under a statute that required full disclosure for amnesty |
| **Criminal trials** | notably **Eugene de Kock's**, which produced extensive testimony |
| **Inquests reopened after 1994** | which reversed earlier findings |
| **Court records and declassified documents** | |

**So the record is unusually good**, because the amnesty mechanism gave perpetrators a reason to tell the truth. **From stage 1's commission lesson: these are findings and confessions, not convictions in most cases** — and the distinction holds.

---

**Detention without trial.** From the security laws lesson: 90 days from 1963, 180 from 1965, **indefinite and incommunocado under section 6 of the Terrorism Act from 1967**, and section 29 of the Internal Security Act from 1982.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Detained over the period** | **tens of thousands** |
| **Under the 1986 emergency alone** | **about 25,000 in the first year**, including **thousands of children** |
| **Access to a court** | **none**, by statute |
| **Access to a lawyer or family** | **none**, at the security police's discretion |

**Children in detention is the fact that most shocked international opinion in the late 1980s**, and the Detainees' Parents Support Committee's documentation of it is the primary record.

---

**Deaths in detention.** The documented figure is **at least 73 people who died in security detention between 1963 and 1990.**

**The official explanations, as recorded at inquests:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Fell down a flight of stairs"** | |
| **"Slipped in the shower"** | |
| **"Jumped from a window"** | |
| **"Hanged himself with his own clothing"** | |
| **"Natural causes"** | |

**And the inquests: in virtually every case before 1990, the finding was that no one was responsible.**

**That pattern is itself the evidence.** Seventy-three deaths, a consistent repertoire of explanations, and no finding of responsibility in any of them — **a legal system functioning exactly as designed to produce that result.**

**The TRC established, from perpetrators' own accounts, that deaths occurred during interrogation and from torture**, and the inquest findings in several cases have since been formally reversed — **Ahmed Timol's in 2017, Neil Aggett's reopened in 2019–20** — decades later, on the same evidence plus the testimony.

---

**Torture. The TRC documented the methods and they recur across the country, which establishes that they were taught:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"The bag"** | suffocation with a wet canvas bag or tube |
| **Electric shock** | applied to the genitals, hands, head |
| **The "helicopter"** | suspension from a pole between bound wrists and ankles |
| **Prolonged standing, sleep deprivation, solitary confinement** | |
| **Beating** | |
| **Threats and mock executions**, including against family | |

**The consistency is the finding.** The same techniques in Johannesburg, Port Elizabeth, Durban and Cape Town, over decades, **is a training programme, not a set of individual excesses** — and the TRC said so.

---

**The death squads**, which are a distinct matter from detention.

| Unit | |
| --- | --- |
| **C1 / C10 — "Vlakplaas"** | a Security Branch unit on a farm near Pretoria, using "askaris" — turned former MK members — **to abduct and kill.** Commanded by **Dirk Coetzee**, then **Eugene de Kock** |
| **The Civil Cooperation Bureau (CCB)**, from 1986 | a military covert unit, operating domestically and abroad |
| **Various Security Branch units** | regionally |

**Established operations, among many:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Cradock Four, 1985** | **Matthew Goniwe**, Fort Calata, Sparrow Mkonto and Sicelo Mhlauli — UDF organisers, abducted and killed. A signal from a Joint Management Centre proposing Goniwe's "permanent removal from society" was later produced |
| **The PEBCO Three, 1985** | abducted and killed; the bodies destroyed |
| **Ruth First, 1982** | **killed by a parcel bomb in Maputo** |
| **Dulcie September, 1988** | **the ANC's representative in Paris, shot dead** |
| **Khotso House, 1988** | **the South African Council of Churches' headquarters bombed** — **Adriaan Vlok, the Minister of Law and Order, admitted to the TRC that he had ordered it on PW Botha's instruction** |
| **Cross-border raids** | **Maseru 1982 (42 killed), Matola 1981, Gaborone 1985, Harare and Lusaka 1986** |

**The Khotso House admission is the one to hold.** A cabinet minister told a commission that he ordered the bombing of a church building in central Johannesburg **on the Prime Minister's instruction.** It is not an allegation; it is an admission on the record.

**And De Kock's trial produced the most detail.** Convicted in 1996 on 89 charges including six murders, sentenced to two life terms plus 212 years, **and he gave extensive evidence to the TRC and in other prosecutions.** He was granted parole in 2015.

---

**The command question, which is the live argument.** How far up did authorisation go?

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Established** | **operational commanders ordered killings**; the Khotso House order came from Vlok on Botha's instruction; **the State Security Council used language — "eliminate", "permanently remove from society" — that its own members told the TRC meant killing** |
| **Argued** | whether the SSC's language was authorisation or deniable encouragement |
| **PW Botha** | **refused to appear before the TRC**, was convicted of that refusal in 1998, and the conviction was overturned on appeal. **He never testified** |
| **The TRC's finding** | that the state had been responsible for gross human rights violations, and that the SSC had created a climate in which killing was understood as authorised |

**Both sides of that argument are in the TRC's own volumes**, and it is the most careful place to read it.

---

**And the accountability outcome, which is stage 11's subject.** The TRC referred roughly **300 cases** for prosecution where amnesty had been refused or not sought.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Prosecutions brought** | **very few** |
| **Convictions** | fewer still — De Kock, and a handful |
| **Inquests reopened** | **several, from 2017 onward**, decades late |
| **The NPA's record** | **the subject of sustained criticism and litigation by families**, and of an official inquiry |

**So: a commission established a great deal, perpetrators admitted a great deal, and almost nobody was prosecuted.** That sentence is true of apartheid-era crimes and it is true of state capture — which is stage 11's parallel and stage 12's argument.

**Practice.** Find the documented number of deaths in security detention. Then read the standard inquest explanations and the findings. Then find Adriaan Vlok's TRC testimony on Khotso House. Then look up how many TRC referrals resulted in prosecutions, and the families' litigation about it.
Wiehahn and Riekert, 1979:
The two commissions that tried to save apartheid by reforming it, the one that worked for the state and the one that destroyed it.

**The problem, by 1977.** Three pressures converging:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The skills constraint** | from the boom lesson: the economy needed skilled workers the law forbade training |
| **The unions** | from the Durban lesson: **unregistered African unions were organising and striking, lawfully impossible and actually happening** |
| **Employers** | **wanted a procedure.** Illegal strikes with no recognised counterpart and no binding agreement were worse for business than legal ones |
| **And 1976** | from the Soweto lesson: the townships were no longer governable by administration alone |

**So the state appointed two commissions in 1977, reporting in 1979**, and their recommendations are the first serious reform of apartheid's core.

---

**The Wiehahn Commission**, under Nic Wiehahn, on labour.

**What it recommended:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African trade unions recognised** | and permitted to register |
| **Statutory job reservation abolished** | **the colour bar from stage 3, ended** |
| **A single industrial relations system** | for all workers |
| **An Industrial Court** | to adjudicate unfair labour practices |

**Implemented in the Industrial Conciliation Amendment Act of 1979**, which became the **Labour Relations Act.**

**Why the state agreed to it — and this is the crucial point: it expected to gain.**

| The calculation | |
| --- | --- |
| **Registration means regulation** | registered unions must keep books, hold ballots, follow procedures, and can be deregistered |
| **Recognition means bureaucratisation** | officials, offices and agreements rather than mass action |
| **Legal strikes are procedurally constrained** | notice periods, ballots, defined disputes |
| **And it would separate the industrial from the political** | which was the whole hope |
| **The skills problem is relieved** | without conceding political rights |

**It was a co-option strategy, explicitly, and it is defensible on its own terms.** Bringing an insurgent labour movement inside a legal framework has worked for states before.

**It failed completely.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1979** | **FOSATU founded** — unions register and grow |
| **1979–85** | **membership grows from tens of thousands to over a million** across the federations |
| **1985** | **COSATU founded**, around half a million members at launch |
| **1987** | **COSATU adopts the Freedom Charter** — the industrial and the political fuse, exactly as the state had hoped to prevent |
| **1980s** | **the unions become the most effective opposition in the country** — stayaways, consumer boycotts, strikes with political demands, and the organisational backbone of the UDF period |
| **1990s** | **COSATU is a partner in the governing alliance** |

**Why the co-option failed, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of the state's cleverness.** Legal standing gave the unions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The right to organise openly** | which is worth more than any constraint it came with |
| **Recognition agreements with employers** | enforceable, nationwide |
| **Stop orders for dues** | **a reliable income**, which the ICU never had, from stage 4 |
| **Shop stewards with legal protection** | **an organisational structure inside every plant** |
| **A legal arena** | the Industrial Court, which they used relentlessly |

**That last point is the one to notice.** The Industrial Court, created to channel disputes, **became a venue in which black workers won cases against employers and against the state** — and in a country with no other rights-based forum, it was the only one that worked. **Lawyers and unions used it as a substitute constitutional court for a decade.**

---

**The Riekert Commission**, under Piet Riekert, on influx control and urban Africans — and it is the one that reveals the strategy.

**What it recommended:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ease controls on urban "insiders"** | Africans with section 10 rights from the pass lesson — give them security, housing, mobility between urban areas |
| **Tighten controls on "outsiders"** | **those without section 10 rights, in the homelands and on farms** |
| **Make employers liable** | for employing or housing unqualified people |

**So: a two-tier African population.** A privileged urban insider class with rights, and an excluded majority rigorously confined.

**The strategy is clear and it was stated: create a black urban middle class with something to lose.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The hope** | a propertied, employed, housed urban African population would prefer stability to revolution |
| **The measures that followed** | **99-year leasehold from 1978, freehold for urban Africans from 1986**, home ownership schemes, trading rights, and township upgrading |
| **Why it was a reasonable bet** | it is a strategy that has worked elsewhere |

**It failed too, and for an instructive reason: the division it tried to create did not hold, because the township was not divided that way.** An insider with a house and a job lived next door to his brother without papers; **the rent increases of 1984 fell on insiders; and the political organisations that formed were township-wide.** The Vaal Triangle revolt that began the 1980s rising, in the next lesson, **was started by insiders over rent.**

---

**The combined verdict, which is this lesson's point.**

**1979 is the moment the apartheid state began reforming its own core, and both reforms strengthened its opponents.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Wiehahn** | **created a legal, funded, organised mass movement** where there had been none |
| **Riekert** | **failed to split the township** and provoked the grievance that lit it |

**And the general lesson is worth taking out of South Africa:** an authoritarian state that reforms under pressure frequently gives its opponents the organisational capacity they lacked. **The concession that relieves an economic constraint can create a political one.** Stage 6 argues about whether the same is true of the 1990 decision.

**Practice.** Find Wiehahn's recommendations and the 1979 Act that implemented them. Then find union membership figures for 1979 and 1985. Then read Riekert's insider/outsider distinction and work out what it required of an employer. Then establish what started the 1984 Vaal Triangle revolt, and whether those people were insiders or outsiders.
Total Strategy, and PW Botha:
Militarisation, destabilisation, selective reform, and the speech that cost the country its credit.

**The man. P. W. Botha**, Minister of Defence for twelve years, **Prime Minister from 1978** after the Information Scandal destroyed Vorster, **and State President under the new constitution from 1984 to 1989.**

**Botha came from the Defence portfolio and governed as a defence minister.** That single fact explains the period.

**The doctrine: "total onslaught" and "total strategy".**

| The analysis | |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa faces a "total onslaught"** | Soviet-directed, operating through the ANC, the unions, the churches, the press, foreign governments and the UN |
| **It is not primarily military** | it is political, economic, psychological, diplomatic and military at once |
| **Therefore the response must be total** | coordinating every arm of the state |
| **Which requires** | **a restructured state, with security at its centre** |

**And the practical corollary, which is the doctrine's one accurate insight: 80% political, 20% military.** Botha's strategists held that insurgency is defeated by addressing grievances as well as by force — **which is why Total Strategy included real reform.** That combination is what makes the period hard to read.

**The institutional restructuring, which was substantial:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The State Security Council** | **elevated above the cabinet** as the central decision-making body, dominated by the military and the security services |
| **The National Security Management System** | **a parallel state structure** — Joint Management Centres covering every region and town, coordinating security, administration and "welfare" |
| **Defence spending** | **up very sharply**, to a large share of the budget |
| **The securocrats** | military and intelligence officers in policy roles across government |

**The NSMS is the thing to understand.** By the mid-1980s there was a shadow administration of Joint Management Centres running parallel to elected local government, gathering intelligence, directing upgrading projects and coordinating security operations. **From the security lesson: the JMC signal about Matthew Goniwe's "permanent removal from society" came out of this structure.**

**Destabilisation of the region**, which is the external half:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Angola** | **sustained SADF operations and support for UNITA** through the 1980s |
| **Mozambique** | **support for RENAMO**, with devastating effects on that country |
| **Lesotho** | raids, and a border blockade in 1986 that contributed to a coup |
| **Zimbabwe, Zambia, Botswana, Swaziland** | raids and covert operations |
| **The Nkomati Accord, 1984** | a non-aggression pact with Mozambique, **which South Africa continued to breach** |

**The regional cost is enormous and is usually a footnote in South African accounts.** The destabilisation of Angola and Mozambique killed very large numbers of people and wrecked two economies for a generation. **A Commonwealth study put the cost to the frontline states in the tens of billions of dollars.** It is a major part of what apartheid did, and it happened outside the borders.

**The reforms, which were real and were selective** — and from the pillars lesson, they were **petty apartheid conceded and grand apartheid retained:**

| Conceded | Retained |
| --- | --- |
| **Mixed Marriages and Immorality Acts repealed, 1985** | **Group Areas, until 1991** |
| **Pass laws and influx control abolished, 1986** | **the homelands and citizenship** |
| **African trade unions legalised, 1979** | **no political rights** |
| **99-year leasehold 1978, freehold 1986** | **in townships only** |
| **Some amenities desegregated**; sport | **schools, hospitals, residence** |
| **The tricameral parliament, 1983** | **Africans excluded entirely** |

**That table is the period.** And the pattern is consistent: **every concession was of something that cost the state little and was internationally visible; nothing was conceded on the distribution of political power.**

**And then the Rubicon speech, which is the single most consequential speech in modern South African history for the wrong reasons.**

**15 August 1985, Durban.** Botha was to address the National Party's Natal congress. **In the weeks before, South African diplomats and officials had briefed foreign governments and bankers that major reform would be announced** — the release of Mandela, the restoration of citizenship, a negotiated future. Foreign Minister Pik Botha had encouraged the expectation.

**It was broadcast live, internationally.**

**What he said: he was defiant.** He rejected the idea of one person one vote in a unitary state, warned against pressure, wagged his finger, and offered nothing of what had been expected. **"I am not going to lead white South Africans on a road to abdication and suicide."**

**What happened next:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rand collapsed** | losing a large share of its value within days |
| **Foreign banks refused to roll over short-term loans** | |
| **Late August 1985** | **South Africa declared a debt standstill** — suspending repayment of principal on a large part of its foreign debt |
| **The Johannesburg Stock Exchange** | closed temporarily |
| **And from then** | **South Africa was effectively cut off from international capital markets** |

**The 1985 debt standstill is the economic turning point of apartheid**, and it is more important than the formal sanctions that followed. **A country that cannot borrow cannot run a deficit, cannot invest, and cannot grow.** For the rest of the decade South Africa had to run trade surpluses to repay debt — **which meant suppressing imports, suppressing investment and suppressing growth**, in the middle of a political emergency.

**And the comparison that makes it vivid: the 1960s boom was financed substantially by foreign capital, which arrived once repression had succeeded.** The 1985 cut-off came once repression had visibly failed. **The same mechanism, in reverse.**

**Why Botha did it**, which is genuinely argued:

| Account | |
| --- | --- |
| **He never intended reform of that kind** | and his officials had over-promised |
| **His caucus and the right wing constrained him** | the Conservative Party had broken away in 1982 over the tricameral plan |
| **He resented being told what to do** | which is the personal account, widely held |
| **The speech was rewritten late** | under pressure from securocrats |

**All four are supported and they are not exclusive.** What is certain is the consequence.

**Practice.** Find the "80% political, 20% military" formulation and work out what it implies about why reforms happened. Then list the NSMS's structure and compare it with elected local government. Then watch or read the Rubicon speech. Then find the rand's exchange rate in July and October 1985, and look up what a debt standstill requires a country to do.
The 1983 constitution, the UDF, and the:
A parliament with three chambers and no African members, the front that formed to oppose it, and the rent increase that began the end.

**The constitution. The Republic of South Africa Constitution Act 110 of 1983** — the **tricameral parliament.**

| Chamber | For | Members |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **House of Assembly** | **white** | **178** |
| **House of Representatives** | **Coloured** | **85** |
| **House of Delegates** | **Indian** | **45** |
| **Africans** | **excluded entirely** | **—** |

**The ratio is the design: 4 : 2 : 1.** In any joint sitting or joint committee, **the white chamber's members outnumbered the other two combined** — by construction, permanently. **So Coloured and Indian representation was real in form and arithmetically incapable of outvoting anything.**

**And the "own affairs" device.** Matters were divided into:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Own affairs"** | education, housing, welfare, local government — **each chamber legislating for its own group** |
| **"General affairs"** | defence, foreign policy, finance, security, African affairs — **decided jointly, where the 4:2:1 ratio applied** |

**So each community could administer its own schools and could not touch anything that mattered.** And **African affairs was a general affair** — decided by a parliament with no African members.

**Plus an executive State President** with greatly enhanced powers, replacing the Prime Minister: **Botha became State President in 1984**, able to legislate for the homelands by proclamation and to determine what counted as an own affair.

**Why the government did it.** Riekert's logic from two lessons ago, applied politically: **co-opt the Coloured and Indian populations into the system, so that the racial order becomes a coalition of minorities against the African majority.** It was a reasonable strategy on its own terms and it required those populations to participate.

**The referendum and the elections, which decided it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **White referendum, 2 November 1983** | **66% in favour**, on a high turnout |
| **Opposition from the right** | **the Conservative Party**, which had broken from the National Party in 1982 over the plan — **because it conceded anything at all** |
| **Opposition from the left** | the Progressive Federal Party, because it conceded nothing that mattered |
| **The Coloured election, August 1984** | **turnout about 31%** |
| **The Indian election, August 1984** | **turnout about 20%** |

**Those turnout figures are the verdict.** The two communities the constitution was designed to co-opt **refused it** — by a boycott organised by their own political organisations. **The strategy failed at the first step.**

**And the boycott campaign built the organisation that then dominated the decade.**

---

**The United Democratic Front, launched 20 August 1983** at Rocklands, Mitchells Plain, Cape Town.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | **a front, not a party** — a coalition of affiliated organisations keeping their own identities |
| **Affiliates** | **around 400 at launch, over 600 later** — civics, youth and student congresses, women's organisations, unions, church groups, sports bodies, professional associations |
| **Politics** | **Charterist** — the Freedom Charter from this stage's lesson, and effectively the ANC's internal expression |
| **Slogan** | **"UDF unites, apartheid divides"** |
| **The call for it** | **Allan Boesak**, in January 1983 |
| **Presidents** | Archie Gumede, Oscar Mpetha, **Albertina Sisulu** |
| **Officials** | Popo Molefe, Patrick Lekota |

**The front structure is the clever part.** A banned organisation cannot operate; **a front of hundreds of legal organisations, each individually small, is very hard to ban** — and when the state eventually restricted it, the affiliates continued.

**And the parallel tradition, which should not be omitted: the National Forum**, formed in June 1983 at Hammanskraal, out of the **Black Consciousness and socialist** traditions — **AZAPO** and others, with the **Azanian Manifesto.** Its objection to the UDF was the old Africanist one from the PAC lesson: **multiracial alliance, and the subordination of class to nation.** It was much smaller and it argued the case throughout.

---

**Then the townships, and the thing that lit them was rent.**

**The Black Local Authorities Act of 1982** had created elected African township councils — **the political answer to Riekert's insider strategy.**

| And they were set up to fail | |
| --- | --- |
| **No rateable tax base** | from stage 4's Native Revenue Account: townships had to finance themselves |
| **No industry or commerce** to tax | by the design of the Group Areas city |
| **So the only revenue** | **rents and service charges** |
| **Therefore** | **the councils' only possible act was to raise rents** |
| **And their legitimacy** | **nil** — turnout in council elections was around 10–20% |

**So the state created councils whose sole available policy was the one guaranteed to produce a revolt**, in communities that regarded them as collaborators. **That is Riekert's strategy and the 1923 Act's financing rule colliding.**

**3 September 1984, the Vaal Triangle.** Rent increases announced in Sharpeville, Sebokeng and Boipatong. **Protests, a stayaway, and the killing of the deputy mayor of Sharpeville on the first day** — which produced the Sharpeville Six trial, in which six people were sentenced to death for a killing in a crowd on the doctrine of common purpose, and were reprieved in 1988 after an international campaign.

**And from the Vaal it spread, and did not stop for six years.**

**What "ungovernability" meant in practice**, after the ANC's January 1985 call to render apartheid unworkable:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Councillors** | **resigned en masse, or were attacked.** By 1985 most township councils had ceased to function |
| **Rent and service boycotts** | sustained for years, and in places never resumed |
| **Street and area committees** | **alternative local government**, organising defence, disputes, cleaning and schooling |
| **People's courts** | which handled disputes — and which in places became instruments of violence |
| **Consumer boycotts** | of white-owned shops, which were extremely effective locally |
| **Stayaways** | general strikes, organised with the unions |
| **School boycotts** | and the argument between **"liberation before education"** and **"people's education"** |

**The alternative structures are the period's most important and least comfortable subject.** Street committees in some places were genuinely democratic local self-government under enormous pressure. **In others the people's courts became arbitrary and violent**, and the punishment of suspected informers included **necklacing** — a burning tyre around the neck.

**This curriculum states that plainly.** Necklacing and the killing of suspected collaborators were carried out by people associated with the liberation movement, **the TRC found the ANC and the UDF responsible for gross human rights violations in this category**, and the ANC accepted a share of that finding. **It is part of the record, it was contested within the movement at the time, and an account of the 1980s that omits it is not honest.**

**Practice.** Find the tricameral chambers' sizes and work out why the ratio was 4:2:1. Then find the 1984 Coloured and Indian turnout figures. Then read the Black Local Authorities Act's revenue provisions and work out what a councillor could actually do. Then find the TRC's findings on the ANC and the UDF, and read what they cover.
States of emergency, 1985-1989:
Five years of rule by regulation, twenty-five thousand detentions, a reporting ban, and a stalemate neither side could break.

**The emergencies:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **20 July 1985** | declared in **36 magisterial districts** |
| **7 March 1986** | lifted |
| **12 June 1986** | **declared nationwide** |
| **1987, 1988, 1989** | **renewed annually** |
| **1990** | lifted in most of the country in June; **in Natal only in October** |

**What an emergency gave the state:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Detention without trial** | by any policeman, initially for 14 days, extendable by the minister indefinitely |
| **Rule by regulation** | the State President legislating by proclamation |
| **Indemnity** | **security forces indemnified for acts done in good faith** |
| **Powers of curfew, cordon, search and seizure** | without warrant |
| **Control of gatherings, funerals, publications** | |
| **And restriction of reporting** | which is the next section |

**The detention figures:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In the first year of the 1986 emergency** | **about 25,000 people detained** |
| **Children** | **thousands** — the figure usually cited for those under 18 detained between 1986 and 1989 is around 10,000, documented by the Detainees' Parents Support Committee |
| **Typical periods** | weeks to many months; some for years |
| **Access to courts** | severely restricted, though **the courts did intervene in some cases** — notably on the validity of regulations |

**The courts' partial resistance is worth noting.** Unlike the 1960s, the 1980s judiciary struck down some emergency regulations as too vague or beyond the enabling power — **and the state simply re-promulgated them in corrected form.** A real but limited check.

**The media restrictions**, which shaped how the world saw the period:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reporting of "unrest"** | restricted and then effectively prohibited without official clearance |
| **Photographing or filming security action** | **banned** |
| **Journalists excluded** from areas of unrest | |
| **The effect** | **television coverage of the townships ended** |
| **And newspapers published blank spaces** | where censored material had been |

**That ban is a significant historical fact for a specific reason: it worked.** International coverage of South Africa declined after mid-1986 because there were no pictures. **The state had learned from 1976 that an image can do more than an army** — from the Soweto lesson — and it removed the cameras.

**The violence, and its composition is the part most often misunderstood.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Political deaths, roughly 1984–89** | **several thousand — the commonly cited figure exceeds 5,000** |
| **A large share** | **was not state-against-activist** |
| **It was** | **between organisations** — UDF/ANC-aligned against **Inkatha**, especially in Natal from 1987; and against **vigilante groups** |

**The vigilantes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The *witdoeke*** | in Crossroads, Cape Town, 1986 — who destroyed squatter settlements **with police complicity**, which the TRC established |
| **The A-Team, the Amabutho, and others** | township-based, aligned with councillors or with Inkatha |
| **And the "third force" question** | whether the state organised and armed them. **The TRC found substantial state involvement in fomenting violence**, and this is stage 6's central argument |

**The Natal conflict from 1987 is the largest single component.** Inkatha against the UDF and then the ANC, in KwaZulu and Natal, **with thousands killed over the following seven years** — and it continued through the transition and past the 1994 election. **Stage 6 takes it up properly, because the question of state involvement in it is the transition's biggest dispute.**

**The international escalation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1985** | **the debt standstill**, from the Botha lesson — the real economic blow |
| **1986** | **the Commonwealth Eminent Persons Group** visits, exploring negotiation — **and its mission collapses on 19 May 1986 when the SADF raids Harare, Lusaka and Gaborone** while the group is in the country |
| **2 October 1986** | **the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act**, passed over Reagan's veto by Congress |
| **September 1986** | **European Community measures** |
| **1985–90** | **around 200 American companies disinvest** |
| **Sport and culture** | total isolation |

**The Eminent Persons Group episode is the clearest evidence of the securocrats' ascendancy.** A Commonwealth mission exploring a negotiated settlement was in the country, and the SADF bombed three capitals. **Whether that was intended to end the mission or was simply the security establishment acting on its own logic is argued; the effect was the same.**

**The 1987 white election**, which is the political indicator to notice:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The National Party won** | comfortably |
| **And the Conservative Party became the official opposition** | **overtaking the Progressive Federal Party** |
| **Which means** | **the white electorate's main opposition was now to Botha's right** — against reform, not for more of it |

**So by 1987 the government faced an ungovernable black majority, a hostile world, no access to credit, and a white electorate whose strongest opposition thought it had conceded too much.** That is the stalemate.

**The stalemate, stated precisely, because it is the condition that produced 1990:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The state could not be overthrown** | **MK never came close**, and the security forces held |
| **The townships could not be governed** | administration had collapsed and emergency rule was not government |
| **The economy could not grow** | **no credit, falling gold price, capital flight, and a skills constraint** |
| **The liberation movement could not win** | militarily or by insurrection |
| **And it could not be defeated** | because every repression produced recruits |

**Neither side could win and neither could be beaten.** That is what a stalemate is, and it is the strongest single explanation for why negotiations began — **because both sides' best alternative to agreement had become worse than agreement.**

**The last year:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1988** | **Cuito Cuanavale** in Angola — a prolonged battle whose outcome both sides claim; and the **New York Accords** in December, leading to **Namibian independence and Cuban withdrawal** |
| **January 1989** | **Botha has a stroke** |
| **February 1989** | **de Klerk elected National Party leader** |
| **1989** | the **Mass Democratic Movement's Defiance Campaign** — hospitals, beaches and schools desegregated by occupation |
| **August 1989** | **Botha resigns**, in anger, after a confrontation with his own cabinet |
| **September 1989** | **de Klerk becomes State President**; the "purple rain" march in Cape Town, and a 70,000-strong march that the police permit |
| **2 February 1990** | **the speech** |

**Namibia matters more than it usually gets credit for.** The New York Accords removed South Africa's northern buffer, delivered an independent Namibia under a SWAPO government in 1990, **and demonstrated that a negotiated transfer of power to a liberation movement was survivable** — a rehearsal, next door, watched closely by everyone.

**Practice.** Find the detention figures for the first year of the 1986 emergency, and the estimates for children. Then find the media regulations and work out what a television news crew could lawfully film. Then look up the Eminent Persons Group and what ended its mission. Then establish who the official opposition was after the 1987 election, and what that implies.
Why it ended: the four accounts:
Stage 5's conclusion, and the second of stage 1's big disagreements — with each account at its strongest and what would settle it.

**The question. Why did the National Party, in February 1990, unban its opponents and begin negotiating itself out of power?**

**It is not an obvious thing to have done.** The state had not been defeated militarily, the security forces were intact and loyal, the government had just won an election, and it held every instrument of coercion. **Regimes in that position usually do not negotiate.**

---

**Account 1: internal resistance.**

| The case | |
| --- | --- |
| **The townships were ungovernable** from 1984 | administration collapsed; councils ceased to function; rents went uncollected for years |
| **The unions** | **a million-plus members, able to stop the economy** — and legal, thanks to Wiehahn |
| **The schools** | a generation outside the state's reach |
| **Every repression produced recruits** | 1976 filled MK; the 1980s filled the UDF |
| **The emergency was not government** | it was the suspension of government |
| **So** | **the state could hold the country and could not run it** |

**What would strengthen it:** evidence that the government's internal assessments identified ungovernability as the binding constraint. **Some such documents exist and point this way.**

**Its weakness:** resistance had been high in 1960 and in 1976 too, and the state had crushed it both times. **Resistance alone does not explain the timing.**

---

**Account 2: economic failure.**

| The case | |
| --- | --- |
| **The skills ceiling** | from the 1960s boom lesson: apartheid forbade producing the workers the economy needed |
| **The 1985 debt standstill** | **no access to international credit for the rest of the decade** |
| **The gold price** | which had saved the 1970s, **fell through the 1980s** |
| **Sanctions and disinvestment** | real, and compounding |
| **Military spending** | consuming a large share of the budget |
| **Growth** | **near zero per capita through the 1980s**, with high inflation |
| **So** | **the state could no longer afford itself** |

**What would strengthen it:** the sequence. **Does the decision follow the economic deterioration closely?** The 1985 standstill, the 1986 sanctions and the gold price's decline all precede 1990 by three to five years, which fits.

**Its weakness:** poor states repress for decades. **Economic failure creates pressure, not a decision** — and South Africa in 1990 was far from collapse.

---

**Account 3: the end of the Cold War.**

| The case | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC's patron collapsed** | Soviet support for the armed struggle ended; **Gorbachev's USSR was pressing for negotiated settlements across the region** |
| **And the government's best argument collapsed with it** | **"total onslaught" was a Soviet onslaught.** Without the USSR, what was the threat? |
| **The West's calculation changed** | a non-communist ANC was acceptable where a Soviet-backed one had not been |
| **Timing** | **the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989; de Klerk's speech was in February 1990** |
| **De Klerk said so** | repeatedly, in his own account: the fall of communism made the risk acceptable |

**What would strengthen it:** the timing is the strongest evidence any of the four accounts has. **Three months.**

**Its weakness:** it explains the moment and not the necessity. **Something had to make negotiation desirable; the Cold War's end made it safe.** And it has an uncomfortable implication: **it credits South Africans least for their own liberation**, which is why it is resisted — and resistance to a conclusion is not evidence against it.

---

**Account 4: the elite decision, which is the fourth and is often left out.**

| The case | |
| --- | --- |
| **The National Party chose the moment of its greatest remaining strength** | not its weakest. **It still held the army, the civil service, the economy and the negotiating initiative** |
| **Secret talks had run for years** | **with Mandela in prison from 1985, and with the ANC in exile at Mells Park in England from 1987** |
| **Business had been talking to the ANC** | the 1985 Lusaka delegation of South African businessmen |
| **Afrikaner intellectuals and the Broederbond** | **had begun arguing internally for a negotiated settlement** from the mid-1980s |
| **The calculation** | **negotiate now, from strength, and secure property, pensions, the civil service and the constitution — or wait and negotiate from weakness** |
| **And they largely achieved it** | which is stage 6's subject and stage 1's third disagreement |

**What would strengthen it:** the record of the secret talks, the Broederbond's internal documents, and **what the National Party actually secured in the settlement.** All three are substantially available.

**Its weakness:** it understates the pressure that made the calculation necessary. **Elites do not decide to give up power because they have reconsidered.**

---

**The composite, which is where most serious historians now sit:**

> **A stalemate made negotiation necessary; economic failure made it urgent; the Cold War's end made it safe; and the National Party chose the timing to negotiate from strength.**

**Each account supplies one element and none is sufficient alone.** And the stalemate from the last lesson is the frame: **neither side could win, both sides' alternatives were getting worse, and the question became who would move first and on what terms.**

**Why this disagreement matters so much politically**, which is stage 1's point about these four questions:

| If you believe | Then |
| --- | --- |
| **Resistance won** | **the settlement was a victory**, and those who fought for it earned the right to govern |
| **The economy failed** | the transition was **a managed handover**, and the economic order was never defeated |
| **The Cold War ended it** | **South Africans were less the authors of their liberation than any account prefers** |
| **The elite chose it** | **the settlement's terms were set by the outgoing power**, which is the strongest form of the "compromise" case in stage 1's third disagreement |

**Those four conclusions license four different politics**, and that is why the argument is conducted with heat. **Stage 6 is the transition itself, where the same dispute becomes concrete: what was actually on the table, who could have got more, and what was traded.**

**Practice.** Write each of the four accounts in one sentence, then rank them by how well they explain the **timing** and separately by how well they explain the **necessity**. Note that the rankings differ. Then find de Klerk's own account of why he acted, and ask what a self-interested narrator would say. Then write down what evidence would move you between accounts, and whether it exists.
2 February 1990:
The speech, what it actually said, and why it was a greater break than anyone in the chamber expected.

**The occasion.** The State President's address at the opening of Parliament, Cape Town, **2 February 1990.** De Klerk had been in office five months.

**What he announced:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC, the PAC, the SACP and 33 other organisations unbanned** | |
| **Political prisoners released** | those imprisoned only for membership of banned organisations |
| **Restrictions lifted** on about 374 people | the banning orders from stage 5 |
| **The death penalty suspended**, pending reform | |
| **Media restrictions** eased | |
| **Negotiations** | an undertaking to negotiate a new constitution |
| **And, nine days later** | **Mandela's release** |

**11 February 1990: Mandela walked out of Victor Verster prison** after twenty-seven years, and addressed a crowd on the Grand Parade in Cape Town that evening.

**Why the speech was a greater break than the chamber understood.** Three things in it were irreversible, and de Klerk may not have appreciated all three.

**1. Unbanning the SACP.** The National Party's entire claim since stage 4 had been that the opposition was a communist front. **Unbanning the Communist Party conceded that the threat it had described for forty years was no longer the point** — and from stage 5's final lesson, the Cold War's end is what made that concession possible.

**2. Releasing Mandela without conditions.** Previous offers had been conditional — on renouncing violence, or on going to the Transkei. **Mandela had refused them all, from prison, over years.** Releasing him unconditionally meant the state had stopped trying to set the terms of his politics.

**3. Committing to negotiate a constitution.** Not reform. **A new constitution** — which necessarily meant the end of the existing order, because any constitution negotiated with the unbanned organisations would have to enfranchise the majority.

**What the speech did not say, which is the subject of the next lesson.** It did not concede majority rule. **De Klerk's position, held through 1990 and 1991, was that the outcome would be "power-sharing"** — group rights, minority vetoes, a rotating or collective presidency, and constitutional protection for communities. **He later said explicitly that he had not anticipated simple majority rule.**

**So the two sides came to the table with incompatible understandings of what had been agreed**, and the next four years are the working out of that.

**The reaction, in four directions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Internationally** | immediate and enormous. Sanctions began to be relaxed through 1990–91 |
| **The ANC** | welcomed it and was substantially unprepared — **an exile organisation with no legal internal structures suddenly had to build a national party** |
| **The white right** | **the Conservative Party and the AWB called it treason.** Their constituency was large, from stage 5's 1987 election |
| **The townships** | and here the thing nobody expected: **the violence got worse** |

**That last row is the transition's central fact and it needs stating before anything else.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Political deaths, 1984–89** | several thousand |
| **Political deaths, 1990–94** | **about 14,000** |

**More people were killed in the four years of negotiation than in the preceding decade of insurrection and emergency.** The lesson on the violence is three ahead, and the question of who was responsible is the transition's biggest unresolved dispute.

**And a detail about the speech worth keeping, from stage 1's method.** De Klerk's own later accounts emphasise his decisiveness and his moral motivation. **The record shows:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
