| **2005** | **dissolved itself and its remaining members joined the ANC** |

**The party that governed South Africa for forty-six years dissolved itself eleven years after leaving power and its remnant joined the ANC.** That is one of the more remarkable endings in modern political history, and stage 10 covers how it happened.

**The IFP stayed in cabinet** — until 2004, with Buthelezi at Home Affairs throughout. **A party that had boycotted the election until eight days before it served in the national cabinet for ten years.**

---

**And the programme, which is the GNU period's substantive story.**

**The Reconstruction and Development Programme — the RDP.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | **the ANC's 1994 programme**, developed with COSATU and the civics, published as a base document and then a White Paper |
| **Content** | housing, water, electrification, health, education, land reform, jobs — **a developmental, redistributive programme** |
| **Institutionally** | **an RDP office in the Presidency** under Jay Naidoo, to drive it across departments |
| **Its fate** | **the RDP office was closed in March 1996** |

**And in June 1996, two months later: GEAR** — the Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy.

| | **RDP** | **GEAR** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Logic** | **redistribution driving growth** | **growth enabling redistribution** |
| **Fiscal stance** | expansionary where needed | **deficit reduction** |
| **Developed by** | the ANC with COSATU and the mass movement | **a team of officials and economists, substantially in confidence** |
| **Presented as** | a programme for negotiation | **non-negotiable** |
| **The alliance's role** | central | **not consulted** |

**GEAR's adoption is the single most contested act of the post-1994 ANC**, and it is the subject of stage 9's lesson. **What belongs here is the timing: it came two months after the final constitution was adopted and one month before the National Party left the cabinet** — which is to say, at the moment the transition's political settlement was completed.

**Practice.** Find the GNU's cabinet composition and who held Finance in 1994, 1995 and 1996. Then establish the dates of the constitution's adoption and the NP's withdrawal announcement, and work out the connection. Then trace the National Party's vote share from 1994 to 2004. Then set the RDP's base document beside GEAR and list what changed.
The Constitutional Assembly:
Two years, two million submissions, and the most participatory constitution-making process attempted anywhere — plus what it could not resolve.

**The body.** From the interim constitution lesson: **the National Assembly and the Senate sitting together — 490 members** — as the Constitutional Assembly, with two years to adopt a final text by a two-thirds majority, bound by the thirty-four principles.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Chairperson** | **Cyril Ramaphosa** (ANC) |
| **Deputy** | **Leon Wessels** (NP) |
| **Structure** | six **theme committees**, a constitutional committee, technical committees of experts, and a management committee |
| **Duration** | May 1994 to May 1996 |

**The pairing of Ramaphosa and Wessels is the Kempton Park bilateral channel, institutionalised** — and from the CODESA lesson, that is how the real work got done.

**The public participation programme, which is the thing this process is known for internationally:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Submissions received** | **around two million** |
| **Methods** | public meetings across the country, a national media campaign, a newspaper (*Constitutional Talk*), a radio programme, phone-in lines, and workshops |
| **Scale of outreach** | **millions of copies of working drafts distributed**, in all official languages |
| **The slogan** | "You've made your mark, now have your say" |

**Was it genuine or was it theatre?** Both, in proportions that are argued about:

| For | Against |
| --- | --- |
| **Submissions were read, catalogued and reported to the theme committees** | **the great majority could not be and were not individually addressed** |
| **Some provisions demonstrably came from it** | notably on **children's rights, animal welfare, and the environment** |
| **The legitimating effect was real** | and it was partly the point |
| | **the hard questions were settled by negotiation between two parties**, not by submission |

**The honest assessment: the public process shaped the document at the margins and legitimated it substantially, and the central bargains were struck elsewhere.** Which is true of every constitution ever written and is not a scandal — **the comparison that matters is that most constitutions are written without any public process at all.**

**What the Assembly had to resolve, and these were the live fights:**

| Issue | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **Property** | **section 25** — property protected, with expropriation permitted for a public purpose or in the public interest, with compensation that is "just and equitable", and an explicit mandate for land reform. **A negotiated compromise, and stage 7 and stage 12's subject** |
| **The death penalty** | **excluded** — and the Constitutional Court had already decided it in *Makwanyane* in 1995 |
| **Lockouts** | employers' right to lock out **omitted** from the final text — which the Court raised at certification, from the principles lesson |
| **Provincial powers** | **the big one.** The ANC wanted a strong centre; the IFP and NP wanted federalism. **The Court's certification refusal turned on it** |
| **Education in a mother tongue** | section 29(2), compromise language — and still litigated |
| **Language** | eleven official languages, with no single dominant one specified |
| **Traditional leadership** | **recognised**, with its powers left to legislation — stage 8's unresolved question |
| **Socio-economic rights** | **included and made justiciable**, which was internationally unusual — stage 7 |
| **The security services** | civilian oversight, constitutional provisions |

**The two abstentions and the boycott:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The IFP** | **withdrew from the Constitutional Assembly in early 1995** and did not return — maintaining that international mediation had been promised and not delivered. **So the final constitution was written without the party governing KwaZulu-Natal** |
| **The Freedom Front** | participated, and **abstained** on the final vote, on self-determination grounds |
| **The ACDP** | **voted against**, on abortion and the death penalty |

**The vote, 8 May 1996: 421 in favour, 2 against, 10 abstentions.**

**The IFP's absence is the most significant gap in the final constitution's legitimacy**, and it is why the provincial powers question stayed live, why KwaZulu-Natal pursued its own provincial constitution (which the Constitutional Court struck down in 1996), and why federalism recurs in stage 12.

---

**Then the certification, which the principles lesson covered: refused on 6 September 1996, amended, certified on 4 December, signed at Sharpeville on 10 December, in force 4 February 1997.**

**What the final Constitution is, in one paragraph, as an orientation to stage 7.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Supreme law** | **section 2** — law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid |
| **A Bill of Rights** | **chapter 2**, justiciable, binding the state and in some respects private persons |
| **Including socio-economic rights** | housing, health care, food, water, social security, education |
| **Three spheres of government** | national, provincial, local — **"distinctive, interdependent and interrelated"** |
| **Chapter 9 institutions** | **Public Protector, Human Rights Commission, Auditor-General, Electoral Commission** and others |
| **A Constitutional Court** | with final authority on constitutional matters |
| **Co-operative government** | chapter 3 |
| **Founding values** | **human dignity, equality, non-racialism, non-sexism, supremacy of the Constitution and the rule of law, universal adult suffrage** |

**And the thing that distinguishes it from most constitutions: it was written to prevent a specific recurrence.** Every major feature answers something from stages 3 to 5:

| The Constitution has | Because |
| --- | --- |
| **Constitutional supremacy** | **parliamentary sovereignty produced apartheid** |
| **A justiciable Bill of Rights** | **entrenched clauses did not hold** — the 1950s crisis |
| **A Judicial Service Commission** | **the Appeal Court was packed in 1955** |
| **Chapter 9 institutions** | **nothing had held the executive to account** |
| **Socio-economic rights** | **the dispossession was material, not only political** |
| **Eleven languages** | the language politics of stages 3 to 5 |
| **Section 25's land mandate** | **1913 and 1936** |

**Stage 7 reads it chapter by chapter.**

**Practice.** Find the Constitutional Assembly's public participation figures and one provision that demonstrably came from a submission. Then establish when the IFP withdrew and what it said. Then find the 8 May 1996 vote. Then take three features of the final Constitution and name what each was designed to prevent.
The economic settlement:
What was decided about the economy, where it was decided, and the observation that makes the third disagreement sharp.

**The claim to examine. That political power changed hands in 1994 and economic power did not** — stage 1's third disagreement.

**This lesson sets out what was actually settled, and the striking thing is where.**

---

**1. The apartheid debt was honoured.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The debt** | large, and **mostly domestic** — held by South African banks, pension funds and insurers |
| **The argument for repudiation** | **"odious debt"** — that debt incurred by an illegitimate regime to suppress its own population should not bind its victims. Argued by **Jubilee South Africa** and others |
| **The decision** | **honour it** |
| **Where decided** | **not at Kempton Park.** It followed from legal continuity — from the Multi-Party Forum lesson, the old Parliament enacted the new constitution, so obligations survived |
| **The consequence** | **debt service was one of the largest items in the first democratic budgets**, crowding out the RDP |

**The debt point is the strongest single exhibit for the "compromise" case**, and the strongest answer to it is that most of the creditors were South African pension funds — **so repudiation would have destroyed the savings of, among others, the civil servants and workers the new government represented.** Both are true.

---

**2. Reserve Bank independence was constitutionalised.**

**Section 224 of the final Constitution:**

> **The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth… and it must perform its functions independently.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What that does** | **monetary policy is removed from the elected government's control** |
| **Why it was agreed** | market confidence; and it was a National Party and business requirement |
| **An oddity** | **the SARB is one of very few central banks with private shareholders**, inherited from 1921 |
| **The live argument** | **nationalising the Bank and amending its mandate** are standing ANC conference resolutions that have never been implemented — stage 8 and stage 12 |

---

**3. Property rights were entrenched — section 25.**

**From the Constitutional Assembly lesson: a negotiated compromise.** Property protected; expropriation permitted for a public purpose or in the public interest, **with "just and equitable" compensation**; and an explicit land-reform mandate in subsections (5) to (9).

**It is not the absolute property clause business wanted, and it is not the Freedom Charter's clause either.** Stage 7 reads it properly.

---

**4. Trade liberalisation was committed before 1994.**

**From the TEC lesson: the Uruguay Round tariff commitments were agreed by the outgoing government in 1993–94**, binding the new one. **Stage 9 covers what that did to clothing, textiles and footwear employment.**

---

**5. Nationalisation was abandoned — and this one was the ANC's own decision.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **February 1990** | Mandela affirmed nationalisation as ANC policy, from the release lesson |
| **January 1992, Davos** | **Mandela's own account is that he was persuaded against it at the World Economic Forum** — reportedly by Chinese and Vietnamese delegates, who told him their own countries were moving the other way |
| **1992–94** | the commitment fades from ANC documents |
| **1996** | **GEAR** |

**And the alternative that existed.** The **Macroeconomic Research Group (MERG)** produced a report in 1993 — a more interventionist programme, developed with the alliance, with public investment, a minimum wage and a developmental state. **It was shelved.** Stage 9 covers MERG and GEAR together.

---

**6. Civil service jobs and pensions were guaranteed** — from the sunset lesson, and the **Government Employees Pension Fund was brought to full funding at very substantial cost.**

---

**Now the observation this lesson exists for.**

**Look at where each decision was made:**

| Decision | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **The debt honoured** | **a consequence of legal continuity**, not a negotiated item |
| **Reserve Bank independence** | **in the constitutional negotiations** |
| **Property rights** | **in the constitutional negotiations** |
| **Tariff commitments** | **by the outgoing government**, 1993–94 |
| **The IMF facility's terms** | **by the outgoing government**, December 1993 |
| **Civil service guarantees** | **in the sunset clauses** |
| **Nationalisation abandoned** | **by the ANC, 1992–94** |
| **GEAR** | **by the ANC government, 1996** |

**Three of the eight were negotiated with the National Party. Two were decided by the outgoing government. Two were the ANC's own decisions after 1990. One followed from legal continuity.**

**Which means the common formulation — "the ANC was outnegotiated on the economy at Kempton Park" — is not quite right.** The constitutional negotiations settled property and the Reserve Bank. **Everything else was either inherited, pre-committed, or chosen by the ANC itself.**

**And that matters for how the third disagreement is argued:**

| If the economic settlement was negotiated | If it was substantially chosen |
| --- | --- |
| **the ANC's negotiators conceded too much** | **the ANC's leadership was persuaded**, by circumstances, by markets, by advice, or by conviction |
| the remedy is to renegotiate | **the remedy is a different politics** |
| the villain is the other side | **the question is internal** |

**The second column is the harder argument and it is the better-supported one** — which is why the dispute inside the ANC alliance about GEAR, from 1996 to the present, has been more bitter than any argument with the National Party. **Stage 9 and stage 12 are its continuation.**

**The strongest form of the "compromise" case, stated fairly:** that the ANC's leadership entered negotiations with the state in crisis, emerged having secured the franchise and the constitution, **and accepted a macroeconomic framework that foreclosed the redistribution its own programme promised** — and that it did so because the alternative appeared to be capital flight, currency collapse and a failed state. **Whether that appearance was accurate is the question**, and it is genuinely unsettled.

**Practice.** List the eight decisions and where each was made. Then find the odious-debt argument and the pension-fund answer to it, and weigh them. Then read section 224 and work out what it removes from an elected government's control. Then find the MERG report of 1993 and compare its programme with GEAR's.
The TRC: design and mandate:
The commission's legal basis, the choices made in designing it, and the bargain at its centre.

**The authority. From the interim constitution lesson: the postamble required that "amnesty shall be granted in respect of acts, omissions and offences associated with political objectives", with Parliament to legislate the mechanism.**

**Parliament legislated the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 34 of 1995.**

**And the critical design choice was made there, not in the negotiations: the amnesty would be individual and conditional, not blanket.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The security establishment had expected** | a general amnesty — an indemnity covering the past |
| **What it got** | **amnesty you must apply for, by name, for specific acts, on conditions** |
| **Why that matters** | **it is the difference between a line drawn under the past and a process that extracts the past** |

**The three conditions for amnesty:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Full disclosure** | **the applicant must tell the whole truth about the act** |
| **2. A political objective** | the act must have been associated with a political objective, in the Act's defined sense |
| **3. Proportionality** | the act must have been proportionate to that objective |

**So the bargain is: truth for amnesty.** An applicant who disclosed fully got amnesty; one who lied or withheld got neither amnesty nor immunity, **and their admissions could be used against them.**

**That is why the apartheid-era record is as good as it is**, from stage 5's security lesson: **perpetrators had a strong incentive to describe their own crimes in detail.**

---

**The structure. Seventeen commissioners, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, with Alex Boraine as deputy, and three committees:**

| Committee | |
| --- | --- |
| **Human Rights Violations** | **took statements and held the public hearings** |
| **Amnesty** | **quasi-judicial** — heard applications and decided them. Chaired by a judge |
| **Reparation and Rehabilitation** | made recommendations on reparations |

**The mandate's limits, which are the subject of much of the criticism:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Subject matter** | **"gross violations of human rights"** — killing, abduction, torture and severe ill-treatment |
| **Period** | **1 March 1960 to 10 May 1994** — Sharpeville to Mandela's inauguration |
| **Who** | **all sides** — the state, the liberation movements, the homelands, the IFP, the right |
| **Not covered** | **the ordinary operation of apartheid** — forced removals, pass laws, Bantu Education, Group Areas, the migrant labour system |

**That last row is the mandate's central limitation and the TRC said so about itself.** The commission's own report acknowledges that by focusing on gross violations it necessarily treated as background the system that produced them — **and that the great majority of apartheid's harm was lawful, administrative and daily rather than criminal and exceptional.**

**Which is a profound problem.** From stages 3 to 5: **the dispossession of 3.5 million people was done by proclamation, not by death squad.** A commission investigating torture and murder will not find the Group Areas Act.

**The TRC's partial answer was the institutional hearings** — on business, the health sector, the legal profession, the media, the churches, prisons and the armed forces. **They produced valuable material and had no amnesty or sanction attached**, so participation was voluntary and uneven. **Business's engagement in particular was widely regarded as inadequate.**

---

**The design choices that made it different from other truth commissions:**

| Choice | Against the alternative |
| --- | --- |
| **Public hearings** | **Chile's and Argentina's commissions worked largely in private** |
| **Broadcast** | **the SABC's weekly *Special Report*, presented by Max du Preez** — which is free to watch, and is the single most powerful primary source on this subject |
| **Named perpetrators** | rather than anonymised findings |
| **Amnesty powers** | **unique** — no other truth commission could grant it |
| **Victim-centred** | with a reparations mandate |

**The broadcast decision is the one with the longest reach.** For two years South Africans watched, weekly, the testimony of victims and perpetrators. **It is why the TRC's findings are part of public knowledge in a way that no commission's report alone could be** — and it is why stage 5's lessons can cite what the country watched.

---

**And then the legal challenge, which settled the bargain's constitutionality.**

***Azanian Peoples Organisation (AZAPO) v President of the Republic of South Africa*, 1996.** The applicants included **the families of Steve Biko, Griffiths Mxenge and Fabian Ribeiro** — people killed by the state.

**Their argument:** the amnesty provisions were unconstitutional because they deprived victims and families of **the right to have a legal dispute settled by a court** — a right in the interim constitution's Bill of Rights.

**It is an extremely strong argument.** Their relatives had been murdered; the killers could obtain amnesty; **and the families would have no civil or criminal remedy.**

**The Constitutional Court upheld the amnesty.** Its reasoning, in summary:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The postamble** | was part of the Constitution and specifically authorised amnesty |
| **The purpose** | **without amnesty, the truth would not emerge** — perpetrators would not disclose, and the record would be lost |
| **The trade** | **truth and reconciliation, against individual claims** |
| **And the context** | a negotiated transition in which the security forces' acquiescence had been necessary |

**So the highest court in the country told the family of Steve Biko that they could not sue or prosecute, because the country needed the truth more.** That is the transition's hardest single moment, it was decided openly, with reasons, and **the judgment is worth reading because it states the bargain more honestly than any political speech did.**

**Practice.** Find the three conditions for amnesty and work out why full disclosure was the operative one. Then read the TRC's own acknowledgement of its mandate's limits. Then watch an episode of the SABC's *TRC Special Report*. Then read the *AZAPO* judgment and decide whether you think the Court was right.
The TRC: what it achieved, and what it d:
The numbers, the record it produced, the reparations that were not paid, and the prosecutions that did not follow.

**The numbers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Victim statements taken** | **about 21,000** |
| **Victims who testified at public hearings** | **about 2,000** |
| **Amnesty applications** | **7,112** |
| **Amnesty granted** | **849** — **about 12%** |
| **Amnesty refused** | **over 5,000** |
| **Report** | **volumes 1–5 in October 1998; volumes 6–7 in March 2003** |

**The 12% grant rate is the figure that corrects the common impression.** The TRC is often described as having traded blanket amnesty for truth. **It refused seven applications in eight** — because most applicants either failed the full-disclosure test, or could not show a political objective, or were applying for ordinary crimes.

---

**What it achieved, and these are real:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The record** | **the most detailed account of state criminality any such commission has produced** — from stage 5's security lesson, perpetrators described their own acts under oath |
| **Victims heard in public** | **about 21,000 statements and 2,000 testimonies**, broadcast weekly |
| **Specific truths established** | Khotso House, Vlakplaas, the Cradock Four, Operation Marion, the chemical and biological programme, cross-border operations |
| **Findings against all sides** | **the state, the IFP, the right, and the ANC** |
| **The prevention of a blanket amnesty** | from the last lesson, which was the security establishment's expectation |
| **A model** | studied and copied, with variations, in more than thirty countries |

**The findings against the ANC deserve emphasis**, because they are the strongest evidence of the commission's independence. **The TRC found the ANC responsible for gross violations** — the camps in exile where suspected infiltrators were tortured, civilian deaths from MK operations, and the township killings of suspected collaborators from stage 5's UDF lesson.

**And the ANC went to court in October 1998 to stop the publication of those findings. It lost.** The report was published with them in. **De Klerk, separately, obtained an interdict that removed a passage about him** — so one party failed to suppress findings and the other partly succeeded.

**That pair of facts is the best short summary of the TRC's standing: both principal parties tried to censor it, and it published anyway.**

---

**What it did not achieve.**

**1. Reparations — the clearest failure.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The TRC recommended** | **about R21,700 per year for six years** for each identified victim — on the order of **R3 billion** in total |
| **The government paid** | **a once-off payment of R30,000** to around 16,000 identified victims, from 2003 |
| **Which is roughly** | **a sixth of what was recommended, once** |
| **The President's Fund** | established to hold reparations money — **and it has held large unspent balances for years**, which is a standing scandal |
| **Community reparations** | recommended, and largely not delivered |

**The reparations failure is the TRC's deepest wound** and it is not the commission's fault: **it recommended, and the government decided.** Victims who had testified publicly, often at great cost, received a fraction of what the commission had said they were owed, years late.

**And it broke the bargain.** The deal was that victims gave up their legal claims — upheld in *AZAPO* — **in exchange for truth and reparation.** The truth was delivered; the reparation was not.

**2. Prosecutions — the second failure, and it is stage 11's parallel.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cases referred for prosecution** | **around 300**, where amnesty had been refused or not sought |
| **Prosecutions brought** | **very few** |
| **Convictions** | **a handful** |
| **Why** | **a political decision not to pursue them**, which successive NPA leaderships have been found to have made or acquiesced in |
| **The families' response** | **litigation**, sustained over two decades |
| **Inquests reopened** | **Timol (2017), Aggett (2019–20)**, and others — decades late, on the TRC's evidence |
| **A dedicated NPA unit** | **established and resourced only in the 2020s** |

**The Nokuthula Simelane case is the emblem.** An MK operative abducted in 1983 and never found; her family litigated for decades; **four former policemen were eventually charged in 2016, more than thirty years after.** The case has proceeded slowly and the family's pursuit of it is one of the longest private campaigns for accountability in South African history.

**3. The systemic harm went unaddressed**, from the design lesson: **removals, pass laws, Bantu Education and the migrant system were outside the mandate.**

**4. Business** — the institutional hearings produced little, and the question of corporate complicity and restitution was left open. **It resurfaced in foreign litigation and in the reparations debate, and is unresolved.**

**5. "Reconciliation" itself**, which is the most-argued criticism:

| The criticism | |
| --- | --- |
| **It placed the burden on victims** | to forgive, in public, with a bishop presiding |
| **Tutu's framing was Christian** | in a process that was legally secular, and some victims found it coercive |
| **It individualised a systemic crime** | **"a few bad apples" is the risk of any perpetrator-focused process** |
| **It conflated truth with closure** | and many victims have said explicitly that they received neither |

**The defence, which is also strong:** that reconciliation in the TRC's statutory sense meant **a shared factual record and the avoidance of further violence**, not the obligation of personal forgiveness, **and that the alternative was either a blanket amnesty with no truth or trials that could not have been held.**

---

**The honest summary, which this curriculum offers as a judgement because the facts support it:**

> **The TRC did the job it was given well and the government did not do its part.** The commission established the record, heard the victims and refused most amnesty applications. **The reparations it recommended were largely not paid and the prosecutions it referred were largely not brought** — and both of those were decisions by the democratic government, not by the commission.

**Practice.** Find the amnesty application and grant figures. Then find the TRC's reparations recommendation and what was actually paid. Then establish how many referrals produced prosecutions. Then read about the Nokuthula Simelane case. Then decide whether the bargain in *AZAPO* was kept.
What was traded:
Stage 6's conclusion, and stage 1's third disagreement: both cases at their strongest, and what would settle it.

**The question. Was the negotiated settlement a victory, or a compromise that left economic power untouched?**

---

**The case that it was a victory.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Universal franchise** | **achieved in full**, with no qualification, no separate rolls, no group representation |
| **A justiciable Bill of Rights** | including socio-economic rights, which few constitutions have |
| **Constitutional supremacy with a real court** | which refused to certify the constitution, and later ruled against a president |
| **Group rights and minority vetoes** | **defeated completely** — the National Party's central objective |
| **Power-sharing** | **expired in five years**, and the party that wanted it dissolved itself in eleven |
| **The homelands** | **abolished and reincorporated**; citizenship restored |
| **No civil war** | with 14,000 already dead in four years and armed forces on several sides |
| **And in 1990 none of this looked likely** | which is the strongest form of the argument |

**That last row is the case's core and it should be taken seriously.** In February 1990 the plausible futures included partition, a *volkstaat*, a federal arrangement with entrenched group vetoes, a Lebanese-style collapse, or a long war in KwaZulu-Natal. **The settlement delivered a unitary democratic state with one franchise, and it held.**

---

**The case that it was a compromise.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Property rights entrenched** | **section 25**, which constrains land reform |
| **The apartheid debt honoured** | consuming a large share of the early budgets |
| **Reserve Bank independence constitutionalised** | monetary policy outside elected control |
| **Tariff commitments pre-agreed** | by the outgoing government |
| **Civil service jobs and pensions guaranteed** | **with no sunset** |
| **Amnesty** | and from the TRC lesson, **reparations unpaid and prosecutions unbrought** |
| **GEAR in 1996** | **the redistributive programme replaced two months after the constitution was adopted** |
| **And the distribution of wealth** | **which has barely moved** — stage 9 has the numbers |

**And the pattern from the sunset lesson, which is the case's sharpest observation:**

> **The concessions with sunsets were political. The concessions without sunsets were economic and administrative.**

**Power-sharing expired. Property, the Reserve Bank, the debt, the pensions and the amnesty did not.**

---

**Now what this curriculum can add, from the economic settlement lesson, which sharpens both cases.**

**Three of the economic decisions were negotiated with the National Party. The rest were inherited, pre-committed by the outgoing government, or taken by the ANC itself after 1990.**

| Decision | Whose |
| --- | --- |
| **Property clause, Reserve Bank independence, civil service guarantees** | **negotiated** |
| **The debt, the tariff commitments, the IMF terms** | **inherited or pre-committed** |
| **Abandoning nationalisation, shelving MERG, adopting GEAR** | **the ANC's own** |

**Which means the two cases are not quite arguing about the same thing.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The "victory" case** | is about **the constitutional settlement**, and it is largely right about it |
| **The "compromise" case** | is about **the economic trajectory**, and it is largely right about that |
| **And the economic trajectory was not mostly settled at Kempton Park** | which is why blaming the negotiators is the weakest version of the second case, and examining the ANC's own choices is the strongest |

---

**What would settle it, which is stage 1's requirement.**

**It cannot be settled by evidence, because it is a comparison with a counterfactual: what could have been obtained instead.** But **what can be established** — and substantially has been:

| Question | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **What was actually on the table?** | **the CODESA and MPNF records, and the O'Malley interviews**, which were taken as it happened |
| **What was the state's real condition in 1992?** | the fiscal, debt and security records |
| **Could the ANC have pushed harder on the economy?** | **the record of what was asked for and refused** — and on property and the Reserve Bank, the answer appears to be that it tried and settled |
| **Was nationalisation abandoned under pressure or by persuasion?** | **the ANC's own internal documents**, and Mandela's and others' accounts |
| **Would capital flight have followed a different course?** | **unknowable** |

**So: the terms are checkable, the alternative is not.** Which is why the disagreement persists and will.

---

**One further observation worth making, because it belongs to neither case.**

**The settlement's architecture assumed a competent, honest state would use it.** The Constitution gives extensive powers to a national government: to legislate, to tax, to expropriate with compensation, to regulate, to build, to educate.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 25 permits expropriation** | in the public interest, including for land reform, with just and equitable compensation |
| **The state may legislate** | on labour, on wages, on competition, on mineral rights — **and has** |
| **The fiscal power** | is substantial |
| **The socio-economic rights** | are justiciable, and have been enforced against the state |

**So a serious question, which stage 9 and stage 12 both press: how much of what has not changed was foreclosed by the settlement, and how much by thirty years of what the state did with it?**

**That question does not resolve the third disagreement. It relocates part of it** — from 1993 to the decades after — and it is why stages 8 to 12 exist.

**Practice.** Write both cases in a paragraph each, as strongly as you can. Then take the economic settlement's eight decisions and sort them by who decided. Then find one thing section 25 permits that has not been done, and ask why. Then write down what evidence would move you, and whether it is obtainable.
How to read a constitution:
The method for this stage, which is different from reading a statute — and the three things in the text that are not rules.

**The document. The Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996.**

**And a detail that tells you something: it has no Act number.** It was passed as Act 108 of 1996, **and the Citation of Constitutional Laws Act of 2005 provided that it be cited without one** — because a supreme constitution is not one statute among others. **From stage 6: its whole design answers parliamentary sovereignty.**

**Its shape:**

| Chapter | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Founding provisions** — sections 1 to 6 |
| **2** | **The Bill of Rights** — sections 7 to 39 |
| **3** | Co-operative government |
| **4** | Parliament |
| **5** | The President and national executive |
| **6** | Provinces |
| **7** | Local government |
| **8** | Courts and the administration of justice |
| **9** | **State institutions supporting constitutional democracy** |
| **10** | Public administration |
| **11** | Security services |
| **12** | Traditional leaders |
| **13** | Finance |
| **14** | General provisions, and the schedules |

**It is about 110 pages. Read it.** It is free, it is in plain English by the standards of such documents, **and almost nobody arguing about it has.**

---

**How to read it, in five rules.**

**1. Read the text, then the cases.** The words matter and they are not self-executing. **Section 26 says everyone has the right to adequate housing; what that requires was decided in *Grootboom* in 2000**, and the case is as much the law as the section.

**2. Rights are not absolute, and the limitation clause is where that happens.** Every right in chapter 2 is subject to **section 36**, which sets out when a right may be limited. **So "the Constitution guarantees X" is never the end of an argument** — the question is whether a limitation on X is reasonable and justifiable. Lesson 17 of this stage.

**3. Watch for the verbs.** The Constitution distinguishes carefully:

| Verb | Means |
| --- | --- |
| **"has the right to"** | a right, enforceable |
| **"must"** | an obligation |
| **"may"** | a power |
| **"must take reasonable measures, within its available resources, to achieve the progressive realisation of"** | **a qualified obligation** — and that formula is the whole socio-economic rights debate |
| **"is entitled to"** | |

**The fourth row is the one to learn.** It appears in sections 26 and 27, and it means the state must act reasonably toward a goal rather than deliver the thing immediately. **Lessons 12 and 13.**

**4. Read the obligations as well as the rights.** **Section 7(2): the state must respect, protect, promote and fulfil the rights in the Bill of Rights.** Four verbs, four different duties:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Respect** | do not infringe |
| **Protect** | **prevent others from infringing** |
| **Promote** | create the conditions |
| **Fulfil** | **take positive steps to deliver** |

**That structure is why South African rights jurisprudence reaches private conduct and requires state action**, and it is unusual.

**5. Know what is not in the text.** Three categories:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Deliberate omissions** | the Freedom Charter's nationalisation clause, from stage 5 |
| **Left to legislation** | **traditional leadership's powers, the electoral system's detail, land reform's mechanisms** |
| **Decided by courts since** | the content of almost every right |

---

**And the three things in the text that are not rules.**

**First, section 1's values** — dignity, equality, non-racialism, non-sexism, the rule of law, universal suffrage. **These are not directly enforceable rights; they are the standard against which everything else is interpreted**, and the Court uses them constantly.

**Second, the interpretation clause, section 39** — and it is remarkable:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **39(1)(a)** | a court interpreting the Bill of Rights **must promote the values that underlie an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom** |
| **39(1)(b)** | **must consider international law** |
| **39(1)(c)** | **may consider foreign law** |
| **39(2)** | when interpreting any legislation or developing the common law, **every court must promote the spirit, purport and objects of the Bill of Rights** |

**Section 39(1)(b) is unusual: a constitutional instruction to consider international law.** And 39(1)(c)'s permission to consider foreign law is why South African judgments cite Canadian, German, Indian and American decisions — **which is both a strength and a criticism made of the Court.**

**Third, the postamble's descendant: the preamble**, which is not a rule and is quoted constantly:

> **We, the people of South Africa, recognise the injustices of our past… Believe that South Africa belongs to all who live in it, united in our diversity.**

**"South Africa belongs to all who live in it" is from the Freedom Charter of 1955**, from stage 5. **The preamble carries the Charter's opening line into the Constitution** — which is one answer to the question of whether the Charter was honoured.

---

**The method for this stage, then.** Each lesson takes a section or a group of them, says what the text provides, gives the case that decided what it means, and says what is still argued. **Where a provision is contested — section 25 above all — both readings get their strongest form, per stage 1.**

**Practice.** Download the Constitution and read chapter 1 — six sections, ten minutes. Then find section 7(2) and write out what each of its four verbs requires. Then find section 39 and note what a court must and may consider. Then find the preamble's phrase from the Freedom Charter.
The founding provisions:
Chapter 1 — six sections that are the hardest part of the Constitution to change, and why section 1 is protected more than the Bill of Rights.

**Section 1, in full, because it is six lines and it governs everything:**

> **The Republic of South Africa is one, sovereign, democratic state founded on the following values:**
> **(a) Human dignity, the achievement of equality and the advancement of human rights and freedoms.**
> **(b) Non-racialism and non-sexism.**
> **(c) Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law.**
> **(d) Universal adult suffrage, a national common voters roll, regular elections and a multi-party system of democratic government, to ensure accountability, responsiveness and openness.**

**Read each value against stages 3 to 5:**

| Value | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| **Human dignity** | the whole apparatus of classification and humiliation |
| **The achievement of equality** | note **"achievement"** — a goal to be reached, not a state already attained. **That word is the constitutional basis of redress** |
| **Non-racialism** | **stage 5's Freedom Charter fight, and the defeat of group rights in stage 6** |
| **Non-sexism** | and stage 4's women's politics |
| **Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law** | **parliamentary sovereignty, and the 1950s court-packing** |
| **A national common voters roll** | **the Cape common roll, lost in 1936 and 1956** |
| **Multi-party democracy, regular elections** | |

**Every clause is a specific historical repudiation.** Section 1 is the shortest summary of this curriculum's first six stages that exists.

**And "non-racialism" rather than "multiracialism"** — from stage 1's lesson on words, and stage 5's: **the doctrinal distinction the Congress tradition fought over for decades is in the founding provisions.**

---

**The amendment threshold, which is the point of this lesson.**

| To amend | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 1** | **75% of the National Assembly** plus **six of the nine provinces in the NCOP** |
| **The Bill of Rights (chapter 2)** | **two-thirds of the National Assembly** plus six provinces |
| **Most other provisions** | **two-thirds of the National Assembly** |
| **Provisions affecting provinces** | two-thirds plus six provinces |

**So section 1 is harder to amend than the Bill of Rights.** That is deliberate and it is the Constitution's answer to the 1950s: **the values and the fact of constitutional supremacy are protected above the specific rights**, because a government that could amend the supremacy clause could then do anything.

**No party has ever had 75% of the National Assembly.** The ANC's highest was just under 70%, in 2004.

**Which means section 1 has been, in practice, unamendable since 1997** — and that is the strongest structural protection in the document.

---

**Sections 2 to 6, briefly, with the one that matters most next lesson.**

**Section 2 — supremacy**, which is the next lesson.

**Section 3 — citizenship.** Common citizenship; all citizens equally entitled to the rights, privileges and benefits of citizenship. **From stage 5's 1970 Act: this sentence is the answer to denationalisation**, and it is why the homelands' citizenship laws could not survive.

**Sections 4 and 5 — the national anthem and the flag.** Worth a note:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The anthem** | **a combination of *Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika* and *Die Stem van Suid-Afrika*** — the liberation hymn and the old national anthem, in one piece, in five languages |
| **The flag** | designed in 1994, deliberately with no reference to any previous flag |

**The anthem's construction is the transition's aesthetic in one object**, and it is argued about — some find it a genuine synthesis, others a forced splice. **Both readings are defensible and the splice was the point.**

**Section 6 — languages**, and this one has changed:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Official languages** | **twelve, since 2023** — Sepedi, Sesotho, Setswana, siSwati, Tshivenda, Xitsonga, Afrikaans, English, isiNdebele, isiXhosa, isiZulu, **and South African Sign Language** |
| **The Eighteenth Amendment** | **signed 19 July 2023**, adding SASL after three decades of campaigning by the deaf community |
| **The state's duty** | to take practical and positive measures to elevate the status and advance the use of the indigenous languages |
| **Parity** | national and provincial government must use at least two official languages; **all official languages must enjoy parity of esteem and be treated equitably** |
| **Also protected** | **the Khoi, Nama and San languages** — to be promoted, per section 6(5) |
| **The institution** | the **Pan South African Language Board** |

**Section 6 is the Constitution's most-ignored provision.** In practice English dominates government, business, higher education and the courts; **Afrikaans retains substantial institutional presence; and the nine African official languages are used far less than the text requires.** Stage 9's education lesson and stage 12 both touch it.

**And the Khoi, Nama and San clause connects to stage 2**: the Constitution undertakes to promote the languages of the people whose land claims predate the 1913 cut-off and who were classified Coloured. **The undertaking has been very thinly honoured, and ǀXam from stage 2 has no speakers to promote it to.**

**Practice.** Read section 1 and match each value to something from stages 3 to 5. Then find the amendment thresholds in section 74 and note which provision is hardest to change. Then read section 6 and count the languages, then establish which the government you deal with actually uses.
Supremacy, and what it changed:
Section 2 — twenty-eight words that reverse the entire previous constitutional order, and what they oblige.

**Section 2, in full:**

> **This Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic; law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid, and the obligations imposed by it must be fulfilled.**

**Three clauses, and each does distinct work.**

---

**1. "This Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic."**

**From stage 3's Union lesson and stage 5's constitutional crisis: the previous order was parliamentary sovereignty.** Parliament could enact anything; courts interpreted and could not invalidate; entrenched clauses were defeated by changing the procedure.

| Then | Now |
| --- | --- |
| **Parliament supreme** | **the Constitution supreme** |
| Courts interpret | **courts may invalidate** |
| Entrenchment by special majority, defeasible | **a justiciable text, with a court** |

**And the reversal was demonstrated before the Constitution took effect** — from stage 6: **the Constitutional Court refused to certify the Constitutional Assembly's text in September 1996.** A supreme constitution's first act was to be enforced against the body that wrote it.

---

**2. "Law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid."**

**Two words to notice: *law* and *conduct*.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Law** | statutes, regulations, by-laws, common law, customary law — **all of it reviewable** |
| **Conduct** | **the acts of officials, ministers, the police, a president** |

**"Conduct" is the word that makes the Constitution bite on administration rather than only on legislation.** It is why a president's decision, a minister's appointment, a police operation or a parliamentary procedure can be declared invalid.

**And the cases that used it are stage 11's:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***EFF v Speaker* (2016)** | **the President's failure to comply with the Public Protector's remedial action was inconsistent with the Constitution** |
| ***UDM v Speaker* (2017)** | the Speaker's belief that she lacked a discretion on a secret ballot was wrong in law |
| **The Zuma contempt judgment (2021)** | a former President's refusal to appear before a commission |

**All three are "conduct", not law.**

---

**3. "And the obligations imposed by it must be fulfilled."**

**This is the clause people forget and it is the one with the most work left in it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It makes the Constitution's duties mandatory** | not aspirational |
| **Combined with section 7(2)** | **respect, protect, promote and fulfil** |
| **And section 237** | **"all constitutional obligations must be performed diligently and without delay"** |

**Section 237 is the sleeper provision of the whole document.** *Diligently and without delay.* **It has been used to compel the state to act** — on appointments not made, reports not filed, decisions not taken — and it is the textual basis for a great deal of the litigation that has substituted for administration in South Africa.

---

**What supremacy made possible, with the examples:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Striking down statutes** | ***Makwanyane*** (1995) — the death penalty; ***Bhe*** (2004) — the customary succession rules codified in 1927, from stage 4 |
| **Striking down conduct** | the Nkandla line of cases |
| **Compelling the state to act** | ***TAC*** (2002) — provide nevirapine; ***Glenister*** (2011) — create an adequately independent anti-corruption body |
| **Developing the common law** | section 39(2) — **so private law changes too** |
| **Reviewing customary law** | against the Bill of Rights, which is lesson 14's subject |
| **Refusing a constitution** | 1996 |

---

**Now the limit, which is this lesson's honest second half.**

**Supremacy makes a judgment binding. It does not make it happen.**

| Case | Judgment | Implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***Grootboom*** (2000) | housing policy must be reasonable and include the desperate | **Irene Grootboom died in 2008 without a house** |
| ***TAC*** (2002) | provide nevirapine | **complied with, eventually and slowly** |
| ***Glenister*** (2011) | create an independent anti-corruption body | **the Hawks' independence is still argued about** — stage 8 |
| **Numerous orders** on school infrastructure, textbooks, sanitation | | **repeat litigation on the same issues for years** |

**So the pattern: South Africa has an extremely strong constitutional law and a weak state.** The courts order; the administration does not always deliver; the applicants return.

**And that produces a specific phenomenon worth naming: litigation as a substitute for government.** Civil society organisations — the Treatment Action Campaign, Section27, Equal Education, the Legal Resources Centre, SERI, Corruption Watch — **sue the state to compel it to do what it has already undertaken to do.**

| The reading that this is a success | The reading that it is a failure |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism works** — rights are enforced against a reluctant state | **a state that must be sued to supply textbooks is not functioning** |
| **It is what a justiciable Bill of Rights is for** | **and courts are a terrible way to run a schools system** |
| Without it, far less would be delivered | **it advantages those with access to lawyers** |

**Both are true and stage 12 argues about which matters more.** What is not in doubt is that section 2 and section 237 are what made it possible — **and that in a country with the previous constitutional order, none of it could have happened at all.**

**Practice.** Read sections 2, 7(2) and 237 together. Then find one case that invalidated a statute and one that invalidated conduct. Then look up what happened to Irene Grootboom after her judgment. Then find a current case in which an organisation is suing the state to deliver something it has already promised.
The Bill of Rights: structure and applic:
Chapter 2's architecture — who is bound, who is entitled, how a rights case actually works, and the two-stage analysis every argument follows.

**The sections that make the machine work, before any individual right.**

---

**Section 7 — the obligations.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **7(1)** | the Bill of Rights is **"a cornerstone of democracy"** and **"affirms the democratic values of human dignity, equality and freedom"** |
| **7(2)** | **"The state must respect, protect, promote and fulfil the rights in the Bill of Rights."** |
| **7(3)** | the rights are **subject to the limitations in section 36 or elsewhere in the Bill** |

**From the method lesson, the four verbs in 7(2) are four duties**, and the third and fourth — promote and fulfil — are what make this a Bill of Rights that requires the state to act rather than merely to refrain.

---

**Section 8 — application, and this is the technical heart.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **8(1)** | the Bill of Rights **binds the legislature, the executive, the judiciary and all organs of state** |
| **8(2)** | **"A provision of the Bill of Rights binds a natural or a juristic person if, and to the extent that, it is applicable, taking into account the nature of the right and the nature of any duty imposed by the right."** |
| **8(3)** | courts must apply or develop the common law to give effect to a right, and may develop rules to limit it |
| **8(4)** | **"A juristic person is entitled to the rights in the Bill of Rights to the extent required by the nature of the rights and the nature of that juristic person."** |

**Section 8(2) is "horizontal application" and it is unusual.** Most bills of rights bind only the state. **South Africa's binds private persons too, where the right's nature makes that appropriate.**

| Practical consequences | |
| --- | --- |
| **A private employer** | cannot unfairly discriminate — section 9(4) |
| **A private school or club** | may be bound by equality provisions |
| **A newspaper** | the right to dignity operates against private defamation |
| **A landlord** | eviction must comply with section 26(3) and the courts' requirements |
| **A private hospital** | may be bound in some respects |

**And 8(4) means companies have constitutional rights** — to property, to privacy in some respects, to just administrative action, to access to courts. **Not to dignity or life, by nature.** This matters enormously in practice: **much constitutional litigation is brought by companies**, and stage 12's arguments about corporate power run through it.

---

**Section 9 onward are the rights themselves, which the next lessons take.**

**Sections 36 to 39 are the machinery at the other end:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **36** | **the limitation clause** — lesson 17 |
| **37** | **states of emergency** — lesson 18 |
| **38** | **enforcement** — who may approach a court, and the remedies |
| **39** | **interpretation** — from the method lesson |

---

**Now the two-stage analysis, which is how every constitutional rights argument in South Africa is structured.** Learn this and you can follow any judgment.

**Stage one: has a right been infringed?**

| Ask | |
| --- | --- |
| **Does the claimant hold the right?** | section 8(4) for a company; some rights are for citizens only |
| **Is the respondent bound?** | section 8(1) or 8(2) |
| **What does the right mean?** | interpretation, section 39 |
| **Has it been infringed?** | on the facts |

**Stage two: is the infringement justified?** **Section 36.**

| Ask | |
| --- | --- |
| **Is the limitation by "law of general application"?** | **if not, it fails immediately.** Arbitrary executive action cannot be justified under section 36 |
| **Is it reasonable and justifiable** in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom? | weighing the five listed factors |

**The burden shifts between the stages.** The claimant proves the infringement; **the respondent must justify it.** That allocation is doing a great deal of work — **it means the state has to explain itself.**

**And if the limitation is not justified: section 172 governs the remedy** — a declaration of invalidity, with the court able to suspend it to allow Parliament to fix the defect, or to limit its retrospective effect. **Lesson 19.**

---

**Three things about this structure that are worth noticing.**

**1. "Law of general application" excludes a great deal.** A policy, a practice, an instruction, a discretionary decision — **none of these is a law of general application**, so a right infringed by them cannot be saved by section 36. **It must be justified, if at all, under the specific right's internal qualifications.** This is why administrative conduct that infringes a right very often simply fails.

**2. Some rights have internal limitations, and they are not all subject to the same analysis.** Section 26's "within its available resources… progressive realisation" is an internal qualification; **so is section 25(1)'s "arbitrary"; so is section 33's "just" administrative action.** Where a right is internally qualified, much of the weighing happens inside stage one.

**3. The Bill of Rights binds the judiciary**, section 8(1) — **so the courts' own conduct and the common law they apply are constrained by it.** Section 39(2) requires every court, in every case, to develop the common law in the Bill of Rights' spirit. **Which means South African private law has been changing continuously since 1994**, in defamation, in delict, in contract, in eviction, in family law.

**Practice.** Read sections 7, 8, 36, 38 and 39 together — that is the machinery. Then find one case where a company relied on a right under section 8(4). Then take any rights judgment and identify where stage one ends and stage two begins. Then find a case in which the limitation failed because there was no law of general application.
Equality — section 9:
The most litigated provision in the Constitution, the clause that makes redress constitutional, and the test for unfair discrimination.

**Section 9, in its five subsections:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **9(1)** | **"Everyone is equal before the law and has the right to equal protection and benefit of the law."** |
| **9(2)** | equality includes the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms. **"To promote the achievement of equality, legislative and other measures designed to protect or advance persons, or categories of persons, disadvantaged by unfair discrimination may be taken."** |
| **9(3)** | **the state may not unfairly discriminate** directly or indirectly on listed grounds |
| **9(4)** | **no person may unfairly discriminate** — horizontal, from the last lesson |
| **9(5)** | **discrimination on a listed ground is unfair unless it is established that the discrimination is fair** |

**The listed grounds in 9(3):**

> **race, gender, sex, pregnancy, marital status, ethnic or social origin, colour, sexual orientation, age, disability, religion, conscience, belief, culture, language and birth.**

**Sixteen grounds, and "sexual orientation" among them** — which in 1996 made South Africa the first country in the world to include it in a constitution. **That clause produced the same-sex marriage judgment, *Fourie*, in 2005, and South Africa was the fifth country to recognise it.**

---

**Now section 9(2), which is the provision this lesson exists for.**

**Read it again: "To promote the achievement of equality, legislative and other measures designed to protect or advance persons… disadvantaged by unfair discrimination may be taken."**

**That is the constitutional basis of employment equity, B-BBEE, preferential procurement, land reform's redistributive mechanisms and every other redress measure.** And the way it is drafted matters enormously.

**The key case: *Minister of Finance v Van Heerden* (2004).**

**The question: is a redress measure a form of discrimination that has to be justified, or is it part of equality itself?**

**The Court's answer: part of equality.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The wrong analysis** | a redress measure discriminates on race, so it must be shown to be fair under 9(3) and 9(5) |
| **The right analysis** | **a measure that genuinely satisfies 9(2) is not "discrimination" to be excused — it is a measure in service of the equality 9(1) and 9(2) establish** |
| **The test for a 9(2) measure** | **does it target persons disadvantaged by unfair discrimination · is it designed to protect or advance them · and does it promote the achievement of equality** |

**So the constitutional structure is: formal equality in 9(1) and 9(3), substantive equality in 9(2), and 9(2) is not an exception to equality but a component of it.**

**That is the single most important thing to understand about South African equality law**, and it is why arguments that BEE is "reverse discrimination" fail as constitutional arguments. **They may succeed as policy arguments** — that a particular measure is badly designed, captured, or no longer targeting the disadvantaged — **and stage 9 and stage 12 take those seriously.** But the constitutional objection does not run.

**And the limit, which is real.** A measure must actually satisfy the three-part test. **A measure that does not target the disadvantaged, or that is not designed to advance them, or that does not promote equality, is not protected by 9(2)** — and courts have said so. **Whether specific BEE measures now satisfy it, thirty years on, is a live and legitimate question**, and it is stage 12's.

---

**The unfair discrimination test, from *Harksen v Lane* (1997)**, which is the sequence every discrimination case follows:

| Step | |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Is there differentiation?** | and does it bear a rational connection to a legitimate government purpose? If not, it violates 9(1) |
| **2. Does it amount to discrimination?** | **on a listed ground** — then it is discrimination. **On an unlisted ground** — then only if it is based on attributes with the potential to impair fundamental human dignity |
| **3. Is the discrimination unfair?** | **on a listed ground, unfairness is presumed** (9(5)); otherwise the claimant must show it |
| **4. If unfair** | can it be justified under **section 36**? |

**Step 2's distinction between listed and unlisted grounds is where new grounds enter.** **Citizenship** was recognised as an analogous ground in *Larbi-Odam*; **HIV status** in *Hoffmann v South African Airways* (2000), where the Court held that refusing employment to an HIV-positive cabin attendant was unfair discrimination.

**And the presumption in 9(5) is a powerful allocation of burden.** Discriminate on race, sex or religion and **you must prove it was fair.**

---

**The implementing legislation.** Section 9(4) required Parliament to enact national legislation to prevent unfair discrimination, and it did:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **PEPUDA** — the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act 4 of 2000 | the general statute |
| **Equality Courts** | **every magistrates' court and High Court sits as one** — accessible, with simplified procedure |
| **The Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998** | in the workplace |
| **The Labour Relations Act** | unfair discrimination as an unfair labour practice |

**The Equality Courts are the most under-used institution in South African law.** They are designed for an unrepresented complainant, they can hear hate-speech and discrimination complaints, and most people do not know they exist. **Stage 8's lesson on institutions returns to the pattern.**

**Practice.** Read section 9 and list its sixteen grounds. Then read *Van Heerden*'s holding on section 9(2) and state in one sentence why redress is not an exception to equality. Then work through the *Harksen* steps on a concrete example — a retirement age, say. Then find your nearest Equality Court.
Dignity, life, and the person:
Sections 10 to 13 — the rights the Constitutional Court has used most, the judgment that abolished the death penalty, and the right that reaches furthest into private life.

**Section 10: "Everyone has inherent dignity and the right to have their dignity respected and protected."**

**Dignity is the Constitution's organising value and it does three jobs:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A right in itself** | enforceable |
| **A value** | in section 1, and in section 39's interpretive instruction |
| **The content of other rights** | **equality, privacy, bodily integrity and the socio-economic rights are all explained in dignity terms by the Court** |

**Why dignity rather than liberty as the central value — and this is a real and deliberate choice.** The American tradition organises rights around liberty; **the German Basic Law, written after Nazism, puts dignity first, and South Africa followed it.**

**The reason is in stages 3 to 5.** The injury of apartheid was not principally a restriction of liberty: **it was classification, humiliation, the pass, the removal, the bench, the compound.** A liberty-centred constitution would have struggled to name that. **A dignity-centred one names it exactly.**

**And the consequence is that South African rights law is more comfortable with positive obligations than American law is** — because dignity requires provision, and liberty mainly requires restraint.

---

**Section 11: "Everyone has the right to life."**

***S v Makwanyane* (1995)** — the Constitutional Court's first major judgment, under the interim constitution, **abolishing the death penalty.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reasoning** | the death penalty infringed the rights to life and to dignity and the prohibition on cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment, and **could not be justified** |
| **Chaskalson P's analysis** | deterrence was not established; the penalty was arbitrary in application; and **it was incompatible with the values the Constitution established** |
| **Public opinion** | **strongly in favour of the death penalty, then and now** |
| **The Court's answer** | that the question is not what the majority wants but what the Constitution requires — **and that a Bill of Rights exists precisely to protect against majorities** |

***Makwanyane* is the founding judgment of South African constitutionalism** for that reason: it did the unpopular thing, immediately, with full reasons, and it held. **Reinstating the death penalty remains a popular political demand and would require a constitutional amendment the Court has made very difficult.**

**Section 11 has also been argued in other contexts** — on abortion (where the Court has not held that the foetus holds section 11 rights), on the state's duty to protect life from violent crime, and on access to life-saving treatment, which is section 27's territory.

---

**Section 12: freedom and security of the person**, and it is the longest of these:

| 12(1) — everyone has the right | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **not to be deprived of freedom arbitrarily or without just cause** |
| **(b)** | **not to be detained without trial** |
| **(c)** | **to be free from all forms of violence from either public or private sources** |
| **(d)** | **not to be tortured in any way** |
| **(e)** | not to be treated or punished in a cruel, inhuman or degrading way |

| 12(2) — bodily and psychological integrity, including | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **to make decisions concerning reproduction** |
| **(b)** | **to security in and control over their body** |
| **(c)** | **not to be subjected to medical or scientific experiments without informed consent** |

**Read 12(1)(b) against stage 5: "not to be detained without trial."** Section 6 of the Terrorism Act, 90 days, 180 days, the states of emergency — **all of it, in six words.**

**And 12(1)(d): "not to be tortured in any way."** From stage 5's security lesson. **There is no qualification, and torture is also non-derogable under section 37** — it cannot be suspended even in a state of emergency.

**12(1)(c) is the one doing unexpected work: "free from all forms of violence from either public or private sources."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Private sources"** | **so the state has a duty to protect people from violence by other people** |
| **Which produces** | state liability for failures to protect — ***Carmichele v Minister of Safety and Security* (2001)**, where the Court held the state could be liable in delict for failing to protect a woman from a known dangerous man |
| **And it is the constitutional root** | of the state's obligations on **gender-based violence**, which stage 12 covers |

***Carmichele* is one of the most consequential judgments in South African private law**, because it used section 39(2) to develop the common law of delict to impose a duty on the state — **and the state's failures to protect have been litigated on that basis ever since.**

**And 12(2)(a), "decisions concerning reproduction"**, is the textual basis of the **Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act 92 of 1996** — one of the most liberal abortion laws in the world, enacted the same year as the Constitution, and the subject of continuing political contest.

---

**Section 13: "No one may be subjected to slavery, servitude or forced labour."**

**Short, absolute, and from stages 3 and 4: Cape slavery, indenture, the masters and servants laws, labour tenancy, and the pass-law farm labour system.** It is not a dead letter — **it has been argued in cases on human trafficking and on exploitative labour conditions.**

**Practice.** Read *Makwanyane*'s treatment of public opinion and decide whether you find it convincing. Then read section 12(1) and match each paragraph to something from stage 5. Then read *Carmichele* and work out what duty it created. Then find the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act and its constitutional basis.
Privacy, religion, belief and opinion:
Sections 14 and 15 — the right that decriminalised cannabis and struck down bulk surveillance, and the one that governs religion in a secular state with a religious population.

**Section 14: "Everyone has the right to privacy, which includes the right not to have — (a) their person or home searched; (b) their property searched; (c) their possessions seized; or (d) the privacy of their communications infringed."**

**The structure: a general right, with four specified instances.** The general right is broader than the list.

**And the Court's framework, from *Bernstein v Bester* (1996): privacy operates on a continuum.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Strongest** | **the inner sanctum — the home, the body, intimate relationships** |
| **Weaker** | as a person moves into community and commercial life |
| **Weakest** | business and regulated activity |

**Which is why a search of a home is harder to justify than an inspection of a company's records**, and why both are section 14 questions.

**Two judgments that show its reach.**

***Minister of Justice v Prince* (2018)** — **the private use and cultivation of cannabis by an adult in a private place decriminalised**, on privacy grounds.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The earlier attempt** | ***Prince* (2002)**, on **religious** grounds — a Rastafari lawyer — **failed** |
| **The successful ground** | **privacy**, sixteen years later |
| **What it covers** | **private use and cultivation by adults in private**; not dealing, not public use |
| **The follow-up** | **the Cannabis for Private Purposes Act, signed in 2024**, legislating the detail |

**The two *Prince* cases together are a lesson in constitutional litigation: the same conduct, two different rights, one failure and one success.**

***AmaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism v Minister of Justice* (2021)** — **the Constitutional Court held key provisions of RICA unconstitutional**, including the bulk interception of communications and the absence of safeguards for journalists' and lawyers' communications and for post-surveillance notification.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Who brought it** | **the investigative journalism outfit from stage 1's press lesson** — after discovering that one of its journalists had been surveilled |
| **What it established** | **mass surveillance requires constitutional authority and safeguards**, and South Africa's did not have them |

**And the general statute: POPIA — the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013**, fully in force from 2021, with an **Information Regulator.** It is section 14's legislative expression and it governs how any organisation may process personal information.

---

**Section 15: freedom of conscience, religion, thought, belief and opinion.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **15(1)** | the right |
| **15(2)** | **religious observances may be conducted at state or state-aided institutions** — provided they are **free and voluntary**, **equitable**, and follow rules made by the appropriate authority |
| **15(3)** | **legislation recognising marriages concluded under religious or customary systems is permitted** — subject to consistency with the Constitution |

**South Africa is a secular state with a strongly religious population, and section 15(2) is the compromise.** Religious observance in state schools is permitted and must be voluntary and equitable — **so a school may have a religious ethos and may not compel participation or favour one faith.**

**The litigation shows where the line sits:**

| Case | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| ***Christian Education SA v Minister of Education* (2000)** | **corporal punishment in religious schools: the ban upheld.** The religious interest did not outweigh the children's rights |
| ***MEC for Education: KZN v Pillay* (2007)** | **a Hindu Tamil pupil's nose stud: the school's code could not prohibit it.** Religious and cultural practice must be accommodated unless it is unreasonable to do so |
| ***OGOD v Laerskool Randhart* (2017)** | **a public school may not brand itself as adhering to a single religion**, though religious observance remains permitted under 15(2) |

***Pillay* is the important one** and it introduced **"reasonable accommodation"** into South African law: **a rule of general application that burdens a religious or cultural practice must be adjusted unless adjustment is unreasonable.** That principle now runs through employment, education and public administration.

**And section 15(3) on religious marriages is the unfinished business.** It permits legislation; **Parliament has not fully delivered it**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Customary marriages** | **recognised** — the Recognition of Customary Marriages Act 120 of 1998 |
| **Civil unions** | the Civil Union Act 17 of 2006, after *Fourie* |
| **Muslim marriages** | **not recognised by general legislation for decades**, which left women in them without the protections of marriage. **The Constitutional Court in *Women's Legal Centre Trust v President* (2022) declared the failure unconstitutional and ordered Parliament to legislate** |
| **Hindu and other religious marriages** | similarly addressed through litigation rather than legislation |

**The *Women's Legal Centre* case is a good illustration of stage 7's recurring pattern**, from the supremacy lesson: **a constitutional obligation unperformed for twenty-five years, enforced eventually by litigation.** Section 15(3) said Parliament *may* legislate; **section 9's equality and section 10's dignity meant it had to.**

**Practice.** Read sections 14 and 15. Then read both *Prince* judgments and identify which right succeeded. Then read *Pillay*'s reasonable accommodation test. Then find out whether Parliament has yet legislated on Muslim marriages, and when the Court's deadline was.
Expression, and its limits:
Section 16 — the right with the most unusual structure in the Bill of Rights, and the hate-speech judgment that rewrote a statute.

**Section 16(1): "Everyone has the right to freedom of expression, which includes — (a) freedom of the press and other media; (b) freedom to receive or impart information or ideas; (c) freedom of artistic creativity; and (d) academic freedom and freedom of scientific research."**

**Four specified inclusions, and the explicit protection of the press and of academic freedom is notable** — from stage 5, where both had been comprehensively suppressed.

---

**And then section 16(2), which is the unusual part:**

> **The right in subsection (1) does not extend to — (a) propaganda for war; (b) incitement of imminent violence; or (c) advocacy of hatred that is based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion, and that constitutes incitement to cause harm.**

**Read "does not extend to".** This is **not** a limitation under section 36. **It is an internal exclusion: these three categories are not protected expression at all.**

**The consequence is technical and important:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For ordinary expression** | a restriction infringes section 16(1) and **must be justified under section 36** |
| **For the three excluded categories** | **there is nothing to justify.** The expression is simply outside the right |

**So the two-stage analysis from the structure lesson does not apply to them** — which makes the definition of each category decisive, because everything turns on whether speech falls inside or outside.

**And each category is narrowly drafted:**

| Category | Note the narrowing words |
| --- | --- |
| **Propaganda for war** | not discussion of war |
| **Incitement of *imminent* violence** | **"imminent"** — not advocacy of violence generally |
| **Advocacy of hatred based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion that *constitutes incitement to cause harm*** | **two requirements: advocacy of hatred, and incitement to harm.** And only four grounds — **not sexual orientation, not disability** |

**So a great deal of offensive and even hateful speech is inside section 16(1)** and can be restricted only if the restriction survives section 36. **That is a genuinely protective structure** and it is why South African expression law is closer to the American position than its reputation suggests.

---

**The hate-speech judgment: *Qwelane v South African Human Rights Commission* (2021).**

**The background.** Jon Qwelane, a journalist, published a column in 2008 attacking same-sex relationships. **He was found to have committed hate speech under section 10 of PEPUDA** — the equality statute from the equality lesson.

**And section 10 of PEPUDA was drafted much more broadly than section 16(2):** it prohibited words based on a prohibited ground that could reasonably be construed to demonstrate a clear intention to **be hurtful**, be harmful or incite harm, or **promote or propagate hatred.**

**The Constitutional Court's decision:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The "hurtful" limb** | **unconstitutional and struck out** — too broad, catching speech that merely offends |
| **The rest** | **upheld, and reformulated** — hate speech requires harm or incitement to harm, or the promotion of hatred |
| **PEPUDA's grounds** | **broader than section 16(2)'s four**, and that was held permissible as a justified limitation under section 36 |
| **Qwelane's column** | **found to be hate speech** on the reformulated test |

**So PEPUDA may prohibit more than section 16(2) excludes — because the extra prohibition is a section 36 limitation that was justified — but it may not prohibit speech merely for being hurtful.**

**That is the current law and it is the thing to know: "hurtful" is not the test; harm or the promotion of hatred is.**

---

**The other cases worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
