| ***Islamic Unity Convention v IBA* (2002)** | a broadcasting code clause prohibiting material **"likely to prejudice relations between sections of the population"** — **struck down as overbroad** |
| ***Print Media SA v Minister of Home Affairs* (2012)** | **prior classification of publications struck down** — prior restraint is particularly suspect |
| ***EFF v Manuel* (2021)** | defamation, and the limits of political speech about officials |

**And the statute that was passed and never signed: the Protection of State Information Bill — the "Secrecy Bill".** Passed by Parliament in 2013, **and never signed into law** by the President after sustained campaigning against it by the Right2Know campaign and the media.

**That is stage 1's Gazette lesson again, in reverse: a Bill passed and not assented to is not law**, and the Bill has been sitting unsigned for over a decade. **It is a live political question whether it ever will be.**

---

**The practical state of media freedom, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** South Africa has a free press by any international comparison, with constitutional protection, active investigative journalism and no prior censorship. **The pressures on it are commercial — declining revenue, shrinking newsrooms, concentrated ownership — rather than legal**, from stage 1's press lesson. **The SABC's independence and funding remain contested.**

**And the structural point this stage keeps making: the Constitution protects expression very strongly, and a press that cannot afford reporters is not protected by any clause.** Stage 10's lesson on the press takes it up.

**Practice.** Read section 16 in full and note that 16(2) says "does not extend to". Then work out which of these is inside 16(1): a column arguing against immigration; a speech urging a crowd to attack a shop now; a pamphlet advocating hatred of a religion and calling for harm. Then read *Qwelane*'s reformulation of PEPUDA section 10. Then establish whether the Secrecy Bill has been signed.
Assembly, association, and political rig:
Sections 17 to 19 — the rights that make opposition possible, the judgment that decriminalised protest, and the case that forced independent candidates onto the ballot.

**Section 17: "Everyone has the right, peacefully and unarmed, to assemble, to demonstrate, to picket and to present petitions."**

**The qualifications are in the right itself: "peacefully and unarmed".** So a violent or armed assembly is outside section 17 — the internal-exclusion technique from the expression lesson.

**The governing statute: the Regulation of Gatherings Act 205 of 1993** — passed during the transition, and notably a product of the **Goldstone Commission's** recommendations from stage 6.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it requires** | **notice** to the local authority for a gathering of more than fifteen people, with a convener |
| **What it is not** | **a permit system** — the authority cannot simply refuse; it may impose conditions or, on narrow grounds, prohibit |
| **The structure** | negotiation between convener, authority and police |

**And the judgment: *Mlungwana v S* (2018).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The provision** | **section 12(1)(a) of the Act made it a criminal offence to convene a gathering without giving notice** |
| **The applicants** | members of the Social Justice Coalition, convicted for a protest about sanitation in Khayelitsha |
| **The holding** | **the criminalisation was unconstitutional** — it limited section 17 and was not justified, because the Act's other mechanisms were sufficient |
| **Consequence** | **failing to give notice is no longer a crime.** The notice obligation remains |

**That matters for poor communities above all**, which the Court said: **the people most likely to protest without a lawyer's notice are the people with the least access to one**, and criminalising the failure fell on them.

---

**Section 18: "Everyone has the right to freedom of association."**

**Short, and it carries a great deal** — trade unions (with section 23), political parties (with section 19), religious bodies, professional associations, and the right **not** to associate.

---

**Section 19 — political rights, and this is the one that structures South African electoral politics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **19(1)** | **every citizen is free to make political choices**, including to **form a political party**, to **participate in its activities and recruit members**, and to **campaign** |
| **19(2)** | **every citizen has the right to free, fair and regular elections for any legislative body established under the Constitution** |
| **19(3)** | **every adult citizen** has the right **to vote in elections for any legislative body, and to do so in secret**, and **to stand for public office and, if elected, to hold office** |

**Note "citizen" throughout.** Section 19 is one of the few rights restricted to citizens — **permanent residents may not vote.**

**The cases, and each changed something:**

| Case | Held |
| --- | --- |
| ***August v Electoral Commission* (1999)** | **prisoners have the right to vote**, and the IEC must make arrangements for them |
| ***Minister of Home Affairs v NICRO* (2004)** | an attempt to disenfranchise certain sentenced prisoners **struck down** |
| ***Richter v Minister of Home Affairs* (2009)** | **South Africans abroad may vote** in national elections |
| ***My Vote Counts v Minister of Justice* (2018)** | **information on private funding of political parties must be recorded and made accessible** |
| ***New Nation Movement v President* (2020)** | **the Electoral Act was unconstitutional in requiring candidates for the National Assembly and provincial legislatures to stand only through parties** |

**The last two are the ones with current consequences.**

***My Vote Counts* produced the Political Party Funding Act 6 of 2018**, in force from 2021: **parties must disclose donations above a threshold, foreign donations are restricted, and the IEC administers a Multi-Party Democracy Fund.** From stage 10's party funding lesson: **before 2021, South African party funding was entirely undisclosed.**

***New Nation Movement* produced the Electoral Amendment Act of 2023**, which allowed **independent candidates** to contest national and provincial elections for the first time — **used in the 2024 election, with negligible success**, because the system's seat allocation makes an independent's path very hard. **Stage 10 and stage 12 argue about whether the Act satisfied the judgment.**

---

**And the gap in section 19 that the electoral reform argument turns on.**

**Section 19 guarantees free, fair and regular elections and the right to vote and stand.** **It does not specify an electoral system.**

| What the Constitution requires | What it leaves open |
| --- | --- |
| Elections, free and fair and regular | **the system** |
| **A national common voters roll** (section 1) | |
| **"Results in general, in proportional representation"** — Schedule 6 and section 46(1)(d) | **but not closed national lists specifically** |

**So the closed-list proportional system South Africa uses since 1994 — from stage 6, chosen for a first election with no voters' roll — is a statutory choice, not a constitutional requirement.**

**And the consequence, which is stage 10's central institutional point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Under closed lists** | **a member of the National Assembly owes their seat to the party, not to a constituency** |
| **So** | **accountability runs to the party's list committee** |
| **Which means** | an MP who defies the party loses their livelihood |
| **And** | **no MP has a geographic constituency to answer to** |

**That is the single most-argued institutional feature of South African democracy**, it could be changed by ordinary legislation, and nothing in the Constitution prevents a mixed or constituency system. **Stage 12 puts both sides.**

**Practice.** Read sections 17 to 19. Then read *Mlungwana* and work out why criminalising notice failures fell hardest on the poor. Then find the Political Party Funding Act's disclosure threshold. Then establish whether the Constitution requires closed-list proportional representation, and what it does require.
Movement, trade, labour, environment:
Sections 21 to 24 — four rights that each answer something specific from the preceding stages.

**Section 21 — freedom of movement and residence.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **21(1)** | everyone has the right to freedom of movement |
| **21(2)** | everyone has the right to leave the Republic |
| **21(3)** | **every citizen has the right to enter, to remain in and to reside anywhere in the Republic** |
| **21(4)** | every citizen has the right to a passport |

**Read 21(3) against stages 4 and 5.** The pass laws, section 10 rights, influx control, endorsing out, the 72-hour rule, the Group Areas Act, the homelands' borders — **all of it answered by one sentence.** *To reside anywhere in the Republic.*

**And 21(4) against stage 5's citizenship lesson**: the TBVC passports nobody accepted.

**Section 21 is the least litigated right in the Bill of Rights precisely because the thing it prohibits was abolished before it came into force.** Its practical work now is in immigration law, where the rights of non-citizens are at issue and section 21 largely does not reach them — **which stage 12's lesson on migration takes up.**

---

**Section 22 — freedom of trade, occupation and profession.**

> **Every citizen has the right to choose their trade, occupation or profession freely. The practice of a trade, occupation or profession may be regulated by law.**

**Against stage 3 and stage 4: the colour bar, job reservation, the civilised labour policy, trading licences refused to Indian businesses under the Group Areas Act.**

**And note the second sentence: regulation is expressly permitted.** So professional bodies, licensing, qualification requirements and business regulation are all within section 22 — **the right is to choose, not to be unregulated.**

**Its live use is in challenges to licensing and regulatory schemes**, and it is the clause business litigants reach for most often after section 25 and section 33.

---

**Section 23 — labour relations, and this one is substantial:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **23(1)** | **"Everyone has the right to fair labour practices."** |
| **23(2)** | **workers** may form and join a trade union, participate in its activities, and **strike** |
| **23(3)** | **employers** may form and join employers' organisations and participate in their activities |
| **23(4)** | unions and employers' organisations have organisational rights |
| **23(5)** | **the right to engage in collective bargaining**, with legislation permitted to regulate it |
| **23(6)** | legislation may recognise union security arrangements in a collective agreement |

**Three things to notice.**

**First: "everyone has the right to fair labour practices" is extraordinarily broad.** Not "every worker" — **everyone.** It has been read to cover job applicants and, in some circumstances, relationships that are not strictly employment.

**Second: the right to strike is constitutional, and there is no corresponding right to lock out.** From stage 6's certification lesson: **the Constitutional Court raised the asymmetry when it refused to certify the Constitution**, and the final text still confers a right to strike on workers without conferring a right to lock out on employers. **The Labour Relations Act provides for lockouts as a matter of statute, not of constitutional right.** That asymmetry is deliberate and is defended on the ground that the parties are not equally situated.

**Third: from stage 4 and stage 5 — Africans were excluded from the statutory definition of "employee" from 1924 to 1979**, so had no legal union, no lawful strike and no bargaining. **Section 23 is the answer, and it is why South African labour law is among the most protective in the world** — which stage 9's unemployment lesson treats as both an achievement and a contested cause.

**The implementing statutes:** the **Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995**, the **Basic Conditions of Employment Act**, the **Employment Equity Act**, and the **National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018.**

---

**Section 24 — the environment:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **24(a)** | everyone has the right **to an environment that is not harmful to their health or well-being** |
| **24(b)** | **and to have the environment protected, for the benefit of present and future generations**, through reasonable legislative and other measures that prevent pollution and ecological degradation, promote conservation, and secure ecologically sustainable development and use of natural resources **while promoting justifiable economic and social development** |

**Note the final clause: environmental protection is balanced against development in the text itself.**

**And it has teeth.** Section 24 has produced real litigation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Fuel Retailers* (2007)** | sustainable development must be considered in authorisation decisions |
| **The "Deadly Air" case (2022)** | the Highveld's air quality held to breach section 24; the Minister ordered to act |
| **The Thabametsi and Khanyisa coal cases** | **climate change impacts must be assessed** before a power station is authorised |
| **Shell seismic survey cases (2022)** | authorisations set aside for failures of consultation with coastal communities |
| **The Karpowership and gas procurement challenges** | ongoing |

**The "Deadly Air" judgment is the one to know**: a court held that the air in the Mpumalanga Highveld — where South Africa's coal power stations are — **breached the constitutional right**, and ordered the Minister to prescribe regulations. **From stage 9's Eskom lesson: the country's electricity and its constitutional environmental obligations are in direct conflict**, and that conflict is now being litigated rather than legislated.

**Practice.** Read section 21(3) and list the apartheid measures it reverses. Then read section 23 and note what employers are and are not given. Then find the "Deadly Air" judgment and what it ordered. Then ask what section 24's final clause — "while promoting justifiable economic and social development" — does to an argument about a coal plant.
Property — section 25:
The most contested provision in the Constitution, read closely — and the thing almost everybody gets wrong about compensation.

**Section 25 has nine subsections and they do four different jobs.** Read in order they look like a property clause; **read by function they are a land reform clause with a property clause attached.**

---

**Job one: protect property from arbitrary state action.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **25(1)** | **"No one may be deprived of property except in terms of law of general application, and no law may permit arbitrary deprivation of property."** |

**Two requirements: a law of general application, and non-arbitrariness.** The test for arbitrariness comes from ***First National Bank v Commissioner, SARS* (2002)**: there must be **sufficient reason** for the deprivation, assessed against the relationship between purpose, person and property.

**And note what 25(1) does *not* say: it does not guarantee a right to property.** The Constitution protects against arbitrary deprivation; **it does not confer property.** That drafting was deliberate and it was a negotiated outcome from stage 6.

---

**Job two: regulate expropriation.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **25(2)** | property may be expropriated **only in terms of law of general application**, **(a) for a public purpose or in the public interest**, and **(b) subject to compensation**, the amount and timing of which is **agreed or decided or approved by a court** |

**So expropriation requires: a statute, a public purpose or public interest, and compensation determined by agreement or by a court.**

---

**Job three — and this is the subsection everybody misquotes: how compensation is calculated.**

> **25(3) The amount of the compensation and the time and manner of payment must be just and equitable, reflecting an equitable balance between the public interest and the interests of those affected, having regard to all relevant circumstances, including —**
> **(a) the current use of the property;**
> **(b) the history of the acquisition and use of the property;**
> **(c) the market value of the property;**
> **(d) the extent of direct state investment and subsidy in the acquisition and beneficial capital improvement of the property; and**
> **(e) the purpose of the expropriation.**

**The point to take away, and it is the most consequential misunderstanding in South African public debate:**

> **Market value is one of five listed factors. It is not the measure of compensation.**

**The standard is "just and equitable", reflecting "an equitable balance".** Market value informs it; **so does how the property was acquired, what the state put into it, and what the expropriation is for.**

**So "expropriation without compensation" and "expropriation at market value" are both departures from the text.** The text requires an amount that is just and equitable in the circumstances — **which in some circumstances could be below market value, and in principle could be nil.** Whether it could be nil under section 25 as it stands is the question the next lesson is about.

**And the subsection that enlarges "public interest":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **25(4)(a)** | **"the public interest includes the nation's commitment to land reform, and to reforms to bring about equitable access to all South Africa's natural resources"** |
| **25(4)(b)** | **"property is not limited to land"** |

**So land reform is expressly a public interest for expropriation purposes.** That is in the text; it is not an interpretation.

---

**Job four: the land reform mandate — subsections (5) to (9), which are the clause's other half and are routinely ignored.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **25(5)** | **redistribution** — the state **must take reasonable legislative and other measures, within its available resources, to foster conditions which enable citizens to gain access to land on an equitable basis** |
| **25(6)** | **tenure security** — a person or community whose tenure is legally insecure **as a result of past racially discriminatory laws or practices** is entitled, **to the extent provided by an Act of Parliament**, to legally secure tenure or comparable redress |
| **25(7)** | **restitution** — a person or community **dispossessed of property after 19 June 1913** as a result of past racially discriminatory laws or practices is entitled, **to the extent provided by an Act of Parliament**, to restitution or equitable redress |
| **25(8)** | **"No provision of this section may impede the state from taking legislative and other measures to achieve land, water and related reform"** — provided any departure complies with section 36 |
| **25(9)** | **Parliament must enact the legislation referred to in subsection (6)** |

**Four observations about these five subsections.**

**The 1913 date in 25(7) is the 1913 Natives Land Act's**, from stage 4 — **so the Constitution adopts that Act's date as the boundary of restitution**, and everything in stages 2 and 3 falls outside. **Khoe and San dispossession is not claimable.**

**"To the extent provided by an Act of Parliament" in 25(6) and 25(7) means the rights are not self-executing.** They depend on legislation — the **Restitution of Land Rights Act 22 of 1994** and the tenure statutes. **A right whose content Parliament defines is a weaker right.**

**25(8) is an anti-impediment clause**, and it is unusual: it instructs that nothing in the section may be read to block land, water and related reform. **It is the textual answer to the claim that section 25 prevents reform.**

**And 25(5) is an obligation on the state that has never been fully enforced.** Nobody has successfully compelled a national land redistribution programme under 25(5), **and the state's own performance against it is stage 9's subject.**

---

**What the courts have decided, and what they have not.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***FNB* (2002)** | the arbitrariness test under 25(1) |
| ***Agri SA v Minister for Minerals and Energy* (2013)** | the conversion of old-order mineral rights under the MPRDA **was not an expropriation** — a significant narrowing of what counts |
| **Land Claims Court cases on compensation** | **have held that just and equitable compensation can be below market value**, with the factors weighed |
| **The Constitutional Court** | **has never decided a section 25(3) compensation case** |

**That last line is the important one.** The meaning of just and equitable compensation has **not** been settled by the highest court. **So the most consequential question in South African property law is open** — and the next lesson is about what has been done in its absence.

**Practice.** Read section 25 in full, twice. Then write out 25(3)'s five factors and note where market value sits. Then read 25(4)(a) and 25(8) and ask what work each does against the claim that section 25 blocks reform. Then establish whether the Constitutional Court has ruled on compensation.
The Expropriation Act, and the failed am:
What has actually happened on section 25 since 2018 — the amendment that failed, the statute that passed, and the fact that it is not in force.

**The sequence matters, so take it in order.**

---

**2017–18: the political turn.** The ANC's December 2017 national conference resolved to pursue **"expropriation of land without compensation"**, and in February 2018 the National Assembly adopted a motion to review section 25.

**From stage 1's lesson on party documents: a conference resolution is ANC policy.** What followed is what happens to ANC policy.

---

**2018–19: the parliamentary review.** A Joint Constitutional Review Committee held public hearings across the country — **among the largest public participation exercises since 1996** — and reported that section 25 should be amended to make explicit what was already possible.

**Note the formulation: "to make explicit what is already possible".** That is the committee's own framing, and it concedes the previous lesson's point — **the argument was about clarity, not about creating a new power.**

---

**2021: the amendment, and it failed.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Bill** | would have amended section 25 to **provide expressly for nil compensation** in circumstances to be set out in national legislation |
| **The vote, 7 December 2021** | **204 in favour** |
| **Required** | **two-thirds — 267 votes** |
| **So** | **it failed** |
| **Who voted against** | **the DA and others, because it went too far; and the EFF, because it did not go far enough** |

**The EFF's position is the detail that explains the outcome.** The EFF wanted **state custodianship of all land** — the state as owner, with use rights allocated — **which is a different and more radical proposal than nil compensation.** It would not support an amendment that stopped short of it.

**So the amendment failed because its opponents on both sides outnumbered its supporters**, and the ANC did not have two-thirds on its own. **From stage 6's election lesson: the arithmetic of 1994 recurring in 2021.**

---

**2024–25: the statute, which did pass.**

**The Expropriation Act 13 of 2024**, signed by the President on **23 January 2025** — replacing the Expropriation Act of 1975, which was an apartheid-era statute that had survived three decades of democracy.

**What it does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Provides the procedure** | for expropriation by organs of state, which the 1975 Act did badly and unconstitutionally |
| **Requires** | a public purpose or the public interest, attempts to negotiate, notice, and a determination of compensation |
| **Section 12(3)** | **provides that compensation may be nil in specified circumstances** |
| **Those circumstances** | **limited to expropriation of land "in the public interest"**, and the listed cases are narrow — abandoned land, land held purely for speculation, land where the state already holds an interest, land whose market value is less than state investment in it |
| **Disputes** | compensation determined by a court if not agreed |

**So nil compensation is in the Act, it is narrow, and it applies only to land expropriated in the public interest.** The common description — "the government can now take your land for nothing" — is not what the Act says.

**And whether section 12(3) is constitutional under section 25 as it stands is contested** — which is precisely what the failed amendment would have settled.

---

**And now the fact that makes this lesson a worked example of stage 1.**

> **As of 14 October 2026, the Expropriation Act 13 of 2024 has not come into force.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Signed** | **23 January 2025** |
| **Commencement** | **on a date determined by the President by proclamation in the Gazette** |
| **Proclamation issued** | **none, more than twenty months later** |
| **So the operative law of expropriation** | **is still the 1975 Act** |

**From stage 1's Gazette lesson: "an Act can be signed and not in force."** This is the most politically prominent current example. **Check it before relying on it** — a proclamation may have issued since this was written.

**And it is under litigation.** The Act has been challenged in court, and the challenges are proceeding.

---

**Why the Act matters internationally, as a dated note.**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the Expropriation Act became a subject of diplomatic dispute, with **United States criticism of it and executive action citing it** during 2025. **South Africa's response has been that the Act is a domestic law aligning expropriation procedure with the Constitution.**

**The episode is a good illustration of stage 1's method.** The Act's content is checkable in three pages; **the international characterisation of it was not drawn from the text.** Anyone arguing about it should read section 12(3) and the definition of public interest before accepting any description of what it permits.

---

**What has actually happened to land, which is the question underneath all of it — and stage 9 answers it properly.** In short:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Restitution** | about 80,000 claims lodged by 1998; most urban claims settled, **largely in cash** |
| **Redistribution** | targets repeatedly missed; the original 30% by 1999 target was not met, and successive targets have been reset |
| **Tenure reform** | **the weakest leg** — the 25(6) legislation Parliament was required to enact under 25(9) is substantially incomplete |
| **Expropriation used for land reform** | **almost never.** The state has acquired land overwhelmingly by purchase, on a willing-buyer basis |

**That last line is the one that reframes the whole argument.** The state has had the power to expropriate for land reform since 1994 — **section 25(2) and 25(4)(a)** — and has essentially not used it. **So whether the constraint has been the Constitution or the state's own capacity and choices is stage 12's argument**, and the record points substantially at the second.

**Practice.** Find section 12(3) of the Expropriation Act and read the circumstances in which nil compensation may apply. Then establish whether the Act has yet been brought into force, and on what date. Then find the 7 December 2021 vote figures and the EFF's stated reason for voting against. Then find how many hectares the state has acquired for land reform by expropriation rather than purchase.
Housing — section 26:
The socio-economic right with the most litigation, the judgment that invented reasonableness review, and the woman who died without a house.

**Section 26:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **26(1)** | **"Everyone has the right to have access to adequate housing."** |
| **26(2)** | **"The state must take reasonable legislative and other measures, within its available resources, to achieve the progressive realisation of this right."** |
| **26(3)** | **"No one may be evicted from their home, or have their home demolished, without an order of court made after considering all the relevant circumstances. No legislation may permit arbitrary evictions."** |

**Three things to notice in the drafting.**

**"Access to" adequate housing, not "adequate housing".** The state must make housing accessible; **it does not guarantee a house to everyone on demand.**

**26(2)'s formula — "reasonable measures, within available resources, progressive realisation"** — is the qualified-obligation formula from the method lesson, **and it is what the next judgment is about.**

**And 26(3) is unqualified.** No "within available resources", no "progressive realisation". **A court order, after considering all relevant circumstances, is required for every eviction.** From stages 4 and 5: the Group Areas Act, the removals, the demolitions behind the departing families. **One sentence.**

---

***Government of the Republic of South Africa v Grootboom* (2000)** — the most important socio-economic rights judgment in the world, by citation.

**The facts.** About 900 people, including 390 children, had moved from an informal settlement called Wallacedene onto private land. **They were evicted, their shelters and possessions destroyed, and they had nowhere to go.** They sued.

**The two possible approaches, and the Court chose the second:**

| **The minimum core approach** | **The reasonableness approach** |
| --- | --- |
| The right has a **minimum content** the state must deliver immediately | **the state must have a reasonable programme** |
| Courts determine what the minimum is | **courts review the programme for reasonableness** |
| Argued by the applicants' supporters, drawing on international law | **adopted by the Court** |

**Why the Court refused the minimum core**, in its own reasoning: **it lacked the information and the institutional competence to determine what a minimum adequate house is, for a whole country, across every circumstance** — and the Constitution's text, with its "available resources" and "progressive realisation", pointed to a programme standard rather than an entitlement standard.

**So what does "reasonable" require? The Court's criteria:**

| A reasonable programme must | |
| --- | --- |
| **Be comprehensive, coherent and co-ordinated** | across spheres of government |
| **Be balanced and flexible** | with **short, medium and long-term** provision |
| **Allocate responsibilities and resources clearly** | |
| **Not exclude a significant segment of society** | |
| **And — the holding** | **respond to those in desperate need** |

**The state's housing programme was found unreasonable for one reason: it had no provision for people in crisis.** It built houses for people on waiting lists and had nothing for a family evicted today with nowhere to go. **That is what the Court ordered to be fixed.**

**And the criticism of reasonableness review, which is serious:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It gives no individual entitlement** | Mrs Grootboom won and got no house |
| **It is deferential** | the state chooses the programme; the court reviews it |
| **It is hard to enforce** | a declaration that a policy is unreasonable requires a new policy, not a delivery |
| **And** | **Irene Grootboom died in 2008, still living in a shack** |

**That last fact is cited in every discussion of South African socio-economic rights and it should be.** The applicant in the world's leading housing-rights case was never housed.

**The defence of reasonableness review is also serious:** it has produced real, repeated, enforceable obligations on the state, **it avoided courts setting national housing budgets**, and the alternative — judges determining minimum entitlements — has not obviously worked better anywhere it has been tried.

---

**What has been built on 26(3) and the eviction cases, which is where the right has bitten hardest:**

| Case | Holding |
| --- | --- |
| **PIE Act** — Prevention of Illegal Eviction from and Unlawful Occupation of Land Act 19 of 1998 | the statute implementing 26(3) |
| ***Port Elizabeth Municipality v Various Occupiers* (2004)** | a court must consider **whether alternative accommodation is available** before ordering eviction |
| ***Olivia Road* (2008)** | **"meaningful engagement"** with occupiers required before eviction |
| ***Blue Moonlight* (2011)** | **a city must provide temporary accommodation to those it evicts, and cannot plead a budget it failed to plan for** |
| ***Daniels v Scribante* (2017)** | **a farm occupier may make improvements to her dwelling** without the owner's consent |

***Blue Moonlight* is the one with teeth.** The City of Johannesburg argued it had no budget for emergency housing; **the Court held that a city which knows evictions happen and budgets nothing for them has not acted reasonably.** It converted a planning failure into a legal obligation.

**And *Daniels v Scribante* is the one that reaches furthest** — a woman living on a farm under the Extension of Security of Tenure Act, held entitled to make her home habitable, **against the owner's objection.** From stages 3 and 4: labour tenancy, and the farm removals.

---

**The practical state of housing, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** South Africa has delivered several million subsidised houses and serviced sites since 1994 — **one of the largest state housing programmes anywhere** — and the housing backlog has not fallen, because urbanisation and household formation have outpaced delivery. **And from stage 5's Group Areas lesson, most of it was built on cheap peripheral land, which has reproduced the apartheid city's shape.**

**Stage 9 does the numbers.**

**Practice.** Read section 26 and note which subsection is unqualified. Then read *Grootboom*'s reasonableness criteria and ask what the state's programme lacked. Then read *Blue Moonlight* and work out what a city must now budget for. Then find out what happened to Irene Grootboom.
Health, food, water, social security:
Section 27 — the right that produced the antiretroviral programme, the case the state won, and the grants that reach a third of the country.

**Section 27:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **27(1)** | everyone has the right to have access to **(a) health care services, including reproductive health care; (b) sufficient food and water; (c) social security, including, if they are unable to support themselves and their dependants, appropriate social assistance** |
| **27(2)** | **reasonable measures, within available resources, progressive realisation** — the same formula as section 26 |
| **27(3)** | **"No one may be refused emergency medical treatment."** |

**27(3) is unqualified**, like 26(3). **No available resources, no progressive realisation.** An emergency case may not be turned away.

---

**The three cases that define the right, and they went three different ways.**

***Soobramoney v Minister of Health* (1997)** — **the state won.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The facts** | a man with chronic renal failure, needing dialysis to survive; the hospital's dialysis capacity was rationed by criteria he did not meet |
| **He argued** | section 27(3) — emergency medical treatment — and 27(1)(a) |
| **The Court held** | **27(3) covers a sudden catastrophe, not an ongoing condition requiring continuing treatment**; and the rationing was a reasonable allocation of scarce resources |
| **He died shortly afterwards** | |

***Soobramoney* established the Court's deference on resource allocation**, and it is the case cited whenever the state says it cannot afford something.

---

***Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign* (2002)** — **the state lost, and this is the most consequential socio-economic rights judgment in South African history.**

**The background, which is stage 11's material and belongs here in outline.** The Mbeki government's position on HIV/AIDS was shaped by **AIDS denialism** — questioning whether HIV causes AIDS and whether antiretrovirals were safe. **The state restricted nevirapine, a drug that substantially reduces mother-to-child transmission, to two pilot sites per province.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The applicants** | **the Treatment Action Campaign**, with Section27's predecessors |
| **The claim** | the restriction was unreasonable under section 27 |
| **The Court held** | **it was.** The policy excluded a significant segment of those in need and was not justified by the reasons given |
| **The order** | **the state must remove the restrictions and permit and facilitate nevirapine's use throughout the public health system**, and must take reasonable measures to extend it |

**And the state complied, slowly, and the programme that followed is now the largest antiretroviral treatment programme in the world** — reaching millions of people.

**The mortality consequence of the delay is a matter of published estimate**, and the figures for excess deaths attributable to the denialist period run into the hundreds of thousands. **Stage 11 treats it as the subject it is.**

**What *TAC* established legally:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reasonableness review has force** | a policy with a plausible rationale was struck down |
| **Courts will grant mandatory relief** | not merely declarations |
| **And the social-movement route works** | **the TAC's combination of litigation, mass mobilisation and expert evidence is the model** every subsequent South African rights campaign has copied |

---

***Mazibuko v City of Johannesburg* (2009)** — **the state won, and it is the limit case.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The issue** | **Johannesburg's free basic water allocation (six kilolitres per household per month) and its prepaid water meters** in Phiri, Soweto |
| **The applicants argued** | the allocation was insufficient and the meters unlawfully disconnected supply without process |
| **The Court held** | **it would not quantify "sufficient water"**; the city's policy was reasonable and under continuous review; **and prepaid meters were lawful** |
| **The reasoning** | **determining a numerical entitlement is a legislative and executive function**, not a judicial one |

***Mazibuko* is the clearest statement of reasonableness review's limits** and it disappointed many who had read *TAC* as the start of a judicially enforced social minimum. **It is also where the Court's institutional reasoning is most explicit: judges will review a programme and will not write one.**

---

**And one more that matters for a current argument: *Khosa v Minister of Social Development* (2004).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The issue** | social grants restricted to citizens, excluding **permanent residents** |
| **Held** | **unconstitutional** — section 27(1)(c) says **"everyone"**, and the exclusion violated equality and dignity |
| **Significance** | **a socio-economic right extending to non-citizens** |

***Khosa* is the reference point for every argument about migrants' access to services**, which stage 12 covers — and it establishes that where the text says "everyone", citizenship is not a permissible filter without justification.

---

**Social security in practice, which is South Africa's largest and least-discussed achievement:**

> **As of 2025–26:** the social grant system reaches a very large share of the population — **roughly 19 million permanent grants** (old age, child support, disability and others), **plus the Social Relief of Distress grant**, with total beneficiaries on the order of **28 million people** in a population of about 63 million. **Check the current figures with SASSA and the Budget Review.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Child Support Grant** | **the largest**, reaching well over ten million children |
| **The old age grant** | nearly universal above the age threshold |
| **The SRD grant** | introduced in 2020 for Covid relief and extended repeatedly, for unemployed adults with no other income |
| **The effect on poverty** | **large and measurable** — South African inequality after taxes and transfers is appreciably lower than before them, from stage 1's Gini lesson |

**And the live argument: a basic income grant.** The SRD grant's extension has effectively created a partial income support for working-age adults, **and whether to formalise it as a permanent basic income grant is one of the central fiscal and political questions of the present.** Stage 9 and stage 12 take it.

**Practice.** Read section 27 and note which subsection is unqualified. Then read *TAC*'s order and establish what the state was required to do. Then read *Mazibuko* and state why the Court would not quantify sufficient water. Then find the current number of social grant beneficiaries and what share of the population that is.
Children, and education:
Sections 28 and 29 — the two places where the Constitution imposes immediate obligations rather than progressive ones, and what has been done with them.

**Section 28 — children's rights, and it is the longest provision in the Bill of Rights.**

**Section 28(1) gives every child the right:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | to a name and a nationality from birth |
| **(b)** | **to family care or parental care, or to appropriate alternative care** when removed from the family |
| **(c)** | **to basic nutrition, shelter, basic health care services and social services** |
| **(d)** | to be protected from maltreatment, neglect, abuse or degradation |
| **(e)** | to be protected from exploitative labour practices |
| **(f)** | not to be required or permitted to do work inappropriate for their age |
| **(g)** | **not to be detained except as a measure of last resort**, for the shortest appropriate period, **separately from persons over 18** |
| **(h)** | **to a legal practitioner assigned by the state, at state expense, in civil proceedings affecting the child** |
| **(i)** | not to be used directly in armed conflict |

**And then section 28(2), which is the provision that does the most work in South African law:**

> **"A child's best interests are of paramount importance in every matter concerning the child."**

**"Paramount" is a strong word and the Court has treated it as one.** It applies in custody, in sentencing a parent, in eviction, in immigration, in schooling — **every matter concerning a child.**

***S v M* (2007)** is the case: **when sentencing a primary caregiver, a court must consider the impact on the children** and may not treat it as incidental. **That is section 28(2) reaching into criminal sentencing.**

**Now the technical point that matters most about section 28(1)(c).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"basic nutrition, shelter, basic health care services and social services"** | |
| **And note what is missing** | **no "within available resources", no "progressive realisation"** |

**So children's socio-economic rights are drafted unqualified**, unlike adults' in sections 26 and 27.

**And the Court's answer in *Grootboom* complicated it:** it read 28(1)(c) as imposing the **primary** obligation on **parents and families**, with the state's obligation arising where a child is **without family care** — so the unqualified drafting does not give every child a direct claim against the state for shelter. **That reading has been criticised** and it is the live question in children's rights litigation.

---

**Section 29 — education, and this is where the distinction matters most:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **29(1)(a)** | **"Everyone has the right to a basic education, including adult basic education."** |
| **29(1)(b)** | **"and to further education, which the state, through reasonable measures, must make progressively available and accessible."** |

**Read the two together.** **29(1)(b) carries the progressive-realisation formula. 29(1)(a) does not.**

**And the Constitutional Court confirmed the consequence in *Governing Body of the Juma Musjid Primary School* (2011):**

> **The right to a basic education in section 29(1)(a) is immediately realisable. It is not subject to internal limitation, and the state's obligation is not qualified by available resources or progressive realisation.**

**That is the strongest socio-economic right in the Constitution** and it is the basis of a whole litigation programme:

| Case | What was ordered |
| --- | --- |
| ***Section27 v Minister of Basic Education* (2012)** | **textbooks** — the state's failure to deliver textbooks in Limpopo breached section 29(1)(a). **Every learner must have a textbook for every subject** |
| ***Madzodzo* (2014)** | **furniture** — desks and chairs |
| ***Equal Education* cases** | **norms and standards for school infrastructure**, promulgated after litigation |
| ***Komape v Minister of Basic Education*** | **Michael Komape, aged five, drowned in a school pit latrine in 2014.** The litigation that followed addressed sanitation and the state's liability |

**The Komape case is the one to know.** A five-year-old died in a pit toilet at a school in Limpopo in 2014. **The family litigated for years**; the courts dealt with liability, damages and the state's obligations; **and the eradication of pit latrines at schools has been a declared government programme for a decade and is still incomplete.**

**From the supremacy lesson's pattern: textbooks, desks, toilets and infrastructure norms have all been obtained by litigation** — an immediately realisable right, enforced case by case, because the administration did not deliver.

---

**Section 29(2) — language of instruction, and it is the most politically contested education clause:**

> **Everyone has the right to receive education in the official language or languages of their choice in public educational institutions where that education is reasonably practicable. In order to ensure the effective access to, and implementation of, this right, the state must consider all reasonable educational alternatives, including single medium institutions, taking into account — (a) equity; (b) practicability; and (c) the need to redress the results of past racially discriminatory laws and practices.**

**Read the structure: a right to choose, qualified by "reasonably practicable", with the state required to consider single-medium institutions while taking account of equity and redress.**

**That is a compromise and it has produced two decades of litigation**, almost all of it about **Afrikaans**:

| Case | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Mikro* (2005)** | a single-medium Afrikaans primary school could not be compelled to become parallel-medium |
| ***Hoërskool Ermelo* (2010)** | a provincial department could intervene where a school's language policy excluded learners who had nowhere else to go |
| ***AfriForum v University of the Free State* (2017)**, ***Gelyke Kanse v Stellenbosch* (2019)** | **universities' moves away from Afrikaans upheld**, on practicability and equity grounds |

**The pattern: single-medium Afrikaans schooling is constitutionally permissible and is not constitutionally protected against change where equity and practicability point the other way.** And the live argument is the **BELA Act** — the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act — whose provisions on school language and admission policy were the most contested legislation of 2024, **and parts of which were held back from commencement for further consultation.** Stage 12 takes it.

**Section 29(3) permits independent schools**, at private expense, subject to registration and non-discrimination.

**Practice.** Read sections 28 and 29 and mark which provisions carry the progressive-realisation formula and which do not. Then read *Juma Musjid* on basic education's immediate realisability. Then find the Komape case and what it established. Then read section 29(2) and work out how its three factors interact.
Language, culture and community:
Sections 30 and 31 — the rights that recognise group life in a non-racial constitution, and the judgments that remade customary law.

**The tension this lesson is about.** From stage 6: **the ANC defeated group rights in the negotiations**, because recognising groups was apartheid's own premise.

**And yet the Constitution recognises cultural, religious and linguistic communities.** How?

**The answer is in how sections 30 and 31 are drafted: as individual rights to participate in community life, not as rights held by communities against the state.**

---

**Section 30:**

> **Everyone has the right to use the language and to participate in the cultural life of their choice, but no one exercising these rights may do so in a manner inconsistent with any provision of the Bill of Rights.**

**Section 31:**

> **(1) Persons belonging to a cultural, religious or linguistic community may not be denied the right, with other members of that community — (a) to enjoy their culture, practise their religion and use their language; and (b) to form, join and maintain cultural, religious and linguistic associations and other organs of civil society.**
> **(2) The rights in subsection (1) may not be exercised in a manner inconsistent with any provision of the Bill of Rights.**

**Four observations.**

**1. The rights are held by persons, not communities.** "Everyone", "persons belonging to". **No community has standing as such**, and no community has a veto, a reserved seat or a territorial claim. **That is how group rights were refused while group life was protected.**

**2. "Of their choice"** in section 30. **Membership is elective.** Nobody is assigned to a culture — which is the exact inverse of stage 5's Population Registration Act.

**3. Both sections carry the same internal limit: these rights may not be exercised inconsistently with the Bill of Rights.** So culture and religion do not override equality, dignity or children's rights. **That clause is where every hard case is decided.**

**4. There is no constitutional right to a *volkstaat*.** From stage 6: **Constitutional Principle XXXIV allowed for the possibility**, the Volkstaat Council investigated, and **section 235 of the final Constitution recognises the right to self-determination of any community sharing a common cultural and language heritage "within a territorial entity in the Republic or in any other way, determined by national legislation"** — which is a permission to legislate, not a right. **No such legislation exists.**

---

**Now the judgments that remade customary law**, which are the most consequential application of these sections.

**The background, from stage 4's 1927 Act lesson: customary law was codified by colonial officials in the 1920s, in a version systematically more patriarchal than the practice it recorded** — and that codification governed until 1994.

***Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha* (2004).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rule** | **male primogeniture** in customary succession — the eldest male relative inherits, as codified under the Black Administration Act |
| **The facts** | two young daughters excluded from their father's estate in favour of his father |
| **Held** | **unconstitutional.** The rule, as codified and applied, violated equality and dignity |
| **The remedy** | the Intestate Succession Act applied, pending legislation |

***Bhe* is the case where the internal limit in section 31(2) did its work:** a customary rule, protected in principle by sections 30 and 31, **struck down because it was inconsistent with equality.**

***Shilubana v Nwamitwa* (2008)** — and this is the more interesting judgment.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The facts** | the Valoyi community resolved that a woman, Ms Shilubana, should become **hosi** — traditional leader — a position customarily held by men. Her cousin challenged it on the basis of customary law |
| **Held** | **the community's own decision to develop its custom was valid** |
| **The principle** | **living customary law** — custom is what a community actually practises and may change, not what was written down in 1927 |

**That distinction is the central move in South African customary law:**

| **Official customary law** | **Living customary law** |
| --- | --- |
| **The colonial codification** | **the community's actual, current practice** |
| Fixed in the 1920s | **develops** |
| More patriarchal than the practice | |
| **What the courts apply** | **this one** |

***Shilubana* means a community may develop its own custom toward constitutional values**, which is a far better outcome than courts striking custom down — **and it is the answer to the charge that constitutionalism simply overrides African law.** The Court's position is that it applies African law, in its living form, and that African law develops.

**The other cases in the line:** ***Gumede* (2009)** on customary marriage property regimes; ***MM v MN* (2013)** on consent to a further customary marriage; ***Mayelane* (2013)** on the first wife's consent.

---

**Chapter 12 — traditional leaders**, for completeness, because sections 211 and 212 belong with this:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **211(1)** | **the institution, status and role of traditional leadership, according to customary law, is recognised, subject to the Constitution** |
| **211(3)** | **courts must apply customary law when it is applicable**, subject to the Constitution and legislation |
| **212** | **national legislation may provide for a role for traditional leadership** at local level, and houses of traditional leaders may be established |

**"Subject to the Constitution" appears twice, and it is the whole settlement on traditional authority: recognised, and subordinate.**

**And section 212's "may provide for a role" is the great unfinished business**, from stage 4's chiefs lesson and stage 5's homelands. **What traditional leaders may actually decide — land allocation, dispute resolution, local development — has been legislated and relegislated and remains contested.** Stage 8's lesson on traditional authority takes it, and the **Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019** from stage 2's Khoisan lesson is part of it.

**Practice.** Read sections 30 and 31 and identify the internal limit in each. Then read *Bhe* and *Shilubana* and state the difference in approach. Then write out the distinction between official and living customary law. Then read section 235 and establish whether a right to self-determination exists or a power to legislate for one.
Information, and administrative justice:
Sections 32 and 33 — the two rights that do more day-to-day work against the state than any others, and the statutes they required.

**These two sections are the least glamorous and most used provisions in the Bill of Rights.** Almost all litigation against the South African state runs through them.

---

**Section 32 — access to information:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **32(1)(a)** | **"Everyone has the right of access to any information held by the state"** |
| **32(1)(b)** | **"and any information held by another person that is required for the exercise or protection of any rights"** |
| **32(2)** | **national legislation must be enacted** to give effect to it, and may provide for reasonable measures to alleviate the administrative and financial burden on the state |

**32(1)(b) is unusual internationally.** Most access-to-information rights reach only the state. **South Africa's reaches private persons — including companies — where the information is required to exercise or protect a right.**

**The statute: PAIA — the Promotion of Access to Information Act 2 of 2000.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How it works** | a written request to the body's information officer; a decision within 30 days; **grounds of refusal are listed and limited**; internal appeal, then court or the Information Regulator |
| **Grounds of refusal** | privacy of a third party, commercial information, legal privilege, defence and security, the economic interests of the Republic, and others |
| **The mandatory disclosure override** | **section 46: disclosure must be granted despite a refusal ground if it reveals a substantial contravention of the law or an imminent and serious public safety or environmental risk, and the public interest in disclosure clearly outweighs the harm** |

**Section 46 is the public-interest override and it is the provision investigative journalism relies on.**

**And the practical reality, which is this lesson's honest note:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Compliance is poor** | **a large share of PAIA requests are simply ignored** — a "deemed refusal" |
| **Enforcement** | required a court application for two decades; **the Information Regulator took over PAIA enforcement in 2021**, which has helped unevenly |
| **Who uses it** | journalists, NGOs, lawyers and researchers — **rarely individuals** |
| **Its successes** | substantial. **Much of what is known about state capture, arms procurement, party funding and public contracts came through PAIA** |

---

**Section 33 — just administrative action:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **33(1)** | **"Everyone has the right to administrative action that is lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair."** |
| **33(2)** | **"Everyone whose rights have been adversely affected by administrative action has the right to be given written reasons."** |
| **33(3)** | national legislation must be enacted, provide for review by a court or independent tribunal, impose a duty on the state to give effect to the rights, and promote an efficient administration |

**Three requirements in 33(1), and they are the whole of administrative law:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Lawful** | **within the power conferred** — the official must have had authority, and must have used it for its purpose |
| **Reasonable** | **rationally connected to the purpose, and not so unreasonable that no reasonable decision-maker could have reached it** |
| **Procedurally fair** | **notice, an opportunity to be heard, an unbiased decision-maker, and reasons** |

**And 33(2)'s right to written reasons is the one most often forgotten and most useful.** A decision that adversely affects your rights must be explained in writing on request. **Reasons are the prerequisite of review — you cannot challenge what you have not been told.**

**The statute: PAJA — the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act 3 of 2000.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | codifies the grounds of review, requires reasons, and sets the procedure |
| **The grounds** | section 6 — about a dozen, covering unauthorised action, bias, procedural unfairness, irrelevant considerations, bad faith, irrationality, unreasonableness, and failure to decide |
| **The time limit** | **180 days**, extendable by a court on good cause — and this catches a great many applicants |
| **Who it binds** | organs of state, and natural or juristic persons exercising a public power or performing a public function |

**That last row matters: PAJA follows the function, not the body.** A private entity exercising a public power is reviewable.

---

**Why these two sections do so much work, which is the point of the lesson.**

**From the supremacy lesson's pattern: South Africa has strong constitutional law and a weak administration.** Sections 32 and 33 are the tools that pattern runs on:

| Problem | Remedy |
| --- | --- |
| **An appointment made irregularly** | **PAJA review** |
| **A tender awarded corruptly** | **PAJA review, and the principle of legality** |
| **A licence refused without reasons** | **section 33(2)** |
| **A decision taken without consulting those affected** | procedural fairness |
| **Documents withheld** | **PAIA** |
| **A report not released** | PAIA, with section 46 |

**And the doctrine that has grown alongside PAJA: the principle of legality.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | a constitutional requirement, derived from the rule of law in section 1, that **all exercises of public power be lawful and rational** |
| **Why it matters** | **it applies to the exercise of power that is not "administrative action" under PAJA** — executive and policy decisions, a president's appointments, parliamentary processes |
| **The cases** | the state capture litigation of stage 11 runs almost entirely on legality rather than PAJA — **because a president's decisions are executive, not administrative** |

**So the division: PAJA for administration, legality for executive power.** And legality's core requirement is **rationality** — there must be a rational connection between the decision, the reasons and the purpose.

***Democratic Alliance v President* (2012)**, on the appointment of a National Director of Public Prosecutions, is the case that established how far rationality review reaches into executive appointments — **and it is the foundation of stage 11's litigation.**

**Practice.** Make a PAIA request for something you are curious about and see what happens. Then read PAJA's section 6 grounds of review. Then find a decision affecting you and ask whether you were given written reasons. Then read *DA v President* (2012) on rationality, and note what it allows a court to examine in an executive appointment.
Courts, and the rights of the accused:
Sections 34 and 35 — the right to a hearing, and the longest list of criminal procedure protections in any constitution, read against stage 5.

**Section 34:**

> **Everyone has the right to have any dispute that can be resolved by the application of law decided in a fair public hearing before a court or, where appropriate, another independent and impartial tribunal or forum.**

**Four elements: a dispute resolvable by law, a fair hearing, in public, before an independent and impartial forum.**

**And from stage 6's TRC lesson: this is the right the Biko and Mxenge families relied on in *AZAPO*** — and the Constitutional Court held that the amnesty provisions limited it justifiably. **Section 34 is why that case was arguable at all.**

**Its other main use is access:** court fees, legal aid, the cost of litigation, and the rules that keep people out of court. **Legal Aid South Africa** exists under it, and the shortage of civil legal aid — **criminal legal aid is far better provided than civil** — is a standing section 34 problem.

---

**Section 35 — arrested, detained and accused persons.** It is the longest provision in the Bill of Rights, in three parts, and **every clause of it answers something from stage 5.**

**35(1) — arrested persons:**

| | Answering |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** to remain silent | |
| **(b)** to be informed promptly of the right to remain silent and of the consequences of not doing so | |
| **(c)** **not to be compelled to make any confession or admission** that could be used in evidence | **the interrogations of stage 5** |
| **(d)** **to be brought before a court as soon as reasonably possible, and not later than 48 hours after the arrest** | **90-day, 180-day and indefinite detention** |
| **(e)** at the first court appearance, to be charged or informed of the reason for continued detention, or released | |
| **(f)** **to be released from detention if the interests of justice permit**, subject to reasonable conditions | |

**The 48-hour rule in 35(1)(d) is the single most important clause in section 35.** From stage 5's security laws lesson: **section 6 of the Terrorism Act permitted indefinite detention with no court able to pronounce on it.** Forty-eight hours, in the Constitution, with no exception.

**35(2) — detained persons, including sentenced prisoners:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** to be informed promptly of the reason | |
| **(b)** **to choose, and to consult with, a legal practitioner** | **and from stage 5: detainees had no access to lawyers** |
| **(c)** **to have a legal practitioner assigned by the state at state expense, if substantial injustice would otherwise result** | |
| **(d)** **to challenge the lawfulness of the detention in person before a court**, and to be released if unlawful | **the provision that section 6 had expressly excluded** |
| **(e)** **to conditions of detention consistent with human dignity**, including adequate accommodation, nutrition, reading material and medical treatment | |
| **(f)** to communicate with, and be visited by, a spouse or partner, next of kin, religious counsellor and medical practitioner | |

**35(2)(d) is *habeas corpus*, constitutionalised** — and it is the direct answer to the clause that made the seventy-three deaths in detention possible.

**35(2)(e) on conditions is actively litigated**, and South African prison conditions — overcrowding above all — have been found to breach it repeatedly.

---

**35(3) — accused persons: the right to a fair trial, with fifteen listed elements:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** to be informed of the charge with sufficient detail to answer it | |
| **(b)** **to have adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence** | |
| **(c)** to a public trial before an ordinary court | **and note "ordinary court" — no special courts** |
| **(d)** **to have the trial begin and conclude without unreasonable delay** | |
| **(e)** to be present | |
| **(f)** to choose and be represented by a legal practitioner | |
| **(g)** **to have one assigned at state expense if substantial injustice would otherwise result** | |
| **(h)** **to be presumed innocent, to remain silent, and not to testify** | **and from stage 5: the sabotage law reversed the onus of proof** |
| **(i)** to adduce and challenge evidence | |
| **(j)** **not to be compelled to give self-incriminating evidence** | |
| **(k)** **to be tried in a language the accused understands**, or to have the proceedings interpreted | **and in a twelve-language country this is substantial** |
| **(l)** **not to be convicted for an act that was not an offence when it was committed** | |
| **(m)** **not to be tried twice** for the same offence | |
| **(n)** **to the benefit of the least severe prescribed punishment** if it has changed between offence and sentencing | |
| **(o)** **of appeal to, or review by, a higher court** | |

**And then 35(5), the exclusionary rule:**

> **Evidence obtained in a manner that violates any right in the Bill of Rights must be excluded if the admission of that evidence would render the trial unfair or otherwise be detrimental to the administration of justice.**

**Note it is not an automatic exclusion.** The test is whether admission would render the trial unfair **or** be detrimental to the administration of justice — **so a court weighs it.** That is a deliberately more flexible rule than the American one, and it has produced a substantial body of case law on confessions, searches and identification.

---

**Why section 35 is drafted at this length**, which is the lesson's point.

**Most constitutions state fair trial rights in a sentence or two.** South Africa's lists fifteen.

**The reason is in stage 5.** A country whose previous order included:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Indefinite incommunicado detention** | |
| **Reversed onus of proof** for political offences | |
| **Statutory exclusion of judicial review** of detention | |
| **Confessions obtained by torture** | |
| **Seventy-three deaths in custody with no finding of responsibility** | |
| **Trials conducted in languages the accused did not speak** | |
| **Special courts** | |

**...does not leave fair trial rights to be inferred.** It writes them out. **Section 35 is the most explicitly historical provision in the Constitution**, and reading it as a list of what was done before is the quickest way to understand both the section and stage 5.

**Practice.** Read section 35 in full and mark each clause with what from stage 5 it answers. Then find the 48-hour rule and compare it with section 6 of the Terrorism Act. Then read 35(5) and note that exclusion is not automatic. Then find a recent judgment in which evidence was excluded under 35(5) and one in which it was admitted.
The limitation clause — section 36:
The provision that decides most constitutional cases, its five factors, and the two words that defeat a great deal of state conduct before any weighing begins.

**Section 36(1), in full:**

> **The rights in the Bill of Rights may be limited only in terms of law of general application to the extent that the limitation is reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom, taking into account all relevant factors, including —**
> **(a) the nature of the right;**
> **(b) the importance of the purpose of the limitation;**
> **(c) the nature and extent of the limitation;**
> **(d) the relation between the limitation and its purpose; and**
> **(e) less restrictive means to achieve the purpose.**

**And 36(2): except as provided in 36(1) or elsewhere in the Constitution, no law may limit any right in the Bill of Rights.**

---

**First: the threshold requirement, and it does more work than the five factors.**

**"Only in terms of law of general application."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A statute, regulation or by-law** | **qualifies** |
| **The common law** | qualifies |
| **A policy, a circular, an instruction, a practice** | **does not** |
| **A discretionary decision by an official** | **does not** |
| **Arbitrary executive action** | **does not** |

**So if a right is infringed by something that is not a law of general application, section 36 cannot save it.** There is nothing to justify — **the infringement simply fails.**

**That is why so much litigation against the South African state succeeds without reaching the five factors.** The state acts by circular, by practice, by decision; **and a circular cannot limit a constitutional right.**

---

**Second: the standard. "Reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on human dignity, equality and freedom."**

**This is a proportionality enquiry, and the Court set it out in *Makwanyane* from the dignity lesson.** The five factors are the weighing:

| Factor | The question |
| --- | --- |
| **(a) the nature of the right** | **how central is it?** Dignity and life are weighed differently from a commercial interest |
| **(b) the importance of the purpose** | **is the state pursuing something that matters?** Public safety and crime prevention weigh heavily |
| **(c) the nature and extent of the limitation** | **how much of the right is taken?** A total prohibition is harder to justify than a restriction |
| **(d) the relation between the limitation and its purpose** | **does it actually achieve the purpose?** A measure that does not work cannot be justified by the goal it fails to reach |
| **(e) less restrictive means** | **could the purpose be achieved with less intrusion?** |

**Factor (d) is the one litigants most often win on.** A state that cannot show its measure achieves its stated purpose has not justified the limitation — **and in *Makwanyane*, the failure to establish deterrence was central.**

**And factor (e) is the one that produces the most careful judgments:** a court asking whether a narrower measure would have done, and frequently finding that it would.

---

**Third: the burden.** From the structure lesson: **the claimant proves the infringement; the state must justify it.** So the state has to put up evidence, in affidavits, about purpose, effect and alternatives — **and failures to do so are a common reason for losing.**

---

**Fourth: the factors are not exhaustive.** "All relevant factors, including" — **so other considerations may enter**, and the Court has considered international practice, the position in comparable democracies, and the historical context.

---

**Fifth, and this is the thing most often got wrong: section 36 is not the only limitation mechanism.**

| Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 36** | the general clause |
| **Internal qualifications in a right** | **"within available resources", "progressive realisation"** (ss 26, 27); **"arbitrary"** (s 25(1)); **"just"** administrative action (s 33); **"reasonably practicable"** (s 29(2)) |
| **Internal exclusions** | **section 16(2)** — the three categories outside expression entirely |
| **Internal limits on community rights** | **ss 30 and 31's "not inconsistent with the Bill of Rights"** |
| **Section 37** | **states of emergency** — the next lesson |

**Where a right is internally qualified, much of the weighing happens inside stage one** — so a case about housing turns on whether the state's measures were *reasonable*, not on whether an infringement was justified. **That is why *Grootboom* does not contain a section 36 analysis.**

---

**What section 36 means practically, which is the lesson's conclusion.**

**It means "the Constitution guarantees X" is never an argument by itself.** The real question is always:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Is there a law of general application?** | if not, the state loses |
| **What is the purpose?** | and is it important |
| **Does the measure achieve it?** | |
| **Is there a less restrictive way?** | |

**Four questions, applied to anything — a lockdown regulation, a hate-speech provision, a firearms law, a minimum sentence, a school language policy, a surveillance statute.** From stage 1's method: **it gives you a structure for reading any rights argument, including your own.**

**Practice. Read section 36 and memorise the five factors** — they are worth knowing. Then take one restriction you have an opinion about and work through the four questions. Then find a judgment where the limitation failed on factor (d) or (e). Then find one where the state lost because there was no law of general application.
States of emergency — section 37:
The most carefully drafted provision in the Constitution, why it has never been used, and the Act that was used instead.

**Section 37 is the Bill of Rights' answer to stage 5's states of emergency** — 1985 to 1990, 25,000 detentions, rule by proclamation, security forces indemnified, reporting banned.

**And the drafting is correspondingly severe.**

---

**When an emergency may be declared — 37(1):**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Only in terms of an Act of Parliament** | not by proclamation alone |
| **Only when the life of the nation is threatened** | by **war, invasion, general insurrection, disorder, natural disaster or other public emergency** |
| **And only if** | the declaration is **necessary to restore peace and order** |

**"The life of the nation is threatened" is a high threshold**, borrowed from international human rights instruments.

**How long — 37(2):**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Prospective only** | **it cannot be backdated** |
| **21 days** | and then it lapses |
| **A first extension** | up to three months, **by a resolution of the National Assembly, by majority** |
| **Subsequent extensions** | up to three months each, **and requiring 60% of the National Assembly** |
| **With a public debate** | required before each extension |

**The escalating majority is the clever part: the longer an emergency runs, the larger the majority needed to continue it.**

**Who may review it — 37(3): "Any competent court may decide on the validity of — (a) a declaration of a state of emergency; (b) any extension; or (c) any legislation enacted, or other action taken, in consequence of a declaration."**

**Read that against stage 5's section 6 of the Terrorism Act, which provided that no court could pronounce on a detention.** Section 37(3) is its exact reversal.

**What may be derogated — 37(4):** emergency legislation may limit rights **only** to the extent that:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is consistent with the Republic's international obligations** | |
| **It is strictly required by the emergency** | |
| **It is published in the national Gazette** as soon as reasonably possible | |
| **And it does not derogate from the Table of Non-Derogable Rights** | |

**And 37(5) is the provision aimed directly at 1985–90:**

| No Act of Parliament may | |
| --- | --- |
| **Permit or authorise indemnity** for the state or any person **for an unlawful act** | **the emergency indemnities of stage 5** |
| **Derogate from sections 1 or 37** | |
| **Authorise derogation from a non-derogable right** | |

---

**The Table of Non-Derogable Rights**, which cannot be suspended in any emergency:

| Right | Extent |
| --- | --- |
| **Equality** | in respect of unfair discrimination **solely** on race, colour, ethnic or social origin, sex, religion or language |
| **Human dignity** | **entirely** |
| **Life** | **entirely** |
| **Freedom and security of the person** | **torture, cruel treatment, and bodily and psychological integrity** |
| **Slavery and servitude** | |
| **Children** | protection from abuse and exploitation, detention as a last resort, and not being used in armed conflict |
| **Arrested, detained and accused persons** | **most of section 35**, including the right to challenge detention before a court and the fair trial rights |

**Dignity and life are absolutely non-derogable** — no emergency, no war, no insurrection.

**And detention during an emergency, if permitted at all, is subject to 37(6)'s conditions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The detainee's name and place of detention** | **published in the Gazette within five days** |
| **A court review within ten days**, and every ten days thereafter | **with release ordered if detention is not necessary** |
| **Legal representation and a medical practitioner** of the detainee's choice | |
| **The right to appear in person and make representations** | |
| **Adult family member or friend to be notified** | |

**Compare that with stage 5: indefinite, incommunicado, no publication, no court, no lawyer, no doctor, and seventy-three deaths.** Section 37(6) is written line by line against it.

---

**And now the thing that makes this lesson important: section 37 has never been used.**

**No state of emergency has been declared in South Africa since 1994.**

**What was used instead: the Disaster Management Act 57 of 2002.**

> **On 15 March 2020 a national state of disaster was declared under the Disaster Management Act, and it ran until 4 April 2022 — more than two years.**

**And the two instruments are not comparable in their safeguards:**

| | **Section 37 state of emergency** | **Disaster Management Act state of disaster** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Declared by** | **Act of Parliament** | **a minister, by notice in the Gazette** |
| **Initial duration** | **21 days** | **three months** |
| **Extension** | **National Assembly resolution, then 60%** | **by ministerial notice, monthly** |
| **Parliamentary approval** | **required** | **not required** |
| **Non-derogable rights table** | **applies** | **does not** |
| **Regulations made by** | Parliament, with limits | **a minister** |
| **Court review** | **expressly provided** | available on ordinary grounds |

**So the most extensive restriction of rights in democratic South Africa's history — the Covid lockdowns, with limits on movement, assembly, trade, education and religious observance, enforced criminally for two years — was imposed under a statute with fewer safeguards than section 37.**

**That is not a legal technicality and it is the central lesson of this provision.** Section 37 was drafted with extraordinary care to constrain emergency rule, and it was bypassed — **not unlawfully, because the Disaster Management Act is a valid statute, but completely.**
