**The litigation.** Regulations were challenged repeatedly; **in *De Beer v Minister of Cooperative Governance* (2020) a High Court found many of them irrational**, a decision varied on appeal; **other challenges succeeded in part** (on, among other things, the ban on certain trade and aspects of the funeral and movement rules). **The courts reviewed the regulations on rationality rather than under section 37's framework**, because section 37 did not apply.

**The question stage 12 asks: should the Disaster Management Act's emergency powers be brought closer to section 37's standard?** It is a live legislative question and an unresolved one.

**Practice.** Read section 37 and the Table of Non-Derogable Rights. Then list which of your rights could not have been suspended even in a declared emergency. Then compare the two columns of the table above. Then establish how many months the 2020–22 state of disaster ran and how each extension was made.
Enforcement, standing and remedies:
Who may bring a constitutional case, what a court may order, and the two features that make South African public interest litigation unusually effective.

**Section 38 — enforcement, and the list is the point:**

> **Anyone listed in this section has the right to approach a competent court, alleging that a right in the Bill of Rights has been infringed or threatened, and the court may grant appropriate relief, including a declaration of rights. The persons who may approach a court are —**
> **(a) anyone acting in their own interest;**
> **(b) anyone acting on behalf of another person who cannot act in their own name;**
> **(c) anyone acting as a member of, or in the interest of, a group or class of persons;**
> **(d) anyone acting in the public interest; and**
> **(e) an association acting in the interest of its members.**

**Paragraph (d) is the one that matters: "anyone acting in the public interest".**

**Most legal systems require a litigant to have a personal interest — *standing*.** South Africa does not, for constitutional cases.

| Consequence | |
| --- | --- |
| **An NGO may challenge a law** that does not affect it | |
| **A journalist may sue** over a provision affecting others | |
| **A person with no stake** may act for a class that cannot | |
| **Which means** | **a constitutional defect does not go unchallenged merely because its victims cannot litigate** |

**And that is why South Africa has the public interest litigation sector it has** — the Treatment Action Campaign, Section27, Equal Education, the Legal Resources Centre, SERI, Corruption Watch, the Helen Suzman Foundation, amaBhungane, the Centre for Child Law, Lawyers for Human Rights, the Socio-Economic Rights Institute.

**From the supremacy lesson: litigation as a substitute for administration.** Section 38(d) is the provision that makes it possible, **and the sector it created is one of the most consequential features of post-1994 South Africa.**

**The counter-argument, which stage 12 takes seriously:** that broad standing hands policy questions to whoever can fund a case, **that unelected organisations with foreign funding set national priorities through the courts**, and that courts are a poor forum for distributive choices. **Both the achievements and the objection are real.**

---

**Section 172 — remedies, and what a court must and may do:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **172(1)(a)** | **a court deciding a constitutional matter *must* declare law or conduct inconsistent with the Constitution invalid to the extent of its inconsistency** |
| **172(1)(b)** | **and *may* make any order that is just and equitable, including — (i) limiting the retrospective effect of the declaration; and (ii) suspending the declaration for any period and on any conditions, to allow the competent authority to correct the defect** |

**The "must" in (a) is mandatory: a court cannot find an invalidity and leave it.** And the "may" in (b) is extraordinarily broad — **"any order that is just and equitable"** is close to an unlimited remedial discretion.

**The remedies the courts have developed from it:**

| Remedy | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Declaration of invalidity** | the baseline |
| **Suspension of invalidity** | **the defect stands for a period while Parliament fixes it** — avoiding a legal vacuum |
| **Severance** | striking out the offending words and leaving the rest |
| **Reading-in** | **adding words to a statute to cure it** — used in *Fourie* on same-sex marriage, and controversially |
| **Reading-down** | interpreting a provision narrowly to save it |
| **Mandatory order** | **do the thing** — *TAC*'s nevirapine order |
| **Structural interdict** | **do the thing, and report back to the court on progress** |
| **Constitutional damages** | money, where no other remedy suffices — rare |
| **Costs orders against officials personally** | increasingly used |

**Two of those deserve explanation.**

**Suspension of invalidity** is how the Court avoids chaos. **In *Bhe*, striking down the customary succession rules immediately would have left estates ungoverned**, so the Court applied the Intestate Succession Act pending legislation. **It is also criticised as leaving unconstitutional law in force** — sometimes for years, and sometimes the legislature misses the deadline and must ask for an extension.

**The structural interdict** is the strongest tool and the most contested. **A court orders the state to act and requires it to report back** — so the court retains supervision. It has been used on school infrastructure, on prisons, on sanitation and in the Komape line from the education lesson.

| The case for it | The case against |
| --- | --- |
| **Declarations alone are ignored** | **courts become administrators** |
| **It is the only remedy that produces delivery** | separation of powers |
| **Repeat litigation is worse** | **judges have no capacity to run a programme** |

---

**And the costs principle that changed behaviour: *Biowatch*.**

***Biowatch Trust v Registrar, Genetic Resources* (2009)** established that **in constitutional litigation against the state, a private litigant who loses should not ordinarily be ordered to pay the state's costs.**

**Why that matters enormously:** the ordinary rule is that the loser pays. **For an NGO with a small budget, the risk of paying the state's legal costs is prohibitive** — so the ordinary rule would have shut down public interest litigation entirely.

**The *Biowatch* principle, with section 38(d)'s standing, is the reason the sector exists.** Two rules — one on who may sue, one on what losing costs — **and between them they produced a mechanism that has delivered textbooks, antiretrovirals, emergency housing, party funding disclosure, independent candidates and the unravelling of state capture.**

**Practice.** Read section 38 and note paragraph (d). Then read section 172(1) and distinguish what a court must do from what it may do. Then find one judgment that used a structural interdict and one that suspended an invalidity. Then read the *Biowatch* principle and work out what public interest litigation would cost without it.
Three spheres, and co-operative governme:
How the state is arranged — the word the Constitution deliberately avoided, the schedules that divide power, and the provision that lets one sphere take over another.

**Section 40(1): "In the Republic, government is constituted as national, provincial and local spheres of government which are distinctive, interdependent and interrelated."**

**"Spheres", not "tiers" or "levels".** That word was chosen deliberately.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Tiers" implies a hierarchy** | with the national government on top |
| **"Spheres" implies distinct domains** | each with its own constitutional standing |
| **And it matters legally** | **a municipality is not a creature of the province; its powers come from the Constitution** |

**So a province cannot simply instruct a municipality, and the national government cannot simply instruct a province, in their own areas of competence.** From stage 6: this is Constitutional Principle XVIII's legacy — **the provinces' powers could not be reduced below the interim constitution's.**

---

**How powers are divided: the schedules.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Schedule 4** | **concurrent national and provincial competences** — **both may legislate** |
| **Schedule 5** | **exclusive provincial competences** |
| **Schedule 4 Part B and Schedule 5 Part B** | **local government matters**, which municipalities administer |
| **Everything else** | national |

**Schedule 4's concurrent list is where most government happens:**

> **agriculture, education at all levels except tertiary, environment, health services, housing, indigenous and customary law, police (to the extent provided), population development, public transport, social welfare, trade, urban and rural development, welfare services.**

**Schedule 5's exclusive provincial list is short and minor:**

> **abattoirs, ambulance services, provincial archives, libraries other than national, liquor licences, museums other than national, provincial planning, provincial cultural matters, provincial recreation, provincial roads and traffic, veterinary services.**

**Read those two lists together and the structure is clear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The provinces' real work is concurrent** | **health, education, housing, welfare — delivered provincially, legislated substantially nationally** |
| **Their exclusive powers are small** | liquor licences and provincial roads |
| **So a province is largely an implementing agency** | with legislative powers it rarely uses |

**That is the single most important fact about South African provinces and it is stage 8's subject.** They spend enormous budgets — **health and education are provincial functions** — and they legislate very little. **Whether nine provinces are worth their cost is one of stage 12's arguments.**

**And section 146 resolves conflicts** in the concurrent sphere: **national legislation prevails over provincial in defined circumstances** — uniformity needed for the nation, national standards, prevention of unreasonable action by a province. **In practice, national legislation usually prevails.**

---

**Chapter 3's principles of co-operative government — section 41**, which requires all spheres to:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Preserve the peace, national unity and the indivisibility of the Republic** | |
| **Respect the constitutional status, institutions, powers and functions** of government in other spheres | |
| **Not assume any power or function except those conferred** | |
| **Exercise powers so as not to encroach** on another sphere's integrity | |
| **Co-operate in mutual trust and good faith** | and **"avoid legal proceedings against one another"** |

**That last obligation is real and it is enforced.** A sphere of government that sues another without exhausting intergovernmental mechanisms **may have its case struck out** — the Constitutional Court has said so, and section 41(3) requires that every reasonable effort be made to settle disputes before litigation.

---

**Local government — chapter 7, and it is stronger than most countries':**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **152 — the objects** | democratic and accountable government, **sustainable services**, social and economic development, a safe and healthy environment, **and the involvement of communities** |
| **153 — developmental duties** | **a municipality must structure its administration and budget to prioritise the basic needs of the community** |
| **156 — powers** | the matters in Schedules 4B and 5B, plus anything assigned |
| **Fiscal powers** | **property rates and service charges**, from section 229 |
| **Equitable share** | a constitutional entitlement to a share of nationally raised revenue, section 227 |

**Section 152(1)(b) — "to ensure the provision of services to communities in a sustainable manner" — is the clause most litigation about water, electricity and sanitation runs on.**

**And section 153's "developmental duties" is a constitutional instruction about how a municipality must budget**, which is unusual and is almost never enforced.

---

**And the intervention provisions, which are where the spheres' independence has a limit:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 100** | **the national executive may intervene in a province** that cannot or does not fulfil an executive obligation — by directive, or by **assuming responsibility** for the obligation |
| **Section 139** | **a province may intervene in a municipality** in the same way, including by **dissolving the municipal council** and appointing an administrator |

**Section 139 is used frequently.** Dozens of municipalities have been placed under provincial administration, **and the record is that intervention rarely fixes them** — which is stage 8's local government lesson.

**Section 100 is used rarely and has been politically explosive when it has been** — most prominently in the Eastern Cape and in North West's health departments.

**Practice.** Read Schedules 4 and 5 and note what is concurrent and what is exclusively provincial. Then read sections 152 and 153 and ask what they oblige a municipality to do. Then find how many municipalities are currently under section 139 intervention. Then read section 41(3) and work out what a province must do before suing the national government.
The courts, and Chapter 9:
The judiciary's constitutional position, how judges are appointed, and the six institutions created to watch the state.

**Section 165 — judicial authority:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **165(1)** | judicial authority **vests in the courts** |
| **165(2)** | **"The courts are independent and subject only to the Constitution and the law, which they must apply impartially and without fear, favour or prejudice."** |
| **165(3)** | **no person or organ of state may interfere** with the functioning of the courts |
| **165(4)** | **"Organs of state, through legislative and other measures, must assist and protect the courts to ensure the independence, impartiality, dignity, accessibility and effectiveness of the courts."** |
| **165(5)** | **an order or decision issued by a court binds all persons and organs of state** |

**165(4) is an affirmative duty on the executive and legislature to protect the courts** — which has been invoked when ministers or party officials attacked judges, and in the Zuma contempt litigation of stage 11.

**And 165(5) is the provision the Constitutional Court relied on in holding a former President in contempt**: an order binds all persons, including him.

---

**The court structure — section 166:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Constitutional Court** | **the highest court in all matters** since the Seventeenth Amendment (2013) — before that, only in constitutional matters |
| **The Supreme Court of Appeal** | |
| **The High Court** | with divisions |
| **The Magistrates' Courts** | |
| **Any other court** | established by an Act of Parliament — Labour, Land Claims, Competition Appeal, Electoral, Equality, Tax |

**The 2013 change is worth noting: the Constitutional Court became the apex court for everything**, not only constitutional questions, and it may hear any matter raising an arguable point of law of general public importance.

**The Constitutional Court: eleven judges**, and a matter must be heard by at least eight.

**Terms — section 176:** a non-renewable term of **twelve years, or until age seventy**, whichever comes first, **unless an Act of Parliament extends it.** The non-renewability is the key protection: **a judge seeking reappointment is a judge with an interest.**

---

**Appointment — section 174, and the two routes differ:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Chief Justice and Deputy Chief Justice** | **the President appoints, after consulting the Judicial Service Commission and the leaders of the parties in the National Assembly** |
| **President and Deputy President of the SCA** | the President appoints after consulting the JSC |
| **Other Constitutional Court judges** | **the President appoints from a list prepared by the JSC** — and may ask for more names, with reasons |
| **All other judges** | **the President must appoint on the advice of the JSC** |

**Note the difference: for the Chief Justice the President *consults*; for other judges the President acts *on the advice of* the JSC.** "On the advice of" is binding; "after consulting" is not.

**Which means the Chief Justice's appointment is substantially the President's choice**, and it has been contested — **the 2021–22 process for Chief Justice, in which the President called for public nominations and then appointed someone other than the JSC's recommended candidate, is the live example.**

**The Judicial Service Commission — section 178**, and its composition is the point:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Chief Justice**, who presides | |
| **The President of the SCA** | |
| **A Judge President** designated by the Judges President | |
| **The Minister of Justice**, or an alternate | |
| **Two practising advocates** and **two practising attorneys** | nominated by their professions |
| **One teacher of law** | |
| **Six members of the National Assembly**, **at least three from opposition parties** | |
| **Four delegates of the National Council of Provinces** | |
| **Four persons designated by the President** after consulting party leaders | |

**Twenty-three members, with a politically appointed majority** — and that is the deliberate design, answering stage 5's court-packing: **appointments are neither the executive's alone nor the judiciary's alone.**

**Whether the balance is right is argued.** Critics say the political members dominate and that interviews have been used for political ends; **defenders say judicial self-selection is worse.** Stage 8 covers the JSC's record.

---

**Chapter 9 — "State institutions supporting constitutional democracy", section 181:**

| The six | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Public Protector** | investigates improper conduct in state affairs, and **its remedial action is binding unless set aside on review** — *EFF v Speaker* (2016) |
| **The South African Human Rights Commission** | promotes and monitors rights, and may investigate and litigate |
| **The Commission for the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Cultural, Religious and Linguistic Communities** | from the community rights lesson |
| **The Commission for Gender Equality** | |
| **The Auditor-General** | **audits and reports on all national, provincial and local accounts** |
| **The Electoral Commission** | |

**Plus, under section 192, an independent authority to regulate broadcasting — ICASA.**

**Section 181's protections:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **181(2)** | **independent, impartial, and must exercise their powers "without fear, favour or prejudice"** |
| **181(3)** | **other organs of state must assist and protect them** to ensure their independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness |
| **181(4)** | **"No person or organ of state may interfere with the functioning of these institutions."** |
| **181(5)** | **accountable to the National Assembly**, and must report on their activities and performance at least annually |

**Appointment — section 193: by the President on the recommendation of the National Assembly**, with **60% of the Assembly required for the Public Protector and the Auditor-General** and a majority for the others.

**The 60% threshold is a protection and a weakness.** It requires cross-party support — **and it has produced appointments by negotiation, with mixed results.** Stage 8 and stage 11 cover the Public Protector's record, which is the clearest case of a Chapter 9 institution both constraining a president and then being used against his opponents.

**And section 194 — removal: only on a finding by a committee of the National Assembly of misconduct, incapacity or incompetence, and a resolution supported by two-thirds.** **That procedure was used for the first time against a Public Protector in 2022–23**, which stage 11 covers.

**Practice.** Read section 165 and note the duty in 165(4). Then read section 174 and distinguish "after consulting" from "on the advice of". Then count the JSC's political and professional members. Then read section 181(4) and ask what "interference" would consist of.
Amending the Constitution:
Section 74 — the thresholds, how often they have been met, and the question nobody has had to answer.

**Section 74 sets three thresholds, and from the founding provisions lesson:**

| To amend | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 1, or section 74 itself** | **75% of the National Assembly**, plus **six of the nine provinces in the NCOP** |
| **Chapter 2 — the Bill of Rights** | **two-thirds of the National Assembly**, plus **six provinces** |
| **Any other provision** | **two-thirds of the National Assembly** — plus six provinces if it affects the NCOP, provincial boundaries, powers, functions or institutions |

**And the procedural requirements, in 74(5) to (8):**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Publication** | **the proposed amendment must be published for public comment at least 30 days before introduction** |
| **Submission** | to the provincial legislatures and, where relevant, the NCOP |
| **No omnibus amendments** | **74(4): a constitutional amendment Bill may not include provisions other than constitutional amendments and connected matters** |
| **Provincial consent** | where an amendment concerns only one or some provinces, **those provinces' legislatures must approve** |

**74(4) is a good provision: it prevents a constitutional amendment being slipped into an unrelated Bill.**

---

**How often it has been done: eighteen amendments, as of the Eighteenth in 2023.**

**The ones worth knowing:**

| Amendment | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| **Early amendments (1997–2003)** | technical and transitional corrections; municipal arrangements; **and the floor-crossing provisions** |
| **The floor-crossing amendments (2002–03)** | **permitted MPs and councillors to change parties without losing their seats** — upheld by the Constitutional Court in *UDM v President* (2002), **and repealed in 2008** |
| **The Sixth Amendment (2001)** | court structures |
| **The Seventeenth Amendment (2012)** | **made the Constitutional Court the apex court for all matters**, and established the Chief Justice as head of the judiciary with responsibility for the courts' norms and standards |
| **The Eighteenth Amendment (2023)** | **South African Sign Language as the twelfth official language** |

**The floor-crossing episode is the most instructive.** It was enacted because the ANC and the New National Party wanted it; **it was upheld as constitutional**; it was widely regarded as corrosive of accountability under a closed-list system; **and it was repealed six years later.** From stage 10's electoral lesson: under closed lists, a seat belongs to the party, so permitting a member to keep it on defection was an odd fit — and both the enactment and the repeal were self-interested.

**And the amendment that failed, from the property lesson: the attempt to amend section 25 in 2021 — 204 votes of the 267 required.**

---

**Now the question nobody has had to answer: is there an unamendable core?**

**The text says no.** Section 74 provides a procedure for amending anything, including section 1, at 75%.

**But consider the implication.** A party with 75% of the National Assembly and six provinces could, on the text:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Amend section 1** | removing non-racialism, or universal suffrage |
| **Amend the Bill of Rights** | at two-thirds |
| **Abolish the Constitutional Court's powers** | |
| **In principle, dismantle the democracy** | by following the procedure |

**Which raises the "basic structure" question**, named after the Indian doctrine: **are there constitutional provisions so fundamental that an amendment destroying them would itself be unconstitutional, however large the majority?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **India** | **yes** — the Supreme Court's basic structure doctrine, from *Kesavananda Bharati* (1973) |
| **Germany** | **yes, textually** — the Basic Law's "eternity clause" protects human dignity and the federal democratic order from amendment |
| **South Africa** | **undecided** |

**What the South African courts have said is suggestive and not a holding.** In ***Premier of KwaZulu-Natal v President* (1996)** the Constitutional Court observed, in passing, that **an amendment purporting to abolish the Bill of Rights or to dismantle the democratic state might raise questions the Court would have to consider** — but it did not decide it, because it did not have to.

**So the position is: the text permits anything by the procedure, and the Court has hinted that there may be a limit, and nobody has tested it.**

**And the practical protection is arithmetic.** From the founding provisions lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No party has ever had 75% of the National Assembly** | the ANC's peak was just under 70%, in 2004 |
| **And as of the 2024 election** | **no party has a majority at all** |
| **Nor six provinces** | without coalition partners |

**So section 1 has been, in practice, unamendable for the Constitution's entire life** — and the structural protection the drafters built has been reinforced by the electorate rather than tested by it.

---

**Which closes stage 7 on the observation it has been building toward.**

**The 1996 Constitution is an extremely well-designed document, written by people who knew exactly what they were preventing.** From stages 3 to 5: parliamentary sovereignty, court-packing, defeasible entrenchment, detention without trial, dispossession, and a state accountable to nobody. **Every one of them is answered by a specific provision, and the answers have largely held.**

**And the thing the design assumed — a state with the capacity and the will to use the powers the Constitution gives it — is the subject of stages 8 to 12.**

**Practice.** Read section 74 and write out the three thresholds. Then read 74(4) and work out what it prevents. Then look up the floor-crossing amendments and their repeal. Then read the *Premier of KwaZulu-Natal* dictum on the limits of amendment, and decide what you think the answer should be.
The gap between design and capacity:
Why the institutions get a stage of their own, and the single observation that organises it.

**Stage 7 established that South Africa's constitutional design is excellent and was written by people who knew exactly what they were preventing.**

**This stage is about what happens when that design meets an administration.**

**The observation, stated once and then demonstrated twenty-one times:**

> **South Africa's institutional failures are overwhelmingly failures of capacity and of appointment, not of design.**

**The powers exist. The mandates are clear. The accountability mechanisms are constitutionally entrenched.** And:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Parliament has extensive oversight powers** | **and did not use them for a decade** |
| **The Auditor-General reports in detail every year** | **and the findings recur** |
| **The NPA is constitutionally independent** | **and its leadership was contested for twenty years** |
| **SARS was among the best revenue services in the world** | **and was dismantled in four years and partly rebuilt** |
| **Municipalities have constitutional powers and an equitable share** | **and most cannot produce a clean audit** |
| **The courts work** | **and are asked to do the administration's job** |

**That last row is stage 7's pattern, from the supremacy lesson, and it is the symptom.**

---

**Why "capacity, not design" is a claim and not a platitude.** It is one answer to stage 1's fourth big disagreement — **corruption or design?** — and this stage's version of it is narrower and more specific:

| The claim | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not** | that the Constitution is at fault |
| **Not** | that the institutions were badly designed |
| **But** | **that the people appointed to them, the skills available to them, and the political incentives acting on them have determined their performance far more than their mandates have** |

**And the evidence for it is the variance.** Institutions with the same constitutional standing have performed extremely differently:

| Held, broadly | Did not |
| --- | --- |
| **The Constitutional Court** | **the National Prosecuting Authority** |
| **The Reserve Bank** | **most state-owned enterprises** |
| **National Treasury** (with a severe wobble) | **the police's detective and crime intelligence capacity** |
| **The Auditor-General** | **most municipalities** |
| **StatsSA** | **the Public Protector, for a period** |
| **The IEC** | **the Post Office** |

**The left column and the right column have identical constitutional protections.** So what distinguishes them is not the design.

**What does distinguish them is this stage's subject, and the candidates are:**

| Factor | |
| --- | --- |
| **Leadership appointment** | **who was appointed, and by what process** |
| **Technical professionalisation** | whether the institution's work requires measurable expertise |
| **Visibility** | whether failure is publicly obvious |
| **Insulation from political appointment** | **the Reserve Bank's governor is appointed differently from an SOE board** |
| **Whether capture was attempted** | **and the right column is substantially the list of what was attacked** |
| **Whether the institution's staff resisted** | **which in several cases they did, at personal cost** |

**The fifth row is the one stage 11 develops.** A great deal of the right-hand column is explained by state capture having targeted it — **revenue, prosecution, intelligence, procurement and the SOEs** — and the left-hand column substantially by its having failed there.

---

**The structure of this stage.**

| Lessons | |
| --- | --- |
| **2–6** | **the elected institutions** — Parliament, the NCOP, the President and the Cabinet |
| **7** | **the public service**, and the appointment question |
| **8–11** | **the criminal justice and revenue institutions** — the NPA, the police, intelligence, SARS |
| **12–13** | **the economic institutions** — the Reserve Bank and Treasury |
| **14–16** | **the watchdogs** — the Auditor-General, the Public Protector, the other Chapter 9s |
| **17** | **the judiciary**, and how judges are held to account |
| **18–21** | **the other spheres** — provinces, local government twice, traditional authority |
| **22** | **state-owned enterprises** |

**And what this stage is careful about, under stage 1's rules.** The performance of these institutions is a matter of record — **audits, judgments, commission findings, published reports.** The *reasons* for it are contested, and where they are the lesson gives both.

**One more thing, which is this curriculum's posture applied to a subject where cynicism is cheap.**

**South Africa's institutions are not uniformly failing and saying so is not loyalty.** The Constitutional Court has ruled against two presidents. The Auditor-General names officials. StatsSA's numbers are trusted. The Reserve Bank has held inflation in a target band for twenty-five years. An election has been run every five years, and in 2024 it produced a change in how the country is governed without anybody dying.

**And South Africa's institutions are failing badly in specific, identifiable, measurable ways**, which the rest of this stage sets out.

**Both are true, and an account with only one of them is not a description of the country.**

**Practice.** Take the two columns above and write down, for one institution in each, what you think distinguishes them. Then find the Auditor-General's most recent general report and read its summary. Then come back to this lesson at the end of the stage and see whether your answer has changed.
Parliament: how a law is made:
The four kinds of Bill, the committee stage where everything happens, and the constitutional requirement to consult the public.

**The two Houses:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The National Assembly** | **400 members**, elected proportionally — **half from a national list, half from regional lists** |
| **The National Council of Provinces** | **90 delegates — ten per province**: six permanent and four special, the special including the Premier |

**And the four kinds of Bill, which determine the procedure:**

| Section | Kind | Procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **s74** | **constitutional amendment** | **the thresholds from stage 7** |
| **s75** | **ordinary Bill not affecting provinces** | NA decides; **the NCOP may amend or reject, and the NA can override it** |
| **s76** | **ordinary Bill affecting provinces** | **the NCOP has real power** — provinces vote by province, and a deadlock goes to a mediation committee, with the NA able to override only by two-thirds |
| **s77** | **money Bill** | **introduced only by the Minister of Finance**, and only in the NA |

**So the NCOP's power depends entirely on whether a Bill is tagged section 75 or section 76** — and the tagging is itself contested, because it decides who has a say. **The Constitutional Court has adjudicated tagging disputes**, and the *Tongoane* case struck down the Communal Land Rights Act in 2010 **purely because it had been wrongly tagged as a section 75 Bill when it affected provinces.**

**That is worth noticing: an Act invalidated on procedure alone**, after six years in force.

---

**How a Bill actually passes:**

| Step | Where the work happens |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Policy and drafting** | **in the department.** By the time a Bill reaches Parliament, the content is largely set |
| **2. Cabinet approval** | and publication for comment |
| **3. Introduction**, first reading | formal |
| **4. The portfolio committee** | **this is the stage that matters.** Public hearings, submissions, clause-by-clause consideration, amendments |
| **5. Second reading debate** and NA vote | |
| **6. The NCOP** | and its committee |
| **7. Assent** by the President, and publication | |
| **8. Commencement** | **by proclamation, which from stage 1 may never come** |

**Step 4 is where a Bill is made or broken**, and it is the step the public can reach. **Submissions to a portfolio committee are read, hearings are held, and Bills change** — the BELA Act, the NHI Bill, the Expropriation Bill and the Electoral Amendment Bill were all substantially altered in committee.

**And from stage 1: PMG exists because the press does not cover committees.** If you want to know what Parliament is doing, that is where to look.

---

**Public participation, which is a constitutional requirement and not a courtesy.**

**Sections 59 and 72 require the National Assembly and the NCOP to "facilitate public involvement" in their legislative processes.**

***Doctors for Life International v Speaker* (2006)** is the case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | the NCOP had failed to facilitate public involvement in four health Bills |
| **Held** | **it had.** The obligation is real and justiciable, and what it requires depends on the Bill's nature and the circumstances |
| **The remedy** | **four Acts declared invalid** |

**So a Bill passed without adequate public involvement is unconstitutional** — which is an unusual and strong requirement, and it has been litigated repeatedly since, including on provincial processes and on the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act.

**And the practical consequence: South African legislative committees hold more public hearings than most parliaments**, because the alternative is invalidation.

---

**Money Bills, and the power Parliament acquired and barely uses.**

**Before 2009, Parliament could approve or reject a budget and could not amend it.** Section 77(3) required an Act to provide the procedure for amending money Bills, **and Parliament did not enact one for thirteen years.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Money Bills Amendment Procedure and Related Matters Act 9 of 2009** | finally provided it |
| **What it allows** | **Parliament may amend the budget**, subject to a procedure and to fiscal framework constraints |
| **It also created** | **the Parliamentary Budget Office** — independent analytical capacity for MPs |
| **How often it has been used to amend a budget** | **essentially never** |

**That is the stage's thesis in one institution.** Parliament spent thirteen years without the power, acquired it, and has not used it. **The constraint is not the design.**

---

**Who may introduce a Bill.** Ministers, committees, and — **after *Oriani-Ambrosini v Sisulu* (2012)** — **an individual member.** The Court held that an MP has a constitutional right to introduce legislation and that the NA's rules could not require prior permission. **Private members' Bills are now possible and remain rare.**

**Practice.** Find a Bill currently before a portfolio committee on PMG and read the submissions. Then establish whether it is tagged section 75 or section 76 and what that means for the NCOP. Then read *Doctors for Life* on what facilitating public involvement requires. Then find out how many times Parliament has amended a budget since 2009.
Parliament's oversight, and why it faile:
The powers Parliament has to hold the executive to account, the decade in which it did not, and the judgments that told it so.

**The powers, and the list is substantial:**

| Power | Section |
| --- | --- |
| **Portfolio committees** | may summon any person to give evidence or produce documents — **section 56** |
| **Questions to ministers**, oral and written | and the President's question time |
| **Debates**, including on matters of public importance | |
| **SCOPA** — the Standing Committee on Public Accounts | **examines the Auditor-General's reports and the accounts of every department and entity** |
| **Budget votes** | the opportunity to refuse money |
| **Motion of no confidence** | **section 102 — a majority removes the Cabinet or the President** |
| **Impeachment** | **section 89 — two-thirds, for a serious violation of the Constitution or law, serious misconduct, or inability** |
| **Removal of Chapter 9 heads** | **section 194 — two-thirds** |
| **Ad hoc committees and inquiries** | with full powers to summon |

**Section 56's summons power is as strong as any parliament's.** A committee may compel attendance and the production of documents, **and refusal is an offence.**

---

**And from roughly 2009 to 2017 it was substantially not used against the executive.**

**The mechanism of the failure is not mysterious and it is structural, from stage 7's political rights lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Closed-list proportional representation** | **a member's seat belongs to the party** |
| **So** | an MP who votes against the party loses their livelihood |
| **The party's caucus** | **instructs; the committee chair is a party appointee** |
| **And the majority party's MPs** | **are the executive's party's MPs** |
| **Therefore** | **oversight of a president by his own party's members, whose careers he influences** |

**That is not a South African peculiarity — every parliamentary system has it.** What is peculiar is the **closed list**, which removes the one counterweight: **an MP with a constituency has an independent base.** A South African MP has none.

**The consequences, documented:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Eight motions of no confidence in President Zuma** | **all defeated** |
| **The Nkandla report** | **an ad hoc committee established and then a majority report that exonerated the President** — later found by the Constitutional Court to have been invalid |
| **The SABC inquiry, 2016–17** | **an exception: a genuine, cross-party inquiry that produced a damning report** |
| **The Eskom inquiry, 2017–18** | **another exception, and a very good one** — the Public Enterprises committee under Zukiswa Rantho's chairing did real work on state capture |
| **SCOPA** | **functioned better than most committees throughout**, by convention chaired by an opposition member |

**The two exceptions matter.** They show the powers work when a committee chooses to use them, **and both came late — after the political cost of not acting had become higher than the cost of acting.**

---

**The judgments that told Parliament it had failed.**

***Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly* (2016)** — the Nkandla judgment:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **the Public Protector's remedial action is binding unless set aside on review** |
| **And** | **the President's failure to comply with it was inconsistent with the Constitution** |
| **And crucially** | **the National Assembly's resolution absolving him was invalid** — Parliament had failed in its constitutional obligation to hold the executive to account |

**That last finding is the important one: a court told Parliament that it had not done its job and that its resolution was unconstitutional.**

***United Democratic Movement v Speaker* (2017)** — the secret ballot case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The question** | whether a motion of no confidence could be held by secret ballot |
| **Held** | **the Speaker has a discretion to allow one**, and had wrongly believed she did not |
| **The reasoning** | **MPs' constitutional obligation is to the Constitution and the people, not to the party**, and a secret ballot may be necessary where members cannot vote their conscience openly |
| **What happened** | the Speaker allowed one; **the motion was defeated, with about 26 ANC members apparently voting for it** |

***UDM* is the most direct judicial statement of the closed-list problem.** The Court said, in effect: **we know your seat depends on the party, and a secret ballot is the remedy available.**

***Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker* (2017)** — the impeachment rules case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **Parliament had failed for over twenty years to make rules for a section 89 impeachment**, and was obliged to make them |
| **Consequence** | rules adopted, and **used for the first time in the section 194 removal of the Public Protector in 2022–23** |

**Three judgments, each finding that Parliament had not performed a constitutional function.** From stage 7's section 237: obligations must be performed diligently and without delay.

---

**What has changed, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** since the **2024 election produced no single-party majority**, parliamentary arithmetic has altered. **Committee chairmanships are shared among more parties, the governing arrangement must negotiate its legislation, and the executive's majority is coalitional.** Whether that has improved oversight is early to judge and is stage 11's and stage 12's question.

**The structural point is unchanged: the closed list is still in place**, so the incentive that produced the failure is still in place. **Stage 12's electoral reform argument is about exactly this.**

**Practice.** Read section 56 and note what a committee may compel. Then find the Eskom inquiry's report of 2018 and read its findings. Then read *UDM v Speaker* on why a secret ballot might be necessary. Then look up how many motions of no confidence have been brought and how many have succeeded.
The NCOP, and the provinces' voice:
The second chamber, what it was for, and the general verdict on it.

**What it is. The National Council of Provinces — 90 delegates, ten per province.**

| Per province | |
| --- | --- |
| **Six permanent delegates** | appointed by the provincial legislature, in proportion to its party composition |
| **Four special delegates** | **including the Premier** or a designated member, rotating according to the business before the Council |
| **The delegation votes** | **as a province** on section 76 Bills — one vote per province, cast by the head of the delegation |

**The "votes as a province" feature is the point.** On Bills affecting provinces, **the NCOP is not a chamber of 90 individuals; it is nine provincial votes** — which is what makes it a federal institution rather than a second chamber of the same electorate.

**What it was for**, from stage 6's negotiations:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The federalists' guarantee** | the IFP and the National Party wanted provinces with real power |
| **Constitutional Principle XVIII** | provincial powers not substantially less than the interim constitution's |
| **So** | a chamber in which provinces could block legislation affecting them |
| **Replacing** | **the Senate of the interim constitution**, which had been the instrument of the 1950s court-packing in its earlier form |

**Its powers:**

| On | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 76 Bills** | **real power** — amendment, rejection, mediation, and the NA can override only by two-thirds |
| **Section 75 Bills** | **weak** — the NA can override by a simple majority |
| **Constitutional amendments** | **six of nine provinces required** for amendments affecting provinces, the Bill of Rights, or section 1 |
| **Section 100 interventions** | must be approved by the NCOP |
| **Oversight** | of national matters affecting provinces |

---

**And the verdict, which is close to unanimous among people who study it: the NCOP has not worked as intended.**

**The reasons:**

| Reason | |
| --- | --- |
| **One party governed almost everywhere** | **from 1994 to 2024 the ANC held seven to eight provinces.** A chamber of provincial delegations in which one party controls eight of nine is not a check on that party's national government |
| **Delegates are party appointees** | from provincial legislatures, subject to the same caucus discipline as MPs |
| **Mandates** | **a delegation votes on its legislature's mandate** — and the mandating process is weak, late and frequently nominal |
| **Capacity** | **provincial legislatures have little research capacity** to form a view on national legislation |
| **Attendance** | **poor**, particularly by special delegates and Premiers |
| **Tagging** | **most Bills are tagged section 75**, which reduces the Council to a revising chamber it can be overridden in |

**The tagging point is the quiet one.** From the legislation lesson: **whether the NCOP has power depends on the tag**, and the Joint Tagging Mechanism's decisions have tended toward section 75. ***Tongoane*** is the case where the Court corrected one, and it is rare.

---

**What it has done, because the picture is not blank:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Provincial week and Taking Parliament to the People** | public engagement programmes that reach places the NA does not |
| **Section 100 and 139 oversight** | reviewing interventions in provinces and municipalities |
| **Mediation on section 76 Bills** | occasionally substantive |
| **A forum for premiers** | though the **President's Co-ordinating Council** does that better |

**And the comparison that explains its weakness: intergovernmental coordination happens elsewhere.**

| Body | |
| --- | --- |
| **The President's Co-ordinating Council** | the President, premiers and ministers — **where national-provincial business actually gets settled** |
| **MinMECs** | a minister with the nine provincial MECs for that function — **where health, education and housing policy is coordinated** |
| **The Budget Council and Budget Forum** | where the division of revenue is negotiated |
| **The Financial and Fiscal Commission** | a constitutional body advising on the division of revenue |

**So the executive's intergovernmental machinery is substantial and the legislative chamber built for the purpose is marginal.** That is the NCOP's situation.

---

**Whether it should exist is a live argument, and both sides are serious.**

| Abolish or reform it | Keep it |
| --- | --- |
| **It does not perform its function** | **because one party held eight provinces — and that has now changed** |
| **It duplicates the NA** on most Bills | the section 76 power is real when used |
| **It costs money** | small relative to the budget |
| **Provinces themselves may not be worth their cost** | **which is the deeper argument** — see the provinces lesson |
| | **a federal element is part of the 1993 settlement** and removing it reopens stage 6 |

**And the 2024 change matters here more than anywhere.** From the oversight lesson: **with provincial governments now more varied in composition, a chamber of provincial delegations could become what it was designed to be.** Whether it has is stage 11's and stage 12's question.

**Practice.** Find the NCOP's composition and work out how a province's single vote is determined. Then find a Bill tagged section 76 and follow what the NCOP did with it. Then look up the President's Co-ordinating Council and a MinMEC, and ask what the NCOP adds. Then decide whether you would keep it.
The President, and the executive:
The office, its powers, how a president is removed, and the two cases that tested both.

**The office. Sections 83 to 92.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **83** | the President is **head of state and head of the national executive** |
| **84** | the powers of head of state — assent to Bills, appointments, pardons, **commissions of inquiry**, referendums, honours |
| **85** | **executive authority** — implementing legislation, developing and implementing national policy, co-ordinating departments, preparing legislation |
| **86** | **elected by the National Assembly** from among its members |
| **88** | **a maximum of two terms** |
| **91** | the Cabinet — **the President appoints and dismisses ministers**, who must be Assembly members **except for a maximum of two** |
| **92** | **ministers are accountable collectively and individually to Parliament** |

**Two structural facts about the office.**

**It is a parliamentary presidency, not a directly elected one.** The President is elected by the National Assembly, from among its members, and **can be removed by it.** So South Africa has a president with the powers of a head of state and the tenure of a prime minister.

**And the two-minister exception in section 91 is small but real:** a president may appoint two people from outside Parliament. **It has been used for technocratic appointments** — and the 2024 Government of National Unity's cabinet drew on it.

---

**How a president leaves office, and there are four routes:**

| Route | Threshold |
| --- | --- |
| **Resignation** | |
| **Section 102(2) — motion of no confidence in the President** | **a majority of the National Assembly.** The President and Cabinet must resign |
| **Section 89 — removal** | **two-thirds**, for **a serious violation of the Constitution or the law, serious misconduct, or inability to perform** |
| **Recall by the party** | **not constitutional at all** — but it is how it has actually happened |

**The fourth row is the one that matters in practice.**

| President | How office ended |
| --- | --- |
| **Mandela** | **did not seek a second term** |
| **Mbeki** | **recalled by the ANC's NEC in September 2008**, and resigned |
| **Motlanthe** | caretaker, until the 2009 election |
| **Zuma** | **recalled by the ANC's NEC in February 2018**, and resigned |
| **Ramaphosa** | in office |

**So two presidents have been removed, and neither by a constitutional mechanism.** They were removed by their party's National Executive Committee, which has no constitutional standing whatever, **and they complied because their parliamentary majority was the party's.**

**That is the most important fact about South African executive accountability.** From stage 1's lesson on party documents: **the ANC's NEC is an organ of a voluntary association and it has twice changed the head of state.** The constitutional mechanisms were available and were not used; the party mechanism was used and worked immediately.

**Which cuts both ways:**

| It shows accountability exists | It shows it runs the wrong way |
| --- | --- |
| **A president who loses his party's confidence goes** | **to a party body, not to the electorate or to Parliament** |
| It is faster than impeachment | **and it is not transparent, not reasoned, and not reviewable** |
| | **and the removal of Mbeki in 2008 was a factional act**, not an accountability one |

---

**The difference between sections 102 and 89**, which is more than the threshold:

| | **102(2) no confidence** | **89 removal** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Threshold** | **majority** | **two-thirds** |
| **Grounds** | **none required** — it is political | **specified grounds**, requiring a finding |
| **Consequence** | **the President and the entire Cabinet must resign** | **the President is removed** |
| **Additional consequence** | none | **on grounds of violation or misconduct, the person may be barred from benefits and from holding public office** |

**Section 89's extra consequence is why it is the more serious route** and why it has never been completed. **From the oversight lesson: Parliament had no rules for it until a court ordered them in 2017.**

---

**The two cases that tested the office.**

***Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker* (2016)**, from the oversight lesson: **the President's failure to comply with the Public Protector's remedial action on Nkandla was inconsistent with the Constitution.** The Court made a declaration and the National Assembly's exonerating resolution was invalidated.

***Democratic Alliance v President* (2012)**, on the appointment of a National Director of Public Prosecutions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **the President's appointment of Menzi Simelane was irrational and was set aside** |
| **Why it matters** | **it established that an executive appointment is reviewable for rationality** under the principle of legality from stage 7 |
| **What that opened** | **the whole state capture litigation** — appointments, dismissals, decisions, all reviewable for a rational connection to a legitimate purpose |

**The rationality standard is deferential and it has teeth.** A court will not ask whether an appointment was wise; **it will ask whether the decision was rationally connected to the purpose of the power** — and a great many were not.

---

**The Presidency as an institution, which is a distinct question.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Presidency** | the department supporting the President — **small relative to the centre of government in comparable states** |
| **The Director-General in the Presidency** | and the Secretary of Cabinet |
| **Policy coordination** | **weak, and repeatedly reorganised** — the National Planning Commission (2010), Operation Vulindlela (2020), and various delivery units |
| **The problem named repeatedly** | **South Africa has a strong constitutional executive and a weak centre of government** — departments operate in silos and the Presidency lacks the capacity to drive implementation |

**The National Planning Commission produced the National Development Plan in 2012**, which from stage 1's party documents lesson is **the current official long-term plan, cited by everyone and implemented by almost nobody.** Stage 9 and stage 12 return to why.

**Practice.** Read sections 83 to 92. Then distinguish sections 102 and 89 on grounds, threshold and consequence. Then establish how Mbeki and Zuma left office and under what authority. Then read *DA v President* (2012) and state the rationality test in one sentence.
The public service, and appointment:
A million employees, the constitutional values they are bound by, and the practice a commission found unlawful.

**The constitutional frame — chapter 10.**

**Section 195(1) sets out the values the public administration must be governed by**, and the list is unusually explicit:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **a high standard of professional ethics** |
| **(b)** | efficient, economic and effective use of resources |
| **(c)** | **a development-oriented** administration |
| **(d)** | **services provided impartially, fairly, equitably and without bias** |
| **(e)** | people's needs responded to, and the public encouraged to participate in policy-making |
| **(f)** | **accountable** administration |
| **(g)** | **transparency**, with timely, accessible and accurate information |
| **(h)** | **good human-resource management and career-development practices, to maximise human potential** |
| **(i)** | **"Public administration must be broadly representative of the South African people, with employment and personnel management practices based on ability, objectivity, fairness, and the need to redress the imbalances of the past"** |

**Read 195(1)(i) carefully, because it contains both requirements at once: ability and objectivity, *and* redress.** It is section 9(2) from stage 7, applied to employment in the state — **and it means neither "merit only" nor "representivity only" is the constitutional position.**

**And section 196 establishes the Public Service Commission** — independent, impartial, with power to investigate, monitor and evaluate personnel practices and to report to Parliament. **It has been consistently under-powered and under-used.**

---

**The scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Public servants** | **on the order of 1.2 to 1.3 million**, counting national and provincial departments |
| **Plus** | municipal employees, SOE employees, and the security services |
| **The wage bill** | **one of the largest items in the budget** — roughly a third of consolidated non-interest spending, and the subject of continuous fiscal argument |
| **Where they are** | **the great majority in provinces** — because health and education are provincial functions |

**The wage bill's growth is stage 9's subject.** What belongs here: **public service remuneration rose substantially faster than inflation for most of the 2007–2020 period**, while employment numbers were roughly flat — **so the state spent much more on roughly the same number of people**, which is a fact both sides of the fiscal argument use.

---

**Now cadre deployment, which is the lesson's substance.**

**What it is. The ANC's practice of having party structures recommend or determine appointments to positions in the state** — through deployment committees at national, provincial and local level.

**The ANC's own account of it** is doctrinal and open, from stage 4's Native Republic lesson: **under the National Democratic Revolution, the movement must control the levers of state power**, and deploying cadres to the state is how a liberation movement transforms an inherited administration. **It is written in ANC documents and has been for decades.**

**The objections, and they are of three kinds:**

| Objection | |
| --- | --- |
| **Constitutional** | **a party body determining state appointments is inconsistent with sections 195 and 197**, and with the impartiality the administration is required to show |
| **Legal** | the appointing authority is the relevant executive authority or accounting officer under the Public Service Act; **a party committee has no legal standing in it** |
| **Practical** | **it selects for loyalty over competence**, and it is the mechanism through which capture operated |

**And the Zondo Commission's finding, which is the thing to know.**

**The commission examined cadre deployment and found, in its report, that the practice as operated was unlawful and unconstitutional, and recommended that it be discontinued and that appointments be made on merit through transparent processes.** It also recommended legislation on public service appointments.

**That is a commission's finding, not a court's** — from stage 1's lesson on commissions — **and the ANC has disputed it**, maintaining that recommending candidates is lawful political activity and that the formal appointment remains the executive's.

**The litigation.** The Democratic Alliance sought the deployment committee's records; **after extended proceedings the ANC produced minutes**, and the practice's details — including discussion of judicial appointments — became public. **A further challenge to the practice's lawfulness has been pursued.**

**Where it stands, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the practice has been formally reconsidered within the ANC, a **Public Service Amendment Act and Public Administration Management Amendment Act** have been enacted to shift appointment powers from ministers to heads of department and to professionalise recruitment, and **a National Framework towards the Professionalisation of the Public Sector** was adopted in 2022. **Whether practice has changed is contested.**

---

**The related and less-discussed problems, which capacity failures actually consist of:**

| Problem | |
| --- | --- |
| **Acting appointments** | **senior posts filled by acting officials for years** — which removes accountability and deters decisions |
| **Vacancy rates** | high in technical functions — engineers, planners, finance, IT |
| **Turnover at director-general level** | **very high**, and a DG's tenure is often shorter than a policy's implementation |
| **The loss of technical skills** | **from stage 5's Bantu Education lesson and from emigration** |
| **Consultants** | **large spending on consultants to do work the state cannot**, which the Auditor-General reports on |
| **Discipline** | **slow and rarely concluded**; officials on precautionary suspension for years on full pay |

**The director-general turnover point is the one specialists emphasise most.** A department whose accounting officer changes every two years cannot execute a ten-year plan, **and no legislation fixes that.**

**Practice.** Read section 195(1) and note that (i) requires ability *and* redress. Then find the Zondo Commission's findings on cadre deployment and the ANC's response. Then find your nearest department's vacancy rate and the number of acting senior managers. Then look up consultant spending in the Auditor-General's latest general report.
The National Prosecuting Authority:
Constitutionally independent, politically contested for twenty years, and the institution whose condition explains why so few prosecutions follow so many findings.

**The constitutional provision — section 179:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **179(1)** | **a single national prosecuting authority**, headed by a National Director of Public Prosecutions **appointed by the President** |
| **179(2)** | the authority has the power to institute criminal proceedings on behalf of the state |
| **179(4)** | **"National legislation must ensure that the prosecuting authority exercises its functions without fear, favour or prejudice."** |
| **179(5)** | the NDPP determines prosecution policy, may review decisions, and must consult the Directors of Public Prosecutions |
| **179(6)** | **"The Cabinet member responsible for the administration of justice must exercise final responsibility over the prosecuting authority."** |

**Read 179(4) and 179(6) together and the tension is in the text.** The authority must act without fear or favour, **and a minister has final responsibility over it.** The courts have read 179(6) narrowly — **as responsibility for the institution's functioning rather than for individual prosecution decisions** — but the drafting is the source of twenty years of argument.

**And the appointment is the President's alone.** No commission, no parliamentary approval, no required consultation. **Compare the Public Protector from stage 7, who requires 60% of the National Assembly.**

---

**The record of the office, which is the lesson:**

| NDPP | Tenure | End |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bulelani Ngcuka** | 1998–2004 | resigned, after conflict over the arms deal and the "spy" allegations |
| **Vusi Pikoli** | 2005–2009 | **suspended in 2007 days after obtaining an arrest warrant for the National Police Commissioner, then dismissed** — and the Ginwala inquiry found him fit for office |
| **Menzi Simelane** | 2009–2012 | **appointment set aside as irrational** — *DA v President* (2012) |
| **Nomgcobo Jiba** | acting | **later struck from the roll of advocates** |
| **Mxolisi Nxasana** | 2013–2015 | **paid a very large settlement to leave** |
| **Shaun Abrahams** | 2015–2018 | **appointment invalidated** — *Corruption Watch v President* (2018) |
| **Shamila Batohi** | 2019– | |

**Six NDPPs in twenty-one years, of whom two had their appointments set aside by courts, one was dismissed after acting against a police commissioner, and one was paid to leave.**

**The Pikoli episode is the clearest.** He obtained a warrant for **Jackie Selebi**, the National Police Commissioner and then president of Interpol; **he was suspended within days** on grounds of a breakdown in the relationship with the minister; the **Ginwala inquiry found him fit to hold office**; and **he was dismissed anyway.** Selebi was later convicted of corruption.

***Corruption Watch v President* (2018)** is the judgment that set the record straight:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **Nxasana's removal by settlement was invalid** — an NDPP cannot be bought out, because that is how independence is destroyed |
| **And consequently** | **Abrahams's appointment was invalid**, since the vacancy had been created unlawfully |
| **And** | **sections 12(4) and 12(6) of the NPA Act — allowing the President to suspend an NDPP indefinitely and without pay — were unconstitutional** |

**The last finding is the structural one: an NDPP who can be suspended indefinitely without pay is not independent.**

---

**The Scorpions, and their disbandment.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Directorate of Special Operations** | established 1999 **inside the NPA** — prosecutors and investigators working together on organised crime and corruption |
| **Its record** | **very high conviction rates**, and it investigated senior politicians, including the arms deal and Selebi |
| **2007** | **the ANC's Polokwane conference resolved to dissolve it** |
| **2009** | **legislation disbanded it**, and the **Hawks** were created inside the police instead |

**The disbandment is the single clearest institutional act of the period** and it was done by resolution of a party conference, then by statute. **From stage 1: a conference resolution is ANC policy, and here it became law in eighteen months.**

**And the Constitutional Court's response, in *Glenister II* (2011):**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **the Constitution requires an adequately independent anti-corruption entity**, derived from the state's obligations and from international agreements |
| **And** | **the Hawks as legislated lacked adequate independence** — the legislation was invalid |
| **Parliament amended it** | and in ***Helen Suzman Foundation v President* (2014)** further provisions were struck down |

***Glenister* established a constitutional right to an effective anti-corruption capacity.** It is one of the most creative judgments the Court has given and it has not been fully satisfied — **which is the Hawks lesson, next.**

---

**The current position, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the NPA has an **Investigating Directorate Against Corruption (IDAC)**, made a permanent statutory body by the **NPA Amendment Act of 2024** — giving it its own investigators rather than relying on the police. **Shamila Batohi has led the NPA since 2019.**

**And the question that hangs over it, which is stage 11's and stage 12's:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The TRC referred about 300 cases** | from stage 6: **almost no prosecutions** |
| **The Zondo Commission referred a large volume of matters** | from 2022: **a small number of prosecutions, slowly** |
| **The arms deal** | **no successful prosecution of a South African official** |
| **The capture-era SOE contracts** | some prosecutions, mostly of less senior people, mostly unresolved |

**So two commissions, three decades apart, both produced extensive findings and almost no criminal consequence** — and the NPA's record above is the principal reason. **An institution whose leadership was contested for twenty years does not build the capacity to prosecute complex financial crime**, and that capacity takes a decade to build.

**The honest counterweight:** complex corruption prosecutions are slow everywhere, the NPA has had its budget constrained, and **the cases now before the courts are genuinely difficult.** Stage 12 weighs it.

**Practice.** Read section 179 and note the tension between (4) and (6). Then establish how each NDPP since 1998 left office. Then read *Glenister II* on the constitutional requirement of an independent anti-corruption body. Then find how many Zondo referrals have resulted in convictions, and the date you checked.
The police, and the Hawks:
A police service with a constitutional mandate, among the world's highest murder rates, and the investigative capacity that is the actual problem.

**The constitutional provisions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **205(3)** | the objects of the police: **"to prevent, combat and investigate crime, to maintain public order, to protect and secure the inhabitants of the Republic and their property, and to uphold and enforce the law"** |
| **206** | **a member of Cabinet is responsible for policing** and must determine national policing policy; **provinces have oversight functions** |
| **206(6)** | **a province may investigate, or appoint a commission to investigate, complaints of police misconduct** |
| **207** | **a National Commissioner appointed by the President**, to control and manage the police |
| **208** | **a civilian secretariat** for the police |

**And the independent oversight body: IPID — the Independent Police Investigative Directorate**, under the IPID Act of 2011, which must investigate deaths in police custody, deaths as a result of police action, torture, rape by police and corruption.

***McBride v Minister of Police* (2016)**: **the provisions allowing the minister to suspend and remove the IPID head were unconstitutional** — the same reasoning as the NDPP's in the last lesson. **An oversight body whose head the overseen minister can remove is not independent.**

---

**The National Commissioners, and the pattern is the NPA's:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **George Fivaz** | 1995–2000 |
| **Jackie Selebi** | 2000–2009 — **convicted of corruption in 2010** |
| **Bheki Cele** | 2009–2012 — **removed after a board of inquiry found lease deals unlawful**; later Minister of Police |
| **Riah Phiyega** | 2012–2017 — **suspended; a board of inquiry recommended removal** following Marikana |
| **Khehla Sitole** | 2017–2022 — **resigned**, after judicial findings about his conduct in a procurement matter |
| **Fannie Masemola** | 2022– |

**Six commissioners in thirty years, with one convicted, two removed or resigned after inquiries, and one found unfit.**

**And the structural point: the appointment is the President's alone**, as with the NDPP. **No commission, no parliamentary process** — and the Zondo Commission recommended that this change.

---

**Now the numbers, dated, because they are the context for everything else:**

> **As of the 2023–24 and 2024–25 police statistics: South Africa records on the order of 26,000 to 27,000 murders a year** — a rate among the highest in the world outside active conflict. **Plus very high rates of rape, aggravated robbery and assault.** **Check the current quarterly release from SAPS and StatsSA.**

**And the Victims of Crime Survey from StatsSA**, which measures reported experience rather than recorded cases, **consistently shows under-reporting**, particularly of sexual offences.

---

**The thing that is actually broken, and it is not the number of police.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Personnel** | **South Africa has a large police service by international comparison** — roughly 180,000 to 190,000 members |
| **The deficit** | **investigative capacity** |

**The detective service is the problem.** From the published figures and the Auditor-General's and parliamentary committee reports:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Detection and conviction rates for murder** | **low** — a substantial majority of murder dockets do not end in a conviction |
| **Detective-to-docket ratios** | far above any reasonable workload |
| **Forensic capacity** | **backlogs in DNA analysis running to hundreds of thousands of cases** at points in the 2020s |
| **Training and experience** | the loss of experienced detectives, and the promotion of inexperienced ones |
| **Crime intelligence** | **repeatedly compromised** — the secret service account, successive heads suspended or charged |

**Crime intelligence deserves its own note.** It is funded from a **secret services account** with limited audit visibility, **and it has been the subject of repeated allegations of abuse for factional purposes** — with heads of the division suspended, charged and in one case convicted. **The Zondo Commission and the 2018 intelligence review both addressed it.**

**And the consequence of weak investigation is the one that matters for everything else in this curriculum: impunity.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For ordinary crime** | a murder that will not be solved deters nobody |
| **For political violence** | from stage 6: **the train massacres are substantially unsolved**; political killings in KwaZulu-Natal continue with few convictions |
| **For corruption** | **a prosecution requires an investigation**, and the Hawks depend on the same pool of skills |

---

**The Hawks — the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Created** | 2009, replacing the Scorpions from the last lesson |
| **Located** | **inside the police**, not in the NPA |
| **Its independence** | **litigated twice** — *Glenister II* (2011) and *Helen Suzman Foundation* (2014), both finding the legislation inadequate |
| **Its record on capture-era cases** | **weak**, which is why IDAC was given its own investigators in 2024 |
| **Its heads** | contested, including **Berning Ntlemeza**, whose appointment was set aside by a court in 2017 after findings that he lacked integrity |

**The structural criticism of locating the Hawks inside the police is the one *Glenister* turned on: an anti-corruption unit inside the institution it may have to investigate, reporting to a commissioner appointed by the President, is not insulated.** The Scorpions had been in the NPA, with prosecutors and investigators together, **and that is the model IDAC partially restores.**

---

**Marikana, which belongs in this lesson because it is the institution's worst single event.**

> **On 16 August 2012, police shot dead 34 striking mineworkers at Marikana**, in the North West, during a wildcat strike at Lonmin's platinum operations. Ten people, including two police officers and two Lonmin security guards, had been killed in the preceding week.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Farlam Commission** | 2012–2015, reported 2015 |
| **Its findings** | **the police operation was defective and dangerous**; the plan was unlawful in material respects; **the police misled the commission and altered documents** |
| **Accountability** | **the National Commissioner was found unfit for office; a board of inquiry followed** |
| **Prosecutions** | **no police officer has been convicted of the killings** |
| **Compensation** | civil claims settled, slowly, over years |

**Marikana is stage 11's material as a political event.** As an institutional matter it is the clearest demonstration of the chapter's thesis: **the constitutional mandate, the oversight bodies and the commission all functioned, and nobody was prosecuted.**

**Practice.** Find the latest quarterly crime statistics and the murder figure. Then find the detective service's case load per detective and the DNA backlog. Then read *Glenister II* on why the Hawks' location matters. Then establish how many police officers have been convicted for the Marikana killings.
Intelligence:
The least visible institution, the review panel that found it had been repurposed, and the reform that followed.

**The constitutional frame — chapter 11, sections 198 to 210.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **198** | the governing principles: **national security must reflect the resolve to live as equals, in peace and harmony, free from fear and want**; and **national security is subject to the authority of Parliament and the national executive** |
| **199(5)** | the security services **must act, and teach and require their members to act, in accordance with the Constitution and the law, including customary international law** |
| **199(6)** | **"No member of any security service may obey a manifestly illegal order."** |
| **199(7)** | **the security services may not prejudice a political party interest that is legitimate**, nor further, in a partisan manner, any interest of a political party |
| **209** | intelligence services may be established **only by the President, as head of the national executive, and only in terms of national legislation** |
| **210** | **national legislation must provide for civilian monitoring by an inspector appointed by the President and approved by two-thirds of the National Assembly** |

**Read 199(6) and 199(7) against stage 5's security state.** *No member may obey a manifestly illegal order* — and *may not further a political party's interest in a partisan manner.* **Both clauses are written against specific history.**

---

**The institutions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The State Security Agency (SSA)** | created in **2009 by proclamation**, merging the domestic **National Intelligence Agency** and the foreign **South African Secret Service** into one body |
| **Crime intelligence** | **inside the police**, from the last lesson |
| **Defence intelligence** | inside the SANDF |
| **The Inspector-General of Intelligence** | **the civilian monitor under section 210**, appointed with two-thirds approval |
| **The Joint Standing Committee on Intelligence (JSCI)** | **parliamentary oversight, meeting in closed session** |

**The 2009 merger is where the trouble begins, in most accounts.** Combining domestic and foreign intelligence in one agency, created by proclamation rather than by legislation debated in public, **removed a separation that had existed since 1994** and concentrated capability under a single minister.

---

**The finding, and this is the lesson's substance.**

**The High-Level Review Panel on the State Security Agency**, appointed in 2018 and chaired by **Sydney Mufamadi**, reported that year.

**What it found, in substance:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A "doctrinal shift"** | **the SSA had been repurposed from protecting the constitutional order to serving factional political ends** |
| **Parallel structures** | operating outside the lawful command chain |
| **Large volumes of unaccounted cash** | and procurement without controls |
| **Political operations** | directed at domestic political actors, including within the governing party |
| **Loss of capability** | **the agency's core intelligence function had degraded** |
| **Oversight failure** | the Inspector-General's office under-resourced, and the JSCI inadequately informed |

**And the Zondo Commission heard evidence to similar effect**, including on cash payments, unauthorised operations and the funding of media and political projects.

**That is as serious a finding as can be made about an intelligence service in a constitutional democracy: that it was turned on the democracy it existed to protect.** From stage 5's security lesson: **the clauses in sections 199(6) and 199(7) exist because this had happened before.**

---

**The reform, as a dated note:**
