> **As of 14 October 2026:** the **General Intelligence Laws Amendment Act** was enacted in 2024 to give effect to the review panel's central recommendation — **splitting the SSA back into separate domestic and foreign services** — and to strengthen the Inspector-General's office and tighten vetting and procurement. **Implementation is in progress and its effect is not yet assessable.**

**And one provision of that Bill was contested on constitutional grounds**: the breadth of the vetting powers over individuals and organisations, which civil society argued could reach lawful political and journalistic activity. **Parts were amended in response.**

---

**The structural problem with intelligence oversight, which is general and not South African:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Secrecy is necessary** | an intelligence service that publishes its operations cannot operate |
| **And secrecy defeats oversight** | **the overseers must be trusted with what they cannot disclose** |
| **So oversight depends on the overseers** | the Inspector-General, and a committee meeting in closed session |
| **Which means** | **if the overseers are captured or incapable, there is no backstop** |
| **And South Africa's experience** | **is that they were under-resourced and under-informed for a decade** |

**That is why the Inspector-General's independence and capacity matter more than any statutory wording**, and why the review panel's recommendations concentrated on them.

**And the transparency that does exist, from stage 1's sources lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The secret services account** | **audited by the Auditor-General**, with a classified report to the JSCI |
| **The Inspector-General's reports** | **classified**, with limited public summaries |
| **Parliamentary budget votes** | public in aggregate |
| **Commission evidence** | **the single most informative public source** — Zondo, and the review panel's released report |

**So almost everything known publicly about South African intelligence since 1994 comes from commissions and from journalism**, not from the oversight architecture. **That is the measure of the oversight architecture.**

**Practice.** Read sections 198 to 210. Then find the High-Level Review Panel's report of 2018 and read its findings on the doctrinal shift. Then establish what the 2024 amendment Act changed. Then look up the Inspector-General of Intelligence's budget and staff complement, and compare it with the SSA's.
SARS:
The clearest case study available of an institution built, captured, and partly rebuilt — with a commission's findings on all three.

**Why SARS gets its own lesson.** It is the one South African institution whose rise, destruction and partial recovery are all documented, measurable and within twenty-five years. **If you want to understand what capacity is and how it is lost, this is the case.**

---

**The building, 1997–2009.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Created** | as an autonomous revenue authority outside the public service, with its own employment terms |
| **Led by** | **Pravin Gordhan as Commissioner from 1999 to 2009** |
| **What was built** | **e-filing, risk-based audit, a Large Business Centre, specialist enforcement units, customs modernisation, and a professional staff** |
| **The outcomes** | **revenue collection consistently above target for most of a decade**; tax-to-GDP ratio rising; **and a compliance culture, which is the asset that takes longest to build and is easiest to lose** |
| **Reputation** | **internationally regarded as among the best revenue administrations in the developing world** |

**The compliance point is the one to understand.** A revenue service's real asset is **taxpayers' belief that evasion will be detected and that the money is used properly.** That belief is built over years and it can be destroyed in months.

---

**The destruction, 2014–2018.**

**Tom Moyane was appointed Commissioner in September 2014.**

**What happened, as the Nugent Commission found it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A restructuring** | **the executive committee dissolved, the Large Business Centre dismantled, enforcement and compliance units broken up** |
| **Consultants** | **a large contract with a management consultancy** to design and implement the restructuring |
| **Senior staff** | **a mass exodus** — the great majority of the senior leadership left within two years |
| **The "rogue unit" narrative** | **an allegation that SARS had run an unlawful covert intelligence unit**, used to justify suspensions, dismissals and the removal of senior officials |
| **The reports behind it** | **the Sikhakhane panel (2014), and a KPMG report (2015) which KPMG later withdrew and apologised for** |
| **Revenue** | **substantial shortfalls against target**, year after year |

**The "rogue unit" story is the mechanism and it is worth understanding as a technique.** An allegation of unlawful conduct, supported by reports later discredited, **was used to remove the officials who had built the enforcement capacity** — and the allegation was repeated in media aligned with the project. **The KPMG report's withdrawal is the documented part.**

**And the revenue consequence was measurable.** The Nugent Commission put the shortfall attributable in part to the institution's deterioration in the tens of billions of rands.

---

**The Nugent Commission, 2018**, chaired by Judge Robert Nugent.

**Its findings, and the language is unusually blunt for a commission:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"A massive failure of integrity and governance"** | |
| **The restructuring** | **had been destructive and was not justified by any coherent rationale** |
| **Moyane** | **recommended for removal**, which followed |
| **The consultancy's role** | criticised; **the firm subsequently repaid its fees** |
| **The "rogue unit" allegations** | **found to have no proper basis as used** |
| **And the recommendation** | **restore the capability, and insulate the appointment of the Commissioner** |

**Nugent's report is short, readable and free**, and it is the single best document on how a competent South African institution was dismantled.

---

**The rebuilding, 2019 onward.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Edward Kieswetter** | Commissioner from May 2019 |
| **What was restored** | **the Large Business Centre, enforcement and compliance capacity, the illicit economy unit, and specialist audit** |
| **Recruitment** | including the return of some who had left |
| **Revenue** | **recovered and has exceeded estimates in several subsequent years**, with substantial amounts attributed to compliance and enforcement work |
| **Technology** | continued modernisation, with high e-filing rates |

**And the recovery is the most hopeful fact in this stage.** An institution can be rebuilt — **in about five years, with a competent appointment, a clear mandate and political support.**

**But note the asymmetry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **To build it** | **about twelve years** |
| **To break it** | **about four** |
| **To rebuild it** | **about five, and the compliance culture is slower than the systems** |

---

**What SARS demonstrates for the stage's thesis**, which is why it is here:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The design was not the problem** | SARS's legislation did not change materially |
| **The appointment was** | **one appointment, in 2014** |
| **The institution's staff were the asset** | and they left |
| **The oversight bodies worked, eventually** | the commission, the courts, Parliament's finance committee — **all after four years** |
| **And the recovery required** | **a competent appointment and nothing else legislative** |

**That is the capacity thesis in one institution**, and it is why a stage on institutions is worth having.

**One further lesson, from stage 1's method.** The "rogue unit" narrative was carried in published reports by reputable firms and reported widely as fact. **It was wrong, and establishing that it was wrong took a judicial commission four years.** From stage 1: **place the source, ask what it is for, and notice that an allegation repeated in aligned media is not corroboration.**

**Practice.** Read the Nugent Commission's report — it is short. Then find SARS's revenue collection against target for each year from 2013 to 2019. Then look up the KPMG report's withdrawal and apology. Then find what the Large Business Centre does and why dismantling it mattered.
The Reserve Bank:
The institution that has held, its unusual ownership, and the mandate argument that recurs at every ANC conference.

**The constitutional provisions — sections 223 to 225:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **223** | **"The South African Reserve Bank is the central bank of the Republic"** |
| **224(1)** | **"The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth in the Republic."** |
| **224(2)** | **"The South African Reserve Bank, in pursuit of its primary object, must perform its functions independently and without fear, favour or prejudice, but there must be regular consultation between the Bank and the Cabinet member responsible for national financial matters."** |
| **225** | the Bank's powers and functions are those customarily exercised by central banks, as determined by an Act of Parliament |

**From stage 6's economic settlement lesson: this clause was a negotiated requirement**, and it removes monetary policy from elected control. **It is one of only a handful of constitutions in the world that entrenches central bank independence.**

**And note what 224(1) actually says: protect the value of the currency — *in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth*.** The mandate is price stability **with a stated purpose**, which is a textual hook for the argument that growth and employment are part of it.

---

**How it operates:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Monetary Policy Committee** | sets the repurchase rate, meeting several times a year, with published statements and minutes-equivalent |
| **Inflation targeting** | **a 3–6% band, adopted in 2000** |
| **The Governor** | **appointed by the President**, for a five-year term, after consultation |
| **Other functions** | banknote issue, the national payment system, **bank supervision through the Prudential Authority**, financial stability, and management of the gold and foreign exchange reserves |
| **Financial stability mandate** | formalised by the **Financial Sector Regulation Act of 2017** — the "twin peaks" reform |

**The target band is worth a dated note:**

> **As of 2025–26 the inflation target has been under formal review, with argument for lowering it toward 3%** rather than the 3–6% band's midpoint of 4.5%. **Check the current position with the Reserve Bank and Treasury.**

---

**The ownership, which is genuinely odd.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The SARB has private shareholders** | about **two million shares**, held by **roughly 600 to 800 shareholders** |
| **What they get** | **a capped dividend**, and they **elect seven of the fifteen board directors** |
| **What they do not get** | **any influence over monetary policy**, which is the MPC's, or over the Bank's regulatory functions |
| **How many central banks are like this** | **very few** — Belgium, Switzerland, Japan and Turkey have variants; most are wholly state-owned |

**And it is a standing political irritant out of proportion to its substance.** Shareholders have no policy influence; **the arrangement nonetheless invites the claim that the central bank is privately owned**, which is formally true and practically misleading.

**Nationalising the shareholding is an ANC conference resolution** — adopted at Nasrec in 2017 and reaffirmed — **and has never been implemented.** The reasons given are cost, the absence of any policy benefit, and the signalling risk.

---

**The mandate argument, which is the live one.**

| The case for changing the mandate | The case against |
| --- | --- |
| **224(1) already mentions "balanced and sustainable economic growth"** — so employment is within the purpose | **the primary object is price stability**, and the growth clause states the purpose of that stability rather than a second target |
| **Unemployment above 30%** is the country's defining problem, and a central bank that targets only inflation is ignoring it | **a central bank cannot create jobs**; it can create inflation, which falls hardest on the poor |
| Other central banks have dual mandates — **the US Federal Reserve** | and have higher inflation tolerance with contested results |
| **Quantitative easing** could fund development | **South Africa borrows in rand and in dollars**, and monetary financing in an open emerging economy risks a currency and debt spiral |
| | **the Bank's independence is one of the few institutions that held** — stage 8's thesis — and reopening it is a risk |

**Both sides are serious and the argument is not settled by economics alone**, because it turns on how much the costs of inflation fall on the poor against how much the costs of unemployment do. **Stage 9 and stage 12 take it up with the numbers.**

---

**And the episode that shows the institution's standing.**

**In 2017 the Public Protector issued a report on an apartheid-era Bankorp lifeboat** that included remedial action **directing Parliament to amend section 224 of the Constitution** to change the Reserve Bank's mandate.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What happened** | **the courts set it aside** |
| **The findings** | **the Public Protector had acted beyond her powers, had not acted with an open mind, and had met the Presidency and the SSA without disclosing it** |
| **The costs** | **a personal costs order against the Public Protector** — unusual, and deliberate |
| **The significance** | **a Chapter 9 institution attempted to direct a constitutional amendment, and the courts stopped it** |

**That episode is the clearest demonstration in the period both of a watchdog being misused and of the courts functioning** — and it belongs to the next lesson as much as to this one.

**Practice.** Read sections 223 to 225 and note the full wording of 224(1). Then find the current inflation target and the review's status. Then establish how the SARB's shareholders are constituted and what rights they hold. Then read the mandate argument's two columns and decide what evidence would move you.
Treasury, and the budget:
The institution capture most needed and least achieved, the cycle that governs every other institution, and the four days in December 2015.

**The constitutional provisions — sections 213 to 219 and 226 to 230:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **213** | **a National Revenue Fund** — all money received by the national government must be paid into it, and may be withdrawn only in terms of an appropriation or a direct charge |
| **215** | **budgets must promote transparency, accountability and the effective financial management** of the economy, debt and the public sector |
| **216** | **the national treasury must prescribe uniform treasury norms and standards** — and **may stop the transfer of funds to an organ of state that commits a serious or persistent material breach** |
| **217** | **procurement must be fair, equitable, transparent, competitive and cost-effective** — and **may provide for preferential procurement and protect or advance disadvantaged persons** |
| **218–219** | guarantees, and the remuneration of office-bearers |
| **227** | **provinces and municipalities are entitled to an equitable share of nationally raised revenue** |

**Section 216's power to stop transfers is the strongest administrative weapon in South African government**, and it has been used — most prominently against provinces and municipalities in serious breach.

**And section 217 is the constitutional basis of both the procurement rules and BEE procurement** — note that it **permits** preferential procurement, within a framework of fairness, competitiveness and cost-effectiveness. **Stage 9 and stage 12 argue about the balance.**

---

**The budget cycle, which is worth knowing because it is when things can be influenced:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **Through the year** | departments prepare bids; **the Medium Term Expenditure Framework** sets three-year envelopes |
| **October / November** | **the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement** — the fiscal framework and the division of revenue, with the macro forecasts |
| **February** | **the Budget** — the Minister of Finance's speech, the **Budget Review**, the Division of Revenue Bill and the Appropriation Bill |
| **February–July** | **parliamentary committees consider the fiscal framework, then the Division of Revenue Bill, then the Appropriation Bill**, with public hearings |
| **During the year** | adjustments appropriation, and the Special Appropriation Bills |
| **After** | **annual reports and audited financial statements**, then **SCOPA and the Auditor-General** |

**From stage 1's sources lesson: the Budget Review each February is the clearest single document on what the South African state actually does.** It is free, it is several hundred pages, and the overview and the chapter on the division of revenue answer most questions anybody has.

**And the statutes that govern spending:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Public Finance Management Act 1 of 1999 (PFMA)** | national and provincial departments and public entities — **accounting officers, irregular expenditure, and the duty to prevent it** |
| **The Municipal Finance Management Act 56 of 2003 (MFMA)** | municipalities |
| **The Public Procurement Act 28 of 2024** | **the new consolidated procurement framework**, replacing a patchwork |

---

**Now Treasury as an institution, and the stage's thesis.**

**Treasury was the institution state capture most needed and least achieved**, and the reason is structural: **every large irregular payment must pass through a procurement process and a budget.** Capturing SOEs delivers contracts; **capturing Treasury would have delivered the whole fiscus.**

**And it was attacked.**

**December 2015 — "Nenegate":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **9 December 2015** | **Finance Minister Nhlanhla Nene dismissed**, and **David van Rooyen**, a little-known backbencher, appointed |
| **The reaction** | **the rand fell sharply; bond yields spiked; bank shares collapsed** — a very large loss of value within days |
| **13 December 2015** | **van Rooyen replaced by Pravin Gordhan** |
| **Duration** | **four days** |

**The four days are the most instructive episode in modern South African political economy.** A single appointment produced a market reaction severe enough to force its reversal in under a week — **and the reversal was secured by business leaders, ANC figures and the markets rather than by any constitutional mechanism.**

**March 2017:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gordhan and his deputy Mcebisi Jonas dismissed** | after being recalled from an investor roadshow in London |
| **Malusi Gigaba appointed** | |
| **Consequence** | **S&P and Fitch downgraded South Africa's foreign-currency debt to sub-investment grade in April 2017**; Moody's followed in 2020 |

**Jonas's evidence to the Zondo Commission** — that he had been offered a very large sum and the finance ministership by members of the Gupta family in the presence of the President's son — is among the most serious testimony the commission heard. **He refused.**

**And what Treasury's officials did**, which is the part the stage's thesis rests on: **they resisted**. The nuclear procurement programme, the SAA guarantees, specific irregular transactions — **Treasury officials declined, delayed, insisted on processes and in some cases went to court.** Several lost their jobs.

---

**The fiscal position, as a dated note, because it is the constraint on everything in stages 9 and 12:**

> **As of the 2025–26 Budget: gross national debt is in the region of 75–77% of GDP**, up from about 26% in 2008; **debt-service costs are among the largest single items of spending**, exceeding what is spent on several major functions; and **the primary balance has recently moved into surplus**, with debt projected to stabilise. **Check the current Budget Review.**

**Debt-service cost is the number that matters.** From stage 6's economic settlement: the apartheid debt was honoured and crowded out the RDP. **The current debt crowds out the same things, and it was accumulated after 2008** — which is stage 9's subject.

**Practice.** Download the most recent Budget Review and read the overview chapter. Then find debt-service costs and compare them with spending on health, or on police. Then find section 216 and establish when Treasury has stopped transfers. Then read Mcebisi Jonas's Zondo evidence.
The Auditor-General:
The institution that held, whose reports are the evidence base for everything else in this stage, and whose new powers are the one real constitutional innovation of the past decade.

**The constitutional provisions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **181** | the Auditor-General is **a Chapter 9 institution** — independent, subject only to the Constitution and the law, impartial, and **accountable to the National Assembly** |
| **188(1)** | **must audit and report on the accounts, financial statements and financial management of all national and provincial departments and administrations, all municipalities, and any other institution required by legislation** |
| **188(3)** | **must submit audit reports to any legislature with a direct interest, and all reports must be made public** |
| **181(3)** | **other organs of state must assist and protect these institutions** to ensure their independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness |

**From stage 7's Chapter 9 lesson, the design.** Here, the practice — **and it is the most successful of the six.**

---

**The audit opinions, which you need in order to read the reports:**

| Opinion | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Unqualified with no findings** | **"clean audit"** — the statements are reliable **and** there are no material findings on performance reporting or compliance |
| **Unqualified with findings** | the numbers are reliable, **but** there are findings on compliance or on performance information |
| **Qualified** | **parts of the statements are materially misstated** |
| **Adverse** | **the statements as a whole are materially misstated** |
| **Disclaimer** | **the auditee could not provide enough evidence to form an opinion at all** |
| **Outstanding** | the statements were not submitted |

**"Clean audit" is the one to be careful with.** It means the records are in order and the rules were followed. **It does not mean the money achieved anything** — a department can receive a clean audit and deliver nothing, and the AG says so.

**And the expenditure categories:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Irregular expenditure** | **incurred in contravention of legislation** — it is a compliance finding, **not a finding of loss or of theft** |
| **Fruitless and wasteful** | **made in vain and would have been avoided had reasonable care been exercised** |
| **Unauthorised** | **outside the vote or the purpose appropriated** |

**The distinction between irregular expenditure and loss is the most commonly abused statistic in South African politics.** A large irregular expenditure figure means rules were broken — procurement without three quotes, a contract extended without approval — **and some of it is theft and some of it is paperwork.** From stage 1's statistics lesson: **the AG says this explicitly in every general report, and it is routinely reported as if the whole figure were stolen.**

---

**The 2018 amendment, which is the real innovation.**

**The Public Audit Amendment Act of 2018, effective from April 2019**, gave the AG powers no comparable audit office has:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Material irregularity** | **the AG may identify a "material irregularity"** — non-compliance, fraud, theft or a breach of fiduciary duty that **has caused or is likely to cause a material financial loss**, or harm to the public or to an institution |
| **Referral** | **may refer it to a public body with a mandate to investigate** — the Hawks, the NPA, the Public Protector |
| **Remedial action** | **may take binding remedial action** where the accounting officer fails to act |
| **Certificate of debt** | **may issue a certificate of debt against an accounting officer personally** for the loss, recoverable by the relevant executive authority |

**Personal liability for an accounting officer is the point.** From this stage's thesis: the consistent failure in South African public administration is **consequence management** — findings are made and nobody is affected. **The certificate of debt attaches the loss to a person.**

**And it is used sparingly and slowly.** The first material irregularities were raised from 2019 and the number has grown; **certificates of debt have been rare.** The honest assessment is that the power is real, the process is deliberately heavy, and **its deterrent effect is not yet established.**

---

**What the reports say, as a dated snapshot:**

> **As of the general reports for 2023–24 and 2024–25:** at national and provincial level, **roughly a quarter to a third of auditees achieve clean audits**, with the position having improved slowly. **At local government level it is far worse — on the order of 10 to 15% of 257 municipalities**, with dozens receiving qualified, adverse or disclaimed opinions and some failing to submit statements at all. **Irregular expenditure across government runs to tens of billions of rands a year**, and the AG reports a large accumulated balance of irregular expenditure never dealt with. **Check the current MFMA and PFMA general reports at agsa.co.za.**

**And the AG's standing diagnosis, repeated across general reports for a decade:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Instability in key positions** | vacancies and acting appointments in accounting-officer and chief-financial-officer posts |
| **Lack of basic financial controls** | **not sophisticated fraud — record-keeping** |
| **Non-compliance with supply chain rules** | and inadequate contract management |
| **No consequence management** | **the central finding: findings are not acted on** |
| **Reliance on consultants** | including to prepare the financial statements the officials should prepare |

**Read that list against the rest of the stage.** It is the capacity thesis stated by the institution with the best evidence.

---

**Why the AG held, which is the question the stage keeps asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Appointment** | **nominated by a National Assembly committee and appointed by the President on a resolution of the Assembly** — a non-renewable term of between five and ten years |
| **Funding** | **largely self-funding through audit fees**, which reduces dependence on a departmental vote |
| **Mandate** | **technical and rule-bound** — an audit opinion is an exercise with professional standards behind it |
| **Profession** | staffed by chartered accountants with an external professional identity |
| **Leadership** | **Kimi Makwetu to 2020, then Tsakani Maluleke — the first woman to hold the office** |

**Compare the Public Protector, next.** Same chapter, same independence clause, **different appointment process and a discretionary mandate — and a very different history.**

**Practice.** Open the latest MFMA general report and find the clean-audit count. Then find the AG's definition of irregular expenditure and write down why it is not a measure of theft. Then find how many certificates of debt have been issued since 2019. Then look up one municipality near you and read its audit outcome.
The Public Protector in practice:
The clearest single demonstration of this stage's thesis: the design was adequate, one appointment broke it, the removal mechanism worked, and it took seven years.

**The mandate — section 182:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **182(1)(a)** | **investigate any conduct in state affairs, or in the public administration in any sphere of government, that is alleged or suspected to be improper or to result in any impropriety or prejudice** |
| **182(1)(b)** | **report on that conduct** |
| **182(1)(c)** | **take appropriate remedial action** |
| **182(3)** | **may not investigate court decisions** |
| **182(4)** | **must be accessible to all persons and communities** |

**That is an extraordinarily broad jurisdiction** — any conduct in state affairs, alleged or suspected, improper or prejudicial. **And the three words that carried the office's whole history are "appropriate remedial action", because the Constitution does not say whether it binds.**

---

**Thuli Madonsela, 2009–2016.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Secure in Comfort* (2014)** | the **Nkandla** report — on the roughly R246m of state spending at the President's private residence, finding he had unduly benefited and directing that he repay a reasonable portion |
| ***State of Capture* (October 2016)** | released on her last day in office — on the Gupta family's influence over appointments and contracts, **and its remedial action directed the President to appoint a commission of inquiry headed by a judge selected by the Chief Justice** |

**The second report produced the Zondo Commission**, which is stage 11's material. **A Chapter 9 institution, with a R200m budget and no police powers, produced the commission that produced 5,000 pages on the executive.**

---

**And the judgment that settled the central question.**

***Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly* (2016)** — the Nkandla judgment.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Held** | **the Public Protector's remedial action is binding unless set aside by a court** |
| **The reasoning** | **a watchdog whose findings may simply be ignored is "a toothless bulldog"** — the office would be meaningless, and the Constitution does not create meaningless offices |
| **And** | **the National Assembly's resolution absolving the President was unlawful**, and **the President had failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution** |
| **Remedy** | the Treasury to determine the amount; the President to repay it; **which he did** |

**That holding is one of the most consequential in South African constitutional law**, and note what it means in both directions: **a Public Protector's remedial action binds the President — and it binds whoever holds the office, whatever the quality of the report.** Which is the next part.

---

**Busisiwe Mkhwebane, 2016–2023.**

**The record, as the courts found it:**

| Report | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **The Bankorp / CIEX report (2017)** | **set aside; she was found to have acted beyond her powers and not with an open mind, and to have met the Presidency and the SSA without disclosure; a personal costs order** — and the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2019, in unusually severe terms |
| **The Vrede dairy report** | **set aside**, as failing to investigate the implicated senior politicians at all |
| **The "rogue unit" report on Pravin Gordhan** | **set aside** — relying on the discredited material from the SARS lesson |
| **The CR17 / Bosasa donation report** | **set aside** |
| **Others** | a sustained pattern of adverse findings and costs orders across the high courts and the Constitutional Court |

**An office whose remedial action binds unless set aside, held by someone whose reports were repeatedly set aside, is a weapon.** From the thesis: **the binding-remedial-action holding was correct, and it made the appointment far more consequential.**

**And the removal, which is the part that matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism** | **section 194** — removal on the grounds of misconduct, incapacity or incompetence, **on a finding by a National Assembly committee and a resolution supported by two-thirds of its members** |
| **The process** | **the first section 194 inquiry ever held**, running from 2022, with rules the Constitutional Court had to clarify in litigation first |
| **The finding** | **guilty of incompetence and misconduct** |
| **The vote** | **the National Assembly removed her on 11 September 2023** |
| **Afterwards** | **she was elected to the National Assembly in 2024** for a different party |
| **Successor** | **Kholeka Gcaleka, from November 2023** |

**Seven years, a two-thirds threshold, an inquiry that had to be litigated into existence, and about a dozen reports set aside at public expense before it concluded.** That is what accountability for a Chapter 9 office-holder actually costs.

---

**The lesson, stated as the stage's thesis:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Was the design wrong?** | **mostly no.** A broad mandate, binding remedial action, a 60% appointment threshold and a two-thirds removal threshold are a defensible design |
| **What failed?** | **the appointment** — and the record of the preceding office-holder shows the same design producing the opposite result |
| **What worked?** | **the courts, throughout, and the National Assembly, eventually** |
| **What is the structural weakness?** | **the office's power now depends almost entirely on the holder's judgment, and the correction runs through litigation at the complainant's cost** |
| **And one real design question** | whether a single-person office with that jurisdiction should be a collegial body, which **the Asmal review raised in 2007** and nobody implemented |

**Practice.** Read sections 182 and 194. Then read the *EFF v Speaker* (2016) holding on binding remedial action and the "toothless bulldog" reasoning. Then find three Mkhwebane reports that were set aside and what the court said in each. Then read the section 194 committee's final report and find what it had to establish.
The other Chapter 9s:
Six institutions, one review that recommended consolidating them nineteen years ago, and the funding problem none of them has solved.

**Section 181 lists them:**

| Institution | Section | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Public Protector** | 182–183 | the last lesson |
| **The South African Human Rights Commission** | 184 | promote, protect and monitor human rights; **and require organs of state to report annually on their realisation of socio-economic rights** |
| **The Commission for the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Cultural, Religious and Linguistic Communities** | 185–186 | the **CRL Rights Commission** |
| **The Commission for Gender Equality** | 187 | promote respect for and the attainment of gender equality |
| **The Auditor-General** | 188–189 | the lesson before last |
| **The Electoral Commission** | 190–191 | **manage elections, ensure they are free and fair, declare the results** |

**And section 192** requires an independent broadcasting authority — **ICASA**, established by statute rather than directly by the Constitution, which is why it is usually discussed separately.

**The common provisions, in section 181, are the important part:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **181(2)** | **independent, and subject only to the Constitution and the law**, impartial, without fear, favour or prejudice |
| **181(3)** | **other organs of state, through legislative and other measures, must assist and protect these institutions** to ensure their independence, impartiality, dignity and effectiveness |
| **181(4)** | **no person or organ of state may interfere with their functioning** |
| **181(5)** | **accountable to the National Assembly**, and must report on their activities at least once a year |

---

**The Electoral Commission, which is the other success.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The record** | **seven national elections and six local elections since 1994, none of whose results has been successfully overturned** |
| **Why it holds** | a technical mandate, **a visible and auditable process**, party agents at every voting station, and the Electoral Court as a dedicated forum |
| **The one serious episode** | **the chairperson's position in 2014–15**, where a lease procurement finding led the Electoral Court to conclude she should vacate office, and she resigned |
| **The structural challenge** | ***New Nation Movement* (2020)** — the Constitutional Court held that the Electoral Act was unconstitutional in **requiring candidates to stand only through parties**, producing the 2023 amendment permitting independent candidates |
| **The persistent problem** | **the voters' roll and address data**, which the Court addressed in the *Kham* and *Tlokwe* litigation, requiring addresses on the roll |

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the IEC is running the municipal elections of **4 November 2026**. The 2024 national election was administered without a successful legal challenge to the result, including under the new independent-candidate provisions.

**And the IEC's own constraint, which is stage 10's material: it manages elections; it does not regulate political finance beyond the Political Party Funding Act's disclosure regime**, and that Act is enforced through the IEC with limited capacity.

---

**The SAHRC**, which does the most with the least.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its powers** | **investigate, report, subpoena, and litigate** — it may take cases to court in its own name, and does |
| **The socio-economic rights reports** | **section 184(3)** requires organs of state to report to it annually on housing, health care, food, water, social security, education and the environment — **the only systematic monitoring of the stage 7 rights that exists** |
| **The Equality Courts** | under PEPUDA, and the Commission refers and supports cases |
| ***SAHRC v Qwelane*** | the hate speech litigation, decided by the Constitutional Court in **2021**, which struck part of PEPUDA's section 10 as overbroad and reformulated the test |
| **The criticism** | **slow complaint handling, uneven provincial capacity, and a tendency to report rather than enforce** |
| **The structural criticism** | it is asked to adjudicate the most inflamed public disputes in the country on a small budget |

**The Commission for Gender Equality** has a comparable mandate — promote, monitor, investigate, subpoena, litigate — **and has been persistently under-resourced and troubled by internal governance disputes.** Its most substantial work has been on reproductive rights, on forced sterilisation findings, and on gender-based violence reporting.

**The CRL Rights Commission** is the least prominent, and its most notable intervention is instructive: **its 2017 report on the "commercialisation of religion"** proposed a statutory peer-review body to license religious practitioners. **It was strongly contested on section 15 grounds and was not implemented** — and it is a good example of a commission proposing a remedy its own founding provision could not carry.

---

**The Asmal review, which is the unfinished business.**

**In 2007 an ad hoc National Assembly committee chaired by Kader Asmal reviewed all the Chapter 9 institutions.**

**What it recommended:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Consolidation** | **merging the SAHRC, the CGE and the CRL Commission into a single human rights commission** with specialised units, to end duplication and spread scarce capacity |
| **Funding** | **a direct charge on the National Revenue Fund or an Assembly-determined allocation**, rather than budgets routed through a department |
| **Appointments** | a single, consistent, more transparent process |
| **Reporting** | **a dedicated parliamentary committee** to receive and act on their reports |
| **Status** | **almost none of it implemented, nineteen years later** |

**The funding point is the one that matters most and is least discussed.** With the partial exception of the self-funding Auditor-General:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **a body that must oversee the executive receives its budget through the executive's budget process** |
| **What that produces** | chronic under-funding, vacancies, and an incentive not to be troublesome |
| **What section 181(3) says** | **organs of state must assist and protect them to ensure their effectiveness** |
| **Whether under-funding breaches it** | **arguable, and never litigated** |

**That is a live constitutional question nobody has taken to court**, and it is a good candidate for stage 12.

**And the reporting point.** Section 181(5) makes them accountable to the National Assembly — **and the Assembly has no dedicated committee for them**, so their annual reports are received by whichever portfolio committee is nearest. **From the Parliament lesson: a power that exists and is not exercised.**

**Practice.** Read section 181 in full. Then find the Asmal report of 2007 and list its recommendations against what was implemented. Then find the SAHRC's and the CGE's budgets and vacancy rates and compare them with their mandates. Then find out which parliamentary committee received the last SAHRC annual report, and what it did with it.
The judiciary, and the JSC:
The institution that held most clearly, the appointment process that is the reason, and the two judges Parliament removed.

**The provisions, and read them against the NDPP's appointment from earlier in this stage:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **165(1)–(2)** | **judicial authority vests in the courts, which are independent and subject only to the Constitution and the law**, and must apply them impartially and without fear, favour or prejudice |
| **165(3)–(4)** | **no person or organ of state may interfere**, and **organs of state must assist and protect the courts** to ensure their independence, impartiality, dignity, accessibility and effectiveness |
| **165(5)** | **an order or decision of a court binds all persons and organs of state** |
| **174(3)** | **the President appoints the Chief Justice and Deputy Chief Justice after consulting the Judicial Service Commission and the leaders of the parties in the National Assembly**, and the President of the SCA on the JSC's advice |
| **174(4)** | **Constitutional Court judges are appointed from a list prepared by the JSC containing three names more than the number of vacancies** — the President may reject nominees with reasons, and the JSC must supplement the list |
| **174(6)** | **all other judges are appointed by the President on the advice of the JSC** — and "advice" here is binding in substance |
| **174(2)** | **the need for the judiciary to reflect broadly the racial and gender composition of South Africa must be considered** |

**That is the decisive institutional difference in this whole stage.** The National Director of Public Prosecutions and the National Commissioner of Police are **appointed by the President alone.** Judges are appointed **through a commission, from a published list, after public interviews.**

**And the outcomes track it.** The judiciary is the institution that held most clearly. **The stage's thesis in one comparison.**

---

**The Judicial Service Commission — section 178.**

| Members | Count |
| --- | --- |
| **The Chief Justice (presiding)**, the President of the SCA, and **one Judge President designated by the Judges President** | 3 |
| **The Cabinet member responsible for the administration of justice**, or an alternate | 1 |
| **Two practising advocates** nominated by the advocates' profession and appointed by the President | 2 |
| **Two practising attorneys** nominated by the attorneys' profession and appointed by the President | 2 |
| **One teacher of law** designated by the teachers of law at South African universities | 1 |
| **Six members of the National Assembly**, **at least three of whom must be from opposition parties** | 6 |
| **Four delegates of the NCOP**, supported by **at least six of the nine provinces** | 4 |
| **Four persons designated by the President** after consulting the leaders of all the parties in the Assembly | 4 |
| **Total** | **23** |

**Plus, when considering a specific division's matters, that division's Judge President and the relevant province's Premier — 25.**

**Count the politically designated members: six from the Assembly, four from the NCOP, four presidential designees, and the minister — fourteen of twenty-three.** A majority. **That is deliberate**, and it was defended in 1994 on the grounds that judicial appointment in a constitutional democracy should not be a closed professional guild, and that **the bench inherited in 1994 was 97% white and 99% male** and would not transform itself.

**And it is the standing criticism.** The counter-arguments:

| For the current composition | Against |
| --- | --- |
| **appointment should have a democratic element**; a self-selecting judiciary is also a political choice | **the overseen branch's politicians hold a majority on the body that appoints its overseers** |
| **transformation required it**, and the bench has in fact transformed | **interview quality has been poor** — the 2021 Chief Justice interviews were very widely criticised, including by former JSC members |
| the JSC has made good appointments, including of judges who then ruled against the executive | **unsuccessful candidates have litigated**, and the JSC has been found to have acted irrationally or opaquely in specific processes |
| | **party-political questioning of candidates** about rulings and affiliations |

**Both columns are serious, and the evidence cuts both ways**: the JSC has a political majority **and** the judiciary it has appointed produced *Glenister*, *Nkandla*, *Corruption Watch*, *Doctors for Life* and the Zondo rulings. **Not to arrive at a position — but notice which evidence weighs on which side.**

---

**Tenure and removal.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **176(1)** | **a Constitutional Court judge holds office for a non-renewable term of twelve years, or until the age of 70**, whichever comes first — subject to an Act of Parliament extending it on length-of-service grounds |
| **176(2)** | other judges hold office **until discharged in terms of an Act of Parliament** |
| **176(3)** | **salaries, allowances and benefits may not be reduced** — a standard independence protection |
| **177(1)** | **removal requires (a) a JSC finding of incapacity, gross incompetence or gross misconduct, and (b) a National Assembly resolution supported by at least two-thirds of its members** |
| **177(2)** | the President must then remove the judge |
| **177(3)** | the President may suspend a judge on the JSC's advice pending that process |

**Non-renewable terms matter.** A judge who cannot be reappointed cannot be courted, **which is why the twelve-year non-renewable Constitutional Court term is one of the strongest independence provisions in the document.**

**And section 177 was used for the first time in 2024.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Judge Nkola Motata** | after a 2007 incident and a long disciplinary history, **found guilty of gross misconduct** |
| **Judge President John Hlophe** | **found guilty of gross misconduct for attempting to influence two Constitutional Court justices in 2008** — a matter that took **fifteen years** to resolve through the JSC and the courts |
| **The vote** | **the National Assembly removed both in February 2024**, by the required two-thirds — **the first judges removed under the Constitution** |
| **Afterwards** | **Hlophe was elected to the National Assembly in 2024** and his party's designation of him to the Judicial Service Commission was litigated and found unlawful |

**Fifteen years for the Hlophe matter, in the institution with the best accountability record in the country.** From the Public Protector lesson: **this is what accountability actually costs in time.** Both sides of that are worth holding — **it was eventually done, and it took fifteen years.**

---

**The capacity problems, which are real and under-discussed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Backlogs** | long delays in the high courts and in the criminal courts, with the criminal backlog tied to the police and NPA capacity from earlier in this stage |
| **Access** | **litigation is expensive**; Legal Aid South Africa is comparatively well run and under-funded; the small claims courts and the Equality Courts are the accessible forums and are under-used |
| **Administration** | **the Office of the Chief Justice became a separate department in 2010** — judicial administration moved out of the Department of Justice, which was an independence gain |
| **Judicial education** | the South African Judicial Education Institute, created 2008 |
| **The bench's composition** | **transformed substantially since 1994** — a majority of judges are now black, and **women are roughly a third**, which is the live gap. **Check the Office of the Chief Justice's figures.** |

---

**And the argument the judiciary's success produces.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The criticism** | **the courts decide too much** — "juristocracy", or the judicialisation of politics. Political disputes that should be settled in Parliament or at the ballot box arrive as litigation |
| **The evidence for it** | *EFF v Speaker*, *UDM v Speaker*, the impeachment rules, the secret ballot, cadre deployment, the NDPP appointments — **courts repeatedly setting the terms of political contests** |
| **The answer** | **the Court's own**, in *Doctors for Life* and elsewhere: it decides what is brought to it, it has declined to prescribe where it can order a process instead, and **it cannot refuse a case because the subject is political** |
| **The deeper point** | **the courts fill the space the other institutions vacate.** Parliament's oversight failed; the NPA's leadership was contested; the Public Protector's office was misused. **The litigation went up because the alternatives went down** |
| **And the risk** | an institution carrying that much weight **attracts attacks on its legitimacy**, which is stage 12's material |

**Practice.** Read sections 165 to 178. Then count the JSC's politically designated members and write out the strongest argument for that composition. Then read the Hlophe JSC history and date each step. Then find the current gender composition of the bench from the Office of the Chief Justice.
The provinces in practice:
Nine governments that spend a third of the budget, raise almost none of it, and deliver the two services that matter most.

**What a province is, from stage 7's three-spheres lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **104** | a provincial legislature may legislate on the **Schedule 4 concurrent** functional areas and the **Schedule 5 exclusive** ones |
| **125** | executive authority vests in the **Premier**, exercised with the **Executive Council** — **a maximum of ten MECs** |
| **105** | **30 to 80 members**, elected by proportional representation |
| **127, 133** | the Premier assents to provincial Bills; MECs are **accountable collectively and individually to the legislature** |
| **139** | **provincial intervention in a municipality** |
| **100** | **national intervention in a province** |

**And what they actually administer**, which is the thing to hold on to:

| Schedule 4 (concurrent) | Schedule 5 (exclusive) |
| --- | --- |
| **basic education**, excluding tertiary | provincial planning |
| **health services** | provincial roads and traffic |
| **housing** | liquor licences |
| **social welfare services** | **abattoirs, ambulance services** |
| agriculture, environment, tourism, public transport | provincial cultural matters and sport |

**Basic education and public health are provincial.** So are housing delivery and social welfare services. **About a third of all government spending passes through provincial budgets**, and almost all of it is on those four.

---

**The fiscal fact that explains most provincial politics.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 227** | provinces are **entitled to an equitable share of nationally raised revenue** |
| **Section 228** | a province may impose **surcharges on tax bases** and limited taxes, levies and duties — **not income tax, VAT, or corporate tax** |
| **In practice** | **roughly 95% or more of provincial revenue comes from national transfers** — the equitable share plus conditional grants |

**So a province spends enormous sums it did not raise and cannot increase.** From the Treasury lesson: **this is the opposite of a municipality**, which has rates and service surcharges. **A province is an administration with a legislature attached**, and its accountability runs mostly to the national budget process rather than to its own taxpayers.

**And that cuts both ways in the argument about abolishing them**, below.

---

**The performance variance, which is the stage's thesis at provincial scale.**

**From the Auditor-General's PFMA general reports, consistently over a decade:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Consistently better outcomes** | **the Western Cape and Gauteng** — more clean audits, fewer disclaimers, better financial controls |
| **Consistently worse** | **the Eastern Cape, Limpopo, Mpumalanga, North West and the Free State** |
| **The same Constitution, the same transfers formula, the same legislation** | **and very different results** |

**That variance is the single best argument for the capacity thesis.** The design is identical across all nine; **the outcomes are not.**

**And section 100 has been used.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Limpopo, December 2011** | **five provincial departments placed under national administration** after the province ran out of money and went into unauthorised overdraft — Treasury took over payments |
| **North West, 2018** | **an intervention centred on the health department** after a collapse in services |
| **The pattern** | **interventions stabilise the finances and rarely build the capacity**, so the position deteriorates again after they end |

---

**Two cases that show what provincial failure means in practice.**

**Life Esidimeni.**

> **In 2015–16 the Gauteng health department terminated a contract with the Life Esidimeni facilities and moved about 1,700 psychiatric patients to NGOs, many unlicensed and unequipped. At least 144 patients died.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Health Ombud's report (2017)** | found the decision unlawful, the NGOs unfit, and the deaths avoidable |
| **The arbitration (2018)** | conducted by **former Deputy Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke**, awarding **constitutional damages** to the families and setting out the state's conduct in detail |
| **Afterwards** | **an inquest ran for years**, and found grounds on which the former MEC and a senior official could be held liable, referring the matter for prosecution. **Check the current position** |

**Nobody has been convicted. From the NPA lesson, that is the pattern.**

**The Eastern Cape schools and the textbook litigation.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | mud schools, schools without water or sanitation, and undelivered textbooks |
| **The litigation** | a sustained campaign, including ***Section 27 v Minister of Basic Education*** on textbooks in Limpopo and the Equal Education litigation on norms and standards for school infrastructure |
| **The result** | **binding minimum norms and standards, with deadlines, and repeated returns to court over compliance** |
| **The lesson** | **section 29's right to basic education, from stage 7, is immediately realisable — and it took litigation to get a plan with dates** |

---

**The argument about the provinces.**

| Abolish or reduce them | Keep them |
| --- | --- |
| **duplication** — nine health departments, nine education departments, nine legislatures, nine executives | **the Constitution entrenches them**, and removing them needs a 75% or two-thirds amendment plus six provinces, so the question is partly moot |
| **concurrency muddles accountability** — when a hospital fails, is it the national or the provincial department? | **the alternative is a single national health and education administration** for 63 million people, which no comparable country manages well |
| **capacity is spread too thin** — nine sets of scarce skills | **variance proves provinces can work**: the Western Cape's outcomes are a provincial achievement |
| **they raise almost nothing**, so they are not accountable as taxing governments | **removing them removes the NCOP's basis** and the only sub-national check on the centre |
| the ANC has itself debated reducing the number | **re-engineering delivery is the biggest administrative reform imaginable**, during a service crisis |

**Note that the reduction argument is mostly about the number, not the existence** — six provinces instead of nine would not resolve the concurrency problem and would need the same amendment.

**Practice.** Read Schedules 4 and 5 and note where education and health sit. Then find the equitable share formula in the current Division of Revenue Act. Then compare two provinces' latest audit outcomes. Then read the Moseneke arbitration award in Life Esidimeni.
Local government: the system:
The sphere with the strongest constitutional status, the only real own-revenue base, and the most visible failures.

**Chapter 7 is unusually strong, and the wording matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **151(1)** | **the local sphere consists of municipalities, which must be established for the whole of the territory of the Republic** |
| **151(3)** | **"A municipality has the right to govern, on its own initiative, the local government affairs of its community, subject to national and provincial legislation, as provided for in the Constitution."** |
| **151(4)** | **"The national or a provincial government may not compromise or impede a municipality's ability or right to exercise its powers or perform its functions."** |
| **152** | the objects: **democratic and accountable government; sustainable services; social and economic development; a safe and healthy environment; and encouraging community involvement** |
| **153** | **developmental duties** — structure budgeting, planning and administration to prioritise the basic needs of the community |
| **156** | **executive authority over the Schedule 4 Part B and Schedule 5 Part B matters**, and any matter assigned to it |
| **229** | **a municipality may impose rates on property and surcharges on fees for services** — plus other taxes if national legislation allows |

**Section 151(3) and (4) make a municipality a government, not a branch office.** From stage 7's co-operative government lesson: **this is why a province cannot simply take over a failing municipality** — it must use section 139, and the courts police it.

**And section 229 is the fiscal difference from a province.** A municipality has **its own tax**: property rates, plus surcharges on the services it sells. **That is the whole key to municipal finance.**

---

**The functions, which are the ones people notice:**

| Schedule 4B | Schedule 5B |
| --- | --- |
| **electricity and gas reticulation** | **refuse removal, refuse dumps and solid waste disposal** |
| **water and sanitation services** limited to potable water and domestic waste-water and sewage disposal systems | **street lighting, streets and traffic** |
| **municipal health services** | **municipal parks and recreation, cemeteries** |
| municipal planning, building regulations, public transport | **licensing of dogs, noise pollution, pounds, public places** |
| fire fighting, markets, airports, roads, stormwater | billboards, street trading, local amenities |

**Note what is not there: housing, education, health care beyond municipal health, policing and social welfare.** Those are provincial or national — **and the municipality is who residents go to anyway.**

---

**The structures:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Category A — metropolitan** | **eight metros**: Johannesburg, Tshwane, Ekurhuleni, Cape Town, eThekwini, Nelson Mandela Bay, Buffalo City, Mangaung — **exclusive executive and legislative authority in their areas** |
| **Category B — local** | **about 205**, sharing authority with a district |
| **Category C — district** | **about 44**, covering the local municipalities, with specified shared functions |
| **Total** | **257 municipalities** |
| **Councillors** | **half elected in wards by first-past-the-post, half from party lists to make the council proportional** |
| **Executive systems** | executive mayor, or an executive committee — set by the province under the Structures Act |

**The statutory framework:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Municipal Demarcation Act 27 of 1998** | the Demarcation Board draws the boundaries, independently |
| **Municipal Structures Act 117 of 1998** | categories, types, councils, ward committees |
| **Municipal Systems Act 32 of 2000** | **the IDP, performance management, service delivery agreements, and the staff establishment** |
| **Municipal Finance Management Act 56 of 2003** | budgets, borrowing, supply chain, the accounting officer |
| **Municipal Property Rates Act 6 of 2004** | the valuation roll and the rating of property |

**And the planning instrument: the Integrated Development Plan (IDP)** — a five-year plan, adopted by the council with public participation, **to which the budget must be aligned by law.** From stage 1's sources lesson: **a municipality's IDP and its budget, read together, are the clearest public statement of what it intends**, and they are free on its website.

---

**How a municipality is funded, and this is the part worth understanding properly:**

| Source | Note |
| --- | --- |
| **Property rates** | **the own-revenue base** — strong in metros, negligible in poor rural municipalities |
| **Service charges** | **electricity, water, sanitation, refuse** — and electricity is the big one |
| **The local government equitable share** | **around 9 to 10% of nationally raised revenue** for the sphere that delivers the most visible services |
| **Conditional grants** | the Municipal Infrastructure Grant, the Urban Settlements Development Grant, the free basic services subsidy |
| **Borrowing** | metros can issue bonds; most municipalities cannot borrow at all |

**The electricity surplus is the hinge of municipal finance.** A municipality **buys bulk electricity from Eskom and resells it to residents at a regulated markup** — and that surplus **cross-subsidises everything else it does**, from parks to libraries to roads.

**Which means three things at once:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Eskom tariff increases** | squeeze the municipality from below |
| **Rooftop solar and large-user defection** | **remove the highest-paying customers from the base**, which is a structural threat rather than a cyclical one |
| **Non-payment and losses** | **electricity distribution losses, technical and non-technical, are large** and come straight off the surplus |

**So the municipal fiscal crisis of the 2020s is substantially an electricity story**, and that is why the reforms in stage 9 concentrate on ring-fencing municipal trading services.

---

**Intervention — section 139:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **139(1)** | a province **may** intervene when a municipality fails to fulfil an executive obligation — by directive, assumption of responsibility, or **dissolution of the council** |
| **139(4)** | if a municipality cannot approve a budget or revenue-raising measures, the province **must** intervene |
| **139(5)** | **if a municipality is in a serious or persistent material breach of its financial commitments, the province must impose a recovery plan**, and may dissolve the council |
| **In practice** | **dozens of municipalities are under some form of intervention at any time**, and most interventions end without the municipality recovering |

**Practice.** Read sections 151 to 156 and Schedules 4B and 5B. Then open your own municipality's IDP and budget and find what share of its revenue is electricity. Then find the local government equitable share in the current Division of Revenue Act. Then find how many municipalities are currently under section 139 intervention.
Local government: why it fails:
The diagnosis, in order of weight — and the structural point that most of the 257 cannot fund themselves under the model as designed.

**Start with the measured position, as a dated snapshot:**

> **As of the Auditor-General's MFMA general reports for 2023–24 and 2024–25:** **on the order of 10 to 15% of the 257 municipalities achieve clean audits**; dozens receive qualified, adverse or disclaimed opinions; **irregular expenditure in the sphere runs to tens of billions of rands**; **municipal debt to Eskom and the water boards is on the order of a hundred billion rands and rising**; and **consumer debt owed to municipalities is larger still, most of it older than a year and largely irrecoverable.** **Check the current MFMA general report and the Treasury's local government revenue and expenditure review.**

---

**The causes, in order of how much they explain.**

**1 — The revenue model does not fit most municipalities.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The design assumption** | **section 229**: a municipality funds itself substantially from **property rates and service surcharges** |
| **Where that works** | **the eight metros and roughly twenty secondary cities** — a rateable property base, paying customers, and scale |
| **Where it cannot** | **most of the remaining 230**, especially those drawn over former homeland territory, where there is **little rateable property, high unemployment and no industrial or commercial base** |
| **What they get instead** | the equitable share, which is redistributive but **not sized to run a water utility** |
| **The consequence** | **a structural deficit that no amount of competence closes** |

**This is the part of the municipal story that is not about corruption or competence at all**, and it is why the serious reform proposals are for a **differentiated model** — different powers, funding and reporting for a metro and for a small rural municipality — rather than for better management of a uniform one.

**2 — Political instability.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Since 2016, and far more after 2021** | **many councils are hung**, with no party holding a majority |
| **The effect** | **mayors and councils change frequently**, sometimes several times in a year, and **each change replaces the senior management** |
| **Johannesburg** | the standing example — **a succession of mayors since 2016**, several within single years. **Check the current position** |
| **Why it matters more here than nationally** | **a municipality's work is operational.** A water network needs a five-year capital plan, and **no plan survives a management change every nine months** |

**3 — Appointment and competence.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The posts** | **municipal manager and the section 56 managers** — the accounting officer and the heads of the service departments |
| **The problem** | appointment on political rather than technical grounds, **high vacancy and acting rates**, and the loss of engineers |
| **The engineering point** | **a water and sanitation function requires registered professional engineers**, and a large share of municipalities employ none |
| **The legislative response** | **the Municipal Systems Amendment Act of 2022** — minimum competency requirements, **a bar on municipal managers holding political office in a party**, and regulated appointment procedures. An earlier 2011 version was **struck down in 2017 on the tagging ground**, like *Tongoane* in stage 7, and had to be re-enacted |
| **Status** | **the legislation is in place; the evidence that it has changed appointments is thin so far** |

**4 — Infrastructure and the services themselves.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Water losses** | **non-revenue water — leaks plus unbilled use — is around 40 to 50% nationally**, against a well-run utility's 15% |
| **Treatment** | the Department of Water and Sanitation's **Blue Drop and Green Drop** reports place **a large proportion of water and waste-water systems in high or critical risk categories** |
| **Maintenance** | **repairs and maintenance budgets are consistently below the 8% of asset value benchmark**, which converts an operating saving into a capital loss |
| **Electricity distribution** | an estimated maintenance and refurbishment backlog in the tens of billions |
| **The concrete instance** | **the Hammanskraal cholera outbreak of May 2023**, which killed about 30 people, following the long-known failure of the Rooiwal waste-water treatment works |

**Hammanskraal is the lesson in one event: a known, documented, funded-and-unspent treatment works failure killed people.** Not a policy dispute — **an unmaintained plant.**

**5 — Accountability that does not bite.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The AG's finding** | **no consequence management**, repeated for a decade |
| **Councils as overseers** | **the municipal public accounts committee** exists in most councils and is often chaired by a party with an interest in the outcome |
| **Section 139** | **interventions stabilise and withdraw** — administrators arrive without engineers, so capacity is not imported |
| **The courts** | residents and civil society litigate successfully and repeatedly, **and a court order does not fix a pump** |

---

**What has been tried, and why little has stuck:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Local Government Turnaround Strategy (2009)** | diagnosis correct, implementation thin |
| **Back to Basics (2014)** | the right list — deliver services, govern properly, pay suppliers — **without the capacity to do it** |
| **The District Development Model (2019)** | a coordination layer on top of the existing failures |
| **Operation Vulindlela's local government work** | **the most serious attempt**: ring-fencing metro trading services, licensing and performance conditions on electricity and water, and professional appointment requirements — **stage 9's material, and still in progress** |

**And the honest structural conclusion**, which is the stage's thesis in its hardest form: **about thirty municipalities are viable institutions with fixable problems; about two hundred are administering a mandate they were never funded to carry, with staff they cannot recruit, over infrastructure they cannot maintain.** Those are different problems and they have been treated as one.

**Practice.** Open the Blue Drop and Green Drop reports and find your nearest system's risk rating. Then find your municipality's non-revenue water percentage and its repairs and maintenance as a share of asset value. Then find how many mayors your metro has had since 2016. Then read the Treasury's local government revenue and expenditure review on the differentiated model.
Traditional authority:
A recognised institution, a colonial administrative artefact, and both at once — governing land on which about 18 million people live.

**The constitutional provisions — Chapter 12:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **211(1)** | **"The institution, status and role of traditional leadership, according to customary law, are recognised, subject to the Constitution."** |
| **211(2)** | a traditional authority observing a system of customary law **may function subject to any applicable legislation and customs, which includes amendments to, or repeal of, that legislation or those customs** |
| **211(3)** | **"The courts must apply customary law when that law is applicable, subject to the Constitution and any legislation that specifically deals with customary law."** |
| **212(1)** | **national legislation may provide for a role for traditional leadership as an institution at local level** on matters affecting local communities |
| **212(2)** | national or provincial legislation may provide for **houses of traditional leaders** |

**Read 211(1) and 211(2) together and the settlement is visible.** The institution is **recognised** — and it is **subject to the Constitution**, and the legislation and customs it functions under **may be amended or repealed.** From stage 6: this is a negotiated clause, and the IFP's and the traditional leaders' participation in the 1994 election turned partly on it.

**And 211(3) is doing something unusual: it makes customary law a source of law the courts must apply**, not a cultural practice the courts may note. **South African law has three sources — legislation, the common law, and customary law.**

---

**Why this is a politics lesson and not an anthropology one.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Land** | **about 13% of South Africa**, the former reserves and homelands from stages 4 and 5, is held under **communal tenure** — formally **in trust by the state**, administered in practice through traditional councils |
| **People** | **on the order of 17 to 18 million people live in those areas** |
| **The Ingonyama Trust** | **about 2.8 million hectares in KwaZulu-Natal**, with the Zulu king as sole trustee, established by a last-minute 1994 statute |
| **Electoral weight** | traditional leaders are organised, and **rural voter blocs matter to every party** |
| **Function** | traditional councils **allocate residential and arable land, resolve disputes, and consent to or refuse development and mining** |

**So the question "who may sign away land rights in the former homelands" is one of the largest unresolved property questions in the country**, and it sits directly on stage 7's section 25.

---

**The dual nature, which both sides of the argument rely on.**

| Traditional leadership as a living institution | Traditional leadership as a colonial artefact |
| --- | --- |
| **pre-colonial polities had real institutions**, with councils, obligations and law — stage 2 | |
| and customary law is **living law**, which changes | **the Native Administration Act of 1927 made the Governor-General "Supreme Chief" of all Africans** and gave him power to appoint and depose chiefs |
| **communities recognise their leaders**, and the institution survived a century of attempts to use it | **the Bantu Authorities Act of 1951** built the homeland chieftaincies as the administrative base of separate development — stage 5 |
| **section 211 recognises it, and the voters of those areas have not voted to abolish it** | **so a substantial number of today's recognised traditional authorities were constituted or reshaped by apartheid legislation**, and their boundaries are often administrative rather than customary |

**Both columns are historically correct**, which is why this argument does not resolve. **Not to arrive at a position: the question is not whether the institution is authentic, but what powers it should hold over people who cannot vote it out.**

---

**The legislation, and the litigation, which is where the detail lives.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Traditional Leadership and Governance Framework Act 41 of 2003** | recognised traditional communities and councils, **required traditional councils to be 40% elected and one-third women**, and provided for recognition and the withdrawal of recognition of leaders |
| **Communal Land Rights Act 11 of 2004** | would have transferred communal land to traditional councils — **struck down in *Tongoane v Minister for Agriculture and Land Affairs* (2010)**, on the tagging ground from stage 7's Parliament lesson |
| **Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 3 of 2019** | **recognised Khoi-San leadership for the first time** — a genuine advance — and, in section 24, **allowed traditional councils to enter into agreements and partnerships over communal land**, which critics said permitted deals over people's land without their consent |
| ***Mogale v Speaker of the National Assembly* (2023)** | **the Constitutional Court declared the whole 2019 Act unconstitutional for failure to facilitate public involvement**, following *Doctors for Life*; **the declaration was suspended to allow Parliament to re-enact it properly** |
| **The Ingonyama Trust litigation (2021)** | the high court held that **converting residents' permission-to-occupy rights into rent-paying leases was unlawful**, and ordered rentals repaid |
| **The Traditional Courts legislation** | **fought over for more than a decade**, with the central question being **whether a person may opt out** of a traditional court's jurisdiction |

**Note the pattern across those entries: three major statutes on this subject struck down or partly invalidated, twice on process grounds — tagging and public involvement.** From stage 7: **the procedural requirements are not technicalities when the people affected have the least access to Parliament.**

**And one more line of cases, on custom and equality:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Bhe v Magistrate, Khayelitsha* (2004)** | **struck down male primogeniture in customary intestate succession** as inconsistent with section 9 |
| ***Shilubana v Nwamitwa* (2008)** | **upheld a community's own development of its custom** to appoint a woman as hosi — holding that **a traditional community may change its own law** |

**Read those two together and you have the constitutional approach: customary law is living and the community may develop it; where it discriminates and has not been developed, section 9 applies.**

> **As of 14 October 2026:** the replacement for the invalidated 2019 Act and the communal tenure question remain unresolved. **Check the current status of the traditional leadership and communal tenure legislation in the Gazette and on PMG.**

**Practice.** Read sections 211 and 212. Then read *Mogale* on why the 2019 Act fell. Then find the Ingonyama Trust's 2021 judgment and what it ordered. Then read *Bhe* and *Shilubana* together and state the rule they produce.
State-owned enterprises:
The vehicle state capture used, the reason it used them, and the condition they are in.

**What they are and how they are governed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The major ones** | **Eskom, Transnet, PRASA, SAA, Denel, the South African Post Office, the SABC**, plus the Land Bank, the IDC, the DBSA and about 300 smaller entities |
| **Legal form** | mostly companies under the Companies Act, **with the state as sole shareholder**, listed in **Schedule 2 of the PFMA** as major public entities |
| **Governance** | **a shareholder minister appoints the board; the board appoints the executive; the entity reports through the minister to Parliament** |
| **Oversight** | the PFMA, the Auditor-General, the relevant portfolio committee, and shareholder compacts |
| **Finance** | own revenue, plus **government guarantees** that let them borrow at near-sovereign rates |

**Now the four features that made them the instrument of choice**, which is the Zondo Commission's central structural finding:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Very large procurement budgets** | **capital programmes in the tens of billions**, with technical specifications few can evaluate |
| **Board appointment by a single minister** | **no commission, no public interviews, no parliamentary confirmation** — the appointment problem from this whole stage, in its purest form |
| **Weaker oversight than a department** | an entity is one step removed from the vote, its reporting is less granular, and **a portfolio committee gets an annual report rather than a budget line** |
| **Guaranteed borrowing** | **they can raise money against the state's credit**, so capture does not require an appropriation |

**That is the architecture. Capturing a department gets you a budget vote scrutinised line by line; capturing an SOE gets you a procurement programme.**

---

**Eskom**, which is the one that changed the country's economics.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **generation, transmission and much of distribution**, with roughly 48 GW of nominal capacity, mostly coal |
| **The warning** | **a 1998 White Paper stated that new capacity would be needed by about 2007**, and the decision was deferred |
