> **Check the current Budget Review's revenue chapter and SARS's annual Tax Statistics, which is the single best free document on this subject.**

---

**Now the fact that shapes every fiscal argument: the base is extraordinarily narrow.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Population** | **about 63 million** |
| **Employed** | **on the order of 16 to 17 million** |
| **Registered individual taxpayers expected to submit returns** | **on the order of 7 million** |
| **Who pays most of the personal income tax** | **the top decile of taxpayers pays the clear majority of it**, and taxpayers earning above about a million rand a year — a few hundred thousand people — **pay on the order of 40% of all personal income tax** |
| **Companies** | **a small number of large companies pay most of the corporate tax** |

**So a few hundred thousand individuals and a few hundred companies fund a very large share of a state serving 63 million people.** **Both political conclusions drawn from that are coherent:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One** | **the base cannot bear more** — raising rates on a narrow base risks emigration, avoidance and a shrinking base, and the arithmetic is fragile |
| **Two** | **the narrowness is a symptom of the unemployment rate**, not of over-taxation — **broaden the base by employing people**, and note that the top decile's income share is two-thirds, so its tax share is not disproportionate to its income share |

**And the honest technical note on emigration: the claim that high earners are leaving is asserted far more often than it is measured.** The SARS data on tax emigration and the StatsSA migration estimates exist; **go to them rather than to the assertion.**

---

**Is the system progressive? Yes, and the parts work differently:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Personal income tax** | **strongly progressive** — marginal rates rise to 45%, with rebates and thresholds that exempt low earners entirely |
| **VAT** | **mildly regressive in itself** — the poor spend a larger share of income — **but** South Africa **zero-rates a basket of about 19 basic foodstuffs**, extended in 2019 to include bread flour, cake flour and sanitary products, which blunts it |
| **Excise** | regressive in incidence (tobacco, alcohol, fuel), defended on other grounds |
| **The net system, including spending** | **strongly progressive** — the fiscal incidence finding from the inequality lesson |

**The VAT zero-rating argument is a good one to understand**, because it is a trade-off with no clean answer: **zero-rating is poorly targeted** — a wealthy household buying brown bread also benefits, and in rand terms benefits more — **and it is administratively simple and immediate**, where a targeted transfer requires a working transfer system. South Africa has a working transfer system, **which is why the economists' preference is to tax VAT broadly and compensate through grants, and the political preference is to zero-rate.**

---

**The 2025 VAT episode, as a dated case study — and it is the best single illustration of what the coalition changed.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **19 February 2025** | **the Budget was postponed on the day it was due to be delivered** — the first time in South African history — because the Cabinet had not agreed the fiscal framework, which reportedly included **a two-percentage-point VAT increase** |
| **12 March 2025** | the Budget was tabled, proposing **a 0.5 percentage point VAT increase in 2025 and another in 2026** |
| **April 2025** | **the fiscal framework was adopted in Parliament on a contested vote** that split the governing coalition, and **two parties took the matter to court**, arguing the process was unlawful |
| **Then** | **the VAT increase was withdrawn**, and the court proceedings were resolved on that basis |
| **21 May 2025** | **a third Budget was tabled**, without the VAT increase, with spending reductions and other revenue measures instead |

**What that sequence demonstrates**, and each point is stage 11's and stage 12's material:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A budget is now negotiated** | **the executive can no longer assume its fiscal framework will pass**, because no party holds a majority |
| **Parliament's budget powers became real** | the **Money Bills Act** powers from stage 8 — described there as acquired and essentially never used — **were used** |
| **Tax policy is now coalition policy** | the VAT increase failed on politics, not on economics |
| **And the fiscal hole did not go away** | **it was closed with spending restraint and other measures**, which is where the debt lesson picks up |

**Practice.** Open SARS's latest Tax Statistics and find the number of individual taxpayers by income band and the share of PIT each band pays. Then find the zero-rated VAT basket. Then find the three 2025 Budget Reviews and compare the fiscal frameworks. Then work out what a one percentage point VAT increase raises, and compare it with the annual cost of the SRD grant.
Debt, and the fiscal question:
From 26% of GDP to the high seventies in fifteen years, where it went, and the argument about what to do now.

**The path, which is the fact to hold:**

| Year | Gross national debt, share of GDP |
| --- | --- |
| **2008–09** | **about 26%** |
| **2012–13** | about 40% |
| **2016–17** | about 50% |
| **2020–21** | **a sharp jump**, with the Covid contraction and revenue collapse |
| **2024–25 onward** | **mid-to-high 70s, projected to stabilise** |

> **As of the 2025–26 Budget: gross loan debt is in the region of 75 to 77% of GDP, a primary surplus has been achieved, and debt is projected to stabilise and then decline slowly. Debt-service costs are on the order of R400bn a year — more than 20% of main budget revenue, and more than is spent on health, or on police, or on basic education's national transfers.** **Check the current Budget Review's chapter 3.**

**Debt-service cost is the number that matters, not the ratio.** A ratio is a claim about sustainability; **the interest bill is money that cannot be spent.** From stage 6: the apartheid debt was honoured and crowded out the RDP — **and this debt, accumulated after 2008, crowds out the same things.**

---

**Where it went, which is the part that is actually contested.**

**Five causes, and they are not equally weighted:**

| Cause | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| **The 2008–09 revenue collapse, and the counter-cyclical response that became structural** | **large.** Spending was raised in a downturn, correctly; **revenue never returned to the pre-crisis path and spending was not brought back** |
| **The public wage bill** | **large** — the next lesson. Average real remuneration rose substantially while headcount was roughly flat |
| **SOE bailouts and guarantees** | **large and visible** — **Eskom alone has received support in the hundreds of billions**, including the roughly R254bn relief package of 2023, plus SAA, SANRAL, the Post Office, Denel and the Land Bank |
| **Slow growth** | **the denominator.** A debt ratio falls with growth; **1% growth with 4 to 5% nominal interest costs raises the ratio mechanically** |
| **The cost of borrowing** | **the downgrades** of 2017 and 2020 to sub-investment grade raised the interest rate on new issuance, and the **long end of the yield curve is unusually steep**, so South Africa pays a large premium to borrow long |

**Note what is not on that list: social grants.** Grant spending has grown, and it is **not** the principal driver — **the wage bill, the SOEs and the interest bill are.** That is a factual point worth being precise about, because grants are the most frequently blamed item and the Budget Review's own figures do not support it.

**And one accounting manoeuvre worth knowing**, because it came up in 2024: **the Gold and Foreign Exchange Contingency Reserve Account (GFECRA)** — the account holding the Reserve Bank's valuation gains on foreign reserves — **was drawn down to reduce borrowing**, on the order of R150bn over three years. **A legitimate use of a real asset, and not a repeatable source of revenue.**

---

**The argument, which is the central fiscal dispute in South African politics.**

| The consolidation case | The expansion case |
| --- | --- |
| **the interest bill is the fastest-growing line item** and every rand of it is a rand not spent on anything | **the consolidation since 2020 has been real austerity** — spending per person on health, education and infrastructure has fallen in real terms |
| **a debt spiral is a real risk**: if the interest rate exceeds the growth rate, the ratio rises without any new spending | **the growth rate is itself depressed by the consolidation** — cutting capital spending reduces future growth and therefore worsens the ratio |
| **South Africa borrows in a currency it does not control at the long end** and has already been downgraded twice | **the debt is overwhelmingly rand-denominated and domestically held**, which removes the classic emerging-market currency-mismatch crisis mechanism |
| **the primary surplus achieved by 2024–25 is the stabilising condition** and should be held | **the composition of the consolidation is wrong** — it fell on capital budgets and on non-wage goods and services rather than on the wage bill |
| **no country has grown out of a debt problem without stabilising it first** | **the binding constraints are electricity and logistics, which require capital spending** |

**The strongest point on each side, honestly:** for consolidation, **the interest bill's crowding-out is arithmetic, not opinion.** For expansion, **the composition critique is correct** — the consolidation protected the wage bill and cut maintenance and capital, which is the worst available combination because it converts an operating saving into a capital loss. **Both can be true at once, which means the real argument is about the wage bill.**

---

**And the thing to watch, in one line:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The sustainability condition** | **nominal GDP growth above the average interest rate on debt, with a primary surplus** |
| **So the three numbers** | **nominal growth, the effective interest rate, and the primary balance** — all three in chapter 3 of every Budget Review |
| **The contingent liabilities** | **guarantees to SOEs**, which are not in the debt figure until they are called |

**Practice.** Find the current debt-to-GDP ratio, debt-service cost, and primary balance in the Budget Review. Then put debt-service cost next to the health budget. Then find the contingent liabilities table and the total of government guarantees. Then take the composition critique and check it: find real growth in capital spending and in compensation of employees over the last five years.
The public wage bill:
A third of spending, roughly flat headcount, and the court case that established the state cannot sign what it cannot afford.

**The scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **National and provincial government employees** | **on the order of 1.2 to 1.3 million** |
| **Plus** | local government and public entities, taking the total public sector workforce higher |
| **Compensation of employees** | **on the order of R700 to R800bn a year** |
| **Share of consolidated non-interest spending** | **roughly a third** |
| **Share of GDP** | **around 10 to 11%** — **high by international comparison**, including against both OECD and middle-income peers |

> **Check the Budget Review's chapter on expenditure and the annexures, which break compensation down by sphere and function.**

**And the composition, which is the thing that makes this hard:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Teachers** | the largest single group — roughly 400,000 |
| **Health personnel** | nurses, doctors, support staff |
| **Police** | roughly 180,000 to 190,000 |
| **Everything else** | the administrative public service, correctional services, defence |

**So "cut the wage bill" means, in practice, "employ fewer teachers, nurses or police, or pay them less."** From stage 8: **the capacity problem is a shortage of skilled people in the state, and the wage bill is how skilled people are paid.** The slogan and the arithmetic do not meet.

---

**Now the analytical point, which is the one that resolves most of the confusion.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Headcount** | **roughly flat since about 2012**, and falling in some functions |
| **Average remuneration** | **rose substantially in real terms** over the 2007–2020 period — the published estimates put the real increase at a large fraction, with some functions roughly doubling in nominal terms over a decade |
| **Therefore** | **the wage bill grew through pay per employee, not through the number of employees** |

**That matters in four ways:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The critique is not "a bloated bureaucracy"** | by headcount per capita, South Africa's public service is **not unusually large**; it is unusually **well-paid relative to the private sector at comparable skill levels**, particularly in the middle and lower grades |
| **The composition is wrong at the top** | **senior management pay is high**, and the stage 8 findings on acting appointments and turnover mean that money buys instability |
| **Occupation-specific dispensations** | special salary arrangements for teachers, nurses, doctors and police drove much of the increase, and were introduced to retain skills — with mixed evidence that they did |
| **The freeze that followed** | **the consolidation after 2020 held compensation roughly flat in nominal terms, which means vacancies went unfilled** — so the state got fewer people at the same cost, which is the worst outcome for capacity |

**That last row is the honest verdict on the past five years: the wage bill was contained by not hiring, which protected the salaries of those in post and starved the functions that needed staff.**

---

**The 2018 agreement and the court case, which set the constitutional position.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2018** | **a three-year public service wage agreement** was concluded in the Public Service Co-ordinating Bargaining Council |
| **2020** | **the state did not implement the third year's increases**, citing unaffordability and the Covid fiscal position |
| **The litigation** | the unions went to the Labour Appeal Court |
| **The finding (2020)** | **clause 3.3 of the agreement was unlawful and invalid** — it had been concluded **without compliance with the Treasury regulations requiring that a collective agreement with budget implications be certified as affordable** |
| **On appeal** | **the Constitutional Court declined to disturb that outcome** |
| **The principle** | **a collective agreement in the public service that does not comply with the statutory and regulatory affordability requirements is invalid** |

**Read that against stage 8's Treasury lesson.** **Section 216 and the PFMA framework bind the bargaining process**, which means **the state's negotiators cannot sign what the fiscus cannot carry — and if they do, the agreement falls.**

**The two readings of that judgment, and both have force:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The state's** | **a necessary constraint.** Public money is appropriated by Parliament, and a bargaining council cannot appropriate |
| **The unions'** | **the state broke a freely concluded agreement and was rescued by its own non-compliance with its own regulations** — which is a poor basis for good faith bargaining, and the breach was the state's |

**And the politics of it, from the stage's wages lesson: COSATU's largest affiliates are public service unions.** **So the wage bill is simultaneously the governing party's largest fiscal problem and its alliance partner's core interest.** That is not resolvable by better analysis; **it is the structural reason the consolidation fell on capital budgets instead.**

**Practice.** Find compensation of employees in the current Budget Review as a share of consolidated spending and of GDP. Then find the public service headcount trend over the last ten years and the average remuneration trend next to it. Then read the Labour Appeal Court judgment on the 2018 agreement. Then find the current vacancy rate in one provincial health department.
Electricity as an economic constraint:
What load-shedding cost, how the price path changed the economy's shape, and the reform that is either the biggest success since 1994 or a correction of a self-inflicted wound.

**Stage 8 covered Eskom as an institution. This lesson is electricity as an input price and a supply constraint.**

**The physical record:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Load-shedding began** | **2007**, after the new-capacity decision warned of in 1998 was deferred |
| **2021** | roughly 2,500 GWh shed |
| **2022** | **on the order of 11,500 GWh shed, across roughly 3,800 hours** |
| **2023** | **the worst year — over 15,000 GWh, across roughly 6,900 hours**, which is more than 70% of the year's hours at some stage of shedding |
| **2024 onward** | **largely suspended, with intermittent returns** |

> **Check the CSIR's annual Statistics of Utility-Scale Power in South Africa, which is free and the authoritative source, and Eskom's weekly system status reports.**

**The GDP cost estimates:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Per-stage-per-day estimates** | on the order of **hundreds of millions of rands per stage per day**, with higher figures at the deeper stages |
| **Annual** | the Reserve Bank and Treasury put the 2022 and 2023 drag at **one to two percentage points of GDP growth** |
| **The cumulative** | **the clearest single explanation of why growth in those years was near zero** |
| **The caveat** | these are estimates with wide confidence intervals and they double-count in places; **the direction and order of magnitude are solid, the precise figures are not** |

---

**The price path, which matters more over twenty years than the outages did over three.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Before 2007** | **South Africa had among the cheapest electricity in the world**, which was the industrial strategy of the minerals-energy complex lesson |
| **Since 2008** | **Eskom's standard tariff has risen several hundred per cent in nominal terms, far faster than inflation** — a very large real increase |
| **Why** | **the capital cost of Medupi and Kusile, falling sales volumes, rising coal and diesel costs, and the debt** |
| **The effect on the economy's shape** | **the energy-intensive industries built on cheap power — smelters, ferrochrome, aluminium — lost their reason to be here**, which is a chapter of the deindustrialisation lesson |
| **The regulatory mechanism** | **NERSA** determines tariffs through the Multi-Year Price Determination and the Regulatory Clearing Account, with Eskom litigating repeatedly over the outcome |
| **The municipal layer** | from stage 8: **municipalities add their own markup**, so a household or business in a metro pays Eskom's tariff plus the municipality's surplus |

**The combination of outages and a large real price increase in the same fifteen years is what makes this an economic rather than a technical story.** **A business cannot plan around either.**

---

**The reform, and it has moved further than almost anything else since 2019.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **REIPPPP** | the **Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme**, from 2011 — competitive bidding for renewable capacity |
| **What the bidding showed** | **prices fell dramatically across bid windows** — early solar PV bids around R3.50 per kWh, by the fourth window around **R0.62 per kWh.** One of the clearest demonstrations anywhere that competitive procurement collapses renewable costs |
| **The stall** | **the programme was obstructed between roughly 2015 and 2018**, when Eskom declined to sign power purchase agreements — a state capture-era episode documented in the Zondo material |
| **The licensing threshold** | **raised from 1 MW to 100 MW for embedded generation in August 2021, and then the licensing requirement was removed entirely** — registration instead |
| **The consequence** | **a very large private build-out**, especially **rooftop and commercial solar**, reaching several gigawatts within a few years |
| **Unbundling** | the National Transmission Company, and the **Electricity Regulation Amendment Act of 2024** creating a market operator and third-party access to the grid |
| **The remaining constraint** | **transmission.** The best wind and solar resource is in the Cape, the grid capacity is in Mpumalanga, **and new transmission lines take years and very large capital** |

**That last row is the current binding constraint and the one to watch**: **the generation problem has largely been solved by allowing private capital in; the transmission problem cannot be solved that way without resolving who builds and owns the lines.**

---

**The just transition, which is where the politics is.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The coal economy** | **Mpumalanga** — on the order of 80,000 to 90,000 direct coal mining jobs plus Eskom's own employment, concentrated in a handful of towns |
| **The commitment** | South Africa's Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement, and the **Just Energy Transition Partnership announced at COP26 in 2021** — initially **$8.5bn pledged**, later raised, largely in **loans rather than grants**, which is the substance of the complaint about it |
| **The cautionary case** | **Komati power station**, decommissioned in 2022 as the pilot, where the repurposing lagged badly behind the closure and the town suffered — **cited by everyone who argues the transition is being done to Mpumalanga rather than with it** |
| **The carbon tax** | in force since 2019, rising under a published schedule, with allowances that substantially reduce the effective rate |
| **The external pressure** | **the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism**, phasing in from the mid-2020s, which prices the carbon content of imports — **a direct commercial threat to South African steel, aluminium and cement exports** |

**And the argument, stated fairly:**

| Move faster | Move carefully |
| --- | --- |
| **renewables are now the cheapest new capacity**, demonstrated by the bid windows | **the coal fleet is paid for**, and closing it early has a capital cost |
| **the export economy faces carbon pricing at the border** regardless of domestic policy | **Mpumalanga's towns have no alternative economy** and the Komati experience is the evidence |
| **the health cost of coal burning** — the Highveld priority area's air quality, and the ***Deadly Air* judgment of 2022**, which held that poor air quality there breached section 24 of the Constitution | **security of supply first**: renewables need storage and transmission, and the 2023 experience is recent |
| the finance is available and conditional on moving | **the finance is mostly loans**, adding to the debt problem of the last lesson |

**Practice.** Find the CSIR's figures for energy shed in 2022, 2023 and the latest year. Then find Eskom's standard tariff increase since 2008 and compare it with cumulative CPI. Then find the REIPPPP bid window prices for solar PV across windows. Then read the *Deadly Air* judgment's finding on section 24.
Logistics: rail, ports and roads:
The constraint that has overtaken electricity, measured in tonnes that were mined and not moved.

**Why logistics gets a lesson of its own.** From the mining lesson: **mining is roughly half of merchandise exports.** Bulk minerals move by rail to a port or they do not move. **So the rail network's capacity is the export economy's capacity**, and since about 2018 it has been the binding one.

**The structure:**

| Division | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Transnet Freight Rail** | **the national freight rail network**, about 20,000 route kilometres, including the two dedicated heavy-haul export lines |
| **Transnet National Ports Authority** | **the landlord of the eight commercial ports** — infrastructure, dredging, marine services |
| **Transnet Port Terminals** | **the operator of most container, bulk and break-bulk terminals** |
| **Transnet Pipelines** | the fuel and gas pipeline network |
| **Transnet Engineering** | rolling stock manufacture and maintenance |

**Note the structural oddity: Transnet is both the ports landlord and the main terminal operator**, which means **the regulator of port access competes with the people who want access.** That is the same structural problem the electricity reform addressed by separating the grid — and it is what the current port reforms are about.

---

**The numbers, which are stark:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Rail freight volume, 2017–18** | **about 226 million tonnes** |
| **Rail freight volume, 2022–23** | **about 149 million tonnes** |
| **Since** | **a partial recovery**, with the Freight Logistics Roadmap targeting a return to 250 million tonnes by the end of the decade |
| **The coal export line to Richards Bay** | **capacity on the order of 81 million tonnes; railed volumes fell to around 47 to 50 million** |
| **The iron ore line to Saldanha** | **capacity around 60 million tonnes**, with railed volumes well below it |

> **Check Transnet's annual results, the Minerals Council's commentary, and the Treasury's reporting on the Freight Logistics Roadmap.**

**A third of the rail volume disappeared in five years.** The causes, in rough order:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Locomotive availability** | **the 1,064-locomotive programme that Zondo examined** left a large part of the fleet without spares or support after the contractual relationship with the supplier broke down, **with hundreds of locomotives standing** |
| **Cable theft and vandalism** | **the signalling and overhead cabling of whole corridors stripped**, with the Johannesburg–Durban container corridor repeatedly out of service |
| **Maintenance backlog** | track, wagons and signalling |
| **Skills loss** | from stage 8 — engineers and experienced operating staff |
| **Derailments and operating discipline** | |

**The ports.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The measure** | **the World Bank and S&P Global Container Port Performance Index**, which ranks ports by vessel turnaround time |
| **The result** | **South Africa's container ports — Durban, Cape Town and Ngqura — have ranked near the very bottom of the global index**, with Durban at times ranked in the last handful of several hundred ports |
| **The causes** | **equipment availability** — ship-to-shore and straddle carriers out of service — **wind delays at Cape Town, landside congestion, and software and systems failures** |
| **The visible cost** | **ships waiting at anchor for days**, which carriers price into freight rates on South African routes, and **fruit and other perishables missing their markets** |

**And the consequence: freight shifted to road.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The shift** | **coal, chrome, manganese and containers moving by truck** on corridors designed for a fraction of that traffic |
| **The cost** | **road haulage of bulk minerals is several times the cost per tonne-kilometre of rail** — money off the exporter's margin, or ore left in the ground |
| **The externality** | **the N3 and N4 corridors' road damage**, congestion and accident rates |
| **The visible instance** | **queues of coal trucks on the roads into Richards Bay and across the Mpumalanga corridors** |

---

**The reform, which is roughly where electricity's was in 2021:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The National Logistics Crisis Committee (2023)** | a Presidency-led structure modelled on the energy equivalent |
| **The Freight Logistics Roadmap (December 2023)** | **separate infrastructure from operations, open the network to third-party operators, and bring in private capital at terminals** |
| **The Economic Regulation of Transport Act (2024)** | **creates a Transport Economic Regulator** — an independent economic regulator for ports, rail and pipelines, which is the precondition for third-party access to be fair |
| **Third-party access** | **a network statement and slot allocation process**, with private operators obtaining access to the rail network |
| **Ports** | **private partner processes at container terminals**, including at Durban's Pier 2 — **which has itself been litigated by an unsuccessful bidder**, delaying the transaction |
| **The remaining question** | **capital.** Transnet's debt and its ability to fund the locomotive and infrastructure programme |

> **As of 14 October 2026: third-party access and the terminal concessions are in progress, with volumes recovering from the 2022–23 low but well short of the 2017–18 level. Check Transnet's latest results and the roadmap's reported milestones.**

**And the honest assessment**, which parallels electricity: **the diagnosis is agreed across the political spectrum, the institutional reforms are correct in design, and the implementation is slower than the electricity equivalent because rail is harder — a single network with one operator, high capital intensity, and no equivalent of rooftop solar to let users bypass it.**

**Practice.** Find Transnet's latest annual rail volume and compare it with 2017–18. Then find South Africa's ports in the latest Container Port Performance Index. Then work out the cost difference per tonne-kilometre between rail and road for bulk minerals. Then find the current status of third-party access on the rail network.
Land: the figures everybody cites:
The numbers used in every land argument, where each comes from, and what each one does and does not say.

**This lesson is about the statistics, because the land debate is conducted almost entirely in numbers that are quoted without their definitions.** From stage 1: **establish what a figure measures before using it.**

**The total:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa's land area** | **about 122 million hectares** |
| **Agricultural land** | **on the order of 96 to 100 million hectares**, most of it suitable only for extensive grazing |
| **Arable land** | **a small fraction — roughly 12 to 13% of the surface** — because most of the country is dry |

**That last row is worth noting before any argument about redistribution: South Africa is a dry country and most of its land cannot be cropped.**

---

**The 2017 Land Audit, and the figure everyone cites.**

**The Department of Rural Development and Land Reform's land audit** reported in 2017. **The widely quoted finding:**

> **Of the 37 million hectares of farms and agricultural holdings held by individuals — natural persons — white South Africans hold about 26.7 million hectares, or roughly 72%.**

**Now the definitions, which are essential:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What that 72% is a share of** | **37 million hectares of individually owned farmland — not of South Africa, and not of all farmland** |
| **What the other 85 million hectares are** | **state land, trust land including the former homelands, land held by companies, trusts, close corporations, community property associations, and churches** |
| **Why that matters** | **a very large share of commercial farmland is held by companies and trusts, whose ownership the audit did not pierce** — so the racial composition of that land's ownership is **not measured** by this figure |
| **State land** | **on the order of 14% of the surface**, including the former homeland land held in trust |
| **The honest summary** | **ownership is heavily racially skewed and the exact degree is not precisely measured**, because the corporate and trust layer was not penetrated and because of the communal land question |

**Both misuses of this figure are common.** One side quotes "72% of the land is white-owned", **which the audit does not say.** The other says "the audit is meaningless because it covers only a third of the country", **which overstates the objection** — the individually held farmland is a large category and the skew within it is not in doubt.

---

**The restitution numbers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The statute** | **the Restitution of Land Rights Act 22 of 1994**, giving a right to restitution to those dispossessed **after 19 June 1913** by racially discriminatory law or practice |
| **The claims deadline** | **31 December 1998**, by which **about 80,000 claims** were lodged |
| **Settled** | the large majority, **and most urban claimants took financial compensation rather than land** — on the order of tens of billions of rands paid out |
| **Land restored** | **on the order of 3.5 to 4 million hectares** |
| **The reopening** | **the Restitution of Land Rights Amendment Act of 2014 reopened the claims window**, and about 160,000 new claims were lodged |
| **And then** | ***Land Access Movement of South Africa v Chairperson, NCOP* (2016)** — **the Constitutional Court declared the 2014 Act invalid for inadequate public involvement**, the same ground as *Doctors for Life* and *Mogale*. **The new claims are in limbo and thousands of old claims remain unsettled** |

**That is the third major piece of land legislation struck down on public participation grounds** — with the Communal Land Rights Act in *Tongoane* (2010) and the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act in *Mogale* (2023). **From stage 8: the pattern is not coincidence.**

**The 1913 cut-off is itself contested**, and reasonably: dispossession of the Khoe, the San and the frontier societies happened long before 1913 — stages 2 and 3 — **and restitution's own statute excludes it.** The response is that an earlier cut-off makes overlapping claims unresolvable; **the objection stands anyway.**

---

**The redistribution numbers, and the target that moved:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The original target** | **30% of commercial agricultural land transferred** — set in 1994 for five years, then moved to 2014, then to 2025 |
| **Achieved** | **on the order of 10%** of commercial farmland transferred through all programmes, on most published estimates |
| **The budget** | **land reform has consistently received well under 1% of the national budget** — on the order of 0.4%, and declining in real terms through the 2010s |
| **The arithmetic point** | **the target was never funded.** The Motlanthe panel calculated what 30% would cost at market value and compared it with the allocation |

**And the phrase to retire: "willing buyer, willing seller."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | **a policy choice made by the government after 1994**, not a constitutional requirement |
| **What section 25(3) actually requires** | **"just and equitable" compensation, reflecting an equitable balance between the public interest and the interests of those affected**, having regard to **five listed factors** — current use, history of acquisition and use, market value, **the extent of direct state investment and subsidy**, and the purpose of the expropriation |
| **So market value is one of five factors** | **not the measure.** From stage 7's section 25 lesson |
| **The implication** | **the constraint on land reform was never the Constitution's compensation standard**, because that standard was never tested. Which is the next lesson |

**Practice.** Find the 2017 Land Audit and read its definitions before its findings. Then find the restitution programme's settled claims, hectares restored and financial compensation paid. Then find land reform's allocation in the current Budget Review as a share of the total. Then read section 25(3) and list the five factors.
Land reform: why it has not worked:
The diagnosis two official panels reached, which is not the one the public argument assumes.

**The constitutional obligation first, because it is three separate duties and they are usually conflated:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **25(5) — redistribution** | **"The state must take reasonable legislative and other measures, within its available resources, to foster conditions which enable citizens to gain access to land on an equitable basis."** |
| **25(6) — tenure security** | a person or community whose tenure is legally insecure **as a result of past racially discriminatory laws or practices** is entitled to **legally secure tenure or comparable redress** |
| **25(7) — restitution** | a person or community dispossessed **after 19 June 1913** by such laws or practices is entitled to **restitution or equitable redress** |
| **25(8)** | **no provision of section 25 may impede the state from taking measures to achieve land, water and related reform** to redress past discrimination — subject to section 36 |

**Three programmes, and the public argument is almost entirely about one of them.** **Restitution** has a claims process and a court. **Redistribution** has a budget. **Tenure reform — section 25(6), which affects the most people — is the weakest leg and is barely discussed.**

---

**The official diagnosis.**

**The High Level Panel on the Assessment of Key Legislation and the Acceleration of Fundamental Change**, chaired by **former President Kgalema Motlanthe**, reported in **2017** after extensive public hearings. **Its finding on land was explicit:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The obstacle is not section 25** | the panel found **no evidence that the Constitution's property clause was the binding constraint** |
| **What was** | **"increasing evidence of corruption by officials, the diversion of the land reform budget to elites, lack of political will, and lack of training and capacity"** |
| **The budget** | **far too small for the stated targets** |
| **The recommendation** | **do not amend section 25; implement the existing law, fund it, and fix the administration** |

**And the 2019 Presidential Advisory Panel on Land Reform and Agriculture** reached broadly the same conclusion, with **a majority against amendment and a dissenting minority in favour** — the split itself being worth reading.

**That is the most important fact in this lesson, and it cuts against both political positions:** the state's own expert panels concluded that **land reform failed for administrative and fiscal reasons, under a Constitution that permitted far more than was attempted.**

---

**The specific failures, which are stage 8's capacity findings in land form:**

| Failure | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Budget** | **under half a per cent of the national budget** for a programme with a 30% target |
| **Post-settlement support** | **land transferred without finance, equipment, extension advice, water or market access** — the two-agricultures problem. A substantial proportion of redistributed farms ceased commercial production |
| **The leasehold turn** | **the State Land Lease and Disposal Policy of 2013 stopped transferring title**, so **the state retains ownership and grants leases** — which means **the beneficiary has no collateral and no asset**, and the state becomes the landlord of farmers |
| **Elite capture** | the Motlanthe panel's finding, repeated in audit reports — **well-connected applicants obtaining farms and leases** |
| **Communal Property Associations** | the vehicle for community ownership, **widely dysfunctional**, with unresolved governance and membership disputes, and an annual report to Parliament that documents it |
| **Beneficiary selection and records** | **poor record-keeping on who received what**, which is why even the 10% figure is estimated rather than counted |
| **Capacity** | **the department's own audit outcomes and vacancy rates** |

**And the tenure leg, where the clearest judicial finding is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Land Reform (Labour Tenants) Act of 1996** | gave labour tenants a right to claim the land they occupied and used |
| **What happened** | **roughly 20,000 claims were lodged by the 2001 deadline and the department failed, for two decades, to process them** |
| ***Mwelase v Director-General, Department of Rural Development and Land Reform* (2019)** | **the Constitutional Court appointed a special master to oversee the processing of labour tenant claims**, finding the department's failure so persistent that ordinary remedies had not worked |
| **Why that matters** | **a court taking over the administration of a statutory programme is an extraordinary remedy**, and the Court said so. **It is the clearest judicial statement that the land reform failure is administrative** |

**And ESTA**, from the agriculture lesson: **tenure rights for farm dwellers, widely assessed as poorly enforced**, with evictions continuing.

---

**So what is the argument actually about?**

| The case for amending section 25 / expropriation without compensation | The case against |
| --- | --- |
| **the compensation standard raises the cost** of each hectare and therefore limits what a budget can buy | **the panels found the Constitution was not the constraint**, and the compensation standard has never been litigated to its limits |
| **it is a statement of political intent** that changes the bargaining position of the state | **it addresses the price of land, not the state's inability to support farmers on it** — so it would produce more unproductive transfers |
| **section 25(8) and the "just and equitable" standard are untested**, so clarifying them legislatively removes uncertainty | **policy uncertainty itself has a cost** — on agricultural investment, on bank lending against farmland, and on the broader investment climate |
| **the 1913 cut-off and the market-value anchor are both political choices** that favour current holders | **the Expropriation Act of 2024 already provides for nil compensation in defined circumstances**, so the statutory route has been taken without an amendment — stage 7 |
| | **the binding constraints are budget, post-settlement support and administration**, and none of them is fixed by an amendment |

**From stage 7: the constitutional amendment failed in Parliament in December 2021, and the Expropriation Act 13 of 2024 was signed on 23 January 2025 and is not yet in force as of 14 October 2026.** **Stage 12 takes the argument forward from there.**

**Practice.** Read sections 25(5) to 25(8) and separate the three obligations. Then find the Motlanthe High Level Panel's land chapter and its conclusion on section 25. Then read *Mwelase* on the special master. Then find how much of the redistributed land is held under state lease rather than transferred title.
BEE: what the law requires:
The statute, the five elements of the scorecard, the procurement rules that were struck down, and what the law does and does not compel.

**Most arguments about BEE are conducted without reference to what the legislation actually says.** This lesson is the text; the next is the evidence.

**The constitutional basis, from stage 7:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 9(2)** | **"Equality includes the full and equal enjoyment of all rights and freedoms. To promote the achievement of equality, legislative and other measures designed to protect or advance persons, or categories of persons, disadvantaged by unfair discrimination may be taken."** |
| **Section 217(2)** | procurement policy **may** provide for **categories of preference in the allocation of contracts** and **the protection or advancement of persons disadvantaged by unfair discrimination** |
| **The test** | ***Minister of Finance v Van Heerden* (2004)** — a measure must **target** the disadvantaged, be **designed to protect or advance** them, and **promote the achievement of equality** |

**So preferential measures are constitutionally authorised, and they are not exempt from scrutiny: a measure that fails the *Van Heerden* test is unconstitutional.**

---

**The statute:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment Act 53 of 2003** | the framework; **"black people" is defined to mean Africans, Coloureds and Indians** who are South African citizens by birth or descent, or naturalised before 1994 |
| **The B-BBEE Amendment Act 46 of 2013** | **created the B-BBEE Commission**, **made fronting a criminal offence**, and inserted a **trumping provision** making the Act's status requirements prevail over other legislation in case of conflict |
| **The Codes of Good Practice** | **issued by the Minister under the Act and gazetted** — this is where the scorecard lives, and it is amended by notice rather than by statute |
| **Compliance** | **voluntary in itself** — the Act compels nobody to have a BEE score. **It becomes compulsory through procurement, licensing and sector regulation** |

**That last row is the most misunderstood point in the whole subject.** **The B-BBEE Act does not require any private company to do anything.** It creates **a measurement system**. The system bites because:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The state buys** | public procurement is on the order of a trillion rand a year, and **a scorecard affects your bid** |
| **Licences and rights are conditional** | **mining rights under the MPRDA and the Mining Charter**, telecommunications licences, liquor and gambling licences, financial services |
| **Large firms' own scorecards depend on their suppliers** | **enterprise and supplier development points**, so a large customer requires its suppliers to be compliant — the mechanism that reaches the whole private economy |

---

**The scorecard, under the amended Codes:**

| Element | Weight | What it measures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ownership** | **25 points** | black ownership of the entity, by voting rights and economic interest — **a priority element** |
| **Management control** | **19 points** | board, executive and senior/middle/junior management representation |
| **Skills development** | **20 points** | **spend on training black employees** as a share of payroll, plus learnerships — **a priority element** |
| **Enterprise and supplier development** | **40 points** | **preferential procurement from compliant and black-owned suppliers, plus support to black-owned suppliers and new enterprises** — **a priority element** |
| **Socio-economic development** | **5 points** | contributions to community and social causes |
| **Total** | **105 to 109 with bonus points** | |

**Read the weights.** **Ownership is 25 of about 109.** **Enterprise and supplier development is 40** — the largest element — **and skills development is 20.** **So on the law's own arithmetic, 60 of 109 points are about procurement, supplier support and training, and 25 are about ownership.**

**That matters for the next lesson's argument**, because the critique of BEE is overwhelmingly about ownership deals, which is the smallest of the three priority elements.

**The mechanics:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Levels** | **a score converts to Level 1 (best) through Level 8**, with a non-compliant category below |
| **The discounting principle** | **miss the sub-minimum on any priority element and your level drops by one**, which is what makes those three elements "priority" |
| **Exempted Micro Enterprises (EMEs)** | **turnover under R10 million — automatically Level 4**, and **Level 1 if at least 51% black-owned**, with no scorecard required |
| **Qualifying Small Enterprises (QSEs)** | a reduced scorecard |
| **Sector codes** | **mining, ICT, financial services, agriculture (AgriBEE), construction, property, tourism, transport, forestry** — each with its own weights and targets |

---

**Procurement, and the judgment that reset it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Preferential Procurement Policy Framework Act 5 of 2000** | gives effect to section 217(2) — a points system for price and for specific goals |
| **The 2017 Preferential Procurement Regulations** | introduced **pre-qualification criteria**, allowing an organ of state to require a minimum B-BBEE level or black ownership percentage **to bid at all** |
| ***Minister of Finance v Afribusiness NPC* (2022)** | **the Constitutional Court held the 2017 Regulations invalid** — the Minister had **exceeded the powers the PPPFA gave him**; the declaration was suspended for twelve months to allow a replacement |
| **The ground** | **not that preference is unconstitutional** — that **these regulations were not authorised by the empowering statute.** From stage 1: read what a judgment actually decided |
| **The replacement** | **the Public Procurement Act 28 of 2024** — a consolidated framework with an explicit statutory basis for preferential procurement and set-asides, and a single regulator |

> **As of 14 October 2026: the Public Procurement Act's regulations and the framework for set-asides and preference points are the operative rules. Check the Treasury's procurement regulations and instruction notes for the current position.**

**And employment equity**, from the labour law lesson: **the Employment Equity Amendment Act of 2022, in force 1 January 2025, empowers the Minister to set sectoral numerical targets, with a compliance certificate required to do business with the state.** **That is the enforcement mechanism BEE and employment equity now share: access to public contracts.**

**Practice.** Find the current Codes of Good Practice and the generic scorecard, and write out the five elements and their weights. Then find the definition of "black people" in the Act. Then read the *Afribusiness* judgment's actual holding. Then find the Public Procurement Act's preference and set-aside provisions.
BEE: the evidence, both sides:
What is measurable after twenty-two years, what is not, and why the same evidence supports two opposite conclusions.

**Start with what can actually be measured, because much of this argument runs on assertion.**

**1 — Ownership of listed companies.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The JSE's own 2017 study** | found **black South Africans held on the order of 23% of the shares in the top 100 companies that were available to be held** — counting **direct holdings plus mandated investments**, principally pension funds, of which the Government Employees Pension Fund is the largest |
| **An earlier NEF-commissioned study** | put the figure around **27%** of available shares, on a similar method |
| **Direct black ownership** | **much lower** — a single-digit to low-double-digit percentage, depending on method |
| **The measurement problem** | **"available shares" excludes the large foreign-held free float**, and **counting a pension fund's holding as black ownership** is contested: it is economically real for the member and it confers **no control** |

**So the honest statement is: measured black ownership of the listed economy is somewhere between roughly 5% and roughly 27% depending on what you count, and the pension fund question is the whole spread.** **From stage 1: a figure whose range is five-fold is a definitional dispute, not a factual one.**

**2 — Management, where the data is better and the picture is clearer.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The source** | **the Commission for Employment Equity's annual report**, which every designated employer files into |
| **The finding, consistently** | **African South Africans remain a small minority of top management** — on the order of a sixth to a fifth of top management posts — **against roughly 80% of the economically active population**; white South Africans hold a clear majority of top management |
| **Lower levels** | **much more transformed** — junior and middle management, and the professional grades, have changed substantially |
| **The pattern** | **transformation has moved up the hierarchy slowly and stalled near the top** |

**That is the strongest single piece of evidence in the whole argument, and it is public and annual.**

**3 — The black middle class.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The growth** | **substantial and not seriously disputed** — the various survey-based estimates show the black middle class growing several-fold since the early 2000s, into the millions |
| **Where it came from** | **the public service, state-owned enterprises, the professions, financial services and management posts in large firms** — so **substantially from employment and employment equity, rather than from ownership deals** |
| **Why that matters** | **the most consequential redistribution of the post-1994 period happened through jobs and salaries, not through equity** |

**4 — What cannot be measured.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The aggregate cost of the BEE system** | **there is no credible aggregate estimate.** Claims circulate; none rests on a defensible method |
| **The counterfactual** | **what ownership and management composition would look like with no BEE at all** is unknowable, and both sides' assertions about it are assertions |
| **The growth effect** | **studies exist in both directions and none is decisive** |

**Saying so is not evasion. It is the state of the evidence, and anybody claiming a precise aggregate number for BEE's cost or benefit is going beyond it.**

---

**Now the two cases, each in its strongest form.**

| The case that BEE has failed | The case that BEE has worked, within its limits |
| --- | --- |
| **inequality has not fallen** — the Gini is where it was, and **within-African inequality rose**, which is consistent with a programme that moved a minority up | **it was never designed to reduce the Gini** — it was designed to change who owns and manages the economy, and on management's lower and middle tiers **it demonstrably did** |
| **ownership deals enriched a small, politically connected group**, often funded by vendor finance that left the beneficiary with debt rather than an asset | **ownership is 25 of 109 points**; the system's weight is on **skills development and supplier development**, which reach far more people and get no attention |
| **fronting is pervasive** — the B-BBEE Commission's own reports document it, and prosecution is rare | **fronting was criminalised in 2013 and a Commission exists**; under-enforcement is a stage 8 capacity failure, not a design failure |
| **procurement preference became a capture vehicle** — Zondo's evidence repeatedly shows BEE requirements used to justify inflated pricing and intermediary companies that added nothing | **the capture was of the procurement system generally**, and the same contracts would have been looted under any preference regime |
| **it taxes the economy** at the margin — compliance cost, a narrower supplier pool, and a disincentive for small firms to grow past the EME threshold | **the EME and QSE thresholds exist precisely to exempt small firms**, and compliance cost for a large firm is a rounding error |
| **thirty years is long enough** — a measure under section 9(2) must be **temporary in principle**, and no sunset has ever been contemplated | **the top-management numbers show the job is not done**, and a measure whose objective is unmet cannot be sunsetted for reaching an anniversary |
| **it entrenches a racial classification** in law, perpetuating apartheid's categories in order to undo them | **the classification exists because the disadvantage was imposed by it**, and *Van Heerden* permits targeting the disadvantaged by the characteristic used to disadvantage them |

**Both columns are serious. Not to arrive at a position.**

---

**What would settle it**, which is what stage 1 trains for and stage 12 formalises:

| Question | The evidence that would answer it |
| --- | --- |
| **Has BEE changed who runs the economy?** | **the Commission for Employment Equity's top-management series over time** — it is published annually and the trend is the answer |
| **Has it changed ownership?** | **an ownership study that reports direct and mandated holdings separately**, consistently, across years |
| **Does it cost growth?** | **firm-level data on compliance cost and on supplier pool restriction**, which would require research access nobody has funded |
| **Does fronting dominate?** | **the B-BBEE Commission's investigation outcomes and prosecution rate**, which it publishes |
| **Would a class-based alternative work better?** | **a trial.** Several proposals exist — means-testing, or weighting by poverty rather than race — and **none has been piloted** |

**The last row is the most interesting fact in this lesson: the obvious alternative to a race-based criterion is a class-based one, it is widely proposed across the political spectrum, and nobody has tested it at scale.** **From stage 1: that is a live empirical question being argued as a moral one.**

**Practice.** Find the latest Commission for Employment Equity report and the top-management composition table. Then find the JSE ownership study and separate direct from mandated holdings. Then find the B-BBEE Commission's latest annual report and its fronting investigation numbers. Then write the strongest version of the column you disagree with.
RDP, GEAR, the NDP and Vulindlela:
Six economic plans in thirty years, what each promised, what each delivered, and the pattern in the difference.

**This lesson is the policy record, and the pattern it reveals is more useful than any of the individual plans.**

---

**1994 — the RDP.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | **the Reconstruction and Development Programme** — the ANC's election platform, turned into a government White Paper, with an RDP office in the Presidency and an RDP Fund |
| **The content** | **meeting basic needs** — housing, water, electrification, health, education — **developing human resources, democratising the state, and building the economy** |
| **What it delivered** | **the electrification and water programmes are its real achievements** — millions of households connected, which is measurable and was done |
| **What happened to it** | **the RDP office was closed in 1996** and its functions distributed across departments. The name survives attached to houses |
| **The critique** | it was a programme of **spending without a stated means of financing it**, and the fiscal position of 1994 — the inherited debt from stage 6 — did not permit it |

**2 — 1996: GEAR.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it was** | **Growth, Employment and Redistribution** — a macroeconomic framework announced in **February 1996**, **not negotiated with the alliance partners**, and presented as **"non-negotiable"** |
| **The targets** | **6% growth and 400,000 new jobs a year by 2000**; the deficit cut to 3% of GDP; inflation controlled; tariffs reduced; **exchange controls relaxed; some privatisation** |
| **What it delivered** | **the macroeconomic stabilisation worked** — the deficit fell, inflation came down, **debt fell toward the 26% of GDP that the debt lesson starts from**, and inflation targeting followed in 2000 |
| **What it did not** | **the growth and employment targets were missed substantially**, and formal employment fell in the late 1990s |
| **Its political legacy** | **the alliance rupture.** COSATU and the SACP regarded GEAR as a betrayal of the RDP, and the argument shaped internal ANC politics for a decade — stages 10 and 11 |
| **The honest assessment** | **it bought the fiscal space that funded the grant system and the 2000s infrastructure programme** — and it did so with a social cost that its own authors did not anticipate |

**3 — 2006: ASGISA**, the Accelerated and Shared Growth Initiative, targeting 6% growth by 2010 — **arriving during the commodity boom when growth was already above 5%**, and overtaken by the financial crisis.

**4 — 2010: the New Growth Path**, targeting **5 million jobs by 2020** through identified "jobs drivers" — infrastructure, agriculture, mining, the green economy, manufacturing and tourism. **The target was not met and the framework was superseded within two years.**

**5 — 2012: the National Development Plan.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **Vision 2030**, produced by the **National Planning Commission** chaired by Trevor Manuel, after extensive consultation — **a 400-page diagnostic and plan**, and the most intellectually serious document of the six |
| **The targets** | **11 million new jobs by 2030; unemployment down to 6%; growth averaging 5.4%; gross fixed capital formation at 30% of GDP; the elimination of income poverty** |
| **Its diagnosis** | **nine challenges, headed by "too few people work" and "the standard of education for most black learners is of poor quality"** — which the unemployment lesson in this stage reaches independently |
| **Its status** | **adopted by Cabinet and endorsed by the ANC's 2012 conference** |
| **What happened** | **it was never translated into departmental mandates, budgets or accountability.** No minister's performance was measured against it; **the planning commission had no implementation authority**; and the state capture years followed |
| **Where the targets stand** | **not close.** Employment, growth and investment are all far below the trajectory; **the investment rate is roughly half the 30% target** |

**6 — 2020: Operation Vulindlela.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **a joint Presidency and National Treasury unit** — deliberately small — **that selects a short list of specific structural reforms and tracks them to completion** |
| **The first phase** | **electricity** (the licensing threshold, unbundling, the market), **logistics** (the roadmap, third-party access), **water** (licensing turnaround, the water resources agency), **telecommunications** (the spectrum auction of 2022, finally held after years of delay), **and skilled immigration** (the visa system) |
| **The second phase, from 2024** | **local government, and spatial and housing reform** |
| **Why it has worked better** | **it is not a plan with targets. It is a list of regulatory obstacles with named owners and deadlines, published quarterly** |
| **Its limits** | **it does not address the schooling system, the labour market or inequality** — the things that need money and decades rather than a regulatory change |

---

**The pattern, which is the lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The plans with targets** | **RDP, GEAR, ASGISA, the New Growth Path, the NDP** — **all specified outcomes** (growth rates, job numbers), **none specified who would be accountable for which action by when**, and **none met its headline target** |
| **The programme without targets** | **Vulindlela specified actions, owners and dates and published progress** — and **delivered a substantial share of them** |
| **The lesson** | **an economic plan that names an outcome is a wish; one that names a regulatory change, an owner and a date is an instrument** |
| **The limit of the lesson** | **Vulindlela works on things a regulation can fix.** It has no answer to the reading outcomes of the unemployment lesson, which is the largest constraint of all |

**And a note on the pattern's political meaning**, which stage 11 picks up: **GEAR was imposed and achieved its macro targets at the cost of alliance unity; the NDP was consensual and was never implemented.** **Those two facts together are the central dilemma of South African economic policymaking**, and nobody has a general solution to it.

**Practice.** Find the NDP's chapter 3 diagnostic and compare its nine challenges with the explanations in this stage's unemployment lesson. Then find GEAR's targets and the actual outcomes for 1996 to 2000. Then find Operation Vulindlela's latest quarterly progress report and count the reforms completed against those outstanding. Then pick one NDP 2030 target and work out what annual rate would now be needed to reach it.
Growth, and how to argue about the econo:
Two very different fifteen-year periods, five explanations for the second, and the stage's close.

**The record, and this is the single most important chart in South African economics:**

| Period | Real GDP growth, annual average |
| --- | --- |
| **1994–2008** | **on the order of 3.3 to 3.6%** |
| **2009–2024** | **on the order of 1%** |
| **2012 onward, per capita** | **falling** — population growth above 1% against output growth below it, so **GDP per person has declined for more than a decade** |

> **Check the Reserve Bank's Quarterly Bulletin for the series and StatsSA's GDP releases. The per capita series is the one to look at, because it is what a person experiences.**

**Say the per capita point plainly, because it is the fact underneath every political development in stages 11 and 12: the average South African has been getting poorer since roughly 2014.** Not stagnant — **poorer.** That is the economic condition in which the 2024 election happened.

**And the investment rate, which is the cleanest single diagnostic:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Gross fixed capital formation** | **around 14 to 15% of GDP** |
| **The NDP's target** | **30%** |
| **Fast-growing middle-income comparators** | **25 to 35%** |
| **What that means** | **the economy is not replacing and expanding its capital stock fast enough to grow**, and both public and private investment are weak |

---

**Five explanations for the post-2009 collapse.** Each has real evidence; **they are not mutually exclusive; and the weighting is the whole argument.**

**1 — State capacity and state capture.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | from stage 8 — **the institutions that deliver electricity, rail, ports, water and municipal services degraded, and that degradation is a direct supply constraint** |
| **The evidence** | **the timing matches closely**: Eskom's availability factor, Transnet's volumes, municipal audit outcomes and the investment rate all deteriorate over the same period |
| **The strongest form** | **this is not a story about corruption's moral cost. It is a story about electricity you cannot buy and ore you cannot move** |

**2 — The commodity cycle.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | **the 1994–2008 growth was substantially a global commodity boom driven by Chinese industrialisation**, and its end explains the slowdown without any domestic story |
| **The evidence** | **the boom's timing is exact** — 2003 to 2008 — and growth exceeded 5% in its peak years; the 2021 commodity spike produced a large revenue windfall and brief growth |
| **The counter** | **other commodity exporters did not stagnate for fifteen years**, and South Africa failed to supply during the 2021 spike **because of rail and electricity** — which is explanation 1 |

**3 — Electricity and logistics.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | the narrow version of 1 — **two specific physical constraints**, quantified in this stage's two lessons on them |
| **The evidence** | **the Reserve Bank's and Treasury's estimates put load-shedding alone at one to two percentage points of growth** in the worst years |
| **The test now available** | **load-shedding has largely stopped since 2024. If this explanation carries most of the weight, growth should recover materially. Watch it — this is a live, falsifiable prediction** |

**4 — Policy uncertainty and the cost of doing business.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | **expropriation, mining charters, NHI, BEE requirements, labour regulation and visa delays** together deter investment, independent of any individual policy's merits |
| **The evidence** | **business confidence indices, the investment rate itself, and the mining investment attractiveness surveys** |
| **The counter** | **confidence indices measure sentiment, which follows outcomes as much as it causes them**; and the single largest investment deterrent in the surveys is **electricity and logistics**, not policy |

**5 — Structure and demand.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | **an economy where 40% of working-age people have income and inequality is the world's highest has a demand problem**: the domestic market is small relative to the population, so investment in production for it is unattractive |
| **The evidence** | the composition of growth — **credit-driven household consumption drove the 2000s expansion**, and household debt limits its repetition |
| **The implication** | **growth requires either exports — hence logistics — or broadening the domestic market, which means jobs and transfers** |

---

**How to argue about this, which is the stage's close and the handover to stage 12.**

**Four rules, each drawn from stage 1 and tested against this stage's material:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Name the base of every number** | **an unemployment rate without its definition, a Gini without its base, a land percentage without its denominator, and a BEE ownership figure without its method are all unusable.** Most economic disagreement in South Africa is definitional |
| **2 — Separate the inherited from the current** | the minerals-energy complex, the spatial geography and the schooling system's deficit are **inherited and slow**; electricity, logistics, appointment and procurement are **current and fast.** **A policy argument that confuses the two is arguing for the wrong time horizon** |
| **3 — State the counterfactual** | **"BEE cost the economy X" and "without land reform there would be stability" are both counterfactual claims.** Ask what the comparison case is and whether it is observable |
| **4 — Name the test** | **for each of the five explanations above, there is evidence that would raise or lower its weight.** The post-2024 electricity recovery is a live test of explanation 3. The Commission for Employment Equity series is a live test of BEE's effect on management. **A position that specifies no test is not an analysis** |

**And the one-sentence summary of the stage, which is deliberately not a conclusion:**

> **South Africa has an economy built for extraction, a labour market that cannot absorb its population, the most redistributive fiscal system measured and the highest measured inequality, a competent revenue service and central bank, a failing logistics and municipal infrastructure, and fifteen years of per capita decline. Whether the binding constraint is inherited structure or current capacity is the central economic argument, and it is settled differently by each of the five explanations above.**

**Stage 12 takes the live arguments — land, NHI, BEE's future, the fiscal question — and sets out what evidence would settle each.**

**Practice.** Find real GDP per capita for 2008, 2014 and the most recent year. Then find gross fixed capital formation as a share of GDP and compare it with the NDP's target. Then take explanation 3 and check its prediction: find growth for the years since load-shedding was suspended. Then write a paragraph arguing for the explanation you find weakest, using its strongest evidence.
Why the parties are the unit:
The stage's thesis: in South Africa the party is the political unit, not the politician — and that is a design choice with consequences you can trace.

**The thesis:**

> **South Africa's electoral system makes parties, rather than individuals, the units of political competition. A national or provincial legislator is on a list that the party controls, owes their seat to the party rather than to any voter, and can be removed from the list by the party. Almost every accountability failure in stage 8 runs through that fact — and almost every proposal for reform addresses it.**

**And the counter-case, which the electoral reform lesson gives in full:**

> **Closed-list proportional representation gave South Africa a Parliament that is accurately proportional, has a high representation of women, gives small parties and minority views real seats, and has never produced a disputed national result. Constituency systems deliver local accountability and systematically distort the national result. The trade-off is real, and the 1994 choice was made deliberately.**

---

**What this stage covers, and in what order:**

| Lessons | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1–3** | **the machinery** — how a ballot becomes a seat, nationally and locally |
| **4–7** | **the ANC** — as a movement, as an organisation, as the national political arena, and the alliance |
| **8–11** | **the opposition and the newer parties** — the DA's lineage, the EFF, the IFP and the regionals, and MK |
| **12–13** | **what the results show** — why the majority went, and what coalitions have done |
| **14** | **money** — the party funding law and what it discloses |
| **15–16** | **the press** — who owns it, and what protects it |
| **17–19** | **outside the parties** — courts, protest, and migration politics |
| **20** | **what the system is becoming** |

---

**Three things to carry through the stage.**

**1 — Parties are private organisations with public power.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Constitution assumes them** | section 1 names **a multi-party system of democratic government**; section 19 gives every citizen the right to **form a political party, to participate in its activities and to recruit members** |
| **And they are voluntary associations** | **their internal rules are their constitutions**, and a dispute about a branch meeting or a leadership election is a contract and association matter |
| **Which the courts enforce** | **repeatedly**, including by setting aside provincial conferences of the governing party. **From stage 8: the courts end up adjudicating internal party disputes because the party's own processes fail** |
| **And the consequence** | **when a party holds a parliamentary majority, its internal rules are effectively part of the constitutional order** — the recall lesson shows why |

**2 — The closed list is the hinge.** It is the single institutional fact that connects this stage to stage 8:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Zondo's recommendation** | the Commission ended its institutional recommendations by **questioning the closed-list system's effect on accountability** |
| **The *UDM* and *EFF* litigation** | **secret ballots and impeachment rules** were litigated precisely because an MP voting against their party faces delisting |
| **Oversight** | stage 8's finding that Parliament's powers exist and are not used — **a committee chair who embarrasses the executive is on a list the executive's party controls** |

**3 — Not to arrive at a position, which in this stage means something specific.** Parties are the subject most likely to be described partisanly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For each party**, this stage gives | **its own account of itself**, its record where that is measurable, and the strongest criticism made of it |
| **It does not** | rank them, recommend one, or treat any party's self-description as a finding |
| **From stage 1's party document lesson** | **a manifesto is a statement of intent by an interested party.** Read it as evidence of what the party wants said about it |
| **And the test** | **if you cannot state a party's case in the terms its own supporters would recognise, you do not understand it well enough to criticise it** |

**Practice.** Read section 19 of the Constitution. Then find one party's constitution and establish how its leader is elected and how a member is expelled. Then take the party you like least and write its strongest claim about itself in a sentence it would accept.
How a ballot becomes a seat:
Three ballots, 400 seats, a quota, and the two hundred compensatory seats that make the result almost exactly proportional.

**The constitutional frame, from stage 7:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 46** | the National Assembly has **between 350 and 400 members**, elected under a system prescribed by national legislation that is **based on the national common voters' roll**, provides for **a minimum voting age of 18**, and **"results, in general, in proportional representation"** |
| **Section 105** | the same for provincial legislatures — **30 to 80 members**, proportional |
| **Section 1(d)** | **universal adult suffrage, a national common voters' roll, regular elections and a multi-party system of democratic government** |

**Note what section 46 does and does not require: proportionality is constitutionally mandated; closed party lists are not.** **The list system is in the Electoral Act, which Parliament can change by ordinary legislation.** That matters for the reform lesson at the end of this stage.

---

**The National Assembly's 400 seats:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **200 regional seats** | **allocated province by province, from each party's regional list for that province** — so the provinces' seat totals are fixed by their share of registered voters |
| **200 compensatory seats** | **allocated from a national list, to bring each party's total up to its national proportion** |
| **The effect** | **the regional half gives provincial representation; the compensatory half corrects any disproportionality the regional allocation produces.** The combined result is **almost exactly proportional to the national vote** |

**The arithmetic, in the form you can actually use:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The quota** | **total valid votes divided by 401, plus one** — the **Droop quota** |
| **Seats** | each party gets one seat per full quota, then **the remaining seats go to the largest remainders** |
| **In practice** | with roughly 16 million valid votes, **a seat costs on the order of 40,000 votes** |
| **The threshold** | **there is none.** A party with one quota's worth of votes — **roughly a quarter of one per cent** — gets a seat |
| **The consequence** | **very small parties win seats**, which is why the Assembly contains more than a dozen parties |

**And the provincial ballot is separate.** A voter in a general election now marks **three ballots**:

| Ballot | What it elects |
| --- | --- |
| **The national compensatory ballot** | a party, for the 200 national seats |
| **The regional ballot** | **a party or an independent candidate**, for that province's share of the 200 regional seats |
| **The provincial ballot** | a party, for the provincial legislature |

---

**The closed list, and what it means in practice:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The voter chooses a party** | **not a person** — except on the regional ballot's independent candidates |
| **The party ranks its candidates** | and **the order determines who sits** |
| **Vacancies** | **filled by the party from its list**, not by a by-election |
| **So an MP's seat depends on** | **the party's internal list process**, which is an internal party matter |
| **And section 47(3)(c)** | **a member loses their seat if they cease to be a member of the party that nominated them** — the anti-defection rule |

**Floor-crossing**, briefly, because it is a good illustration of the system being amended and then unamended: **constitutional amendments permitted members to cross the floor without losing their seats from 2002**, producing several party realignments, and **the permission was removed by amendment in 2009.** The anti-defection position is now the default again.

---

**Independent candidates, and the 2023 amendment.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The judgment** | ***New Nation Movement v President* (2020)** — **the Electoral Act was unconstitutional in requiring that candidates stand only through parties**, because section 19(3)(b) gives every citizen the right **to stand for public office** |
| **The fix** | **the Electoral Amendment Act of 2023** |
| **What it allows** | **an independent may contest the regional ballot only** |
| **The requirements** | **signatures from registered voters** in the region, set as a percentage of the previous election's quota, lodged with a deposit |
| **The ceiling** | **an independent cannot access the 200 compensatory seats**, and **any votes above one quota are not transferable** — so an independent's votes beyond one seat's worth elect nobody |
| **The criticism** | **that this makes the independent route formally available and practically unusable**, and that it is **less favourable than the judgment required**. Further litigation followed |
| **The result in 2024** | **no independent candidate won a seat** |

**That is a live constitutional question**: whether the 2023 Act actually satisfies *New Nation Movement*. **From stage 1: read the judgment and then the Act and form your own view.**
