**Practice.** Open the IEC's results site for 2024 and find the total valid votes, then calculate the quota. Then find the smallest party that won a seat and its vote total. Then read section 47(3)(c) on losing a seat. Then read the Electoral Amendment Act's signature requirement for an independent and work out how many signatures that is in your province.
The local ballots, and the district oddi:
Where a voter does choose a person, how a hung council happens, and the one tier of South African government almost nobody can explain.

**Local government, from stage 8, has three categories: eight metros, about 205 local municipalities, and about 44 districts. The ballots differ by where you live.**

**If you live in a metro — two ballots:**

| Ballot | What it elects |
| --- | --- |
| **The ward ballot** | **a person**, by first-past-the-post, in your ward |
| **The proportional ballot** | **a party**, for the list seats |
| **The composition** | **half the council is ward councillors, half is list councillors** — and **the list seats are allocated so that the council as a whole is proportional to the PR vote** |

**That last point is the one to understand, and it is the same principle as the national compensatory list.** **If a party wins more wards than its PR share would justify, it gets correspondingly fewer list seats.** So **winning wards does not win you a council** — **the PR vote determines the council's composition, and the ward vote determines who occupies your party's share of it.**

**If you live in a local municipality inside a district — three ballots:**

| Ballot | What it elects |
| --- | --- |
| **The ward ballot** | your local council's ward councillor |
| **The local PR ballot** | the local council's list seats |
| **The district PR ballot** | **the 40% of the district council that is directly elected** |

**And the district council's other 60%** is made up of **councillors appointed by the local councils in the district**, in proportion to their populations. **So a district council is 40% directly elected and 60% delegated** — which means **you cannot vote a district council out**, and its accountability runs through the local councils.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What districts do** | **bulk water and sanitation in many areas, district health services, regional planning, firefighting and disaster management**, and in some provinces most of the water function |
| **Why it matters** | from stage 8's local government lessons — **the water function in much of rural South Africa sits with a district whose councillors most residents did not elect and cannot identify** |
| **The reform argument** | **districts are widely proposed for abolition or for reassignment of functions**, and the **District Development Model of 2019 went the other way**, adding a coordination role |

**Note that about 4,400 to 4,500 wards exist countrywide**, and **the ward ballot is the only place in South African elections where a voter directly chooses a named individual who then holds office.** **Independents have always been able to contest wards**, and some win.

---

**How a hung council happens, and why it happens so much more locally than nationally.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism** | **proportional composition with no threshold**, plus a large number of parties contesting, means **a council frequently has no majority** |
| **The scale** | after the **2016** elections, hung metros appeared for the first time; after the **2021** elections, **on the order of 60 to 70 of the 257 councils had no majority party** |
| **The mayoral election** | **the council elects the mayor** (or the executive committee), **by majority, at its first sitting**, chaired by a judicial officer |
| **The instability** | **a mayor can be removed by a simple council majority at any time**, so **any shift of two or three councillors can change the government of a city** |
| **And the small parties' leverage** | **a party with one or two seats can hold the balance**, which is both the system working as designed and the source of the churn |

**That is the structural reason stage 8's local government lesson lists political instability as the second-largest cause of municipal failure.** **The national Parliament's five-year terms and the section 102 motion of no confidence make national government far more stable than a council.**

---

**The 2021 result, as the reference point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC** | **below 50% of the national local government vote for the first time** — in the mid-40s |
| **The DA** | in the low 20s |
| **The EFF** | around 10% |
| **The IFP** | **a strong recovery in KwaZulu-Natal** |
| **Turnout** | **low — on the order of 46% of registered voters**, the lowest of any South African election to that point |
| **The pattern** | **fragmentation**, with a long tail of small and local parties and independents winning council seats |

> **As of 14 October 2026 the next municipal elections are on 4 November 2026. Everything in this lesson is the machinery those elections will run on, and the results will be on the IEC's site within days. Check them against the 2021 figures above.**

**Practice.** Find your own ward and its councillor. Then open the IEC's 2021 results for your municipality and work out how the PR seats corrected the ward result. Then find out which district municipality you fall under, if any, and what functions it holds. Then find how many councils had no majority after 2021.
The ANC as a movement:
A 114-year-old organisation that describes itself as a liberation movement rather than a political party — and the specific consequences of that self-understanding.

**The claim, in the ANC's own language:** it is **"a national liberation movement"** whose task is **"the National Democratic Revolution"** — the transfer of power to the people as a whole, of which winning elections is one instrument. **From stage 1's party document lesson: that is a self-description, and it is also an analytically useful one, because it explains behaviour that a party-political frame does not.**

---

**The history in the form it is used politically**, with stages 4 to 6 holding the detail:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1912** | founded as **the South African Native National Congress** in Bloemfontein — a deputation-and-petition organisation of ministers, teachers, lawyers and chiefs, formed in direct anticipation of the 1913 Land Act |
| **1923** | renamed the **African National Congress** |
| **1943–44** | **the Youth League** — Mandela, Sisulu, Tambo, Lembede — pushing mass action against the petitioning tradition |
| **1949** | **the Programme of Action** adopted: boycotts, strikes, civil disobedience |
| **1952** | **the Defiance Campaign**, and the membership rising into the tens of thousands |
| **1955** | **the Freedom Charter**, adopted at the Congress of the People at Kliptown — the founding statement of the movement's politics |
| **1960** | **banned**, after Sharpeville |
| **1961** | **Umkhonto we Sizwe** formed — the armed struggle |
| **1969** | **the Morogoro Conference** — opening membership to all races in exile structures, and the Strategy and Tactics document |
| **1985** | **the Kabwe Conference** — opening the NEC to all races |
| **1990** | **unbanned**, 2 February |
| **1994** | **in government** |

**Four things in that list explain the ANC's self-understanding:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is older than the Union** | **founded in 1912, two years after Union, against the 1913 Act** — so it predates every other party in Parliament and the apartheid state itself |
| **It is a broad front, by design** | **nationalists, communists, trade unionists, Christians, liberals and Africanists in one organisation** — which is why its internal arguments are as wide as a national politics |
| **It was an army and a government-in-exile** | with camps, a treasury, a diplomatic corps and a security department, **which produces a particular organisational culture: discipline, collective decision, and an intolerance of public dissent** |
| **It was the Charter's custodian** | and **the Freedom Charter is still cited in internal arguments as the authority** |

---

**The Freedom Charter, 1955**, which you should read because it is short and because every faction quotes it:

| Clause | Text, in part |
| --- | --- |
| **The People Shall Govern!** | every man and woman the right to vote and to stand |
| **All National Groups Shall have Equal Rights!** | |
| **The People Shall Share in the Country's Wealth!** | **"The mineral wealth beneath the soil, the banks and monopoly industry shall be transferred to the ownership of the people as a whole"** |
| **The Land Shall be Shared Among Those Who Work It!** | **"Restrictions of land ownership on a racial basis shall be ended, and all the land re-divided amongst those who work it"** |
| **All Shall be Equal Before the Law!** | |
| **All Shall Enjoy Equal Human Rights!** | |
| **There Shall be Work and Security!** | |
| **The Doors of Learning and Culture Shall be Opened!** | |
| **There Shall be Houses, Security and Comfort!** | |
| **There Shall be Peace and Friendship!** | |

**The third clause is the one that has been argued about continuously for seventy years**, because it says **transfer to the ownership of the people as a whole** — and whether stage 6's settlement honoured or abandoned it is the argument that produced GEAR's reception, the nationalisation debates, and the EFF.

**The honest reading, which is contested in both directions:** the Charter is **a statement of political aims written in 1955 by a mass gathering**, not a programme with implementation detail. **Those who read it as mandating nationalisation and those who read it as a democratic and anti-discrimination charter are both reading real text.**

---

**And the consequences of the movement self-understanding, which recur in the next three lessons:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal decisions carry public authority** | **a conference resolution is treated as a mandate** — the Scorpions' disbandment from stage 8 is the clearest case |
| **Collective discipline over individual mandate** | **public dissent by a member is a disciplinary matter**, which interacts badly with the closed list and with parliamentary oversight |
| **The movement outranks the state** | **the recall lesson**: two presidents removed by a party body with no constitutional standing |
| **"Deployment" rather than appointment** | stage 8's cadre deployment — **a coherent practice if the party is the custodian of the revolution, unlawful according to the Zondo Commission** |
| **And a defence worth stating** | **the broad-front character is also why the transition held.** An organisation that could contain communists and chiefs, exiles and inkatha-era rivals, could negotiate a constitution that bound all of them. **Stage 6 is the evidence for that** |

**Practice.** Read the Freedom Charter — it is two pages. Then read the ANC's Strategy and Tactics document's definition of the National Democratic Revolution. Then find the 1912 founding conference's resolutions and note what it was formed to oppose. Then write down one behaviour of the ANC in government that the movement frame explains better than a party frame.
The ANC as an organisation:
Branches, conferences and the NEC: how the governing party actually makes decisions, and why its internal procedure is a national concern.

**The structure, from the bottom:**

| Level | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The branch** | **the basic unit** — a minimum membership, meeting in a ward or a zone. **A branch in good standing elects delegates and nominates candidates for leadership** |
| **The Branch General Meeting (BGM)** | where that nomination happens — **the single most contested procedural event in South African politics** |
| **The region** | a cluster of branches, with a Regional Executive Committee |
| **The province** | a Provincial Conference every four years, electing a Provincial Executive Committee and a provincial chairperson |
| **The National Conference** | **every five years** — thousands of voting delegates, **about 90% of them from branches** — which **elects the national leadership and adopts resolutions** |
| **The National General Council** | **mid-term**, reviewing implementation of conference resolutions without electing leadership |
| **The National Executive Committee (NEC)** | **the highest decision-making body between conferences** — around 80 elected members plus the officials and ex officio members |
| **The National Working Committee (NWC)** | the NEC's smaller operational body, meeting more often |
| **The Top Six, now Seven** | **President, Deputy President, National Chairperson, Secretary-General, Deputy Secretary-General (two since 2022), Treasurer-General** |

**And the Secretary-General's office is the one to watch**, because it controls **membership records, branch audits and the organisational machinery** — which means **it controls who is in good standing and therefore who may vote at a conference.** **That is why the Secretary-General's position is contested as hard as the President's.**

---

**Why branch procedure is a national matter.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The chain** | **branch members elect conference delegates → conference elects the NEC and the party President → the party President becomes the country's President if the party holds a majority** |
| **So the decisive electorate** | for most of the period since 1994, **was a few thousand conference delegates**, selected through branch meetings |
| **Which creates an incentive** | **to control branch membership** |
| **The resulting practices** | **"gatekeeping"** — denying membership or blocking meetings to exclude rival factions; **membership fraud** — bulk-paid or fabricated memberships; and **branch audit disputes** |
| **The litigation** | **the courts have repeatedly set aside ANC provincial conferences** — including in KwaZulu-Natal and the Free State — **for non-compliance with the party's own constitution** |
| **The membership numbers** | **peaked above a million around 2012 and have fallen substantially since**, to a figure in the hundreds of thousands at recent conference audits |

**That last row is worth pausing on.** **A governing party's membership fell by a large fraction in a decade** — which has two readings: **declining popular commitment to the organisation**, or **the removal of fraudulent memberships by better auditing.** **Both are claimed and both are partly true.**

---

**Slates, which is how leadership contests actually work.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The practice** | **candidates run as a package** — a presidential candidate with a named Deputy, Secretary-General and so on — and branches nominate the slate |
| **Why** | it concentrates support and makes nominations legible, **and it converts a leadership election into a factional contest** |
| **The party's own position** | **slates have been formally criticised in conference resolutions and by the Secretary-General's organisational reports** as damaging to unity |
| **The consequence after a conference** | **the losing slate holds NEC seats**, so the leadership is divided from the day it takes office — **which is the key to understanding the ANC-in-government's behaviour in stage 11** |

**And the step-aside rule**, which is the most consequential internal rule of the last decade:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The origin** | **the 2017 Nasrec conference resolved** that members facing serious criminal charges should step aside from party and public positions |
| **The implementation** | **NEC guidelines adopted in 2021** required a member **criminally charged with corruption or another serious offence to step aside within 30 days**, failing which they would be suspended |
| **The first major application** | **the Secretary-General was suspended in 2021** under the rule, and litigated against it |
| **Reaffirmation** | **the 2022 conference kept it**, against sustained internal opposition |
| **Why it matters nationally** | it is **the only mechanism in South African politics that removes a person from office on being charged rather than on being convicted** — and it is **a party rule, not a law** |
| **The objection** | **it bypasses the presumption of innocence**, and its critics argue it can be weaponised by inducing charges against rivals |
| **The defence** | **a party is free to set its own standards for holding office in its name**, and the alternative had been office-holders remaining in place through years of trial |

---

**And the rule that connects this lesson to stage 8: deployment.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The practice** | **the National Deployment Committee recommends party members for positions in the state**, including in departments, SOEs and other institutions |
| **The party's defence** | a governing party is entitled to place people who will implement its programme, as parties do elsewhere through political appointments |
| **The Zondo Commission's finding** | **the practice as conducted was unlawful and unconstitutional**, because it extended into appointments that are required by law to be made on merit by the relevant authority |
| **The litigation** | the DA pursued the committee's minutes, and the courts ordered their disclosure |
| **The status** | **contested, and the subject of a formal recommendation to end it** |

**Practice.** Find the ANC's constitution and read the branch and conference provisions. Then find the Secretary-General's organisational report from the last national conference and read what it says about membership and branch health. Then read the step-aside guidelines. Then find one court judgment setting aside an ANC provincial conference and establish which rule was breached.
Recalls, and the party above the state:
Two presidents removed by a party committee with no constitutional standing, and the exact mechanism that made it work.

**What the Constitution says about removing a President**, from stage 8:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 86** | **the National Assembly elects the President** from among its members, at its first sitting and whenever a vacancy occurs |
| **Section 102(2)** | **a motion of no confidence in the President, passed by a majority of the Assembly's members, requires the President and the whole Cabinet to resign** |
| **Section 89** | **removal for a serious violation of the Constitution or the law, serious misconduct, or inability to perform** — requiring **a two-thirds majority**, and carrying the loss of benefits |
| **What is not mentioned** | **any political party, any party committee, or any party conference** |

**And what actually happened, twice:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **September 2008** | **the ANC's National Executive Committee resolved to recall President Thabo Mbeki.** He resigned the following day, nine months before the end of his term. **Kgalema Motlanthe served as caretaker President until the 2009 election** |
| **February 2018** | **after the December 2017 national conference elected a new party President, the NEC resolved to recall President Jacob Zuma.** He resisted for several days, **then resigned** |
| **The constitutional basis of either recall** | **none. The NEC is a party body** |
| **Also recalled this way** | **premiers and mayors, routinely** |

---

**So how does a body with no constitutional power remove a head of state? The mechanism is precise and it is worth setting out, because it explains more of South African politics than any other single chain:**

| Step | Why it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the party holds a majority of the National Assembly's seats** |
| **2** | **those members sit on closed party lists** — from the ballot lesson |
| **3** | **section 47(3)(c): a member who ceases to be a member of the party loses the seat** |
| **4** | **so an MP who defies the party faces expulsion and the loss of their seat and salary** |
| **5** | **therefore the party's instruction to vote for a motion of no confidence is credible** |
| **6** | **so a President who refuses to resign faces a section 102 motion they will lose** |
| **7** | **resignation is therefore the rational response, and no vote is needed** |

**Read steps 2, 3 and 4 again.** **The recall mechanism is a consequence of the electoral system.** In a constituency system, a member whose local voters elected them has an independent base and the threat is weaker. **The closed list is what converts an internal party decision into a constitutional outcome.**

**That is the single clearest demonstration of this stage's thesis.**

---

**The two readings, and both are serious:**

| The recall is legitimate | The recall is a constitutional problem |
| --- | --- |
| **the President is elected by the Assembly, not by voters directly**, so the Assembly's majority party removing its own nominee is within the system's logic | **the Constitution provides two removal routes, with specified grounds and thresholds, and neither was used** |
| **it is faster and less destabilising** than a contested impeachment, and in 2008 and 2018 it avoided a prolonged crisis | **no grounds are stated and no evidence is tested** — a recall requires only a majority of a party committee |
| **parliamentary systems everywhere** see prime ministers removed by their parties — the United Kingdom and Australia have done it repeatedly | **those are parliamentary systems where members have constituencies**; here the members have no independent mandate at all |
| **voters elect a party, and the party's leadership is the party's business** | **the President holds an office with constitutional powers**, and section 83 makes them Head of State, not a party functionary |

**The comparison with Westminster is the strongest argument for the defence and it has a real answer: in those systems a leader's removal is checked by members who hold their own seats.** **Remove that check and a party's internal faction fight becomes the mechanism for changing a head of state.**

---

**And the contrast with a case where the constitutional route was used**, which is instructive:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2022** | an **independent panel under section 89**, appointed by the Speaker and chaired by a former Chief Justice, considered the **Phala Phala** matter and reported that there was **prima facie evidence of a serious violation** warranting a full inquiry |
| **What happened** | **the National Assembly voted not to proceed**, with the governing party's members voting as a bloc |
| **What it shows** | **the section 89 route exists, has now been exercised to the point of a panel report, and was stopped by the same majority-plus-closed-list mechanism** |
| **The comparison** | **a sitting President survived the constitutional removal process and two previous Presidents were removed by a party committee.** **Both outcomes were produced by party discipline rather than by the Constitution's design** |

**From stage 8's conclusion: this is why Zondo's institutional recommendations ended at the electoral system.**

**Practice.** Read sections 86, 89 and 102 together. Then read section 47(3)(c). Then write out the seven-step chain above from memory. Then find the section 89 panel's 2022 report and the Assembly's vote, and establish what each party did.
The Alliance:
A governing party, a communist party that does not contest elections, and a trade union federation — and what has happened to the arrangement.

**The Tripartite Alliance is the ANC, the South African Communist Party and COSATU**, with the civic movement **SANCO** often counted as a fourth partner. **It is not a coalition in the parliamentary sense: only one of the partners contests elections.**

| Partner | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC** | the governing party — the last two lessons |
| **The SACP** | **founded 1921 as the Communist Party of South Africa**, banned in 1950, reconstituted underground in 1953, unbanned in 1990. **It does not contest elections; its members stand on ANC lists** and have held senior Cabinet positions |
| **COSATU** | **the Congress of South African Trade Unions, founded 1985** — the largest federation, from the wages lesson in stage 9 |
| **SANCO** | the South African National Civic Organisation, formed from the 1980s civic associations |

**The arrangement's logic**, which is historical: **the three organisations were the internal and external pillars of the same struggle.** The SACP supplied much of the ANC's theoretical framework and a large share of its exile leadership; **the unions supplied the mass mobilisation of the 1980s that made the country ungovernable** — stage 5. **The alliance is the organisational residue of that.**

---

**What each partner gets:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The ANC gets** | **electoral machinery** — union and civic structures campaigning — **and legitimacy with organised labour and the left** |
| **The SACP gets** | **positions and policy influence without electoral risk** — it has never had to test its support at the ballot box |
| **COSATU gets** | **direct access to government**, the Nedlac seat from stage 9, and a say in ANC policy and lists |
| **The forum** | **the Alliance Political Council and periodic alliance summits**, which are where the real negotiation happens — **and which have no public record** |

**From stage 1's sources lesson: alliance decisions are made in a forum with no minutes, no statutory basis and no public reporting, and they have shaped national policy.** That is a genuine transparency problem and it is rarely named as one.

---

**The ruptures, in order:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1996 — GEAR** | from stage 9. **Announced without alliance consultation and declared non-negotiable.** COSATU and the SACP regarded it as the abandonment of the RDP, and **the argument structured alliance politics for a decade** |
| **2005–07 — the Zuma turn** | **COSATU and the SACP backed Jacob Zuma against Thabo Mbeki**, on the basis that Mbeki's government was technocratic and anti-labour. **Polokwane in 2007 was substantially an alliance revolt** |
| **2012–15 — the NUMSA split** | **NUMSA, COSATU's largest affiliate, called for the federation to break the alliance and for a workers' party**; it was **expelled in 2014**, and the general secretary was removed in 2015 |
| **2017 — SAFTU** | **the South African Federation of Trade Unions was formed**, outside the alliance, around NUMSA and the expelled leadership — **the first serious federation-level challenge to COSATU since 1985** |
| **2017 onward — the SACP's electoral question** | **the SACP's 2017 congress resolved to contest elections "in some form"**, and it has debated and deferred the question since, contesting marginally at local level |
| **2024 — the GNU** | **both COSATU and the SACP opposed including the DA in a government of national unity**, and the ANC did it anyway |

> **As of 14 October 2026: the SACP has resolved to contest elections in its own right, with the municipal elections of 4 November 2026 the test. Check the IEC's registered party list and the result. If the SACP contests independently and COSATU's affiliates divide their support, the alliance as constituted since 1990 will have effectively ended.**

---

**The analytical question, stated as two positions:**

| The alliance still matters | The alliance is a formality |
| --- | --- |
| **COSATU's structures still campaign**, and in a 40% election every point of organisation counts | **the ANC's vote fell to 40% with the alliance intact**, so its electoral value is demonstrably limited |
| **the SACP's and COSATU's policy positions are visible** in the NHI, the wage bill, the labour legislation and the opposition to privatisation | **the partners opposed GEAR, the Scorpions' creation, the NDP's labour chapter and the GNU, and lost each time** |
| **the alliance veto on privatising SOEs has held** for thirty years, which is a significant achieved outcome | **COSATU's membership base is now public sector**, so its interest is the wage bill, which puts it at odds with the governing party's fiscal position |
| **SANCO and the union structures remain the ANC's only mass presence** in many communities | **SAFTU, the EFF and now MK compete for the same constituency**, and are not in the alliance |

**The strongest evidence for the second column is the privatisation record read the other way:** stage 9's reform programme has **introduced private participation in electricity generation, rail operations and port terminals** — **the alliance's central red line, crossed by structural separation rather than by sale.** **Whether that counts as a defeat for the alliance or a compromise it accepted is genuinely unclear, and stage 12 takes it up.**

**Practice.** Find the SACP's most recent congress resolutions on contesting elections. Then find COSATU's submission on the most recent Budget and compare it with the Treasury's position on the wage bill. Then find an alliance summit communiqué and note what it commits anybody to. Then establish which Cabinet members have been SACP central committee members.
The DA and its lineage:
A party descended from the parliamentary opposition to apartheid, grown from under 2% to over 20%, governing one province — and unresolved about what it is.

**The lineage, which the party itself emphasises and which is genuinely relevant:**

| Year | Party |
| --- | --- |
| **1934–1977** | **the United Party** — Smuts's party, the official opposition after 1948, opposing apartheid's implementation while accepting segregation |
| **1959** | **the Progressive Party** — eleven UP MPs broke away over the UP's acceptance of the removal of African representation, adopting a qualified franchise and a bill of rights |
| **1961–1974** | **Helen Suzman was the Progressive Party's only MP** — thirteen years as a one-person opposition, which is the party's founding story |
| **1975–1977** | the Progressive Reform Party |
| **1977–1989** | **the Progressive Federal Party**, which became **the official opposition** after the UP's dissolution |
| **1989** | **the Democratic Party** — a merger of the PFP with two smaller formations |
| **2000** | **the Democratic Alliance** — the DP merged with the **New National Party** (the National Party's successor) and the Federal Alliance |
| **2001–2005** | **the NNP left the DA and then merged into the ANC.** The DA kept the name |

**That history is used in two ways and both readings are available in the record:** **the party that opposed apartheid in Parliament when almost nobody did** — Suzman's record is real and documented — **and the party that absorbed the National Party's remnant in 2000** and inherited part of its electorate.

**The leaders**: Zach de Beer, then **Tony Leon (1994–2007)**, **Helen Zille (2007–2015)**, **Mmusi Maimane (2015–2019)**, **John Steenhuisen (interim 2019, elected 2020)**.

---

**The vote share, which is the clearest growth story in South African politics:**

| Election | Share |
| --- | --- |
| **1994 (DP)** | **1.7%** |
| **1999 (DP)** | **9.6%** |
| **2004 (DA)** | **12.4%** |
| **2009** | **16.7%** |
| **2014** | **22.2%** |
| **2019** | **20.8%** |
| **2024** | **21.8%** |

**From 1.7% to 22% in twenty years, and then a plateau at just over a fifth for three successive elections.** **The plateau is the fact the party's internal argument is about.**

**And the governing record:** **Cape Town from 2006 and the Western Cape from 2009**, continuously.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The claim** | from stage 8's variance table — **the Western Cape and Cape Town consistently produce the best audit outcomes, the best service delivery indicators and among the best health and education outcomes in the country** |
| **The counter-claims** | the province **started from the best inherited base**, has the smallest former-homeland territory and a different demographic and fiscal profile; and **the Cape Town drought of 2017–18** and persistent township service inequality are cited against it |
| **The honest position** | **the governance indicators are real and measurable, and the base effect is also real.** **The best evidence is the trend within the province and the comparison with Gauteng**, which has a similarly urban profile |

---

**The identity argument, which is the party's central unresolved question.**

**The question is simple to state: should the DA accept race-based redress?**

| The position that it should not | The position that it should |
| --- | --- |
| **non-racialism means the state must not classify people by race** — the Constitution's goal is a society where race is irrelevant, and race-based policy entrenches the category | **disadvantage in South Africa was imposed by race and is still distributed by race** — a policy blind to race cannot reach it |
| **means-testing and poverty targeting reach the disadvantaged** without the classification, and reach poor people of every group | **section 9(2) expressly permits race-based measures**, and *Van Heerden* from stage 9 sets the test they must pass |
| **BEE's record** — stage 9 — **shows race-based redress producing an elite** rather than broad gains | **a party that rejects redress cannot win a majority** in a country where the great majority of voters experienced racial dispossession |
| it is **the classical liberal position** the party's lineage comes from | it is **what the party's growth beyond its base required**, which the 2014–2019 period tested |

**The institutional history of that argument:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2014–2019** | **under Maimane the party moved toward accepting redress**, adopting diversity language and a position acknowledging race as a proxy for disadvantage |
| **2019** | **the party's vote fell slightly**, and a post-election review followed. **Maimane resigned**, as did the Johannesburg mayor, both leaving the party |
| **2020** | **a policy conference resolved against using race as a proxy for disadvantage**, in favour of means-based criteria |
| **Since** | **the party has held that position**, with the plateau at 21–22% as the evidence each side cites |

**Both sides read the same numbers.** **The classical liberal wing points to the vote holding at 21.8% in 2024 after the repositioning.** **The other wing points to the party's failure to grow beyond a fifth, and to its support remaining heavily concentrated among minority voters.** **Not to arrive at a position: the two readings are testable against the 2026 and 2029 results.**

---

**And the structural facts worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal structure** | **federal, deliberately** — a Federal Congress elects the leader, and a **Federal Council** with its own elected chairperson runs the organisation between congresses. **The chairperson's role has at times been more powerful than the leader's**, which is unusual |
| **Candidate selection** | **more contested internally than the ANC's**, with electoral colleges and interviews, and recurring disputes about the outcomes |
| **Its position on devolution** | **a consistent push for provincial powers** — policing, rail, ports — **which is stage 12's devolution argument**, and which the Western Cape has pursued through legislation and litigation |
| **The Cape independence question** | **a fringe position the party formally rejects**, and which recurs in Western Cape politics |
| **2024** | **the DA entered the Government of National Unity**, taking Cabinet posts — stage 11 |

**Practice.** Find the DA's 2024 manifesto and its position on BEE and employment equity. Then find Helen Suzman's parliamentary record and one speech. Then compare the Western Cape's and Gauteng's audit outcomes and matric throughput over five years. Then read the party's 2020 policy conference resolution on race as a proxy.
The EFF:
A party founded out of an expulsion, which forced three issues onto the national agenda and litigated Parliament's accountability rules into existence.

**The origin:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The context** | **the ANC Youth League under Julius Malema** campaigned from 2008 on **"economic freedom in our lifetime"**, pressing nationalisation of mines and expropriation of land |
| **2012** | **Malema was expelled from the ANC** after disciplinary proceedings, for sowing division and bringing the organisation into disrepute |
| **July 2013** | **the Economic Freedom Fighters was launched** |
| **The style** | **red overalls and domestic worker uniforms in Parliament** — a deliberate statement that the legislature should look like the people it represents |

**The seven cardinal pillars**, which are the party's programme and should be read in its own words:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **expropriation of South Africa's land without compensation for equal redistribution in use** |
| **2** | **nationalisation of mines, banks and other strategic sectors of the economy, without compensation** |
| **3** | **building state and government capacity**, which will lead to the abolishment of tenders |
| **4** | **free quality education, healthcare, houses and sanitation** |
| **5** | **massive protected industrial development** to create millions of sustainable jobs, including the introduction of minimum wages |
| **6** | **massive development of the African economy** and advocating for a move from reconciliation to justice |
| **7** | **open, accountable, corruption-free government and society** without fear of victimisation by state agencies |

**Note pillars 3 and 7 against stage 8**: **state capacity and the abolition of the tender system** is a substantive institutional position, and it is rarely engaged with when the party is discussed.

---

**The results:**

| Election | Share |
| --- | --- |
| **2014** | **6.35%**, from a standing start fourteen months after founding |
| **2016 (local)** | **8.2%** |
| **2019** | **10.8%** |
| **2021 (local)** | **10.3%** |
| **2024** | **9.5%** — **fourth place**, having been overtaken by MK |

**The 2024 result is the party's first reverse**, and the reason is specific: **MK's emergence took a substantial share of the same constituency**, particularly in KwaZulu-Natal, and the EFF's own former deputy president left to lead MK's parliamentary caucus.

---

**The parliamentary record, which is the most misreported thing about the party.**

**The conduct is well known:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **August 2014** | **"Pay back the money"** — the sustained disruption of question time over the Nkandla findings, leading to removals from the chamber by security |
| **2015–2017** | **repeated State of the Nation Address disruptions**, including the 2015 signal-jamming episode and physical removals |
| **The criticism** | **that it degrades the institution** and substitutes spectacle for legislative work |

**And the litigation record is the part usually left out:**

| Case | What it established |
| --- | --- |
| ***EFF v Speaker* (2016)** | **the Public Protector's remedial action binds unless set aside**, and the Assembly's resolution absolving the President was unlawful — **the Nkandla judgment from stage 8** |
| ***UDM v Speaker* (2017)** | brought with others — **the Speaker has the power to allow a secret ballot** in a motion of no confidence |
| ***EFF v Speaker* (2017)** | **the National Assembly had failed to make rules for a section 89 impeachment inquiry**, and was ordered to make them — **which is why the 2022 Phala Phala panel existed at all** |

**So the party most criticised for disrupting Parliament is the party whose litigation created Parliament's impeachment procedure and established that the Public Protector's findings bind the President.** **Both facts are true and they belong in the same paragraph.**

---

**The criticisms, in their strongest form:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **VBS** | **the collapse of VBS Mutual Bank** — a small bank whose looting cost municipalities and individual depositors on the order of R2bn — **produced a report ("The Great Bank Heist") that traced payments to an entity associated with the brother of the party's deputy president.** The party disputes the characterisation; **the allegations have not been tested in a criminal court against the party's leaders** |
| **Funding opacity** | the party's disclosed donations under the funding law are small relative to its operations, which is a question asked of several parties |
| **Conduct outside Parliament** | **confrontational protest actions** at schools, retailers and farming towns, with litigation following several of them |
| **The "kill the boer" litigation** | the Equality Court found the chant, as used, **was not hate speech** in its context as a historical struggle song, and **the Supreme Court of Appeal upheld that in 2024** — a finding many find indefensible and which is a genuine section 16 question |
| **Coalition behaviour** | **it supported DA mayors in the 2016 metros and then withdrew**, and in 2023 helped install a mayor from a party with a single seat. **Critics call it destabilising; the party calls it leverage** |

**And the defence that even its opponents generally concede:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Agenda-setting** | **expropriation without compensation, free higher education, and the nationalisation question were marginal in 2013 and central by 2017.** The constitutional amendment attempt, the fee-free policy announcement of 2017, and the land debate of stages 7 and 9 all followed the pressure |
| **Accountability** | **the litigation record above** |
| **Representation** | **it gave a political home to a young, unemployed constituency** that abstention had otherwise absorbed — which the turnout lesson makes relevant |

**Practice.** Read the seven cardinal pillars in the party's own founding manifesto. Then read *EFF v Speaker* (2017) on the impeachment rules. Then find the EFF's 2024 result by province and compare it with 2019. Then find the party's disclosed donations in the IEC's funding reports.
The IFP, and the regional parties:
A party that nearly broke the transition, a long decline and a recovery, and the long tail of small parties the system's lack of a threshold produces.

**The IFP, because its history is load-bearing for stages 5 and 6:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1975** | **Inkatha was founded by Mangosuthu Buthelezi**, reviving the name of a 1920s Zulu cultural organisation, as a cultural movement that functioned as **the ruling party of the KwaZulu homeland** |
| **The crucial refusal** | **Buthelezi refused "independence" for KwaZulu** — the only major homeland leader to do so — **which denied the apartheid government its central objective** and is the strongest point in the party's defence of its record |
| **1990–94** | **the violence** of stage 6 — **on the order of 14,000 deaths**, concentrated in Natal and on the Reef, between Inkatha and ANC-aligned forces, **with the state security services' covert support for Inkatha established by the TRC and by the Goldstone Commission** |
| **The Caprivi trainees** | **about 200 Inkatha members trained by the SADF in 1986** in the Caprivi Strip, for offensive operations — a documented finding |
| **April 1994** | **the IFP joined the election a week before it**, after the last-minute constitutional concessions of stage 6. **Its participation is the reason the election was not a civil war** |
| **1994–2004** | **Buthelezi was Minister of Home Affairs**, and the IFP governed KwaZulu-Natal |

**That is a record that cannot be summarised in one direction.** **The party was the apartheid state's covert ally against the ANC, it refused the homeland independence that apartheid needed, and its late entry into the 1994 election prevented a catastrophe.** **All three are established.**

**The decline and the recovery:**

| Election | National share |
| --- | --- |
| **1994** | **10.5%**, and the KwaZulu-Natal government |
| **1999** | 8.6% |
| **2004** | **7.0%** — and **it lost KwaZulu-Natal to the ANC** |
| **2009** | 4.6% |
| **2014** | **2.4%** — after **the National Freedom Party split away in 2011** |
| **2019** | 3.4% |
| **2024** | **3.9% nationally, and a strong second place in KwaZulu-Natal**, entering both the national Government of National Unity and the KwaZulu-Natal provincial coalition |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Leadership** | **Velenkosini Hlabisa became leader in 2019; Buthelezi died in September 2023** at 95, having led the organisation for 44 years |
| **Its politics** | **federalism and devolution of powers to provinces, recognition of traditional leadership, free-market economics, and social conservatism** |
| **Its 2024 position** | **Minister of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs** — which puts the party in charge of the local government portfolio of stage 8 |

---

**The long tail, and why it exists.** From the ballot lesson: **there is no electoral threshold, and a seat costs roughly a quarter of one per cent of the national vote.** **So a party with 40,000 supporters sits in Parliament.** In 2024, **more than fifty parties contested the national ballot and about eighteen won seats.**

| Party | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Freedom Front Plus (FF+)** | **founded 1994 by General Constand Viljoen** as the constitutional route for Afrikaner self-determination, after he declined an armed alternative — stage 6. **Pursues section 235 self-determination, cultural rights and property rights.** Around 1 to 2.5% |
| **African Christian Democratic Party (ACDP)** | **1993**, Christian-conservative; opposed the 1996 Constitution on the abortion and death penalty provisions. Consistently around 1% |
| **United Democratic Movement (UDM)** | **1997**, founded by **Bantu Holomisa**, former Transkei military leader, after his expulsion from the ANC for naming a minister before the TRC. **Brought *UDM v Speaker* (2017)** |
| **Congress of the People (COPE)** | **2008** — **the Mbeki-aligned split after his recall**, led by Mosiuoa Lekota. **Won 7.4% in 2009 and then collapsed**, through internal leadership litigation, to a fraction of a per cent. **The cautionary tale of South African splits** |
| **GOOD** | **2018**, founded by Patricia de Lille after leaving the DA |
| **ActionSA** | **2020**, founded by Herman Mashaba after leaving the DA; contests selectively, strongest in Gauteng metros |
| **Patriotic Alliance (PA)** | **2013**, led by Gayton McKenzie; strongest in coloured working-class communities in the Western and Northern Cape; **in the 2024 national executive** |
| **Al Jama-ah, the African Independent Congress, Rise Mzansi, BOSA, the PAC and AZAPO** | smaller again — **and Al Jama-ah, with one parliamentary seat, held the Johannesburg mayoralty from 2023** with EFF and ANC support |
| **The National Freedom Party (NFP)** | **the 2011 IFP split**, which cost the IFP KwaZulu-Natal seats and then declined itself |

---

**What the long tail does, in both directions:**

| The case for no threshold | The case for one |
| --- | --- |
| **every vote elects somebody** — a system with a 5% threshold would have discarded the votes of millions across these parties | **fragmentation makes coalitions unstable** — stage 8's local government lesson, where a one-seat party can hold a metro |
| **minority and regional views get real representation** — Afrikaner self-determination, Christian conservatism, Muslim representation, coloured working-class politics | **a party with one seat holding a mayoralty** is disproportionate leverage |
| **it lowers the barrier to new entry**, which is why the EFF and MK could appear and grow | **COPE's collapse shows that low barriers also produce parties that cannot sustain themselves**, wasting the mandate given to them |
| **it is what section 46's proportionality requirement most naturally produces** | **coalition legislation or a threshold would require only an ordinary statute** |

**Practice.** Open the IEC's 2024 results and list every party that won a seat, with its vote share. Then find the FF+'s position on section 235 self-determination. Then trace COPE's share from 2009 to 2024 and find out what happened. Then establish which small parties hold executive positions in the national or any provincial government.
MK, and the 2024 realignment:
A party registered eight months before an election, led from outside Parliament by a man the Constitutional Court ruled ineligible to stand, which took third place.

**The sequence, which is worth having exactly:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **September 2023** | **the uMkhonto weSizwe Party was registered with the IEC** by a private individual — using the name of the ANC's former armed wing |
| **16 December 2023** | **Jacob Zuma announced he would campaign for MK and would not vote for the ANC**, while saying he remained an ANC member |
| **January 2024** | **the ANC suspended him**, and later expelled him |
| **Early 2024** | **the ANC litigated** — to deregister the party and over the use of the name and logo — **and failed to have it removed from the ballot**; the trademark dispute continued separately |
| **April 2024** | **the Electoral Court ruled that Zuma could stand** as a candidate |
| **20 May 2024** | **the Constitutional Court held he was ineligible** — **section 47(1)(e)**: a person convicted of an offence and **sentenced to more than twelve months' imprisonment without the option of a fine** may not be a member of the Assembly for five years after the sentence. **His 2021 contempt sentence of fifteen months disqualified him** |
| **29 May 2024** | **MK won 14.58% of the national vote and 58 seats** — third place — **and about 45% in KwaZulu-Natal**, becoming the largest party in that province |
| **His face remained on the ballot** | and the party's campaign was built on him |

**Three things in that sequence are genuinely remarkable:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The speed** | **from registration to third place in eight months**, with no organisational history, no funding disclosure of any scale, and no conventional campaign infrastructure |
| **The candidate** | **a former President, expelled from the governing party, ruled ineligible to sit, leading a party to 58 seats from outside the legislature** |
| **The geography** | **KwaZulu-Natal flipped.** The ANC's KZN vote collapsed, the IFP recovered, and MK took the largest share — **which is the single largest regional realignment since 1994** |

---

**What MK says it stands for**, and this is the part that matters for stages 7 and 12, because it is a constitutional position no other party in Parliament holds:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Parliamentary sovereignty** | **the party's platform proposes replacing constitutional supremacy with the sovereignty of Parliament** — so that **Parliament, not the Constitutional Court, has the final word** |
| **A chamber of traditional leaders** | **an unelected upper house** of traditional leaders with real legislative power |
| **Land** | **expropriation without compensation**, and the return of land to traditional authorities |
| **The economy** | nationalisation of mines, banks and strategic sectors; a sovereign wealth fund; free education and health care |
| **Other positions** | restoring the death penalty; reviewing the Constitution in full |

**The first item is the one to take seriously.** From stage 7: **section 2 — constitutional supremacy — is the founding structural choice of the post-1994 order**, and stages 7 and 8 are an extended demonstration of what it has produced. **A party with 58 seats proposes to reverse it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The case made for it** | **the courts have accumulated power that elected representatives should hold**; the judicialisation-of-politics critique from stage 8, taken to its conclusion; and **an elected majority should be able to act without judicial veto** |
| **The case against** | **every institutional gain in stages 7 and 8 came from justiciable rights and binding judgments** — Nkandla, *Glenister*, *Corruption Watch*, the socio-economic rights cases. **Parliamentary sovereignty was the apartheid order's doctrine**, and stage 5 is what it produced |
| **And the amendment arithmetic** | **section 1 requires 75% of the Assembly plus six provinces** — from stage 7. **This cannot be done by any foreseeable majority** |

**That last row matters: the proposal is constitutionally almost unachievable, which is why it functions as a statement of political orientation rather than a programme.** **From stage 1's party document lesson: read it as evidence of what the party wants said about it.**

---

**And what MK has done since:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It did not join the Government of National Unity** | and sits in opposition |
| **It formed a bloc with the EFF** | a "progressive caucus" arrangement, with the stated aim of coordinating opposition |
| **Leadership instability** | **a rapid turnover of parliamentary leaders and senior office-holders** in its first years, which is the standard pattern for a party assembled quickly around one person |
| **Its KZN position** | **the largest party in the province, in opposition to a provincial coalition** of the ANC, IFP and DA |

> **As of 14 October 2026: MK's durability is untested. The municipal elections of 4 November 2026 are the first local test of whether it has structures or only a vote. Check the result against its 2024 share, especially in KwaZulu-Natal. COPE's 7.4% in 2009 and subsequent collapse is the base rate for parties assembled quickly around a single leader.**

**Practice.** Read section 47(1)(e) and the Constitutional Court's May 2024 judgment. Then find MK's 2024 manifesto and its section on the Constitution. Then compare the ANC's, IFP's and MK's KwaZulu-Natal shares in 2019 and 2024. Then find COPE's 2009 and 2014 results and write down what you would watch for in MK's 2026 result.
Why the ANC lost its majority:
Thirty years of vote shares, a collapse in 2024, and the arithmetic of abstention that most accounts leave out.

**The record:**

| Election | ANC share | ANC votes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1994** | **62.65%** | about 12.2 million |
| **1999** | **66.35%** | about 10.6 million |
| **2004** | **69.69%** | about 10.9 million |
| **2009** | **65.90%** | about 11.7 million |
| **2014** | **62.15%** | about 11.4 million |
| **2019** | **57.50%** | about 10.0 million |
| **2024** | **40.18%** | **about 6.5 million** |

**Read the second column and then the third.** The share declined gradually from 2004 and then fell **seventeen points in one election.** And in absolute votes: **the ANC lost about 3.5 million voters between 2019 and 2024**, and **about 5.7 million against its 2009 peak.**

---

**But the share figures understate what happened, because turnout fell throughout.**

| Election | Turnout, as a share of registered voters |
| --- | --- |
| **1999** | **about 89%** |
| **2004** | **about 77%** |
| **2009** | **about 77%** |
| **2014** | **about 73%** |
| **2019** | **about 66%** |
| **2024** | **about 59%** |
| **2021 (local)** | **about 46%** |

**And registration itself is incomplete.** In 2024: **roughly 27.8 million registered voters, against a voting-age population of roughly 42 million.**

**So do the arithmetic that almost nobody does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Voting-age population** | **about 42 million** |
| **Registered** | **about 27.8 million** — so **roughly 14 million eligible adults were not on the roll** |
| **Voted** | **about 16.2 million** — **roughly 39% of eligible adults** |
| **The ANC's 40.18%** | **of those 16.2 million** = about 6.5 million = **roughly 16% of the voting-age population** |
| **The largest category by far** | **the roughly 26 million eligible adults who did not vote** |

**That is the central fact of South African electoral politics now, and it belongs in every argument about mandates: the governing party's support is about one in six adults, and non-voting is larger than every party combined.**

**And the non-voters are young.** **Registration among 18-to-29-year-olds is far below the older cohorts** — the IEC publishes the breakdown. **The "born free" generation, with no personal memory of 1994, is substantially outside the electoral system rather than voting against the ANC within it.**

---

**Why the 2024 collapse, and the causes are separable:**

| Cause | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| **The MK split** | **the largest single factor. MK took 14.58%, concentrated in KwaZulu-Natal**, and most of it came from the ANC's 2019 vote. **Without MK, the ANC would plausibly have been in the low 50s** |
| **Load-shedding and service failure** | **2022 and 2023 were the worst load-shedding years** — stage 9 — and water failures, potholes and municipal collapse were the daily experience in the run-up |
| **Unemployment and per capita decline** | **a decade of falling GDP per head** — stage 9's central fact |
| **State capture and the Zondo findings** | published 2022, with almost no prosecutions following — stage 8's NPA lesson |
| **July 2021** | **the unrest, with over 350 deaths** — stage 11 — and the state's visible loss of control |
| **Generational replacement** | the oldest voters with direct liberation loyalty are being replaced by a cohort with none, **which is a slow, permanent trend rather than a shock** |
| **Local government** | **the 2021 result at 45% had already signalled it**, and local government is where the ANC's brand is most damaged |

**Note that most of these are stage 8 and stage 9 material.** **The electoral result is the dependent variable**: institutional failure and economic stagnation, measured over a decade, produced it. **That is the whole case for stages 8 and 9 existing.**

---

**And the two readings of the 2024 result, both of which are defensible:**

| A realignment | A rebuke within continuity |
| --- | --- |
| **the dominant-party era ended** — South Africa now has a genuinely competitive system with coalition government as the norm | **the ANC still leads the government, holds the Presidency, and governs seven provinces** in some form |
| **MK's and the EFF's combined 24% is a substantial anti-constitutional-settlement vote**, which is new | **the opposition did not grow** — the DA was flat at 21.8%, the EFF fell, and the ANC's losses went to a party built on a former ANC President. **This was an ANC civil war fought at the ballot box** |
| **the governing party accepted a coalition with its principal opponent**, which is a system-level change | **no new political force with its own programme broke through**; the realignment was within the liberation movement's constituency |
| **turnout at 59% and falling** signals a legitimacy problem for the whole system, not just one party | **turnout declines are normal** in maturing democracies after a founding election |

**Not to arrive at a position. The 2026 local and 2029 national results test both.**

**Practice.** Build the table at the top of this lesson yourself from the IEC's results site. Then find the 2024 registration figures by age band. Then calculate what share of the voting-age population voted for each of the top four parties. Then work out what the ANC's share would have been if MK's votes had gone to it.
Coalitions, 2016 to now:
Ten years of coalition government, from the metros that became ungovernable to the national unity government — and what the record actually shows.

**The sequence, because the local experience came first and shaped expectations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **August 2016** | **the ANC lost Johannesburg, Tshwane and Nelson Mandela Bay.** DA-led administrations took office with **EFF support that was explicitly not a coalition** — the EFF took no positions and gave vote-by-vote backing |
| **2017–2019** | **the arrangement broke down.** The Nelson Mandela Bay mayor was removed in 2018; Tshwane and Johannesburg saw repeated motions, walkouts and administrative paralysis |
| **November 2021** | **about 60 to 70 of 257 councils had no majority.** Coalitions formed everywhere, including in all the major metros |
| **2021–2024, Johannesburg** | **a succession of mayors** — a DA mayor removed and reinstated by court order and removed again; **then a mayor from a party holding a single council seat**, with ANC and EFF support; then an ANC mayor. **On the order of five mayors in three years** |
| **Nelson Mandela Bay and Tshwane** | comparable churn |
| **The consequence** | **stage 8's finding: political instability is among the largest causes of municipal failure**, because each change of mayor changes the senior management, and a water network needs a five-year plan |

**That is the base rate against which the national coalition was formed, and it is why almost nobody expected the national arrangement to hold.**

---

**The 2024 national result, and the government it produced:**

| Party | Share |
| --- | --- |
| **ANC** | **40.18%** |
| **DA** | **21.81%** |
| **MK** | **14.58%** |
| **EFF** | **9.52%** |
| **IFP** | **3.85%** |
| **PA** | **2.06%** |
| **VF+ / FF+** | **1.36%** |
| **ActionSA** | about 1.2% |
| **Others** | the long tail |

**The arithmetic forced a choice.** **The ANC needed partners worth at least 10 points.** The options:

| Option | Why it was not taken |
| --- | --- |
| **ANC + MK** | **MK's price was reportedly the removal of the President**, and the parties had just fought an election against each other |
| **ANC + EFF** | **the policy distance on property and the Reserve Bank**, and the market and investor reaction, which stage 9's Nenegate lesson makes concrete |
| **ANC + EFF + MK** | the same, compounded |
| **ANC + DA + others** | **taken** |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **14 June 2024** | **a Statement of Intent was signed**, and the National Assembly **re-elected Cyril Ramaphosa as President** |
| **The parties** | **ten, in the end** — ANC, DA, IFP, PA, GOOD, PAC, FF+, UDM, Rise Mzansi and Al Jama-ah |
| **30 June 2024** | **the Cabinet was announced** — a large executive, with **roughly a dozen posts going to parties other than the ANC**, the DA taking six |
| **The name** | **a "Government of National Unity"**, deliberately echoing stage 6's 1994 GNU — **although the 1994 version was constitutionally mandated by the interim Constitution and this one is a political agreement** |
| **The decision rule** | **"sufficient consensus"**, with **a clearing house mechanism** for resolving disputes before they become public — both terms borrowed from CODESA, stage 6 |

**And the provinces**, which are usually left out: **Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal both required coalition or minority arrangements**, with KwaZulu-Natal governed by an ANC–IFP–DA–NFP arrangement against an MK opposition.

---

**What the record shows so far**, which is the honest assessment:

| What has held | What has strained |
| --- | --- |
| **the arrangement survived its first budget crisis** — the 2025 VAT episode from stage 9, which took three budgets and a court case | **that same episode showed the executive can no longer assume its fiscal framework will pass** |
| **the structural reforms continued** — electricity, logistics, visas, water licensing | **major policy disputes** — NHI, the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act's language and admissions provisions, expropriation, and foreign policy — **have been managed by deferral rather than resolution** |
| **no party has left**, and the Cabinet has functioned | **the clearing house has been used slowly**, and disputes have been conducted publicly |
| **the markets and the rating agencies responded positively** to the arrangement's formation | **the ANC's alliance partners opposed it** — the Alliance lesson — and the left of the ANC continues to |

**The structural problem both columns point at: the agreement has no enforcement mechanism.** **"Sufficient consensus" means a party can block, and nothing happens if it does.** From the 1994 precedent in stage 6: **the National Party walked out of the 1996 GNU with two years to run, and nothing followed.**

---

**And the reform proposals, which are stage 12's material:**

| Proposal | What it would do |
| --- | --- |
| **A threshold for coalition participation** | require a minimum vote share to hold executive office, ending **one-seat mayoralties** |
| **A constructive vote of no confidence** | **a mayor or President may only be removed if a replacement is simultaneously elected** — the German model, which prevents removal without an alternative |
| **Cooling-off periods** | **bar motions of no confidence in the first and last year** of a council's term |
| **Codified coalition agreements** | enforceable, published, with dispute resolution |
| **Direct election of mayors** | **a separate mandate for the executive**, which removes the council's ability to change the mayor at will |
| **The constraint** | **most of these require only ordinary legislation**; the electoral system itself is in the Electoral Act, not the Constitution |

**The honest counter-argument to all of them: stability and accountability are a trade-off.** **A constructive vote of no confidence makes a bad mayor harder to remove as well as a good one.** From stage 8: **the councils that work best are those where power is contestable.**

**Practice.** Find the June 2024 Statement of Intent and read what it commits the parties to. Then list Johannesburg's mayors since 2016 with dates. Then find the German constructive vote of no confidence and work out what it would have changed in Johannesburg. Then find the current composition of the Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal executives.
Party funding:
The law that finally required disclosure, what the disclosures show, and the gap between the disclosed figures and the campaigns they supposedly funded.

**The constitutional starting point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 236** | **"To enhance multi-party democracy, national legislation must provide for the funding of political parties participating in national and provincial legislatures on an equitable and proportional basis."** |
| **Note** | **this is a duty to fund parties publicly.** It is one of the few positive obligations in the Constitution that is unambiguously met |

**The two public funds:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Represented Political Parties' Fund** | **public money, allocated to parties in the national and provincial legislatures** — on a formula that is **largely proportional with an equitable component**, administered by the IEC |
| **The Multi-Party Democracy Fund** | **private donations pooled and distributed by the IEC** on the same basis, so that a donor can support multi-party democracy without choosing a party |

---

**And then the long period with no disclosure at all.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Until 2021** | **private donations to South African political parties were entirely unregulated and undisclosed.** No ceiling, no reporting, no prohibition on foreign or state-owned sources |
| **What that produced** | **the record is the Zondo Commission's and the journalism of stage 1's press lesson** — the Bosasa donations, Chancellor House's holdings in companies contracting with Eskom, and the funding of competing internal ANC leadership campaigns |
| **The 2017 ANC leadership contest** | **campaign funding on the order of hundreds of millions of rands on the winning side**, with the bank records made public and then sealed by court order on privacy grounds |
| **The point** | **internal party leadership contests were, and remain, outside the disclosure regime entirely** — and from the recall lesson, **an internal leadership contest selects the country's President** |

**That last row is the single largest remaining gap in South African political finance law, and it is deliberate.**

---

**The Political Party Funding Act 6 of 2018, in force 1 April 2021.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Disclosure** | **a party must disclose donations above a threshold** — set at **R100,000 from a single donor in a financial year** — **and the IEC publishes them quarterly** |
| **The cap** | **a single donor may not give more than R15 million to a party in a financial year** |
| **Prohibited sources** | **foreign governments and foreign government agencies** (except for training, skills development or policy research), **organs of state, and state-owned enterprises** |
| **Also prohibited** | **donations made in exchange for a benefit, or for an improper purpose** |
| **Records** | parties must keep records and submit audited statements |
| **Enforcement** | **the IEC**, with limited investigative capacity |
| **The precursor judgment** | ***My Vote Counts v Minister of Justice* (2018)** — **the Constitutional Court held PAIA invalid for failing to provide for the recording, preservation and access to information on private party funding**, which forced the legislation |

> **As of 14 October 2026: the R100,000 threshold and the R15m cap have themselves been litigated, on the argument that they are set too high to achieve meaningful transparency and that the process for determining them was flawed. Check the current thresholds and the status of that litigation.**

---

**What the disclosures actually show, and this is the analytically important part.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The totals** | **the disclosed donations across all parties amount to a few hundred million rands per electoral cycle** |
| **The concentration** | **a small number of individuals and companies account for most of it**, and the largest disclosed donors are generally known |
| **The pattern by party** | **the DA has consistently disclosed the most**, the ANC substantial amounts, and **several parties with large national vote shares have disclosed very little** |
| **The problem** | **the disclosed amounts are implausibly small relative to the campaigns observed** — national billboard, broadcast, transport, rally and digital campaigns across nine provinces |
| **The possible explanations** | **donations below the threshold** (R99,000 from many sources is invisible); **in-kind support** that is poorly captured; **spending by third parties** who are not the party; **and non-compliance** |

**From stage 1: when a published figure is implausible against observable reality, the question is what the measurement excludes.** Here the answer is known: **the threshold, in-kind support, third-party spending and internal party contests.**

**And three things the Act does not do at all:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No spending limits** | **a party may spend whatever it raises**, with no campaign expenditure ceiling |
| **No third-party regulation** | **an organisation campaigning for an outcome without being a party is unregulated** |
| **No regulation of incumbency advantage** | **government advertising, official events and state communication during a campaign period are not constrained** beyond the IEC's code |

**Practice.** Open the IEC's party funding disclosure reports and total the disclosed donations for the last full year, by party. Then compare that with what you observed of the campaigns. Then read section 236 and find the Represented Political Parties' Fund allocation for the current year. Then find the *My Vote Counts* (2018) judgment's reasoning on why funding information is necessary for the section 19 right.
Who owns the press:
Six owners, a collapse in print, the best investigative journalism on the continent, and a documented case of a narrative being bought.

**From stage 1's press lesson: place the outlet before reading it for facts.** This is the ownership map.

| Group | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| **Media24 (Naspers)** | **News24** — the largest news website in the country — **City Press, Rapport, Son, Daily Sun**, and a large magazine stable |
| **Arena Holdings** | **the Sunday Times, Business Day, Sowetan, Financial Mail, TimesLIVE** — formerly Avusa and then Tiso Blackstar, now South African-owned |
| **Independent Media** | **The Star, Cape Times, The Mercury, Pretoria News, Independent on Saturday, Sunday Tribune** — bought from an Irish group in 2013 by a consortium, **financed substantially by the Public Investment Corporation, which manages government employees' pensions** |
| **Caxton** | **The Citizen** and a very large network of free local papers |
| **Daily Maverick** | **independent, reader-funded with philanthropic support**, with the **Scorpio** investigative unit |
| **Mail & Guardian** | the oldest independent weekly, from the *Weekly Mail* of the 1980s |

**Broadcast:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The SABC** | **three television channels and about nineteen radio stations**, including the African-language stations with the largest audiences in the country. **State-owned, with the governance history from stage 8** |
| **eMedia** | **e.tv and Openview** — free-to-air |
| **MultiChoice** | **DStv** — the dominant pay-TV platform, with its own news channel |
| **Primedia** | **702, 947, Cape Talk, and Eyewitness News** |
| **Newzroom Afrika, Kagiso Media** and others | |
| **Community radio** | **on the order of 250 to 300 licensed stations** — **and this is the most under-discussed part of the map.** Community radio reaches rural and poor audiences that no newspaper does, and it is where a great deal of political communication actually happens |

**And the non-profit investigative sector**, which produces a disproportionate share of what is known:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **amaBhungane** | **broke much of state capture**, with the #GuptaLeaks |
| **GroundUp** | **courts, local government, health, housing** — and much of it republishable free |
| **Viewfinder** | **police accountability data journalism** |
| **Open Secrets, Bhekisisa, Spotlight, Oxpeckers** | economic crime, health, and environment |
| **The funding model** | **donor and philanthropic**, which is its strength (no advertiser pressure) and its vulnerability (no revenue from readers) |

---

**The collapse of print, which changes everything else:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Circulation** | **most major South African newspapers have lost half or more of their circulation since around 2010** — several have lost considerably more |
| **Closures** | **a large number of titles and local papers have closed**, and newsroom staff numbers have fallen sharply |
| **What that means for this curriculum** | **court reporting, council reporting and provincial legislature reporting have thinned drastically.** From stage 8: **a municipality with no local newspaper has no routine external scrutiny at all** |
| **What replaced it** | **digital and non-profit journalism in the metros; very little anywhere else** |
| **The paywall question** | the strongest investigative work is increasingly behind paywalls or donor-funded, **while the free-to-read layer is thinner** |

---

**Two episodes that should be in anybody's media literacy.**

**1 — The Guptas' media, and Bell Pottinger.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The outlets** | **The New Age newspaper (2010) and the ANN7 television channel (2013)**, owned by the Gupta family |
| **The funding** | **substantially state advertising and bulk subscriptions taken by government departments and state-owned enterprises** — documented in the Zondo material. **Public money funding a privately owned outlet aligned with the family capturing the public entities** |
| **Bell Pottinger** | **a London public relations firm retained in 2016** to run a campaign built on the phrase **"white monopoly capital"**, deliberately designed to reframe the state capture allegations as an attack by white business on black economic transformation |
| **The outcome** | **the campaign's mechanics were exposed**, the firm was **expelled from its industry body in 2017 and collapsed within weeks** |
| **Why it matters as a lesson** | **it is a fully documented case of a political narrative being commissioned, paid for and distributed** — and the phrase outlived the firm. **From stage 1: ask who benefits from a frame, not only whether a claim is true** |

**2 — The "rogue unit" reporting, from stage 9's SARS lesson.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What happened** | **a major Sunday newspaper ran a sustained series on an alleged unlawful covert unit at SARS**, which was used to justify the removal of the officials who had built SARS's enforcement capacity |
| **The basis** | **panel and consultancy reports that were later discredited, one of them withdrawn with an apology** |
| **The correction** | **the newspaper retracted and apologised**, the Press Ombud ruled against it, and senior editorial staff left |
| **Why it matters** | **this is the self-correction mechanism working, slowly and at great cost** — four years, a judicial commission, and an institution dismantled in the meantime. **From stage 1: a reputable outlet's sustained reporting can be wrong, and the correction is itself evidence** |

**Practice.** Take the last five news stories you read about South African politics and identify the owner of each outlet. Then find the circulation figures for one newspaper in 2010 and now. Then find the Press Council's rulings on the SARS reporting. Then find out whether your own municipality has a local newspaper covering its council, and if not, who does.
Press freedom, and its threats:
A constitutional right, a self-regulation system created under threat, a Bill that has sat unsigned for over a decade, and three judgments that matter.

**The right, from stage 7:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **16(1)** | **"Everyone has the right to freedom of expression, which includes — (a) freedom of the press and other media; (b) freedom to receive or impart information or ideas; (c) freedom of artistic creativity; and (d) academic freedom and freedom of scientific research."** |
| **16(2)** | **the right does not extend to propaganda for war, incitement of imminent violence, or advocacy of hatred based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion that constitutes incitement to cause harm** |
| **32** | **the right of access to information held by the state, and to information held by another person that is required for the exercise or protection of any right** — the basis of PAIA |

**Press freedom is named expressly in the text**, which is not universal in constitutions, and **South Africa consistently ranks among the freest media environments in Africa** on the international indices.

---

**Self-regulation, and the threat that produced it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The threat** | **the ANC's 2007 and 2010 conference and NGC resolutions proposed a statutory Media Appeals Tribunal** — a state body with power over press content, accountable to Parliament |
| **The response** | **the print industry established the Press Freedom Commission**, chaired by **former Chief Justice Pius Langa**, which reported in 2012 |
| **Its recommendation** | **"independent co-regulation"** — a self-regulatory body with **a majority of public (non-press) members**, binding rulings, no state involvement |
| **The outcome** | **the Press Council of South Africa in its current form, with the Press Code, the Press Ombud and an Appeals Panel**, with public-member majorities on its panels |
| **And the tribunal** | **was not established** |

**That is a genuine instance of a credible threat producing institutional reform**, and it is the reason the Press Council's rulings carry weight: **the industry accepted binding adjudication by a body it does not control in order to avoid a statutory one.**

**Broadcast is regulated separately** — **ICASA** licenses, and the **Broadcasting Complaints Commission** adjudicates content.

---

**The Secrecy Bill, which is an unusual constitutional artefact.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Protection of State Information Bill** | introduced in 2010, intended to replace apartheid-era secrecy legislation |
