| **The objection** | **broad classification powers, severe penalties for possession and publication of classified information, and no adequate public interest defence** — the **Right2Know** campaign was formed to oppose it |
| **What happened** | **Parliament passed it in 2013 and the President has never signed it** |
| **Its status** | **passed, unassented, and therefore not law** — for over a decade |
| **Why it matters** | **the old apartheid secrecy statutes remain partly in force**, so the reform did not happen either, **and the Bill remains available to be signed** |

---

**Three judgments that changed the position materially.**

**1 — *amaBhungane Centre for Investigative Journalism v Minister of Justice* (2021).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject** | **RICA**, the statute governing interception of communications |
| **The background** | **an investigative journalist's communications had been intercepted**, which came to light years later |
| **The findings** | **RICA was unconstitutional** for failing to provide **post-surveillance notification** to the subject; for **inadequate safeguards for the designated judge's independence**; for **no safeguards on bulk interception**; and specifically **for failing to provide special protection where the subject is a journalist or a lawyer** |
| **Why it matters** | **a journalist who cannot protect a source cannot do investigative work**, and the state had been intercepting journalists with no mechanism for them ever to find out |

**2 — *Mineral Sands Resources (Pty) Ltd v Reddell* (2022).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The subject** | **SLAPP suits** — Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation: defamation claims brought **not to vindicate a reputation but to exhaust and silence a critic** |
| **The holding** | **abuse of process may be raised as a defence** where proceedings are brought for an ulterior purpose of that kind |
| **Why it matters** | **the cost of defending a defamation claim is itself the weapon**, and a small outlet or an individual activist cannot carry it. **The judgment gives them something to plead** |

**3 — The SANEF harassment litigation**, in which the Equality Court found that **sustained public attacks on named journalists by a political party and its leaders amounted to harassment**, with orders following. **Which establishes that political intimidation of journalists is actionable.**

---

**And the pressures that remain, stated without exaggeration:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Economic** | **the collapse of print revenue from the last lesson** is a larger practical threat to South African journalism than any law. **A newsroom that cannot afford a court reporter is not censored; it is absent** |
| **State advertising** | **unregulated as a lever**, and the Gupta-era outlets from the last lesson show what it can fund |
| **The SABC** | **editorial independence has been breached and recovered** — the 2016 instruction not to broadcast footage of violent protest, the dismissal and Labour Court reinstatement of the journalists who refused, and the 2017 parliamentary inquiry |
| **Intimidation** | threats and online campaigns against named investigative journalists, documented by SANEF |
| **Newer statutes** | **the Cybercrimes Act and POPIA** create offences and data duties that interact awkwardly with journalism, and **the Film and Publications Amendment Act's online classification powers** were contested on section 16 grounds |
| **And the honest other side** | **South Africa has no journalists in prison, a free and adversarial press, successful litigation against the state, and the strongest investigative sector on the continent.** The threats are real and the baseline is good |

**Practice.** Read section 16 in full, including 16(2). Then read the *amaBhungane* RICA judgment's findings on journalists' communications. Then find the Press Council's code and one recent ruling against a major newspaper. Then establish the current status of the Protection of State Information Bill.
Civil society's route through the courts:
Why South African public interest litigation works, the cases that built the record, and the limits the litigants themselves name.

**Four provisions make it possible, and the first is the one that matters most:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 38 — standing** | **anyone may approach a court alleging a right in the Bill of Rights has been infringed or threatened**, acting: **in their own interest; on behalf of another who cannot act in their own name; as a member of, or in the interest of, a group or class; in the public interest; or as an association acting in the interest of its members** |
| **Section 34** | the right to have a dispute decided in a fair public hearing before a court |
| **Section 172(1)(b)** | a court **"may make any order that is just and equitable"** — including **suspending a declaration of invalidity, reading in words, and retaining supervisory jurisdiction** |
| **Section 7(2)** | **"The state must respect, protect, promote and fulfil the rights in the Bill of Rights"** — a positive duty, which makes a failure to act justiciable |

**Section 38's public interest standing is extraordinarily broad by comparative standards.** In many jurisdictions an organisation must show that it is personally affected. **Here, an NGO with no personal interest may litigate on behalf of people it has never met.** From stage 7's enforcement lesson: **that single choice is the reason this stage's lesson exists.**

---

**The record, in the cases that built it:**

| Case | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| ***Grootboom* (2000)** | **the socio-economic rights are justiciable**, and the state's housing programme had to be reasonable — stage 7 |
| ***Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign* (2002)** | **ordered the state to make nevirapine available to prevent mother-to-child HIV transmission.** The single most consequential public interest case in South African history — stage 11 |
| ***Glenister II* (2011)** | **a constitutional requirement of an independent anti-corruption body** — stage 8, brought by a businessman in his own name |
| ***Juma Musjid* (2011)** and the textbook and school infrastructure litigation | **section 29's right to basic education is immediately realisable**, and the norms and standards had to be made with deadlines |
| ***Black Sash v Minister of Social Development* (2017)** | **the Court supervised the social grant payment system through a crisis**, retaining jurisdiction and ordering the contracted company to account for its profits. **Nineteen million people's grants** |
| ***Corruption Watch v President* (2018)** | the NDPP appointments — stage 8 |
| ***My Vote Counts* (2018)** | **party funding disclosure** — the last lesson |
| ***New Nation Movement* (2020)** | **independent candidates** |
| ***Mwelase* (2019)** | **a special master for labour tenant claims** — stage 9 |
| ***Deadly Air* (2022)** | **Highveld air quality breached section 24** |
| ***Mlungwana* (2018)** | **criminalising an unnotified protest was unconstitutional** — the next lesson |

**And the organisations, because knowing who litigates tells you where to find the documents:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Health and education** | **Treatment Action Campaign, Section27, Equal Education, SECTION27's partner clinics** |
| **Housing, land and the city** | **SERI, Ndifuna Ukwazi, the Legal Resources Centre, Abahlali baseMjondolo** |
| **Social security** | **the Black Sash** |
| **Corruption and governance** | **Corruption Watch, OUTA, the Helen Suzman Foundation, Open Secrets** |
| **Information and democracy** | **Right2Know, My Vote Counts, the Open Democracy Advice Centre** |
| **Rights generally** | **Lawyers for Human Rights, the Centre for Applied Legal Studies, the Centre for Child Law, the Legal Resources Centre** |
| **And a Chapter 9 institution** | **the SAHRC litigates in its own name** — stage 8 |

---

**Why it works, which is worth stating as a system:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Broad standing** | section 38 |
| **Justiciable positive rights** | sections 26 to 29, plus section 7(2) |
| **Flexible remedies** | section 172(1)(b) — **a court can order a plan, with dates, and keep the case open** |
| **A judiciary that holds** | stage 8's finding, and the reason the other three matter |
| **Access to information** | **PAIA**, which is slow and much-criticised but exists |
| **Funding** | **foreign and domestic philanthropic funding, pro bono work by commercial firms, and Legal Aid** |
| **The result** | **a thirty-year record of enforceable orders against the state on housing, health, education, social security, the environment, elections and appointments** |

---

**And the limits, which the litigants name themselves:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A court order does not fix a pump** | **an order requires the state to do something the state is incapable of doing.** From stage 8: the capacity problem is not a legal problem, and litigation cannot supply engineers |
| **Non-compliance** | **orders are routinely not complied with**, which is why structural interdicts, supervisory jurisdiction and ultimately *Mwelase*'s special master emerged. **Each escalation is a response to a failure** |
| **The separation of powers objection** | **the state's standing argument is that a court supervising an administration crosses into the executive's function.** It has force, **and the Court's answer is that it escalates only after ordinary remedies have failed** |
| **Cost and delay** | **years, and sums only a funded organisation can carry.** The individual litigant is rare |
| **Donor dependence** | **the sector's funding has tightened sharply**, and several organisations have contracted. **A litigation strategy funded by foreign philanthropy is also politically vulnerable to that fact being pointed out** |
| **Displacement** | **the deepest internal criticism: winning in court can substitute for organising politically**, producing judgments without constituencies. Several of these organisations argue about this openly |

**The displacement point is the one that links back to this stage's thesis.** **Civil society litigates because the parties do not deliver accountability** — stage 8's Parliament lesson. **But a judgment cannot vote, and an organisation of twenty lawyers is not a political base.** **Which is why the protest lesson comes next.**

**Practice.** Read section 38 and section 172(1)(b). Then read the *TAC* judgment's orders — not the reasoning, the orders. Then find one organisation above and read its most recent annual report, including its funding sources. Then find a case where a court retained supervisory jurisdiction and establish whether the state complied.
Protest:
A right, a notification statute, somewhere between ten and fifteen thousand gatherings a year, and the argument about what all that protest means.

**The right:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 17** | **"Everyone has the right, peacefully and unarmed, to assemble, to demonstrate, to picket and to present petitions."** |
| **Note the qualifiers** | **"peacefully and unarmed"** are **internal** to the right — a violent or armed gathering is **not** protected by section 17 at all, and no limitation analysis under section 36 is needed |
| **Section 23** | **the right to strike**, separately, for workers — stage 9 |

**The statute: the Regulation of Gatherings Act 205 of 1993**, passed in the transition period on the recommendation of the Goldstone Commission.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Notice, not permission** | **a convenor must give the municipality notice**, normally seven days ahead, for a gathering of more than fifteen people |
| **The process** | the municipality may call a meeting to agree conditions, and **may prohibit only on specified grounds** — a credible threat of serious disruption, injury or property damage |
| **The convenor's duties** | marshals, route, conduct |
| **Section 11 liability** | **the convenor and the organisation can be held liable for damage caused by the gathering**, subject to a defence |
| ***SATAWU v Garvas* (2012)** | **the Constitutional Court upheld that liability**, holding it a justifiable limitation — a union was liable for damage during a march |
| ***Mlungwana v S* (2018)** | **struck down section 12(1)(a), which made it a criminal offence to convene a gathering without notice** — an unjustifiable limitation of section 17. **So failing to give notice is no longer a crime, though the gathering may be dispersed** |

**Read *Garvas* and *Mlungwana* together: the organiser bears civil liability for damage, and is not criminally liable merely for not notifying.** That is a reasonably coherent position, and it is more protective than most comparable systems.

---

**The scale.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The data** | **SAPS's public order policing records count "crowd management incidents"**, split between peaceful and unrest-related |
| **The order of magnitude** | **on the order of ten to fifteen thousand recorded gatherings a year**, of which **the large majority are recorded as peaceful** |
| **The "protest capital of the world" claim** | **overstated as usually made** — there is no comparable global dataset, so the ranking cannot be established. **But the per-capita rate of recorded gatherings is genuinely high** by any available comparison |
| **The service delivery share** | tracked by **Municipal IQ's service delivery protest index**, which shows a long-term upward trend concentrated in metros and in specific provinces |

**What the protests are about, from the recorded causes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Water** | the most common single trigger — **from stage 8, non-revenue water and treatment failure** |
| **Electricity** | connections, outages, prepaid meters |
| **Housing and land occupation** | |
| **Roads and potholes** | |
| **Jobs** | including demands that local people be employed on local projects, which is where the "construction mafia" overlaps |
| **And frequently, local political disputes** | **the selection of a ward councillor, or a councillor's conduct** — which is the analytically interesting one |

---

**Now the argument about what it means.**

| Protest as a failure of representation | Protest as democratic participation |
| --- | --- |
| **the ward councillor is the only access point**, and is a party appointee answerable to the party — the stage's thesis | **section 17 exists because mass action is legitimate politics**, and the 1980s are stage 5's evidence |
| **people protest because nothing else works** — a complaint to a municipality with no functioning call centre and no local newspaper has nowhere to go | **a high rate of protest in a democracy with a free press and functioning courts is a sign of engagement**, not of breakdown |
| **the frequency tracks municipal audit outcomes and service failure**, which suggests causation | **the large majority are peaceful and lawful**, and the state's response is the variable worth measuring |
| the term used in the research literature — **"the rebellion of the poor"** — captures the pattern | **and some protest is factional**, mobilised in internal party contests rather than against the state |

**Both columns are supported, and the last row of the second column deserves emphasis because it is under-discussed: a significant share of "service delivery protest" is mobilised within local party contests**, over who gets a council nomination or a tender. **That does not make the underlying grievance false; it does mean the protest is not a clean signal of public opinion.**

---

**And the state's response, which is where the serious problem is.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Deaths at protests** | **people are killed at South African protests with some regularity**, by police action |
| **The named case** | **Andries Tatane, killed by police on camera during a service delivery protest in Ficksburg in 2011.** The officers were acquitted |
| **Marikana** | **2012, 34 dead** — stage 8's police lesson and stage 11 |
| **The oversight** | **IPID** must investigate deaths resulting from police action — stage 8 — **and its conviction record is poor** |
| **Rubber bullets and crowd control** | repeated findings of improper use, and litigation |

**And one pattern that is badly under-reported: the killing of activists.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Abahlali baseMjondolo** | **the shack dwellers' movement**, based in Durban, with a membership in the tens of thousands — **has had a large number of its leaders and members assassinated**, by most counts more than twenty since 2018 |
| **Political killings in KwaZulu-Natal** | **a sustained pattern of assassinations of councillors, candidates and local officials**, investigated by a dedicated task team with some convictions |
| **Whistleblowers** | **Babita Deokaran, a senior Gauteng health official who had flagged irregular payments, was assassinated in 2021** — which is the sharpest possible illustration of stage 8's consequence-management failure |

**From stage 8: this is the police lesson's impunity finding in its most serious form. A country where local activists and whistleblowers are killed and the cases are not solved has a specific, identifiable institutional failure, and it is the detective service.**

**Practice.** Read section 17 and note where the qualifiers sit. Then read *Mlungwana* on why criminalising unnotified gatherings failed. Then find the latest SAPS crowd management figures and the peaceful/unrest split. Then find Municipal IQ's protest index and the provinces it concentrates in.
Migration politics:
The numbers, the claims made about them, the law, and the electoral incentive that has formed around the gap.

**Start with the measurement, because the gap between the figures and the claims is the whole political story.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Census 2022** | counted **roughly 2.4 million foreign-born residents** — **about 4% of the population** |
| **Undercount** | **real and acknowledged.** Censuses undercount undocumented people, and the 2022 census had a high overall undercount rate which StatsSA adjusted for |
| **Credible range for total foreign-born** | **roughly 2 to 4 million**, depending on the adjustment used |
| **Claims in public debate** | **frequently 10 to 15 million, and occasionally higher** |
| **What those claims rest on** | **nothing traceable.** Africa Check has repeatedly traced them to assertion, to misread Home Affairs figures, or to multiplying border crossings by a guess |
| **Where most migrants are from** | **Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Lesotho, Malawi, and smaller numbers from Nigeria, Ethiopia, Somalia, Bangladesh and Pakistan** |

**From stage 1's statistics lesson: this is the clearest case in the whole curriculum of a policy argument conducted on a number that is wrong by a factor of four or more.** **A figure of 15 million would mean roughly one in four people in South Africa is foreign-born, which no survey, census, school enrolment record or mortality statistic supports.**

**Note what that does and does not establish.** **It does not** mean local pressure on clinics, schools and housing is imagined — **in specific neighbourhoods the concentration is high and the pressure is real.** **It does** mean a national policy built on 15 million is built on nothing.

---

**The violence, which is the recurring fact:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **May 2008** | **attacks across Gauteng and then nationally — 62 people killed**, about a third of them South African, and roughly 100,000 displaced |
| **2015** | attacks in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng, with deaths and large-scale displacement, and the looting of foreign-owned shops |
| **2019** | attacks in the Johannesburg CBD and surrounds |
| **Recurring** | **lower-level attacks on foreign-owned shops and individuals continue**, and are frequently recorded as ordinary crime |
| **The term** | **"xenophobia" is contested** — many researchers prefer **"Afrophobia"**, noting that the violence targets Black African and South Asian migrants and not European or North American ones |

**And the organised politics since 2021:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Operation Dudula** | **a movement formed in 2021**, which conducts actions against foreign traders, demands employers dismiss foreign workers, and blockades clinics to check documents. **Its name means "push back"** |
| **Party positions** | **the Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA both campaign explicitly on immigration enforcement and deportation**, and both improved their position doing so. **Several other parties have moved in the same direction** |
| **The electoral incentive** | **this is the key structural fact: anti-migrant politics is now electorally rewarded**, which it was not in 2009, and the parties responded to that |
| **The courts** | **actions blocking access to clinics and schools have been found unlawful**, and litigation against Operation Dudula's methods has succeeded |

---

**The law, which is where the administrative failure sits.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Immigration Act 13 of 2002** | work, business, study and visitor visas; the critical practical fact being **Home Affairs' processing capacity** |
| **Refugees Act 130 of 1998** | **a strong statute on paper** — non-refoulement, the right to work and study while a claim is pending |
| **The 2017 Amendment Act**, in force 2020 | **restricted asylum seekers' automatic right to work, and provided for claims to be deemed abandoned** if a seeker fails to renew |
| **The backlog** | **the asylum appeal backlog has run into the hundreds of thousands of cases**, with waits of many years. **A person with a pending claim for a decade is in legal limbo, cannot work formally, and cannot be deported** |
| **The Zimbabwean Exemption Permit** | **about 178,000 permits** issued to Zimbabweans who had been in South Africa for years. **The decision to terminate the dispensation, announced in 2021, was declared unlawful and unconstitutional by the Gauteng High Court in 2023 for procedural unfairness and lack of consultation**, and remitted. **Check the current position** |
| **The Border Management Authority** | established by the **Border Management Authority Act of 2020**, operational from 2023, consolidating border functions |
| **Lindela** | the repatriation centre, **repeatedly criticised by the SAHRC and in litigation over conditions and over detention beyond lawful periods** |

**And two judgments on rights that do not depend on status:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Khosa v Minister of Social Development* (2004)** | **permanent residents could not be excluded from social grants** — section 27 says "everyone" |
| ***Centre for Child Law v Minister of Basic Education* (2020)** | **undocumented children may not be excluded from schools.** Section 29's right to basic education, read with section 28, **attaches to the child and not to the parent's documentation** |

---

**How to argue about it**, which is the point of the lesson:

| The enforcement case | The case against it |
| --- | --- |
| **a state that cannot control entry cannot plan services**, and the asylum system's backlog is itself the failure | **the numbers are a fraction of what is claimed**, so national policy built on the claims will not address the real local pressure |
| **local pressure on clinics, schools and informal trade is real** and falls on the poorest areas | **the evidence on employment mostly finds migrant workers are neutral or net job-creating**, with higher self-employment rates — stage 9's spaza lesson |
| **undocumented status enables exploitation** — below-minimum wages, no recourse — which undercuts local workers too | **the enforcement mechanism in practice is street-level document checks**, which catch South Africans without ID as well, and have been found unlawful |
| **every state regulates entry**, and saying so is not xenophobia | **the violence is real, recurrent and lethal**, and political rhetoric is causally implicated in it |
| **and the honest centre of this column** | **and the honest centre of this one** |
| **the asylum backlog is an administrative catastrophe that harms migrants most of all** | **the single most effective anti-xenophobia measure would be a functioning Home Affairs**, which is a stage 8 capacity problem |

**Note where the two columns converge: both end at Home Affairs' administrative capacity.** **A system that decides claims in months rather than a decade, documents who is here, and processes permits reliably is the one intervention both sides' strongest arguments require.** **That is not a coincidence, and it is the most useful thing in this lesson.**

**Practice.** Find the Census 2022 figure for foreign-born residents and the undercount adjustment. Then find an Africa Check report tracing a large migration claim to its source. Then find the current asylum appeal backlog. Then read *Centre for Child Law v Minister of Basic Education* (2020) on undocumented children and schooling.
What the party system is becoming:
The stage's close: fragmentation measured, the three scenarios, and what to watch on 4 November 2026.

**What has changed, stated as facts rather than as a trend:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Dominant-party rule ended in 2024** | from 69.7% in 2004 to 40.2% in 2024 |
| **The governing party governs in coalition** nationally, in at least two provinces, and in most metros | |
| **The opposition is fragmented** | **the largest opposition party has been at 21 to 22% for three successive elections**, and the second and third largest are both splits from the governing party |
| **Turnout has fallen every election since 1999** | **and the largest single political category is non-voters — roughly 26 million eligible adults** |
| **Two parties with a combined 24% of the vote** stand outside the constitutional consensus in significant respects — the EFF on property and the Reserve Bank, MK on constitutional supremacy itself | |
| **Local government is persistently unstable** | from stage 8 and the coalitions lesson |

**And the measured fragmentation**: the number of parties winning seats has risen steadily, and **the effective number of parties — the standard political science measure, which weights parties by size — has roughly doubled since 2004.** **South Africa has moved from a dominant-party system to a fragmented multi-party one in a single electoral cycle.**

---

**Three scenarios, each with a named mechanism and an observable test.**

**1 — Consolidation into a stable two- or three-bloc system.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism** | **coalition government becomes routine, voters learn to vote for blocs rather than parties**, and the small parties are squeezed out or absorbed |
| **The evidence for** | **the 2024 GNU held through a budget crisis**; voters rewarded the arrangement in the market and confidence data; **European coalition systems are stable** |
| **The evidence against** | **no threshold exists to squeeze small parties out**, and the system rewards splitting |
| **The test** | **do the small parties' shares fall in 2026 and 2029, and do the GNU parties campaign as a bloc?** |

**2 — Continued fragmentation and governing paralysis.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism** | **no threshold, low barriers to entry, declining party loyalty, and a grievance base of 26 million non-voters** produce new parties each cycle |
| **The evidence for** | **MK went from registration to 58 seats in eight months**; the local government record; the long tail of parties |
| **The evidence against** | **COPE's collapse is the base rate** — new parties mostly fail by the second election |
| **The test** | **MK's and ActionSA's 2026 local results, and whether any new party registers and polls above 5%** |

**3 — Realignment around the constitutional question.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The mechanism** | **the dividing line stops being the liberation-movement legacy and becomes whether you accept the 1996 settlement** — constitutional supremacy, an independent judiciary and central bank, property rights |
| **The evidence for** | **MK's parliamentary sovereignty platform, the EFF's property and Reserve Bank positions, and a GNU that united the ANC and DA across that line rather than across any economic one** |
| **The evidence against** | **the 2024 realignment was an ANC civil war, not an ideological one** — MK's vote is substantially a personal and regional vote |
| **The test** | **whether MK and the EFF's combined share rises or falls, and whether their constitutional positions become more or less central to their campaigning** |

**Not to arrive at a position. Each scenario has a test with a date.**

---

**The reform question, which stage 12 takes up.**

| Reform | Status |
| --- | --- |
| **A constituency or mixed-member element in the National Assembly** | **requires only an amendment to the Electoral Act**, not to the Constitution — section 46 requires proportionality, which a mixed-member proportional system satisfies. **Recommended by the Van Zyl Slabbert Electoral Task Team in 2003 and never implemented** |
| **An electoral threshold** | ordinary legislation; **would reduce fragmentation and discard small parties' votes** |
| **Coalition stability legislation** | **a constructive vote of no confidence, cooling-off periods, enforceable agreements** — ordinary legislation |
| **Direct election of mayors** | **probably requires a constitutional amendment**, as it changes the local executive's constitution |
| **Open lists** | **ordinary legislation** — voters rank candidates within a party, which keeps proportionality and restores a personal mandate |
| **Lowering the independent candidate barriers** | **arguably constitutionally required** already, given *New Nation Movement* |

**The Van Zyl Slabbert report of 2003 is the document to know.** It recommended **a mixed system — multi-member constituencies plus a compensatory national list** — keeping proportionality while giving voters a named representative. **It was shelved and has been revived in every reform discussion since, including by the Zondo Commission.** From stage 8: **the Commission's institutional recommendations ended at the electoral system, and this is the proposal they pointed to.**

---

**And what to watch, concretely:**

> **As of 14 October 2026 the municipal elections are three weeks away, on 4 November 2026. They are the first full test of everything in this stage. Watch, in order:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Turnout** | **2021 was about 46%.** Below that and the legitimacy question sharpens for every party |
| **2 — MK's local result** | **does a party built in eight months around one person have ward structures?** Compare its share with its 14.58% of 2024, especially in KwaZulu-Natal |
| **3 — The ANC's floor** | it was 45% locally in 2021 and 40% nationally in 2024. **Which of those is the trend?** |
| **4 — The DA's ceiling** | **three elections at 21–22%.** A fourth confirms a structural ceiling |
| **5 — The SACP** | **if it contests independently, the alliance as constituted since 1990 has ended** |
| **6 — Hung councils** | **more or fewer than the roughly 60 to 70 of 2021?** |
| **7 — Independents and local parties** | **the ward ballot is the one place a voter chooses a person.** Watch how many independents win wards |

**Then do what stage 1 asks: write the seven answers down with the date, and compare them with what you expected.**

**Practice.** Find the Van Zyl Slabbert Electoral Task Team report and read its recommendation. Then calculate the effective number of parties for 2004 and 2024 from the IEC's results. Then write your prediction for each of the seven items above before 4 November 2026. Then check them afterwards, and note which of the three scenarios the result supports.
How to read the last thirty years:
The stage's method: five presidencies, four arguments about what happened, and the trap that every account of this period falls into.

**This stage is narrative, and narrative is where stage 1's warnings bite hardest.** The events are recent, the participants are alive, and **almost every available account was written by somebody with a position in the argument.**

---

**The periodisation, which is itself a claim:**

| Period | The conventional label |
| --- | --- |
| **1994–1999** | **the Mandela presidency** — reconciliation, the Constitution, the TRC |
| **1999–2008** | **the Mbeki presidency** — macroeconomic consolidation, growth, AIDS denialism, the arms deal, centralisation |
| **2008–2009** | **the Motlanthe caretaker** — eight months |
| **2009–2018** | **the Zuma presidency** — state capture, Nkandla, Marikana, #FeesMustFall |
| **2018–2024** | **Ramaphosa's first term** — the commissions, Covid, July 2021, the energy crisis |
| **2024–** | **the coalition** |

**Note the trap: organising thirty years by presidency implies that presidents are the causal unit.** From stages 8, 9 and 10: **the institutional, economic and party-political structures are often doing the causal work**, and a presidency is where it becomes visible. **Keep both frames.**

---

**The four arguments about this period, each of which will be visible in every account you read:**

**1 — Was 1994 a revolution or a negotiated transfer of political power only?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The achievement view** | **universal franchise, a justiciable Bill of Rights, the end of statutory racial law, mass electrification and water delivery, the grant system, and the HIV treatment programme.** Measured by what a 1990 observer would have predicted, **the outcome is extraordinary** |
| **The incomplete-revolution view** | **ownership, land and the labour market are substantially unchanged** — stage 9. **Political power transferred and economic power did not**, which is what stage 6's "what was traded" lesson is about |
| **Both cite the same data** | and the disagreement is about the counterfactual and about the standard |

**2 — Is the decline about one man, or about the organisation?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Zuma-centred account** | **state capture was a project of a specific network around a specific president**, and his removal in 2018 was the turning point |
| **The structural account** | **the arms deal predates him by a decade**; cadre deployment, the conference-resolution mechanism and the closed list are organisational features — stage 10; **and capture required thousands of people to cooperate** |
| **The test** | **what happened after 2018.** The institutional rebuilds at SARS and the NPA were real; the prosecutions were not |

**3 — Was the economic decline a policy failure or a capacity failure?** From stage 9's five explanations. **This is the most consequential disagreement, because the two diagnoses prescribe opposite things.**

**4 — Did the Constitution constrain or enable?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It constrained** | **Nkandla, the NDPP appointments, *Glenister*, the socio-economic rights cases, the 2024 transfer of some power.** The courts held — stage 8 |
| **It was insufficient** | **two commissions, almost no prosecutions.** A document cannot supply detectives |
| **It enabled the wrong things** | **MK's position from stage 10, and the EFF's on property.** The settlement's property and central bank provisions constrained redistribution |

---

**And the method, which is stage 1 applied to living memory:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Date everything** | **a claim about "the Zuma years" that is true of 2015 may be false of 2010.** Nine years is a long time, and the capture project accelerated sharply after 2014 |
| **2 — Separate the finding from the allegation** | **a commission's finding, a court's judgment, a journalist's report and a politician's claim are four different evidentiary classes** — stage 1's commission lesson |
| **3 — Name the source's position** | almost every memoir, biography and analysis of this period is by a participant or an opponent. **Read them; place them first** |
| **4 — Check whether a number was ever substantiated** | **the state capture arithmetic lesson in this stage is the case study.** Figures repeated for years sometimes have no origin |
| **5 — Watch for the achievement that gets forgotten** | **the HIV programme, electrification, water, the grant system and the ART-driven recovery in life expectancy** are the largest measurable changes of the period, and they feature in almost no political account of it |

**Point 5 is deliberate and it is this stage's one editorial commitment: the failures are extensively documented and the deliverables are not.** **Both belong in the record.**

**Practice.** Write down what you currently believe about each of the four arguments above, with the date. Then read one memoir or account by a participant in this period and note where their position shapes the narrative. Then take one claim you hold about "the Zuma years" and establish which years it is actually true of.
The Mandela presidency, 1994-1999:
Five years of simultaneous nation-building, constitution-writing, institution-creating and service delivery — and the criticisms that are made of it.

**What the government inherited in May 1994**, which is the baseline for everything:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Administration** | **eleven separate administrations to merge** — the central state, four provinces, and the homelands and self-governing territories, with incompatible systems and personnel |
| **The civil service** | **guaranteed in post by the sunset clauses** from stage 6, so the apartheid bureaucracy stayed |
| **Debt** | **high, inherited and honoured** — stage 6's economic settlement |
| **Service backlogs** | **roughly a third of households without electricity, millions without piped water, a housing backlog in the millions** |
| **Education** | **nineteen racially separate departments** |
| **Violence** | **the KwaZulu-Natal and Reef conflict of stage 6 had not fully stopped in 1994** |

**The constitutional task was simultaneous**: the Constitutional Assembly sat from 1994 and the final Constitution was certified and signed in 1996 — **stage 6 and 7** — **while the same people were running a new government.**

---

**What was delivered, measurably:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Electrification** | **the national electrification programme connected millions of households** in the 1990s — one of the fastest such programmes anywhere. From 1994's roughly a third of households connected to the large majority within about fifteen years |
| **Water** | millions of people given access to piped water, through the RDP and the Water Services Act |
| **The RDP housing programme** | hundreds of thousands of units in the first five years, with the quality criticisms that followed |
| **Free health care** | **for pregnant women and children under six, from 1994**, and primary health care clinics built in large numbers |
| **School feeding and the single education system** | **nineteen departments merged into one national and nine provincial** |
| **The institutions** | **the Constitutional Court (1995), the Public Protector, the SAHRC, the IEC, the Auditor-General's mandate, the Land Claims Court, the CCMA and the Labour Court, the Human Rights and Gender Commissions** — stages 7 and 8 **all exist because of this period** |
| **The labour legislation** | **the LRA (1995), the BCEA (1997), the Employment Equity Act (1998)** — stage 9 |
| **The TRC** | 1995–1998 — stage 6 |

**That is an extraordinary volume of institution-building in five years**, and it is the strongest answer to the question of what the period achieved.

---

**And the decisions that are criticised, each with its defence:**

| The criticism | The defence |
| --- | --- |
| **GEAR, 1996** — adopted without alliance consultation, abandoning the RDP's redistributive programme for deficit reduction | **the fiscal position was the inherited debt of stage 6**, and the macroeconomic stabilisation GEAR achieved funded the grant system — stage 9 |
| **The sunset clauses** — the apartheid civil service and security establishment kept in post, which shaped the state's capacity and culture for a generation | **they were the price of a peaceful transfer**, and stage 6 is the evidence that the alternative was not obviously available |
| **No prosecutions after the TRC** — about 300 referred cases, almost none pursued | **the political cost of prosecuting in 1999 was judged to threaten the settlement.** Which is a judgment, not a legal position, and the TRC's own report disagreed with it |
| **Reconciliation prioritised over redress** — the Springbok jersey, the lunch with Betsie Verwoerd, the emphasis on reassurance | **it held the country together**, and the counterfactual is stage 6's violence continuing. **This criticism has grown much louder since 2015** |
| **The arms deal was initiated** in this period, concluded in 1999 | and is the next lesson |
| **AIDS** — **the epidemic grew very fast in the mid-1990s and the response was slow**, with Mandela himself later saying he had not given it the attention it required | the scale was not yet clear in 1994, **and the denialism that did the measurable damage came later** |

**The reconciliation criticism deserves careful handling, because it is now the most common one and it is often made anachronistically.** **In 1994 the questions were whether the army would accept the result, whether the right wing would fight, and whether the KwaZulu-Natal conflict would spread.** From stage 6: **those were live. Whether a different balance between reconciliation and redress was available in those conditions is a genuine historical question, and asserting that it obviously was is not an argument.**

---

**And three things about Mandela's own presidency that are usually left out:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **He served one term by choice** | **and did not seek a second**, which set a precedent that has held |
| **He delegated domestic administration substantially to Deputy President Mbeki** | and concentrated on reconciliation, foreign policy and symbolic leadership — **so much of the Mandela-era policy record is Mbeki's work** |
| **The foreign policy was more contested than the hagiography allows** | **the recognition switch from Taiwan to China in 1997, arms sales to questionable buyers, the Nigerian execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa in 1995 after South African intervention failed, and the Lesotho intervention of 1998** — the foreign policy lesson takes these up |

**Practice.** Find the household electrification figures for 1994 and 2004. Then read the RDP White Paper's objectives and compare them with what was delivered by 1999. Then find the sunset clause provisions in the interim Constitution and establish exactly what they guaranteed. Then read one criticism of Mandela's reconciliation politics made before 2000 and one made after 2015, and note the difference.
The arms deal:
The template for everything that followed: a procurement whose cost tripled, a commission whose report was set aside by a court, and no successful prosecution of a South African official.

**What it was:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The name** | **the Strategic Defence Procurement Package**, approved in 1999 |
| **What was bought** | **four frigates and three submarines from German consortia; 24 Hawk trainer and 26 Gripen fighter aircraft from BAE Systems and Saab; and 30 light utility helicopters from Agusta** |
| **The announced cost** | **about R30 billion** |
| **The eventual cost** | **substantially higher — with exchange rate movements and financing, estimates run to R70 billion and above** |
| **The context** | **a country with a massive service backlog, a debt problem and no external military threat, buying fighter jets** |

**The central factual dispute is not whether irregularities occurred. Several are established. It is whether the decisions at the top were corrupt.**

---

**What is established:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Auditor-General, Public Protector and NDPP joint investigation (2001)** | **the Joint Investigation Team report found irregularities in the selection of subcontractors** but **did not find the government's decisions improper**. **It later emerged that the draft report had been materially changed before publication**, which is itself part of the story |
| **Schabir Shaik** | **convicted in 2005 of corruption and fraud** for payments to Jacob Zuma, then Deputy President, in connection with the deal, **and sentenced to 15 years** — released on medical parole in 2009 |
| **The charges against Zuma** | **brought, withdrawn in 2009 on the basis of the "spy tapes", reinstated after litigation in 2016–18**, and **the trial has proceeded slowly since** |
| **BAE Systems** | **paid a very large settlement to the United States Department of Justice in 2010** over, among other matters, payments made in connection with the South African contract, and **the UK Serious Fraud Office investigated** |
| **Saab** | **disclosed in 2011 that its partner BAE had made payments through a subsidiary** that Saab had not known of |
| **Fana Hlongwane** | a defence adviser named in the BAE investigations as having received very large payments |
| **Tony Yengeni** | **convicted of fraud in 2003** over a discounted vehicle from a bidder, and imprisoned |

**So two convictions — a businessman and an MP — and foreign settlements and admissions, with no conviction of a senior South African decision-maker.**

---

**The Seriti Commission, which is the part that matters most for this curriculum.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Established** | **2011**, chaired by Judge Willie Seriti, after sustained pressure, with a broad mandate to investigate the deal |
| **Its conduct** | **two of its own senior staff resigned publicly**, alleging that the commission had a "second agenda" to protect those implicated, and that evidence was not being pursued |
| **Its report (2016)** | **found no evidence of corruption, fraud or improper influence by anybody** |
| **Then** | **Corruption Watch and the Right2Know campaign took the report to court** |
| **The outcome (August 2019)** | **the High Court set the commission's findings aside in full** — holding that **the commission had failed to inquire fully and comprehensively**, had not tested evidence, had not confronted witnesses with contradictory material, **and that its conclusions could not stand** |
| **And then** | **nothing. The report was set aside and no new commission was appointed** |

**A judicial commission's report into the largest procurement scandal in South African history was declared to have been an inadequate inquiry by a court, and the matter was simply left there.** **From stage 1's commission lesson: that is the strongest available demonstration of why a commission is not a court and why its findings are not final.**

---

**Why the arms deal is the template, which is the lesson's point:**

| Feature | Where it recurs |
| --- | --- |
| **A very large procurement with technical specifications few can evaluate** | **the SOEs** — stage 8 |
| **Intermediaries and "advisers" taking fees** | the capture-era contracts |
| **Offsets and industrial participation promises that were never delivered** | the offset commitments were valued in the hundreds of billions and **the delivery was never audited to a conclusion** |
| **An investigation whose report was altered** | the JIT draft |
| **A commission that found nothing and was set aside** | **Seriti**, against which **Zondo should be measured — Zondo's findings have not been set aside** |
| **Prosecutions of intermediaries, not principals** | **the pattern stage 8's NPA lesson describes** |
| **Foreign prosecutors doing the work South African ones did not** | **the US DOJ settlement, and later the ABB, SAP and McKinsey settlements** of the capture era |

**That last row is a recurring and uncomfortable feature of this whole period: the most reliable accountability mechanism for South African corruption has been foreign law enforcement and foreign regulators**, acting on their own anti-bribery statutes. **It is covered again in the state capture arithmetic lesson.**

**Practice.** Read the High Court's 2019 judgment setting aside the Seriti Commission's findings. Then find the BAE Systems settlement with the US Department of Justice and what it covered. Then find the offset obligations promised in 1999 and establish whether anybody has audited their delivery. Then compare the Seriti and Zondo commissions on the three criteria the 2019 judgment used.
Mbeki: the technocratic presidency:
Nine years of growth, institutional centralisation and continental ambition, ended by his own party — and the two decisions that define the period.

**The record on its own terms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Growth** | **GDP growth averaged above 4% from 1999 to 2008, exceeding 5% in the boom years** — stage 9's first fifteen-year period |
| **Fiscal position** | **the deficit eliminated and a surplus achieved by 2006–07; debt fell toward 26% of GDP** — the position that stage 9's debt lesson starts from |
| **Social spending** | **the grant system expanded very substantially** — the Child Support Grant, introduced in 1998, grew to cover millions of children in this period. **The social wage of stage 9 was built here** |
| **The black middle class** | **grew substantially**, through employment equity and public service and corporate advancement — stage 9's BEE lesson |
| **Institutions** | **the Scorpions (1999), SARS's modernisation under Gordhan (stage 9), inflation targeting (2000), and the Treasury's PFMA framework (1999)** |
| **Infrastructure** | the 2010 World Cup programme, Gautrain, and the Medupi and Kusile decisions — **which stage 9 shows went badly** |

**That is the strongest growth and fiscal record of the post-1994 period**, and it is the reason the "lost decade" framing in stage 9 refers to what came after.

---

**And the governing style, which is the other half:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Centralisation** | **the Presidency was substantially strengthened** — a policy unit, a planning capacity, and the coordination of departments from the centre |
| **Technocracy** | **policy made by officials and experts rather than through alliance consultation**, which is what made GEAR's reception a lasting grievance — stage 10's Alliance lesson |
| **Deployment** | **the cadre deployment committee's practice was consolidated** in this period — stage 8 |
| **Intolerance of dissent** | **the 2001 allegations of a plot against him, directed at three senior ANC figures, and the Hefer Commission into whether the NDPP had been an apartheid spy** — both widely read as the use of state and party machinery against rivals |
| **The Scorpions' investigations** | **of Zuma, of the police commissioner, and of the arms deal** — which is why their disbandment after Polokwane happened, from stage 8 |

---

**Two decisions define the presidency, and they pull in opposite directions.**

**One is AIDS denialism**, which is the next lesson and which is the single most costly decision of the post-1994 period.

**The other is Zimbabwe**, and it is the clearest case of a defensible policy with an indefensible outcome:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Quiet diplomacy"** | **engagement with the Zimbabwean government rather than public condemnation or sanctions**, pursued through SADC mediation |
| **The case for it** | **South Africa had no good instruments** — sanctions would have hit Zimbabwean workers hardest; **public condemnation of a fellow liberation movement would have forfeited the mediating role**; and **the mediation did produce the 2008 Global Political Agreement**, which ended the worst of the violence and the hyperinflation |
| **The case against** | **the 2002 and 2008 elections were not free, the land seizures destroyed the agricultural economy, hyperinflation reached figures with no modern parallel, and millions of Zimbabweans came to South Africa** — stage 10's migration lesson |
| **The sharpest single episode** | **the *An Yue Jiang* in 2008** — a Chinese ship carrying arms for Zimbabwe, which **a South African court restrained from transiting South African territory**, after the government had cleared it. **A court stopped an arms transfer the executive had permitted** |
| **The judgment to make** | **whether the mediation's achievement was worth eight years of restraint.** Both sides have a case and the migration consequence is the heaviest weight against |

---

**And the continental project, which is the part Mbeki is most respected for abroad:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The African Renaissance** | the framing idea — African solutions, African institutions, African economic recovery |
| **The African Union** | **the OAU was replaced by the AU in 2002**, with substantial South African drafting input and a Constitutive Act that permits intervention in a member state in grave circumstances |
| **NEPAD** | **the New Partnership for Africa's Development (2001)** — a development compact trading governance reform for investment and aid, **with the African Peer Review Mechanism as its accountability device** |
| **Mediation** | **the DRC and Burundi peace processes**, in which South African mediation was central and substantially successful |
| **The assessment** | **real institutional achievement, with NEPAD's peer review never acquiring teeth** |

---

**The end:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **December 2007** | **he was defeated for the ANC presidency at Polokwane** by Jacob Zuma — the first time a sitting South African President lost control of his party |
| **September 2008** | **recalled by the NEC** — stage 10's recall lesson — after a High Court judgment suggesting political interference in Zuma's prosecution. **That judgment was later overturned on appeal, after the recall had already happened** |
| **The note worth making** | **the finding that triggered the recall did not survive appeal**, and the recall was not reversed |

**Practice.** Find GDP growth and the budget balance for each year from 1999 to 2008. Then find the Child Support Grant's coverage in 1999 and 2008. Then read the *An Yue Jiang* judgment. Then establish what the African Peer Review Mechanism has actually done since 2003.
AIDS denialism:
The most costly single policy decision of the post-1994 period, measured in lives, and the litigation and institutions that reversed it.

**The scale of the epidemic first:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **HIV prevalence** | **rose extremely fast through the 1990s** — from low single-digit percentages of pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in the early 1990s to **around a quarter by the early 2000s** |
| **Life expectancy** | **fell from the low 60s in 1990 to around 53 by the mid-2000s.** **A country's life expectancy falling by a decade in peacetime is a catastrophe of a particular kind** |
| **Deaths** | **adult mortality roughly doubled**, concentrated in the 25-to-49 age band, with the demographic signature visible in StatsSA's mortality data |
| **Orphans** | **on the order of two million children had lost a parent** |

---

**What the denialism consisted of:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The position** | **that HIV does not cause AIDS, or that the link is unproven; that antiretrovirals are toxic and the pharmaceutical industry's interest; and that the epidemic's real causes are poverty and malnutrition** |
| **1997 — Virodene** | **an industrial solvent promoted as a cure**, supported by senior figures against the Medicines Control Council's refusal to permit trials |
| **2000 — the Presidential AIDS Advisory Panel** | **convened with AIDS dissidents among its members**, giving them official standing |
| **July 2000 — the Durban International AIDS Conference** | **the President's opening address did not attribute AIDS to HIV**, prompting the **Durban Declaration**, signed by over 5,000 scientists, asserting that the evidence that HIV causes AIDS is "clear-cut, exhaustive and unambiguous" |
| **The Health Minister** | **advocated garlic, beetroot, lemon and olive oil**, and resisted the antiretroviral programme |
| **The practical effect** | **the state refused to provide antiretrovirals in the public sector** — both for treatment and, critically, **for the prevention of mother-to-child transmission**, where a short course of a single drug at birth dramatically reduces transmission |

---

**The cost, which has been estimated and the estimate matters.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The principal study** | a 2008 analysis by researchers at **Harvard's School of Public Health** (Chigwedere and colleagues), modelling what a timely rollout would have prevented |
| **The finding** | **on the order of 330,000 excess deaths**, and **on the order of 35,000 avoidable infant HIV infections** from the failure to provide mother-to-child prophylaxis |
| **The method** | comparison with feasible rollout scenarios based on what neighbouring countries and the eventual South African programme achieved |
| **The caveat, stated honestly** | **it is a modelled counterfactual, and the number depends on the assumed feasible rollout rate.** Other estimates differ. **The order of magnitude — hundreds of thousands — is not seriously disputed** |

**From stage 1: a modelled number is not a counted one.** **And a modelled number of this magnitude, from a reputable source, with a published method, is evidence.**

---

**How it was reversed, which is the most important public interest litigation story in South African history.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Treatment Action Campaign** | **founded in 1998 by Zackie Achmat and others** — a mass-membership movement of people living with HIV, combining **street mobilisation, scientific literacy and litigation** |
| **2001 — the pharmaceutical case** | **39 pharmaceutical companies sued the South African government** over the Medicines Act's provisions permitting parallel importation and generic substitution. **The TAC joined as amicus; the companies withdrew.** A global turning point in access to medicines |
| **2002 — *Minister of Health v Treatment Action Campaign*** | **the Constitutional Court held the state's restriction of nevirapine to two pilot sites per province unreasonable, and ordered it to make the drug available at public hospitals and clinics without delay** |
| **The legal significance** | from stage 7 — **the clearest application of the *Grootboom* reasonableness standard, with a mandatory order rather than a declaration** |
| **2003** | **the Cabinet approved the Operational Plan for comprehensive HIV and AIDS care**, including antiretroviral treatment |
| **2004** | **the public rollout began**, slowly and unevenly, against continuing resistance from the Health Ministry |
| **2006** | **Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka took over the national AIDS council's leadership**, and the policy shifted decisively |
| **2008** | **a new Health Minister, Barbara Hogan, stated publicly that HIV causes AIDS** |
| **2009 onward** | **Aaron Motsoaledi as Health Minister drove the largest treatment expansion in the world** |

---

**And what the programme became, which is the other half of the record:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **People on antiretroviral treatment** | **on the order of 5.5 million — the largest treatment programme in the world** |
| **Life expectancy** | **recovered from around 53 in the mid-2000s to the mid-60s** — **an increase of over a decade in under twenty years**, almost entirely attributable to ART |
| **Mother-to-child transmission** | **reduced to very low single-digit percentages** |
| **The funding** | **substantially domestic**, with PEPFAR and Global Fund support — and **the domestic share has grown**, which matters as donor funding becomes less reliable |
| **The remaining gap** | **men's testing and treatment adherence, and the adolescent girls' infection rate**, which remain the programme's hardest problems |

> **As of 14 October 2026: the programme's scale and the life expectancy recovery are the largest measurable social achievement of the post-1994 period. Check the Thembisa model estimates and StatsSA's mid-year population estimates for the current figures.**

**Hold both halves of this lesson together, because almost no account does: the same state that caused hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths through denialism then built the largest and one of the most effective HIV treatment programmes in the world.** **Stage 8's thesis — that outcomes turn on specific decisions and specific appointments rather than on design — has no better illustration.**

**Practice.** Read the *Minister of Health v TAC* (2002) judgment's orders. Then find South African life expectancy for 1990, 2005 and the most recent year. Then find the Durban Declaration of 2000 and read it. Then find the current number of people on ART and the domestic share of the programme's funding.
The health system, and NHI:
Two health systems in one country, four simultaneous epidemics, and the largest proposed reform since 1994.

**The structural fact first, and it is the reason NHI exists as a proposal:**

| | Private | Public |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Who it covers** | **roughly 16% of the population** — about 9 to 10 million people on medical schemes | **the remaining 84%** |
| **What it spends** | **roughly half of all health spending in the country** | roughly half |
| **Per person** | **several times the public sector's per capita spend** | |
| **Where the specialists are** | **disproportionately in private practice** | |
| **Total health spending** | **around 8 to 9% of GDP** — high for a middle-income country | |

> **Check the Council for Medical Schemes' annual report for coverage, and the Budget Review's health chapter for the public spend.**

**Two systems, roughly equal money, a five-to-one difference in people covered.** **That is the inequality of stage 9 expressed in a sector**, and **no argument about South African health policy makes sense without it.**

**And the Competition Commission's Health Market Inquiry (final report, 2019)** found the private sector **highly concentrated** — in hospital groups, in funders and in administrators — **with weak competition, opaque pricing, supply-induced demand, and no effective regulator of prices or outcomes.** **So the private half is not a well-functioning market either.**

---

**The burden of disease, which is called the "quadruple burden" because four epidemics run at once:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **HIV and TB** | **the largest ART programme in the world** — the last lesson — **and among the highest TB incidence rates globally**, with hundreds of thousands of cases a year and a persistent drug-resistant component |
| **Maternal, newborn and child mortality** | substantially improved since 2009, largely through the ART programme and PMTCT |
| **Non-communicable disease** | **hypertension, diabetes, obesity and cancers rising sharply** — now a very large share of the burden, and **the system is built for infectious disease** |
| **Injury and violence** | **trauma units carrying a load driven by the murder, assault and road death rates** of the next lesson |

**And the human resources problem**, which is stage 9's wage bill lesson made concrete:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Doctors per capita** | **low** — roughly one per thousand people, counting both sectors, with the public sector far below that |
| **Distribution** | **specialists concentrated in urban centres and in the private sector** |
| **And the paradox of the 2020s** | **qualified doctors completing community service have gone unplaced because provincial posts were frozen** — hundreds of them in some years. **A country with a doctor shortage not employing its own graduates because the compensation budget was held flat.** From stage 9: that is what containing a wage bill by not hiring looks like |
| **Medico-legal claims** | **contingent liabilities against provincial health departments running to many tens of billions of rands** — the consequence of negligence in under-resourced facilities, which then consumes the budget that would have prevented it |

---

**National Health Insurance.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The policy history** | **a Green Paper in 2011, a White Paper in 2015, a Bill in 2019, passed by Parliament in 2023, and signed into law on 15 May 2024** |
| **The core design** | **a single public fund** that **purchases health services** from accredited public and private providers, **funded through taxation**, **with services free at the point of delivery** |
| **The section that produces the litigation** | **medical schemes are restricted to providing complementary cover** — cover for services the Fund does not pay for — **once the Fund is fully implemented** |
| **Status** | **signed, with implementation requiring further legislation, regulations, funding decisions and institutional construction over many years, and multiple court challenges filed immediately** |

> **As of 14 October 2026: the Act is law, substantially unimplemented, and under litigation on several grounds. It is also a point of open disagreement inside the governing coalition. Check the current status of the challenges and of the implementation framework.**

**The arguments, in their strongest forms:**

| For NHI | Against |
| --- | --- |
| **the two-tier system is indefensible** — half the money for a sixth of the people — and **incremental reform has not changed it in thirty years** | **a single fund requires state administrative capacity**, and stage 8's evidence on provincial health departments and procurement is the reason to doubt it |
| **a single purchaser has buying power** — it can set prices, which is the only demonstrated answer to the Health Market Inquiry's concentration finding | **restricting medical schemes removes the exit option** for 10 million people and the funding they currently contribute, with uncertain net effect on the public system |
| **section 27 obliges progressive realisation** of the right to health care, and pooling is the mechanism most countries use | **the fiscal space does not exist** — stage 9's debt lesson — and the Act does not specify the revenue |
| **the principle is mainstream**: most comparable systems pool risk nationally | **the sequencing is wrong** — fix public facilities, procurement and human resources first, then pool. **This is the most serious objection and it is made by supporters of universal coverage** |
| **accreditation gives leverage** over quality in both sectors | **constitutional objections** on section 27, property and the right to choose a provider, now before the courts |

**Note where the argument actually is: almost nobody defends the current two-tier system, and almost nobody disputes that universal coverage is the right objective.** **The dispute is about the vehicle and the sequence.** **From stage 1: that is a much narrower disagreement than the public debate suggests, and stage 12 takes it up.**

**Practice.** Find the medical scheme coverage figure and the public and private per capita health spends. Then read the Health Market Inquiry's findings on hospital concentration. Then find the NHI Act's section on medical schemes' role. Then find the number of unplaced community service doctors in the most recent year.
Crime since 1994:
A murder rate that halved and then rose by half again, and what each movement tells you.

**The single series to know:**

| Year | Murders per 100,000 |
| --- | --- |
| **1994–95** | **around 67** |
| **2002–03** | around 47 |
| **2011–12** | **around 30** — the low point |
| **2016–17** | around 34 |
| **2023–24** | **around 45** |

**In absolute numbers: roughly 26,000 murders in the mid-1990s, falling to about 15,600 in 2011–12, and back above 27,000 by the mid-2020s.**

> **Check the SAPS quarterly and annual crime statistics, and StatsSA's Victims of Crime Survey for reported-experience data.**

**That shape — a halving and then a two-thirds increase — is the most informative crime statistic in the country, because the two movements have different explanations.**

---

**Why it fell, 1994 to 2012:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Political violence ended** | **stage 6's conflict was killing thousands a year into the mid-1990s**, and its cessation accounts for a substantial part of the early decline |
| **Firearms control** | **the Firearms Control Act of 2000, in force from 2004**, tightened licensing substantially. **The published research associates it with a measurable decline in firearm homicide** in the following years |
| **Economic growth** | **stage 9's 1994–2008 period** — rising employment and incomes |
| **Policing investment** | **the 2000s saw real increases in police numbers and in detective and forensic capacity**, plus the Scorpions |
| **Demography** | the young male share of the population began to decline |

**Why it rose again, 2012 onward:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Police capacity** | **stage 8's police lesson — detective capacity, forensic backlogs, crime intelligence compromised, and six national commissioners in thirty years** |
| **Illegal firearms** | **the single most concrete case: a senior police officer was convicted of selling thousands of firearms that had been confiscated and should have been destroyed, substantially to Cape Town gangs, with police analysis linking them to a very large number of murders.** The guns came from the police store |
| **Extortion economies** | **the "construction mafia" halting projects for a cut; protection rackets in township trade and in the taxi industry** — stage 9's informal sector lesson |
| **Gang economies** | principally in the Western Cape, around drug markets and extortion |
| **Economic stagnation** | **stage 9's post-2009 period, and the youth unemployment rate** |
| **Impunity** | **the detection and conviction rates** — from stage 8, a substantial majority of murder dockets do not end in a conviction, **and a murder that will not be solved deters nobody** |

**The explanation that does the most work is the fourth row of the first table read against the first row of the second: policing capacity rose and then fell, and the murder rate fell and then rose, with a lag.** **It is not proof, and it is the strongest available correlation.**

---

**The other crime categories, briefly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Sexual offences** | **on the order of 40,000 to 55,000 reported a year** — and **the Victims of Crime Survey consistently shows that only a small fraction of sexual offences are reported**, so the recorded figure is a reporting rate as much as an incidence rate. The next lesson |
| **Aggravated robbery** | house robbery, business robbery, carjacking and cash-in-transit heists — **the category that most shapes how middle-class South Africans live** |
| **Kidnapping** | **risen very sharply in the 2020s**, from a low base, including for ransom |
| **Stock theft and rural crime** | politically charged and statistically under-discussed |

**And the fact that says most about the state's capacity:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Police** | **roughly 180,000 to 190,000 members** |
| **Registered private security officers** | **on the order of 2.5 million registered with PSIRA, with several hundred thousand actively employed** |
| **The ratio** | **active private security personnel substantially outnumber police** — one of the largest such ratios in the world |
| **What it means** | **personal security in South Africa is substantially a purchased private good**, which means **its distribution follows income** — so the people in the highest-crime areas have the least protection |

**That is stage 9's inequality lesson in the one sector where the state's monopoly is supposed to be absolute.**

---

**And two findings worth knowing because they are precise:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Khayelitsha Commission (2014)** | a Western Cape commission of inquiry, chaired by **former Constitutional Court Justice Kate O'Regan and former NDPP Vusi Pikoli**, into policing inefficiency in Khayelitsha. **It found systemic inefficiencies, a breakdown of trust between police and the community, and — critically — that police resources were allocated in a way that disadvantaged poor, black areas** |
| **The resource allocation litigation** | that finding was taken further, and **the Equality Court held that the police's human resource allocation system unfairly discriminated on the grounds of race and poverty** — **the areas with the most murders had the fewest police per capita** |
| **Prisons** | **on the order of 155,000 to 165,000 inmates against a design capacity well below that**, with **roughly a quarter to a third awaiting trial** — many for long periods. ***Lee v Minister of Correctional Services* (2012)** established state liability for TB infection contracted in prison |

**Practice.** Build the murder rate series yourself from the SAPS annual statistics. Then find the Firearms Control Act's commencement date and the firearm homicide trend after it. Then read the Khayelitsha Commission's findings on resource allocation. Then find the current number of registered private security officers and compare it with police numbers.
Education since 1994:
Near-universal access, among the world's highest education spending as a share of GDP, and reading outcomes at the bottom of every international comparison.

**What was achieved, which is substantial and is usually skipped:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One system** | **nineteen racially separate departments merged into one national and nine provincial departments** |
| **Spending equalised** | **per-learner spending in the early 1990s differed by a factor of four or more between white and African schools.** That gap was closed and then reversed — **poorer schools now receive more per learner through the quintile funding system** |
| **Access** | **enrolment for ages 7 to 15 is near-universal**, and **Grade R attendance is now near-universal too** |
| **No-fee schools** | **roughly 75 to 80% of public schools charge no fees** — stage 9's social wage |
| **School feeding** | **a meal a day to 9 to 10 million learners** |
| **Spending** | **basic plus higher education is on the order of 6% of GDP and close to 20% of consolidated spending** — **among the highest in the world as a share of the economy** |
| **Higher education enrolment** | **roughly doubled since 1994, to on the order of 1.1 million** |

**Access was solved. That is the achievement and it was not trivial.**

---

**And the outcomes, which are the problem:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **PIRLS 2021 (reading, Grade 4)** | **about 81% of South African learners could not read for meaning in any language — the lowest of all participating countries** |
| **TIMSS (maths and science)** | **South Africa has consistently ranked at or near the bottom** of the participating countries |
| **The one encouraging qualification** | **South Africa's TIMSS improvement rate from 1995 to 2019 was among the fastest measured anywhere.** Improving fast from a very low base is still improving fast — **and PIRLS 2021 showed a reversal, attributed substantially to Covid school closures** |

**The matric figure, and how to read it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The National Senior Certificate pass rate** | **rose from around 60% in the late 2000s to the high 80s in the mid-2020s** |
| **The throughput problem** | **of roughly 1.2 million learners who start Grade 1, on the order of 700,000 write matric** — so **a large share leaves the system before the exam** |
| **The arithmetic** | **a pass rate is calculated on those who write.** A rising pass rate with falling throughput can mean the weakest candidates were not entered |
| **The pass requirement** | **30% in some subjects and 40% in others** meets the minimum, which is a real and separate criticism |
| **The useful number instead** | **passes with university entrance ("bachelor passes") as a share of the original Grade 1 cohort** — on the order of 15% or less |

**From stage 1: the matric pass rate is the most widely reported and least informative education statistic in the country.** **Use throughput and bachelor passes against the cohort.**

---

**What the diagnosis points at:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Early grade reading instruction** | **the consensus diagnosis.** Children are not taught to decode and comprehend in the foundation phase, and **the deficit compounds through every later grade.** The Early Grade Reading Study and the Funda Wande work are the evidence base |
| **Teacher subject knowledge** | **the teacher training colleges were closed in the 1990s and 2000s** and teacher education moved to universities, **producing a long supply gap**; studies of teacher content knowledge in mathematics find serious gaps |
| **Time on task** | **measured teaching time is well below the curriculum's requirement** in many schools |
| **Infrastructure** | **pit latrines, no water, no electricity in thousands of schools** — litigated continuously. **The deaths of children in school pit latrines in 2014 and 2018, and the *Komape* litigation, are what forced the norms and standards to have deadlines** |
| **Language of instruction** | the transition to English in Grade 4, which the PIRLS results sit directly on top of |
| **Governance** | **the Ministerial Task Team report of 2016 found the sale of teaching and principal posts — "jobs for cash" — in six provinces**, involving union and departmental officials. **Stage 8's appointment thesis, in schools** |

---

**Higher education:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Access** | **roughly doubled**, with NSFAS funding expanding from single-digit billions to **on the order of R50 billion** after 2018 — stage 11's #FeesMustFall lesson |
| **Throughput** | **dropout rates remain high** — a large share of entrants do not complete, and completion within the minimum time is much lower |
| **The missing middle** | **households too well off for NSFAS and too poor to pay** — the unresolved funding question |
| **TVET colleges** | **on the order of 700,000 enrolments with poor completion and weak employer linkages** — widely identified as the system's biggest unrealised opportunity |

**And the live legislative dispute, as a dated note:**

> **As of 14 October 2026: the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act was signed in September 2024, with its sections on school language and admissions policy — which shift final authority from school governing bodies to provincial heads of department — held back for further consultation before implementation. It is one of the governing coalition's open disagreements.** **Check the commencement proclamations in the Gazette and the status of any litigation.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For the provisions** | **school governing bodies have used language and admissions policy to exclude**, which is documented, and a head of department should be able to override it to place children |
| **Against** | **section 29(2)'s right to education in the language of choice where reasonably practicable, and section 29(3)'s independent schools**, plus the governance principle that school communities run their schools |
| **The underlying fact** | **the dispute is about a small number of schools and a large principle**, and both sides know it |

**Practice.** Find the PIRLS 2021 South African result and the comparator countries. Then calculate the bachelor-pass rate against the Grade 1 cohort of twelve years earlier. Then read the *Komape* judgment. Then find the Ministerial Task Team's 2016 report on the selling of posts.
Gender, and gender-based violence:
Among the world's highest femicide rates, one of the world's most gender-equal legislatures, and the gap between the two.
