**Start with both facts, because they are both true and they are rarely stated together.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Representation** | **women are roughly 45 to 46% of the National Assembly** — **among the highest shares in the world**, achieved through party list quotas rather than statute, principally the governing party's 50/50 rule. **Women have held the Speakership, the Deputy Presidency, and senior Cabinet and judicial positions** |
| **Law** | **section 9 lists gender and sex as prohibited grounds; the Constitution recognises reproductive autonomy (s12(2)(a)); the Choice on Termination of Pregnancy Act (1996) is among the more permissive in the world; *Bhe* struck male primogeniture; the Recognition of Customary Marriages Act (1998) gave customary wives equal status; same-sex marriage was recognised in 2006 after *Fourie*** |
| **And** | **the rate at which women are killed in South Africa is roughly five times the global average** |

**That is the central paradox of this lesson: formal equality is extensive and well-enforced, and the violence is among the worst measured anywhere.**

---

**The numbers, carefully:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Women murdered** | **on the order of 2,500 to 2,900 a year** — SAPS records them separately in the quarterly releases |
| **The rate** | **roughly five times the global average for female homicide** |
| **Intimate partner killing** | **the South African Medical Research Council's femicide studies found that a very large share of women murdered are killed by an intimate partner** — the widely cited finding from the 2009 study being **a woman killed by a partner roughly every eight hours** |
| **Sexual offences reported** | **on the order of 40,000 to 55,000 a year** |
| **Reporting** | **the Victims of Crime Survey indicates only a small fraction of sexual offences are reported** — so the recorded figure is far below incidence |
| **Attrition** | **the published research on rape case attrition found a conviction in well under a tenth of reported cases** — with cases lost at every stage, from docket to court |

> **Check SAPS's quarterly crime statistics, which report contact crimes against women and children separately, and the SAMRC's femicide studies.**

**The attrition finding is the one to hold, because it is the mechanism.** **A reported rape has a small probability of a conviction**, and from stage 8's police lesson the reasons are identifiable: **detective capacity, the DNA backlog, case withdrawal under pressure, and secondary victimisation in the process itself.** **This is not a gap in the law.**

---

**What has been built, and it is not nothing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Thuthuzela Care Centres** | **one-stop facilities at hospitals** providing medical care, forensic examination, counselling and police statement-taking in one place — **on the order of 60 of them**, and **the model is internationally regarded** |
| **Sexual offences courts** | dedicated courts with trained prosecutors and intermediaries, re-established from 2013 |
| **The National Register for Sex Offenders** | expanded by the 2021 legislation |
| **The 2018 turning point** | **the #TotalShutdown marches of August 2018**, followed by **the first Presidential Summit on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide in November 2018** and a declaration with commitments |
| **The National Strategic Plan on GBVF (2020)** | six pillars, with a costed implementation plan |
| **Three Acts signed in January 2022** | **the Domestic Violence Amendment Act** (expanded definitions including coercive control-type conduct, online applications for protection orders, mandatory reporting duties); **the Criminal and Related Matters Amendment Act** (bail and minimum sentence tightening, extended use of intermediaries); and **the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act** (register expansion, reporting obligations) |
| **The National Council on GBVF Act (2024)** | **a statutory council** to coordinate the response |

**And the honest assessment of all of it:** **the legislative and institutional architecture is now extensive, and the conviction rate has not moved correspondingly.** **From stage 8: this is a consequence-management failure, and the binding constraint is the detective service, the forensic laboratories and the courts' capacity — not the statute book.**

---

**Three cases that belong in the record.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***Carmichele v Minister of Safety and Security* (2001)** | **the state can be liable in delict for failing to protect a woman from a known violent offender** — the police and prosecutors had not opposed bail for a man with a history. **A foundational judgment on the state's positive duty under section 12** |
| ***Tshabalala v S* (2020)** | **the Constitutional Court held the doctrine of common purpose applies to rape** — so a participant in a group attack is liable for the rapes committed by others, without having to have perpetrated the act personally |
| **The 2006 rape trial** | **the complainant in the rape trial of the then-Deputy President, known publicly as "Khwezi", was subjected to extensive public hostility; he was acquitted; she left the country and died in 2016.** **In 2016 four women staged a silent protest at the election results announcement holding placards reading "Remember Khwezi"** — one of the most widely recognised political images of the period |

**The third entry is not a legal precedent and it belongs here for a reason: it is the clearest illustration of how a complainant's treatment deters reporting**, which is the attrition finding's social mechanism.

---

**And three structural points that connect to the rest of the curriculum:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The labour market** | **women's labour force participation is lower, unemployment higher, and earnings lower** — and **unpaid care work is overwhelmingly women's**, which is the mechanism. Stage 9's absorption rate is gendered |
| **The grant system** | **the Child Support Grant is received overwhelmingly by women**, which makes it the largest income transfer to women in the country — stage 9 |
| **Media attention** | **the 2014 trial of a celebrity for killing his partner received more South African and global coverage than the roughly 2,700 other women killed that year combined.** **From stage 1's press lesson: what gets covered is not what is most common** |

**Practice.** Find the latest quarterly SAPS figures for women murdered and sexual offences reported. Then find the SAMRC femicide study and its intimate-partner share. Then read *Carmichele* on the state's positive duty. Then find the National Strategic Plan on GBVF's six pillars and establish which of them has a measurable indicator with published results.
The Zuma presidency, 2009-2018:
Nine years in which the institutions of stage 8 were systematically weakened, several courts stopped specific projects, and the record is not uniformly negative.

**How he got there, because the legal history is the political history:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **2005** | **dismissed as Deputy President** after Schabir Shaik's conviction for corrupt payments to him — the arms deal lesson — **and charged** |
| **2006** | **acquitted in a rape trial** — the gender lesson |
| **December 2007** | **defeated Thabo Mbeki for the ANC presidency at Polokwane** |
| **September 2008** | **a High Court judgment suggested political interference in his prosecution**, triggering Mbeki's recall. **The judgment was later overturned on appeal** |
| **April 2009** | **the NDPP withdrew the charges**, citing the **"spy tapes"** — recordings of the former NDPP and a Scorpions head discussing the timing of the charges |
| **2016–2018** | **the High Court set that withdrawal aside as irrational, the Supreme Court of Appeal upheld it, and the charges were reinstated.** The trial has proceeded slowly since |

**So the charges were withdrawn weeks before he became President, and the withdrawal was later held to have been irrational.** **That sequence is the single most consequential prosecutorial decision in South African history** — stage 8's NPA lesson.

---

**What the presidency did to the institutions, in the order stage 8 covers them:**

| Institution | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **The NPA** | **Simelane's appointment set aside (2012); Nxasana paid to leave; Abrahams's appointment later invalidated** — three NDPPs in nine years |
| **The Scorpions** | **disbanded in 2009** on the Polokwane resolution, replaced by the Hawks inside the police |
| **The Hawks** | **their independence litigated twice and found inadequate** — *Glenister II* and *HSF* |
| **The police** | **two commissioners removed after inquiries**; crime intelligence repeatedly compromised |
| **SARS** | **dismantled from 2014** — the Nugent findings, stage 9 |
| **Treasury** | **attacked twice** — Nenegate in December 2015 and the March 2017 dismissals, stage 9 |
| **The State Security Agency** | **repurposed for factional ends** — the 2018 review panel, stage 8 |
| **The SOEs** | **the vehicle** — stage 8, and the next two lessons |
| **The Public Protector** | **the office changed hands in 2016**, with the consequences stage 8 records |

**That is not a list of unrelated events. It is one project, and the Zondo Commission's reports are the documentation.**

---

**And three things the courts stopped, which is the other side of the ledger:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The nuclear programme** | **a 9,600 MW nuclear procurement, with intergovernmental agreements signed including with Russia.** ***Earthlife Africa v Minister of Energy* (2017)** — **the Western Cape High Court set aside the determination and the agreements as unlawful**, for having been made without proper public participation and NERSA concurrence. **A procurement running to perhaps a trillion rand was stopped by two NGOs in a high court** |
| **The Al-Bashir matter** | **the Supreme Court of Appeal held in 2016 that the government's failure to arrest the Sudanese President, who was subject to an ICC warrant, was unlawful** — the foreign policy lesson |
| **The spy tapes** | above |

**From stage 8: the judiciary held, and this is the evidence.**

---

**And the record that is not negative, which belongs in an honest account:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The HIV programme** | **the largest treatment expansion in the world happened in this period** — the AIDS lesson. **Life expectancy rose by roughly a decade** |
| **The social wage** | **grant coverage and value expanded substantially** — stage 9 |
| **Free higher education** | **announced in December 2017**, and the NSFAS expansion that followed — the #FeesMustFall lesson |
| **NHI policy** | developed in this period |
| **BRICS** | **South Africa joined in 2010**, which was a deliberate and consequential foreign policy achievement whatever one thinks of it |
| **The 2010 World Cup** | delivered |
| **Infrastructure** | **the renewable energy programme's first bid windows (2011–2015) were among the most successful public procurements in South African history** — stage 9 — **and then the same administration obstructed them** |

**That last row is the period in one line: the state ran an exemplary competitive renewable procurement and then refused to sign the resulting contracts.**

---

**The end, and the aftermath:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Motions of no confidence** | **eight were brought and all were defeated** — stage 8's Parliament lesson, including the 2017 secret ballot vote |
| **December 2017** | **Cyril Ramaphosa narrowly won the ANC presidency at Nasrec** — the next lessons |
| **February 2018** | **recalled by the NEC**, and resigned — stage 10 |
| **2019–2021** | **summoned by the Zondo Commission, appeared once in July 2019, then refused to return.** The Constitutional Court ordered him to appear; **he defied the order** |
| **June 2021** | **sentenced to fifteen months' imprisonment for contempt of the Constitutional Court** — an extraordinary order against a former head of state |
| **7 July 2021** | **imprisoned**, which triggered the July unrest two days later |
| **September 2021** | **released on medical parole, which the Supreme Court of Appeal later held unlawful**; **returned to prison in August 2023 and released the same day on a remission of sentence** |
| **2023** | **his private prosecution of a journalist and a prosecutor was struck down as an abuse of process** |
| **2024** | **MK** — stage 10 |

**Practice.** Read the SCA's judgment on the spy tapes decision. Then read *Earthlife Africa v Minister of Energy* (2017) and establish what it set aside. Then find the dates of the eight motions of no confidence and the votes. Then list the institutions in the table above and write next to each what stage 8 says its condition is now.
Nkandla:
R246 million of state money at a private homestead, a swimming pool described as a fire-fighting installation, and the first judicial finding that a sitting President had violated the Constitution.

**The facts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The place** | **Nkandla, in KwaZulu-Natal — the President's private residence**, a family homestead |
| **The project** | **"security upgrades"**, undertaken by the Department of Public Works from 2009 |
| **The cost** | **about R246 million of public money**, against an initial estimate a small fraction of that |
| **What was built** | **a swimming pool, an amphitheatre, a cattle kraal and culvert, a chicken run, a visitors' centre, extensive new housing, and relocation of neighbouring families** — alongside genuine security items such as fencing, bulletproofing and access control |

---

**The Public Protector's report, *Secure in Comfort* (March 2014).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The finding on the features** | **the swimming pool, amphitheatre, cattle kraal, chicken run and visitors' centre were not security features** |
| **The finding on benefit** | **the President and his family had unduly benefited** from the non-security installations |
| **The finding on conduct** | **he had failed to act in accordance with the Executive Ethics Code** by not stopping the escalation once he became aware |
| **The remedial action** | **that he repay a reasonable percentage of the cost of the non-security features, as determined by the National Treasury with the SAPS, and report to the National Assembly** |
| **The other findings** | **the procurement was riddled with irregularity and the cost escalation was not controlled** — a Public Works failure as much as anything |

**The swimming pool became the centre of the argument because of what was said about it.** **A ministerial report in 2015 concluded that the pool was a fire-fighting water reservoir — a "fire pool" — and that the President need not repay anything.** **The report included a demonstration video.** **The phrase entered the language.**

---

**What Parliament did**, which is stage 8's oversight lesson in one case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Three processes** | **an ad hoc committee**, a Special Investigating Unit investigation, and **the ministerial report above** |
| **The ad hoc committee** | **boycotted by opposition parties** and criticised as designed to produce absolution |
| **The outcome** | **the National Assembly adopted a resolution accepting the ministerial report and absolving the President of any liability to repay** |
| **Which is the point** | **the Assembly used its majority to set aside a Chapter 9 institution's remedial action** |

---

**Then the courts, in *Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker of the National Assembly; Democratic Alliance v Speaker* (31 March 2016).**

| The holding | |
| --- | --- |
| **On remedial action** | **the Public Protector's remedial action is binding unless set aside by a court** — the "toothless bulldog" reasoning from stage 8 |
| **On the Assembly** | **its resolution absolving the President was unlawful and invalid**, because it had no power to set aside the remedial action |
| **On the President** | **he had failed to uphold, defend and respect the Constitution as the supreme law** — section 83(b) |
| **The remedy** | **the Treasury to determine the amount within 60 days; the President to pay it within 45 days of that** |
| **What followed** | **the Treasury determined about R7.8 million, and he paid it in September 2016** |

**The second and third rows are the historic parts.** **A unanimous Constitutional Court found that the National Assembly had acted unlawfully and that the President had failed in his constitutional duty.** **That had never happened before.**

**And then nothing further happened constitutionally:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **April 2016** | **an impeachment motion under section 89 was brought and defeated** — it needed two-thirds, and the governing party's members voted against |
| **So** | **a court found the President had failed to uphold the Constitution, and the Assembly declined to remove him** |
| **Which is** | **stage 10's closed-list mechanism, operating exactly as that lesson describes** |

---

**Why Nkandla matters more than its cost:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **R246 million is small** | against the capture-era SOE contracts of the next lessons, **and it did more political damage than any of them** |
| **Because it was legible** | **a swimming pool at a private house is a fact anybody can hold.** A locomotive procurement's escalation is not |
| **It produced the binding-remedial-action holding** | **which made the Public Protector's office powerful** — stage 8 — with the consequences that lesson traces under the next office-holder |
| **It demonstrated Parliament's failure** | **more clearly than any committee report could** |
| **And it is the reason the Public Protector had the standing to issue *State of Capture* in October 2016** | **which produced the Zondo Commission.** **Nkandla is the causal chain's first link** |

**From stage 1's method: a small, legible fact can carry more political weight than a large illegible one, and the weight is not proportional to the money.**

**Practice.** Read *Secure in Comfort*'s remedial action paragraph. Then read the Constitutional Court's 2016 orders. Then find the National Assembly's 2015 resolution and the April 2016 impeachment vote. Then compare the R246m with the locomotive contract's escalation in the next lesson, and ask yourself why Nkandla was politically heavier.
The Guptas, and how capture worked:
A family business, a relationship with a president's family, and the mechanism — set out as a method, because the method is what transfers.

**Who they were:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The family** | **three brothers — Ajay, Atul and Rajesh — who arrived in South Africa from India in 1993** |
| **The businesses** | **Sahara Computers**, then **Oakbay Investments** — mining, media, computing and engineering |
| **The relationship** | **with the Zuma family from the early 2000s**, with **Duduzane Zuma, the President's son, a director and shareholder in several Gupta-linked companies** |
| **The media** | **The New Age newspaper (2010) and the ANN7 channel (2013)** — stage 10's press lesson |
| **The residence** | **Saxonwold, Johannesburg** — which became shorthand |

**The signal event, in April 2013: a chartered aircraft carrying about 200 wedding guests from India landed at Waterkloof Air Force Base**, a national key point, **with clearance obtained through officials.** **A private family used a military airbase for a wedding.** **The subsequent inquiry implicated senior officials and nobody of consequence was held accountable.** **That is the whole story in one incident, three years before the term "state capture" entered use.**

---

**The method, which is the part worth learning**, because it generalises:

| Step | How it worked |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Place people** | **get allies appointed to boards, to CEO and CFO positions, and to the relevant ministries.** Stage 8's appointment thesis — **and the Zondo Commission found board appointments at Eskom, Transnet and Denel made at the family's instance** |
| **2 — Control the procurement process** | **restructure procurement, create or capture the committees, and use "advisers"** |
| **3 — Insert an intermediary** | **a company with no capability is placed between the SOE and the real supplier**, taking a fee or a share of the contract for nothing |
| **4 — Use the state's own money as working capital** | **the Eskom prepayment is the clearest case**, below |
| **5 — Buy the narrative** | **the media outlets and the Bell Pottinger campaign** — stage 10 |
| **6 — Discredit the enforcers** | **SARS's "rogue unit", the attacks on Treasury officials, the NPA's leadership** — stages 8 and 9 |
| **7 — Launder and move the proceeds** | **through local and foreign banks and shell companies, substantially to the UAE** |

**Note that steps 1 and 6 are the same insight from two directions: control who is appointed, and remove whoever can investigate.**

---

**The specific transactions, as the Commission found them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Estina dairy (Free State)** | **on the order of R220 million of public money** for a dairy project at Vrede that never functioned as promised, **with funds traced out of the country** |
| **Transnet's locomotives** | **the acquisition of 1,064 locomotives, with the price escalating by many billions from the approved figure**, and **advisory fees of well over a billion rand** paid to intermediary firms. **The Commission devoted a volume to it** |
| **Eskom and Optimum Coal** | **a Glencore-owned colliery supplying Eskom was put under contractual and penalty pressure, went into business rescue, and was acquired by Tegeta — a Gupta-linked company. Eskom then made a prepayment of about R659 million to Tegeta, which the Commission found was used to fund the acquisition itself** |
| **The offer to Mcebisi Jonas** | **in 2016 the Deputy Finance Minister testified he was offered a very large sum of cash and the finance ministership at the Saxonwold residence, in the presence of the President's son. He refused** — stage 9's Treasury lesson |
| **Vytjie Mentor** | testified to a similar offer of a ministerial position |
| **Denel, SAA, SA Express and the SABC** | further transactions and appointments |

**And the two events that broke it open:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **March–April 2016** | **South Africa's major banks closed the Gupta companies' accounts**, citing reputational and compliance risk. **A commercial decision by private banks did more immediate damage than any state action** |
| **May–June 2017 — the #GuptaLeaks** | **roughly 200,000 emails and documents leaked to amaBhungane, Scorpio and News24**, documenting the transactions, the instructions and the money flows. **The single most consequential journalism in South African history** — stage 10 |

---

**What happened to them, which is the accountability record:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **February 2018** | **the family left South Africa**, principally for Dubai, as asset forfeiture raids began |
| **June 2022** | **two of the brothers were arrested in the United Arab Emirates** on South Africa's request |
| **2023** | **the extradition failed.** The UAE declined, and the handling of the request by South African authorities was heavily criticised, including for procedural defects |
| **Convictions in South Africa** | **none of the brothers has been convicted in a South African court** |
| **The Estina prosecution** | brought against a number of accused, **with proceedings struck from the roll at one point owing to the state's lack of readiness**, and reinstituted |
| **Where accountability did come from** | **foreign regulators and the firms' own settlements** — the next lesson |

**That is the arms deal pattern from earlier in this stage, repeated: intermediaries and foreign firms settle, and the principals are not convicted.**

**And one term to use carefully.** **"State capture"** entered South African use through **the Public Protector's October 2016 report title, *State of Capture***. **It has a specific analytical meaning in the political science literature — the systematic repurposing of state institutions to serve private interests, as distinct from episodic bribery — and that meaning is the right one.** **It is not a synonym for corruption, and the distinction is what stage 8's institutional analysis rests on.**

**Practice.** Read the Zondo Commission's volume on Transnet's locomotives. Then read its findings on the Tegeta prepayment. Then find the #GuptaLeaks reporting on one transaction and trace how the documents established it. Then establish the current status of the Estina prosecution and the extradition request.
The Zondo Commission:
Four years, three hundred days of hearings, five thousand five hundred pages — and the one commission in this curriculum whose findings no court has set aside.

**How it came to exist**, which is the causal chain from Nkandla:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **October 2016** | **the Public Protector's report *State of Capture*** — its remedial action **directed the President to appoint a commission of inquiry headed by a judge selected by the Chief Justice** |
| **The President litigated against it** | and **lost in the High Court in December 2017**, which confirmed the remedial action |
| **January 2018** | **the commission was established by proclamation**, with **Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo** as chairperson |
| **The name** | **the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture, Corruption and Fraud in the Public Sector including Organs of State** |
| **Note the mechanism** | **a Chapter 9 institution compelled the President to appoint a commission, through a court, against his resistance.** From stage 8: that is the binding-remedial-action holding doing work |

---

**The scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hearings** | **from August 2018 to mid-2021** — on the order of 300 days of public hearings, broadcast live |
| **Witnesses** | **around 300 gave oral evidence; several hundred more filed affidavits** |
| **Evidence** | **on the order of 1.7 million pages** |
| **Cost** | **on the order of a billion rand**, which is the figure most often raised against it |
| **The reports** | **delivered in parts between January and June 2022 — roughly 5,500 pages in total** |

**What each part covered:**

| Part | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| **One** | **South African Airways, SARS, and the New Age / government advertising** |
| **Two** | **Transnet and Denel** |
| **Three** | **Bosasa, and further Transnet matters** |
| **Four** | **Eskom** |
| **Five** | **the State Security Agency, Parliament, cadre deployment, the ANC, and the recommendations** |

---

**Zuma's defiance, which is a constitutional episode in its own right:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **July 2019** | **he appeared once**, for several days |
| **Then** | **refused to return**, despite summonses |
| **January 2021** | **the Constitutional Court ordered him to appear and answer questions** |
| **He defied the order** publicly | |
| **June 2021** | **the Constitutional Court found him in contempt and sentenced him to fifteen months' imprisonment** — **a former head of state imprisoned for defying a court** |
| **7 July 2021** | **he surrendered** |
| **9 July 2021** | **the unrest began** — the July 2021 lesson |

**The significance for stage 7's constitutional supremacy: a court ordered a former President to testify, he refused, and he went to prison for it.** **There is no more direct demonstration that section 165(5) — a court order binds all persons — is enforceable.**

---

**What the Commission found, in summary by institution:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Transnet** | **"the primary site of state capture"** in the Commission's own characterisation — the locomotives, the advisory fees, the board appointments |
| **Eskom** | board capture, the Optimum and Tegeta transactions, coal contracts, consultancy fees |
| **SAA** | board and procurement capture, with findings against the long-serving chairperson |
| **SARS** | **the dismantling documented in stage 9**, consistent with the Nugent findings |
| **Denel** | board capture and the Denel Asia transaction |
| **The SSA** | **repurposed for factional political ends**, consistent with the 2018 review panel — stage 8 |
| **Bosasa** | **a facilities company whose business model was the systematic bribery of officials and politicians**, with payments to the ANC and to individuals over many years |
| **The government's advertising spend** | directed to Gupta-owned media |
| **Parliament** | **failed in its oversight duty** — the next lesson |
| **The ANC** | **cadre deployment found unlawful and unconstitutional**, and the party itself implicated — the next lesson |

**And the recommendations**, which stage 8's closing lesson sets out: **a permanent independent anti-corruption agency; panel-based appointments for the NDPP, police commissioner and SOE boards; procurement reform with a single regulator; whistleblower protection; the end of cadre deployment; and a reconsideration of the closed-list electoral system.**

---

**Now the two assessments, because both are made seriously.**

| What it achieved | What it did not |
| --- | --- |
| **the record.** **5,500 pages of tested evidence, publicly available and free**, which is why this curriculum can cite findings rather than allegations | **prosecutions.** **The referrals have produced a small number of cases, slowly** — stage 8's NPA lesson |
| **it survived.** **No part of its findings has been set aside by a court** — unlike the Seriti Commission's report on the arms deal | **recovery.** The money recovered has come mostly from **settlements with implicated firms**, not from the commission's referrals — the next lesson |
| **the institutional reform agenda** it produced is the most coherent available, and parts have been implemented — IDAC, the Public Procurement Act | **implementation.** **The appointment reforms, which are the highest-leverage recommendations, have largely not been enacted** |
| **it made defiance costly** — the contempt sentence | **the political consequence was electoral, not legal** — stage 10's 2024 lesson |
| **it was televised**, so the evidence entered public memory directly rather than through intermediaries | **the cost — about a billion rand — is a fair criticism to weigh against what followed** |

**The honest summary, which is this curriculum's position on commissions generally, from stage 1: Zondo produced an excellent record and almost no consequences, and those are separate functions.** **A commission establishes what happened. A prosecution requires a prosecutor, an investigator and a court — and stage 8 explains why those were not available.**

**Practice.** Download one part of the Zondo report and read its executive summary. Then read the Commission's recommendations on appointments in Part Five. Then compare the Seriti and Zondo commissions on whether their findings survived judicial review. Then find how many Zondo referrals have resulted in a conviction, and the date you checked.
What Zondo found about Parliament and th:
Part Five's two hardest chapters: that the legislature failed, and that the governing party's own practices made the capture possible.

**Most summaries of the Zondo Commission stop at the SOEs. The findings that matter most for stages 8 and 10 are in Part Five, and they are about Parliament and about the ANC.**

---

**On Parliament.**

**The Commission's finding, in substance:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The conclusion** | **Parliament failed in its constitutional duty to hold the executive accountable** throughout the period under investigation |
| **How** | **portfolio committees did not pursue warnings that were put to them**; **SCOPA's work was not acted on**; and **the executive's accounts went substantially untested** |
| **The mechanism** | **the governing party's parliamentary caucus acted to shield the executive** — opposing motions, voting down inquiries, and in the Nkandla case **adopting a resolution absolving the President** |
| **The evidence that it was possible** | **the Portfolio Committee on Public Enterprises' Eskom inquiry of 2017–18** — which did the work, called the witnesses, and produced findings. **The Commission used it to show that the failure was a choice, not an incapacity** |

**And the recommendations, which stage 8's conclusion lists:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Oversight of the President** | **a dedicated parliamentary mechanism for overseeing the Presidency**, which does not exist |
| **Committee capacity** | **research and investigative support for committees**, which are presently under-resourced |
| **The member's duty** | **that an MP's constitutional oversight obligation must prevail over a party instruction** — which the Commission recognised is unenforceable without the next item |
| **The electoral system** | **that a constituency element be introduced**, so that **members have a base independent of the party list** |

**That last recommendation is why stage 10 exists.** **A judicial commission investigating corruption concluded that the electoral system was part of the causal chain**, because **a member whose seat depends entirely on a party list cannot be expected to defy the party in the public interest.** From stage 10's recall lesson: **the seven-step chain is the same mechanism.**

---

**On the ANC**, which is the more remarkable set of findings, because **a commission appointed by the governing party's President made findings against the party itself.**

| Finding | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Cadre deployment** | **the practice as conducted was unlawful and unconstitutional** — because the deployment committee's recommendations extended into appointments that the law requires to be made on merit by a designated authority. **The Commission obtained the committee's minutes** |
| **Knowledge** | **the minutes showed the committee's involvement in appointments across the state**, including to positions where party involvement had been denied |
| **Party funding** | **the party received money from entities implicated in the capture** — including from Bosasa, whose business model the Commission found was the systematic bribery of officials — **and the Commission recommended a review of the Political Party Funding Act's thresholds** |
| **The recommendation** | **legislation making it unlawful for a political party to be involved in appointments to positions in the state** |
| **The step-aside rule** | **the Commission regarded it as insufficient** on its own as an integrity mechanism |
| **The structural warning** | **that the concentration of power in a dominant party, combined with internal processes that select the state's leadership, had made the capture possible** — and that the remedy was institutional, not personal |

**And the finding that is most often misstated: the Commission dealt with President Ramaphosa's own role as chair of the deployment committee between 2013 and 2017**, and **it made findings about the committee's conduct in that period** while **not finding that he had personally directed unlawful appointments.** **Read the actual passage rather than either side's summary of it.**

---

**And on whistleblowers**, which produced the clearest practical recommendation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The finding** | **whistleblowers were persecuted, dismissed, intimidated and in cases killed**, and the existing framework — **the Protected Disclosures Act** — had failed them |
| **The evidence** | the Commission heard from a succession of officials who had reported irregularities and lost their careers |
| **The recommendation** | **a comprehensive whistleblower protection regime**, including financial support, physical protection and a reward mechanism |
| **The event that proved the point** | **Babita Deokaran, a senior Gauteng health official who had flagged irregular payments, was assassinated in August 2021** — stage 10's protest lesson |
| **Status** | **a discussion paper and draft amendments have followed; a comprehensive regime has not been enacted.** **Check the current position** |

---

**Why these findings matter more than the transaction findings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The transactions are history** | the locomotives were bought, the coal was supplied, the money is gone |
| **The mechanisms are current** | **cadre deployment, the closed list, committee under-resourcing, party funding thresholds and whistleblower exposure all still exist** |
| **So the implementation record is the real measure** | **IDAC was made permanent and the Public Procurement Act was passed — both real.** **The appointment reforms, the electoral reform and the whistleblower regime were not** |
| **From stage 8's conclusion** | **the highest-leverage recommendations are the ones that have not been enacted**, and they are the ones that reduce patronage |

**Practice.** Read Part Five's chapter on Parliament. Then read its recommendations on cadre deployment and on the electoral system. Then find the deployment committee minutes that were disclosed and read a page of them. Then establish what has happened to the whistleblower protection proposals since 2022.
The state capture arithmetic:
What it cost, what was recovered, and why the honest answers are "nobody knows" and "about a tenth of what you have heard."

**The figure everybody quotes.**

> **"State capture cost South Africa R500 billion."**

**Where it comes from:** **it was used by the President and by senior officials from around 2019, and it entered general circulation.** **What it does not have is a published method.** **No document sets out what was counted, over what period, on what basis.** **The Zondo Commission did not endorse a single aggregate figure**, and the serious researchers in the field decline to.

**From stage 1's statistics lesson: a figure with no traceable method is not a measurement, however senior the person repeating it.** **That does not mean the cost was small. It means the number is not evidence.**

---

**What can actually be measured, in four separate categories that are often conflated:**

**1 — Money stolen or paid irregularly.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Irregular expenditure** | **the Auditor-General's figures** — tens of billions a year across government — **which from stage 8 is a compliance measure and not a theft measure** |
| **Documented overpayments** | **the locomotive contract's escalation, the Tegeta prepayment, the consultancy fees, the Estina transfers** — these are specific, documented and total in the tens of billions |
| **The Special Investigating Unit** | has contracts and payments under investigation running into many tens of billions of rands of value, which is **the value of contracts reviewed, not the amount stolen** |

**2 — Money recovered.**

| Source | Order of magnitude |
| --- | --- |
| **McKinsey** | **repaid about a billion rand of Transnet and Eskom fees in 2018**, with further repayments; **and in 2024 its Africa unit entered a deferred prosecution agreement with the United States Department of Justice with a penalty of well over a hundred million dollars** for the same conduct |
| **SAP** | **repaid several hundred million rand**, and **settled with the US Department of Justice and SEC in 2024 for a sum in the hundreds of millions of dollars** |
| **ABB** | **settled with South African authorities for about R2.5 billion**, and separately **paid a very large US penalty** |
| **Bain & Company** | **repaid its SARS fees**, and was **barred from United Kingdom government contracting for three years and restricted in the United States** |
| **KPMG** | **repaid its SARS fees** |
| **The Asset Forfeiture Unit** | **preservation and forfeiture orders in the low billions of rands a year**, with the amount actually forfeited substantially less than the amount restrained |
| **The plausible total recovered** | **on the order of ten billion rand**, overwhelmingly from the settlements above |

**3 — Prosecutions.** **From stage 8: a small number, slowly, mostly not of principals.**

**4 — The institutional damage, which is larger than all of the above.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Eskom** | **the load-shedding of 2022–23 cost one to two percentage points of GDP growth in each of those years** — stage 9. **That is far more than the money stolen from Eskom** |
| **Transnet** | **a third of rail volume lost** — stage 9's logistics lesson. **The export revenue foregone exceeds the contract irregularities by a wide margin** |
| **SARS** | **the revenue shortfall the Nugent Commission attributed in part to the institution's deterioration ran to the tens of billions a year** — stage 9 |
| **The NPA and the police** | **the capacity that was not built**, which is why the prosecutions did not follow |
| **The conclusion** | **the theft was the mechanism; the destruction of the institutions was the cost.** A rand stolen from Eskom is a rand; **a rand's worth of damage to Eskom's ability to generate electricity is a multiple of that** |

---

**Now the pattern that is the most important thing in this lesson.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where recovery came from** | **voluntary repayment by implicated firms, and foreign law enforcement** — the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, the UK's procurement bans, Swiss and other jurisdictions' asset freezes |
| **Where it did not** | **South African criminal prosecution of principals** |
| **The same pattern earlier** | **the arms deal** — the BAE settlement with the US Department of Justice, and no South African conviction of a decision-maker |
| **Why** | **stage 8's NPA and police lessons.** Complex financial prosecution requires forensic accountants, experienced prosecutors and a functioning investigative capacity, **and those were the specific capacities that the capture project destroyed** |
| **Which is the point** | **capture's most effective self-protection was the destruction of the institutions that would have prosecuted it**, and that protection has outlasted the project |

**That is a complete and sufficient explanation for why two commissions thirty years apart produced extensive findings and almost no criminal consequence.** **It is not a mystery and it does not require a conspiracy.**

---

**And the honest summary to carry:**

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| **What did it cost?** | **unknown in aggregate. Tens of billions demonstrably stolen or irregularly paid; far more than that in institutional damage, measurable through Eskom's and Transnet's output** |
| **What has been recovered?** | **on the order of ten billion rand, mostly from firms that settled** |
| **How many principals convicted?** | **very few** |
| **What recovered the most?** | **foreign regulators and the firms' own compliance departments** |
| **Is R500 billion right?** | **it has no published method. Do not use it as a fact. Use the measurable components instead** |

**Practice.** Try to find a published method for the R500 billion figure. Then find the McKinsey, SAP and ABB settlement amounts and dates. Then find the Asset Forfeiture Unit's recoveries in the NPA's latest annual report. Then put Eskom's 2023 GDP cost next to the total recovered, and write down which number is larger.
Marikana:
Thirty-four people shot dead by police in one afternoon, the largest such killing since Sharpeville, and the political consequences that followed.

**The context, which is stage 9's labour material:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The place** | **Lonmin's platinum operations at Marikana, in the North West** |
| **The industry** | **the platinum belt** — from stage 9, the largest mineral earner, with mineworkers living in informal settlements around the shafts |
| **The union conflict** | **the National Union of Mineworkers was losing members to the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union**, with violence between them — stage 9's wages lesson |
| **The demand** | **rock drill operators struck for a monthly wage of R12,500**, outside the recognised bargaining process — a **wildcat strike**, so not protected under the LRA |
| **The preceding week** | **from 11 to 13 August 2012, ten people were killed** — including **two police officers and two Lonmin security guards**, and several mineworkers |

**The killing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **16 August 2012** | **police moved to disperse and disarm strikers gathered at a koppie** |
| **"Scene One"** | **a group of strikers moving toward police was fired on — 17 killed, in front of television cameras** |
| **"Scene Two"** | **a further 17 killed at and around the koppie, out of camera view, many shot at close range** — and **the existence and character of Scene Two only became clear through the commission's forensic work and subsequent research** |
| **Total** | **34 killed on the day, 78 wounded** |
| **And then** | **about 270 arrested mineworkers were initially charged with the murders of their own colleagues, on a common purpose theory. The charges were withdrawn after public outcry** |

**The Scene Two distinction matters because of what it shows about the record.** **The televised killing was immediately known; the larger and more serious killing was not**, and establishing it took a commission and independent researchers. **From stage 1: what is on camera is not the whole event.**

---

**The Farlam Commission**, 2012 to 2015, chaired by retired Justice Ian Farlam.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On the police operation** | **the plan was defective and dangerous**, adopted late, and **unlawful in material respects**; the decision to disarm the strikers on that day was taken for reasons that were not properly explained |
| **On police conduct afterwards** | **the police misled the commission and altered and withheld documents** — a finding in the commission's own words |
| **On the National Commissioner** | **found not to be a fit and proper person to hold office**, which led to a board of inquiry |
| **On Lonmin** | **criticised for failing to address the living conditions it had undertaken to improve and for not engaging the strikers** |
| **On the unions** | findings against both NUM and AMCU in relation to the violence of the preceding week |
| **On political responsibility** | **no finding that any politician had ordered the operation.** The commission considered **the emails of Cyril Ramaphosa, then a Lonmin non-executive director**, including one urging **"concomitant action"** against what he characterised as criminal conduct, and his contacts with ministers, **and found they did not amount to improper influence on the police operation** |
| **Prosecutions** | **no police officer has been convicted for the killings** |
| **Compensation** | **civil claims for loss of support and for the wounded and arrested were settled over subsequent years**, slowly, running to hundreds of millions of rands |

**The political responsibility finding is contested and will remain so.** **The commission's reasoning is published; the criticism is that it accepted the account of the sequence of decisions too readily.** **Read the chapter and form a view — and note that "no finding of improper influence" is not the same as "no involvement", which is what both sides' summaries tend to elide.**

---

**What followed, which is why Marikana is a political event and not only a policing one:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Sharpeville comparison** | **the largest number of people killed by South African police in a single incident since Sharpeville in 1960** — stage 5. **That comparison was made immediately, by everyone, and it is the reason the event had the weight it did** |
| **AMCU's rise** | **and the five-month platinum strike of 2014**, the longest in South African history |
| **The EFF** | **founded in 2013, explicitly invoking Marikana**, and it made the event central to its politics — stage 10 |
| **The ANC's standing with workers** | **damaged in a way that has not recovered**, and the alliance's claim to represent mineworkers was directly challenged |
| **Ramaphosa** | **the association has followed him through every subsequent political contest**, including 2017 and 2024 |
| **The living conditions** | **Lonmin's unfulfilled housing undertakings under its social and labour plan** — stage 9's mining lesson — **became the standing example of what a social and labour plan is worth unenforced** |

---

**And the institutional reading, which is stage 8's:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The constitutional mandate functioned** | section 205, the right to assemble, the right to strike |
| **The commission functioned** | **it was thorough, its findings were severe, and it was not set aside** |
| **The oversight bodies functioned** | **IPID investigated; a board of inquiry removed the commissioner** |
| **And nobody was prosecuted** | |
| **Which is the thesis** | **the design worked, the inquiry worked, and the consequence did not** — stage 8's gap between design and capacity, in the single worst case available |

**Practice.** Read the Farlam Commission's findings on the police plan and on the police's conduct before the commission. Then read its chapter on the political responsibility question and form your own view. Then establish whether any police officer has been prosecuted, and the current status. Then find Lonmin's social and labour plan housing commitments and what was delivered.
RhodesMustFall and FeesMustFall:
The first mass political movement of the post-apartheid generation, organised outside the parties, which changed higher education funding in two years.

**The sequence:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **March 2015** | **#RhodesMustFall began at the University of Cape Town**, with a protest at the statue of Cecil John Rhodes. **The statue was removed on 9 April 2015** |
| **What it was about** | **the statue, and then far more** — the racial composition of senior academic staff, the curriculum, institutional culture, outsourced workers' conditions, and what "transformation" had meant in twenty years |
| **October 2015** | **#FeesMustFall began at Wits** over a proposed 10.5% fee increase, spread to almost every campus within days |
| **21 October 2015** | **a march on Parliament during the medium-term budget statement** |
| **23 October 2015** | **a march on the Union Buildings** — and **the President announced a 0% fee increase for 2016** |
| **2016** | **an 8% cap announced for 2017 with the state covering the increase for students from households below a threshold.** Protests resumed, with **campus closures, substantial arson and property damage running into hundreds of millions of rands, and large numbers of arrests** |
| **January 2016** | **the Commission of Inquiry into Higher Education and Training was appointed**, chaired by Justice Jonathan Heher |
| **November 2017** | **the Heher Commission reported** — **recommending against fee-free university education for all**, and proposing **an income-contingent loan scheme** backed by government, repayable through the tax system |
| **16 December 2017** | **at the ANC's Nasrec conference, the President announced fee-free higher education for students from households earning below R350,000** — **against the Commission's central recommendation** |

**Note the last two rows together.** **A judicial commission was appointed, deliberated for two years, recommended an income-contingent loan scheme, and the decision announced weeks later was the opposite.** **From stage 1's commission lesson: a commission advises, and the executive decides.**

---

**What actually changed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **NSFAS funding** | **from single-digit billions of rands in the mid-2010s to on the order of R50 billion** |
| **Students funded** | **on the order of a million** |
| **What it covers** | **fees, accommodation, learning materials and a living allowance** for students from households below the threshold — **a bursary, not a loan, for those who qualify** |
| **The access effect** | **real and large.** Higher education participation among poorer students rose substantially |
| **Insourcing** | **cleaning and security staff at several universities were brought in-house** on better terms — **a concrete win that the movement is rarely credited with** |

**And what did not change:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The missing middle** | **households above the NSFAS threshold and unable to pay** — the group the Heher Commission's loan scheme was designed for. **Still unresolved, and the subject of repeated proposals** |
| **Throughput** | **dropout rates remain high** — stage 11's education lesson. **Funding access does not by itself produce graduates, and the school system's outputs are the binding constraint** |
| **Accommodation** | **a severe national shortage**, which is now the most common cause of start-of-year campus disruption |
| **NSFAS administration** | **serious failures** — a direct-payment arrangement that went badly wrong, defunding errors, and **the dissolution of the scheme's board.** From stage 8: a well-funded programme administered badly |
| **The curriculum question** | **#RhodesMustFall's original demand about curriculum and staff composition produced debate, some appointments and some course changes, and no systematic reform** |

---

**Why it matters politically, which is the stage's point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It was the born-free generation's own movement** | **organised by people with no personal memory of apartheid**, about their own conditions, **and it was not led by any political party** |
| **The parties competed to claim it** | **the EFF's student command and the ANC-aligned student organisation both sought ownership**, and neither controlled it |
| **It used horizontal organisation and social media** | **no single leadership, decisions by mass meeting** — which made it fast and made it impossible to negotiate with |
| **It split over tactics** | **the arson and the disruption of examinations divided the movement**, and that split is why it did not consolidate into a durable organisation |
| **It won** | **a 0% increase in three weeks, and a fee-free policy in two years.** **From stage 10's protest lesson: mass action worked where the formal channels had not** |
| **And it did not become a party** | **unlike the 1980s student movement, which fed into the ANC.** Several of its figures entered politics individually; the movement itself dissolved |

**That last row is worth sitting with.** **A generation mobilised, achieved a major policy change, and produced no organisation.** **From stage 10's turnout lesson: the same cohort is substantially outside the electoral system.** **Whether those two facts are connected is a genuinely open question and a good one.**

**Practice.** Read the Heher Commission's recommendation on an income-contingent loan scheme. Then find NSFAS's budget for 2015 and for the most recent year. Then find the current proposals for the missing middle. Then establish what happened to the insourcing agreements at one university.
Nasrec 2017, and the turn:
A party conference decided by 179 votes out of about 4,700, which produced a President, a divided leadership, and the commissions.

**The 54th National Conference of the ANC, 16 to 20 December 2017, at Nasrec in Johannesburg.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The contest** | **Cyril Ramaphosa against Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma** |
| **The result** | **Ramaphosa 2,440; Dlamini-Zuma 2,261** |
| **The margin** | **179 votes, of roughly 4,700 cast** |
| **What it decided** | **who would be President of South Africa** — from stage 10's chain: branches elect delegates, delegates elect the party president, the party president becomes the country's President |

**Hold the arithmetic: a margin of about 3.8% of a few thousand delegates, selected through branch meetings, determined the national executive for the following six years.** **That is stage 10's thesis in a single number.**

---

**And the part that explains everything about the following five years: the leadership that emerged was split between the two slates.**

| Position | From which slate |
| --- | --- |
| **President — Ramaphosa** | his own |
| **Deputy President** | **the opposing slate** |
| **National Chairperson** | Ramaphosa's |
| **Secretary-General** | **the opposing slate** |
| **Deputy Secretary-General** | **the opposing slate** |
| **Treasurer-General** | Ramaphosa's |

**From stage 10's organisation lesson: the Secretary-General's office controls membership records, branch audits and the organisational machinery.** **So the new party President did not control the party's machinery**, and three of the six senior officials had campaigned against him.

**That is the single most useful fact for understanding the pace of 2018 to 2022.** Every assessment of Ramaphosa's first term — **"too slow", "incremental", "constrained"** — rests on it. **He held the Presidency of the country and a minority of the party's officials.**

---

**The resolutions**, which became national policy questions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Land** | **expropriation of land without compensation**, adopted on the conference floor against the leadership's drafted position. **Which produced the 2018–2021 constitutional amendment attempt — stage 7 — and the Expropriation Act of 2024** |
| **The Reserve Bank** | **nationalisation of the SARB's private shareholding** — stage 8's Reserve Bank lesson. **Never implemented** |
| **A state bank** | **Never implemented as resolved** |
| **Free higher education** | announced days before the conference ended — the last lesson |
| **The step-aside principle** | **adopted here**, and implemented by NEC guidelines in 2021 — stage 10 |
| **Cadre deployment** | **retained** |

**From stage 10's movement lesson: a conference resolution is treated as a mandate.** **Three of these six became national policy debates within months, and two were never acted on at all.** **Which is worth knowing when a conference resolution is cited as settled policy.**

---

**What followed, in eight weeks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **January 2018** | **the Eskom board was replaced** — the first substantive institutional intervention |
| **January 2018** | **the Zondo Commission was established by proclamation** |
| **February 2018** | **the NEC recalled President Zuma, and Ramaphosa was elected President by the National Assembly** |
| **February 2018** | **the Nugent Commission into SARS followed in May** — stage 9 |
| **February 2019** | **Shamila Batohi was appointed NDPP** |
| **May 2019** | **Edward Kieswetter was appointed SARS Commissioner** |

**Those six items are the substance of "the turn", and they are all appointments and inquiries.** **From stage 8's conclusion: appointment is the highest-leverage lever available to a president, and it is the one Ramaphosa used.** **The SARS recovery of stage 9 and the NPA's reconstruction both date from this list.**

---

**And the 2022 conference, briefly, because it settled the question:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **December 2022, the 55th Conference** | **Ramaphosa re-elected, 2,476 to 1,897** — a far wider margin |
| **The officials** | **his slate took the Secretary-General's position**, so the machinery problem was resolved |
| **The step-aside rule** | **retained, against sustained internal opposition** |
| **Structure** | **expanded to a Top Seven**, with a second Deputy Secretary-General |
| **What it means** | **the factional contest inside the party was decided in 2022, not 2017** — and **the 2024 election result followed eighteen months later** |

**Practice.** Find the Nasrec 2017 voting figures for all six positions and note which slate each winner came from. Then read the conference's land resolution. Then list the six post-conference actions above with their dates. Then compare the 2017 and 2022 margins and consider what the difference allowed.
Ramaphosa's first term:
Six years of institutional repair, three crises nobody planned for, and the argument about whether the pace was a choice.

**The record, organised by what it actually was:**

**1 — Appointments and inquiries**, from the last lesson: **the Zondo and Nugent commissions; the Eskom, Transnet, SAA and Denel boards replaced; a new NDPP, SARS Commissioner, Chief Justice and Public Protector; and IDAC established.** **This is the substantive record and it is the part that worked.**

**2 — Structural economic reform.** From stage 9:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Operation Vulindlela (2020)** | **the one economic programme of the post-1994 period that delivered a substantial share of what it set out to do** — electricity licensing, the spectrum auction of 2022, water use licensing turnaround, the skilled immigration visa system, the logistics roadmap |
| **Electricity** | **the embedded generation threshold raised and then removed; Eskom unbundled; the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act of 2024; the National Transmission Company operational.** **Load-shedding largely suspended from 2024** |
| **Logistics** | **the Freight Logistics Roadmap and the Economic Regulation of Transport Act of 2024** — slower, and in progress |
| **Procurement** | **the Public Procurement Act of 2024** |
| **The investment conferences** | from 2018, with pledges in the hundreds of billions of rands and **a mixed record on conversion to actual investment** |

**3 — The crises:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Covid-19** | 2020–22 — the next lesson |
| **July 2021** | the lesson after that |
| **The energy crisis** | **2022 and 2023 were the worst load-shedding years on record** — stage 9. **The Energy Action Plan of July 2022 and a Minister of Electricity appointed in 2023** |

**4 — What did not move:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Prosecutions** | **the central failure.** Two commissions' worth of findings, very few convictions — stage 8's NPA lesson and this stage's arithmetic lesson |
| **Local government** | **stage 8's local government lessons.** The 2021 result and the municipal audit outcomes |
| **The wage bill and the fiscus** | **contained by not hiring** — stage 9 |
| **Unemployment** | **higher at the end of the term than at the start** |
| **Appointment reform** | **the Zondo recommendations on the NDPP, the police commissioner and SOE boards were not enacted** |
| **Cadre deployment** | **retained by the party, found unlawful by the Commission** |

**5 — Phala Phala**, two lessons on.

---

**The elections in between:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2019** | **57.5%** — a decline, and the Cabinet was reduced from 36 ministers to 28 |
| **2021 local** | **45.6%** — below half for the first time |
| **2024** | **40.18%**, and the coalition — stage 10 |

---

**Now the argument, which is the live assessment of the period.**

| "Too slow, and it was a choice" | "That was the available pace" |
| --- | --- |
| **the prosecutions did not follow**, which was the test everybody named in 2018, and six years is long enough | **the NPA had to be rebuilt first** — stage 8. A prosecution service with three contested NDPPs in nine years does not acquire forensic capacity quickly, and complex cases take years |
| **cadre deployment continued** throughout, and the party's own committee was found unlawful | **the party's machinery was held by the opposing faction until December 2022** — the last lesson |
| **the pace was a negotiating position**, protecting party unity ahead of accountability | **a faster pace risked the party splitting, and the 2024 result shows what a split cost even when managed** |
| **local government was not addressed at all** in the first term | **the electricity crisis was existential and absorbed the available political capital** |
| **"Ramaphoria" in 2018 was spent on commissions rather than on reform legislation** | **the commissions produced the evidence base without which nothing else was arguable**, and the institutional repairs at SARS and the NPA are real and measurable |

**The strongest point on each side, honestly stated:** **against — the single highest-leverage reform available was appointment reform, it required only legislation, and it was not done.** **For — the SARS recovery and the end of load-shedding are both large, measurable improvements that did not happen by themselves, and both took about five years, which is how long institutional repair takes.**

**And the structural reading, which stages 8 and 10 support: a President who holds the office through a party whose machinery he does not control, with a closed-list caucus whose members' seats depend on that machinery, has a narrow set of levers.** **The ones he used — appointment and regulatory reform — are precisely the ones that do not require a parliamentary majority or party consensus.** **That is not a defence or an indictment. It is the mechanism.**

**Practice.** List the institutional appointments made between February 2018 and May 2019 and establish the condition of each institution now. Then find Operation Vulindlela's reform list and count the completed items. Then find the unemployment rate in February 2018 and in May 2024. Then write the strongest version of whichever column above you disagree with.
Covid-19:
One of the world's strictest lockdowns, two years of government by regulation, about three hundred thousand excess deaths, and world-class science.

**The sequence:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **5 March 2020** | **the first confirmed case** |
| **15 March 2020** | **a national state of disaster declared under the Disaster Management Act 57 of 2002** |
| **26 March 2020** | **a hard lockdown — among the strictest in the world.** No leaving home except for essential purposes, **no outdoor exercise, no sale of alcohol or tobacco, no hot food delivery** |
| **1 May 2020** | **a five-level "risk-adjusted strategy"**, with restrictions eased and re-imposed through successive waves |
| **4 April 2022** | **the state of disaster ended — two years and three weeks after it began** |

---

**The constitutional point first, because it is the one that belongs in this curriculum.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What was used** | **the Disaster Management Act — ordinary legislation.** Regulations were made **by a minister, by notice in the Gazette** |
| **What was not used** | **section 37 of the Constitution — a state of emergency** — which **requires an Act of Parliament, a declaration lasting 21 days unless the Assembly extends it, automatic judicial reviewability, and a list of non-derogable rights** |
| **The consequence** | **for two years, rights of movement, assembly, trade and religious practice were limited by ministerial regulation**, with **Parliament's role reduced to oversight after the fact** |
| **The litigation** | substantial. ***De Beer v Minister of Cooperative Governance* (2020)** held a large tranche of regulations irrational and unconstitutional; **the tobacco sales ban was found unconstitutional after it had ended**; and numerous specific restrictions were challenged |
| **The argument for** | **the Act was designed for exactly this, it allowed rapid response, and a section 37 emergency carries far graver connotations and would have suspended more** |
| **The argument against** | **section 37's safeguards exist precisely for prolonged rights limitation**, and **a two-year regime of ministerial regulation is what the drafters of section 37 were guarding against** |

**From stage 7's states of emergency lesson: this is the most important untested question about section 37, and it was answered in practice by avoiding it.**

---

**The deaths, measured honestly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Recorded Covid-19 deaths** | **on the order of 102,000** |
| **Excess natural deaths** | **the South African Medical Research Council's weekly excess mortality series estimated roughly 300,000 excess natural deaths** over the pandemic period |
| **The attribution** | **the SAMRC's estimate was that the large majority of the excess — on the order of 85 to 95% — was Covid-attributable** |
| **Why the gap** | **limited testing, deaths at home, and deaths from untreated other conditions** when the health system was overwhelmed |
| **Which number to use** | **the excess deaths series.** From stage 1's statistics lesson: **a recorded cause-of-death count is a function of testing capacity; excess mortality is not** |

**That makes Covid, on the excess-death measure, roughly the same order of magnitude as the cumulative AIDS denialism cost of earlier in this stage** — and **both are modelled or estimated, and both are the best available figures.**

---

**The science, which was genuinely world-leading:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Genomic surveillance** | **the Network for Genomic Surveillance in South Africa** sequenced at a scale and speed few countries matched |
| **The Beta variant** | **identified and characterised by South African scientists in December 2020** |
| **Omicron** | **identified and announced by South African and Botswanan scientists in late November 2021** |
| **What followed the Omicron announcement** | **immediate travel bans on southern African countries**, imposed within days by many states |
| **The consequence** | **the bans were widely criticised, including by the WHO, as penalising the transparency that had identified the variant** — and the government protested them as unjustified |
| **The lesson** | **the global incentive structure punished the country that did the surveillance**, which is a real policy problem and was named as one at the time |

**The vaccine rollout, more mixed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The false start** | **an AstraZeneca purchase was abandoned in early 2021** after South African trial data showed poor efficacy against the Beta variant, and the doses were transferred on |
| **The health worker programme** | **a large implementation trial vaccinated health workers from February 2021** |
| **The mass rollout** | **from May 2021**, reaching **roughly half of adults with at least one dose** — **short of the target**, with **hesitancy, access and demand rather than supply the binding constraint in the later phases** |
| **Equity** | **South Africa was among the leading voices for the TRIPS waiver on vaccine intellectual property**, which was substantially unsuccessful — the foreign policy lesson |

---

**The economy and the schools:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **GDP** | **fell by roughly 6% in 2020** — the largest single-year contraction in the post-1994 period |
| **Employment** | **on the order of two million jobs lost in the second quarter of 2020**, with the recovery in output faster than the recovery in employment |
| **The relief package** | **announced at R500 billion**, comprising **the R350 SRD grant** (stage 9), **grant top-ups**, **UIF wage support paying out tens of billions**, and **a R200 billion loan guarantee scheme that was very poorly taken up** |
| **Schools** | **closed from March 2020, with rotational attendance into 2021.** **Studies estimate roughly a year of learning lost for primary learners** — and **the PIRLS 2021 reading result's reversal from stage 11's education lesson is attributed substantially to this** |

**The learning loss is the pandemic's longest-lasting South African cost**, and from the education lesson's compounding argument: **a cohort that lost a year of foundation-phase learning carries it to matric.**

---

**And the corruption, which was immediate:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **PPE procurement** | **emergency procurement rules were relaxed, and the Special Investigating Unit investigated contracts worth many billions of rands, finding a large proportion irregular** |
| **Digital Vibes** | **a communications contract at the Department of Health, worth on the order of R150 million, found by the SIU to have been irregularly awarded to associates of the Minister of Health**, who **resigned in 2021** |
| **The killing** | **Babita Deokaran, who had flagged irregular Gauteng health payments including PPE contracts, was assassinated in August 2021** — stage 10 |
| **Recovery** | **the SIU obtained setting-aside orders and recoveries**, and **prosecutions have been limited** |
| **The pattern** | **relaxed procurement controls plus urgency plus weak consequence management** — stage 8's thesis, under emergency conditions |

**Practice.** Find the SAMRC's excess deaths estimate and the recorded Covid death toll, and note the ratio. Then read section 37 and list the safeguards that a Disaster Management Act declaration does not carry. Then find the SIU's reported findings on PPE contracts. Then find an estimate of Covid learning losses for South African primary learners.
July 2021:
A week in which the state lost control of two provinces, three hundred and fifty-four people died, and the official inquiry declined to call it what the President had called it.

**The sequence:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **29 June 2021** | **the Constitutional Court sentenced Jacob Zuma to fifteen months for contempt** — the Zondo lesson |
| **7 July 2021** | **he surrendered to serve the sentence** |
| **8–9 July** | **blockades began on the N3** — the corridor between Durban's port and Gauteng, which is the country's economic artery — **with trucks stopped and burned** |
| **9–18 July** | **widespread looting, arson and destruction across KwaZulu-Natal and parts of Gauteng** |
| **The scale** | **about 3,000 retail stores looted; on the order of 200 shopping centres and malls; more than a thousand ATMs destroyed; warehouses, distribution centres, factories and a Durban-area oil refinery affected** |
| **Deaths** | **354 people**, on the official count |
| **Arrests** | **on the order of 5,500** |
| **The military** | **the SANDF was deployed, initially in small numbers, with a much larger deployment authorised as the week went on** |

---

**The damage, and the character of it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Economic cost** | **estimates of around R50 billion of GDP, with R20 billion or more in direct stock and property loss** |
| **Jobs** | **on the order of 150,000 jobs affected**, many in retail and logistics |
| **Food and fuel** | **supply chains into KwaZulu-Natal broke**, with queues and shortages, and **the port and the N3 corridor halted** |
| **Insurance** | **Sasria, the state-owned special risks insurer, paid out the largest claims in its history and required recapitalisation** |

**And the deaths were of two kinds, which matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Most** | **in and around the looting itself** — crushes, shootings, and deaths at the sites |
| **Phoenix** | **36 people were killed in Phoenix, north of Durban**, in confrontations between residents who had set up blockades and Black people travelling through or near the area. **The great majority of those killed were Black; the area is predominantly Indian** |
| **What it did** | **the Phoenix killings opened the most serious public argument about race between Black and Indian South Africans since the 1949 Durban riots** — stage 4 — and **prosecutions followed, with mixed outcomes** |
| **Why it is in this lesson** | **because a week of state absence produced armed community defence, and armed community defence produced a racial massacre.** That is the most important single consequence to understand |

---

**The state's failure, as the official inquiry found it.**

**The Expert Panel into the July 2021 Unrest**, appointed by the President and chaired by **Professor Sandy Africa**, reported in **February 2022**.

| Its findings, in substance | |
| --- | --- |
| **Preparedness** | **the state was unprepared**, despite available indications |
| **Intelligence** | **there was no coherent intelligence picture**; the State Security Agency — stage 8's intelligence lesson — **failed to provide actionable warning, or its warnings were not acted on** |
| **Policing** | **the police were overwhelmed and in places simply absent**; command and control broke down; the public order policing capacity was inadequate in numbers, equipment and doctrine |
| **The security cluster** | **failed to coordinate**, and the relationship between the police, the military and intelligence did not function |
| **The characterisation** | **the panel was careful.** It found **evidence of orchestration and instigation**, and it **declined to adopt the term "insurrection" as the explanation**, concluding that **the state's own failures were the proximate cause of the scale of what happened** |

**That last row is the lesson's most important point, and it is a stage 1 point about language.** **The President described the events as "an attempted insurrection".** **The panel he appointed found orchestration at the start and state failure as the reason it spread.** **Those are different claims, and the difference matters: an insurrection is something done to a state; a collapse of policing is something a state does to itself.**

---

**Accountability:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The instigators** | **a small number of people were charged with incitement; very few convictions have followed** |
| **The security cluster** | **the National Police Commissioner left office in 2022** after separate judicial findings; **the State Security Agency was moved into the Presidency** and subsequently restructured by the 2024 intelligence legislation — stage 8 |
| **The intelligence reform** | **the General Intelligence Laws Amendment Act of 2024** is substantially a response to this and to the 2018 review panel |
| **Public order policing** | capacity has been increased, and the doctrine review continues |
| **Prosecution of the Phoenix killings** | **brought, with convictions in some cases** |

---

**And the two structural implications, which recur in stages 8 and 12:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The state's monopoly on force is incomplete** | **for a week, in two provinces, order was maintained — where it was maintained — by private security, by community structures, by taxi associations and by armed residents.** From stage 11's crime lesson: **private security personnel substantially outnumber police**, and July 2021 is what that means under stress |
| **A political dispute inside one party produced a national emergency** | **the trigger was the imprisonment of a former President on a contempt order arising from a commission.** From stage 10: **the party's internal conflict was conducted with national consequences, and the state could not contain it** |

**Practice.** Read the Expert Panel's report of February 2022 and its findings on intelligence and policing. Then compare its characterisation with the President's "attempted insurrection" statement. Then find Sasria's payouts for the unrest. Then establish how many people have been convicted of instigating the unrest, and the date you checked.
Phala Phala:
The first time the section 89 impeachment mechanism reached a panel finding against a sitting President — and the vote that stopped it.

**The facts that are not disputed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **February 2020** | **a burglary at the President's private game farm, Phala Phala, in Limpopo** |
| **What was taken** | **a very large sum in United States dollars — on the order of $580,000 — which had been concealed inside furniture** |
| **The handling** | **the theft was not reported through the ordinary police channels.** It was handled by **the Presidential Protection Unit**, and suspects were traced and questioned privately |
| **The President's account** | **that the money was the proceeds of a sale of buffalo to a foreign buyer**, held pending the animals' collection |
| **How it became public** | **in June 2022 the former Director-General of the State Security Agency filed an affidavit** with the police, alleging money laundering, kidnapping and defeating the ends of justice |
