**What remains unexplained, and this is the honest list:** **why a cash sum of that size was held in furniture at a farm; the full circumstances of the sale and the buyer; why the theft was not reported to the police in the ordinary way; and what was done with the suspects.**

---

**The section 89 process, which is the constitutionally significant part.**

**From stage 8: section 89 allows the Assembly to remove the President for a serious violation of the Constitution or the law, serious misconduct, or inability — on a two-thirds majority.** **And from stage 10: the rules for conducting such an inquiry existed only because *EFF v Speaker* (2017) ordered the Assembly to make them.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The panel** | **an independent panel appointed by the Speaker under those rules**, chaired by **former Chief Justice Sandile Ngcobo**, with a retired judge and a senior advocate |
| **Its task** | **not to decide guilt** — **to determine whether there was sufficient evidence to show that the President had a prima facie case to answer**, which would then trigger a full Assembly inquiry |
| **Its report, late 2022** | **that there was prima facie evidence of a serious violation of the Constitution and of serious misconduct**, specifically that he may have **acted in a way inconsistent with his office and exposed himself to a conflict between his official responsibilities and his private business**, and may have **failed to report the theft as required** |
| **13 December 2022** | **the National Assembly voted not to adopt the report** — by a substantial margin, with the governing party's members voting against — **so no inquiry was held** |

**That is the mechanism in stage 10's recall lesson, operating in the opposite direction.** **The same closed-list discipline that removed two presidents by party decision protected one from a constitutional process.** **Both outcomes were produced by party discipline, and neither by the Constitution's design.**

---

**The other investigations, and their outcomes:**

| Body | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| **The South African Reserve Bank** | investigated the exchange control aspects and **found no contravention**, on the basis that the funds had not been a completed transaction in the relevant sense |
| **SARS** | examined the tax aspects |
| **The Public Protector** | **reported in 2023, clearing him of a breach of the Executive Ethics Code** |
| **The police and the NPA** | **the criminal complaints did not result in charges against the President** |
| **Parliament** | **no inquiry, following the December 2022 vote** |

**So: a panel found a prima facie case, and every other body that examined it found no contravention or declined to proceed.** **From stage 1: those are not contradictory findings, because they were answering different questions on different standards** — **a prima facie case to answer is a much lower threshold than a contravention proved.** **Both results can be correct, and anybody citing only one of them is making an argument rather than reporting.**

---

**Why it matters, which is not mainly about the money:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The mechanism was tested** | **section 89 had never before reached a panel finding.** It now has, and **the procedure exists and works up to the point of the vote** |
| **2 — And the vote is the binding constraint** | **two-thirds of the Assembly is unattainable against an incumbent whose party holds a plurality and whose members sit on its list.** **The threshold is the protection** |
| **3 — The asymmetry with the recalls** | **a party committee can remove a President with no grounds and no evidence; the Constitution's own procedure requires two-thirds and was stopped.** **Stage 10's seven-step chain explains both** |
| **4 — The accountability test** | **the President who established the commissions, rebuilt SARS and the NPA, and campaigned on accountability was himself the subject of the first section 89 panel finding — and his party's caucus protected him** |
| **5 — The source of the allegation** | **a former head of the State Security Agency, whose own conduct the 2018 review panel and the Zondo Commission had addressed** — stage 8. **From stage 1: place the source. That does not make the affidavit false, and it is relevant to why it appeared in June 2022** |

> **As of 14 October 2026: no charges have been brought against the President, the unexplained items above remain unexplained, and the matter recurs in political argument rather than in litigation. Check whether any further proceedings have been instituted.**

**Practice.** Read the section 89 panel's report and note the standard it applied. Then read the Reserve Bank's finding and establish what question it answered. Then find the December 2022 Assembly vote and how each party voted. Then write down the difference between "a prima facie case to answer" and "a contravention established".
2024, and the coalition:
The election that ended single-party majority rule, the three weeks that produced a ten-party government, and its first two years.

**The result, from stage 10:**

| Party | Share | Seats |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ANC** | **40.18%** | **159** |
| **DA** | **21.81%** | **87** |
| **MK** | **14.58%** | **58** |
| **EFF** | **9.52%** | **39** |
| **IFP** | **3.85%** | 17 |
| **PA** | **2.06%** | 9 |
| **VF Plus** | **1.36%** | 6 |
| **Others** | | the balance |
| **Turnout** | **about 58.6% of registered voters** | |

**Three firsts:** **the first time the ANC fell below 50%; the first time a party other than the ANC won a province from it since 1994 in the sense that MK became the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal; and the first national coalition government not mandated by the Constitution.**

---

**The three weeks:**

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **29 May 2024** | polling |
| **2 June** | **the IEC declared the result.** The Constitution requires **the National Assembly's first sitting within 14 days**, at which it **must elect a President** — so the parties had under two weeks |
| **The options** | stage 10's table — **MK's reported price was the President's removal; an EFF arrangement carried the policy and market risk of stage 9's Nenegate lesson; a minority government had no majority for a budget** |
| **14 June 2024** | **a Statement of Intent was signed, and the National Assembly re-elected Cyril Ramaphosa as President.** The Assembly also elected its Speaker and the NCOP its chairperson, with positions distributed among the parties |
| **30 June 2024** | **the Cabinet was announced** — a large executive, **with roughly a dozen positions held by parties other than the ANC, the DA taking six**, and the IFP, PA, GOOD, FF+, UDM, Rise Mzansi, PAC and Al Jama-ah also represented |

**The Statement of Intent's substance:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The stated priorities** | **rapid, inclusive and sustainable economic growth; job creation; reducing poverty and the cost of living; building state capability; and stabilising local government** |
| **The decision rule** | **"sufficient consensus"** |
| **The dispute mechanism** | **a clearing house**, to resolve disagreements before they become public |
| **What it does not contain** | **a binding programme, an enforcement mechanism, or a procedure for a party's exit** |

**And the provinces:** **Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal both required coalition or minority arrangements**, with **KwaZulu-Natal governed by an ANC–IFP–DA–NFP combination against an MK opposition** — which is the inverse of the national picture and worth noting.

---

**The first two years, as a dated assessment:**

> **As of 14 October 2026, the record is as follows. Check each item against the current position.**

| What held | What strained |
| --- | --- |
| **the arrangement survived the 2025 budget crisis** — stage 9's VAT lesson: **a Budget postponed on the day it was due for the first time in South African history, a second Budget with a VAT increase, a contested fiscal framework vote, litigation, the withdrawal of the increase, and a third Budget in May 2025** | **that episode showed the executive can no longer assume its fiscal framework will pass** — and **Parliament's Money Bills Act powers, described in stage 8 as acquired and never used, were used** |
| **the structural reform programme continued** — electricity, logistics, water, visas; **load-shedding has stayed largely suspended** | **the policy disputes were deferred rather than resolved**: **NHI**, the **Basic Education Laws Amendment Act's language and admissions sections**, **expropriation**, and **foreign policy** |
| **no party has left the arrangement**, and the Cabinet has functioned | **disputes have been conducted publicly** rather than through the clearing house |
| **the markets and rating agencies responded positively** to its formation | **the ANC's alliance partners opposed it** — stage 10 — and **both MK and the EFF sit outside it in a declared bloc** |
| **two of the three largest parties are inside a single government**, which removes the sharpest form of political conflict from the streets | **the arrangement has no enforcement mechanism**, and the 1996 precedent — the National Party walking out of the mandated GNU — is the warning |

---

**The three questions the arrangement has not answered**, which is where this stage hands over to stage 12:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Can a coalition make a contested decision?** | **It has reformed by regulation and deferred by legislation.** **NHI, expropriation, BELA and the fiscal question are all live and all unresolved** |
| **2 — Does it change the accountability picture?** | **appointment reform — the Zondo recommendations of stage 8 — has not been enacted, and a coalition is in principle better placed to enact it than a single party**, because the patronage is no longer one party's to protect |
| **3 — What does it do to the parties?** | **the ANC's and DA's own supporters are divided about it**, and **the 2026 municipal and 2029 national elections are the test.** From stage 10's three scenarios |

**And one observation worth making plainly, because it is easy to miss while living through it: on 29 May 2024 a governing party of thirty years lost its majority, and on 14 June its leader was re-elected President by an assembly in which his party held 40% of the seats, in a government including its principal opponent.** **No institution failed, no result was disputed, nobody was killed, and the transfer of partial power was effected in sixteen days.** **Measured against stage 6's fears and against the comparable cases on the continent, that is the single strongest piece of evidence for the constitutional order's durability.**

**Practice.** Read the Statement of Intent of 14 June 2024. Then list the Cabinet posts held by each party. Then trace the 2025 budget sequence through the three Budget Reviews. Then write down what you would expect to see if the arrangement were failing, and check it against the current position.
Foreign policy since 1994:
A moral foreign policy, a continental project, a non-aligned posture, and the contradictions that have attached to all three.

**The founding claim**, from a 1993 article under Mandela's name: **that human rights would be "the light that guides our foreign affairs"**, and that South Africa would promote democracy, peaceful conflict resolution and African development.

**And the asset nobody else has:** **South Africa built nuclear weapons and then dismantled them**, acceding to the Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1991 — **the only state ever to have done so voluntarily.** That gives it standing on disarmament that no other country can claim, and it has used it.

---

**The Mandela period, and its contradictions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Readmission** | **to the Commonwealth, the United Nations General Assembly, the OAU and SADC**, from near-total isolation |
| **Nigeria, 1995** | **intervention to prevent the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and the Ogoni Nine failed**, and the subsequent attempt to isolate Nigeria found no African support — **the first demonstration that moral leadership without continental agreement achieves nothing** |
| **Arms sales** | **South Africa continued to sell arms to buyers whose conduct the policy condemned**, which was raised at the time and has been ever since |
| **Taiwan to the PRC** | **recognition switched in 1996–98**, abandoning a relationship with a government that had funded the ANC's opponents and supported it in other ways — a straightforwardly interest-based decision |
| **Libya** | **Mandela visited Gaddafi against United States and United Kingdom objections**, with the stated reason that **those who had supported the struggle would not be abandoned.** He then helped broker the Lockerbie trial arrangement |
| **Lesotho, 1998** | **a military intervention**, SADC-mandated, **with deaths and looting in Maseru** — and sustained criticism of its legality and conduct |

**The pattern is set in this period and it has not changed: a declared values-based policy, operated alongside interest-based decisions, with the tension managed rather than resolved.**

---

**The Mbeki period: the continental project.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The African Union** | **the OAU replaced in 2002**, with heavy South African input, and a Constitutive Act permitting intervention in grave circumstances |
| **NEPAD (2001)** | **a development compact** — governance reform in exchange for investment and aid — **with the African Peer Review Mechanism as its accountability device.** The review mechanism never acquired teeth |
| **Mediation** | **the DRC and Burundi peace processes**, in both of which South African mediation was central and substantially successful. **This is the strongest part of the record** |
| **Zimbabwe** | **"quiet diplomacy"** — the Mbeki lesson. **The mediation produced the 2008 agreement; the eight preceding years are the cost** |
| **The Security Council** | **non-permanent terms in 2007–08, 2011–12 and 2019–20**, with **some votes — notably on Myanmar in 2007 — drawing heavy criticism** for subordinating human rights to a non-interference principle |

**The Zuma period: alignment and an obligation breached.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **BRICS** | **South Africa joined in 2010** — by far the smallest economy in the group, and **the admission was a deliberate diplomatic achievement**. The **New Development Bank** followed |
| **The Dalai Lama** | **visas refused or delayed on three occasions**, widely read as deference to China, and litigated |
| **Al-Bashir, June 2015** | **the Sudanese President, subject to an ICC arrest warrant, attended an AU summit in Johannesburg and was allowed to leave despite a court order.** **The Supreme Court of Appeal held in 2016 that the government's conduct was unlawful** |
| **The ICC withdrawal** | **announced in October 2016 and declared unconstitutional by the High Court in February 2017** for want of parliamentary approval. **It was revoked** |
| **The AU Commission** | **Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma chaired it from 2012 to 2017** |

**The Al-Bashir sequence is the clearest case of the courts constraining foreign policy** — and from stage 7: **section 231's treaty obligations and the Implementation Act made the ICC obligation domestic law, so breaching it was unlawful in South Africa, not merely internationally.**

---

**The Ramaphosa period: non-alignment under pressure.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **AfCFTA** | **the African Continental Free Trade Area**, ratified in 2019 with trading from 2021 — **the largest free trade area by membership in the world, and South Africa's principal trade policy bet** |
| **AU chair, 2020** | during the pandemic, including the **African Vaccine Acquisition Trust** and the push for a TRIPS waiver on vaccine intellectual property |
| **Russia and Ukraine** | **South Africa abstained on the key UN General Assembly resolutions from 2022**, on a stated non-aligned position, **and led an African Peace Initiative mission to Kyiv and St Petersburg in June 2023** |
| **The *Lady R*** | **in December 2022 a sanctioned Russian vessel docked at the Simon's Town naval base.** In 2023 **the United States ambassador publicly alleged that arms had been loaded.** **A judicial inquiry chaired by a retired judge reported later that year and found no evidence that weapons were loaded onto the vessel** |
| **The 2023 BRICS summit** | held in Johannesburg, **with the Russian President not attending — which resolved the ICC arrest obligation that his attendance would have created**. BRICS expansion was agreed there |
| **The ICJ case** | **South Africa instituted proceedings against Israel under the Genocide Convention on 29 December 2023.** **The Court ordered provisional measures in January, March and May 2024.** The merits remain pending. **This is the most consequential foreign policy action South Africa has taken since 1994**, and it is defended as the direct application of the founding values claim and criticised as selective |

> **As of 14 October 2026: South Africa held the G20 presidency through 2025, hosting the summit in Johannesburg — the first G20 presidency held by an African state. Relations with the United States deteriorated sharply over the same period, with aid reductions, diplomatic expulsions, tariff measures and the lapse of AGOA preferences all in issue. Check the current trade and diplomatic position, because it is moving.**

---

**The argument about non-alignment, stated fairly:**

| The case for it | The case against |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa is a middle power that gains nothing from choosing a bloc**, and non-alignment is the position most of the Global South holds | **the economic exposure is asymmetric** — **the United States and the European Union are far larger markets for South African manufactured and agricultural exports than Russia is for anything**, so the posture carries a measurable cost |
| **the liberation history creates obligations** that Western governments do not recognise, and **consistency about the ICC, Palestine and international law is itself a values position** | **the consistency is contested** — the Myanmar vote, the Dalai Lama, Zimbabwe and Al-Bashir are cited against it |
| **the ICJ case applies the Genocide Convention through the proper institution**, which is precisely what a rules-based order requires | **"strategic ambiguity" reads as indecision**, and it has cost South Africa influence in both directions |
| **the AfCFTA and the continental project are the long-term interest**, and they require African rather than Western alignment | **the continental project's institutions — NEPAD's peer review, the AU's intervention power — have not delivered**, so the bet is unhedged |

**Practice.** Read Mandela's 1993 statement of the foreign policy and compare it with three decisions in this lesson. Then read the SCA's Al-Bashir judgment. Then find South Africa's ICJ application of December 2023 and the January 2024 provisional measures order. Then find South Africa's top five export markets by value and set them against its diplomatic alignments.
The SANDF, and the regional deployments:
A defence force built by integrating five armies, funded down to a fraction of its former share of the economy, and deployed anyway.

**The constitutional frame, from stage 8's chapter 11:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **200(1)** | the defence force must be **structured and managed as a disciplined military force** |
| **200(2)** | **"The primary object of the defence force is to defend and protect the Republic, its territorial integrity and its people in accordance with the Constitution and the principles of international law regulating the use of force."** |
| **201(2)** | **"Only the President, as head of the national executive, may authorise the employment of the defence force"** — in co-operation with the police, in defence of the Republic, or **in fulfilment of an international obligation** |
| **201(3)** | **the President must inform Parliament promptly** of the reasons, the place, the number of people and the period |
| **202** | **the President is Commander-in-Chief**, and appoints the military command |
| **204** | **a civilian secretariat for defence** |

**Note 201(2)'s third ground — fulfilment of an international obligation — because it is the basis of every deployment in this lesson.**

---

**The integration, which was a genuine achievement:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1994** | **the SANDF was formed by integrating the South African Defence Force, Umkhonto we Sizwe, the Azanian People's Liberation Army, and the armed forces of the four nominally independent homelands** |
| **The difficulty** | **a conventional army and two guerrilla armies that had been fighting each other, with incompatible ranks, training and doctrine** |
| **The outcome** | **it held.** There was no military coup, no mutiny of consequence, and the force remained under civilian control throughout — **which was not the expected outcome in 1993** |
| **The cost** | **a force with a large, ageing personnel complement**, because integration meant absorbing rather than selecting |

---

**And then the funding, which is the lesson's central fact:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Defence spending in the late 1980s** | **on the order of 4% of GDP or more** |
| **Defence spending now** | **on the order of 0.7% of GDP** |
| **The decline** | **among the steepest peacetime reductions in defence spending anywhere** |
| **Why** | **the peace dividend was real and was deliberately taken** — the money went to the social wage of stage 9 |
| **The consequence** | **the 2015 Defence Review found the force to be in "a critical state of decline"**, set out a recovery trajectory, **and was never funded** |

**What that means in practice:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Personnel** | **a complement in the seventies of thousands, with a high average age** — so a large share of the budget is salaries for people who are not deployable |
| **Air force** | **very low serviceability.** The Gripen fighters acquired in the arms deal of earlier in this stage have spent long periods largely unflown for want of maintenance funding, and transport and helicopter availability is limited |
| **Navy** | **the frigates and submarines acquired in the same arms deal have had limited availability**, with maintenance capacity constrained by Denel's collapse — stage 8's SOE lesson |
| **Army** | vehicle serviceability and ammunition stocks |
| **The irony worth naming** | **the equipment bought in the 1999 arms deal cannot be operated for lack of operating budget.** **A procurement criticised at the time for buying capability the country did not need has produced capability the country cannot use** |

---

**The deployments:**

| Where | What |
| --- | --- |
| **Burundi, from 2001** | **protection and then peacekeeping**, in support of the mediation of the Mbeki lesson. **Substantially successful** |
| **The DRC, from 2013** | **the UN's Force Intervention Brigade within MONUSCO**, a combat-mandated formation |
| **The Central African Republic, March 2013** | **13 to 15 SANDF soldiers were killed at Bangui**, in a deployment whose legal basis and purpose were heavily questioned in Parliament afterwards |
| **Mozambique, 2021–2024** | **SAMIM**, the SADC mission in Cabo Delgado against an insurgency — **withdrawn in 2024** |
| **The eastern DRC, from December 2023** | **SAMIDRC**, a SADC mission |
| **Internally** | **Operation Corona** on the borders; **Operation Prosper** for Covid enforcement and for the July 2021 unrest |

**And the event that forced the argument into the open:**

> **In late January 2025, fourteen SANDF soldiers were killed in the eastern DRC as the M23 armed group advanced on Goma. The deployment's supply, air support and medical evacuation capability were publicly questioned, the mission's mandate and sustainability were debated in Parliament, and the withdrawal of SAMIDRC was announced in the months that followed.** **Check the current position and the parliamentary record.**

**That is the clearest possible demonstration of the gap: a combat deployment under section 201(2)'s international obligation ground, by a force funded at 0.7% of GDP.**

---

**The argument, which is genuinely open:**

| Fund it properly | Keep it small |
| --- | --- |
| **South Africa has an 11,000-kilometre land border**, major sea lanes around the Cape, an exclusive economic zone to police, and **standing regional commitments it has itself sought** | **there is no credible external threat to South African territory**, and the primary object in section 200(2) is defence of the Republic |
| **deploying soldiers without air support, medical evacuation and logistics is indefensible** — if the commitments are kept, they must be funded | **the money is the social wage's** — stage 9's fiscal lesson — and an extra percentage point of GDP on defence is the health budget |
| **the border is the migration and smuggling problem** of stage 10 | **border management is a police and Border Management Authority function**, not a military one |
| **capability lost takes decades to rebuild**, as the air force demonstrates | **the honest alternative is to reduce the commitments rather than raise the budget** — and nobody has proposed that |

**The last row is the real question and it is rarely asked: if the force cannot be funded, which commitments should be dropped?** **From stage 9's method: a position that specifies no trade-off is not an analysis.**

**Practice.** Read sections 200 to 204. Then find defence spending as a share of GDP for 1989, 2000 and the most recent Budget. Then find the 2015 Defence Review's assessment and its funding trajectory. Then read the parliamentary record on the SAMIDRC deployment and establish what Parliament was told under section 201(3).

How to hold a live argument:
The stage's method, which is the whole curriculum's standing ruling made into a procedure.

**The ruling, restated:** **this curriculum does not arrive at a position where a question is live.** It gives **the strongest form of each answer** and says **what evidence would settle it.** **This stage is where that is done deliberately, seventeen times.**

---

**Why that is not fence-sitting, which is the objection to it.**

| The objection | The answer |
| --- | --- |
| **"Refusing to conclude is itself a position"** | **sometimes.** It is a position on questions where the evidence is actually decisive, and this stage does not treat those as live — **the migration numbers, the R500 billion figure, the Motlanthe panel's finding on section 25 and the PIRLS result are settled, and the lessons say so** |
| **"Both-sidesing gives bad arguments equal standing"** | **the procedure below requires the strongest form of each side**, not any form. **A position with no evidence and no test does not get a column** |
| **"You are avoiding the hard part"** | **the hard part is specifying what would change your mind.** Most public argument never does it, and this stage requires it in every lesson |

---

**The procedure. Every lesson in this stage has the same five parts, and you should be able to do this yourself for any question.**

| Part | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — State the question precisely** | **most disagreements dissolve or narrow at this step.** "Is BEE good?" is not a question. "Does a race-based procurement preference reduce aggregate inequality?" is |
| **2 — State what is agreed** | **almost always more than the participants admit.** Nobody defends the two-tier health system; nobody disputes that land ownership is racially skewed; nobody argues for load-shedding |
| **3 — The strongest form of each side** | **as its own best advocate would put it**, with its evidence. **If you cannot state it in terms its holders would accept, you do not understand it yet** |
| **4 — What evidence would settle it** | **named, findable, and ideally already being generated.** "More research" is not an answer; "the Commission for Employment Equity's top-management series over the next five years" is |
| **5 — What each side would have to concede** | **the most useful part, and the rarest.** A position that cannot name a fact that would damage it is not an analysis |

---

**Three failure modes to watch for in yourself**, each of which this curriculum has an example of:

| Failure | Example from earlier stages |
| --- | --- |
| **Using a number without its definition** | **the Gini, the unemployment rate, the 72% land figure, BEE ownership** — stage 9's four rules |
| **Arguing a counterfactual as if it were observable** | **"BEE cost the economy X"; "without land reform there would be stability"; "a different transition was available in 1994"** — stage 6 and stage 9 |
| **Treating an allegation as a finding** | **the SARS "rogue unit"; the R500 billion; the migration figures** — stage 1's commission and statistics lessons |

**And one more, which is specific to this subject: attributing a position to the whole of a group.** **"Black South Africans believe", "business wants", "the ANC thinks" — all of these conceal the actual disagreement**, which usually runs *within* each of those groups more sharply than between them. **Stage 9's inequality decomposition is the evidence: within-group inequality is now the larger share, and interests follow it.**

---

**The seventeen arguments this stage takes, and where each one's material is:**

| Lessons | Argument | Material in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2–3** | **land** — expropriation, and communal tenure | stages 7, 9, 8 |
| **4–5** | **the fiscus** — consolidation or expansion, and a basic income grant | stage 9 |
| **6** | **NHI** | stage 11 |
| **7** | **BEE's future** | stage 9 |
| **8** | **the labour market** | stage 9 |
| **9–10** | **electricity's market structure, and the Reserve Bank's mandate** | stages 8 and 9 |
| **11–12** | **electoral reform, and coalition durability** | stage 10 |
| **13** | **devolution** | stages 8 and 10 |
| **14** | **the Constitution itself** | stages 7, 8 and 10 |
| **15** | **crime and policing** | stages 8 and 11 |
| **16** | **migration** | stage 10 |
| **17** | **foreign policy** | stage 11 |
| **18** | **the close — how to keep all of this current** | stage 1 |

**None of these lessons introduces new facts.** **They are the argument structures for facts you already have**, which is why this stage is last.

**Practice.** Take a question in South African politics you hold a confident view on, and run it through the five parts. Write out part 5 — what you would have to concede — before you write part 3. Then find one person who holds the opposite view and check whether your part 3 is one they would accept.
Land: expropriation:
The argument stated precisely, which immediately narrows it — because almost everything the public debate disputes is already settled in law.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should the state be able to expropriate land for land reform with compensation below market value or at nil compensation; and if the law already permits that, why has land reform not happened?**

**2 — What is agreed, and it is a great deal:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ownership is racially skewed** | **not disputed by anybody.** The degree is imprecisely measured — stage 9's land figures lesson — **and the direction is not in question** |
| **Section 25(3) does not require market value** | **"just and equitable" compensation, with market value as one of five factors.** **"Willing buyer, willing seller" was a policy choice, not a constitutional requirement** |
| **The Expropriation Act 13 of 2024** | **signed 23 January 2025, and expressly provides for nil compensation in defined circumstances** — abandoned land, land held purely speculatively, land where the state's investment exceeds its market value, and land already occupied by beneficiaries |
| **Its status** | **as of 14 October 2026 it is signed and not yet in force.** **Check the commencement proclamation in the Gazette** |
| **The constitutional amendment failed** | **in December 2021, in the National Assembly, for want of a two-thirds majority** — stage 7 |
| **Two official panels found section 25 was not the constraint** | **the Motlanthe High Level Panel (2017) and the 2019 Presidential Advisory Panel**, which named budget, corruption, elite capture, post-settlement support and administrative capacity instead — stage 9 |
| **Land reform receives about 0.4% of the national budget** | against a 30% transfer target |
| **Transferred land substantially stopped producing** | without finance, water, extension and market access — stage 9 |

**That list is the lesson.** **Both political positions in the public argument are substantially arguing about a question the law has already answered**, while **the finding of the state's own two expert panels — that the constraint is administrative and fiscal — is accepted by neither side's rhetoric.**

---

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Expropriation without compensation should be used, and the constitutional position clarified further | It should not, and the Act should be applied narrowly if at all |
| --- | --- |
| **the 1913 cut-off is itself arbitrary** — dispossession began in 1652, and a remedy limited to post-1913 claims entrenches the earlier conquest. Stages 2 and 3 are the evidence | **the two panels found the Constitution was not the constraint**, so the reform's failure will not be cured by expanding the power; it will produce more unproductive transfers |
| **compensation at any level diverts a tiny budget** — at 0.4% of the budget, every rand of compensation is a hectare not transferred. **Nil compensation multiplies what the same money can do** | **policy uncertainty has a measurable cost** — on agricultural investment, on bank lending against farmland, and on the broader investment climate of stage 9's fifth explanation |
| **the power already exists in the Act**, so the argument is now about whether the state will use it, not whether it may | **food security**: commercial agriculture is unsubsidised, export-competitive and concentrated — stage 9's two agricultures. **Disruption is not recoverable within a season** |
| **the state has used section 216 and other coercive powers freely elsewhere** — it is land where it has been timid | **expropriation's constitutional limits are untested**, so the first nil-compensation expropriation will be litigated for years, achieving nothing in the interim |
| **the political cost of inaction is rising**, and parties offering more radical remedies gained in 2024 | **the beneficiaries are not served by receiving land they cannot farm** — the leasehold turn and the CPA failures of stage 9 |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Is the compensation standard the binding constraint?** | **the Act is in force and the state expropriates at nil compensation several times. Then measure the hectares transferred per rand of budget against the previous decade.** This is a directly testable claim and the test is now available |
| **Does expropriation damage agricultural investment?** | **agricultural gross fixed capital formation, and bank lending secured on farmland, before and after commencement** — both published |
| **Does transferred land produce?** | **the production record of redistributed farms, by tenure type** — and **the state does not systematically collect this, which is itself a finding** |
| **Is the obstacle administrative?** | **the department's audit outcomes, vacancy rates, and the special master's reports in *Mwelase*** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The expropriation side** | **if nil-compensation expropriations occur and the transfer rate does not rise, the constraint was never compensation** — and the two panels were right |
| **The opposing side** | **if the Act commences, is used, and agricultural investment and lending do not fall materially, the uncertainty argument was overstated** |
| **Both** | **neither position has an answer to post-settlement support**, which is where the evidence says the failure actually is, and **neither party's manifesto has a costed programme for it** |

**Practice.** Find the Expropriation Act's nil-compensation provisions and read them. Then check the Gazette for a commencement proclamation. Then find agricultural GFCF for the last five years. Then write down what you would expect to see in three years if your own view is right.
Land: communal tenure:
The land question affecting the most people, which the public argument almost never reaches.

**1 — The question.**

> **Who should hold and control the land in the former homelands — about 13% of South Africa, on which something like 17 to 18 million people live — and what form of tenure should the people living on it have?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The land is formally held in trust by the state** | and administered in practice through **traditional councils** — stage 8's traditional authority lesson |
| **Residents' tenure is legally insecure** | which **section 25(6) specifically entitles them to have remedied** — "legally secure tenure or comparable redress" |
| **It has not been remedied in thirty-two years** | **the Communal Land Rights Act was struck down in *Tongoane* (2010); the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act in *Mogale* (2023); and no replacement is in force** |
| **The consequence is economic** | **land that cannot be used as collateral, and a farmer who cannot borrow** — stage 9's two agricultures |
| **Traditional leadership is both a living institution and partly an apartheid administrative artefact** | both halves documented — stage 8 |
| **And the Ingonyama Trust litigation found** | that **converting residents' permission-to-occupy rights into rent-paying leases was unlawful** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

**Note that there are three positions here, not two**, which is why this argument does not resolve into a familiar shape.

| Individual title to residents | Communal title held by the community, with democratic governance | Continued administration through traditional councils |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **it is what section 25(6) most plainly means** — secure, legally recognised, defensible tenure in the holder's own name | **the land was held collectively before conquest, and individual titling would fragment it** and open it to distress sales | **the institution is constitutionally recognised in section 211 and the residents of those areas have not voted to abolish it** |
| **collateral**: a titled plot can secure a loan, which is the single binding constraint on smallholder agriculture | **communal property associations are the existing statutory vehicle** — the failure has been administrative support, not the model | **councils allocate land, resolve disputes and mediate development** — removing them leaves no local administration at all |
| **it ends the position where a person's home depends on an unelected authority's goodwill** | **individual title in a community with no credit market produces landlessness within a generation** — the historical comparison is the Glen Grey Act and the Natives Land Act's aftermath | **the customary system is living law under section 211(3) and communities may develop it themselves** — *Shilubana* |
| **women's tenure** — customary allocation has historically run through male household heads, and individual title can fix that directly | **and collective title can be constituted to include women as members**, which *Bhe*'s reasoning supports | **and traditional councils are statutorily required to be partly elected and one-third women** — a requirement widely unmet |

**And the fourth position, which is the one actually in the drafts:** **a hybrid — statutorily recognised, individually held, transferable use rights within a communally held title, with the allocation function regulated and appealable.** **It is the technically obvious answer and it has been drafted several times and never enacted.**

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Does securing tenure unlock credit?** | **the pilot areas where occupancy has been formalised** — compare agricultural lending and investment against matched areas. **The data exists and has not been systematically analysed** |
| **Does individual title lead to distress sales?** | **the record of the former homeland areas where title was issued**, and the comparative literature from other African titling programmes, which is substantial and mixed |
| **Do traditional councils comply with their statutory composition requirements?** | **auditable, and the answer from the available surveys is largely no** — which weakens the third column's democratic claim |
| **What do residents want?** | **surveyed repeatedly, with the consistent finding that residents want secure, inheritable, individually held rights and do not want the land alienable to outsiders** — which is the hybrid position |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The individual title position** | **titling without a functioning land administration produces unregistered transfers and disputes**, and the deeds office cannot currently carry it |
| **The communal title position** | **CPAs have failed at scale**, and the annual reports to Parliament document it |
| **The traditional authority position** | **the statutory composition requirements are not met, the Ingonyama litigation established that residents' rights were converted unlawfully, and three statutes have been struck down on process grounds for failing to consult the people affected** |
| **Everybody** | **the residents' own stated preference has been measured and does not match any pure position** |

**And the honest closing observation:** **this is the land question that affects the most people, it has a technically available answer, the people affected have said what they want, and it has been unresolved for thirty-two years — while the national land argument is conducted almost entirely about commercial farmland.** **That asymmetry is itself a political fact worth explaining.**

**Practice.** Read section 25(6). Then read *Mogale* on why the 2019 Act fell. Then find a survey of communal area residents' tenure preferences. Then find the Communal Property Associations annual report to Parliament.
The fiscal question:
Consolidation or expansion: the argument that constrains every other argument in this stage.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should fiscal policy prioritise stabilising and reducing the debt ratio, or should it accept a higher debt path in order to fund investment and social spending that would raise growth?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The numbers** | **debt at 75 to 77% of GDP, from 26% in 2008; debt-service costs among the largest single spending items, exceeding health and police; a primary surplus achieved; debt projected to stabilise** — stage 9 |
| **Where the debt came from** | **the post-2008 revenue collapse and a counter-cyclical response that became structural; the wage bill; SOE bailouts; slow growth; and the downgrades' borrowing cost.** **Not principally social grants** |
| **The sustainability condition** | **nominal growth above the effective interest rate, with a primary surplus** |
| **The composition problem** | **the consolidation since 2020 fell on capital budgets and on maintenance rather than on the wage bill** — which **both sides agree was the wrong composition** |
| **The debt is mostly rand-denominated and domestically held** | which removes the classic emerging-market currency-mismatch crisis mechanism |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Consolidate | Expand |
| --- | --- |
| **the interest bill's crowding-out is arithmetic, not opinion.** Every rand of debt service is a rand not spent, and it is the fastest-growing line | **the consolidation has been real austerity**: real per-person spending on health, education and infrastructure has fallen, and **the social wage of stage 9 is being eroded while measured need rises** |
| **the spiral risk is real**: if the effective interest rate exceeds nominal growth, the ratio rises with no new spending, and South Africa has already been downgraded twice | **the growth rate is partly endogenous to the fiscal stance.** Cutting capital spending lowers future growth and therefore worsens the ratio — **so consolidation can be self-defeating** |
| **the long end of the yield curve is unusually steep**, which is the market pricing exactly this risk | **the binding constraints are electricity, logistics and water** — stage 9 — **and all three require capital spending.** Vulindlela's regulatory reforms are free; the transmission lines are not |
| **no country has grown out of a debt problem without stabilising it first** | **the comparison set matters**: several countries have run higher ratios with lower spreads, and the ratio alone does not determine the spread |
| **and the political economy point**: fiscal space is what made the 2008 counter-cyclical response possible, and rebuilding it is insurance | **and the political economy point in reverse**: a decade of austerity with no growth is what produced the 2024 result, and there is a cost to that too |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Is the fiscal stance the constraint on growth, or is capacity?** | **the post-2024 period is a natural experiment.** **Load-shedding has largely stopped without a fiscal expansion.** If growth recovers materially, the constraint was electricity. **If it does not, the expansion case strengthens considerably** |
| **Is consolidation self-defeating?** | **the fiscal multiplier on South African public investment**, which the Reserve Bank and Treasury have both estimated and which the independent literature disputes. **Published, contested, and improvable** |
| **Is the debt path credible?** | **the spread between South African and comparable sovereign yields, and the rating agencies' stated reasons** — all public, all updated continuously |
| **Does the composition critique hold?** | **real growth in capital spending versus compensation of employees over the last five years** — directly checkable in the Budget Review's annexures |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The consolidators** | **if growth recovers with load-shedding's end and debt stabilises, the space created should be spent on the capital and maintenance budgets that were cut — not banked.** And **the consolidation's composition was indefensible** |
| **The expanders** | **the wage bill is where the money is.** An expansion case that does not address compensation of employees — **stage 9's wage bill lesson** — is asking for borrowing to fund a line item that grew through pay rather than through staff. **And COSATU's membership composition is why that concession is hard** |
| **Both** | **the contingent liabilities** — SOE guarantees in the hundreds of billions — **are outside the debt figure until they are called**, and neither side's arithmetic includes them |

**And the observation that makes this stage's first lesson's point:** **the two sides agree on the composition critique and disagree about the level.** **That is a much narrower argument than the public one, and it means the operative question is the wage bill — which neither side's principals want to be the question.**

**Practice.** Find real growth in capital spending and in compensation of employees over five years. Then find South Africa's sovereign spread against two comparators. Then find the contingent liabilities table. Then write down what growth rate over the next three years would change your view, and check it.
A basic income grant:
The largest proposed change to South African social policy since 1994, and the argument is about affordability and about work.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should the Social Relief of Distress grant be replaced by a permanent income grant for working-age adults, at what level, on what means test, and funded how?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The gap it fills** | **before 2020 South Africa paid grants to children, the elderly and the disabled and nothing to an unemployed working-age adult without a disability** — stage 9's poverty lesson |
| **The SRD grant exists** | introduced in 2020, **reaching 8 to 9 million people**, **below the food poverty line**, administered on a budget line renewed annually |
| **It cannot be withdrawn politically** | and every party's position now assumes some form of continuation |
| **The transfer system works administratively** | **SASSA pays about 19 million regular grants monthly with low leakage** — and the SRD's own administration has had failures |
| **The evidence on grants and work** | **grant receipt is associated with more job search, not less** — stage 9's unemployment lesson. **This is the strongest finding in the area and it cuts against the reservation-wage objection** |
| **Cost** | **arithmetic, not opinion.** A grant at the food poverty line to all working-age adults who qualify on a means test runs to a substantial percentage of the budget; **the precise figure depends entirely on the level and the means test, and both sides use the same spreadsheet** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Introduce it | Do not, or not yet |
| --- | --- |
| **the labour market will not absorb these people** — stage 9's absorption rate has been flat for fifteen years, and a policy that waits for employment is a policy of indefinite destitution | **it is permanent spending funded from a narrow and fragile tax base** — stage 9's tax lesson — **with no identified revenue source**, which means borrowing, which means the fiscal question of the last lesson |
| **the fiscal incidence evidence shows transfers work** — stage 9's redistribution paradox: the system takes the Gini from about 0.77 to about 0.59 | **the in-kind half of that redistribution is overvalued** — the same lesson's strongest objection — **so the measured success overstates what more transfers would achieve** |
| **a grant pays the transport fare**, so it raises job search and smallholder activity rather than suppressing it. **This is measured** | **the money has an alternative use with a higher growth return**: transmission lines, water infrastructure, early childhood development, or teacher training |
| **the SRD exists, so the question is only whether to formalise it** — and an annually renewed emergency line is the worst available way to run permanent spending | **formalising it removes the option of ending it**, and a permanent entitlement is politically irreversible whatever happens to revenue |
| **the political economy**: 26 million non-voters, a third of working-age adults without work, and parties outside the constitutional consensus gaining — stage 10 | **the political economy in reverse**: a grant funded by borrowing, in an economy at 1% growth, is a transfer from future spending to present consumption |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Does an income grant reduce labour supply?** | **the SRD is a five-year natural experiment covering 8 to 9 million people.** **Compare labour force participation and job search among recipients and non-recipients, controlling for selection.** The QLFS data and the SASSA records would support this and **the linked analysis has not been done at scale** |
| **What does it do to poverty?** | **the Living Conditions Survey, which is run too rarely** — stage 9. **Running it more often is itself the recommendation** |
| **Is it affordable?** | **the Budget Review's own projections at specified levels and means tests.** This is arithmetic and both sides can do it |
| **What is the growth return of the alternative use?** | **the public investment multiplier** — the last lesson's contested estimate |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Supporters** | **a revenue source must be named.** A grant funded by unspecified borrowing is the fiscal question's expansion case without its argument, and **the VAT episode of 2025 showed how hard naming one is** |
| **Opponents** | **the labour supply objection is not supported by the available evidence**, and continuing to lead with it is arguing against the data. **And the SRD already exists, so "do not introduce it" is not the status quo option** |
| **Both** | **the administration.** SASSA's regular grants work; **the SRD's verification and payment systems have failed repeatedly**, and a permanent grant at scale on those systems is a stage 8 capacity question before it is a fiscal one |

**Practice.** Find the SRD grant's current value and compare it with the food poverty line. Then cost a grant at the food poverty line for all qualifying working-age adults, using the Budget Review's own figures. Then find the research on SRD recipients' labour force participation. Then name the revenue source you would use, and work out what it raises.
NHI:
Where the argument actually is — not whether universal coverage, but through what vehicle and in what order.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should South Africa move to a single public purchaser of health services, with medical schemes restricted to complementary cover, and should that be done before or after the public health system's capacity is repaired?**

**2 — What is agreed, and this is unusually extensive:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The two-tier system is indefensible** | **16% of the population accounts for roughly half of health spending** — stage 11. **Almost nobody defends this** |
| **Universal coverage is the right objective** | **and section 27 obliges progressive realisation of access to health care services** |
| **The private sector is not a well-functioning market** | **the Health Market Inquiry (2019) found high concentration, opaque pricing, supply-induced demand and no effective price or outcome regulator** |
| **Public facility quality is the binding constraint on the public side** | infrastructure, human resources, management and medico-legal liability — stage 11 |
| **Incremental reform has not changed the split in thirty years** | which is the strongest argument for a structural change of some kind |
| **The Act is law** | **signed 15 May 2024, substantially unimplemented, under litigation.** **Check the current position** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Implement NHI as legislated | Sequence it differently, or redesign it |
| --- | --- |
| **a single purchaser has monopsony power**, which is **the only demonstrated answer to the Health Market Inquiry's concentration finding** — it can set prices, which regulation has failed to do | **the Fund requires the state to run the largest procurement operation in the country's history**, and stage 8's procurement and provincial health findings are the reason to doubt it |
| **pooling is mainstream**: most comparable systems pool risk nationally, and the principle is not radical | **restricting medical schemes removes the exit option for 10 million people and the contributions they currently make**, with an uncertain net effect on public capacity |
| **accreditation is leverage over quality in both sectors** — a facility that cannot be accredited must improve or lose its revenue | **the Act does not specify the revenue.** Stage 9's fiscal position means the money is either new taxes or reallocation, and neither is in the statute |
| **the two-tier system's defenders have had thirty years** to produce an incremental alternative and have not | **the sequencing objection is made by supporters of universal coverage, not opponents**: fix facilities, human resources and procurement first, then pool. **This is the most serious objection in the argument** |
| **the constitutional objections are weak**: section 27 is a positive obligation and the state has wide latitude on the means | **the constitutional challenges are on section 27, on property, and on the right to choose a provider**, and at least the property and procedural grounds are substantial |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Can the state administer it?** | **the Fund's own establishment is the test.** Watch its procurement, its board appointment process, its audit outcomes and its accreditation capacity in the first three years. **Stage 8's appointment correlation is the thing to apply: how is the board appointed?** |
| **Does the private sector's pricing fall under a single purchaser?** | **the first national price determinations against current scheme tariffs** |
| **Does public facility quality improve under accreditation?** | **the Office of Health Standards Compliance's inspection results**, which already exist and are published |
| **What is the fiscal cost?** | **the Treasury's own costing**, which has been requested repeatedly and not published in full. **That absence is itself the most telling fact in the argument** |
| **Does the exit of medical scheme funding harm or help?** | **no South African evidence exists; the comparative literature is mixed and depends on the quality of the public system at the point of transition** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Supporters** | **a full public costing is a precondition, not an inconvenience**, and the absence of one is the single largest weakness in the case. **And the Fund's governance must be appointed by a commission-type process** — stage 8's whole conclusion — **or the Fund becomes the largest procurement entity in the country with a minister appointing its board** |
| **Opponents** | **"fix the public system first" requires a programme with dates and money, and the people making the argument have not produced one.** **Thirty years of incrementalism is the evidence against it** |
| **Both** | **the Health Market Inquiry's findings have not been acted on through any other mechanism**, so the private sector's concentration remains unaddressed on either path |

**And the stage 1 point: this is the clearest case in the curriculum where the public argument misstates the disagreement.** **It is presented as universal coverage against private medicine.** **It is actually a dispute about institutional capacity and sequencing between people who agree on the objective.**

**Practice.** Read section 27 and the NHI Act's provisions on the Fund's governance and on medical schemes. Then find the Health Market Inquiry's concentration findings. Then look for Treasury's published costing of NHI. Then find out how the Fund's board is to be appointed, and compare that with stage 8's appointment table.
BEE's future:
Thirty-two years in, with a measurable record and an untested alternative.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should empowerment measures continue to use race as the criterion, shift to a class or disadvantage criterion, be refocused on different elements, or be sunsetted?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The B-BBEE Act compels nobody directly** | it creates a measurement system that bites through **procurement, licensing and supplier scorecards** — stage 9 |
| **The scorecard's weights** | **ownership 25 of about 109; enterprise and supplier development 40; skills development 20** |
| **Top management has barely changed** | **the Commission for Employment Equity's annual series: African South Africans remain a small minority of top management against roughly 80% of the economically active population** |
| **Lower and middle management have changed substantially** | |
| **The black middle class grew several-fold** | **principally through employment — the public service, SOEs, the professions, financial services — not through ownership deals** |
| **Within-group inequality rose** | and the between-group share of total inequality fell from around 60% to roughly 40 to 50% **while total inequality did not fall** — stage 9 |
| **No credible aggregate cost estimate exists** | and the counterfactual is unobservable. **Claims in either direction are assertions** |
| **Section 9(2) permits such measures**, subject to the *Van Heerden* test | and **the 2017 procurement regulations were struck down in *Afribusiness* (2022) on ultra vires grounds, not on the permissibility of preference** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Continue, and enforce it properly | Shift to a class criterion |
| --- | --- |
| **the top-management series shows the job is unfinished** — a measure whose objective is unmet cannot be sunsetted for reaching an anniversary | **the measure's own data shows it produced an elite**: within-group inequality rose, and the beneficiaries of ownership deals were a small, connected group |
| **disadvantage was imposed by race and is still distributed by race** — a criterion blind to race cannot reach it, and **means-testing does not capture networks, inherited wealth or the credential gap** | **a poverty or disadvantage criterion reaches the poor of every group, including the poorest, and is not gameable by a wealthy beneficiary of the designated group** |
| **the critique attacks the smallest element** — ownership is 25 of 109; **enforce skills development and supplier development instead**, which reach far more people | **fronting is pervasive**, documented by the B-BBEE Commission itself, and **criminalisation in 2013 has produced almost no prosecutions** — stage 8's consequence-management failure |
| **procurement leverage is the only enforcement that has ever worked** — which is why the 2022 Employment Equity amendment used it | **procurement preference became a capture vehicle** — Zondo's evidence on intermediary companies and inflated pricing, stage 11 |
| **and the constitutional point**: *Van Heerden* permits targeting the disadvantaged by the characteristic used to disadvantage them | **and the constitutional point in reverse**: a measure under section 9(2) must be **designed to achieve equality**, and a measure that demonstrably has not after three decades fails its own test |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Has it changed who runs the economy?** | **the Commission for Employment Equity's top-management series, which is published annually.** **The trend over the next five years is the answer**, and it is the single best indicator in this argument |
| **Has it changed ownership?** | **an ownership study reporting direct and mandated holdings separately, consistently, year on year** — which nobody currently produces |
| **Does fronting dominate?** | **the B-BBEE Commission's investigation outcomes and prosecution rate**, which it publishes |
| **Does it cost growth?** | **firm-level data on compliance cost and supplier pool restriction** — which would need research access nobody has funded |
| **Would a class criterion work better?** | **a trial.** **This is the most important row in the table: the class-based alternative is proposed across the political spectrum and has never been piloted at scale.** A sectoral or provincial pilot with published outcomes would settle more than a decade of argument |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Continuation's supporters** | **if the top-management series does not move over the next five years under the 2022 amendment's sectoral targets, the mechanism does not work** — and procurement leverage will have been tried and failed |
| **The class-criterion side** | **a class criterion has never been tested here**, so its superiority is a prediction. **And it would not reach the credential and network gap**, which is the part the designated-group criterion is actually targeting |
| **Both** | **the enforcement gap is the real problem.** Fronting is criminal and almost never prosecuted; the ownership figures are not properly measured; the Commission is under-resourced. **Stage 8's thesis again: the design is not the binding constraint** |

**Practice.** Find the latest Commission for Employment Equity top-management table and the five-year trend. Then find the 2022 amendment's sectoral targets for one sector. Then find the B-BBEE Commission's fronting investigation numbers. Then design the class-based pilot yourself: what would you measure, where, and over how long?
The labour market:
The argument with the highest stakes and the weakest evidence on both sides.

**1 — The question.**

> **Does South Africa's labour market regulation materially reduce employment, and if so which parts — and what would be given up by changing them?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The absorption rate is about 40%**, against about 60% in middle-income peers | stage 9 |
| **The eight explanations, in order of evidential weight** | **schooling; spatial geography; demand and growth; capital-intensive production; the small informal sector; wages and regulation; concentration; and grants** — with **regulation sixth and grants eighth** |
| **So regulation is a real factor and not the largest** | **this is the honest starting point, and both sides tend to misstate it** |
| **The national minimum wage's measured effects** | **the predicted large employment losses did not materialise in the published studies**, with wage gains and smaller-than-predicted employment effects — though **domestic work is disputed** |
| **Section 32's extension power is the contested mechanism** | not the minimum wage — stage 9's wages lesson |
| **The CCMA works** | free, fast at conciliation, high volume — stage 9 |
| **Union density is around a quarter to a third of formal employees**, and COSATU's base is now public sector | stage 9 |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Reform the regulation | Leave it, and fix the real constraints |
| --- | --- |
| **section 32's extension binds firms that were not represented in the bargaining**, and **the parties to the agreement — established firms and established unions — have a shared interest in raising entrants' costs.** The Newcastle clothing cases are the concrete evidence | **South African wages at the bottom are low in absolute terms**, and productivity-adjusted unit labour costs are not an international outlier |
| **dismissal procedure raises the cost of a marginal hire**, which falls hardest on small firms with no HR capacity — and stage 9's missing middle of firms is the symptom | **the sectors that grew — automotive — are heavily unionised and covered**, so coverage is not the determinant |
| **exemption procedures are administered by the interested bargaining council**, which is a straightforward conflict of interest | **the minimum wage evidence is the best natural experiment available and it went against the prediction**, which should lower confidence in the regulation case generally |
| **in an economy with a third of working-age people out of work, a wage floor set by insiders excludes outsiders** — and the excluded have no seat at Nedlac | **the exclusion argument proves too much**: it implies wages should fall until the surplus is absorbed, which at South Africa's inequality produces working poverty rather than a labour market |
| **a differentiated regime** — lower minima for small firms, new entrants or distressed regions — **is standard in comparable systems** | **differentiation is how the 1980s wage structure worked**, and it would be administered by the same under-capacity inspectorate |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Does extension reduce employment in affected sectors?** | **compare employment in sectors with extended agreements against similar uncovered sectors, controlling for demand.** The data exists in the QLFS and the bargaining council records and **the linked analysis is thin** |
| **Does the minimum wage cost jobs at higher levels?** | **the annual increases are a continuing natural experiment.** **At some level there will be an effect; the question is where, and the annual reviews are generating the data** |
| **Does dismissal procedure deter hiring?** | **firm surveys plus the CCMA's own case data on cost and duration**, and an experiment is possible: a small-firm exemption pilot with measured hiring |
| **Which of the eight explanations dominates?** | **the post-2024 electricity recovery tests demand; the PIRLS cohort tests schooling over a decade.** **Regulation's share is the residual and is the hardest to isolate** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reformers** | **the minimum wage prediction was wrong**, and that should discount the confidence of the broader claim. **And regulation is sixth of eight — a reform programme that leads with it is addressing a minor factor while schooling and spatial geography go unaddressed** |
| **The defenders** | **the insider–outsider structure is real**, Nedlac excludes the unemployed by construction, and **the extension power's conflict of interest in exemptions is indefensible on any view** |
| **Both** | **there is no South African evidence of the quality this argument's stakes deserve**, and that is a research and data-access failure that either side could fix by funding it |

**Practice.** Read section 32 of the LRA. Then find the published evaluations of the national minimum wage's employment effects. Then find one bargaining council's exemption process and who decides. Then rank the eight explanations yourself and write down what evidence moved you on each.
Electricity: who owns the grid:
The reform that is working, and the argument about the part that has not been done.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should transmission and distribution stay in state hands while generation is competitive, or should private capital and ownership extend to the network — and who pays for the transmission build?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The generation reform worked** | **the licensing threshold went from 1 MW to 100 MW in 2021 and then licensing was dropped; a very large private build-out followed; load-shedding has been largely suspended since 2024** — stage 9 |
| **The REIPPPP bid windows proved the price case** | **early solar PV around R3.50 per kWh falling to around R0.62 by the fourth window** |
| **Unbundling is in progress** | **the National Transmission Company became operational in 2024**, and **the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act of 2024** creates a market operator and third-party grid access |
| **Transmission is now the binding constraint** | **the best wind and solar resource is in the Cape; the grid capacity is in Mpumalanga; new lines take years and very large capital** |
| **Municipal distribution is in serious trouble** | **municipalities depend on the electricity surplus, face defection by their best customers, and have a maintenance backlog in the tens of billions** — stage 8 |
| **Eskom's debt** | peaked above R400bn with about R254bn of relief in 2023 |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Keep the network public | Open the network to private capital and ownership |
| --- | --- |
| **a transmission network is a natural monopoly** — selling it creates a private monopoly whose incentive is price, and regulation of a private monopoly is harder than operating a public one | **the state cannot fund the transmission build** — stage 9's fiscal question — and the lines are the binding constraint on everything the generation reform unlocked |
| **the generation reform succeeded precisely because the network stayed neutral** — a privately owned grid with its own generation interests would not be | **independent transmission projects** are standard internationally: private capital builds and operates lines under a regulated concession, with ownership of the asset reverting or remaining regulated |
| **universal service and cross-subsidy** depend on public ownership: a private network operator has no reason to connect a remote village | **the regulator now exists** — the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act and NERSA — **so the precondition for private participation is met** |
| **the pricing problem is regulatory, not ownership-based**: NERSA's tariff determinations are the mechanism, and they can be fixed without selling anything | **Transnet's ports are the cautionary parallel from stage 9**: a state landlord that also operates the terminals produced the worst-ranked ports in the world. **Vertical separation plus private operation is the demonstrated fix** |

**And on municipal distribution, the argument is different and more advanced:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reform in progress** | **ring-fencing municipal electricity and water as separate trading entities**, with licensing conditions, so the surplus cannot be spent on general expenses and the maintenance budget is protected |
| **The further step proposed** | **transferring distribution in failing municipalities to a regional distributor or to Eskom**, which **section 156(4) and the intergovernmental framework permit** |
| **The objection** | **it removes the main revenue instrument of a sphere the Constitution makes a government** — section 151(3) and (4), stage 8 |
| **The counter** | **stage 8's finding that about two hundred municipalities cannot fund themselves under the current model**, so protecting their revenue instrument protects a notional power |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Can the state build the transmission?** | **the transmission build programme's delivery against its published kilometre targets over the next three to five years.** This is the single number to watch in South African electricity policy |
| **Does third-party access work?** | **the volume of energy traded by parties other than Eskom** once the market operator is running |
| **Does ring-fencing fix municipal distribution?** | **compare ring-fenced metros' maintenance spending and loss figures against unreformed municipalities** |
| **What does a private concession cost?** | **the first independent transmission project's tariff**, against Eskom's own cost of capital |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Public-ownership advocates** | **if the transmission build misses its targets for three years, the funding constraint is real and the ideological preference is costing the generation reform.** **And NERSA's performance is itself part of the problem — a regulator litigated against annually is not a working regulator** |
| **Private-participation advocates** | **the generation reform's success came from removing a licensing barrier, not from selling an asset** — the cheapest reforms have been regulatory, and **the ports concession litigation of stage 9 shows that private participation processes can also stall for years** |
| **Both** | **the distribution problem is larger than the transmission problem and gets a fraction of the attention**, because it is municipal and therefore belongs to stage 8's hardest chapter |

**Practice.** Find the transmission build programme's published targets and its delivery to date. Then find the current status of third-party grid access and the market operator. Then find one metro's ring-fenced electricity accounts. Then work out what share of national electricity sales passes through municipal distributors.
The Reserve Bank's mandate:
A clause in the Constitution, a conference resolution, and an argument that turns on whose costs you count.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should the Reserve Bank's mandate be changed to include employment or growth as a target, should the inflation target band be changed, and should the private shareholding be nationalised?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The text** | **section 224(1): "The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth in the Republic."** **224(2): independence, with regular consultation with the finance minister** |
| **It was a negotiated requirement of the 1993–96 settlement** | stage 6 |
| **The Bank held** | **one of the institutions stage 8 lists as having functioned throughout** |
| **The inflation target** | **a 3 to 6% band adopted in 2000**, under formal review in the mid-2020s with argument for lowering it |
| **The shareholding** | **about two million shares held by 600 to 800 shareholders, with a capped dividend, who elect seven of fifteen board directors and have no influence on monetary policy** |
| **Nationalising it is an ANC conference resolution from 2017** | **never implemented** |
| **The Public Protector's 2017 attempt to direct an amendment of section 224 was set aside with a personal costs order** | stage 8 |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Change the mandate | Leave it |
| --- | --- |
| **224(1) already says "in the interest of balanced and sustainable economic growth"** — so growth is textually part of the purpose, and a Bank that treats price stability as the whole object is reading the clause too narrowly | **the primary object is price stability; the growth clause states the purpose of that stability rather than adding a second target.** **This is the natural reading and the Bank's own** |
| **unemployment above 30% for fifteen years is the country's defining problem**, and an institution with the most powerful macroeconomic instrument treating it as somebody else's concern is a policy choice, not a neutral stance | **a central bank cannot create jobs; it can create inflation** — and **inflation falls hardest on the poor**, who hold no inflation-hedged assets and whose wages adjust last |
| **dual mandates exist** — the United States Federal Reserve is the standard example, and its employment mandate has not produced hyperinflation | **South Africa is not the United States**: **a reserve-currency issuer's constraints are not an open emerging economy's**, and the rand's depth and the foreign holding of local-currency bonds are the difference |
| **the real interest rate has been high** relative to peers for long periods, which transmits to investment — stage 9's capital formation lesson | **the Bank's credibility is a public asset that took twenty-five years to build** and can be destroyed in one cycle; **the yield curve's long end already prices fiscal risk** — stage 9 |
| **and the political point**: a monetary policy insulated from elected control was negotiated by people who are not the current electorate | **and the political point in reverse**: it was negotiated precisely because it protects the currency from the electoral cycle, and that is the function |

**On the inflation target band**, the argument is narrower and more technical: **lowering the target to around 3% would reduce long-term inflation expectations and the nominal interest rate, at the cost of a tighter stance during the transition.** **Both Treasury and the Bank have engaged with it publicly, which makes it the most tractable part of this lesson.**

**On the shareholding:** **almost nobody argues it affects policy** — shareholders have no monetary policy role. **The argument for nationalisation is symbolic and the argument against is cost and signalling.** **It is the least consequential and most frequently raised item.**

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
