| **Has monetary policy been too tight?** | **the real repo rate against comparable emerging economies, and the inflation outcomes against the band** — both published monthly. **The Bank has undershot the band's midpoint in several recent periods, which is the strongest single point for the critics** |
| **Would a dual mandate raise employment?** | **the comparative record of dual-mandate central banks in open emerging economies**, which is thin and mixed — **so this is genuinely unsettled rather than conveniently so** |
| **Is the growth constraint monetary?** | **stage 9's five explanations.** **If electricity and logistics explain the stagnation, monetary policy is not the binding constraint, and the post-2024 recovery is the test** |
| **Would lowering the target work?** | **the Bank's and Treasury's published modelling, and the experience of countries that have lowered targets** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Mandate reformers** | **the shareholding question is a distraction** and raising it weakens the serious argument. **And if growth recovers after 2024 without a mandate change, the monetary constraint was not the binding one** |
| **Defenders** | **undershooting the target band is a policy error on their own terms**, and **"the mandate is price stability" does not answer whether the target itself is set correctly** — which is where the real argument is |
| **Both** | **the institution held, and that is worth something that is hard to price.** **Stage 8's appointment correlation suggests the independence is more fragile than it looks, because the Governor is a presidential appointment** |

**Practice.** Read section 224 in full. Then find the inflation outcomes against the 3–6% band for the last five years and note any undershoot. Then find the real repo rate against two emerging market comparators. Then find the current status of the inflation target review.
Electoral reform:
The one reform in this stage that requires no constitutional amendment, has been recommended three times, and has never been done.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should the National Assembly be elected on a mixed constituency-and-list system rather than closed party lists; should there be a threshold; and should lists be open?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 46 requires only that the system "results, in general, in proportional representation"** | **closed lists are in the Electoral Act, not the Constitution** — stage 10 |
| **So a mixed-member proportional system is constitutionally available by ordinary legislation** | as are a threshold and open lists |
| **The closed list's effect** | **stage 10's seven-step recall chain, Parliament's oversight failure, and the litigation over secret ballots and impeachment rules** |
| **The Zondo Commission recommended a constituency element** | in its Part Five institutional recommendations — stage 11 |
| **The Van Zyl Slabbert Electoral Task Team recommended it in 2003** | **multi-member constituencies plus a compensatory national list.** **Shelved** |
| ***New Nation Movement* (2020) required independent candidates to be permitted** | and **the 2023 Act's implementation of that is contested as inadequate** — stage 10 |
| **The current system has produced accurate proportionality, high women's representation, real seats for small parties, and no disputed national result** | **in seven elections** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Introduce constituencies | Keep closed-list PR |
| --- | --- |
| **accountability**: an MP with constituents has a mandate independent of the party, which is the precondition for the oversight Zondo found absent | **proportionality**: every constituency system distorts, and the distortion falls on small parties and dispersed minorities. **South Africa's present system wastes almost no votes** |
| **the recall mechanism depends on the closed list** — stage 10. **Remove it and a party committee can no longer remove a head of state** | **women's representation came from party list quotas.** **Constituency systems worldwide produce lower women's representation**, and the drop would be immediate |
| **a voter can name their representative** — at present only the local ward ballot allows that, and the national legislature is entirely anonymous to voters | **the 1994 choice was deliberate**: constituencies in a country with apartheid's spatial geography would have produced racially defined seats, and the drafters knew it |
| **mixed-member proportional keeps proportionality** — Germany and New Zealand demonstrate it, and the Van Zyl Slabbert design is specifically built for it | **the capacity question**: a constituency system needs a boundary authority, by-elections, and constituency offices — **and the Demarcation Board's municipal work is already contested** |
| **the 2024 result makes it easier**: no party has the majority to block it, and a coalition has less to lose from it | **and the honest point**: **constituency MPs are not automatically better overseers.** Westminster's constituency MPs are also whipped |

**On a threshold:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For** | **ends one-seat mayoralties and reduces coalition fragmentation** — stage 10's local government record |
| **Against** | **discards the votes of millions** across the long tail, and **raises the barrier against the new entry that produced the EFF and MK** |

**On open lists**, which is the under-discussed option: **voters rank or select candidates within their chosen party's list.** **It keeps full proportionality, needs no boundaries, no by-elections and no new institutions, and gives every MP a personal mandate.** **It is the cheapest available fix to the accountability problem and almost nobody proposes it.**

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Do constituency MPs oversee better?** | **the comparative record is mixed and the honest answer is that party discipline dominates in most systems.** **So the strongest case for constituencies is not oversight quality but the removal of the delisting threat** |
| **Would women's representation fall?** | **the comparative data is clear that it would, absent a quota design that compensates** — which the Van Zyl Slabbert model can accommodate and should be required to |
| **Does a threshold improve stability?** | **the comparative evidence is reasonably strong**, and South Africa's own local government record is a natural experiment in the other direction |
| **What would open lists do?** | **untested here**, and **testable at provincial or local level first** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reformers** | **the system they want to change produced seven credible elections and the best women's representation in the region**, and **the burden is on them.** **And the accountability gain is from removing the delisting threat, not from constituencies as such — which points to open lists as the cheaper reform** |
| **Defenders** | **Zondo and Van Zyl Slabbert both recommended change, twenty years apart, and the oversight failure the Commission documented is real.** **"The system works" is not an answer to "Parliament did not hold the executive accountable for a decade"** |
| **Both** | **this is the only reform in this stage achievable by ordinary legislation with no fiscal cost**, and **it has not been done because every party in Parliament benefits from the current system.** **That is the explanation, and it should be stated** |

**Practice.** Read section 46 and establish what it does and does not require. Then read the Van Zyl Slabbert report's recommended design. Then read Zondo's Part Five recommendation on the electoral system. Then work out what an open-list ballot paper would look like and what it would cost to implement.
Coalition durability:
Whether coalition government is now the permanent condition, and whether it can be made to work.

**1 — The question.**

> **Is the 2024 arrangement durable; should coalition government be regulated by legislation; and what would make a coalition capable of a contested decision?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The arithmetic** | **no party is near a majority, and on current trends none will be in 2029** — stage 10 |
| **The local record** | **60 to 70 hung councils after 2021, with mayoral churn and administrative paralysis** — stage 8's second-largest cause of municipal failure |
| **The national arrangement** | **ten parties, "sufficient consensus", a clearing house, no enforcement mechanism, no exit procedure** — stage 11 |
| **It survived its first budget crisis** | three Budgets, a contested fiscal framework vote and litigation, in 2025 |
| **And it has deferred rather than resolved** | **NHI, BELA's language and admissions sections, expropriation and foreign policy** |
| **The reform options need only ordinary legislation** | **except direct mayoral election, which probably needs an amendment** |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

**On durability:**

| It will hold | It will not |
| --- | --- |
| **the alternatives are worse for both principals**: the ANC's are MK or the EFF, and the DA's is opposition. **Mutual lack of alternatives is the strongest glue there is** | **the local record is the base rate**, and councils with the same arithmetic have failed repeatedly |
| **it survived the hardest possible test early** — a budget, which is the one thing a coalition must pass | **it survived by withdrawing the measure**, not by agreeing one. **A coalition that can only pass a budget by dropping its revenue measure is not resolving, it is deferring** |
| **both parties' voters have not punished them** materially yet | **both parties' internal factions oppose it**, and the 2026 and 2029 results are the enforcement mechanism their critics will use |
| **the reform programme gives both sides deliverables** — the electricity recovery is claimed by both | **the deferred questions are the ones their bases care most about**, and deferral has a shelf life |

**On regulation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A constructive vote of no confidence** | **a mayor or President may be removed only if a replacement is elected in the same vote** — the German model. **Directly addresses the churn, and requires ordinary legislation locally** |
| **A threshold for executive office** | ends one-seat mayoralties |
| **Cooling-off periods** | bar no-confidence motions in a term's first and last year |
| **Codified, published, enforceable coalition agreements** | with a dispute mechanism that binds |
| **Direct election of mayors** | gives the executive its own mandate, and probably needs an amendment |
| **The objection to all of them** | **stability and accountability trade off.** **A constructive vote makes a bad mayor harder to remove as well as a good one**, and from stage 8 **the councils that work best are those where power is contestable** |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Is the national arrangement durable?** | **the 4 November 2026 municipal results, and then whether any party leaves before 2029.** **Specifically: whether the coalition parties campaign against each other locally while governing together nationally, which is the hardest test of a coalition anywhere** |
| **Can it make a contested decision?** | **NHI, expropriation's commencement, BELA's sections 4 and 5, and the next budget's revenue measures.** **Each one is a dated, observable test** |
| **Does the constructive vote work?** | **it has a long comparative record in Germany and Spain and is well documented** — **this is the best-evidenced reform in the whole stage** |
| **Does regulating coalitions help?** | **the municipal sphere could be legislated first and the national sphere later**, which is a sequenced natural experiment nobody has proposed |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Coalition optimists** | **deferral is not resolution**, and a government that cannot legislate on health, land or education is governing by regulation only. **Stage 9's Vulindlela point cuts both ways: regulatory reform is what you do when you cannot legislate** |
| **Coalition sceptics** | **sixteen days from a lost majority to a functioning government, with no institution failing and no result disputed** — stage 11 — **is a substantial achievement, and the local record's instability may reflect councils' removability rather than coalition as such** |
| **Both** | **the one reform with the strongest evidence — the constructive vote of no confidence — requires only ordinary legislation and has not been introduced**, which is the same explanation as the electoral reform lesson's |

**And the observation worth carrying: a coalition is in principle better placed to enact stage 8's appointment reforms than a single party**, because **the patronage is no longer one party's to protect.** **Whether it does is the single best test of whether this arrangement is a change of government or a change of system.**

**Practice.** Read the Statement of Intent and list what it commits the parties to. Then find Germany's constructive vote of no confidence and its record. Then list the four deferred decisions above and check the status of each. Then write down what you would expect to see in the 2026 local results if the coalition is durable.
Devolution:
Whether provinces and metros should hold policing, rail and port functions — and what the Constitution already allows.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should provinces and metropolitan municipalities be given operational control of policing, passenger rail, ports and other functions currently held nationally — and is that a constitutional question or a political one?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Schedules 4 and 5 set the functional areas** | and **policing, rail and ports are national** — stages 7 and 8 |
| **Provinces have oversight but not operational policing powers** | **section 206 gives a province oversight functions and the power to investigate complaints; section 207 puts the National Commissioner's appointment with the President** |
| **Assignment is already possible** | **section 99 permits a national minister to assign a function to a province, and section 156(4) requires assignment to a municipality of a Schedule 4A or 5A matter that necessarily relates to local government, if the municipality has the capacity and it would be more effectively administered locally** |
| **So the main route does not need an amendment** | **it needs a minister's decision** |
| **The performance variance is real** | **the Western Cape and Cape Town consistently produce the best audit and service outcomes; the Eastern Cape, Limpopo, North West, Mpumalanga and Free State the worst** — stage 8 |
| **The City of Cape Town has already procured independent power** | and several metros have begun rail and policing feasibility work |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Devolve | Do not |
| --- | --- |
| **subsidiarity**: a metro police service answerable to a mayor who can be voted out is more accountable than a national service answerable to a President | **the variance argument cuts both ways**: devolving to the Western Cape devolves to a capable administration; **devolving the same function to the provinces at the bottom of stage 8's table devolves it to failure** |
| **the national functions are the ones that failed**: policing, prosecution, passenger rail and ports are all national, and all are in the condition stages 8 and 9 describe | **national standards and redistribution**: a devolved function is funded from the provincial equitable share, and **provinces raise almost nothing** — stage 8. So devolution without fiscal devolution is an unfunded mandate |
| **the capacity exists in the metros**: Cape Town, Johannesburg, eThekwini and Tshwane have larger budgets than several provinces, and Cape Town's independent power procurement proved a metro can execute | **policing specifically**: **a fragmented police service loses national intelligence, serious and organised crime capacity, and the ability to pursue criminals across boundaries** — and stage 11's problem is investigative capacity, which fragments badly |
| **passenger rail is the clearest case**: a metro rail service serves one city's commuters and has no national dimension; **PRASA's collapse — from hundreds of millions of journeys to a fraction — is the evidence** | **the political motive is visible**: devolution is pursued hardest where the opposition governs, which means the national interest and the party interest coincide — **and that is true of both sides of this argument** |
| **and the legal point**: the assignment routes already exist and have not been used, which is a choice | **and the constitutional point**: section 44(2) lets Parliament legislate on a Schedule 5 matter to maintain national security, economic unity or essential national standards — **the centre has an override by design** |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Can a metro run passenger rail?** | **the feasibility and business cases already produced by Cape Town and others, and then a pilot.** **A single devolved commuter corridor with published performance data would settle more than a decade of argument** |
| **Does devolved policing improve outcomes?** | **the metro police services that already exist** — Johannesburg, Tshwane, Cape Town, Durban and Ekurhuleni have municipal police with by-law and traffic powers. **Compare their performance and accountability with SAPS units in the same areas** |
| **Is the capacity claim right?** | **stage 8's audit outcomes, by province and by metro**, which is the best available proxy and is published annually |
| **Does devolution become an unfunded mandate?** | **the fiscal framework attached to any assignment** — and the Financial and Fiscal Commission's assessments of past assignments |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Devolutionists** | **asymmetric devolution is what they are actually proposing** — different powers for capable and incapable provinces — **and they should say so, because it has a serious objection: it entrenches the inequality between provinces it is responding to.** **And section 99 assignment is available, so the constitutional argument is largely unnecessary** |
| **Centralists** | **the national functions are the ones that failed**, and "national standards" is a weak defence when the national standard is PRASA's. **And refusing a pilot is refusing the evidence** |
| **Both** | **the honest answer is function by function.** **Commuter rail devolves cleanly; serious and organised crime investigation does not; ports are somewhere in between.** **Arguing about "devolution" in the abstract is arguing about nothing** |

**Practice.** Read sections 99, 156(4) and 44(2). Then find a metro's rail devolution business case. Then compare a metro police service's and SAPS's performance data in the same city. Then pick one function and write the asymmetric-devolution case for it, with its strongest objection.
The Constitution itself:
The argument underneath all the others: whether the 1996 settlement should be kept, amended or replaced.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should constitutional supremacy be retained; should the property, central bank and judicial independence provisions be amended; and is there an unamendable core?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Section 2** | **the Constitution is the supreme law; law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid** — stage 7 |
| **The amendment thresholds** | **section 1 and section 74 itself: 75% of the Assembly plus six provinces. The Bill of Rights: two-thirds plus six provinces. Anything else: two-thirds** |
| **No amendment has ever come close to the Bill of Rights thresholds** | **the 2021 property amendment failed at two-thirds in the Assembly** |
| **The courts have held** | **stage 8's variance table, and the judgments stages 7 to 11 are built on** |
| **And the courts could not supply capacity** | **two commissions, almost no prosecutions** |
| **A party with 58 seats proposes parliamentary sovereignty** | **MK** — stage 10 — **and the arithmetic makes it unachievable** |

**3 — The strongest form of each position.** **There are three, not two.**

| Keep it as it is | Amend specific provisions | Replace constitutional supremacy with parliamentary sovereignty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the institutional record**: the courts, the AG, the IEC and the Reserve Bank held while the appointment-driven institutions failed. **The design was not the problem** — stage 8 | **the property clause's compensation standard and the central bank's mandate were negotiated concessions** — stage 6's "what was traded" — **not consensus choices, and the people who negotiated them are not the current electorate** | **the courts have accumulated power that elected representatives should hold** — the judicialisation critique of stage 8 taken to its conclusion |
| **justiciable socio-economic rights produced the HIV treatment order, the housing jurisprudence, the school infrastructure norms and the grant payment supervision** — stage 10's civil society lesson | **the two expert panels found section 25 was not the land constraint** — so this position is weaker on land than it appears, **and stronger on the Reserve Bank, where the clause is genuinely unusual** | **an elected majority should be able to act without a judicial veto**, and no comparable country entrenches central bank independence constitutionally |
| **the amendment thresholds have protected it from every majority since 1996**, which is the point of thresholds | **the Constitution has been amended eighteen times**, so amendment is normal and not a crisis — stage 7 | **and the deepest version**: the settlement was a negotiated constraint on majority rule, and its legitimacy rests on a bargain struck by people now dead or retired |
| **and the comparative point**: constitutional democracies with weak judicial review have worse rights records, and **stage 5 is what parliamentary sovereignty produced here** | **and the honest version**: amendment is the legitimate route, it exists, and using it is not an attack on the Constitution | |

**The strongest answer to the third column is stage 5.** **Apartheid was built under parliamentary sovereignty, by a Parliament that amended its own constitution to remove the coloured franchise and packed the Senate to do it.** **The Constitution's drafters knew exactly what they were guarding against.** **That is not a conclusive argument — it is the strongest one available, and the third column has to answer it.**

**4 — The basic structure question, which is genuinely unsettled.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The text** | **section 74 provides a procedure for amending anything, including section 1** — so **textually there is no unamendable core** |
| **The comparison** | **India has a judicially created basic structure doctrine; Germany has a textual eternity clause.** **South Africa has neither** |
| **The dictum** | in ***Premier of KwaZulu-Natal v President* (1996)** the Court observed **in passing** that an amendment abolishing the Bill of Rights or dismantling the democratic state might raise questions it would have to consider |
| **Status** | **untested, and the practical protection has been arithmetic** |
| **Which means** | **if a 75% majority ever existed, nobody knows what would happen** — and that is a real gap rather than a settled position |

**5 — What evidence would settle the larger argument, and what each side concedes.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Did the Constitution constrain the capture?** | **stage 8's variance table and stage 11's list of what the courts stopped** — the nuclear procurement, the Al-Bashir warrant, the NDPP appointments, Nkandla. **This is the strongest evidence in the whole curriculum and it is on the record** |
| **Did it prevent redress?** | **the two panels on land; the fiscal incidence studies on redistribution; stage 9's BEE evidence.** **The constitutional constraints on redistribution are weaker than claimed, and the administrative constraints are stronger** |
| **Would a different settlement have delivered more?** | **unobservable.** **Both sides' claims here are counterfactual and should be labelled as such** |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Keep-it-as-it-is concedes** | **the document could not supply capacity, and treating every failure as an implementation problem is unfalsifiable.** **And the property and central bank clauses were negotiated under duress, which is a legitimacy argument it has no answer to** |
| **Amenders concede** | **the thresholds exist for a reason and they have held; and on land, their own state's panels say the clause is not the constraint** |
| **Replacers concede** | **stage 5**, and **that every institutional gain since 1994 came from justiciable rights and binding judgments** |

**Practice.** Read sections 1, 2 and 74. Then count the amendments to date and establish what each did. Then read the *Premier of KwaZulu-Natal* dictum on an unamendable core. Then write the strongest answer the parliamentary sovereignty position could give to stage 5.
Crime and policing:
The argument where the evidence is clearest and the policy is least contested — and the gap between those two facts is the subject.

**1 — The question.**

> **What would actually reduce South Africa's murder rate, and why has it not been done?**

**2 — What is agreed, and it is almost everything:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rate** | **about 67 per 100,000 in 1994–95, about 30 in 2011–12, about 45 now** — stage 11 |
| **The number of police is not the problem** | **180,000 to 190,000 members is large by international comparison** — stage 8 |
| **Investigative capacity is** | **low murder detection and conviction rates, detective case loads far above workable levels, DNA backlogs in the hundreds of thousands, and crime intelligence repeatedly compromised** |
| **Impunity is the mechanism** | **a murder that will not be solved deters nobody** |
| **Resource allocation is skewed** | **the Equality Court held that police human resource allocation unfairly discriminated on race and poverty** — the areas with the most murders have the fewest police per capita |
| **The appointment problem** | **the National Commissioner is appointed by the President alone**, with the record stage 8 sets out, **and Zondo recommended changing it** |
| **The firearms link** | **the Firearms Control Act's commencement coincided with a measurable fall in firearm homicide; and thousands of confiscated firearms were sold out of a police store to gangs** |

**3 — Where the argument actually is.** **Not about the diagnosis — about the sequence and the money.**

| Rebuild detective and forensic capacity first | Visible policing and deployment first |
| --- | --- |
| **the whole causal chain runs through detection**: no detection, no prosecution, no deterrence. **Stage 8's and stage 11's evidence points at one thing** | **the public's demand is presence**, and a state that cannot show visible order loses legitimacy — **July 2021 is the evidence** |
| **detectives and forensic scientists take five to ten years to train**, so starting late is the worst option | **the political cycle is five years**, and a programme whose results arrive in a decade will not be funded |
| **the DNA backlog is a solvable, budgeted, technical problem** with a direct conviction-rate effect | **and station-level resourcing in the highest-crime areas is what the Equality Court judgment actually requires** |

**And two further arguments that are genuinely contested:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Private security** | **active private security personnel substantially outnumber police** — stage 11. **One position: formalise and regulate the relationship, use the capacity.** **The other: it entrenches security as a purchased good, so the people in the highest-crime areas have the least protection, and public resources should not be organised around it** |
| **Extortion economies** | **the construction mafia, township protection rackets and the taxi conflict** — **one position treats these as organised crime requiring a specialist national capacity; the other treats them as a symptom of unemployment and exclusion requiring economic remedies.** **Both are partly right, and the first is actionable now** |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Does detection drive deterrence here?** | **the murder detection rate against the murder rate, by province and by station, over time.** **SAPS holds this data and publishes little of it** — which is itself the finding |
| **Does the DNA backlog affect convictions?** | **directly measurable**: conviction rates in cases where DNA evidence was and was not available in time. **The forensic laboratories' own data** |
| **Does the resource allocation remedy work?** | **the Equality Court's order has a compliance timetable.** **Watch whether allocation shifts and whether murder rates in the reallocated areas move** |
| **Does appointment reform matter?** | **stage 8's appointment correlation.** **If the National Commissioner's appointment is ever put through a panel process, the subsequent tenure record is the test** |

**5 — What each side would have to concede, and the real answer.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Capacity-first** | **it has no answer for the next five years**, and a political system cannot run on a decade-long programme with no interim deliverable |
| **Visibility-first** | **thirty years of visible policing has coincided with the rate it has**, and presence without detection is theatre |
| **Both** | **neither addresses the firearms stock, which the Firearms Control Act evidence suggests is among the highest-leverage available interventions, and which requires a functioning police firearms registry — currently one of the weakest systems in the service** |

**And the honest closing point, which is why this lesson is short on argument and long on agreement:** **the diagnosis is not contested, the remedies are known, they are mostly technical and budgetable, and they have not been done.** **From stage 8's conclusion: that is a consequence-management and appointment problem, not a knowledge problem.** **Of everything in this stage, this is the argument least in need of being had and most in need of being acted on.**

**Practice.** Find the murder detection rate in the latest SAPS annual report, and if it is not there, note that. Then find the DNA backlog figure. Then find the Equality Court's police allocation order and its compliance timetable. Then write down the three interventions you would fund first and what each costs.
Migration:
The argument where the facts are clearest, the claims are furthest from them, and both sides' strongest positions converge.

**1 — The question.**

> **How many foreign nationals are in South Africa, what should the policy be, and what would actually change the outcomes that people are reacting to?**

**2 — What is agreed, or should be:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The numbers** | **Census 2022 counted roughly 2.4 million foreign-born residents, about 4%; allowing for undercount a credible range is roughly 2 to 4 million** — stage 10 |
| **The claims of 10 to 15 million rest on nothing traceable** | **Africa Check has repeatedly traced them to assertion or misread departmental figures.** **15 million would mean one in four people is foreign-born, which no census, school enrolment or mortality statistic supports** |
| **Local pressure is real** | **in specific neighbourhoods the concentration is high and the pressure on clinics, schools and informal trade is genuinely felt** |
| **The asylum system has failed** | **an appeal backlog in the hundreds of thousands, with waits of many years** — so a person with a pending claim cannot work formally and cannot be deported |
| **The violence is real and lethal** | **62 killed in 2008; recurrences in 2015 and 2019; continuing lower-level attacks** |
| **Some rights do not depend on status** | ***Khosa* (2004)** on permanent residents and grants; ***Centre for Child Law* (2020)** on undocumented children and schooling |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Enforce | Regularise |
| --- | --- |
| **a state that cannot control entry cannot plan services** — and the asylum backlog is itself the clearest evidence that it cannot | **the numbers are a fraction of what is claimed**, so a policy built on the claims will not address the real local pressure and will consume capacity doing it |
| **undocumented status enables exploitation** — below-minimum wages, no recourse, no inspection — **which undercuts local workers too.** This is the strongest version of the enforcement case and it is a labour argument | **the employment evidence mostly finds migrant workers neutral or net job-creating**, with higher self-employment rates — stage 9's spaza lesson. **And the informal retail they run supplies the cheapest food in the poorest areas** |
| **every state regulates entry, and saying so is not xenophobia** — the reflexive accusation suppresses a legitimate policy discussion | **the enforcement mechanism in practice is street-level document checks, which catch South Africans without ID and have repeatedly been found unlawful** |
| **the Border Management Authority was created for this** and should be resourced | **political rhetoric is causally implicated in the violence**, and a policy framed around nationality rather than documentation licenses it |
| **and the local government point**: a municipality planning water and clinic capacity needs to know who is there | **and the local government point in reverse**: stage 8 says municipalities cannot plan for the population they already count |

**4 — Where the two sides converge, which is the lesson's point.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Both require** | **a functioning Home Affairs** |
| **Specifically** | **asylum claims decided in months rather than a decade; permits processed reliably; a population register that works; and documentation of who is here** |
| **Why the enforcement case needs it** | **you cannot deport people whose claims are undecided, and you cannot plan services without knowing the numbers** |
| **Why the regularisation case needs it** | **a person with papers can work legally, be inspected, pay tax and not be exploited** |
| **And the obstacle is the same in both cases** | **stage 8's administrative capacity** |

**That convergence is not a compromise position. It is the one intervention both sides' strongest arguments require, and it is the thing nobody campaigns on.**

**5 — What evidence would settle it, and what each side concedes.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **How many people are here?** | **Census 2022 plus the undercount adjustment, plus the asylum and permit records.** **The data problem is real and fixable, and fixing it would remove the argument's most inflamed element** |
| **What is the employment effect?** | **the published South African studies, which mostly find neutral to positive** — and **better data would improve them** |
| **What is the fiscal effect?** | **unmeasured in South Africa**, and the comparative literature is mixed and depends on the migrants' skill profile |
| **Does enforcement reduce the violence?** | **untested, and the available evidence is that enforcement drives and rhetoric precede attacks rather than reducing them** |

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The enforcement side concedes** | **the numbers it campaigns on are wrong by a factor of four or more, and using them is indefensible.** **And its own policy requires the asylum system to work, which means funding Home Affairs rather than deportation** |
| **The regularisation side concedes** | **local pressure is real and dismissing it as xenophobia loses the argument and the election.** **And a state that cannot say who is in its territory has a genuine problem that "the numbers are small" does not answer** |
| **Both concede** | **the asylum backlog harms migrants most of all**, and it is the clearest single failure in the whole area |

**Practice.** Find the Census 2022 foreign-born figure. Then find an Africa Check report tracing a large claim to its source. Then find the asylum appeal backlog and the average waiting time. Then cost what it would take to clear the backlog in two years, and compare it with the Home Affairs budget.
Foreign policy: non-alignment's cost:
Whether the non-aligned posture is a principled position, a strategic choice or an expensive habit.

**1 — The question.**

> **Should South Africa maintain its non-aligned posture given its trade exposure, and is its application of international law consistent?**

**2 — What is agreed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The founding claim** | **human rights as "the light that guides our foreign affairs"** — stage 11 |
| **The unique asset** | **the only state ever to have built nuclear weapons and voluntarily dismantled them** |
| **The continental commitments** | **the AU, SADC, the AfCFTA, and a mediation record in the DRC and Burundi that was substantially successful** |
| **The ICJ case** | **instituted against Israel under the Genocide Convention in December 2023, with provisional measures ordered in 2024 and the merits pending** |
| **The trade exposure** | **China is the largest single trading partner; the United States and the European Union are the largest markets for South African manufactured and agricultural exports.** **This asymmetry is the whole economic argument** |
| **The Al-Bashir breach** | **the SCA held the government's conduct unlawful in 2016** |
| **The *Lady R* inquiry found no evidence that weapons were loaded** | |

**3 — The strongest form of each side.**

| Maintain non-alignment | Realign toward the major markets |
| --- | --- |
| **a middle power gains nothing from choosing a bloc**, and non-alignment is the position most of the Global South holds, which is where South Africa's diplomatic weight comes from | **the exposure is asymmetric and measurable**: the markets that matter for jobs are the ones the posture antagonises, and **stage 9's unemployment is the cost** |
| **the ICJ case is the rules-based order working** — a state using the proper institution to enforce a treaty obligation is precisely what international law requires | **the consistency is contested**: **the Myanmar Security Council vote, the Dalai Lama visas, Zimbabwe's elections and the Al-Bashir breach** are cited against the principle, and **a selectively applied principle is a policy** |
| **the liberation history creates obligations** Western governments do not recognise, and abandoning them for market access is the position being criticised | **the African mediation record is the real asset and it has been neglected** — SADC's recent record in the eastern DRC, and the SANDF's condition, are the evidence |
| **the AfCFTA and the continental project are the long-term interest**, which requires African rather than Western alignment | **the continental institutions have not delivered**: NEPAD's peer review never acquired teeth and the AU's intervention power has not been used as designed. **The bet is unhedged** |
| **and the sovereignty point**: a trade partner that demands alignment as a condition is demanding something no sovereign state should concede | **and the realist point**: **every state's foreign policy is interest-based, and South Africa's own history — the Taiwan switch, the arms sales — shows it has always been.** The dispute is only about which interests |

**4 — What evidence would settle it.**

| Question | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **What does the posture cost?** | **export volumes and tariff treatment in the affected markets, against a counterfactual of unchanged treatment.** **The tariff and preference changes of 2025 are a natural experiment and the trade data will show it within two years** |
| **Is the application consistent?** | **a list of comparable cases and the position taken in each.** **This is a straightforwardly checkable exercise and almost nobody does it** |
| **Does non-alignment buy diplomatic weight?** | **the G20 presidency, the Security Council terms, and the AU and BRICS positions** — against **what was achieved with them** |
| **Do the continental institutions work?** | **the APRM's reviews and their consequences; the AU's interventions; the AfCFTA's trade volumes** — all published and all currently underwhelming |

**5 — What each side would have to concede.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Non-alignment's defenders** | **the consistency objection is strong and has not been answered.** **A principled position requires the principle to be applied to Zimbabwe, Myanmar, Sudan and Russia as it is applied elsewhere**, and the record does not show that |
| **The realignment case** | **a foreign policy conducted for market access is not a principled one either**, and **its advocates should say which of the principled positions they would drop** |
| **Both** | **the instruments have decayed.** **The SANDF cannot sustain the deployments the policy commits to — stage 11 — and the diplomatic service's capacity has been questioned repeatedly.** **A foreign policy of either kind requires functioning instruments, and that is stage 8's problem again** |

**Practice.** Find South Africa's top five export markets by value and set them against its diplomatic alignments. Then make the consistency list: pick five comparable international law situations since 1994 and record the position taken in each. Then find the AfCFTA's current intra-African trade volumes. Then find what the 2025 tariff changes did to the affected export categories.
How to keep this current:
The close: what to read, how often, and the discipline that makes the rest of it hold.

**This is the last lesson of twelve stages and about two hundred and sixty lessons.** **It is short, and it is the one you should come back to.**

---

**What this curriculum was for, stated once.**

> **Not to arrive at a position.** Where a question is live, you now have the strongest form of each answer and a named test. Where a question is settled — the migration numbers, the R500 billion figure, section 25's compensation standard, the PIRLS result, the Motlanthe panel's finding, the attrition rate in rape cases — **you have the evidence that settles it, and the stage that says so.**

**And the thing it was really for**, which is stage 1: **to be able to place a source, read a statistic, read a judgment, read a commission report and read a party document** — so that **the next thirty years of this subject can be followed without anybody's help.**

---

**The reading list, by frequency.** **All of it is free.**

| How often | What |
| --- | --- |
| **Daily or weekly** | **Daily Maverick** and **News24** for the record; **GroundUp** for courts, local government and housing; **amaBhungane** for investigations |
| **Quarterly** | **StatsSA's Quarterly Labour Force Survey** — the unemployment, expanded and absorption rates; **SAPS's quarterly crime statistics**; **the Reserve Bank's Quarterly Bulletin** |
| **Twice a year** | **the Budget Review (February)** and **the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement (October or November)** — stage 9's clearest single documents |
| **Annually** | **the Auditor-General's PFMA and MFMA general reports**; **SARS's Tax Statistics**; **the Commission for Employment Equity report**; **the IEC's party funding disclosures**; **the SAHRC's and other Chapter 9 institutions' annual reports** |
| **When they appear** | **Constitutional Court judgments** at collections.concourt.org.za; **the Government Gazette** at opengazettes.org.za — **for commencement proclamations, which is where a signed Act becomes law**; **PMG** for committee proceedings |
| **Before an election** | **the IEC's results site**, and the manifestos — read as stage 1's party document lesson says |
| **Once, properly** | **the Constitution** — it is short; **the Zondo report's executive summaries**; **the Nugent report**; **the TRC's final chapter**; **the Freedom Charter** |

---

**The routine, which is the actual deliverable of this curriculum.**

| Frequency | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| **Quarterly** | **update the scorecard from stage 11's last lesson.** Four numbers minimum: **the absorption rate, the murder rate, Eskom's EAF, and the debt-service figure.** Write the date |
| **Annually** | **do the whole scorecard.** Note which rows moved against the direction you expected, **and write down why you were wrong before you look for a reason you were right** |
| **After each election** | **stage 10's seven things to watch**, with your prediction written down beforehand |
| **When a commission reports** | **stage 1's commission lesson: a finding is not a conviction; check whether the report survives review** — Seriti and Zondo are the two outcomes |
| **When a number surprises you** | **find its definition and its source before you use it.** Stage 9's four rules |
| **When you find yourself certain** | **stage 12's lesson 1, part 5: name the fact that would damage your position.** If you cannot, you are not finished |

---

**Five habits, which are the whole method compressed:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **date every figure you write down.** An undated number is a memory, not evidence |
| **2** | **name the base** — of the Gini, the unemployment rate, the land percentage, the ownership figure |
| **3** | **separate the inherited from the current.** Structure, geography and schooling are slow; appointment, procurement, electricity and logistics are fast. **Most bad policy argument confuses the two** |
| **4** | **read something you expect to disagree with, monthly, and state its argument before rejecting it.** Stage 1's last lesson, and stage 12's first |
| **5** | **check whether the thing you are angry about is a design failure or a capacity failure.** **Stages 8 and 9 say it is almost always the second, and the remedy is completely different** |

---

**And the last thing, which is why the curriculum is ordered as it is.**

**Stage 1 is first because a reader who cannot place a source reads a committed account as a neutral one.** **Stages 2 to 6 are the history, because the present is unintelligible without it.** **Stage 7 is the document. Stages 8 to 10 are the machinery — institutions, economy, parties — because the machinery is more durable and more useful than the events.** **Stage 11 is the events. Stage 12 is the arguments.**

**If you ever forget the order, remember the reason: the events change constantly, the machinery changes slowly, and the method does not change at all.**

**Practice.** Set the quarterly and annual reminders now, with the four numbers and the full scorecard. Then write down, on one page, the three things you believed about South African politics before this curriculum that you no longer believe, and the evidence that changed each. Date it. Then come back in a year and read it.
